. Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa.

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Aṅguttaranikāye

The Numerical Discourses

Pañcakanipāta-ṭīkā

The Book of the Fives—Subcommentary

1. Paṭhamapaṇṇāsakaṃ

1. The First Fifty

1. Sekhabalavaggo

1. The Chapter on the Powers of a Learner

1. Saṃkhittasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Concise Discourse

1. Pañcakanipātassa [V 3.0001][M 3.0001] paṭhame kāmaṃ sampayuttadhammesu thirabhāvopi balaṭṭho eva, paṭipakkhehi pana akampanīyattaṃ sātisayaṃ balaṭṭhoti vuttaṃ – “assaddhiye na kampatī”ti.

1. In the first [discourse] of the Book of the Fives, indeed, even steadfastness in associated states is a strength, but unshakability by opposing factors is said to be strength in the highest degree—"he is unshaken by lack of faith."

Saṃkhittasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Concise Discourse is concluded.

2-6. Vitthatasuttādivaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Extensive Discourses, etc.

2-6. Dutiye [V 3.0002] hirīyatīti lajjati virajjati. Yasmā hirī pāpajigucchanalakkhaṇā, tasmā “jigucchatīti attho”ti vuttaṃ. Ottappatīti utrasati. Pāputrāsalakkhaṇañhi ottappaṃ.

In the second [discourse], "is ashamed" means one is ashamed and shrinks back. Since shame is characterized by disgust at evil, it is said, "the meaning is 'is disgusted.'" "Is apprehensive" means one is terrified. For apprehension has the characteristic of fear of evil.

Paggahitavīriyoti [M 3.0002] saṅkocaṃ anāpannavīriyo. Tenāha “anosakkitamānaso”ti. Pahānatthāyāti samucchinnatthāya. Kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ upasampadā nāma samadhigamo evāti āha “paṭilābhatthāyā”ti.

"One with aroused energy" means energy free from contraction. Hence it is said, "with a mind unretreating." "For the sake of abandoning" means for the sake of complete destruction. The attainment of wholesome qualities means acquisition itself. Hence it is said, "for the sake of acquisition."

Gatiatthā dhātusaddā buddhiatthā hontīti āha “udayañca vayañca paṭivijjhituṃ samatthāyā”ti. Missakanayenāyaṃ desanā gatāti āha “vikkhambhanavasena ca samucchedavasena cā”ti. Tenāha “vipassanāpaññāya ceva maggapaññāya cā”ti. Vipassanāpaññāya vikkhambhanakiriyato sā ca kho padesikāti nippadesikaṃ katvā dassetuṃ “maggapaññāya paṭilābhasaṃvattanato”ti vuttaṃ. Dukkhakkhayagāminibhāvepi eseva nayo. Sammāti yāthāvato. Akuppadhammatāya hi maggapaññāya khepitaṃ khepitameva, nāssa puna khepanakiccaṃ atthīti upāyena ñāyena sā pavattatīti āha “hetunā nayenā”ti. Tatiyādīsu natthi vattabbaṃ.

Root-words that mean 'going' also mean 'understanding'; hence it is said, 'for the power to penetrate arising and passing away.' This teaching is presented in a mixed manner. Hence it is said, 'both by suppression and by eradication.' Therefore, it is said, 'by insight-wisdom and by path-wisdom.' Though insight-wisdom performs the function of suppression, it is localized. To show it as complete, it is said, 'because it leads to the attainment of path-wisdom.' The same principle applies to its leading to the destruction of suffering. 'Rightly' means according to reality. For what is eliminated by the unshakable path-wisdom is truly eliminated; there is no further need for eliminating it. It proceeds with means and method; hence it is said, 'by cause and by method.' There is nothing further to say about the third and following.

Vitthatasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Extensive Discourses, etc., is concluded.

7. Kāmasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Discourse on Sensuality

7. Sattame asanti lūnanti tenāti asitaṃ, dāttaṃ. Vividhā ābhañjanti bhāraṃ olambenti tenāti byābhaṅgī, vidhaṃ. Kulaputtoti ettha duvidho kulaputto jātikulaputto, ācārakulaputto ca. Tattha “tena kho pana samayena raṭṭhapālo nāma kulaputto tasmiṃyeva thullakoṭṭhike aggakulikassa putto”ti (ma. ni. 2.294) evaṃ āgato uccakulappasuto jātikulaputto nāma. “Ye te kulaputtā saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajitā”ti (ma. ni. 1.34) evaṃ āgatā pana yattha katthaci kule pasutāpi ācārasampannā ācārakulaputto nāma. Idha pana ācārakulaputto adhippeto. Tenāha “kulaputtoti ācārakulaputto”ti. Yuttanti anucchavikaṃ, evaṃ vattabbataṃ arahatīti attho. Sesamettha uttānameva.

7. In the seventh [discourse], asitaṃ and dāttaṃ: because they cut (asanti, lūnanti) with it, it is called asitaṃ or dāttaṃ (sickle). Byābhaṅgī and vidhaṃ: because they bend in various ways (vividhā ābhañjanti) or make a load hang down (bhāraṃ olambenti) with it, it is called byābhaṅgī or vidhaṃ (carrying pole). 'Kulaputto' (son of a good family) here refers to two types: jātikulaputto (son of a good family by birth) and ācārakulaputto (son of a good family by conduct). In this context, the passage "At that time, Raṭṭhapāla, a son of a good family, was the son of the chief family in Thullakoṭṭhika" (MN 2.294) refers to one born into a high family, called jātikulaputto. On the other hand, the passage "Those sons of good families who, out of faith, have gone forth from the household life into homelessness" (MN 1.34) refers to those born in any family but endowed with good conduct, called ācārakulaputto. Here, ācārakulaputto is intended. Hence it is stated, "‘Kulaputto’ means ācārakulaputto." 'Yuttaṃ' means suitable, appropriate (anucchavikaṃ), signifying that it is fitting to be said thus. The remainder here is clear.

Kāmasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on Sensuality is concluded.

8. Cavanasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Discourse on Passing Away

8. Aṭṭhame [V 3.0003][M 3.0003] saddhāyāti iminā adhigamasaddhā dassitā. Catubbidhā hi saddhā – āgamanīyasaddhā, adhigamasaddhā, pasādasaddhā, okappanasaddhāti. Tattha āgamanīyasaddhā sabbaññubodhisattānaṃ pavattā hoti. Āgamanīyappaṭipadāya āgatā hi saddhā sātisayā mahābodhisattānaṃ paropadesena vinā saddheyyavatthuṃ aviparītato gahetvā adhimuccanato. Saccappaṭivedhato āgatasaddhā adhigamasaddhā suppabuddhādīnaṃ viya. “Sammāsambuddho bhagavā”tiādinā buddhādīsu uppajjanakappasādo pasādasaddhā mahākappinarājādīnaṃ viya. “Evameta”nti okkanditvā pakkhanditvā saddahanavasena kappanaṃ okappanaṃ, tadeva saddhāti okappanasaddhā. Tattha pasādasaddhā paraneyyarūpā hoti, savanamattenapi pasīdanato. Okappanasaddhā saddheyyaṃ vatthuṃ ogāhitvā anupavisitvā “evameta”nti paccakkhaṃ karontī viya pavattati.

8. In the eighth [discourse], by "faith" the faith of attainment is shown. For faith is fourfold: faith as tradition, faith as attainment, faith as serenity, and faith as conviction. Among these, faith as tradition occurs among the all-knowing bodhisattas. It is the faith that arises through the practice leading to tradition, which is extraordinary for the great bodhisattas, who, without relying on others' instruction, grasp the object of faith correctly and become resolved. Faith that arises from the realization of truth is the faith of attainment, as seen in Suppabuddha and others. The faith as serenity arises in relation to the Buddha and others, with thoughts like "The Blessed One is fully enlightened," as seen in the great king Kappina and others. Faith as conviction is when one accepts, assents, and firmly believes, thinking, "It is thus." This very faith is called faith as conviction. Among these, faith as serenity is for those who need guidance, for it brings serenity merely upon hearing. Faith as conviction operates by immersing in and penetrating the object of faith, settling into it and making it evident, as if seen directly.

Cavanasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on Passing Away is concluded.

9. Paṭhamaagāravasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the First Discourse on Irreverence

9. Navame appatissayoti appatissavo va-kārassa ya-kāraṃ katvā niddeso. Garunā kismiñci vutto gāravavasena patissavanaṃ, patissavo, patissavabhūtaṃ, taṃsabhāvañca yaṃ kiñci gāravaṃ. Natthi etasmiṃ patissavoti appatissavo, gāravavirahito. Tenāha “ajeṭṭhako anīcavuttī”ti.

9. In the ninth [discourse], 'appatissaya' means 'appatissava'; this is an explanation made by changing the letter 'va' to 'ya'. When something is said by a teacher, 'patissava' is the assenting out of reverence; it is compliance, the state of being compliant, and any reverence of that nature. One in whom there is no such compliance is 'appatissavo' (non-compliant), one devoid of reverence. Therefore, it is said: 'not having a senior, not acting humbly'.

Paṭhamaagāravasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the First Discourse on Irreverence is concluded.

10. Dutiyaagāravasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Second Discourse on Disrespect

10. Dasame vuddhintiādīsu sīlena vuddhiṃ, maggena viruḷhiṃ, nibbānena vepullaṃ. Sīlasamādhīhi vā vuddhiṃ, vipassanāmaggehi viruḷhiṃ, phalanibbānehi vepullaṃ. Ettha ca yassa catubbidhaṃ sīlaṃ akhaṇḍādibhāvappavattiyā suparisuddhaṃ visesabhāgiyattā appakasireneva maggaphalāvahaṃ saṅgharakkhitattherassa viya, so tādisena sīlena imasmiṃ dhammavinaye vuddhiṃ [M 3.0004] āpajjissati. Tena vuttaṃ – “sīlena vuddhi”nti. Yassa pana ariyamaggo uppanno, so virūḷhamūlo viya pādapo suppatiṭṭhitattā sāsane virūḷhiṃ āpanno nāma hoti. Tena vuttaṃ [V 3.0004] – “maggena virūḷhi”nti. Yo sabbakilesanibbānappatto, so arahā sīlādidhammakkhandhapāripūriyā sati vepullappatto hoti. Tena vuttaṃ “nibbānena vepulla”nti. Dutiyavikappe attho vuttanayānusārena veditabbo.

10. In the tenth [discourse], in the phrase 'growth,' etc., growth is by virtue, flourishing is by the path, and abundance is by Nibbāna. Alternatively, growth is by virtue and concentration, flourishing is by the insight paths, and abundance is by fruition and Nibbāna. Here, for one whose fourfold virtue is supremely pure due to its being unbroken, etc., and because it is conducive to distinction, it leads effortlessly to the path and fruition, like for the Elder Saṅgharakkhita; such a person will attain growth in this Dhamma-Vinaya through such virtue. Therefore it is said: 'growth by virtue.' But for one in whom the Noble Path has arisen, like a tree with well-established roots, they are said to have attained flourishing in the Dispensation because of its firm establishment. Therefore it is said: 'flourishing by the path.' One who has attained the Nibbāna of all defilements, that arahant, attains abundance through the complete fulfillment of the aggregates of virtue and other qualities. Therefore it is said: 'abundance by Nibbāna.' In the second alternative, the meaning should be understood in accordance with the method explained.

Dutiyaagāravasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Second Discourse on Disrespect is concluded.

Sekhabalavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Chapter on the Powers of a Trainee is concluded.

2. Balavaggo

2. The Chapter on Powers

1. Ananussutasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Discourse on the Unheard

11. Dutiyassa paṭhame abhijānitvāti abhivisiṭṭhena ñāṇena jānitvā. Aṭṭhahi kāraṇehi tathāgatassāti “tathā āgatoti tathāgato. Tathā gatoti tathāgato. Tathalakkhaṇaṃ āgatoti tathāgato. Tathadhamme yāthāvato abhisambuddhoti tathāgato. Tathadassitāya tathāgato. Tathāvāditāya tathāgato. Tathākāritāya tathāgato. Abhibhavanaṭṭhena tathāgato”ti evaṃ vuttehi aṭṭhahi kāraṇehi. Usabhassa idanti āsabhaṃ, seṭṭhaṭṭhānaṃ. Tenāha “āsabhaṃ ṭhānanti seṭṭhaṭṭhāna”nti. Parato dassitabalayogena “dasabaloha”nti abhītanādaṃ nadati. Brahmacakkanti ettha seṭṭhapariyāyo. Brahmasaddoti āha “seṭṭhacakka”nti. Cakkañcetaṃ dhammacakkaṃ adhippetaṃ.

11. In the first [discourse] of the second [section], 'having known thoroughly' means knowing with superior wisdom. The [explanation] of 'Tathāgata' is by eight reasons: 'Because he has come thus, he is the Tathāgata. Because he has gone thus, he is the Tathāgata. Because he has arrived at the true characteristic, he is the Tathāgata. Because he has fully awakened to the realities in their actuality, he is the Tathāgata. Because of his showing things as they are, he is the Tathāgata. Because of his speaking things as they are, he is the Tathāgata. Because of his doing things as they are, he is the Tathāgata. By reason of his overcoming, he is the Tathāgata.' Thus it is stated for eight reasons. 'This of the bull' means āsabha, the supreme position. Therefore it is said: 'the āsabha position means the supreme position.' By virtue of the strength demonstrated subsequently, he roars the fearless roar, 'I possess the ten powers.' 'Brahmacakka' here is a synonym for 'supreme'. Because of the word 'brahma', it is said 'supreme wheel'. And this wheel is intended to be the Dhamma-wheel.

Ananussutasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on the Unheard is concluded.

3. Saṃkhittasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Concise Discourse.

13. Tatiye kāmaṃ sampayuttadhammesu thirabhāvopi balaṭṭho eva, paṭipakkhehi pana akampanīyattaṃ sātisayaṃ balaṭṭhoti vuttaṃ “muṭṭhassacce na kampatī”ti.

13. In the third [discourse], although even stability in associated states is indeed a manifestation of strength, yet the unshakeability by opposing factors is an especially strong manifestation of strength, as it is said, 'He does not waver in the face of unmindfulness and lack of clear comprehension.'

Saṃkhittasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Concise Discourse is concluded.

4. Vitthatasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Expanded Discourse.

14. Catutthe [V 3.0005][M 3.0005] satinepakkenāti satiyā nepakkena, tikkhavisadasūrabhāvenāti attho. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana nepakkaṃ nāma paññāti adhippāyena “nepakkaṃ vuccati paññā”ti vuttaṃ. Evaṃ sati añño niddiṭṭho nāma hoti. Satimāti ca iminā savisesā sati gahitāti paratopi “cirakatampi cirabhāsitampi saritā anussaritā”ti satikiccameva niddiṭṭhaṃ, na paññākiccaṃ, tasmā satinepakkenāti satiyā nepakkabhāvenāti sakkā viññātuṃ labbhateva. Paccayavisesavasena aññadhammanirapekkho satiyā balavabhāvo. Tathā hi ñāṇavippayuttacittenapi sajjhāyanasammasanāni sambhavanti.

14. In the fourth [discourse], 'with mindfulness and skill' means with the skill of mindfulness, the meaning being by being sharp, clear, and courageous. In the commentary, however, 'skill' is called wisdom, with the intention that 'skill is called wisdom' has been stated. Thus, in that case, another [meaning] is specifically defined. And by 'mindful,' a distinctive mindfulness is grasped, as elsewhere it is also specifically defined as the function of mindfulness itself, not the function of wisdom, when it is said: 'remembering and recollecting what was done long ago and spoken long ago.' Therefore, 'with mindfulness and skill' can indeed be understood as the state of mindfulness being skillful. Through the distinction of conditions, the strength of mindfulness is independent of other phenomena. For thus, even with a consciousness dissociated from knowledge, recitation and reflection can occur.

Cirakatampīti attanā vā parena vā kāyena cirakataṃ cetiyaṅgaṇavattādimahāvattappaṭipattipūraṇaṃ. Cirabhāsitampīti attanā vā parena vā vācāya cirabhāsitaṃ sakkaccaṃ uddisanauddisāpanadhammāsāraṇadhammadesanāupanisinnakaparikathāanumodanīyādivasena pavattitaṃ vacīkammaṃ. Saritā anussaritāti tasmiṃ kāyena cirakate kāyo nāma kāyaviññatti, cirabhāsite vācā nāma vacīviññatti, tadubhayampi rūpaṃ, taṃsamuṭṭhāpakā cittacetasikā arūpaṃ. Iti ime rūpārūpadhammā evaṃ uppajjitvā evaṃ niruddhāti sarati ceva anussarati ca, satisambojjhaṅgaṃ samuṭṭhāpetīti attho. Bojjhaṅgasamuṭṭhāpikā hi sati idha adhippetā. Tāya satiyā esa sakiṃ saraṇena saritā, punappunaṃ saraṇena anussaritāti veditabbā.

'What was done long ago' refers to the fulfillment of the practice of great duties, such as tending to shrine grounds, performed long ago by oneself or others through bodily action. 'What was spoken long ago' refers to verbal actions performed long ago by oneself or others through speech, such as careful recitation, causing others to recite, sharing the essence of the Dhamma, Dhamma talks, seated conversations, and expressions of rejoicing, and so forth. 'Remembering and recollecting' means that in those long-ago bodily actions, the body, that is, bodily intimation, and in long-ago speech, speech, that is, verbal intimation, are both form. The consciousness and mental factors that produce them are formless. Thus, one remembers and recollects that these material and immaterial phenomena have arisen in such a way and ceased in such a way, thereby arousing the enlightenment factor of mindfulness—this is the meaning. For mindfulness that arouses the enlightenment factors is intended here. By that mindfulness, it should be understood that one 'remembers' by recollecting once, and one 'recollects' by recollecting again and again.

Vitthatasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Expanded Discourse is concluded.

5-10. Daṭṭhabbasuttādivaṇṇanā

5-10. Commentary on the Daṭṭhabba Sutta, etc.

15-20. Pañcame savisayasmiṃyevāti attano attano visaye eva. Lokiyalokuttaradhamme kathetunti lokiyadhamme lokuttaradhamme ca tena tena pavattivisesena kathetuṃ. Catūsu sotāpattiyaṅgesūti sappurisasaṃsevo saddhammassavanaṃ yonisomanasikāro dhammānudhammappaṭipattīti imesu catūsu sotāpattimaggakāraṇesu. Kāmañca tesu satiādayopi dhammā icchitabbāva tehi vinā tesaṃ asambhavato[M 3.0006], tathāpi cettha saddhā visesato kiccakārīti veditabbā. Saddho eva hi sappurise payirupāsati, saddhammaṃ suṇāti, yoniso ca aniccādito manasi karoti, ariyamaggassa [V 3.0006] ca anudhammaṃ paṭipajjati, tasmā vuttaṃ “ettha saddhābalaṃ daṭṭhabba”nti. Iminā nayena sesabalesupi attho daṭṭhabbo.

In the fifth, “in their own spheres” means in their respective spheres. “To speak of worldly and supramundane phenomena” means to discuss worldly and supramundane phenomena according to their various modes of occurrence. “In the four factors of stream-entry” refers to these four causes of the stream-entry path: associating with good people, listening to the true Dhamma, wise attention, and practicing in accordance with the Dhamma. And though mindfulness and other qualities should also be desired in them, since without them those factors are impossible, even so, here faith especially should be understood as the active agent. For it is the faithful who associate with good people, listen to the true Dhamma, wisely attend to impermanence, etc., and practice in accordance with the Dhamma of the noble path. Therefore, it is said, “Here, the power of faith is to be seen.” In this way, the meaning should be seen in the remaining powers as well.

Catūsu sammappadhānesūti catubbidhasammappadhānabhāvanāya. Catūsu satipaṭṭhānesūtiādīsupi eseva nayo. Ettha ca sotāpattiaṅgesu saddhā viya, sammappadhānabhāvanāya vīriyaṃ viya ca satipaṭṭhānabhāvanāya yasmā “vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassa”nti (dī. ni. 2.373; ma. ni. 1.106) vacanato pubbabhāge kiccato sati adhikā icchitabbā, evaṃ samādhikammikassa samādhi, “ariyasaccabhāvanā paññābhāvanā”ti katvā tattha paññā pubbabhāge adhikā icchitabbāti pākaṭoyamattho. Adhigamakkhaṇe pana samādhipaññānaṃ viya sabbesampi balānaṃ saddhādīnaṃ samatāva icchitabbā. Tathā hi “ettha saddhābala”ntiādinā tattha tattha etthaggahaṇaṃ kataṃ.

“In the four right efforts” refers to the development of the fourfold right efforts. The same method applies to “the four foundations of mindfulness” and so on. Here, just as faith is predominant among the factors of stream-entry, and energy is predominant in the development of right effort, so too in the development of the foundations of mindfulness, because it is said, “having subdued covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world” (DN 2.373; MN 1.106), mindfulness should be desired as predominant in function in the preliminary stage. Similarly, for one whose work is concentration, concentration should be desired as predominant. Since it is held that “the development of the noble truths is the development of wisdom,” wisdom should be desired as predominant in the preliminary stage. This meaning is clear. At the moment of attainment, however, just as with concentration and wisdom, the equality of all the powers—faith and so on—should be desired. For thus, by the phrase “here the power of faith,” etc., the word “here” is used in each case.

Idāni saddhādīnaṃ tattha tattha atirekakiccataṃ upamāya vibhāvetuṃ “yathā hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tatridaṃ upamā saṃsandanaṃ – rājapañcamasahāyā viya vimuttiparipācakāni pañca balāni. Nesaṃ kīḷanatthaṃ ekajjhaṃ vīthiotaraṇaṃ viya balānaṃ ekajjhaṃ vipassanāvīthiotaraṇaṃ, sahāyesu paṭhamādīnaṃ yathāsakaṃ geheva vicāraṇā viya saddhādīnaṃ sotāpattiaṅgādīni patvā pubbaṅgamatā. Sahāyesu itaresaṃ tattha tattha tuṇhībhāvo viya sesabalānaṃ tattha tattha tadanvayatā, tassa pubbaṅgamassa balassa kiccānugatā. Na hi tadā tesaṃ sasambhārapathavīādīsu āpādīnaṃ viya kiccaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti, saddhādīnaṃyeva pana kiccaṃ vibhūtaṃ hutvā tiṭṭhati puretaraṃ tathāpaccayehi cittasantānassa abhisaṅkhatattā. Ettha ca vipassanākammikassa bhāvanā visesato paññuttarāti dassanatthaṃ rājānaṃ nidassanaṃ katvā paññindriyaṃ vuttaṃ. Chaṭṭhādīni suviññeyyāni.

Now, to clarify by a simile the pre-eminent function of faith and the others in their respective places, the phrase “just as” and so on is stated. Here is the application of the simile: The five powers that ripen liberation are like a king with his four companions. Their descending into a street together for amusement is like the powers descending into the path of insight together. Among the companions, the deliberation of the first and others each in their own house is like faith and the others, upon reaching the factors of stream-entry and so on, taking the lead. The silence of the other companions in their respective places is like the remaining powers following suit in their respective places, in accordance with the function of that leading power. For at that time, their function is not manifest, just as the function of the water element and so on is not manifest in the earth element with its constituents. However, the function of faith and the others alone remains manifest, having been prepared beforehand because the mental continuum has been conditioned by such causes. And here, to show that the development of one practicing insight is especially led by wisdom, the faculty of wisdom is mentioned, making the king the example. The sixth and others are easily understood.

Daṭṭhabbasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Daṭṭhabba Sutta, etc., is concluded.

Balavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Chapter on Powers is concluded.

3. Pañcaṅgikavaggo

3. The Chapter on the Five-Factored.

1-2. Paṭhamaagāravasuttādivaṇṇanā

1-2. Commentary on the First Āgārava Sutta, etc.

21-22. Tatiyassa [V 3.0007][M 3.0007] paṭhame ābhisamācārikanti abhisamācāre uttamasamācāre bhavaṃ. Kiṃ pana tanti āha “vattavasena paññattasīla”nti. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva. Dutiye natthi vattabbaṃ.

21-22. In the first of the third, “ābhisamācārika” means existing in superior conduct, in the highest conduct. But what is that? He says, “the virtue laid down by way of practice.” The rest is easily understood. In the second, there is nothing to be said.

Paṭhamaagāravasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the First Āgārava Sutta, etc., is concluded.

3-4. Upakkilesasuttādivaṇṇanā

3-4. Commentary on the Upakkilesa Sutta, etc.

23-24. Tatiye na ca pabhāvantanti na ca pabhāsampannaṃ. Pabhijjanasabhāvanti tāpetvā tāḷakajjanapabhaṅguraṃ. Avasesaṃ lohanti vuttāvasesaṃ sajātilohaṃ, vijātilohaṃ, pisācalohaṃ, kittimalohanti evaṃpabhedaṃ sabbampi lohaṃ. Uppajjituṃ appadānenāti ettha nanu lokiyakusalacittassapi suvisuddhassapi uppajjituṃ appadāneneva upakkilesatāti? Saccametaṃ, yasmiṃ pana santāne nīvaraṇāni laddhappatiṭṭhāni, tattha mahaggatakusalassapi asambhavo, pageva lokuttarakusalassa. Parittakusalaṃ pana yathāpaccayaṃ uppajjamānaṃ nīvaraṇehi upahate santāne uppattiyā aparisuddhaṃ hontaṃ upakkiliṭṭhaṃ nāma hoti aparisuddhadīpakapallikavaṭṭitelādisannissayo padīpo viya. Apica nippariyāyato uppajjituṃ appadāneneva tesaṃ upakkilesatāti dassento “yadaggena hī”tiādimāha. Ārammaṇe vikkhittappavattivasena cuṇṇavicuṇṇatā veditabbā. Catutthe natthi vattabbaṃ.

23-24. In the third, “not radiant” means not possessing radiance. “Of a breaking nature” means fragile, like a heated and split tāḷaka fruit. “The remaining metal” means all remaining metal, classified as metal of the same kind, of different kinds, pisāca metal, and artificial metal. Regarding “by preventing [wholesome states] from arising”—here, is it not the case that even a very pure worldly wholesome consciousness is defiled precisely by preventing [higher states] from arising? This is true. However, in a mental continuum where the hindrances have taken root, even sublime wholesome states are impossible, let alone supramundane wholesome states. But a limited wholesome state, arising according to conditions, being impure at the moment of arising in a continuum afflicted by hindrances, is called defiled—like a lamp dependent on an impure wick, oil, or similar materials. Furthermore, to show that their nature as a defilement is, without qualification, precisely due to preventing [wholesome states] from arising, he says, “yadaggena hī,” etc. The state of being crushed to powder should be understood as the occurrence of distraction towards the object. In the fourth, there is nothing to be said.

Upakkilesasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Upakkilesa Sutta, etc., is concluded.

5. Anuggahitasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Anuggahita Sutta.

25. Pañcame sammādiṭṭhīti vipassanāsammādiṭṭhītiādinā aṅguttarabhāṇakānaṃ matena ayaṃ atthavaṇṇanā āraddhā, majjhimabhāṇakā panettha aññathā atthaṃ vadanti. Vuttañhetaṃ majjhimaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.452) –

25. Regarding the fifth, the explanation of the meaning here, beginning with “right view” as “the right view of insight,” etc., was commenced according to the view of the Aṅguttara reciters. However, the Majjhima reciters explain the meaning differently here. For this was stated in the Majjhima Commentary (Ma. Ni. Aṭṭha. 1.452)—

“Anuggahitā”ti [V 3.0008][M 3.0008] laddhūpakārā. Sammādiṭṭhīti arahattamaggasammādiṭṭhi. Phalakkhaṇe nibbattā cetovimutti phalaṃ assāti cetovimuttiphalā. Tadeva cetovimuttisaṅkhātaṃ phalaṃ ānisaṃso assāti cetovimuttiphalānisaṃsā. Dutiyapadepi eseva nayo. Ettha catutthaphalapaññā paññāvimutti nāma, avasesā dhammā cetovimuttīti veditabbā. “Sīlānuggahitā”tiādīsu sīlanti catupārisuddhisīlaṃ. Sutanti sappāyadhammassavanaṃ. Sākacchāti kammaṭṭhāne khalanapakkhalanacchedanakathā. Samathoti vipassanāpādikā aṭṭha samāpattiyo. Vipassanāti sattavidhā anupassanā. Catupārisuddhisīlañhi pūrentassa, sappāyadhammassavanaṃ suṇantassa, kammaṭṭhāne khalanapakkhalanaṃ chindantassa vipassanāpādikāsu aṭṭhasu samāpattīsu kammaṃ karontassa, sattavidhaṃ anupassanaṃ bhāventassa arahattamaggo uppajjitvā phalaṃ deti.

“Supported” (anuggahitā) means having received assistance. “Right view” (sammādiṭṭhi) is the right view of the Arahantship path. “Having the fruit of liberation of mind” (cetovimuttiphalā) means that the liberation of mind that arises at the moment of fruition is its fruit. “Having the benefit of the fruit of liberation of mind” (cetovimuttiphalānisaṃsā) means that the very fruit, called liberation of mind, is its benefit. The same method applies to the second term as well. Here, the wisdom of the fourth fruit is called “liberation by wisdom” (paññāvimutti), while the remaining qualities are to be understood as “liberation of mind” (cetovimutti). In phrases such as “supported by virtue” (sīlānuggahitā), “virtue” (sīla) is the fourfold purity of virtue. “Listening” (suta) is listening to suitable teachings. “Discussion” (sākacchā) is talk that cuts off wavering and stumbling in the meditation subject. “Serenity” (samatha) is the eight attainments that are a basis for insight. “Insight” (vipassanā) is the seven kinds of contemplation. For one who fulfills the fourfold purity of virtue, listens to suitable teachings, cuts off wavering and stumbling in the meditation subject, performs the work in the eight attainments that are a basis for insight, and develops the seven kinds of contemplation, the path to Arahantship arises and gives its fruit.

“Yathā hi madhuraṃ ambapakkaṃ paribhuñjitukāmo ambapotakassa samantā udakakoṭṭhakaṃ thiraṃ katvā bandhati, ghaṭaṃ gahetvā kālena kālaṃ udakaṃ āsiñcati, udakassa anikkhamanatthaṃ mariyādaṃ thiraṃ karoti. Yā hoti samīpe valli vā sukkhadaṇḍako vā kipillikapuṭo vā makkaṭakajālaṃ vā, taṃ apaneti, khaṇittiṃ gahetvā kālena kālaṃ mūlāni parikhaṇati, evamassa appamattassa imāni pañca kāraṇāni karoto so ambo vaḍḍhitvā phalaṃ deti, evaṃ sampadamidaṃ veditabbaṃ. Rukkhassa samantato koṭṭhakabandhanaṃ viya hi sīlaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, kālena kālaṃ udakasiñcanaṃ viya dhammassavanaṃ, mariyādāya thirabhāvakaraṇaṃ viya samatho, samīpe valliādīnaṃ haraṇaṃ viya kammaṭṭhāne khalanapakkhalanacchedanaṃ, kālena kālaṃ khaṇittiṃ gahetvā mūlakhaṇanaṃ viya sattannaṃ anupassanānaṃ bhāvanā, tehi pañcahi kāraṇehi anuggahitassa ambarukkhassa madhuraphaladānakālo viya imassa bhikkhuno imehi pañcahi dhammehi anuggahitāya sammādiṭṭhiyā arahattaphaladānaṃ veditabba”nti.

“Just as one who wishes to enjoy a ripe, sweet mango would firmly construct a water basin around the mango sapling, take a pot and water it from time to time, and firmly establish a boundary to prevent the water from escaping. Whatever creeping vine, dry stick, anthill, or spiderweb is nearby, they remove it. Taking a hoe, they dig around the roots from time to time. For one who diligently performs these five actions, that mango tree grows and bears fruit. Similarly, this should be understood: the firm construction of a basin around the tree is to be seen as virtue; watering from time to time is like listening to the Dhamma; establishing a firm boundary is like serenity; removing nearby vines and such is like cutting off wavering and stumbling in the meditation subject; taking a hoe and digging around the roots from time to time is like cultivating the seven kinds of contemplation. Just as a mango tree, supported by these five actions, in time gives sweet fruit, so too should it be understood that for this monk, right view, supported by these five qualities, gives the fruit of Arahantship.”

Ettha ca laddhūpakārāti yathārahaṃ nissayādivasena laddhapaccayā. Vipassanāsammādiṭṭhiyā anuggahitabhāvena gahitattā maggasammādiṭṭhīsu ca arahattamaggasammādiṭṭhi[M 3.0009]. Anantarassa hi vidhi paṭisedho vā, aggaphalasamādhimhi tapparikkhāradhammesuyeva ca kevalo cetopariyāyo niruḷhoti sammādiṭṭhīti arahattamaggasammādiṭṭhi. Phalakkhaṇeti anantaraṃ kālantare cāti duvidhepi phalakkhaṇe. Paṭippassaddhivasena sabbasaṃkilesehi cetovimuccati etāyāti cetovimutti, aggaphalapaññaṃ ṭhapetvā avasesā phaladhammā. Tenāha “cetovimutti phalaṃ assāti, cetovimuttisaṅkhātaṃ [V 3.0009] phalaṃ ānisaṃso”ti. Sabbakilesehi cetaso vimuccanasaṅkhātaṃ paṭippassambhanasaññitaṃ pahānaṃ phalaṃ ānisaṃso cāti yojanā. Idha cetovimuttisaddena pahānamattaṃ gahitaṃ, pubbe pahāyakadhammā. Aññathā phaladhammā eva ānisaṃsoti gayhamāne punavacanaṃ niratthakaṃ siyā. Paññāvimuttiphalānisaṃsāti etthāpi evameva attho veditabbo. Sammāvācākammantājīvā sīlasabhāvattā visesato samādhissa upakārā, tathā sammāsaṅkappo jhānasabhāvattā. Tathā hi so “appanā”ti niddiṭṭho. Sammāsatisammāvāyāmā pana samādhipakkhiyā evāti āha “avasesā dhammā cetovimuttīti veditabbā”ti.

Here, “having received assistance” (laddhūpakārā) means having received the necessary conditions by way of support, etc., as appropriate. Because it is grasped by being supported by insight right view, and among the path right views, it is the right view of the Arahantship path. For there is either a rule or a prohibition for what is immediate; and in the concentration of the supreme fruition, only the penetration of mind becomes established concerning its requisite qualities. Thus, “right view” is the right view of the Arahantship path. “At the moment of fruition” (phalakkhaṇe) means at both kinds of fruition moments: immediately and after a time. “Liberation of mind” (cetovimutti) means that the mind is liberated from all defilements by this through the subsiding of defilements; these are the remaining fruition qualities, excluding the wisdom of the supreme fruition. Therefore, it is said: “liberation of mind is its fruit,” and “the fruit, called liberation of mind, is its benefit.” The connection is that the abandoning, characterized by the mind’s liberation from all defilements and designated as subsiding, is both the fruit and the benefit. Here, by the word “liberation of mind,” only the act of abandoning is taken, whereas previously it referred to the qualities that cause abandoning. Otherwise, if the fruition qualities themselves were taken as the benefit, the repetition would be meaningless. The meaning of “having the benefit of the fruit of liberation by wisdom” (paññāvimuttiphalānisaṃsā) should be understood in the same way here as well. Right speech, right action, and right livelihood, being of the nature of virtue, are particularly helpful for concentration. Likewise, right intention, being of the nature of absorption, is also helpful. For it is designated as “attainment.” Right mindfulness and right effort, however, belong specifically to the side of concentration. Thus, it is said: “the remaining qualities are to be understood as liberation of mind.”

Catupārisuddhisīlanti ariyamaggādhigamassa padaṭṭhānabhūtaṃ catupārisuddhisīlaṃ. Sutādīsupi eseva nayo. Attano cittappavattiārocanavasena saha kathanaṃ saṃkathā, saṃkathāva sākacchā. Idha pana kammaṭṭhānappaṭibaddhāti āha “kammaṭṭhāne…pe… kathā”ti. Tassa kammaṭṭhānassa ekavāraṃ vidhiyā appaṭipajjanaṃ khalanaṃ, anekavāraṃ pakkhalanaṃ, tadubhayassa vicchedanī apanayanī kathā khalanapakkhalanacchedanakathā. Pūrentassāti vivaṭṭasannissitaṃ katvā pālentassa brūhentassa ca. Suṇantassāti “yathāuggahitakammaṭṭhānaṃ phātiṃ gamissatī”ti evaṃ suṇantassa. Teneva hi “sappāyadhammassavana”nti vuttaṃ. Kammaṃ karontassāti bhāvanānuyogakammaṃ karontassa. Pañcasupi ṭhānesu anta-saddo hetuatthajotano daṭṭhabbo. Evañhi “yathā hī”tiādinā vuccamānā ambūpamā yujjeyya.

“The fourfold purity of virtue” (catupārisuddhisīla) is the fourfold purity of virtue that serves as the foundation for the attainment of the Noble Path. The same method applies to “listening” (suta) and so on. “Conversation” (saṃkathā) is talking together in such a way as to make known the activity of one’s own mind; conversation itself is “discussion” (sākacchā). But here, because it is connected with the meditation subject, it is said: “talk that cuts off wavering and stumbling in the meditation subject.” For that meditation subject, failing to apply it correctly once is a “wavering” (khalana); repeatedly failing is a “stumbling” (pakkhalana); and talk that severs and removes both is “talk that cuts off wavering and stumbling” (khalanapakkhalanacchedanakathā). “For one who fulfills” (pūrentassa) means for one who protects and develops it, having made it a basis for turning away from the cycle of rebirth. “For one who listens” (suṇantassa) means for one who listens with the thought, “How will the meditation subject I have grasped come to fruition?” Therefore, it is said: “listening to suitable teachings.” “For one who performs the work” (kammaṃ karontassa) means for one who performs the work of dedication to meditation. In all five places, the word “anta” should be understood as indicating the meaning of “reason.” For in this way, the simile of the mango tree, which is stated beginning with “just as,” would be fitting.

Udakakoṭṭhakanti jalāvāṭaṃ. Thiraṃ katvā bandhatīti asithilaṃ daḷhaṃ nātimahantaṃ nātikhuddakaṃ katvā yojeti. Thiraṃ karotīti udakasiñcanakāle tato tato pavattitvā udakassa anikkhamanatthaṃ jalāvāṭapāḷiṃ thirataraṃ karoti. Sukkhadaṇḍakoti tasseva ambagacchassa sukkhako sākhāsīsako[M 3.0010]. Kipillikapuṭoti tambakipillikapuṭo. Khaṇittinti kudālaṃ. Koṭṭhakabandhanaṃ viya sīlaṃ sammādiṭṭhiyā vaḍḍhanūpāyassa mūlabhāvato. Udakasiñcanaṃ viya dhammassavanaṃ bhāvanāya paribrūhanato. Mariyādāya thirabhāvakaraṇaṃ viya samatho yathāvuttāya bhāvanādhiṭṭhānāya sīlamariyādāya daḷhībhāvāpādanato. Samāhitassa hi sīlaṃ thirataraṃ hoti. Samīpe valliādīnaṃ haraṇaṃ viya kammaṭṭhāne khalanapakkhalanacchedanaṃ icchitabbabhāvanāya vibandhanāpanayanato. Mūlakhaṇanaṃ viya sattannaṃ anupassanānaṃ bhāvanā tassā vibandhassa mūlabhūtānaṃ taṇhāmānadiṭṭhīnaṃ palikhaṇanato. Ettha ca yasmā suparisuddhasīlassa kammaṭṭhānaṃ anuyuñjantassa sappāyadhammassavanaṃ icchitabbaṃ, tato yathāsute atthe sākacchāsamāpajjanaṃ, tato kammaṭṭhānavisodhanena samathanibbatti, tato samāhitassa āraddhavipassakassa vipassanāpāripūri, paripuṇṇā [V 3.0010] vipassanā maggasammādiṭṭhiṃ brūhetīti evametesaṃ aṅgānaṃ paramparāya sammukhā anuggaṇhanato ayamānupubbī kathitāti veditabbaṃ.

“Water basin” (udakakoṭṭhaka) is a water pit. “Firmly made and bound” (thiraṃ katvā bandhati) means one joins it, having made it firm, not loose, not too large, and not too small. “Makes it firm” (thiraṃ karoti) means that when watering, to prevent the water from flowing out from various places, one makes the banks of the water pit firmer. “Dry stick” (sukkhadaṇḍako) refers to the dry branch tip of that same mango tree. “Ant nest” (kipillikapuṭo) means a red ant nest. “Hoe” (khaṇitti) means a spade. Binding the basin is like virtue, because it is the root of the means for the growth of right view. Watering is like listening to the Dhamma, because it fosters development through cultivation. Making the boundary firm is like serenity, because it brings about the strengthening of the boundary of virtue, which is the foundation for the prescribed meditation. For one who is concentrated, virtue becomes even firmer. Removing nearby vines and so on is like cutting off stumbling and slipping in the meditation subject, because it removes the hindrance to the desired cultivation. Digging at the roots is like the cultivation of the seven contemplations, because it digs up craving, conceit, and views, which are the root of that hindrance. Here, it should be understood that this gradual progression is stated because for one of perfectly purified virtue who applies themself to a meditation subject, it is desirable to listen to suitable teachings; from that, one engages in discussion on the meaning as heard; from that, through purifying the meditation subject, serenity arises; from that, for one who is concentrated and has undertaken insight, insight reaches fulfillment; and fulfilled insight nurtures the right view of the path. Thus, because these factors support one another face-to-face in sequence, this gradual progression is spoken of.

Anuggahitasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Anuggahita Sutta is concluded.

6. Vimuttāyatanasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Discourse on the Grounds for Liberation

26. Chaṭṭhe vimuttiyā vaṭṭadukkhato vimuccanassa āyatanāni kāraṇāni vimuttāyatanānīti āha – “vimuccanakāraṇānī”ti. Pāḷiatthaṃ jānantassāti “idha sīlaṃ āgataṃ, idha samādhi, idha paññā”tiādinā taṃtaṃpāḷiatthaṃ yāthāvato jānantassa. Pāḷiṃ jānantassāti tadatthabodhiniṃ pāḷiṃ yāthāvato upadhārentassa. Taruṇapītīti sañjātamattā mudukā pīti jāyati. Kathaṃ jāyati? Yathādesitaṃ dhammaṃ upadhārentassa tadanucchavikameva attano kāyavācāmanosamācāraṃ pariggaṇhantassa somanassaṃ pattassa pamodalakkhaṇaṃ pāmojjaṃ jāyati. Tuṭṭhākārabhūtā balavapītīti purimuppannāya pītiyā vasena laddhāsevanattā ativiya tuṭṭhākārabhūtā kāyacittadarathassa passambhanasamatthatāya passaddhiyā paccayo bhavituṃ samatthā balappattā pīti jāyati. Yasmā nāmakāye passaddhe rūpakāyopi passaddho eva hoti, tasmā “nāmakāyo passambhati”cceva vuttaṃ.

26. In the sixth, the grounds for liberation are the causes for being liberated from the suffering of the round of existence—thus it is said: 'the causes of liberation.' 'One who understands the meaning of the Pāli' means one who knows the true meaning of each Pāli passage, such as 'here virtue is mentioned, here concentration, here wisdom,' and so on. 'One who knows the Pāli' means one who attends properly to the Pāli that reveals its meaning. 'Tender joy' means a soft joy arises as soon as it is born. How does it arise? For one who attends to the Dhamma as taught and accordingly adopts one's own bodily, verbal, and mental conduct, having attained gladness, joy arises, characterized by delight. 'Strong joy that has become a state of satisfaction' means that due to the power of having cultivated the previously arisen joy, a strong joy arises that has become an extreme state of satisfaction. This strong joy, being capable of calming the agitation of body and mind, is able to become a condition for tranquility. Because when the mental body is tranquil, the physical body is also tranquil, therefore it is said only: 'the mental body becomes tranquil.'

Sukhaṃ [M 3.0011] paṭilabhatīti vakkhamānassa cittasamādhānassa paccayo bhavituṃ samatthaṃ cetasikaṃ nirāmisasukhaṃ paṭilabhati vindati. Samādhiyatīti ettha pana na yo koci samādhi adhippeto, atha kho anuttarasamādhīti dassento “arahatta…pe… samādhiyatī”ti āha. “Ayaṃ hī”tiādi tassaṃ desanāyaṃ tādisassa puggalassa yathāvuttasamādhipaṭilābhassa kāraṇabhāvavibhāvanaṃ, yaṃ tathā vimuttāyatanabhāvo. Osakkitunti dassituṃ. Samādhiyeva samādhinimittanti kammaṭṭhānapāḷiyā āruḷho samādhi eva parato uppajjanakabhāvanāsamādhissa kāraṇabhāvato samādhinimittaṃ. Tenāha “ācariyassa santike”tiādi.

'He attains happiness' means he obtains, he finds, the spiritual mental happiness that is capable of being a condition for the concentration of mind that will be spoken of. Regarding 'he is concentrated,' it is not just any concentration that is intended here, but rather, to indicate the unsurpassed concentration, it is said: 'arahantship...pe... he is concentrated.' 'This is indeed' and so on, in that teaching, is an explanation of the causal nature of the attainment of concentration as described for such a person, which is thus the state of being a ground for liberation. 'To recoil' is to show this. 'Concentration itself is the sign of concentration' means the concentration established in the meditation subject of the Pāli text is itself the sign of concentration, because it is the cause for the meditative concentration that is to arise subsequently. Therefore, it is said: 'in the teacher's presence' and so on.

Vimuttāyatanasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on the Grounds for Liberation is concluded.

7. Samādhisuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Samādhi Sutta

27. Sattame [V 3.0011] sabbaso kilesadukkhadarathapariḷāhānaṃ vigatattā sātisayamettha sukhanti vuttaṃ “appitappitakkhaṇe sukhattā paccuppannasukho”ti. Purimassa purimassa vasena pacchimaṃ pacchimaṃ laddhāsevanatāya santapaṇītatarabhāvappattaṃ hotīti āha “purimo…pe… sukhavipāko”ti. Kilesappaṭippassaddhiyāti kilesānaṃ paṭippassambhanena laddhattā. “Kilesappaṭippassaddhibhāvanti kilesānaṃ paṭippassambhanabhāvaṃ. Laddhattā pattattā tabbhāvaṃ upagatattā. Lokiyasamādhissa paccanīkāni nīvaraṇapaṭhamajjhānanikantiādīni niggahetabbāni, aññe kilesā vāretabbā. Imassa pana arahattasamādhissa paṭippassaddhasabbakilesattā na niggahetabbaṃ vāretabbañca atthīti maggānantaraṃ samāpattikkhaṇe ca appayogena adhigatattā appitattā ca aparihānivasena vā appitattā na sasaṅkhāraniggayhavāritagato. Sativepullappattattāti etena appavattamānāyapi satiyā satibahulatāya sato eva nāmāti dasseti. Yathāparicchinnakālavasenāti etena paricchinnassatiyā satoti dasseti. Sesesūti ñāṇesu.

27. In the seventh, because all defilements, suffering, distress, and fever have completely vanished, the bliss here is said to be exceeding. It is said: 'blissful in the present, because of the bliss at each moment of application.' Because by means of each preceding one, each subsequent one, having been obtained and cultivated, attains a state of being more peaceful and sublime, it is said: 'The former... results in bliss.' 'Through the pacification of defilements' means because it is attained by the calming of defilements. 'The state of pacification of defilements' means the state of the calming of defilements, because it is obtained, attained, and that state is entered into. For mundane concentration, the opponents—the hindrances, the factors of the first jhāna, and so on—should be suppressed, and other defilements should be warded off. But for this concentration of arahantship, because all defilements are pacified, there is nothing to be suppressed or warded off. Because it is attained without effort at the moment of attainment immediately after the path, and because it is applied—or applied by way of non-decline—it is not accompanied by forceful suppression and warding off. 'Because of having attained abundance of mindfulness'—by this it is shown that even when mindfulness is not occurring, one is still called 'mindful' due to the abundance of mindfulness. 'According to the defined period'—by this it is shown that one is called 'mindful' due to having a defined mindfulness. 'In the remaining' refers to the knowledges.

Samādhisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Samādhi Sutta is concluded.

8-9. Pañcaṅgikasuttādivaṇṇanā

8-9. Commentary on the Pañcaṅgika Sutta and Others

28-29. Aṭṭhame [M 3.0012] karo vuccati pupphasambhavaṃ “gabbhāsaye kirīyatī”ti katvā. Karato jāto kāyo karajakāyo, tadupanissayo catusantatirūpasamudāyo. Kāmaṃ nāmakāyopi vivekajena pītisukhena tathāladdhūpakāro, “abhisandetī”tiādivacanato pana rūpakāyo idha adhippetoti āha “imaṃ karajakāya”nti. Abhisandetīti abhisandanaṃ karoti. Taṃ pana abhisandanaṃ jhānamayena pītisukhena karajakāyassa tintabhāvāpādanaṃ sabbatthakameva lūkhabhāvāpanayananti āha “temetī”tiādi. Tayidaṃ abhisandanaṃ atthato yathāvuttapītisukhasamuṭṭhānehi paṇītarūpehi kāyassa parippharaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Parisandetītiādīsupi eseva nayo. Sabbaṃ etassa atthīti sabbāvā, tassa sabbāvato. Avayavāvayavisambandhe avayavini sāmivacananti avayavavisayo sabba-saddo, tasmā vuttaṃ “sabbakoṭṭhāsavato”ti. Aphuṭaṃ nāma na hoti yattha yattha kammajarūpaṃ, tattha tattha cittajarūpassa abhibyāpanato. Tenāha “upādinnakasantatī”tiādi.

In the eighth, `karo` is said to be the producer of the flower, because 'it is done in the womb.' The body born from the maker is the `karajakāya`; its supporting condition is the collection of the four continuities of matter. Indeed, the mental body is also supported by the joy and happiness born of seclusion, but from statements like 'it suffuses,' the material body is intended here; hence, it is said, 'this `karajakāya`.' 'It suffuses' means it performs suffusion. That suffusion is the causing of the `karajakāya` to become moist and the removal of all coarseness by the joy and happiness of jhāna; thus it is said, 'it moistens,' and so on. This suffusion should be understood, in its real meaning, as the pervading of the body with the sublime material phenomena originated from the aforesaid joy and happiness. The same method applies to 'it saturates' and so on. `Sabbāvā` means 'possessing all'; `sabbāvato` is the genitive form of that. In the relationship between part and whole, the word `sabba` refers to the whole; therefore, it is said, 'possessing all parts.' There is no part that is untouched (`aphuṭaṃ`), because wherever kamma-born matter exists, mind-born matter pervades it. Hence, it is said, 'the continuity of what is appropriated,' and so on.

Chekoti [V 3.0012] kusalo. Taṃ panassa kosallaṃ nahānīyacuṇṇānaṃ karaṇe piṇḍikaraṇe ca samatthatāvasena veditabbanti āha “paṭibalo”tiādi. Kaṃsa-saddo “mahatiyā kaṃsapātiyā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.61) suvaṇṇe āgato.“Kaṃso upahato yathā”tiādīsu (dha. pa. 134) kittimalohe. Katthaci paṇṇattimatte “upakaṃso nāma rājāsi, mahākaṃsassa atrajo”tiādi (jā. aṭṭha. 4.10.164 ghaṭapaṇḍitajātakavaṇṇanā). Idha pana yattha katthaci loheti āha “yena kenaci lohena katabhājane”ti. Snehānugatāti udakasinehena anuppavisanavasena gatā upagatā. Snehaparetāti udakasinehena parito gatā samantato phuṭā. Tato eva santarabāhirā phuṭā snehena. Etena sabbaso udakena temitabhāvamāha. Na ca pagghariṇīti etena tintassapi tassa ghanathaddhabhāvaṃ vadati. Tenāha “na bindubindū”tiādi.

‘Skilled’ means expert. That skill of his should be understood as his ability in making bathing powders and kneading them into a ball, as it is said, ‘capable,’ and so on. The word ‘kaṃsa’ appears referring to gold in contexts like ‘in a large bronze bowl’ (Majjhima Nikāya 1.61). In phrases like ‘as a broken bronze vessel’ (Dhammapada 134), it denotes an alloy. In some places, it is merely a designation, as in ‘There was a king named Upakaṃsa, son of Mahākaṃsa’ (Jātaka Aṭṭhakathā 4.10.164, the commentary on the Ghaṭapaṇḍita Jātaka). Here, however, it refers to any metal, as stated: ‘in a vessel made of any metal.’ ‘Permeated by moisture’ means entered and penetrated by the moisture of water. ‘Saturated with moisture’ means completely pervaded and suffused on all sides by the moisture of water. Thus, it is suffused inside and out with moisture. By this, he indicates it is entirely soaked with water. And ‘not oozing’ shows that even when soaked, it remains dense and firm. Hence, it is said, ‘not drop by drop,’ and so on.

Tāhi tāhi udakasirāhi ubbhijjatīti ubbhidaṃ, ubbhidaṃ udakaṃ etassāti ubbhidodako. Ubbhinnaudakoti nadītīre khatakūpako viya ubbhijjanakaudako. Uggacchanaudakoti dhārāvasena uṭṭhahanaudako. Kasmā panettha ubbhidodakova [M 3.0013] rahado gahito, na itaroti āha “heṭṭhā uggacchanaudakañhī”tiādi. Dhārānipātabubbuḷakehīti dhārānipātehi ca udakabubbuḷehi ca. “Pheṇapaṭalehi cā”ti vattabbaṃ, sannisinnameva aparikkhobhatāya niccalameva, suppasannamevāti adhippāyo. Sesanti “abhisandetī”tiādikaṃ.

It springs up from these and those water veins, thus it is ‘ubbhidaṃ’ (a spring). It has spring water, thus it is ‘ubbhidodako’ (having spring water). ‘Ubbhinnaudako’ means water that springs up, like in a well dug on a riverbank. ‘Uggacchanaudako’ means water that rises up as a stream. Why is a lake with spring water taken here, and not another kind? It is said, ‘For the water rises from below,’ and so on. ‘By the falling of streams and by bubbles’ means by falling streams and by water bubbles. It should also be said, ‘and with layers of foam.’ The meaning is that it is very settled, utterly still, and perfectly clear due to being undisturbed. The rest is ‘he suffuses,’ and so on.

Uppalānīti uppalagacchāni. Setarattanīlesūti uppalesu, setuppalarattuppalanīluppalesūti attho. Yaṃ kiñci uppalaṃ uppalameva sāmaññaggahaṇato. Satapattanti ettha sata-saddo bahupariyāyo “satagghī”tiādīsu viya. Tena anekasatapattassapi saṅgaho siddho hoti. Loke pana rattaṃ padumaṃ, setaṃ puṇḍarīkanti vuccati. Yāva aggā yāva ca mūlā udakena abhisandanādisambhavadassanatthaṃ udakānuggataggahaṇaṃ. Idha uppalādīni viya karajakāyo, udakaṃ viya tatiyajjhānasukhaṃ.

‘Uppalāni’ means clumps of lotuses. ‘In the white, red, and blue’ means among lotuses: white lotuses, red lotuses, and blue lotuses. Whatever lotus there is, it is simply a ‘lotus,’ from the general term. Regarding ‘satapatta’ (hundred-petaled), here the word ‘sata’ (hundred) is a synonym for ‘many,’ as in phrases like ‘worth a hundred.’ Thus, the inclusion of a lotus with many hundreds of petals is established. In the world, however, a red one is called ‘paduma’ and a white one is called ‘puṇḍarīka.’ The mention of them ‘not having risen from the water’ is to show the possibility of their being suffused by water from tip to root. Here, the body born of kamma is like the lotuses, and the bliss of the third jhāna is like the water.

Yasmā parisuddhena cetasāti catutthajjhānacittamāha, tañca rāgādiupakkilesamalāpagamato nirupakkilesaṃ nimmalaṃ, tasmā āha “nirupakkilesaṭṭhena parisuddha”nti. Yasmā pana pārisuddhiyā eva paccayavisesena pavattiviseso pariyodātatā sudhantasuvaṇṇassa nighaṃsanena pabhassaratā viya, tasmā āha “pabhassaraṭṭhena pariyodātaṃ veditabba”nti. Idanti odātavacanaṃ. Utupharaṇatthanti utuno pharaṇadassanatthaṃ. Utupharaṇaṃ na hoti sesanti adhippāyo. Tenāha “taṅkhaṇa [V 3.0013] …pe… balavaṃ hotī”ti. Vatthaṃ viya karajakāyoti yogino karajakāyo vatthaṃ viya daṭṭhabbo utupharaṇasadisena catutthajjhānasukhena pharitabbattā. Purisassa sarīraṃ viya catutthajjhānaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ utupharaṇaṭṭhāniyassa sukhassa nissayabhāvato. Tenāha “tasmā”tiādi. Tattha ca “parisuddhena cetasā”ti cetogahaṇena jhānasukhaṃ vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tenāha “utupharaṇaṃ viya catutthajjhānasukha”nti. Nanu ca catutthajjhāne sukhameva natthīti? Saccaṃ natthi, sātalakkhaṇasantasabhāvattā panettha upekkhā “sukha”nti adhippetā. Tena vuttaṃ sammohavinodaniyaṃ (vibha. aṭṭha. 232) “upekkhā pana santattā, sukhamicceva bhāsitā”ti.

Because ‘with a purified mind’ refers to the consciousness of the fourth jhāna, and that is undefiled and stainless due to the removal of the stains of defilements such as lust, therefore it is said, ‘purified in the sense of being undefiled.’ And because its distinctive manifestation of purity, due to that very purity as a special condition, is like the radiance of well-smelted gold from polishing, therefore it is said, ‘It should be understood as pure in the sense of being radiant.’ ‘This’ refers to the word ‘white.’ ‘For the purpose of suffusing with warmth’ means for the purpose of showing the suffusion of warmth. The meaning is that no part is left unsuffused by warmth. Therefore it is said, ‘at that moment… it becomes strong.’ The yogi’s kamma-born body should be seen as the cloth, as it is to be suffused by the bliss of the fourth jhāna, which is similar to the suffusion of warmth. The fourth jhāna should be seen as the man’s body, as it is the basis for the bliss that stands in the place of the suffusion of warmth. Hence it is said, ‘Therefore,’ and so on. And here, by the taking of ‘mind’ in ‘with a purified mind,’ the bliss of jhāna should be understood as stated. Therefore it is said, ‘the bliss of the fourth jhāna is like the suffusion of warmth.’ But is there not in fact any bliss in the fourth jhāna? True, there is not; but here equanimity, due to its nature of pleasantness and its peaceful state, is intended by ‘bliss.’ Thus it is stated in the Sammohavinodanī: ‘Equanimity, being peaceful, is spoken of as bliss.’

Tassa [M 3.0014] tassa samādhissa sarūpadassanassa paccayattā paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ paccavekkhaṇanimittaṃ. Samabharitoti samapuṇṇo.

The knowledge of reviewing is the sign for reviewing because it is the condition for seeing the intrinsic nature of each concentration. ‘Evenly filled’ means completely full.

Maṇḍabhūmīti papāvaṇṇabhūmi. Yattha salilasiñcanena vināva sassāni ṭhitāni sampajjanti. Yuge yojetabbāni yoggāni, tesaṃ ācariyo yoggācariyo. Tesaṃ sikkhāpanato hatthiādayopi “yoggā”ti vuccantīti āha pāḷiyaṃ “assadammasārathī”ti. Yena yenāti catūsu maggesu yena yena maggena. Yaṃ yaṃ gatinti javasamajavādibhedāsu gatīsu yaṃ yaṃ gatiṃ. Navame natthi vattabbaṃ.

‘Maṇḍabhūmi’ means ground the color of a dove's wing, where standing crops flourish even without watering. ‘Yoggāni’ are those to be yoked; their teacher is a ‘yoggācariya.’ Because they are trained, even elephants and other animals are called ‘yoggā,’ as the Pāli states in ‘a charioteer of horses to be tamed.’ ‘By whichever way’ means by whichever of the four paths. ‘To whichever going’ means to whichever kind of going among the different types, such as swift or even. Regarding the ninth sutta, there is nothing to be said.

Pañcaṅgikasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Pañcaṅgika Sutta and others is concluded.

10. Nāgitasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Nāgita Sutta.

30. Dasame uccāsaddamahāsaddāti uddhaṃ uggatattā ucco patthaṭo mahanto vinibbhijjitvā gahetuṃ asakkuṇeyyo saddo etesanti uccāsaddamahāsaddā. Vacīghosopi hi bahūhi ekajjhaṃ pavattito atthato saddato ca duravabodho kevalaṃ mahānigghoso eva hutvā sotapathamāgacchati. Macchavilopeti macchānaṃ vilumpitvā viya gahaṇe, macchānaṃ vā vilumpane. Kevaṭṭānañhi macchapacchiṭhapitaṭṭhāne mahājano sannipatitvā “idha aññaṃ ekaṃ macchaṃ dehi, ekaṃ macchaphālaṃ dehī”ti, “etassa te mahā dinno, mayhaṃ khuddako”ti evaṃ uccāsaddaṃ mahāsaddaṃ karonti. Macchaggahaṇatthaṃ jāle pakkhittepi tasmiṃ ṭhāne kevaṭṭā ceva aññe ca “paviṭṭho gahito”ti mahāsaddaṃ karonti. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Asucisukhanti kāyāsucisannissitattā kilesāsucisannissitattā [V 3.0014] ca asucisannissitasukhaṃ. Nekkhammasukhassāti kāmato nikkhamantassa sukhassa. Pavivekasukhassāti gaṇasaṅgaṇikato kilesasaṅgaṇikato ca vigatassa sukhassa. Upasamasukhassāti rāgādivūpasamāvahassa sukhassa. Sambodhasukhanti maggasaṅkhātassa sambodhassa niṭṭhappattatthāya sukhaṃ. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

30. In the tenth sutta, ‘loud and great noise’ means they have a sound that is high because it has risen upwards, extensive, and great, a sound impossible to grasp distinctly. For even the clamor of voices, when produced by many at once, becomes difficult to understand in meaning and sound, reaching the path of the ear as merely a great roar. ‘At the plundering of fish’ means at the seizing of fish as if plundering, or at the plundering of fish. For at the place where fishermen have set out fish in baskets, a great crowd gathers and makes a loud and great noise, shouting, ‘Give me another fish here, give me a piece of fish!’ and ‘You were given a big one, mine is small!’ Even when a net is cast to catch fish, the fishermen and others in that place make a great noise, shouting, ‘It’s in, it’s caught!’ This is stated in reference to that. ‘Impure pleasure’ means pleasure connected with impurity, because it is based on the impurity of the body and based on the impurity of the defilements. ‘The bliss of renunciation’ is the bliss of one who is renouncing sensual pleasures. ‘The bliss of seclusion’ is the bliss of one who is secluded from association with crowds and from association with defilements. ‘The bliss of peace’ is the bliss that brings the calming of lust and so on. ‘The bliss of enlightenment’ is the bliss for the purpose of attaining the culmination of enlightenment, which is designated as the path. The rest is easily understood.

Nāgitasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Nāgita Sutta is concluded.

Pañcaṅgikavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Pañcaṅgika Vagga is concluded.

4. Sumanavaggo

4. The Sumana Vagga.

1. Sumanasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Sumana Sutta.

31. Catutthassa [M 3.0015] paṭhame satakkakūti satasikharo, anekakūṭoti attho. Idaṃ tassa mahāmeghabhāvadassanaṃ. So hi mahāvassaṃ vassati. Tenevāha – “ito cito ca uṭṭhitena valāhakakūṭasatena samannāgatoti attho”ti. Dassanasampannoti ettha dassanaṃ nāma sotāpattimaggo. So hi paṭhamaṃ nibbānadassanato “dassana”nti vuccati. Yadipi taṃ gotrabhu paṭhamataraṃ passati, disvā pana kattabbakiccassa kilesappahānassa akaraṇato na taṃ “dassana”nti vuccati. Āvajjanaṭṭhāniyañhi taṃ ñāṇaṃ. Maggassa nibbānārammaṇatāsāmaññena cetaṃ vuttaṃ, na nibbānappaṭivijjhanena, tasmā dhammacakkhuṃ punappunaṃ nibbattanena bhāvanaṃ appattaṃ dassanaṃ, dhammacakkhuñca pariññādikiccakaraṇena catusaccadhammadassanaṃ tadabhisamayoti natthettha gotrabhussa dassanabhāvāpatti. Sesamettha suviññeyyameva.

31. In the first sutta of the fourth vagga, 'a hundred peaks' means a hundred summits, implying many peaks. This illustrates its nature as a great rain cloud, for it pours down heavy rain. Hence it is said: 'Endowed with a hundred peaks of clouds rising from here and there'—this is the meaning. 'Endowed with vision'—here 'vision' refers to the path of stream-entry. For it is first called 'vision' because of seeing Nibbāna. Although the gotrabhū consciousness sees it earlier, since it does not perform the task to be done, namely, the abandoning of defilements, it is not called 'vision.' For that knowledge is of the nature of directing attention. And this is said because of the path having the common characteristic of Nibbāna as its object, not because of penetrating Nibbāna. Therefore, vision is the Dhamma-eye that has not yet attained development through repeated arising; and the Dhamma-eye is the seeing of the four noble truths and their comprehension by performing the function of full understanding and so on. Thus, the gotrabhū consciousness does not attain the state of 'vision' here. The rest here is easily understood.

Sumanasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Sumanasutta is concluded.

2. Cundīsuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Cundī Sutta

32. Dutiye “ariyakantehi sīlehi samannāgato”tiādīsu (a. ni. 5.179) ariyakantānīti pañcasīlāni āgatāni. Ariyakantāni [V 3.0015] hi pañcasīlāni ariyānaṃ kantāni piyāni, bhavantaragatāpi ariyā tāni na vijahanti. Idha pana “yāvatā, cunda, sīlāni ariyakantāni sīlāni, tesaṃ aggamakkhāyati…pe… agge te paripūrakārino”ti vuttattā maggaphalāni sīlāni adhippetānīti āha “ariyakantāni sīlānīti maggaphalasampayuttāni sīlānī”ti.

32. In the second passage, regarding 'endowed with virtues dear to the noble ones,' etc. (AN 5.179), the term 'virtues dear to the noble ones' refers to the five precepts. Indeed, the five precepts are dear and pleasing to the noble ones; even noble ones who have gone to another existence do not abandon them. Here, however, since it is stated, 'As far as virtues dear to the noble ones, Cunda, the highest is declared... those who perfectly fulfill them,' virtues associated with the path and fruition are intended. Thus, it is said, '“Virtues dear to the noble ones” means the virtues connected with the path and fruition.'

Cundīsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Cundī Sutta is concluded.

3. Uggahasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Uggaha Sutta

33. Tatiye [M 3.0016] sabbapaṭhamaṃ uṭṭhānasīlāti rattiyā vibhāyanavelāya sāmike parijane seyyāya avuṭṭhite sabbapaṭhamaṃ uṭṭhānasīlā. Sāmikaṃ disvā nisinnāsanato aggidaḍḍhā viya paṭhamameva vuṭṭhahantīti vā pubbuṭṭhāyiniyo. Kiṃkāranti kiṃkaraṇīyaṃ, kiṃkaraṇabhāvena pucchitvā kātabbaveyyāvaccanti attho. Taṃ paṭissuṇantā vicarantīti kiṃkārappaṭissāviniyo. Manāpaṃyeva kiriyaṃ karonti sīlenāti manāpacāriniyo. Piyameva vadanti sīlenāti piyavādiniyo.

33. In the third passage, 'first to rise' (uṭṭhānasīlā) means being the first to rise at dawn, when the master and the household are not yet up from bed. Seeing the master, they rise immediately from their seats as if burned by fire; alternatively, they are those who rise early. 'What is to be done?' (kiṃkārā) means 'what needs to be done'; the meaning is that they ask what is to be done, inquiring about the service to be performed. They move about responding to requests, hence they are 'responsive to commands' (kiṃkārappaṭissāviniyo). They perform only pleasing actions by nature, hence they are 'pleasant in conduct' (manāpacāriniyo). They speak only pleasing words by nature, hence they are 'pleasant in speech' (piyavādiniyo).

Tatrupāyāyāti tatra kamme sādhetabbaupāyabhūtāya vīmaṃsāya. Tenāha “tasmiṃ uṇṇākappāsasaṃvidhāne”tiādi. Alaṃ kātunti kātuṃ samatthā. Alaṃ saṃvidhātunti vicāretuṃ samatthā. Tenāha “alaṃ kātuṃ alaṃ saṃvidhātunti attanā kātumpi parehi kārāpetumpī”tiādi. Sesamettha suviññeyyameva.

'Skillful means there' (tatrupāyāya) refers to the investigation that serves as the means to accomplish that task. Hence it is said, 'in that arrangement of wool and cotton,' etc. 'Capable of doing' (alaṃ kātuṃ) means able to do. 'Capable of arranging' (alaṃ saṃvidhātuṃ) means able to deliberate. Hence it is said, 'capable of doing, capable of arranging' means 'able to do it oneself and also have others do it,' etc. The rest here is easily understandable.

Uggahasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Uggaha Sutta is concluded.

4-5. Sīhasenāpatisuttādivaṇṇanā

4-5. Commentary on the Sīhasenāpati Sutta and So Forth

34-35. Catutthe sandiṭṭhikanti asamparāyikatāya sāmaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sayaṃ anubhavitabbaṃ attapaccakkhaṃ diṭṭhadhammikanti attho. Na saddhāmattakeneva tiṭṭhatīti “dānaṃ nāma sādhu sundaraṃ, buddhādīhi paṇḍitehi pasattha”nti evaṃ saddhāmattakeneva na tiṭṭhati. Yaṃ dānaṃ detīti yaṃ deyyadhammaṃ parassa deti. Tassa pati hutvāti tabbisayaṃ lobhaṃ suṭṭhu abhibhavanto tassa adhipati hutvā deti. Tena anadhibhavanīyattā na dāso na sahāyoti. Tattha tadubhayaṃ anvayato [V 3.0016] byatirekato ca dassetuṃ “yo hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Dāso hutvā deti taṇhādāsabyassa upagatattā. Sahāyo hutvā deti tassa piyabhāvāvissajjanato. Sāmī hutvā deti tattha taṇhādāsabyato attānaṃ mocetvā abhibhuyya pavattanato. Atha vā yo dānasīlatāya dāyako puggalo, so dāne pavattibhedena dānadāso, dānasahāyo, dānapatīti tippakāro hoti. Tadassa tippakārataṃ vibhajitvā dassetuṃ “yo hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Dātabbaṭṭhena dānaṃ, annapānādi.

34-35. In the fourth passage, 'immediately visible' (sandiṭṭhikaṃ) means it should be seen for oneself, not pertaining to the hereafter. It is to be personally experienced, directly evident in the present life (attapaccakkhaṃ diṭṭhadhammikaṃ)—this is the meaning. It does not remain merely as faith—thinking, 'Giving is good, beautiful, praised by the wise such as the Buddha'—but goes beyond mere faith. 'One gives a gift' (yaṃ dānaṃ deti) means one offers something to another. 'Being its master' (tassa pati hutvā) means thoroughly overcoming greed regarding that object and giving as its sovereign. Because of not being overpowered by it, one is neither a slave nor a companion. Here, to show both the positive and negative aspects, 'For one who...' etc., is said. One gives as a slave because one is subject to the slavery of craving. One gives as a companion because of not relinquishing affection for it. One gives as a master because one frees oneself from the slavery of craving and gives while exercising control over it. Alternatively, a person who is a giver by virtue of a generous disposition becomes threefold in the act of giving: a slave to giving, a companion in giving, or a master of giving. To explain this threefold nature in detail, 'For one who...' etc., is said. A gift, in the sense of what is to be given, is food, drink, and the like.

Tattha [M 3.0017] yaṃ attanā paribhuñjati, taṇhādhipannatāya tassa vasena vattanato dāso viya hoti. Yaṃ paresaṃ dīyati, tatthāpi annapānasāmaññena idaṃ vuttaṃ “dānasaṅkhātassa deyyadhammassa dāso hutvā”ti. Sahāyo hutvā deti attanā paribhuñjitabbassa paresaṃ dātabbassa ca samasamaṃ ṭhapanato. Pati hutvā deti sayaṃ deyyadhammassa vase avattitvā tassa attano vase vattāpanato. Aparo nayo – yo attanā paṇītaṃ paribhuñjitvā paresaṃ nihīnaṃ deti, so dānadāso nāma tannimittanihīnabhāvāpattito. Yo yādisaṃ attanā paribhuñjati, tādisameva paresaṃ deti, so dānasahāyo nāma tannimittahīnādhikabhāvavivajjanena sadisabhāvāpattito. Yo attanā nihīnaṃ paribhuñjitvā paresaṃ paṇītaṃ deti, so dānapati nāma tannimittaseṭṭhabhāvāpattito.

Here, as for what one enjoys oneself, being overcome by craving, one becomes like a slave, behaving under its power. As for what is given to others, even here, with regard to food and drink in general, it is said that one becomes 'a slave to the giftable thing designated as giving' (dānasaṅkhātassa deyyadhammassa dāso hutvā). One gives as a friend by placing what is to be enjoyed by oneself and what is to be given to others on an equal footing. One gives as a master by not behaving under the power of the giftable thing, but causing it to behave under one's own power. Another explanation: one who enjoys what is excellent oneself but gives what is inferior to others is called a 'slave of giving,' due to incurring an inferior state as a result of that. One who enjoys what is of the same quality as what one gives to others is called a 'friend of giving,' due to avoiding inferior or superior states as a result of that and attaining a similar state. One who enjoys what is inferior oneself but gives what is excellent to others is called a 'master of giving,' due to attaining a superior state as a result of that.

Nittejabhūto tejahānippattiyā. Saha byati gacchatīti sahabyo, sahapavattanako, tassa bhāvo sahabyatā, sahapavattīti āha “sahabhāvaṃ ekībhāvaṃ gatā”ti. Asitassāti vā abandhassa, taṇhābandhanena abandhassāti attho. Pañcamaṃ uttānameva.

'Devoid of radiance' (nittejabhūto) means due to the attainment of loss of radiance. 'Sahabyo' (companion) means 'saha byati gacchati' (goes along with), or 'sahapavattanako' (one who proceeds together). Its state is 'sahabyatā' (companionship) or 'sahapavattī' (co-proceeding); thus it is said, 'having gone to a state of co-existence, a state of unity.' Or, for one who is 'unbound' (asitassa), that is, not bound by the fetter of craving—this is the meaning. The fifth is clear in itself.

Sīhasenāpatisuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Sīhasenāpati Sutta and So Forth is concluded.

6-7. Kāladānasuttādivaṇṇanā

6-7. Commentary on the Kāladāna Sutta and So Forth

36-37. Chaṭṭhe ārāmatoti phalārāmato. Paṭhamuppannānīti sabbapaṭhamaṃ sujātāni. Bhāsitaññūti bhikkhū gharadvāre ṭhitā kiñcāpi tuṇhī honti, atthato pana “bhikkhaṃ dethā”ti vadanti nāma ariyāya yācanāya. Vuttañhetaṃ “uddhissa ariyā tiṭṭhanti, esā ariyānaṃ yācanā”ti. Tatra ye “mayaṃ pacāma, ime na pacanti, pacamāne patvā alabhantā kuhiṃ labhissantī”ti [V 3.0017] deyyadhammaṃ saṃvibhajanti, te bhāsitaññū nāma ñatvā kattabbassa karaṇato. Yuttappattakāleti dātuṃ yuttappattakāle. Appaṭivānacittoti anivattanacitto. Sattamaṃ uttānameva.

36-37. In the sixth, ārāmato means from the fruit garden. Paṭhamuppannāni means those that are the very first, well-grown. Bhāsitaññū refers to monks standing at the door of a house; although they are silent, in essence they are saying, “Give alms,” which is the noble way of asking. For it is said, “The noble stand expecting, this is the asking of the noble.” There, those who think, “We cook, these do not cook; if, coming when we are cooking, they do not receive, where will they receive?” and share the gift, are called bhāsitaññū because of knowing and doing what ought to be done. Yuttappattakāle means at the time fit for giving. Appaṭivānacitto means with a mind that does not turn back. The seventh is straightforward.

Kāladānasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Kāladāna Sutta and So Forth is concluded.

8. Saddhasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Saddha Sutta

38. Aṭṭhame [M 3.0018] anukampantīti “sabbe sattā sukhī hontu averā abyāpajjā”ti evaṃ hitapharaṇena anuggaṇhanti. Apica upaṭṭhākānaṃ gehaṃ aññe sīlavante sabrahmacārino gahetvā pavisantāpi anuggaṇhanti nāma. Nīcavuttinti paṇipātasīlaṃ. Kodhamānathaddhatāya rahitanti kodhamānavasena uppanno yo thaddhabhāvo cittassa uddhumātalakkhaṇo, tena virahitanti attho. Soraccenāti “tattha katamaṃ soraccaṃ? Yo kāyiko avītikkamo, vācasiko avītikkamo, kāyikavācasiko avītikkamo, idaṃ vuccati soraccaṃ. Sabbopi sīlasaṃvaro soracca”nti evamāgatena sīlasaṃvarasaṅkhātena soratabhāvena. Sakhilanti “tattha katamaṃ sākhalyaṃ? Yā sā vācā thaddhakā kakkasā pharusā kaṭukā abhisajjanī kodhasāmantā asamādhisaṃvattanikā, tathārūpiṃ vācaṃ pahāya yā sā vācā nelā kaṇṇasukhā pemanīyā hadayaṅgamā porī bahujanakantā bahujanamanāpā, tathārūpiṃ vācaṃ bhāsitā hoti. Yā tattha saṇhavācatā sakhilavācatā apharusavācatā, idaṃ vuccati sākhalya”nti (dha. sa. 1350) evaṃ vuttena sammodakamudubhāvena samannāgataṃ. Tenāha “sakhilanti sammodaka”nti.

38. In the eighth, anukampanti means they support by pervading with what is beneficial, thinking: “May all beings be happy, free from enmity and affliction.” Moreover, when entering the homes of supporters with other virtuous fellow monastics, they are also said to be supporting. Nīcavutti means the practice of bowing down. Kodhamānathaddhatāya rahitaṃ means devoid of the rigidity of mind characterized by puffing up, which arises from anger and conceit. Soraccena means by the state of gentleness which is designated as moral restraint, as it is said: “What is gentleness? It is the non-transgression by body, non-transgression by speech, non-transgression by body and speech—this is called gentleness. All restraint of virtue is gentleness.” Sakhilaṃ means endowed with a welcoming and amiable disposition, as it is said: “What is kind speech? It is abandoning harsh, rough, bitter, offensive speech that provokes anger and does not lead to concentration, and instead speaking words that are gentle, pleasing to the ear, affectionate, touching the heart, courteous, pleasing to the people, and agreeable to the people. The quality of such gentle, kind, and non-harsh speech is called kind speech.” Hence it is said, “Sakhilaṃ means welcoming.”

Saddhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Saddha Sutta is concluded.

9-10. Puttasuttādivaṇṇanā

9-10. Commentary on the Puttasutta and So Forth

39-40. Navame bhatoti posito. Taṃ pana bharaṇaṃ jātakālato paṭṭhāya sukhapaccayūpaharaṇena dukkhapaccayāpaharaṇena ca pavattitanti dassetuṃ “amhehī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Hatthapādavaḍḍhanādīhīti ādi-saddena mukhena siṅghānikāpanayananahāpanamaṇḍanādiñca saṅgaṇhāti. Mātāpitūnaṃ santakaṃ khettādiṃ avināsetvā rakkhitaṃ tesaṃ paramparāya ṭhitiyā kāraṇaṃ hotīti āha “amhākaṃ santakaṃ…pe… kulavaṃso ciraṃ ṭhassatī”ti. Salākabhattādīni anupacchinditvāti salākabhattādīni avicchinditvā. Yasmā dāyajjappaṭilābhassa yogyabhāvena vattamānoyeva [V 3.0018] dāyassa paṭipajjissati, na itaroti āha “kulavaṃsānurūpāya paṭipattiyā”tiādi[M 3.0019]. Attanā dāyajjārahaṃ karontoti attānaṃ dāyajjārahaṃ karonto. Mātāpitaro hi attano ovāde avattamāne micchāpaṭipanne dārake vinicchayaṃ gantvā aputte karonti, te dāyajjārahā na honti. Ovāde vattamāne pana kulasantakassa sāmike karonti. Tatiyadivasato paṭṭhāyāti matadivasato tatiyadivasato paṭṭhāya. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva. Dasamaṃ uttānameva.

39-40. In the ninth, bhato means nourished. That support, however, is shown to operate from birth onwards by providing comforts and removing discomforts, hence the phrase “by us” and so forth is used. Regarding hatthapādavaḍḍhanādīhi, the word “and so forth” also includes removing mucus from the mouth, bathing, adorning, and so on. Not destroying the parents’ property, such as fields, and protecting it becomes the reason for the continuity of their lineage, hence it is said: “our property… the family line will long endure.” Salākabhattādīni anupacchinditvā means without cutting off the salākabhatta and so forth. Because only one who is fit to receive the inheritance will obtain the inheritance, and not another, it is said: “by conduct befitting the family lineage,” and so forth. Attanā dāyajjārahaṃ karonto means making oneself deserving of inheritance. For parents, when their children do not follow their advice and behave wrongly, they judge them and disinherit them; such children are not worthy of inheritance. But if they follow the advice, they make them owners of the family property. Tatiyadivasato paṭṭhāya means starting from the third day after the death. The rest is easily understood. The tenth is straightforward.

Puttasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Puttasutta and So Forth is concluded.

Sumanavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Sumanavagga is concluded.

5. Muṇḍarājavaggo

5. The Muṇḍarāja Vagga

1-2. Ādiyasuttādivaṇṇanā

1-2. Commentary on the Ādiyasutta and So Forth

41-42. Pañcamassa paṭhame uṭṭhānavīriyādhigatehīti vā uṭṭhānena ca vīriyena ca adhigatehi. Tattha uṭṭhānanti kāyikaṃ vīriyaṃ. Vīriyanti cetasikanti vadanti. Uṭṭhānanti vā bhoguppādane yuttappayuttatā. Vīriyaṃ tajjo ussāho. Pīṇitanti dhātaṃ sutittaṃ. Tathābhūto pana yasmā thūlasarīro hoti, tasmā “thūlaṃ karotī”ti vuttaṃ. Dutiyaṃ uttānameva.

41-42. In the first of the fifth, uṭṭhānavīriyādhigatehi means achieved by effort and energy, or by effort and by energy. Here, uṭṭhāna refers to bodily energy. Vīriya refers to mental energy, they say. Or, uṭṭhāna can mean being constantly engaged in the production of wealth. Vīriya is the effort born of that. Pīṇita means nourished, saturated. Being of such a nature, because one becomes gross in body, it is therefore said, “one makes it gross.” The second is straightforward.

Ādiyasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Ādiyasutta and So Forth is concluded.

3. Iṭṭhasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Iṭṭha Sutta

43. Tatiye appamādaṃ pasaṃsantīti “etāni āyuādīni patthayantena appamādo kātabbo”ti appamādameva pasaṃsanti paṇḍitā. Yasmā vā puññakiriyāsu paṇḍitā appamādaṃ pasaṃsanti, tasmā āyuādīni patthayantena appamādova kātabboti attho. Purimasmiṃ atthavikappe “puññakiriyāsū”ti padassa “appamatto”ti iminā sambandho. Yasmā [V 3.0019] paṇḍitā appamādaṃ pasaṃsanti, yasmā ca puññakiriyāsu appamatto ubho atthe adhigato hoti, tasmā āyuādīni patthayantena appamādova [M 3.0020] kātabbo. Dutiyasmiṃ atthavikappe paṇḍitā appamādaṃ pasaṃsanti. Katthāti? Puññakiriyāsu. Kasmāti ce? Yasmā appamatto ubho atthe adhiggaṇhāti paṇḍito, tasmāti attho. Atthappaṭilābhenāti diṭṭhadhammikādihitappaṭilābhena.

43. In the third sutta, they praise heedfulness: ‘For one who desires long life and other blessings, heedfulness should be practiced’—thus the wise praise only heedfulness. Or, because the wise praise heedfulness in meritorious deeds, therefore, for one desiring long life and other blessings, heedfulness alone should be practiced—this is the meaning. In the former interpretation, the phrase ‘in meritorious deeds’ is connected with ‘the heedful one’. Because the wise praise heedfulness, and because the heedful one attains both goals through meritorious deeds, therefore, for one desiring long life and other blessings, heedfulness alone should be practiced. In the second interpretation, the wise praise heedfulness. Where? In meritorious deeds. Why? Because the heedful one, being wise, attains both goals—this is the meaning. By attaining benefits means by attaining benefits such as those pertaining to this present life and others.

Iṭṭhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Iṭṭha Sutta is concluded.

4. Manāpadāyīsuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Manāpadāyī Sutta

44. Catutthe jhānamanena nibbattaṃ manomayanti āha “suddhāvāsesu ekaṃ jhānamanena nibbattaṃ devakāya”nti. Satipi hi sabbasattānaṃ abhisaṅkhāramanasā nibbattabhāve bāhirapaccayehi vinā manasāva nibbattattā “manomayā”ti vuccanti rūpāvacarasattā. Yadi evaṃ kāmabhave opapātikasattānampi manomayabhāvo āpajjatīti ce? Na, tattha bāhirapaccayehi nibbattetabbatāsaṅkāya eva abhāvato “manasāva nibbattā”ti avadhāraṇāsambhavato. Niruḷho vāyaṃ loke manomayavohāro rūpāvacarasattesu. Tathā hi “annamayo, pāṇamayo, manomayo, ānandamayo, viññāṇamayo”ti pañcadhā attānaṃ vedavādinopi vadanti. Ucchedavādinopi vadanti “dibbo rūpī manomayo”ti (dī. ni. 1.87). Tīsu vā kulasampattīsūti brāhmaṇakhattiyavessasaṅkhātesu sampannakulesu. Chasu vā kāmasaggesūti chasu kāmāvacaradevesu.

44. In the fourth sutta, regarding ‘mind-made’ (manomaya), it is said: ‘A divine body produced by jhāna-mind in the Pure Abodes’. Indeed, although all beings are produced by the mind of volitional formations, form-sphere beings are called ‘mind-made’ because they are produced by the mind alone without external conditions. If so, does this ‘mind-made’ nature also apply to spontaneously arisen beings in the sense-sphere? No, because there, due to the absence of any doubt about their being produced by external conditions, the definitive statement ‘produced by the mind alone’ is not possible. This conventional term ‘mind-made’ is firmly established in the world for form-sphere beings. Thus, even the Vedavadins speak of the self as fivefold: ‘made of food, made of breath, made of mind, made of bliss, made of consciousness’. Even the annihilationists say, ‘divine, having form, mind-made’ (Dīgha Nikāya 1.87). Or, ‘in the three families with good lineage’—namely, in the well-endowed families called brahmins, khattiyas, and vessas. Or, ‘in the six sense-sphere heavens’—namely, among the six classes of sense-sphere deities.

Manāpadāyīsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Manāpadāyī Sutta is concluded.

5-6. Puññābhisandasuttādivaṇṇanā

5–6. Commentary on the Puññābhisanda Sutta and Others

45-46. Pañcame asaṅkheyyoti āḷhakagaṇanāya asaṅkheyyo. Yojanavasena panassa saṅkhā atthi heṭṭhā mahāpathaviyā upari ākāsena parisamantato cakkavāḷapabbatena majjhe tattha tattha ṭhitakehi dīpapabbatapariyantehi paricchinnattā jānantena yojanato saṅkhātuṃ sakkāti katvā.
