Mahāsarīramacchakumbhīlayakkharakkhasamahānāgadānavādīnaṃ saviññāṇakānaṃ balavāmukhapātālādīnaṃ [V 3.0020] aviññāṇakānaṃ bheravārammaṇānaṃ vasena bahubheravaṃ[M 3.0021]. Puthūti bahū. Savantīti sandamānā. Upayantīti upagacchanti. Chaṭṭhaṃ uttānameva.

45–46. In the fifth sutta, ‘immeasurable’ means immeasurable by the measure of āḷhakas. However, its measure exists in terms of yojanas, because below the great earth, above the sky, and all around, it is bounded by the encircling Cakkavāḷa mountains and by the islands and mountains standing here and there in the middle; thus, one who knows can reckon it in yojanas. It is a place of great terror because of great-bodied fish, crocodiles, yakkhas, ogres, great nāgas, dānavas, and other conscious beings, as well as the terrifying objects of Balavāmukha, the abyss, and other unconscious, frightful things. ‘Many’ (puthū) means numerous. ‘Flowing’ (savanti) means streaming. ‘Approaching’ (upayanti) means drawing near. The sixth sutta is self-explanatory.

Puññābhisandasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Puññābhisanda Sutta and Others is concluded.

7-8. Dhanasuttādivaṇṇanā

7–8. Commentary on the Dhana Sutta and Others

47-48. Sattame saddhāti maggenāgatā saddhā. Sīlañca yassa kalyāṇanti kalyāṇasīlaṃ nāma ariyasāvakassa ariyakantaṃ sīlaṃ vuccati. Tattha kiñcāpi ariyasāvakassa ekasīlampi akantaṃ nāma natthi, imasmiṃ panatthe bhavantarepi appahīnaṃ pañcasīlaṃ adhippetaṃ. Aṭṭhamaṃ uttānameva.

47–48. In the seventh sutta, ‘faith’ (saddhā) means the faith that has come through the path. ‘And virtue that is beautiful’ (sīlañca yassa kalyāṇaṃ) means the virtuous conduct of a noble disciple, which is called virtue pleasing to the noble ones. Here, although there is no single virtue of a noble disciple that is not pleasing, in this context, the five precepts not abandoned even in future existences are intended. The eighth sutta is self-explanatory.

Dhanasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Dhana Sutta and Others is concluded.

9. Kosalasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Kosala Sutta

49. Navame patitakkhandhoti sammukhā kiñci oloketuṃ asamatthatāya adhomukho. Nippaṭibhānoti sahadhammikaṃ kiñci vattuṃ avisahanato nippaṭibhāno paṭibhānarahito.

49. In the ninth sutta, ‘with shoulders drooping’ (patitakkhandho) means downcast, due to being unable to look at anything face-to-face. ‘Without response’ (nippaṭibhāno) means being without wit or resource, unable to venture to say anything concerning a fellow practitioner.

Kosalasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Kosala Sutta is concluded.

10. Nāradasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Nārada Sutta

50. Dasame ajjhomucchitoti adhimattāya taṇhāmucchāya mucchito, mucchaṃ mohaṃ pamādaṃ āpanno. Tenāha “gilitvā…pe… atirekamucchāya taṇhāya samannāgato”ti. Mahaccāti mahatiyā. Liṅgavipallāsena cetaṃ vuttaṃ. Tenāha “mahatā rājānubhāvenā”ti.

50. In the tenth sutta, ‘overcome’ (ajjhomucchito) means overcome by excessive craving-infatuation, having fallen into infatuation, delusion, and heedlessness. Hence it is said: ‘having swallowed… possessed by excessive craving’. ‘Great’ (mahaccā) means by a great one. This is said with a reversal of gender. Hence it is said: ‘by great royal power’.

Nāradasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Nārada Sutta is concluded.

Muṇḍarājavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Muṇḍarāja Vagga is concluded.

Paṭhamapaṇṇāsakaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The First Fifty is concluded.

2. Dutiyapaṇṇāsakaṃ

2. The Second Fifty

(6) 1. Nīvaraṇavaggo

(6) 1. The Chapter on the Hindrances

1-2. Āvaraṇasuttādivaṇṇanā

1-2. Commentary on the Āvaraṇa Sutta and Others

51-52. Dutiyassa [V 3.0021][M 3.0022] paṭhame āvarantīti āvaraṇā, nīvārayantīti nīvaraṇā. Ettha ca āvarantīti kusaladhammuppattiṃ ādito parivārenti. Nīvārayantīti niravasesato vārayantīti attho, tasmā āvaraṇavasenāti ādito kusaluppattivāraṇavasena. Nīvaraṇavasenāti niravasesato vāraṇavasenāti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Yasmā pañca nīvaraṇā uppajjamānā anuppannāya lokiyalokuttarāya paññāya uppajjituṃ na denti, uppannāpi aṭṭha samāpattiyo pañca vā abhiññā upacchinditvā pātenti, tasmā “paññāya dubbalīkaraṇā”ti vuccanti. Upacchindanaṃ pātanañcettha tāsaṃ paññānaṃ anuppannānaṃ uppajjituṃ appadānameva. Iti mahaggatānuttarapaññānaṃ ekaccāya ca parittapaññāya anuppattihetubhūtā nīvaraṇadhammā itarāsaṃ samatthataṃ vihanantiyevāti paññāya dubbalīkaraṇā vuttā. Bhāvanāmanasikārena vinā pakatiyā manussehi nibbattetabbo dhammoti manussadhammo, manussattabhāvāvaho vā dhammo manussadhammo, anuḷāraṃ parittakusalaṃ. Yaṃ asatipi buddhuppāde vattati, yañca sandhāyāha “hīnena brahmacariyena, khattiye upapajjatī”ti (jā. 1.8.75). Alaṃ ariyāya ariyabhāvāyāti alamariyo, ariyabhāvāya samatthoti vuttaṃ hoti. Ñāṇadassanameva ñāṇadassanaviseso, alamariyo ca so ñāṇadassanaviseso cāti alamariyañāṇadassanaviseso.

51-52. In the first of the second pair: ‘they obstruct’ (āvaranti), thus they are ‘obstructions’ (āvaraṇā); ‘they hinder’ (nīvārayanti), thus they are ‘hindrances’ (nīvaraṇā). Herein, ‘they obstruct’ means they envelop the arising of wholesome qualities from the very beginning. ‘They hinder’ means they ward off without remainder; this is the meaning. Therefore, ‘by way of obstruction’ means by way of warding off the arising of the wholesome from the start. ‘By way of hindrance’ means by way of warding off without remainder; this is how the meaning should be understood here. For when the five hindrances arise, they do not allow unarisen mundane and supramundane wisdom to arise; and if these have arisen, they cut them off and cause the eight attainments or the five higher knowledges to fall. Therefore they are called ‘weakeners of wisdom.’ Herein, ‘cutting off’ and ‘causing to fall’ simply means not giving an opportunity for those unarisen wisdoms to arise. Thus, the hindering states, being the cause for the non-arising of exalted and unsurpassed wisdom and of certain limited wisdoms, and destroying the competence of others, are called ‘weakeners of wisdom.’ A ‘human quality’ (manussadhammo) is a quality to be generated by humans in the ordinary course of things without meditative development, or it is a quality that leads to a human state of existence; it is limited, minor wholesome action. It is present even when there is no arising of a Buddha, and it is with reference to this that it is said: ‘Through an inferior holy life, one is reborn among the khattiyas’ (Jā 1.8.75). ‘Sufficient for the noble state’ (alaṃ ariyāya ariyabhāvāya), thus ‘sufficiently noble’ (alamariyo); it means being capable of the noble state. ‘A special knowledge and vision’ (ñāṇadassanaviseso) is just knowledge and vision. And that special knowledge and vision is sufficiently noble, thus ‘a special knowledge and vision that is sufficiently noble’ (alamariyañāṇadassanaviseso).

Ñāṇadassananti ca dibbacakkhupi vipassanāpi maggopi phalampi paccavekkhaṇañāṇampi sabbaññutaññāṇampi vuccati. “Appamatto samāno ñāṇadassanaṃ ārādhetī”ti (ma. ni. 1.311) hi ettha dibbacakkhu ñāṇadassanaṃ nāma. “Ñāṇadassanāya cittaṃ abhinīharati abhininnāmetī”ti (dī. ni. 1.234) ettha vipassanāñāṇaṃ. “Abhabbā te ñāṇāya dassanāya anuttarāya sambodhāyā”ti (a. ni. 4.196) ettha maggo. “Ayamañño [M 3.0023] uttarimanussadhammā alamariyañāṇadassanaviseso adhigato phāsuvihāro”ti (ma. ni. 1.328) ettha [V 3.0022] phalaṃ. “Ñāṇañca pana me dassanaṃ udapādi, akuppā me vimutti, ayamantimā jāti, natthi dāni punabbhavo”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.1081; mahāva. 16; paṭi. ma. 2.30) ettha paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ. “Ñāṇañca pana me dassanaṃ udapādi ‘sattāhakālakato āḷāro kālāmo’”ti (ma. ni. 1.284; 2.340) ettha sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ. Idha pana lokuttaradhammo adhippeto. Ettha ca rūpāyatanaṃ jānāti cakkhuviññāṇaṃ viya passati cāti ñāṇadassanaṃ, dibbacakkhu. Sammasanūpacāre ca dhammalakkhaṇattayañca tathā jānāti passati cāti ñāṇadassanaṃ, vipassanā. Nibbānaṃ cattāri vā saccāni asammohappaṭivedhato jānāti passati cāti ñāṇadassanaṃ, maggo. Phalaṃ pana nibbānavaseneva yojetabbaṃ. Paccavekkhaṇā maggādhigatassa atthassa sabbaso jotanaṭṭhena ñāṇadassanaṃ. Sabbaññutā anāvaraṇatāya samantacakkhutāya ca ñāṇadassanaṃ. Byādiṇṇakāloti pariyādinnakālo. Dutiyaṃ uttānameva.

‘Knowledge and vision’ can refer to the divine eye, insight, the path, the fruit, reviewing knowledge, and omniscient knowledge. For it is said: ‘Being diligent, one attains knowledge and vision’ (MN 1.311); here ‘knowledge and vision’ is the divine eye. ‘He directs and inclines his mind toward knowledge and vision’ (DN 1.234); here it is insight-knowledge. ‘They are incapable of knowledge, of vision, of unsurpassed full enlightenment’ (AN 4.196); here it is the path. ‘This other superhuman quality has been attained, a distinction in noble knowledge and vision, a pleasant abiding’ (MN 1.328); here it is the fruit. ‘And knowledge and vision arose in me: “Unshakable is my liberation, this is the last birth, there is now no further state of being”’ (SN 5.1081; Mhv 16; Paṭis II 30); here it is reviewing knowledge. ‘And knowledge and vision arose in me: “Āḷāra Kālāma died seven days ago”’ (MN 1.284; 2.340); here it is omniscient knowledge. Here, however, a supramundane state is intended. In this context, ‘knowledge and vision’ is the divine eye, as ‘it knows the form-base and sees as the eye-consciousness does.’ In the preliminary stage of comprehension, ‘it similarly knows and sees the three characteristics of phenomena’; this is ‘knowledge and vision’ as insight. ‘It knows and sees Nibbāna or the four truths through non-deluded penetration’; this is ‘knowledge and vision’ as the path. The fruit, however, should be construed in terms of Nibbāna. Reviewing knowledge is ‘knowledge and vision’ in the sense of completely illuminating the meaning attained by the path. Omniscience is ‘knowledge and vision’ because of its unobstructedness and its quality of being the all-around eye. ‘Byādiṇṇakālo’ means the time has been completely exhausted. The second sutta is self-evident.

Āvaraṇasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Āvaraṇa Sutta and Others is concluded.

3-4. Padhāniyaṅgasuttādivaṇṇanā

3-4. Commentary on the Padhāniyaṅga Sutta and Others

53-54. Tatiye padahatīti padahano, bhāvanamanuyutto yogī, tassa bhāvo bhāvanānuyogo padahanabhāvo. Padhānamassa atthīti padhāniko, ka-kārassa ya-kāraṃ katvā “padhāniyo”ti vuttaṃ. “Abhinīhārato paṭṭhāya āgatattā”ti vuttattā paccekabodhisattasāvakabodhisattānampi paṇidhānato pabhuti āgatasaddhā āgamanasaddā eva, ukkaṭṭhaniddesena pana “sabbaññubodhisattāna”nti vuttaṃ. Adhigamato samudāgatattā aggamaggaphalasampayuttā cāpi adhigamasaddhā nāma, yā sotāpannassa aṅgabhāvena vuttā. Acalabhāvenāti paṭipakkhena anadhibhavanīyattā niccalabhāvena. Okappananti okkanditvā adhimuccanaṃ, pasāduppattiyā pasādanīyavatthusmiṃ pasīdanameva. Suppaṭividdhanti suṭṭhu paṭividdhaṃ. Yathā tena paṭividdhena sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ hatthagataṃ ahosi, tathā paṭividdhaṃ. Yassa buddhasubuddhatāya saddhā acalā asampavedhi, tassa dhammasudhammatāya saṅghasuppaṭipannatāya [M 3.0024] tena paṭivedhena saddhā na tathāti aṭṭhānametaṃ anavakāso. Tenāha bhagavā – “yo, bhikkhave, buddhe pasanno dhamme pasanno saṅghe pasanno”tiādi. Padhānavīriyaṃ ijjhati “addhā imāya paṭipadāya jarāmaraṇato muccissāmī”ti sakkaccaṃ padahanato.

53-54. In the third sutta: ‘He strives’ (padahati), thus he is a ‘striver’ (padahano), a yogī devoted to development; his state, devotion to development, is the state of striving. ‘He has striving,’ thus he is a ‘striver’ (padhāniko); by changing the letter ‘ka’ to ‘ya,’ it is said ‘padhāniyo.’ Because it is said, ‘having come forth from the aspiration,’ the faith that has come about from the resolve of paccekabodhisattas and disciple-bodhisattas is also ‘faith by way of arrival’ (āgamanasaddhā). However, by way of the supreme designation, it is said of ‘the omniscient Bodhisattas.’ Because it has arisen from attainment, the faith associated with the supreme path and fruit, which is spoken of as a factor of the stream-enterer, is called ‘faith by attainment’ (adhigamasaddhā). ‘By unshakability’ means by its immovability, since it is unconquerable by its opposite. ‘Confidence’ (okappana) is resolving after leaping on; it is simply confidence in a confidence-inspiring object with the arising of confidence. ‘Thoroughly penetrated’ (suppaṭividdhaṃ) means well penetrated; penetrated in such a way that by that penetration the knowledge of omniscience came into his hands. For one whose faith in the Buddha's perfect enlightenment is unshaken and unquivering, it is impossible, there is no opportunity, that his faith in the Dhamma's being the good Dhamma and the Sangha's good practice would not be likewise through that penetration. Therefore the Blessed One said: ‘Monks, one who has confidence in the Buddha, confidence in the Dhamma, confidence in the Sangha,’ and so on. The energy in striving succeeds because one strives earnestly, thinking: ‘Surely, by this practice, I will be freed from aging and death.’

Appa-saddo [V 3.0023] abhāvattho “appasaddassa…pe… kho panā”tiādīsu viyāti āha “arogo”ti. Samavepākiniyāti yathābhuttamāhāraṃ samākāreneva pacanasīlāya. Daḷhaṃ katvā pacantī hi gahaṇī ghorabhāvena pittavikārādivasena rogaṃ janeti, sithilaṃ katvā pacantī mandabhāvena vātavikārādivasena tenāha “nātisītāya nāccuṇhāyā”ti. Gahaṇitejassa mandapaṭutāvasena sattānaṃ yathākkamaṃ sītuṇhasahatāti āha “atisītalaggahaṇiko”tiādi. Yāthāvato accayadesanā attano āvikaraṇaṃ nāmāti āha “yathābhūtaṃ attano aguṇaṃ pakāsetā”ti. Udayatthagāminiyāti saṅkhārānaṃ udayañca vayañca paṭivijjhantiyāti ayamettha atthoti āha “udayañcā”tiādi. Parisuddhāyāti nirupakkilesāya. Nibbijjhituṃ samatthāyāti tadaṅgavasena savisesaṃ pajahituṃ samatthāya. Tassa dukkhassa khayagāminiyāti yaṃ dukkhaṃ imasmiṃ ñāṇe anadhigate pavattirahaṃ, adhigate na pavatti, taṃ sandhāya vadati. Tathāhesa yogāvacaro “cūḷasotāpanno”ti vuccati. Catutthaṃ uttānameva.

The word 'appa' has the meaning of absence, as in such phrases as 'appasadda...' etc.; thus it is said 'free from illness' (arogo). 'Having even digestion' means having the nature of digesting food that has been eaten in an even manner. For if the digestive faculty (gahaṇī) digests too strongly, its intensity generates illness through disorders of bile and the like. If it digests too slackly, its weakness causes disorders of wind and the like. Hence it is said, 'not too cold, not too hot.' Depending on the weakness or sharpness of the heat of the digestive faculty, beings can endure cold and heat respectively; thus it is said, 'one with a very cold digestion,' etc. 'Confession of a transgression as it actually is' is the name for making oneself manifest; thus it is said, 'one who reveals one's own fault as it really is.' 'Leading to arising and passing away' means penetrating the arising and passing away of formations; this is the meaning here, thus it is said 'arising and...' etc. 'Purified' means without defilement. 'Able to penetrate' means able to abandon with distinction by means of that factor. 'Leading to the destruction of that suffering': this is said with reference to that suffering which, so long as this knowledge has not been attained, is liable to continue, but which does not continue once it is attained. Thus this yogi is called a 'lesser stream-enterer' (cūḷasotāpanno). The fourth [factor] is self-evident.

Padhāniyaṅgasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Suttas on the Factors of Striving, etc., is concluded.

5. Mātāputtasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Mother and Son Sutta

55. Pañcame vissāsoti visacchāyasantāno bhāvo. Otāroti tattha cittassa anuppaveso. Gahetvāti attano eva okāsaṃ gahetvā. Khepetvāti kusalavāraṃ khepetvā.

55. In the fifth, 'familiarity' (vissāsa) is a state that is a continuous stream like the shadow of poison. 'Opportunity' (otāra) is the entry of the mind into that. 'Having taken' (gahetvā) is having taken one's own opportunity. 'Having wasted' (khepetvā) is having wasted the opportunity for what is wholesome.

Ghaṭṭeyyāti akkamanādivasena bādheyya. Tīhi pariññāhīti ñātatīraṇappahānasaṅkhātāhi tīhi pariññāhi. Natthi etesaṃ kutoci bhayanti akutobhayā, nibbhayāti attho. Catunnaṃ oghānaṃ, saṃsāramahoghasseva vā pāraṃ pariyantaṃ gatā. Tenāha “pāraṃ vuccati nibbāna”ntiādi.

'One would harm' (ghaṭṭeyya) means one would afflict by way of attacking and so on. 'By the three full understandings' means by the three full understandings designated as full understanding of the known, full understanding by investigation, and full understanding by abandoning. 'There is no fear for them from anywhere' (akutobhayā), thus they are fearless; the meaning is 'without fear.' They have gone to the far shore, the end, of the four floods, or of the great flood of saṃsāra. Hence it is said: 'The far shore is called Nibbāna,' and so on.

Mātāputtasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Mother and Son Sutta is concluded.

6. Upajjhāyasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Preceptor Sutta

56. Chaṭṭhe [M 3.0025] madhurakabhāvo nāma sarīrassa thambhitattaṃ, taṃ pana garubhāvapubbakanti āha “sañjātagarubhāvo”ti[V 3.0024]. Na pakkhāyantīti nappakāsenti, nānākāraṇato na upaṭṭhahanti. Tenāha “catasso disā ca anudisā ca mayhaṃ na upaṭṭhahantī”ti. Sesamettha uttānameva.

56. In the sixth, the 'state of being like a sweet cake' (madhurakabhāva) is the stiffness of the body. But since this is preceded by a state of heaviness, it is said, 'one in whom heaviness has arisen' (sañjātagarubhāvo). 'They do not appear' (na pakkhāyanti) means they do not become clear; they do not present themselves for various reasons. Hence it is said: 'The four directions and the intermediate directions do not present themselves to me.' The rest here is self-evident.

Upajjhāyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Preceptor Sutta is concluded.

7. Abhiṇhapaccavekkhitabbaṭṭhānasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Sutta on Subjects for Frequent Reflection

57. Sattame jarādhammoti dhamma-saddo “asammosadhammo nibbāna”ntiādīsu (su. ni. 763) viya pakatipariyāyo, tasmā jarāpakatiko jiṇṇasabhāvoti attho. Tenāha “jarāsabhāvo”tiādi. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Kammunā dātabbaṃ ādiyatīti kammadāyādo, attanā yathūpacitakammaphalabhāgīti attho. Taṃ pana dāyajjaṃ kāraṇūpacārena vadanto “kammaṃ mayhaṃ dāyajjaṃ santakanti attho”ti āha yathā “kusalānaṃ, bhikkhave, dhammānaṃ samādānahetu, evamidaṃ puññaṃ vaḍḍhatī”ti (dī. ni. 3.80). Yonīhi phalaṃ sabhāvato bhinnampi abhinnaṃ viya missitaṃ hoti. Tenāha “kammaṃ mayhaṃ yoni kāraṇa”nti. Mamattavasena bajjhantīti bandhū, ñāti sālohito ca, kammaṃ pana ekantasambandhavāti āha “kammaṃ mayhaṃ bandhū”ti. Patiṭṭhāti avassayo. Kammasadiso hi sattānaṃ avassayo natthi.

57. In the seventh, regarding 'subject to aging' (jarādhamma): the word dhamma is a synonym for nature, as in such passages as 'Nibbāna is the unconfused Dhamma' (Snp 763). Therefore the meaning is 'of the nature of aging,' 'having a nature that grows old.' Hence it is said, 'the nature of aging,' and so on. This same method applies to the other terms as well. 'Heir to kamma' (kammadāyādo) means one who receives what is to be given by kamma; the meaning is that one is a sharer in the fruit of the kamma one has accumulated. Speaking of that inheritance (dāyajja) by way of a metaphor for the cause, he says, 'Kamma is my inheritance, my property,' just as it is said: 'Bhikkhus, on account of undertaking wholesome states, this merit increases' (DN 3.80). Though by nature the fruit is different from its origin, they are mingled as if inseparable. Hence it is said, 'Kamma is my origin, my cause.' 'Kinsmen' (bandhū) are those who are bound by way of 'mineness'—relatives and blood relations. But since kamma is the one certain connection, he says, 'Kamma is my kinsman.' 'Refuge' (patiṭṭhā) means support. For beings, there is indeed no support like kamma.

Yobbanaṃ ārabbha uppannamadoti “mahallakakāle puññaṃ karissāma, daharamha tāvā”ti yobbanaṃ apassāya mānakaraṇaṃ. “Ahaṃ nirogo saṭṭhi vā sattati vā vassāni atikkantāni, na me harītakakhaṇḍampi khāditabbaṃ, ime panaññe ‘asukaṃ no ṭhānaṃ rujjati, bhesajjaṃ khādāmā’ti vicaranti, ko añño mayā sadiso nirogo nāmā”ti evaṃ mānakaraṇaṃ ārogyamado. Sabbesampi jīvitaṃ nāma pabhaṅguraṃ dukkhānubandhañca, tadubhayaṃ anoloketvā pabandhaṭṭhitiṃ paccayasulabhatañca nissāya “ciraṃ jīviṃ, ciraṃ jīvāmi, ciraṃ jīvissāmi, sukhaṃ jīviṃ, sukhaṃ jīvāmi, sukhaṃ jīvissāmī”ti evaṃ mānakaraṇaṃ jīvitamado.

The intoxication that arises concerning youth is the conceit of relying on one's youth and thinking: 'We will make merit when we are old; for now, we are young.' The intoxication with health is the conceit of thinking: 'I am healthy. Sixty or seventy years have passed, and I haven't had to chew even a piece of myrobalan. But these others wander about saying, "Such and such a part of us is afflicted, let's take medicine." Who else is as healthy as I?' For all, life is fragile and followed by suffering. The intoxication with life is the conceit of not considering both these facts and, relying on the continuity of existence and the ease of obtaining requisites, thinking: 'I have lived long, I am living long, I will live long; I have lived happily, I am living happily, I will live happily.'

Upadhirahitanti [M 3.0026] kāmūpadhirahitaṃ. Cattāro hi upadhī – kāmūpadhi, khandhūpadhi, kilesūpadhi, abhisaṅkhārūpadhīti. Kāmāpi “yaṃ pañca kāmaguṇe paṭicca uppajjati sukhaṃ somanassaṃ, ayaṃ kāmānaṃ assādo”ti (ma. ni. 1.166) evaṃ vuttassa sukhassa adhiṭṭhānabhāvato “upadhiyati ettha sukha”nti iminā vacanatthena “upadhī”ti vuccati, khandhāpi khandhamūlakassa dukkhassa [V 3.0025] adhiṭṭhānabhāvato, kilesāpi apāyadukkhassa adhiṭṭhānabhāvato, abhisaṅkhārāpi bhavadukkhassa adhiṭṭhānabhāvato. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

'Without acquisitions' means without the acquisition of sensual pleasures. For there are four acquisitions: the acquisition of sensual pleasures, the acquisition of the aggregates, the acquisition of defilements, and the acquisition of volitional formations. Sensual pleasures, too, are called an 'acquisition' (upadhi) because they are the basis for the happiness spoken of thus: 'Whatever pleasure and joy arise in dependence on the five cords of sensual pleasure, this is the gratification in sensual pleasures' (MN 1.85). The verbal meaning is 'happiness is placed on this.' Similarly, the aggregates are called an acquisition because they are the basis for suffering rooted in the aggregates; the defilements, because they are the basis for the suffering of the plane of misery; and volitional formations, because they are the basis for the suffering of existence. The rest is easy to understand.

Abhiṇhapaccavekkhitabbaṭṭhānasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Sutta on Subjects for Frequent Reflection is concluded.

8-10. Licchavikumārakasuttādivaṇṇanā

8-10. Commentary on the Sutta to the Licchavi Youth and Others

58-60. Aṭṭhame sāpateyyanti ettha saṃ vuccati dhanaṃ, tassa patīti sapati, dhanasāmiko. Tassa hitāvahattā sāpateyyaṃ, drabyaṃ, dhananti attho. Attano rucivasena gāmakiccaṃ netīti gāmaniyo, gāmaniyoyeva gāmaṇiko.

58-60. In the eighth, regarding 'property' (sāpateyyaṃ): here, saṃ is said to be wealth; its lord (pati) is sapati, the owner of wealth. Because it brings him welfare, it is sāpateyyaṃ; the meaning is goods, wealth. A 'village headman' (gāmanī) is one who directs the village's affairs according to his own preference; a gāmanī is the same as a gāmaṇika.

Anvāya upanissāya jīvanasīlā anujīvinoti āha “ye ca etaṃ upanissāya jīvantī”ti. Ekaṃ mahākulaṃ nissāya paṇṇāsampi saṭṭhipi kulāni jīvanti, te manusse sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva. Navamādīni uttānatthāneva.

'Dependents' (anujīvino) are those whose nature it is to live by following and depending on another; thus he said, 'and those who live in dependence on him.' Fifty or even sixty families might live in dependence on one great family; this was said with reference to those people. The rest is easy to understand. The ninth and the following suttas are clear in meaning.

Licchavikumārakasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Sutta to the Licchavi Youth and Others is concluded.

Nīvaraṇavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Chapter on the Hindrances is concluded.

(7) 2. Saññāvaggo

(7) 2. The Chapter on Perceptions

1-5. Saññāsuttādivaṇṇanā

1-5. Commentary on the Suttas on Perception and Others

61-65. Dutiyassa paṭhame “mahapphalā mahānisaṃsā”ti ubhayampetaṃ atthato ekaṃ, byañjanameva nānanti āha “mahapphalā”tiādi. “Pañcime gahapatayo ānisaṃsā”tiādīsu (udā. 76) ānisaṃsa-saddo phalapariyāyopi hoti[M 3.0027]. Mahato lokuttarassa sukhassa paccayā hontīti mahānisaṃsā. Amatogadhāti amatabbhantarā amataṃ anuppaviṭṭhā nibbānadiṭṭhattā, tato paraṃ na gacchanti. Tena vuttaṃ “amatapariyosānā”ti. Amataṃ pariyosānaṃ avasānaṃ etāsanti [V 3.0026] amatapariyosānā. Maraṇasaññāti maraṇānupassanāñāṇena saññā. Āhāre paṭikūlasaññāti āhāraṃ gamanādivasena paṭikūlato pariggaṇhantassa uppannasaññā. Ukkaṇṭhitassāti nibbindantassa katthacipi asajjantassa. Dutiyādīni uttānatthāneva.

61-65. In the first sutta of the second chapter, concerning 'of great fruit, of great benefit': both of these are one in meaning, only the phrasing is different; thus it says 'of great fruit,' etc. In such phrases as 'these five benefits, householders' (Ud 76), the word 'benefit' can also be a synonym for 'fruit.' They are 'of great benefit' because they are conditions for great, supramundane happiness. 'Grounded in the Deathless' means they are contained within the Deathless, have penetrated the Deathless, because Nibbāna has been seen; they do not go beyond that. Therefore it is said, 'culminating in the Deathless.' They have the Deathless as their culmination, their final end; thus they are 'culminating in the Deathless.' 'Perception of death' is perception by means of the knowledge from contemplating death. 'Perception of the repulsiveness in food' is the perception that arises in one who comprehends food as repulsive in regard to its acquisition and so on. 'Of one who is disenchanted' means of one who is revulsed, not clinging to anything anywhere. The second and following suttas are of clear meaning.

Saññāsuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Suttas on Perception and Others is concluded.

6-10. Sājīvasuttādivaṇṇanā

6-10. Commentary on the Sājīva Sutta and Others

66-70. Chaṭṭhe saha ājīvanti etthāti sājīvo, pañhassa pucchanaṃ vissajjanañca. Tenāha “sājīvoti pañhapucchanañceva pañhavissajjanañcā”tiādi. Abhisaṅkhatanti citaṃ. Sattamādīni uttānatthāneva.

66-70. In the sixth sutta, sājīvo is so called because one lives together (saha ājīvati) with it, that is, with the asking and answering of a question. Hence it is said: 'Sājīvo is both the asking of a question and the answering of a question,' etc. 'Formed' means accumulated. The seventh and following suttas are of clear meaning.

Sājīvasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Sājīva Sutta and others is concluded.

Saññāvaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Chapter on Perceptions is concluded.

(8) 3. Yodhājīvavaggo

(8) 3. The Chapter on the Warrior's Livelihood

1-2. Paṭhamacetovimuttiphalasuttādivaṇṇanā

1-2. Commentary on the First Sutta on the Fruit of the Liberation of Mind and others

71-72. Tatiyassa paṭhame avijjāpalighanti ettha avijjāti vaṭṭamūlikā avijjā, ayaṃ pacurajanehi ukkhipituṃ asakkuṇeyyabhāvato dukkhipanaṭṭhena nibbānadvārappavesavibandhanena ca “paligho viyāti paligho”ti vuccati. Tenesa tassā ukkhittattā “ukkhittapaligho”ti vutto. Punabbhavassa karaṇasīlo, punabbhavaṃ vā phalaṃ arahatīti ponobhavikā, punabbhavadāyikāti attho. Jātisaṃsāroti jāyanavasena ceva saṃsaraṇavasena ca evaṃladdhanāmānaṃ punabbhavakkhandhānaṃ paccayo kammābhisaṅkhāro. Jātisaṃsāroti hi phalūpacārena kāraṇaṃ vuttaṃ. Tañhi punappunaṃ uppattikāraṇavasena parikkhipitvā ṭhitattā “parikhā”ti vuccati santānassa [M 3.0028] parikkhipanato. Tenesa tassa saṃkiṇṇattā vikiṇṇattā sabbaso khittattā vināsitattā “saṃkiṇṇaparikho”ti vutto.

71-72. In the first sutta of the third chapter, regarding 'ignorance as the crossbar': here, 'ignorance' is the ignorance that is the root of the round of existence. Because it cannot be lifted up by many people, and because it is difficult to lift and obstructs entry to the door of Nibbāna, it is called a 'crossbar' since it is like a crossbar. Since this crossbar has been lifted up by him, he is called 'one with crossbar lifted.' 'Conducive to renewed existence' means having the nature of causing renewed existence, or meriting renewed existence as its fruit; the meaning is 'giving rise to renewed existence.' 'The round of birth': this is kamma-formations, the condition for the aggregates of renewed existence, which are so named on account of being born and wandering on. For 'the round of birth' is a term for the cause spoken of by way of a metaphor based on the result. Because it stands encircling the mental continuum as a cause of repeated arising, it is called a 'moat,' as it encloses the continuum. Since this moat has been filled in, scattered, completely cast out, and destroyed by him, he is called 'one with moat filled in.'

Taṇhāsaṅkhātanti [V 3.0027] ettha taṇhāti vaṭṭamūlikā taṇhā. Ayañhi gambhīrānugataṭṭhena “esikā”ti vuccati. Luñcitvā uddharitvā. Orambhāgiyānīti orambhāgajanakāni kāmabhave upapattipaccayāni kāmarāgasaṃyojanādīni. Etāni hi kavāṭaṃ viya nagaradvāraṃ cittaṃ pidahitvā ṭhitattā “aggaḷā”ti vuccanti. Tenesa tesaṃ niggatattā bhinnattā “niraggaḷo”ti vuttoti. Aggamaggena panno apacito mānaddhajo etassāti pannaddhajo. Pannabhāroti khandhabhārakilesabhāraabhisaṅkhārabhārā oropitā assāti pannabhāro. Visaṃyuttoti catūhi yogehi sabbakilesehi ca visaṃyutto. Asmimānoti rūpe asmīti māno, vedanāya, saññāya, saṅkhāresu, viññāṇe asmimāno. Ettha hi pañcapi khandhe avisesato “asmī”ti gahetvā pavattamāno asmimānoti adhippeto.

Regarding 'that designated as craving': here, 'craving' is the craving that is the root of the round of existence. This is called a 'pillar' because it is deep-rooted. 'Having uprooted and pulled it out.' 'Pertaining to the lower shore' means generating the lower part, being conditions for rebirth in the sensual realm, such as the fetter of sensual lust and so on. For these are called 'door-bolts' because they stand having closed off the mind like a door-leaf of a city gate. Therefore, because they have been removed and broken by him, he is called 'one without door-bolts.' 'One with banner lowered': one for whom the banner of conceit has been lowered and removed by the noble path. 'One who has laid down the burden': one for whom the burdens of the aggregates, the defilements, and the formations have been laid down. 'Disengaged': disengaged from the four yokes and from all defilements. 'The conceit "I am"': this is the conceit 'I am' in relation to form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness. Here, what is intended is the conceit 'I am' that proceeds by grasping the five aggregates without distinction as 'I am.'

Nagaradvārassa parissayapaṭibāhanatthañceva sodhanatthañca ubhosu passesu esikāthambhe nikhaṇitvā ṭhapetīti āha “nagaradvāre ussāpite esikāthambhe”ti. Pākāraviddhaṃsaneneva parikhābhūmisamakaraṇaṃ hotīti āha “pākāraṃ bhinditvā parikhaṃ vikiritvā”ti. “Eva”ntiādi upamāsaṃsandanaṃ. Santo saṃvijjamāno kāyo dhammasamūhoti sakkāyo, upādānakkhandhapañcakaṃ. Dvattiṃsakammakāraṇā dukkhakkhandhe āgatadukkhāni. Akkhirogasīsarogādayo. Aṭṭhanavuti rogā, rājabhayādīni pañcavīsatimahābhayāni. Dutiyaṃ uttānameva.

One digs in and sets up pillars on both sides of a city gate to ward off dangers and for purification; thus it says, 'pillars erected at the city gate.' By the very destruction of the wall the ground of the moat is leveled; thus it says, 'having broken the wall and scattered the moat.' 'Thus,' etc., is the connection of the simile. 'Existing body' (sakkāyo) means the existing, present body, which is a collection of phenomena, that is, the five aggregates subject to clinging. The thirty-two parts of the body are the cause for the sufferings that have come to be in this mass of suffering, such as diseases of the eye, diseases of the head, and so on. There are ninety-eight diseases, and the twenty-five great fears, such as fear of kings, and so on. The second sutta is of clear meaning.

Paṭhamacetovimuttiphalasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the First Sutta on the Fruit of the Liberation of Mind and others is concluded.

3-4. Paṭhamadhammavihārīsuttādivaṇṇanā

3–4. Commentary on the First Sutta on the Dhamma-Dweller and others

73-74. Tatiye niyakajjhatteti attano santāne. Mettāya upasaṃharaṇavasena hitaṃ esantena. Karuṇāya vasena anukampamānena. Pariggahetvāti parito gahetvā, pharitvāti attho. Pariccāti parito katvā, samantato pharitvā icceva attho. “Paṭiccā”tipi [M 3.0029] pāṭho. Mā pamajjitthāti “jhāyathā”ti vuttasamathavipassanānaṃ ananuyuñjanena aññena vā kenaci pamādakāraṇena mā pamādaṃ āpajjittha. Niyyānikasāsane akattabbakaraṇaṃ viya kattabbākaraṇampi pamādoti. Vipattikāleti sattaasappāyādivipattiyutte kāle. Sabbepi sāsane guṇā idheva saṅgahaṃ gacchantīti āha “jhāyatha mā pamādattha…pe… anusāsanī”ti. Catutthe natthi vattabbaṃ.

73–74. In the third, 'niyakajjhattaṃ' means within one's own continuum. By one seeking what is beneficial by way of applying loving-kindness. By one sympathizing by way of compassion. 'Pariggahetvā' means having encompassed all around; that is, having pervaded. 'Pariccā' means having made all around; that is, having pervaded completely. There is also the reading 'paṭiccā.' 'Mā pamajjittha' means: do not be negligent, either by not practicing the serenity and insight that have been mentioned with the word 'meditate,' or through any other cause of negligence. In the teaching that leads out, not doing what should be done is also negligence, just as doing what should not be done is. 'Vipattikāle' refers to a time of misfortune, such as a time connected with the seven kinds of unsuitability and so on. Because all the virtues in the teaching are included right here, he said: 'Meditate, do not be negligent... this is the instruction.' In the fourth, there is nothing to say.

Paṭhamadhammavihārīsuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the First Sutta on the Dhamma-Dweller and others is finished.

5. Paṭhamayodhājīvasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the First Sutta on the Warrior's Livelihood

75. Pañcame [V 3.0028] yujjhanaṃ yodho, so ājīvo etesanti yodhājīvā. Tenāha “yuddhūpajīvino”ti. Santhambhitvā ṭhātuṃ na sakkotīti baddho dhitisampanno ṭhātuṃ na sakkoti. Samāgateti sampatte. Byāpajjatīti vikāramāpajjati. Tenāha “pakatibhāvaṃ jahatī”ti.

75. In the fifth, one who fights is a warrior; that is their livelihood, thus they are 'warriors by livelihood.' Therefore it is said, 'those who live by war.' 'Unable to stand firm': he is paralyzed; though endowed with fortitude, he is unable to stand. 'Samāgate': having arrived. 'Byāpajjati': he undergoes a change. Therefore it is said, 'he abandons his natural state.'

Rajaggasminti paccatte bhummavacananti āha “kiṃ tassa puggalassa rajaggaṃ nāmā”ti. Vinibbeṭhetvāti gahitaggahaṇaṃ vissajjāpetvā. Mocetvāti sarīrato apanetvā.

Regarding 'rajaggasmiṃ': this is a locative of place in the individual sense. Thus it is said: 'What is the cloud of dust for that person?' 'Vinibbeṭhetvā': having made him release his firm grip. 'Mocetvā': having removed it from his body.

Paṭhamayodhājīvasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the First Yodhājīva Sutta is finished.

6. Dutiyayodhājīvasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Second Sutta on the Warrior's Livelihood

76. Chaṭṭhe cammanti iminā cammamayaṃ cammamiti sibbitaṃ, aññaṃ vā keṭakaphalakādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Dhanukalāpaṃ sannayhitvāti dhanuñceva tūṇirañca sannayhitvā sajjetvā. Dhanudaṇḍassa jiyāyattabhāvakaraṇādipi hi dhanuno sannayhanaṃ. Tenevāha “dhanuñca sarakalāpañca sannayhitvā”ti. Yuddhasannivesena ṭhitanti dvinnaṃ senānaṃ byūhanasaṃvidhānanayena kato yo sanniveso, tassa vasena ṭhitaṃ, senābyūhasaṃvidhānavasena sanniviṭṭhanti vuttaṃ hoti. Ussāhañca vāyāmañca karotīti yujjhanavasena ussāhaṃ vāyāmañca karoti. Pariyāpādentīti maraṇapariyantikaṃ aparaṃ pāpenti. Tenāha “pariyāpādayantī”ti, jīvitaṃ pariyāpādayanti maraṇaṃ paṭipajjāpentīti vuttaṃ hoti.

76. In the sixth, by 'camma' (hide) is included what is made of hide, stitched with hide, or other things such as a shield or board. 'Having armed himself with bow and quiver' means having armed himself with and prepared both the bow and the quiver. For preparing the bow also includes such things as making the bowstring dependent on the bow-staff. Therefore it is said, 'having armed himself with bow and quiver of arrows.' 'Standing in battle formation' means standing in the formation that is made according to the method of arranging the battle-array of two armies; that is to say, stationed according to the arrangement of the army's battle-array. 'He makes an effort and an exertion' means he makes an effort and an exertion for the sake of fighting. 'They bring to an end' means they bring another to the end which is death. Therefore it is said, 'they bring to an end'; that is to say, they bring life to an end, they make one meet with death.

Arakkhiteneva [M 3.0030] kāyenātiādīsu hatthapāde kīḷāpento gīvaṃ viparivattento kāyaṃ na rakkhati nāma. Nānappakāraṃ duṭṭhullaṃ karonto vācaṃ na rakkhati nāma. Kāmavitakkādayo vitakkento cittaṃ na rakkhati nāma. Anupaṭṭhitāya satiyāti kāyagatāya satiyā anupaṭṭhitāya. Rāgena anugatoti rāgena anupahato. Rāgaparetoti vā rāgena phuṭṭho phuṭṭhavisena viya sappena.

In the passage beginning with 'With an unguarded body,' etc.: one who plays with his hands and feet and twists his neck is called one who does not guard his body. One who utters various kinds of coarse speech is called one who does not guard his speech. One who thinks thoughts of sensual desire and so on is called one who does not guard his mind. 'With mindfulness unestablished' means with mindfulness directed to the body unestablished. 'Pursued by lust' means assailed by lust. Or 'overcome by lust' means touched by lust, like one touched by the venom of a snake.

Anudahanaṭṭhenāti anupāyappaṭipattiyā. Sampati āyatiñca mahābhitāpaṭṭhena. Anavatthitasabhāvatāya ittarapaccupaṭṭhānaṭṭhena. Muhuttaramaṇīyatāya tāvakālikaṭṭhena. Byattehi abhibhavanīyatāya [V 3.0029] sabbaṅgapaccaṅgapalibhañjanaṭṭhena. Chedanabhedanādiadhikaraṇabhāvena ugghaṭṭanasadisatāya adhikuṭṭanaṭṭhena. Avaṇe vaṇaṃ uppādetvā anto anupavisanasabhāvatāya vinivijjhanaṭṭhena. Diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyika anatthanimittatāya sāsaṅkasappaṭibhayaṭṭhena.

In the sense of burning: this is because of wrong practice. In the sense of great torment: this is both now and in the future. In the sense of being of trifling appearance: this is because of its unstable nature. In the sense of being temporary: this is because of its momentary delightfulness. In the sense of shattering all the limbs and members: this is because it is to be overcome by the expert. In the sense of crushing: this is because it is like a pounding, being the basis for cutting, breaking, etc. In the sense of piercing through: this is because of its nature of entering inside after creating a wound where there was no wound. In the sense of being perilous and fearful: this is because it is a sign of harm in the present life and in the future.

Dutiyayodhājīvasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Second Yodhājīva Sutta is finished.

7-8. Paṭhamaanāgatabhayasuttādivaṇṇanā

7–8. Commentary on the First Discourse on Future Dangers and so forth.

77-78. Sattame visesassa pattiyā visesassa pāpuṇanatthaṃ. Vīriyanti padhānavīriyaṃ. Taṃ pana caṅkamanavasena karaṇe “kāyika”ntipi vattabbataṃ labhatīti āha – “duvidhampī”ti. Satthakavātāti sandhibandhanāni kattariyā chindantā viya pavattavātā. Tenāha – “satthaṃ viyā”tiādi. Katakammehīti katacorakammehi. Te kira katakammā yaṃ nesaṃ devataṃ āyācitvā kammaṃ nipphannaṃ, tassa upakāratthāya manusse māretvā galalohitāni gaṇhanti. Te “aññesu manussesu māriyamānesu kolāhalaṃ uppajjissati, pabbajitaṃ pariyesanto nāma natthī”ti maññamānā bhikkhū gahetvā mārenti. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Akatakammehīti aṭavito gāmaṃ āgamanakāle kammanipphattatthaṃ puretaraṃ balikammaṃ kātukāmehi. Tenevāha – “corikaṃ katvā nikkhantā katakammā nāmā”tiādi. Aṭṭhame natthi vattabbaṃ.

77–78. In the seventh, 'for the attainment of distinction' means for the purpose of attaining distinction. 'Energy' means the energy of striving. But when this is done by way of walking meditation, it can also be called 'bodily'; thus it is said, 'of two kinds.' 'Knife-like winds' means winds that occur as if cutting the joints and ligaments with scissors. Therefore it is said: 'like a knife,' etc. 'By those who have done the deed' means by those who have committed theft. It is said that these 'doers of the deed,' having invoked a deity for their deed to succeed, kill people and collect their throat-blood as a service to that deity. Thinking, 'When other people are killed, an uproar will arise, but no one will search for an ascetic,' they seize and kill bhikkhus. This was said in reference to that. 'By those who have not done the deed' means by those who, when coming from the wilderness to a village, wish to perform a preliminary sacrificial offering for the accomplishment of their deed. Therefore it is said: 'Having committed a theft and departed, they are called "those who have done the deed,"' etc. In the eighth, there is nothing to say.

Paṭhamaanāgatabhayasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the First Discourse on Future Dangers and so forth is finished.

9. Tatiyaanāgatabhayasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Third Discourse on Future Dangers

79. Navame [M 3.0031] pāḷigambhīrāti (saṃ. ni. ṭī. 2.2.229) pāḷivasena gambhīrā agādhā dukkhogāhā sallasuttasadisā. Sallasuttañhi (su. ni. 579) “animittamanaññāta”ntiādinā pāḷivasena gambhīraṃ, na atthagambhīraṃ. Tathā hi tattha tā tā gāthā duviññeyyarūpā tiṭṭhanti. Duviññeyyañhi ñāṇena dukkhogāhanti katvā “gambhīra”nti vuccati. Pubbāparaṃpettha kāsañci gāthānaṃ duviññeyyatāya dukkhogāhameva, tasmā pāḷivasena gambhīraṃ. Atthagambhīrāti atthavasena gambhīrā mahāvedallasuttasadisā, mahāvedallasuttassa (ma. ni. 1.449 ādayo) atthavasena gambhīratā pākaṭāyeva. Lokaṃ uttaratīti lokuttaro, so atthabhūto etesaṃ atthīti lokuttarā. Tenāha – “lokuttaradhammadīpakā”ti. Suññatāpaṭisaṃyuttāti sattasuññadhammappakāsakā[V 3.0030]. Tenāha “khandhadhātuāyatanapaccayākārappaṭisaṃyuttā”ti. Uggahetabbaṃ pariyāpuṇitabbanti ca liṅgavacanavipallāsena vuttanti āha “uggahetabbe ceva vaḷañjetabbe cā”ti. Kavino kammaṃ kavitā. Yassa pana yaṃ kammaṃ, taṃ tena katanti vuccatīti āha “kavitāti kavīhi katā”ti. Kāveyyanti kabyaṃ, kabyanti ca kavinā vuttanti attho. Tenāha “tasseva vevacana”nti. Cittakkharāti citrākāraakkharā. Itaraṃ tasseva vevacanaṃ. Sāsanato bahiddhā ṭhitāti na sāsanāvacarā. Bāhirakasāvakehīti “buddhā”ti appaññātānaṃ yesaṃ kesañci sāvakehi. Sussūsissantīti akkharacittatāya ceva sarasampattiyā ca attamanā hutvā sāmaṇeradaharabhikkhumātugāmamahāgahapatikādayo “esa dhammakathiko”ti sannipatitvā sotukāmā bhavissanti.

79. In the ninth, 'profound in the text' (Saṃ. Ni. Ṭī. 2.2.229) means profound, unfathomable, and difficult to penetrate by way of the wording, like the Arrow Sutta. For the Arrow Sutta (Snp 3.8) is profound in its wording—as in the phrase “unindicated and unknown,” etc.—but not profound in meaning. For there, certain verses are difficult to understand. Because what is difficult to understand is difficult to penetrate with knowledge, it is called “profound.” Here too, some verses are difficult to penetrate because they are hard to understand; therefore, they are profound in wording. 'Profound in meaning' means profound by way of the meaning, like the Greater Discourse of Questions and Answers (MN 43), whose profundity of meaning is evident. 'Supramundane': one who transcends the world is `lokuttara`. Because this is their real meaning, they are `lokuttarā` (supramundane). Therefore it is said: “illuminators of the supramundane Dhamma.” 'Connected with emptiness' means they are declarers of the Dhamma that is empty of a self. Hence it is said: “connected with the aggregates, elements, sense bases, and conditional relations.” 'To be learned and to be mastered' is said with an interchange of gender and number; thus it states: “to be learned and to be practiced.” Poetry is the work of a poet. And whatever work is done by someone is said to be done by them; therefore it is said: 'poetry' means 'composed by poets.' 'Poetic compositions' (`kāveyya`) means poetry (`kabya`), and `kabya` means what is spoken by a poet. Hence it is said: “it is a synonym for that.” 'Ornamented letters' means letters of a picturesque form. The other term is a synonym for that. 'Standing outside the Dispensation' means not belonging to the Dispensation. 'By the disciples of outsiders' means by the disciples of some who are not known as “Buddhas.” 'They will be eager to listen' means that, on account of the ornamented letters and the excellence of the melody, they will be pleased—novices, young monks, women, great householders, and others—and will gather, thinking, “This is a Dhamma speaker,” and will become desirous of listening.

Tatiyaanāgatabhayasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Third Discourse on Future Dangers is concluded.

10. Catutthaanāgatabhayasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Fourth Discourse on Future Dangers

80. Dasame pañcavidhena saṃsaggenāti “savanasaṃsaggo, dassanasaṃsaggo, samullāpasaṃsaggo, sambhogasaṃsaggo, kāyasaṃsaggo”ti evaṃ vuttena pañcavidhena saṃsaggena. Saṃsajjati etenāti saṃsaggo, rāgo. Savanahetuko, savanavasena vā pavatto saṃsaggo savanasaṃsaggo. Esa nayo [M 3.0032] sesesupi. Kāyasaṃsaggo pana kāyaparāmāso. Tesu parehi vā kathiyamānaṃ rūpādisampattiṃ attanā vā sitalapitagītasaddaṃ suṇantassa sotaviññāṇavīthivasena uppanno rāgo savanasaṃsaggo nāma. Visabhāgarūpaṃ olokentassa pana cakkhuviññāṇavīthivasena uppanno rāgo dassanasaṃsaggo nāma. Aññamaññaālāpasallāpavasena uppannarāgo samullāpasaṃsaggo nāma. Bhikkhuno bhikkhuniyā santakaṃ, bhikkhuniyā bhikkhussa santakaṃ gahetvā paribhogakaraṇavasena uppannarāgo sambhogasaṃsaggo nāma. Hatthaggāhādivasena uppanno rāgo kāyasaṃsaggo nāma.

80. In the tenth, 'through fivefold association' means through the fivefold association stated as: “association through hearing, association through seeing, association through conversation, association through mutual use, and association through bodily contact.” Association (`saṃsaggo`): one becomes attached by means of this, thus it is association; it is lust (`rāga`). Association that has hearing as its cause, or that proceeds by way of hearing, is association through hearing. This method applies to the rest as well. Association through bodily contact, however, is physical touching. Among these, the lust that arises through the process of ear-consciousness for one who hears others speaking of the perfection of forms and so on, or for one who hears cool sounds, passionate songs, or music, is called association through hearing. The lust that arises through the process of eye-consciousness for one who gazes at an unsuitable form is called association through seeing. The lust that arises by way of mutual talk and conversation is called association through conversation. The lust that arises by way of a bhikkhu taking and using what belongs to a bhikkhunī, or a bhikkhunī taking and using what belongs to a bhikkhu, is called association through mutual use. The lust that arises by way of acts such as holding hands is called association through bodily contact.

Anekavihitanti annasannidhipānasannidhivatthasannidhiyānasannidhisayanasannidhigandhasannidhi- āmisasannidhivasena anekappakāraṃ. Sannidhikatassāti etena “sannidhikāraparibhoga”nti (dha. sa. tikamātikā 10) ettha kāra-saddassa kammatthataṃ dasseti. Yathā vā “ācayaṃ gāmino”ti vattabbe anunāsikalopena “ācayagāmino”ti niddeso kato, evaṃ “sannidhikāraṃ paribhoga”nti vattabbe anunāsikalopena “sannidhikāraparibhoga”nti vuttaṃ, sannidhiṃ katvā paribhoganti attho.

‘Of various kinds’ means of many types: by way of storing food, storing drink, storing robes, storing vehicles, storing bedding, storing scents, and storing material things. ‘Of what has been stored’: by this, in the phrase ‘use involving storing’ (`sannidhikāraparibhoga`), it shows that the word `kāra` is in the objective sense. Just as when `ācayaṃ gāmino` (going to accumulation) should be said, it is stated as `ācayagāmino` by elision of the nasal, so too, when `sannidhikāraṃ paribhoga` should be said, it is stated as `sannidhikāraparibhoga`. The meaning is ‘use after having made a store’ (`sannidhiṃ katvā paribhoga`).

“Sannidhikatassa [V 3.0031] paribhoga”nti ettha (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.12) pana duvidhā kathā vinayavasena sallekhavasena ca. Vinayavasena tāva yaṃ kiñci annaṃ ajja paṭiggahitaṃ aparajju sannidhikāraṃ hoti, tassa paribhoge pācittiyaṃ. Attanā laddhaṃ pana sāmaṇerānaṃ datvā tehi laddhaṃ vā pāpetvā dutiyadivase bhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati, sallekho pana na hoti. Pānasannidhimhipi eseva nayo. Vatthasannidhimhi anadhiṭṭhitāvikappitaṃ sannidhi ca hoti, sallekhañca kopeti. Ayaṃ nippariyāyakathā. Pariyāyato pana ticīvarasantuṭṭhena bhavitabbaṃ, catutthaṃ labhitvā aññassa dātabbaṃ. Sace yassa kassaci dātuṃ na sakkoti, yassa pana dātukāmo hoti, so uddesatthāya vā paripucchatthāya vā gato, āgatamatte dātabbaṃ, adātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Cīvare pana appahonte, satiyā vā paccāsāya anuññātakālaṃ ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭati. Sūcisuttacīvarakārakānaṃ alābhe tatopi vinayakammaṃ katvā ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭati “imasmiṃ jiṇṇe puna īdisaṃ kuto labhissāmī”ti pana ṭhapetuṃ na vaṭṭati, sannidhi ca hoti, sallekhañca kopeti.

Here, concerning ‘the use of what is stored’ (Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 1.12), the discussion is twofold: from the perspective of the Vinaya and from the perspective of the practice of effacement (`sallekha`). First, from the perspective of the Vinaya: any food received today becomes a stored item if kept until the next day, and using it entails an offense of expiation (`pācittiya`). However, if one gives what one has obtained to novices and then receives it back from them, it is allowable to eat it on the second day, but this is not the practice of effacement. This same method applies to the storing of drinks. In the case of storing robes, a robe that is not determined for use or shared with another is both a stored item and it violates the practice of effacement. This is the direct explanation. Indirectly, however, one should be content with the three robes. If a fourth is obtained, it should be given to another. If one cannot give it to just anyone, but wishes to give it to someone who has gone away for the purpose of recitation or inquiry, it should be given to him as soon as he returns; it is not allowable not to give it. But if one's robe is insufficient, it is allowable to set another aside for the permitted time with mindfulness or in expectation. If a needle, thread, and robe-makers are not available, it is also allowable to set it aside after performing a formal act of the Vinaya. But it is not allowable to set it aside thinking, “When this one is worn out, from where will I get another like it?” This is storing, and it violates the practice of effacement.

Yānasannidhimhi [M 3.0033] yānaṃ nāma vayhaṃ ratho sakaṭaṃ sandamānikā pāṭaṅkīti. Na panetaṃ pabbajitassa yānaṃ, upāhanaṃ pana yānaṃ. Ekabhikkhussa hi eko araññavāsatthāya, eko dhotapādakatthāyāti ukkaṃsato dve upāhanasaṅghāṭakā vaṭṭanti, tatiyaṃ labhitvā aññassa dātabbo. “Imasmiṃ jiṇṇe aññaṃ kuto labhissāmī”ti ṭhapetuṃ na vaṭṭati, sannidhi ca hoti, sallekhañca kopeti. Sayanasannidhimhi sayananti mañco. Ekassa bhikkhuno eko sayanagabbhe, eko divāṭṭhāneti ukkaṃsato dve mañcā vaṭṭanti. Tato uttariṃ labhitvā aññassa bhikkhuno, gaṇassa vā dātabbo, adātuṃ na vaṭṭati, sannidhi ceva hoti, sallekho ca kuppati. Gandhasannidhimhi bhikkhuno kaṇḍukacchuchavidosādiābādhe sati gandhā vaṭṭanti. Gandhatthikena gandhañca āharāpetvā tasmiṃ roge vūpasante aññesaṃ vā ābādhikānaṃ dātabbaṃ, dvāre pañcaṅguligharadhūpanādīsu vā upanetabbaṃ. “Puna roge sati bhavissatī”ti ṭhapetuṃ na vaṭṭati, gandhasannidhi ca hoti, sallekhañca kopeti.

In the case of storing vehicles: a vehicle is a palanquin, a chariot, a cart, a sedan chair, or a covered litter. But these are not a vehicle for one who has gone forth; for him, footwear is the vehicle. For one bhikkhu, at most two pairs of footwear are allowable: one for living in the forest and one for when his feet are washed. If a third is obtained, it must be given to another. It is not allowable to keep it thinking, “When this one is worn out, from where will I get another?” This is storing, and it violates the practice of effacement. In the case of storing bedding: bedding is a couch. For one bhikkhu, at most two couches are allowable: one in his sleeping quarters and one in his day-quarters. If more than that are obtained, they must be given to another bhikkhu or to the Sangha. It is not allowable not to give them, for this is storing and it violates the practice of effacement. In the case of storing scents: scents are allowable for a bhikkhu when he has an illness such as an itch, scabies, or a skin disease. One who needs scents may have them brought, but when the illness has subsided, they should be given to other ill persons or used for incense at the door, for five-finger handprint offerings, or for fumigating dwellings. It is not allowable to keep them thinking, “It will be there if I get sick again.” This is storing scents, and it violates the practice of effacement.

Āmisanti vuttāvasesaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ – idhekacco bhikkhu “tathārūpe kāle upakārāya bhavissantī”ti tilataṇḍulamuggamāsanāḷikeraloṇamacchasappitelakulālabhājanādīni āharāpetvā ṭhapeti. So vassakāle kālasseva sāmaṇerehi yāguṃ pacāpetvā paribhuñjitvā “sāmaṇera udakakaddame dukkhaṃ gāmaṃ pavisituṃ, gaccha asukakulaṃ gantvā mayhaṃ vihāre nisinnabhāvaṃ ārocehi, asukakulato dadhiādīni āharā”ti peseti. Bhikkhūhi “kiṃ, bhante[V 3.0032], gāmaṃ pavisissāmā”ti vuttepi “duppaveso, āvuso, idāni gāmo”ti vadati. Te “hotu, bhante, acchatha tumhe, mayaṃ bhikkhaṃ pariyesitvā āharissāmā”ti gacchanti. Atha sāmaṇero dadhiādīni āharitvā bhattañca byañjanañca sampādetvā upaneti, taṃ bhuñjantasseva upaṭṭhākā bhattaṃ pahiṇanti, tatopi manāpamanāpaṃ bhuñjati. Atha bhikkhū piṇḍapātaṃ gahetvā āgacchanti, tatopi manāpamanāpaṃ bhuñjatiyeva. Evaṃ catumāsampi vītināmeti. Ayaṃ vuccati bhikkhu muṇḍakuṭumbikajīvikaṃ jīvati, na samaṇajīvikanti. Evarūpo āmisasannidhi nāma hoti. Bhikkhuno pana vasanaṭṭhāne ekā taṇḍulanāḷi eko guḷapiṇḍo [M 3.0034] kuḍuvamattaṃ sappīti ettakaṃ nidhetuṃ vaṭṭati akāle sampattacorānaṃ atthāya. Te hi ettakaṃ āmisapaṭisanthāraṃ alabhantā jīvitā voropeyyuṃ, tasmā sace hi ettakaṃ natthi, āharāpetvāpi ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭati. Aphāsukakāle ca yadettha kappiyaṃ, taṃ attanāpi paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati. Kappiyakuṭiyaṃ pana bahuṃ ṭhapentassapi sannidhi nāma natthi.

Concerning material things, the remainder should be understood as stated. For instance: Here, a certain bhikkhu, thinking, 'They will be useful at such-and-such a time,' has things like sesame seeds, rice, mung beans, māsa beans, coconuts, salt, fish, ghee, oil, and clay pots brought and stored. When the rains retreat arrives, early in the morning, he has the novices prepare rice-gruel, consumes it, and then sends a novice off, saying: 'Novice, it is difficult to enter the village through the water and mud. Go to such-and-such a family, inform them that I am sitting in my dwelling, and bring back curds and so on from such-and-such a family.' When the bhikkhus say, 'Venerable sir, shall we enter the village?' he replies, 'The village is difficult to enter now, friends.' They say, 'Very well, venerable sir, you stay here. We will go and search for almsfood and bring it back.' Then the novice brings back curds and so on, prepares boiled rice and curry, and presents them. While he is eating, his supporters send more food, and he eats what is agreeable from that. Then the bhikkhus return with almsfood, and from that too he eats what is agreeable. Thus he passes the four months. This is called a bhikkhu who lives the life of a shaven-headed householder, not the life of a recluse. Such is called the storing of material things. However, for a bhikkhu in his dwelling place, it is permissible to store a single nāḷi of rice, a lump of jaggery, and a kuḍuva-measure of ghee—for the sake of thieves who may arrive at an inopportune time. For if they do not obtain even this much material hospitality, they might deprive him of life. Therefore, if even this much is not available, it is permissible to have it brought and stored. And in times of discomfort, whatever is allowable there may also be consumed by oneself. But even if one stores much in an allowable store-room, it does not constitute storing.

Catutthaanāgatabhayasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Fourth Discourse on Future Dangers is finished.

Yodhājīvavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Yodhājīva Chapter is finished.

(9) 4. Theravaggo

(9) 4. The Chapter on the Elders

1-2. Rajanīyasuttādivaṇṇanā

1-2. Commentary on the Discourses Beginning with the Rajanīya Sutta

81-82. Catutthassa paṭhamaṃ suviññeyyameva. Dutiye guṇamakkhanāya pavattopi attano kārakaṃ gūthena paharantaṃ gūtho viya paṭhamataraṃ makkhetīti makkho, so etassa atthīti makkhī. Paḷāsatīti paḷāso, parassa guṇe ḍaṃsitvā viya apanetīti attho. So etassa atthīti paḷāsī. Paḷāsī puggalo hi dutiyassa dhuraṃ na deti, sampasāretvā tiṭṭhati. Tenāha “yugaggāhalakkhaṇena paḷāsena samannāgato”ti.

81-82. The first part of the fourth is very easy to understand. In the second, `makkho` (contempt) is so called because, though it proceeds from denigrating another's virtues, it sullies the perpetrator first, just as dung sullies the one who throws it. One who has this is called a `makkhī`. `Paḷāso` is rivalry; the meaning is that one eliminates another's virtues as if by biting them. One who has this is called a `paḷāsī`. A rivalrous person does not take up another's yoke but stands aloof. Hence it is said: 'endowed with rivalry, characterized by not taking up the yoke.'

Rajanīyasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the discourses beginning with the Rajanīya Sutta is finished.

3. Kuhakasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Kuhaka Sutta

83. Tatiye [V 3.0033] tīhi kuhanavatthūhīti sāmantajappanairiyāpathasannissitapaccayappaṭisevanabhedato tippabhedehi kuhanavatthūhi. Tividhena kuhanavatthunā lokaṃ kuhayati vimhāpayati “aho acchariyapuriso”ti attani paresaṃ vimhayaṃ uppādetīti kuhako. Lābhasakkāratthiko hutvā lapati attānaṃ dāyakaṃ vā ukkhipitvā yathā so kiñci dadāti, evaṃ ukkācetvā kathetīti lapako. Nimittaṃ sīlaṃ tassāti nemittiko, nimittena vā carati, nimittaṃ vā karotīti nemittiko. Nimittanti ca paresaṃ paccayadānasaññuppādakaṃ kāyavacīkammaṃ vuccati[M 3.0035]. Nippeso sīlamassāti nippesiko. Nippisatīti vā nippeso, nippesoyeva nippesiko. Nippesoti ca saṭhapuriso viya lābhasakkāratthaṃ akkosanuppaṇḍanaparapiṭṭhimaṃsikatādi.

83. In the third, 'by three grounds of deceit' means by the three kinds of grounds of deceit, distinguished as hinting, deportment, and the use of requisites. By means of the threefold ground of deceit, one deceives and astonishes the world, making others marvel, thinking, 'Oh, what a wonderful person!'—thus, one is a `kuhaka` (deceiver). Being desirous of gain and honor, one `lapati` (chatters), exalting oneself or a donor so that they give something; one who speaks in this extolling way is a `lapaka` (chatterer). One whose practice is making signs (`nimitta`) is a `nemittika`; or one who acts by means of signs or makes signs is a `nemittika`. A 'sign' refers to a bodily or verbal action that generates in others the idea of giving requisites. One whose practice is belittling (`nippesa`) is a `nippesika`; or one who belittles is a `nippesika`. `Nippesa` refers to things like insulting, ridiculing, and backbiting, done by a crafty person for the sake of gain and honor.

Kuhakasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Kuhaka Sutta is finished.

6-7. Paṭisambhidāppattasuttādivaṇṇanā

6-7. Commentary on the Discourses Beginning with the Paṭisambhidāppatta Sutta

86-87. Chaṭṭhe paṭisambhidāsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva. Uccāvacānīti uccanīcāni. Tenāha “mahantakhuddakānī”ti. Kiṃkaraṇīyānīti “kiṃ karomī”ti evaṃ vatvā kattabbakammāni. Tattha uccakammāni nāma cīvarassa karaṇaṃ, rajanaṃ, cetiye sudhākammaṃ, uposathāgāracetiyagharabodhigharesu kattabbakammanti evamādi. Avacakammaṃ nāma pādadhovanamakkhanādi khuddakakammaṃ. Tatrupāyāsāti tatrupagamaniyā, tatra tatra mahante khuddake ca kamme sādhanavasena upagacchantiyāti attho. Tassa tassa kammassa nipphādane samatthāyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tatrupāyāyāti vā tatra tatra kamme sādhetabbe upāyabhūtāya. Alaṃ kātunti kātuṃ samattho hoti. Alaṃ saṃvidhātunti vicāretuṃ samattho. Sattamaṃ uttānameva.

86-87. In the sixth, what should be said regarding the analytical knowledges has already been stated above. `Uccāvacāni` means high and low. Hence it is said, 'great and small.' `Kiṃkaraṇīyāni` refers to tasks to be done after saying, 'What shall I do?' Here, high tasks include making robes, dyeing, plastering work at a cetiya, and tasks to be done in the Uposatha hall, cetiya house, or Bodhi-tree house, and so on. Low tasks include minor duties like washing feet, anointing, and the like. `Tatrupāyā` means that by which one approaches; the meaning is that one approaches for the sake of accomplishing both great and small tasks here and there. It is said that one is capable of completing any given task. Alternatively, `tatrupāyāya` means being a means to accomplish tasks wherever they need to be done. `Alaṃ kātuṃ` means one is capable of doing. `Alaṃ saṃvidhātuṃ` means one is capable of managing. The seventh is self-evident.

Paṭisambhidāppattasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the discourses beginning with the Paṭisambhidāppatta Sutta is finished.

8. Therasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Sutta on the Elder

88. Aṭṭhame [V 3.0034] thirabhāvappattoti sāsane thirabhāvaṃ anivattibhāvaṃ pattho. Pabbajito hutvā bahū rattiyo jānātīti rattaññū. Tenāha “pabbajitadivasato paṭṭhāyā”tiādi. Pākaṭoti ayathābhūtaguṇehi ceva yathābhūtaguṇehi ca samuggato. Yaso etassa atthīti yasassī, yasaṃ sito nissito vā yasassī. Tenāha “yasanissito”ti. Asataṃ asādhūnaṃ dhammā asaddhammā, asantā vā asundarā gārayhā lāmakā dhammāti asaddhammā. Vipariyāyena saddhammā veditabbā.

88. In the eighth sutta: ‘One who has attained a stable state’ means one who has attained a stable state, an irreversible state, in the Dispensation. ‘One of long standing’ is one who, having gone forth, knows many nights. Hence it is said: ‘from the day of going forth,’ and so on. ‘Manifest’ means one who has become prominent both through qualities that are not as they really are and through qualities that are as they really are. ‘Famous’ is one who has fame, or one who depends on or relies on fame is ‘famous.’ Hence it is said: ‘reliant on fame.’ The dhammas of the bad, the unvirtuous, are the bad Dhamma; or dhammas that are non-existent, not good, blameworthy, and inferior are the bad Dhamma. The good Dhamma is to be understood in the opposite way.

Therasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Sutta on the Elder is finished.

9. Paṭhamasekhasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the First Sutta on the Trainee

89. Navame [M 3.0036] āramitabbaṭṭhena kammaṃ ārāmo etassāti kammārāmo, tassa bhāvo kammārāmatā. Tattha kammanti itikattabbaṃ kammaṃ vuccati. Seyyathidaṃ – cīvaravicāraṇaṃ cīvarakammakaraṇaṃ upatthambhanaṃ pattatthavikaaṃsabaddhakakāyabandhanadhammakaraṇaādhārakapādakathalikasammajjaniādīnaṃ karaṇanti. Ekacco hi etāni karonto sakaladivasaṃ etāneva karoti, taṃ sandhāyesa paṭikkhepo. Yo pana etesaṃ karaṇavelāyameva tāni karoti, uddesavelāya uddesaṃ gaṇhāti, sajjhāyavelāya sajjhāyati, cetiyaṅgaṇavattavelāya cetiyaṅgaṇavattaṃ karoti, manasikāravelāya manasikāraṃ karoti, na so kammārāmo nāma. Bhassārāmatāti ettha yo itthivaṇṇapurisavaṇṇādivasena ālāpasallāpaṃ karontoyeva divasañca rattiñca vītināmeti, evarūpo bhasse pariyantakārī na hoti, ayaṃ bhassārāmo nāma. Yo pana rattimpi divasampi dhammaṃ katheti, pañhaṃ vissajjeti, ayaṃ appabhasso bhasse pariyantakārīyeva. Kasmā? “Sannipatitānaṃ vo, bhikkhave, dvayaṃ karaṇīyaṃ dhammī vā kathā, ariyo vā tuṇhībhāvo”ti (ma. ni. 1.273; udā. 12, 28, 29) vuttattā.

89. In the ninth: ‘Delighting in work.’ Work is his delight, thus he is one who delights in work; the state of that is delight in work. Here, ‘work’ refers to work that is to be done, such as inspecting robes, making robes, providing supports, making bowl-bags, shoulder straps, waistbands, water-strainers, stands, footstools, brooms, and so on. For a certain person, doing these tasks occupies his entire day; this is what is being censured. But one who does these tasks only at the time for them, who takes up a recitation at the time for recitation, who recites at the time for recitation, who performs the duties in the shrine-courtyard at the time for those duties, and who practices contemplation at the time for contemplation—such a person is not called one who delights in work. Regarding ‘delight in talk’: here, one who spends day and night engaged in talk and conversation about the praise of women, the praise of men, and so on, without setting a limit to such talk, is called one who delights in talk. But one who speaks on the Dhamma or answers questions day and night indeed sets a limit to talk. Why? Because it is said: ‘When you have gathered together, monks, there are two things to be done: either talk on the Dhamma or noble silence’ (MN 26; Ud 2.2).

Niddārāmatāti ettha yo gacchantopi nisinnopi nipannopi thinamiddhābhibhūto niddāyatiyeva, ayaṃ niddārāmo nāma. Yassa pana karajakāye gelaññena cittaṃ bhavaṅge otarati, nāyaṃ niddārāmo. Tenevāha – “abhijānāmi kho panāhaṃ, aggivessana, gimhānaṃ pacchime māse pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātappaṭikkanto catugguṇaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ paññāpetvā dakkhiṇena passena sato sampajāno niddaṃ okkamitā”ti (ma. ni. 1.387). Saṅgaṇikārāmatāti ettha [V 3.0035] yo ekassa dutiyo, dvinnaṃ tatiyo, tiṇṇaṃ catutthoti evaṃ saṃsaṭṭhova viharati, ekako assādaṃ na labhati, ayaṃ saṅgaṇikārāmo. Yo pana catūsu iriyāpathesu ekakova assādaṃ labhati, nāyaṃ saṅgaṇikārāmo veditabbo. Sekhānaṃ paṭiladdhaguṇassa parihānāsambhavato “upariguṇehī”tiādi vuttaṃ.

‘Delighting in sleep’: Here, one who, whether walking, sitting, or lying down, is overcome by sloth and torpor and just keeps sleeping—this is called one who delights in sleep. But for one whose mind sinks into the life-continuum due to an illness in his physical body, this is not one who delights in sleep. Thus it is said: ‘I recall, Aggivessana, in the last month of the hot season, after returning from the alms-round after the meal, having folded my outer robe in four, I lay down on my right side, entering sleep mindful and clearly comprehending’ (MN 36). ‘Delighting in company’: Here, one who lives always in association with others—as a second to one, a third to two, a fourth to three—and finds no gratification in being alone, this is one who delights in company. But one who finds gratification in being alone in the four postures is not to be regarded as one who delights in company. Since it is impossible for a trainee to decline from a quality that has been attained, the phrase ‘from higher qualities,’ and so on, is stated.

Paṭhamasekhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the First Sutta on the Trainee is finished.

10. Dutiyasekhasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Explanation of the Second Sutta on the Trainee

90. Dasame [M 3.0037] atipātovāti sabbarattiṃ niddāyitvā balavapaccūse koṭisammuñjaniyā thokaṃ sammajjitvā mukhaṃ dhovitvā yāgubhikkhatthāya pātova pavisati. Taṃ atikkamitvāti gihisaṃsaggavasena kālaṃ vītināmento majjhanhikasamayaṃ atikkamitvā pakkamati. Pātoyeva hi gāmaṃ pavisitvā yāguṃ ādāya āsanasālaṃ gantvā pivitvā ekasmiṃ ṭhāne nipanno niddāyitvā manussānaṃ bhojanavelāya “paṇītabhikkhaṃ labhissāmī”ti upakaṭṭhe majjhanhike uṭṭhāya dhammakaraṇena udakaṃ gahetvā akkhīni puñchitvā piṇḍāya caritvā yāvadatthaṃ bhuñjitvā gihisaṃsaṭṭho kālaṃ vītināmetvā majjhanhe vītivatte paṭikkamati.

90. In the tenth: ‘He enters too early.’ Having slept the whole night, at the crack of dawn he sweeps a little with the tip of a broom, washes his face, and enters the village very early for rice gruel. ‘He returns too late.’ He spends time in association with householders and departs after midday has passed. For having entered the village very early in the morning and obtained rice gruel, he goes to the meeting hall, drinks it, lies down in one spot and sleeps. Then, at the time of the people’s meal, close to midday, he gets up, thinking, ‘I will get choice almsfood.’ Having taken water with a water-strainer and wiped his eyes, he wanders for almsfood, eats as much as he wants, spends time in association with householders, and returns when midday has passed.

Appicchakathāti, “āvuso, atricchatā pāpicchatāti ime dhammā pahātabbā”ti tesu ādīnavaṃ dassetvā “evarūpaṃ appicchataṃ samādāya vattitabba”ntiādinayappavattā kathā. Tīhi vivekehīti kāyaviveko, cittaviveko, upadhivivekoti imehi tīhi vivekehi. Tattha eko gacchati, eko tiṭṭhati, eko nisīdati, eko seyyaṃ kappeti, eko gāmaṃ piṇḍāya pavisati, eko paṭikkamati, eko caṅkamaṃ adhiṭṭhāti, eko carati, eko viharatīti ayaṃ kāyaviveko nāma. Aṭṭha samāpattiyo pana cittaviveko nāma. Nibbānaṃ upadhiviveko nāma. Vuttampi hetaṃ – “kāyaviveko ca vivekaṭṭhakāyānaṃ nekkhammābhiratānaṃ, cittaviveko ca parisuddhacittānaṃ paramavodānappattānaṃ, upadhiviveko ca nirupadhīnaṃ puggalānaṃ visaṅkhāragatāna”nti (mahāni. 57). Duvidhaṃ vīriyanti kāyikaṃ, cetasikañca vīriyaṃ. Sīlanti catupārisuddhisīlaṃ. Samādhinti vipassanāpādakā aṭṭha samāpattiyo. Vimuttikathāti vā ariyaphalaṃ ārabbha pavattā kathā. Sesaṃ uttānameva.

‘Talk on fewness of wishes’: this is talk that proceeds by showing the danger in them, saying: ‘Friend, excessive desire and evil wishes are to be abandoned,’ and advising: ‘One should live having undertaken such fewness of wishes,’ and so on. ‘By the three seclusions’ means by these three seclusions: bodily seclusion, mental seclusion, and seclusion from the substrata. Herein, one goes alone, stands alone, sits alone, lies down alone, enters the village for alms alone, returns alone, undertakes walking meditation alone, walks alone, and dwells alone—this is called bodily seclusion. The eight attainments are called mental seclusion. Nibbāna is called seclusion from the substrata. And this is said: ‘Bodily seclusion for those who delight in renunciation with a secluded body; mental seclusion for those with a purified mind who have attained supreme purification; seclusion from the substrata for those without substrata who have gone to the unconditioned’ (Mahāni 57). ‘Twofold energy’ means bodily and mental energy. ‘Virtue’ means the virtue of fourfold purification. ‘Concentration’ means the eight attainments that are the basis for insight. ‘Talk on liberation’ is talk that proceeds concerning the noble fruit. The rest is self-evident.

Dutiyasekhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Second Sutta on the Trainee is finished.

Theravaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Chapter on the Elders is finished.

(10) 5. Kakudhavaggo

(10) 5. The Kakudha Chapter

1-10. Paṭhamasampadāsuttādivaṇṇanā

1-10. Commentary on the First Accomplishments Sutta, etc.

91-100. Pañcamassa [V 3.0036][M 3.0038] paṭhame dutiye ca natthi vattabbaṃ. Tatiye ājānanato aññā, uparimaggapaññā heṭṭhimamaggena ñātapariññāya eva jānanato. Tassā pana phalabhāvato maggaphalapaññā taṃsahagatā sammāsaṅkappādayo ca idha “aññā”ti vuttā. Aññāya byākaraṇāni aññābyākaraṇāni. Tenevāha “aññābyākaraṇānīti arahattabyākaraṇānī”ti. Adhigatamānenāti appatte pattasaññī, anadhigate adhigatasaññī hutvā adhigataṃ mayāti mānena. Catutthādīni uttānatthāneva.

91-100. In the fifth, there is nothing to be said concerning the first and second. In the third, aññā is distinct from ājānana, for it is the wisdom of the higher path known by means of the full understanding through the lower path. But because it has the nature of fruition, the wisdom of the path and fruition, and right intention and so forth associated with it, are here called 'aññā.' Aññāya byākaraṇāni becomes aññābyākaraṇāni. Therefore it is said: '“Declarations of final knowledge” means declarations of arahantship.' 'With the conceit of attainment' means with the conceit 'I have attained,' on the part of one who perceives as attained what has not been attained, and as realized what has not been realized. The fourth and so on are clear in meaning.

Paṭhamasampadāsuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the First Accomplishments Sutta and so on is concluded.

Kakudhavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Kakudha Chapter is concluded.

Dutiyapaṇṇāsakaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Second Fifty is concluded.

3. Tatiyapaṇṇāsakaṃ

3. The Third Fifty

(11) 1. Phāsuvihāravaggo

(11) 1. The Chapter on Comfortable Abiding

1-4. Sārajjasuttādivaṇṇanā

1-4. Commentary on the Timidity Sutta and so on

101-4. Tatiyassa [V 3.0037][M 3.0039] paṭhame natthi vattabbaṃ. Dutiye piṇḍapātādiatthāya upasaṅkamituṃ yuttaṭṭhānaṃ gocaro, vesiyā gocaro assāti vesiyāgocaro, mittasanthavavasena upasaṅkamitabbaṭṭhānanti attho. Vesiyā nāma rūpūpajīviniyo, tā mittasanthavavasena na upasaṅkamitabbā samaṇabhāvassa antarāyakarattā, parisuddhāsayassapi garahāhetuto, tasmā dakkhiṇādānavasena satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā upasaṅkamitabbaṃ. Vidhavā vuccanti matapatikā, pavutthapatikā vā. Thullakumāriyoti mahallikā anividdhā kumāriyo. Paṇḍakāti napuṃsakā. Te hi ussannakilesā avūpasantapariḷāhā lokāmisanissitakathābahulā, tasmā na upasaṅkamitabbā. Bhikkhuniyo nāma ussannabrahmacariyā. Tathā bhikkhūpi. Aññamaññaṃ visabhāgavatthubhāvato santhavavasena upasaṅkamane katipāheneva brahmacariyantarāyo siyā, tasmā na upasaṅkamitabbā, gilānapucchanādivasena upasaṅkamane satokārinā bhavitabbaṃ. Tatiyacatutthāni uttānatthāneva.

101-4. In the third, there is nothing to be said about the first. In the second, gocara means a suitable place to approach for almsfood and so on. Vesiyāgocara means 'a prostitute's resort,' that is, a place to be approached by way of friendly association. Prostitutes (vesiyā) are those who live by their beauty; they should not be approached by way of friendly association because it endangers the recluse's life and invites blame even for one of pure intention. Therefore, one should approach them mindfully, as recipients of a gift. 'Widows' (vidhavā) refers to those whose husbands are dead or have gone away. 'Thullakumāriyo' means older, unmarried women. 'Paṇḍakā' are eunuchs. They are full of defilements, with unallayed passions, and engrossed in worldly talk, so they should not be approached. 'Bhikkhunīs' are those for whom the holy life is paramount; likewise, bhikkhus too. Because they are of a different nature, if they associate through familiarity, in just a few days an obstacle to the holy life could arise; therefore, they should not be approached. When one approaches for such reasons as inquiring after the sick, one must be mindful. The third and fourth are clear in meaning.

Sārajjasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Timidity Sutta and so on is concluded.

5. Phāsuvihārasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Comfortable Abiding Sutta

105. Pañcame mettā etassa atthīti mettaṃ, taṃsamuṭṭhānaṃ kāyakammaṃ mettaṃ kāyakammaṃ. Esa nayo sesadvayepi. Āvīti pakāsanaṃ. Pakāsabhāvo cettha yaṃ uddissa taṃ kāyakammaṃ karīyati, tassa sammukhabhāvatoti āha “sammukhā”ti. Rahoti appakāsaṃ. Appakāsatā ca yaṃ uddissa taṃ kāyakammaṃ karīyati, tassa apaccakkhabhāvatoti āha “parammukhā”ti. Imāni mettakāyakammādīni bhikkhūnaṃ vasena āgatāni tesaṃ seṭṭhaparisabhāvato, gihīsupi labbhantiyeva. Bhikkhūnañhi mettacittena ābhisamācārikapūraṇaṃ mettaṃ kāyakammaṃ nāma[M 3.0040]. Gihīnaṃ cetiyavandanatthāya [V 3.0038] bodhivandanatthāya saṅghanimantanatthāya gamanaṃ gāmaṃ piṇḍāya paviṭṭhe bhikkhū disvā paccuggamanaṃ pattappaṭiggahaṇaṃ āsanapaññāpanaṃ anugamananti evamādikaṃ mettaṃ kāyakammaṃ nāma. Bhikkhūnaṃ mettacittena ācārapaññattisikkhāpanaṃ kammaṭṭhānakathanaṃ dhammadesanā tepiṭakampi buddhavacanaṃ mettaṃ vacīkammaṃ nāma. Gihīnaṃ “cetiyavandanāya gacchāma, bodhivandanāya gacchāma, dhammassavanaṃ karissāma, dīpamālaṃ pupphapūjaṃ karissāma, tīṇi sucaritāni samādāya vattissāma, salākabhattādīni dassāma, vassāvāsikaṃ dassāma, ajja saṅghassa cattāro paccaye dassāma, saṅghaṃ nimantetvā khādanīyādīni saṃvidahatha, āsanāni paññapetha, pānīyaṃ upaṭṭhapetha, saṅghaṃ paccuggantvā ānetha, paññattāsane nisīdāpetha, chandajātā ussāhajātā veyyāvaccaṃ karothā”tiādikathanakāle mettaṃ vacīkammaṃ nāma. Bhikkhūnaṃ pātova uṭṭhāya sarīrappaṭijagganaṃ katvā cetiyaṅgaṇaṃ gantvā vattādīni katvā vivittasenāsane nisīditvā “imasmiṃ vihāre bhikkhū sukhī hontu averā abyāpajjā”ti cintanaṃ mettaṃ manokammaṃ nāma, gihīnaṃ “ayyā sukhī hontu averā abyāpajjā”ti cintanaṃ mettaṃ manokammaṃ nāma.

105. In the fifth, mettaṃ means 'one who has loving-kindness' (mettā etassa atthīti); the bodily action originating from that is 'bodily action of loving-kindness.' This same method applies to the other two. Āvī means 'openly.' Here the state of being open is because the bodily action is performed in the presence of the one for whom it is intended; thus it is said, 'in person' (sammukhā). Raho means 'in secret.' The state of being secret is because the bodily action is performed when the one for whom it is intended is not present; thus it is said, 'in absence' (parammukhā). These bodily actions of loving-kindness and so on are given with reference to bhikkhus because they are the foremost assembly, but they are certainly found among householders too. For bhikkhus, the fulfillment of the code of conduct with a mind of loving-kindness is called bodily action of loving-kindness. For householders, going to pay homage at a cetiya, to pay homage at a Bodhi tree, or to invite the Sangha; seeing bhikkhus who have entered the village for alms and going out to meet them, taking their bowls, preparing seats, and accompanying them—such things are called bodily action of loving-kindness. For bhikkhus, instructing in the rules of conduct with a mind of loving-kindness, giving a talk on a meditation subject, teaching the Dhamma, and even the Tipiṭaka, the word of the Buddha, are called verbal action of loving-kindness. For householders, when they say such things as: 'Let us go to pay homage at the cetiya, let us go to pay homage at the Bodhi tree, let us listen to the Dhamma, let us make offerings of lamps and flowers, let us undertake and observe the three kinds of good conduct, let us give ticket-food and so on, let us give the rains-residence requisite, today let us give the four requisites to the Sangha, invite the Sangha and prepare food and so on, prepare the seats, set out drinking water, go to meet the Sangha and bring them here, have them sit on the prepared seats, serve them with gladness and enthusiasm'—this is called verbal action of loving-kindness. For bhikkhus, to rise early in the morning, attend to the body, go to the cetiya-terrace, perform one's duties, sit in a secluded lodging, and think, 'May the bhikkhus in this monastery be happy, free from enmity, free from affliction'—this is called mental action of loving-kindness. For householders, to think, 'May the venerable sirs be happy, free from enmity, free from affliction'—this is called mental action of loving-kindness.
