Tattha navakānaṃ cīvarakammādīsu sahāyabhāvagamanaṃ sammukhā kāyakammaṃ nāma, therānaṃ pana pādadhovanasiñcanabījanadānādibhedampi sabbaṃ sāmīcikammaṃ sammukhā kāyakammaṃ nāma, ubhayehipi dunnikkhittānaṃ dārubhaṇḍādīnaṃ tesu avaññaṃ akatvā attanā dunnikkhittānaṃ viya paṭisāmanaṃ parammukhā mettaṃ kāyakammaṃ nāma. “Devatthero tissatthero”ti vuttaṃ evaṃ paggayhavacanaṃ sammukhā mettaṃ vacīkammaṃ nāma, vihāre asantaṃ pana paṭipucchantassa “kuhiṃ amhākaṃ devatthero, kuhiṃ amhākaṃ tissatthero, kadā nu kho āgamissatī”ti evaṃ piyavacanaṃ parammukhā mettaṃ vacīkammaṃ nāma. Mettāsinehasiniddhāni pana nayanāni ummīletvā pasannena mukhena olokanaṃ sammukhā mettaṃ manokammaṃ nāma, “devatthero tissatthero arogo hotu abyāpajjo”ti samannāharaṇaṃ parammukhā mettaṃ manokammaṃ nāma. Kāmañcettha mettāsinehasiniddhānaṃ nayanānaṃ ummīlanaṃ, pasannena mukhena olokanañca mettaṃ kāyakammameva. Yassa pana cittassa vasena nayanānaṃ mettāsinehasiniddhatā, mukhassa ca pasannatā, taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “mettaṃ manokammaṃ nāmā”ti. Samādhisaṃvattanappayojanāni samādhisaṃvattanikāni.

Therein, assisting junior monks in robe-making and other tasks is called bodily action in person. For the elder monks, all respectful services such as washing their feet, sprinkling water, offering a fan, and the like are called bodily action in person. For both, putting away wooden articles and so on that have been badly placed, without showing contempt for them, arranging them as if they were one’s own misplaced items, is called bodily action of loving-kindness in absence. Saying words of praise such as 'Venerable Deva, Venerable Tissa' is called verbal action of loving-kindness in person. When an elder is absent from the monastery, inquiring with kind words such as, 'Where is our Venerable Deva? Where is our Venerable Tissa? When will he return?' is called verbal action of loving-kindness in absence. Opening one's eyes, which are tender with loving-kindness and affection, and looking with a serene face is called mental action of loving-kindness in person. Reflecting, 'May Venerable Deva and Venerable Tissa be healthy and free from affliction,' is called mental action of loving-kindness in absence. Now, the opening of eyes tender with loving-kindness and affection and looking with a serene face are in fact bodily action of loving-kindness. However, it is with reference to the mind by means of which the eyes become tender with loving-kindness and the face becomes serene that this is called 'mental action of loving-kindness.' Those things that serve the purpose of leading to concentration are 'conducive to concentration.'

Samānasīlataṃ [M 3.0041] gatoti tesu tesu disābhāgesu viharantehi bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ samānasīlataṃ gato. Yāyanti yā ayaṃ mayhañceva tumhākañca paccakkhabhūtā. Diṭṭhīti sammādiṭṭhi. Ariyāti niddosā. Niyyātīti vaṭṭadukkhato nissarati niggacchati. Sayaṃ niyyantīyeva hi taṃsamaṅgipuggalaṃ vaṭṭadukkhato niyyāpetīti vuccati. Yā satthu anusiṭṭhi, taṃ karotīti takkaro[V 3.0039], tassa, yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipajjakassāti attho. Dukkhakkhayāyāti sabbadukkhakkhayatthaṃ. Diṭṭhisāmaññagatoti samānadiṭṭhibhāvaṃ upagato.

'He has attained to similarity in virtue' means he has attained to similarity in virtue with the bhikkhus dwelling in the various regions. Yāyanti refers to that which is directly evident to both me and you. 'Diṭṭhi' means right view. 'Ariyā' means faultless. 'Niyyāti' means it leads out, it departs from the suffering of the round of existence. For while leading out itself, it leads the person endowed with it out of the suffering of the round—thus it is said. 'One who does that' (takkaro) means one who does what the Teacher instructs; that is, one who practices in accordance with the instruction. 'For the destruction of suffering' (dukkhakkhayāya) means for the purpose of the destruction of all suffering. 'Has attained to commonality of view' (diṭṭhisāmaññagato) means he has attained a state of shared view.

Phāsuvihārasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Sutta on Comfortable Abiding is concluded.

6-10. Ānandasuttādivaṇṇanā

6-10. Commentary on the Ānanda Sutta and Others

106-110. Chaṭṭhe adhisīleti nimittatthe bhummaṃ, sīlanimittaṃ na upavadati na nindatīti attho. Attani kamme ca anu anu pekkhati sīlenāti attānupekkhī. Sattamādīni uttānatthāneva.

106-110. In the sixth sutta, the word `adhisīle` is a locative used in the sense of a reason. The meaning is that one does not disparage or censure on account of virtue. `Attānupekkhī` means one who repeatedly observes oneself and one's actions by means of virtue. The seventh and the following suttas are of obvious meaning.

Ānandasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Ānanda Sutta and others is concluded.

Phāsuvihāravaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Chapter on Comfortable Abiding is concluded.

(12) 2. Andhakavindavaggo

(12) 2. The Chapter on Andhakavinda

1-4. Kulūpakasuttādivaṇṇanā

1-4. Commentary on the Kulūpaka Sutta and Others

111-114. Dutiyassa paṭhame asanthavesu kulesu vissāso etassāti asanthavavissāsī. Anissaro hutvā vikappeti saṃvidahati sīlenāti anissaravikappī. Vissaṭṭhāni visuṃ khittāni bhedena avatthitāni kulāni ghaṭanatthāya upasevati sīlenāti vissaṭṭhupasevī. Dutiyādīni uttānatthāneva.

111-114. In the first sutta of the second chapter: `asanthavavissāsī` is one who has trust in unfamiliar families. `Anissaravikappī` is one who, being without authority, plans or arranges by means of virtue. `Vissaṭṭhupasevī` is one who, by means of virtue, associates with families that are scattered, cast apart, and established in division, for the purpose of uniting them. The second and the following suttas are of obvious meaning.

Kulūpakasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Kulūpaka Sutta and others is concluded.

5-13. Maccharinīsuttādivaṇṇanā

5-13. Commentary on the Maccharinī Sutta and Others

115-123. Pañcame [V 3.0040][M 3.0042] āvāsamacchariyādīni pañca idha bhikkhuniyā vasena āgatāni, bhikkhussa vasenapi tāni veditabbāni. Āvāsamacchariyena hi samannāgato bhikkhu āgantukaṃ disvā “ettha cetiyassa vā saṅghassa vā parikkhāro ṭhapito”tiādīni vatvā saṅghikaāvāsaṃ na deti. Kulamacchariyena samannāgato bhikkhu tehi tehi kāraṇehi ādīnavaṃ dassetvā attano upaṭṭhāke kule aññesaṃ pavesampi nivāreti. Lābhamacchariyena samannāgato saṅghikampi lābhaṃ maccharāyanto yathā aññe na labhanti, evaṃ karoti attanā visamanissitatāya balavanissitatāya ca. Vaṇṇamacchariyena samannāgato attano vaṇṇaṃ vaṇṇeti, paresaṃ vaṇṇe “kiṃ vaṇṇo eso”ti taṃ taṃ dosaṃ vadati. Vaṇṇoti cettha sarīravaṇṇopi, guṇavaṇṇopi veditabbo.

115-123. In the fifth sutta, the five kinds of stinginess beginning with stinginess about dwellings are presented here in connection with a bhikkhunī, but they are to be understood as applying to a bhikkhu as well. For a bhikkhu endowed with stinginess about dwellings, on seeing a newcomer, says such things as, 'A requisite for the cetiya or for the Sangha has been placed here,' and does not give a dwelling belonging to the Sangha. A bhikkhu endowed with stinginess about families, by pointing out dangers for various reasons, prevents others from even entering the families that support him. A bhikkhu endowed with stinginess about gains, being stingy even with gains belonging to the Sangha, acts so that others do not receive them, because of his own unfair and powerful patronage. A bhikkhu endowed with stinginess about good repute praises his own good repute, and concerning the good repute of others, he points out this or that fault, saying, 'What kind of repute is that?' Here, `vaṇṇa` should be understood as both physical appearance and good qualities.

Dhammamacchariyena samannāgato – “imaṃ dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇitvā eso maṃ abhibhavissatī”ti aññassa na deti. Yo pana – “ayaṃ imaṃ dhammaṃ uggahetvā aññathā atthaṃ viparivattetvā nāsessatī”ti dhammanuggahena vā – “ayaṃ imaṃ dhammaṃ uggahetvā uddhato unnaḷo avūpasantacitto apuññaṃ pasavissatī”ti puggalānuggahena vā na deti, na taṃ macchariyaṃ. Dhammoti cettha pariyattidhammo adhippeto. Paṭivedhadhammo hi ariyānaṃyeva hoti, te ca naṃ na maccharāyanti macchariyassa sabbaso pahīnattāti tassa asambhavo eva. Tattha āvāsamacchariyena lohagehe paccati, yakkho vā peto vā hutvā tasseva āvāsassa saṅkāraṃ sīsena ukkhipitvā carati. Kulamacchariyena appabhogo hoti. Lābhamacchariyena gūthaniraye nibbattati, saṅghassa vā gaṇassa vā lābhaṃ maccharāyitvā puggalikaparibhogena vā paribhuñjitvā yakkho vā peto vā mahāajagaro vā hutvā nibbattati. Vaṇṇamacchariyena bhavesu nibbattassa vaṇṇo nāma na hoti. Dhammamacchariyena kukkuḷaniraye nibbattati. Chaṭṭhādīni uttānatthāneva.

One endowed with stinginess regarding the Dhamma does not give it to another, thinking: 'Having mastered this Dhamma, this person will surpass me.' But if one does not give it out of concern for the Dhamma, thinking: 'Having learned this Dhamma, this person will distort its meaning and ruin it'; or if one does not give it out of concern for the person, thinking: 'Having learned this Dhamma, this person will become arrogant, conceited, with an unpacified mind, and will generate demerit'—that is not stinginess. Here, 'Dhamma' is intended as the Dhamma of learning. The Dhamma of penetration belongs only to the noble ones, and they are not stingy with it since they have completely abandoned stinginess; thus for them it is impossible. In this regard, one who is stingy about dwellings is tormented in a copper house, or becomes a yakkha or a peta and wanders about carrying the rubbish of that very dwelling on one's head. One who is stingy about families has few possessions. One who is stingy about gains is reborn in the dung hell; or, having been stingy with gains meant for the Sangha or a group and having used them for personal enjoyment, one is reborn as a yakkha, a peta, or a great python. One who is stingy about good repute, when reborn in future existences, has no physical beauty. One who is stingy about the Dhamma is reborn in the hell of hot embers. The sixth and the following are of obvious meaning.

Maccharinīsuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Maccharinī Sutta and so on is concluded.

Andhakavindavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Andhakavinda Vagga is concluded.

(13) 3. The Gilāna Vagga

124-130. Tatiyo [V 3.0041][M 3.0043] vaggo uttānatthoyeva.

124-130. The third vagga is of obvious meaning.

(14) 4. Rājavaggo

(14) 4. The Rāja Vagga

1. Paṭhamacakkānuvattanasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the First Cakkānuvattana Sutta

131. Catutthassa paṭhame atthaññūti hitaññū. Hitapariyāyo hettha attha-saddo “attattho parattho”tiādīsu (mahāni. 69; cūḷani. mogharājamāṇavapucchāniddeso 85; paṭi. ma. 3.5) viya. Yasmā cesa paresaṃ hitaṃ jānanto te attani rañjeti, tasmā vuttaṃ “rañjituṃ jānātī”ti. Daṇḍeti aparādhānurūpe daṇḍane. Balamhīti balakāye. Pañca attheti attattho, parattho, ubhayattho, diṭṭhadhammiko attho, samparāyiko atthoti evaṃ pañcappabhede atthe. Cattāro dhammeti catusaccadhamme, kāmarūpārūpalokuttarabhede vā cattāro dhamme. Paṭiggahaṇaparibhogamattaññutāya eva pariyesanavissajjanamattaññutāpi bodhitā hontīti “paṭiggahaṇaparibhogamattaṃ jānāti”icceva vuttaṃ.

131. In the first sutta of the fourth vagga: `atthaññū` (one who knows the goal) means `hitaññū` (one who knows what is beneficial). Here the word `attha` is a synonym for `hita` (benefit), as in such passages as 'one's own benefit, another's benefit,' etc. (Mahāni. 69; Cūḷani. Mogharājamāṇavapucchāniddeso 85; Paṭi. Ma. 3.5). And since this one, knowing what is beneficial for others, makes them devoted to him, it is therefore said: 'he knows how to make them devoted.' `Daṇḍeti` means he imposes punishment appropriate to the offense. `Balamhi` refers to the army. `Pañca atthe` means in the five kinds of benefit: one's own benefit, another's benefit, the benefit of both, the benefit in the present life, and the benefit in the lives to come. `Cattāro dhamme` means the four Noble Truths, or the four dhammas divided into the sensual-sphere, the fine-material-sphere, the immaterial-sphere, and the supramundane. By knowing the measure in receiving and consuming, knowledge of the measure in seeking and giving up is also implied; thus it is just said: 'one knows the measure in receiving and consuming.'

Uttarati atikkamati, abhibhavatīti vā uttaraṃ, natthi ettha uttaranti anuttaraṃ. Anatisayaṃ, appaṭibhāgaṃ vā anekāsu devamanussaparisāsu anekasatakkhattuṃ tesaṃ ariyasaccappaṭivedhasampādanavasena pavattā bhagavato dhammadesanā dhammacakkaṃ. Apica sabbapaṭhamaṃ aññātakoṇḍaññappamukhāya aṭṭhārasaparisagaṇāya brahmakoṭiyā catusaccassa paṭivedhavidhāyinī yā dhammadesanā, tassā sātisayā dhammacakkasamaññā. Tattha satipaṭṭhānātidhammo eva pavattanaṭṭhena cakkanti dhammacakkaṃ. Cakkanti vā āṇā dhammato anapetattā, dhammañca taṃ cakkañcāti dhammacakkaṃ. Dhammena ñāyena cakkantipi dhammacakkaṃ. Yathāha “dhammañca pavatteti cakkañcāti dhammacakkaṃ, cakkañca pavatteti dhammañcāti dhammacakkaṃ, dhammena pavattetīti dhammacakka”ntiādi (paṭi. ma. 2.40-41). Appaṭivattiyanti dhammissarassa bhagavato sammāsambuddhassa dhammacakkassa [V 3.0042] anuttarabhāvato appaṭisedhanīyaṃ. Kehi pana appaṭivattiyanti āha – “samaṇena vā”tiādi. Tattha samaṇenāti pabbajjaṃ upagatena. Brāhmaṇenāti jātibrāhmaṇena. Sāsanaparamatthasamaṇabrāhmaṇānañhi paṭilomacittaṃyeva natthi. Devenāti kāmāvacaradevena. Kenacīti yena [M 3.0044] kenaci avasiṭṭhapārisajjena. Ettāvatā aṭṭhannampi parisānaṃ anavasesapariyādānaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Lokasminti sattaloke.

It surpasses (`uttarati`), goes beyond (`atikkamati`), or overcomes (`abhibhavati`); thus it is `uttaraṃ` (supreme). There is nothing higher than it; thus it is `anuttaraṃ` (unsurpassed). The Wheel of Dhamma (`dhammacakka`) is the Blessed One's teaching of the Dhamma, which is without superior and without rival, set in motion in numerous assemblies of devas and humans hundreds of times for the purpose of effecting their penetration of the noble truths. Moreover, the teaching of the Dhamma that first of all brought about the penetration of the four truths for the eighteen crores of brahmās headed by Aññāta Koṇḍañña has the pre-eminent designation 'Wheel of Dhamma.' Therein, the Dhamma of the foundations of mindfulness and so on is the `dhammacakka` in the sense of setting in motion. Or, `cakka` means command. Because it does not deviate from the Dhamma, and it is both Dhamma and a wheel, it is the `dhammacakka`. It is also the `dhammacakka` because it is a wheel set in motion by means of the Dhamma, by the right method. As it is said: 'He sets in motion the Dhamma and the wheel, thus it is the `dhammacakka`; he sets in motion the wheel and the Dhamma, thus it is the `dhammacakka`; he sets it in motion by means of the Dhamma, thus it is the `dhammacakka`' and so on (Paṭis. Ma. 2.40-41). `Appaṭivattiyaṃ` (that cannot be rolled back) means it cannot be stopped because of the unsurpassed nature of the Wheel of Dhamma of the Blessed One, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, the Lord of the Dhamma. But by whom can it not be rolled back? He says: 'by a recluse,' and so on. Here, `samaṇena` means by one who has gone forth. `Brāhmaṇena` means by a brahmin by birth. For recluses and brahmins in the ultimate sense of the teaching, there is no opposing thought at all. `Devena` means by a deva of the sensual sphere. `Kenaci` means by any remaining member of an assembly. By this, the exhaustive inclusion of all eight assemblies should be understood. `Lokasmiṃ` means in the world of beings.

Paṭhamacakkānuvattanasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the First Cakkānuvattana Sutta is concluded.

2. Dutiyacakkānuvattanasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Second Cakkānuvattana Sutta

132. Dutiye cakkavattivattanti dasavidhaṃ, dvādasavidhaṃ vā cakkavattibhāvāvahaṃ vattaṃ. Tattha antojanasmiṃ balakāye dhammikāyeva rakkhāvaraṇaguttiyā saṃvidhānaṃ, khattiyesu, anuyantesu, brāhmaṇagahapatikesu, negamajānapadesu, samaṇabrāhmaṇesu, migapakkhīsu, adhammikapaṭikkhepo, adhanānaṃ dhanānuppadānaṃ, samaṇabrāhmaṇe upasaṅkamitvā pañhapucchananti idaṃ dasavidhaṃ cakkavattivattaṃ. Idameva ca gahapatike pakkhijāte ca visuṃ katvā gahaṇavasena dvādasavidhaṃ. Pitarā pavattitameva anuppavattetīti dasavidhaṃ vā dvādasavidhaṃ vā cakkavattivattaṃ pūretvā nisinnassa puttassa aññaṃ pātubhavati, so taṃ pavatteti. Ratanamayattā pana sadisaṭṭhena tadevetanti katvā “pitarā pavattita”nti vuttaṃ. Yasmā vā so “appossukko, tvaṃ deva, hohi, ahamanusāsissāmī”ti āha. Tasmā pitarā pavattitaṃ āṇācakkaṃ anuppavatteti nāmāti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Yañhi attano puññānubhāvasiddhaṃ cakkaratanaṃ, taṃ nippariyāyato tena pavattitaṃ nāma, netaranti paṭhamanayo vutto. Yasmā pavattitasseva anuvattanaṃ, paṭhamanayo ca taṃsadise tabbohāravasena vuttoti taṃ anādiyitvā dutiyanayo vutto.

132. In the second sutta, the duty of a wheel-turning monarch is tenfold or twelvefold, the duty that brings about the state of a wheel-turning monarch. Among these, the tenfold duty of a wheel-turning monarch is this: providing righteous protection, shelter, and security for one's own people and the army, for the nobles, for vassals, for brahmins and householders, for town and country folk, for ascetics and brahmins, and for beasts and birds; the warding off of unrighteousness; the giving of wealth to the poor; and approaching ascetics and brahmins to ask questions. This very duty becomes twelvefold by taking householders and the bird species separately. For the son who has fulfilled the tenfold or twelvefold duty of a wheel-turning monarch, continuing what was set in motion by his father, another wheel-treasure appears, and he sets it in motion. But because it is made of jewel, it is the very same in the sense of being similar; having considered this, it is said 'set in motion by his father.' Or, because he said: 'Be without anxiety, Your Majesty, I will rule,' therefore he is said to continue the wheel of command set in motion by his father; this is the meaning to be understood here. For the wheel-treasure accomplished through the power of his own merit is, without qualification, set in motion by him, not by another. This is the first method of explanation. Because it is the continuation of what was already set in motion, and the first method was stated by way of conventional usage regarding something similar to that, having disregarded that, the second method is stated.

Dutiyacakkānuvattanasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Second Cakkānuvattana Sutta is concluded.

4. Yassaṃdisaṃsuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Yassaṃdisaṃ Sutta

134. Catutthe “ubhato sujāto”ti ettake vutte yehi kehici dvīhi bhāgehi sujātatā paññāpeyya, sujāta-saddo ca “sujāto cārudassano”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.399; su. ni. 553; theragā. 818) ārohasampattipariyāyoti [V 3.0043] jātivasena [M 3.0045] sujātataṃ vibhāvetuṃ “mātito ca pitito cā”ti vuttaṃ. Anorasaputtavasenapi loke mātupitusamaññā dissati, idha pana sā orasaputtavasena icchitāti dassetuṃ “saṃsuddhaggahaṇiko”ti vuttaṃ. Gabbhaṃ gaṇhāti dhāretīti gahaṇī, gabbhāsayasaññito mātukucchippadeso. Tenāha “saṃsuddhāya mātukucchiyā samannāgato”ti. Yathābhuttassa āhārassa vipācanavasena gaṇhanato achaḍḍanato gahaṇī, tejodhātu. Pitā ca mātā ca pitaro. Pitūnaṃ pitaro pitāmahā. Tesaṃ yugo pitāmahayugo, tasmā yāva sattamā pitāmahayugā, pitāmahadvandāti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Evañhi pitāmahaggahaṇeneva mātāmahopi gahitoti so aṭṭhakathāyaṃ visuṃ na uddhato. Yuga-saddo cettha ekasesanayena daṭṭhabbo “yugo ca yugo ca yugo”ti. Evañhi tattha tattha dvinnaṃ gahitameva hoti. Tenāha “tato uddhaṃ sabbepi pubbapurisā pitāmahaggahaṇeneva gahitā”ti. Purisaggahaṇañcettha ukkaṭṭhaniddesavasena katanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evañhi “mātito”ti pāḷivacanaṃ samatthitaṃ hoti.

134. In the fourth, when only 'well-born on both sides' is said, some might define well-bornness by any two aspects. And the word 'sujāta' (well-born) in phrases like 'well-born and lovely to behold' is a synonym for the attainment of stature. To clarify well-bornness by way of birth, 'from the mother’s side and the father’s side' is stated. Even in the world, the terms 'mother' and 'father' are used with respect to non-biological offspring, but here it is desired to show that it refers specifically to biological offspring; hence 'of pure conception' is stated. 'It receives and holds the embryo, thus it is the receptacle,' meaning the region of the mother’s womb, known as the womb-chamber. Therefore, it is said, 'endowed with a pure mother’s womb.' Because it receives the eaten food by way of digesting it and not rejecting it, the gahaṇī is the fire element. 'Father and mother are parents.' 'The parents of parents are grandparents.' Their pair is the grandparental pair; thus, 'up to the seventh grandparental pair' means pairs of grandparents—this is how the meaning should be understood here. Thus, by the term 'paternal grandfather,' the maternal grandfather is also included, which is why it is not separately mentioned in the commentary. The word 'yuga' (pair) here should be understood by the principle of ellipsis, as in 'a pair and a pair is a pair.' Thus, in each case, two are taken together. Therefore, it is said, 'from there upwards, all ancestors are included by the term for grandparents.' And here, the term 'purisa' (person) should be understood as used by way of an eminent specification. Thus, the Pāli phrase 'from the mother's side' is supported.

Akkhittoti appattakkhepo. Anavakkhittoti sampattavivādādīsu na avakkhitto na chaḍḍito. Jātivādenāti hetumhi karaṇavacananti dassetuṃ “kena kāraṇenā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ettha ca “ubhato…pe… pitāmahayugā”ti etena khattiyassa yonidosābhāvo dassito saṃsuddhaggahaṇikabhāvakittanato. “Akkhitto”ti iminā kiriyāparādhābhāvo. Kiriyāparādhena hi sattā khepaṃ pāpuṇanti. “Anupakkuṭṭho”ti iminā ayuttasaṃsaggābhāvo. Ayuttasaṃsaggañhi paṭicca sattā akkosaṃ labhanti.

'Uncensured' means one who has not been censured. 'Not despised' means not despised or rejected in any disputes that have arisen. 'On account of birth' is an instrumental of cause; to show this, 'for what reason?' and so on is said. Here, by the passage 'on both sides... up to the seventh grandparental pair,' the absence of any flaw in the khattiya's origin is shown through the proclamation of his pure conception. By 'uncensured,' the absence of transgression in action is indicated, for it is because of transgression in action that beings incur censure. By 'irreproachable,' the absence of unsuitable association is indicated, for it is on account of unsuitable association that beings receive abuse.

Aḍḍhatā nāma vibhavasampannatā, sā taṃ taṃ upādāyupādāya vuccatīti āha “yo koci attano santakena vibhavena aḍḍho hotī”ti. Tathā mahaddhanatāpīti taṃ ukkaṃsagataṃ dassetuṃ “mahatā aparimāṇasaṅkhena dhanena samannāgato”ti vuttaṃ. Bhuñjitabbato paribhuñjitabbato visesato kāmā bhogā nāmāti āha “pañcakāmaguṇavasenā”ti. Koṭṭhaṃ vuccati dhaññassa āvasanaṭṭhānaṃ, koṭṭhabhūtaṃ agāraṃ koṭṭhāgāraṃ. Tenāha “dhaññena ca paripuṇṇakoṭṭhāgāro”ti. Evaṃ sāragabbhaṃ koso, dhaññapariṭṭhapanaṭṭhānañca koṭṭhāgāranti dassetvā idāni tato aññathā taṃ dassetuṃ “atha vā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha yathā asino tikkhabhāvaparihārako [M 3.0046] paṭicchado “koso”ti vuccati. Evaṃ rañño tikkhabhāvaparihāraṃ katvā caturaṅginī senā kosoti āha “catubbidho koso hatthī assā rathā pattī”ti. Vatthakoṭṭhāgāraggahaṇeneva sabbassapi bhaṇḍaṭṭhapanaṭṭhānassa gahitattā “tividhaṃ koṭṭhāgāra”nti vuttaṃ.

Wealthiness is accomplishment in possessions. It is spoken of with reference to this or that; thus it is said: 'Whoever is wealthy by means of their own possessions.' Similarly with great wealth. To show this in its supreme degree, it is said: 'endowed with great, immeasurable wealth.' Because they are to be enjoyed and partaken of, sensual pleasures are specifically called enjoyments; thus it is said: 'by way of the five strands of sensual pleasure.' A koṭṭha is a dwelling place for grain; a house that is a koṭṭha is a koṭṭhāgāra, a granary. Hence it is said: 'with granaries full of grain.' Having thus shown that a treasury (koso) is a storeroom for valuables and a granary is a place for storing grain, now to show it differently, 'or else...' is said. Therein, just as the cover that protects from the sharpness of a sword is called a sheath (koso), so the four-divisioned army, protecting the king from harm, is called a treasury (koso); thus it is said: 'the fourfold treasury: elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry.' Because by the mention of the storeroom for goods, all places for storing goods are included, 'three kinds of storehouses' is said.

Yassā [V 3.0044] paññāya vasena puriso “paṇḍito”ti vuccati, taṃ paṇḍiccanti āha “paṇḍiccena samannāgato”ti. Taṃtaṃitikattabbatāsu chekabhāvo byattabhāvo veyyattiyaṃ. Sammohaṃ hiṃsati vidhamatīti medhā, sā etassa atthīti medhāvī. Ṭhāne ṭhāne uppatti etissā atthīti ṭhānuppatti, ṭhānaso uppajjanapaññā. Vaḍḍhiattheti vaḍḍhisaṅkhāte atthe.

The wisdom by means of which a person is called 'wise' is wisdom (paṇḍicca); thus it is said 'endowed with wisdom.' Competence (veyyattiyaṃ) is skillfulness and expertise in the various things that should be done. Because it injures and dispels delusion, it is called intelligence (medhā); one who possesses it is intelligent (medhāvī). Because its arising occurs in the right situation, it is called timely ingenuity (ṭhānuppatti), that is, wisdom that arises according to the situation. 'In the sense of growth' means in the sense reckoned as growth.

Yassaṃdisaṃsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Yassaṃdisaṃ Sutta is finished.

5-9. Patthanāsuttādivaṇṇanā

5-9. The Commentary on the Patthanasutta and Others

135-9. Pañcame hatthisminti hatthisippe. Hatthīti hi hatthivisayattā hatthisannissitattā ca hatthisippaṃ gahitaṃ. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Vayatīti vayo, sobhanesu katthaci apakkhalanto avitthāyanto tāni sandhāretuṃ sakkotīti attho. Na vayo avayo, tāni atthato saddato ca sandhāretuṃ na sakkoti. Avayo na hotīti anavayo. Dve paṭisedhā pakatiṃ gamentīti āha “anavayoti samattho”ti. Chaṭṭhādīni uttānatthāneva.

135-9. In the fifth, hatthismiṃ means in the elephant-craft. For hatthī is taken as elephant-craft because it is the domain of elephants and is dependent on elephants. This same method applies to the remaining terms. Vayati means vayo; the meaning is that one is able to retain them in excellent matters without stumbling or becoming confused. Na vayo is avayo; one is unable to retain them in terms of meaning and sound. Not being avayo is anavayo. Two negations lead to the original state, thus it is said: “Anavayo means capable.” The sixth and following have a plain meaning.

Patthanāsuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Patthanasutta and Others is finished.

10. Sotasuttavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Sotasutta

140. Dasame tibbānanti tikkhānaṃ. Kharānanti kakkasānaṃ. Kaṭukānanti dāruṇānaṃ. Asātānanti nasātānaṃ appiyānaṃ. Na tāsu mano appeti, na tā manaṃ appāyanti vaḍḍhentīti amanāpā.

140. In the tenth, tibbānaṃ means sharp. Kharānaṃ means coarse. Kaṭukānaṃ means fierce. Asātānaṃ means not pleasant, disagreeable. One does not apply the mind to them, nor do they gratify or augment the mind; thus they are disagreeable.

Sotasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Sotasutta is finished.

Rājavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Chapter on Kings is finished.

(15) 5. Tikaṇḍakīvaggo

(15) 5. The Tikaṇḍakī Chapter

1. Avajānātisuttavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Avajānātisutta

141. Pañcamassa [V 3.0045][M 3.0047] paṭhame datvā avajānātīti ettha eko bhikkhu mahāpuñño catupaccayalābhī hoti, so cīvarādīni labhitvā aññaṃ appapuññaṃ āpucchati. Sopi tasmiṃ punappunaṃ āpucchantepi gaṇhātiyeva. Athassa itaro thokaṃ kupito hutvā maṅkubhāvaṃ uppādetukāmo vadati “ayaṃ attano dhammatāya cīvarādīni na labhati, amhe nissāya labhatī”ti. Evampi datvā avajānāti nāma. Eko pana ekena saddhiṃ dve tīṇi vassāni vasanto pubbe taṃ puggalaṃ garuṃ katvā gacchante gacchante kāle cittīkāraṃ na karoti, āsananisinnaṭṭhānampi na gacchati. Ayampi puggalo saṃvāsena avajānāti nāma. Ādheyyamukhoti ādito dheyyamukho, paṭhamavacanasmiṃyeva ṭhapitamukhoti attho. Tatthāyaṃ nayo – eko puggalo sāruppaṃyeva bhikkhuṃ “asāruppo eso”ti katheti. Taṃ sutvā esa niṭṭhaṃ gacchati, puna aññena sabhāgena bhikkhunā “sāruppo aya”nti vuttepi tassa vacanaṃ na gaṇhāti. Asukena nāma “asāruppo aya”nti amhākaṃ kathitanti purimabhikkhunova kathaṃ gaṇhāti. Aparopissa dussīlaṃ “sīlavā”ti katheti. Tassa vacanaṃ saddahitvā puna aññena “asāruppo eso bhikkhu, nāyaṃ tumhākaṃ santikaṃ upasaṅkamituṃ yutto”ti vuttepi tassa vacanaṃ aggahetvā purimaṃyeva kathaṃ gaṇhāti. Aparo vaṇṇampi kathitaṃ gaṇhāti, avaṇṇampi kathitaṃ gaṇhātiyeva. Ayampi ādheyyamukhoyeva nāma ādhātabbamukho, yaṃ yaṃ suṇāti, tattha tattha ṭhapitamukhoti attho.

141. In the first of the fifth, regarding “gives and then despises”: Here, a monk of great merit is a recipient of the four requisites. Having received robes and so on, he offers them to another monk of little merit. Even when the former repeatedly offers, the latter just takes them. Then the former, becoming slightly angry and wishing to embarrass him, says: “This one does not obtain robes and so on by his own right; he obtains them on account of us.” In this way, it is called “giving and then despising.” Again, a person lives with another for two or three years. At first he treats that person with respect, but as time goes on, he shows him no esteem and does not even go to the place where he is seated. This person, too, is one who despises through familiarity. Ādheyyamukha means one whose opinion is set from the start; the meaning is one whose opinion is fixed at the very first utterance. Herein, this is the method: a person says of a suitable monk, “He is unsuitable.” Hearing this, another takes it as conclusive. Even when later told by another, a fellow monk, “This one is suitable,” he does not accept his word but accepts the word of the first monk, thinking: “So-and-so told us, ‘He is unsuitable.’” Another says of an immoral person, “He is virtuous.” Trusting his word, when later told by another, “This monk is unsuitable; it is not proper for him to approach you,” he does not accept his word but accepts the former’s statement. Another accepts what is said in praise and also accepts what is said in blame. This one too is called ādheyyamukha, one whose opinion is receptive, meaning his opinion is set on whatever he hears.

Loloti saddhādīnaṃ ittarakālappatitattā assaddhiyādīhi lulitabhāvena lolo. Ittarabhattītiādīsu punappunaṃ bhajanena saddhāva bhattipemaṃ. Saddhāpemampi gehassitapemampi vaṭṭati, pasādo saddhāpasādo. Evaṃ puggalo lolo hotīti evaṃ ittarasaddhāditāya puggalo lolo nāma hoti. Haliddirāgo viya, thusarāsimhi koṭṭitakhānuko viya, assapiṭṭhiyaṃ ṭhapitakumbhaṇḍaṃ viya ca anibaddhaṭṭhāne muhuttena kuppati. Mando momūhoti aññāṇabhāvena mando, avisayatāya momūho, mahāmūḷhoti attho.

`Lolo` means fickle. A person is fickle (lolo) because faith and so on are of short duration and because of being stirred up by faithlessness and so on. In such cases as “fleeting devotion,” through repeated engagement, faith itself is devotion and love. Both love based on faith and love associated with the household life are valid. Confidence is confidence rooted in faith. “Thus a person is fickle” means that a person is called fickle because of having fleeting faith and so on. Like the dye of turmeric, like a post struck in a heap of chaff, and like a gourd placed on a horse’s back, he is agitated in a moment in an unfixed position. `Mando momūho` means one is dull (mando) because of ignorance and bewildered (momūho) because of having no proper object; the meaning is greatly deluded.

Avajānātisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Avajānātisutta is finished.

2-3. Ārabhatisuttādivaṇṇanā

2-3. The Commentary on the Ārabhatisutta and Others

142-3. Dutiye [V 3.0046][M 3.0048] ārabhatīti ettha ārambha-saddo kammakiriyahiṃsanavīriyakopanāpattivītikkamesu vattati. Tathā hesa “yaṃ kiñci dukkhaṃ sambhoti, sabbaṃ ārambhapaccayā”ti (su. ni. 749) kamme āgato. “Mahārambhā mahāyaññā, na te honti mahapphalā”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.120; a. ni. 4.39) kiriyāya. “Samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ uddissa pāṇaṃ ārabhantī”ti (ma. ni. 2.51) hiṃsane. “Ārambhatha nikkhamatha, yuñjatha buddhasāsane”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.185; netti. 29; peṭako. 38; mi. pa. 5.1.4) vīriye. “Bījagāmabhūtagāmasamārambhā paṭivirato hotī”ti (dī. ni. 1.10, 195; ma. ni. 1.293) kopane. “Ārabhati ca vippaṭisārī ca hotī”ti (a. ni. 5.142; pu. pa. 191) ayaṃ pana āpattivītikkame āgato, tasmā āpattivītikkamavasena ārabhati ceva, tappaccayā ca vippaṭisārī hotīti ayamettha attho. Yathābhūtaṃ nappajānātīti anadhigatattā yathāsabhāvato na jānāti. Yatthassāti yasmiṃ assa, yaṃ ṭhānaṃ patvā etassa puggalassa uppannā pāpakā akusalā dhammā aparisesā nirujjhantīti attho. Kiṃ pana patvā te nirujjhantīti? Arahattamaggaṃ, phalappattassa pana niruddhā nāma honti. Evaṃ santepi idha maggakiccavasena pana phalameva vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

142-3. In the second, regarding `ārabhati`, the word `ārambha` occurs in the senses of action, performance, harming, effort, damaging, and transgression of a rule. For instance, it occurs in the sense of action in: “Whatever suffering arises, all arises on account of an undertaking” (Snp 749). In the sense of performance: “Great undertakings, great sacrifices—these are not of great fruit” (SN 1.120; AN 4.39). In the sense of harming: “They kill a living being for the ascetic Gotama” (MN 55). In the sense of effort: “Undertake, go forth, apply yourselves to the Buddha’s teaching” (SN 1.185). In the sense of damaging: “He is one who abstains from damaging seed-life and plant-life” (DN 1.10). But this one, “He undertakes and feels remorse” (AN 5.142), occurs in the sense of transgression of a rule. Therefore the meaning here is that he transgresses a rule, and on account of that he feels remorse. “He does not understand as it really is” means that because he has not realized it, he does not know it according to its true nature. “Where for him” means: having reached what state do the evil, unwholesome states that have arisen in this person cease without remainder? This is the meaning. Having reached what do they cease? The path of arahantship. For one who has attained the fruit, they are said to have ceased. This being so, it should be understood that here the fruit is spoken of in terms of the function of the path.

Ārabhatī na vippaṭisārī hotīti āpattiṃ āpajjati, taṃ panesa desetuṃ sabhāgapuggalaṃ pariyesati, tasmā na vippaṭisārī hoti. Na ārabhati vippaṭisārī hotīti āpattiṃ na āpajjati, vinayapaññattiyaṃ pana akovidattā anāpattiyā āpattisaññī hutvā vippaṭisārī hotīti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. “Na ārabhati na vippaṭisārī hotī”ti yo vutto, kataro so puggalo? Ossaṭṭhavīriyapuggalo. So hi “kiṃ me imasmiṃ kāle parinibbānena, anāgate metteyyasammāsambuddhakāle parinibbāyissāmī”ti visuddhasīlopi paṭipattiṃ na pūreti. So hi “kimatthaṃ āyasmā pamatto viharati, puthujjanassa nāma gati anibaddhā, tasmā hi metteyyasammāsambuddhassa sammukhībhāvaṃ labheyyāsi, arahattatthāya vipassanaṃ bhāvehī”ti ovaditabbova.

“He undertakes and does not feel remorse”: he commits an offense, but he seeks a suitable person to whom to declare it; therefore he does not feel remorse. “He does not undertake but feels remorse”: he does not commit an offense, but being unskilled in the Vinaya rules, he perceives what is not an offense as an offense and feels remorse. Thus the meaning should be understood here. As to the one spoken of as “He does not undertake and does not feel remorse,” who is that person? A person who has given up striving. For he, though pure in virtue, does not complete the practice, thinking: “What is final Nibbāna to me at this time? I will attain final Nibbāna in the future, in the time of Metteyya, the Perfectly Enlightened One.” He should indeed be admonished thus: “Venerable sir, why do you dwell negligently? The destination of a worldling is uncertain. Therefore, may you come face to face with Metteyya, the Perfectly Enlightened One; develop insight for the sake of arahantship!”

Sādhūti [M 3.0049] āyācanatthe nipāto. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yāva aparaddhaṃ vata āyasmatā, evaṃ santepi mayaṃ āyasmantaṃ yācāma, desetabbayuttakassa desanāya, vuṭṭhātabbayuttakassa vuṭṭhānena, āvikātabbayuttakassa āvikiriyāya ārambhaje āsave pahāya suddhante ṭhitabhāvapaccavekkhaṇena [V 3.0047] vippaṭisāraje āsave paṭivinodetvā nīharitvā vipassanācittañceva vipassanāpaññañca vaḍḍhetūti. Amunā pañcamena puggalenāti etena pañcamena khīṇāsavapuggalena. Samasamo bhavissatīti lokuttaraguṇehi samabhāveneva samo bhavissatīti evaṃ khīṇāsavena ovaditabboti attho. Tatiyaṃ uttānameva.

`Sādhu` is a particle in the sense of a request. This is what is said: “Venerable sir, you have indeed done wrong. Even so, we request you, venerable sir: by declaring what should be declared, by rehabilitating from what requires rehabilitation, by disclosing what should be disclosed; by abandoning the taints born of undertaking and by dispelling the taints born of remorse through reflecting on one’s state of being established in purity, may you develop both the mind of insight and the wisdom of insight.” “By this fifth person” means by this fifth person, the one whose taints are destroyed. “He will be perfectly equal” means he will be equal through the state of equality in the supramundane qualities. Thus the meaning is that he should be admonished by one whose taints are destroyed. The third is plain in meaning.

Ārabhatisuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Ārabhatisutta and Others is finished.

4-6. Tikaṇḍakīsuttādivaṇṇanā

4-6. Commentary on the Tikaṇḍakī Sutta and Others

144-6. Catutthe paṭikūleti amanuññe aniṭṭhe. Appaṭikūlasaññīti iṭṭhākāreneva pavattacitto. Iṭṭhasmiṃ vatthusmiṃ asubhāya vā pharati, aniccato vā upasaṃharati upaneti pavatteti. Aniṭṭhasmiṃ vatthusminti aniṭṭhe sattasaññite ārammaṇe. Mettāya vā pharatīti mettaṃ hitesitaṃ upasaṃharanto sabbatthakameva vā tattha pharati. Dhātuto vā upasaṃharatīti dhammasabhāvacintanena dhātuto paccavekkhaṇāya dhātumanasikāraṃ vā tattha pavatteti. Tadubhayaṃ abhinivajjetvāti sabhāvato ānubhāvato ca upatiṭṭhantaṃ ārammaṇe paṭikūlabhāvaṃ appaṭikūlabhāvañcāti taṃ ubhayaṃ pahāya aggahetvā, sabbasmiṃ pana tasmiṃ majjhatto hutvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Majjhatto hutvā viharitukāmo pana kiṃ karotīti? Iṭṭhāniṭṭhesu āpāthaṃ gatesu neva somanassito hoti, na domanassito hoti. Upekkhako vihareyyāti iṭṭhe arajjanto aniṭṭhe adussanto yathā aññe asamapekkhanena mohaṃ uppādenti, evaṃ anuppādento chasu ārammaṇesu chaḷaṅgupekkhāya upekkhako vihareyya. Tenevāha “chaḷaṅgupekkhāvasena pañcamo”ti. Iṭṭhāniṭṭhachaḷārammaṇāpāthe parisuddhapakatibhāvāvijahanalakkhaṇāya chasu dvāresu pavattanato “chaḷaṅgupekkhā”ti laddhanāmāya tatramajjhattupekkhāya vasena pañcamo vāro vuttoti attho. Pañcamaṃ chaṭṭhañca uttānameva.

144-6. In the fourth, `paṭikūla` means disagreeable and undesirable. `Appaṭikūlasaññī` refers to one whose mind operates with an agreeable perception. In an agreeable object, one either pervades it with the perception of foulness or adverts to it as impermanent, brings it to mind, and sustains it. `Aniṭṭhasmiṃ vatthusmiṃ` refers to a disagreeable object perceived as a being. `Mettāya vā pharati` means one pervades it with loving-kindness, adverting to it as the wish for welfare, or pervades it universally there. `Dhātuto vā upasaṃharati` means one adverts to it by way of the elements, that is, by contemplating the intrinsic nature of phenomena, one reviews it by way of the elements or directs attention to the elements there. `Tadubhayaṃ abhinivajjetvā` means having abandoned both the repulsive and non-repulsive aspects of the object, without grasping either, and having become neutral towards it in every way. But what does one who wishes to dwell in neutrality do? When agreeable and disagreeable objects come into range, one is neither mentally pleased nor mentally distressed. One should dwell equanimously: not attached to the agreeable nor averse to the disagreeable, one should dwell with equanimity towards the six sense objects with six-factored equanimity, without generating delusion through partiality. Therefore it is said: 'The fifth is by way of six-factored equanimity.' The meaning is that the fifth case is stated by way of that neutrality-equanimity called 'six-factored equanimity' because it operates at the six doors with the characteristic of not abandoning its purified natural state when the six agreeable and disagreeable objects come into range. The fifth and sixth are clear in meaning.

Tikaṇḍakīsuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Tikaṇḍakī Sutta and so forth is completed.

7-10. Asappurisadānasuttādivaṇṇanā

7-10. Commentary on the Asappurisadāna Sutta and Others

147-150. Sattame [M 3.0050] asakkaccanti anādaraṃ katvā. Deyyadhammassa asakkaccakaraṇaṃ nāma asampannaṃ karotīti āha “na sakkaritvā suciṃ katvā detī”ti, uttaṇḍulādidosavirahitaṃ [V 3.0048] sucisampannaṃ katvā na detīti attho. Acittīkatvāti na citte katvā, na pūjetvāti attho. Pūjento hi pūjetabbavatthuṃ citte ṭhapeti, na tato bahi karoti. Cittaṃ vā acchariyaṃ katvā paṭipattivikaraṇaṃ sambhāvanakiriyā, tappaṭikkhepato acittīkaraṇaṃ asambhāvanakiriyā. Agāravena detīti puggale agaruṃ karonto nisīdanaṭṭhāne asammajjitvā yattha vā tattha vā nisīdāpetvā yaṃ vā taṃ vā ādhārakaṃ ṭhapetvā dānaṃ deti. Asahatthāti na attano hatthena deti, dāsakammakarodīhi dāpeti. Apaviddhaṃ detīti antarā apaviddhaṃ vicchedaṃ katvā deti. Tenāha “na nirantaraṃ detī”ti. Atha vā apaviddhaṃ detīti ucchiṭṭhādichaḍḍanīyadhammaṃ viya avakkhittakaṃ katvā deti. Tenāha “chaḍḍetukāmo viya detī”ti. “Addhā imassa dānassa phalameva āgacchatī”ti evaṃ yassa kammassakatādiṭṭhi atthi, so āgamanadiṭṭhiko, ayaṃ pana na tādisoti anāgamanadiṭṭhiko. Tenāha “katassa nāma phalaṃ āgamissatī”tiādi. Aṭṭhamādīsu natthi vattabbaṃ.

147-150. In the seventh, asakkaccaṃ means disrespectfully. To give a gift disrespectfully is to make it deficient, as stated: 'He does not give after honoring it and making it pure.' The meaning is that he does not give it after having made it pure and complete, free from defects such as husks in the rice. Acittīkatvā means not taking it to heart, that is, not honoring it. For one who honors places the object to be honored in his mind and does not put it outside of that. Or, esteeming is an action that modifies one's practice by making the mind hold it in high regard; its rejection, acittīkaraṇaṃ, is the action of not esteeming it. Giving without respect means giving while disrespecting the person, making him sit without sweeping the sitting place, or making him sit just anywhere, or placing just any kind of container and then giving. Asahatthā means he does not give with his own hand but has slaves or workers give it. Apaviddhaṃ deti (he gives what is cast off) means he gives intermittently. Therefore, it is said: 'He does not give continuously.' Alternatively, apaviddhaṃ deti means he gives it contemptuously, like something to be thrown away such as leftovers. Therefore, it is said: 'He gives as if intending to discard it.' 'Surely, the result of this gift will come'—one who has such a view of the ownership of kamma is one with a view of its coming. But this person is not like that, so he is one with no view of its coming. Therefore, it is said: 'Will a result of what has been done really come?' and so on. In the eighth and following, there is nothing to be said.

Asappurisadānasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on the Gifts of an Unworthy Person and so forth is concluded.

Tikaṇḍakīvaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Tikaṇḍakī Chapter is concluded.

Tatiyapaṇṇāsakaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Third Fifty is concluded.

4. Catutthapaṇṇāsakaṃ

4. The Fourth Fifty

(16) 1. Saddhammavaggo

(16) 1. The Chapter on the Good Dhamma

151-160. Paṭhamo [V 3.0049] vaggo uttānatthoyeva.

151-160. The first chapter is clear in meaning.

(17) 2. Āghātavaggo

(17) 2. The Chapter on Ill-will

1-5. Paṭhamaāghātapaṭivinayasuttādivaṇṇanā

1-5. Commentary on the First Discourse on Removing Resentment and so forth

161-165. Dutiyassa [M 3.0051] paṭhame natthi vattabbaṃ. Dutiye āghāto paṭivinayati ettha, etehīti vā āghātapaṭivinayā. Tenāha “āghāto etehi paṭivinetabbo”tiādi.

161-165. In the first part of the second sutta, there is nothing to be said. In the second, āghātapaṭivinayā are so called because resentment (āghāto) is removed (paṭivinayati) here (ettha), or by these means (etehi). Therefore it is said: 'Resentment should be removed by these,' and so on.

Nantakanti anantakaṃ, antavirahitaṃ vatthakhaṇḍaṃ. Yadi hi tassa anto bhaveyya, “pilotikā”ti saṅkhaṃ na gaccheyya.

Nantakaṃ means endless, a piece of cloth without an end. For if it had an end, it would not be designated a 'rag.'

Sevālenāti bījakaṇṇikakesarādibhedena sevālena. Udakapappaṭakenāti nīlamaṇḍūkapiṭṭhivaṇṇena udakapiṭṭhiṃ chādetvā nibbattena udakapiṭṭhikena. Ghammena anugatoti ghammena phuṭṭho abhibhūto. Cittuppādanti paṭighasampayuttacittuppādaṃ.

Sevālena means with algae of various kinds, such as seed, pericarp, and filament. Udakapappaṭakena means with water scum that is produced by covering the water’s surface and has the color of a blue frog’s back. Ghammena anugato means touched and overcome by the heat. Cittuppādaṃ means the arising of a mind associated with repugnance.

Visabhāgavedanuppattiyā kakaceneva iriyāpathapavattinivāraṇena chindanto ābādhati pīḷetīti ābādho, so assa atthīti ābādhiko. Taṃsamuṭṭhānena dukkhito sañjātadukkho. Bāḷhagilānoti adhimattagilāno. Gāmantanāyakassāti gāmantasampāpakassa.

An affliction (ābādho) is so called because it afflicts and torments by cutting off—that is, by preventing the continuation of the postures—like a saw, due to the arising of a disagreeable feeling. One who has this is afflicted (ābādhiko). Pained by what arises from that, he is one for whom suffering has arisen. Bāḷhagilāno means extremely ill. Gāmantanāyakassa means for one who leads to the vicinity of the village.

Pasannabhāvena [V 3.0050] udakassa acchabhāvo veditabboti āha “acchodakāti pasannodakā”ti. Sādurasatāya sātatāti āha “madhurodakā”ti. Tanukameva salilaṃ visesato sītalaṃ, na bahalāti āha “tanusītasalilā”ti. Setakāti nikkaddamā. Sacikkhallādivasena hi udakassa vivaṇṇatā. Sabhāvato pana taṃ setavaṇṇameva. Tatiyādīni uttānatthāneva.

The clarity of the water is to be understood from its limpidity; thus it is said: acchodakā means limpid water (pasannodakā). Because of its sweet taste, it is pleasant; thus it is said: madhurodakā (sweet water). The water is thin and especially cool, not thick; thus it is said: tanusītasalilā (with thin, cool water). Setakā means free from mud. For the water becomes discolored on account of mud and the like, but by nature it is white in color. The third and following are clear in meaning.

Paṭhamaāghātapaṭivinayasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the first Āghātapaṭivinaya Sutta and so forth is concluded.

6. Nirodhasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Nirodha Sutta

166. Chaṭṭhe [M 3.0052] amarisanattheti asahanatthe. Anāgatavacanaṃ katanti anāgatasaddappayogo kato, attho pana vattamānakālikova. Akkharacintakā (pāṇini. 3.3.145-146) hi īdisesu ṭhānesu anokappanāmarisanatthavasena atthisadde upapade vattamānakālepi anāgatavacanaṃ karonti.

166. In the sixth, amarisanattheti means in the sense of not enduring (asahanatthe). Anāgatavacanaṃ katanti means the future tense has been used, but the meaning is actually in the present tense. For grammarians (Pāṇini 3.3.145–146), in such cases, when the word atthi is present, they employ the future tense even for the present time in the sense of disapproval or impatience.

Nirodhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Nirodha Sutta is concluded.

7-9. Codanāsuttādivaṇṇanā

7–9. Commentary on the Codanā Sutta and so on.

167-9. Sattame vatthusandassanāti yasmiṃ vatthusmiṃ āpatti, tassa sarūpato dassanaṃ. Āpattisandassanāti yaṃ āpattiṃ so āpanno, tassā dassanaṃ. Saṃvāsappaṭikkhepoti uposathappavāraṇādisaṃvāsassa paṭikkhipanaṃ akaraṇaṃ. Sāmīcippaṭikkhepoti abhivādanādisāmīcikiriyāya akaraṇaṃ. Codayamānenāti codentena. Cuditakassa kāloti cuditakassa codetabbakālo. Puggalanti codetabbapuggalaṃ. Upaparikkhitvāti “ayaṃ cuditakalakkhaṇe tiṭṭhati, na tiṭṭhatī”ti vīmaṃsitvā. Ayasaṃ āropetīti “ime maṃ abhūtena abbhācikkhantā ayasaṃ byasanaṃ uppādentī”ti bhikkhūnaṃ ayasaṃ uppādeti. Aṭṭhamanavamāni uttānatthāneva.

167–169. In the seventh, vatthusandassanā means showing the matter in which the offense lies, showing it in its own nature. Āpattisandassanā means showing the offense that one has committed. Saṃvāsappaṭikkhepo means the rejection of communion, that is, not performing communal acts such as the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā. Sāmīcippaṭikkhepo means the rejection of proper duties, that is, not performing acts of respect such as paying homage. Codayamānenāti codentena means by one who reproves. Cuditakassa kāloti cuditakassa codetabbakālo means the time for reproving the one who is accused. Puggalanti codetabbapuggalaṃ means the person to be reproved. Upaparikkhitvāti means after having investigated: “Does this person possess the characteristics of one who should be reproved or not?” Ayasaṃ āropetīti means he imputes disgrace to the bhikkhus, thinking: “These bhikkhus, by accusing me falsely, are causing me disgrace and misfortune.” The eighth and ninth are of obvious meaning.

Codanāsuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Codanā Sutta and so on is concluded.

10. Bhaddajisuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Bhaddaji Sutta

170. Dasame [V 3.0051] abhibhavitvā ṭhito ime satteti adhippāyo. Yasmā pana so “pāsaṃsabhāvena uttamabhāvena ca te satte abhibhavitvā ṭhito”ti attānaṃ maññati, tasmā vuttaṃ “jeṭṭhako”ti. Aññadatthu dasoti dassane antarāyābhāvavacanena ñeyyavisesapariggāhikabhāvena [M 3.0053] ca anāvaraṇadassāvitaṃ paṭijānātīti āha “sabbaṃ passatīti adhippāyo”ti.

170. In the tenth, the meaning is: ‘Having overcome these beings, he stands.’ But since he considers himself thus, ‘Having overcome those beings by way of praiseworthiness and superiority, I stand,’ therefore it is said, ‘the eldest.’ Furthermore, as to ‘the tenth,’ by stating that there is no obstruction to vision and that it has the nature of comprehending special knowable things, he professes to have unobstructed vision. Therefore it is said: ‘The meaning is, “He sees all.”’

Bhaddajisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Bhaddaji Sutta is concluded.

Āghātavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Āghāta Vagga is concluded.

(18) 3. Upāsakavaggo

(18) 3. The Chapter on Lay Followers

1-6. Sārajjasuttādivaṇṇanā

1–6. Commentary on the Sārajja Sutta and so on.

171-176. Tatiyassa paṭhamadutiyatatiyacatutthe natthi vattabbaṃ. Pañcame upāsakapacchimakoti upāsakanihīno. “Iminā diṭṭhādinā idaṃ nāma maṅgalaṃ bhavissatī”ti evaṃ bālajanaparikappitakotūhalasaṅkhātena diṭṭhasutamutamaṅgalena samannāgato kotūhalamaṅgaliko. Tenāha “iminā idaṃ bhavissatī”tiādi. Maṅgalaṃ paccetīti diṭṭhamaṅgalādibhedaṃ maṅgalameva patthiyāyati. No kammanti kammassakataṃ no patthiyāyati. Imamhā sāsanāti ito sabbaññubuddhasāsanato. Bahiddhāti bāhirakasamaye. Dakkhiṇeyyaṃ pariyesatīti “duppaṭipannā dakkhiṇeyyā”ti saññī gavesati. Ettha dakkhiṇapariyesanapubbakāre ekaṃ katvā pañca dhammā veditabbā. Chaṭṭhaṃ uttānameva.

171–176. Concerning the third chapter, there is nothing to be said about the first, second, third, and fourth suttas. In the fifth, upāsakapacchimako means an inferior lay follower. A kotūhalamaṅgaliko is one who is given to auspicious signs based on curiosity, one endowed with auspicious signs based on things seen, heard, or sensed, which are concocted by foolish people, thinking: ‘By this seen thing, etc., such and such an auspicious event will occur.’ Hence it is said: ‘By this, this will be,’ and so on. He hopes for an auspicious sign means he desires only auspicious signs of various kinds, such as auspicious things seen. No kammanti kammassakataṃ no patthiyāyati means he does not desire the fruit of his own kamma. From this dispensation means from this dispensation of the Omniscient Buddha. Externally means in an external creed. He seeks a worthy recipient of offerings means he searches with the perception, ‘Those of wrong practice are worthy of offerings.’ Here, the five things are to be understood, with the seeking of a worthy recipient and the prior service being made into one. The sixth is of obvious meaning.

Sārajjasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Sārajja Sutta and so on is concluded.

7-8. Vaṇijjāsuttādivaṇṇanā

7–8. Commentary on the Vaṇijjā Sutta and so on.

177-8. Sattame [V 3.0052] satthavaṇijjāti āvudhabhaṇḍaṃ katvā vā kāretvā vā kataṃ vā paṭilabhitvā tassa vikkayo. Āvudhabhaṇḍaṃ kāretvā tassa vikkayoti idaṃ pana nidassanamattaṃ. Sūkaramigādayo posetvā tesaṃ vikkayoti sūkaramigādayo posetvā tesaṃ maṃsaṃ sampādetvā vikkayo. Ettha ca satthavaṇijjā paroparādhanimittatāya akaraṇīyā vuttā, sattavaṇijjā abhujissabhāvakaraṇato, maṃsavisavaṇijjā vadhahetuto, majjavaṇijjā pamādaṭṭhānato. Aṭṭhamaṃ uttānameva.

177–178. In the seventh, trade in weapons (satthavaṇijjā) is the selling of weapons—whether one has made them, had them made, or obtained them ready-made. The phrase ‘having weapons made and selling them’ is just an illustration. The phrase ‘raising pigs, deer, etc., and selling them’ means raising pigs, deer, etc., preparing their meat, and selling it. Here, trade in weapons is said to be something that should not be done because it is a cause for harming others; trade in living beings, because it leads to a state of non-freedom; trade in meat and poison, because it is a cause of slaughter; and trade in intoxicants, because it is a basis for heedlessness. The eighth is of obvious meaning.

Vaṇijjāsuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Vaṇijjā Sutta and so on is concluded.

9. Gihisuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Gihisutta

179. Navame [M 3.0054] ābhicetasikānanti abhicetoti abhikkantaṃ visuddhacittaṃ vuccati adhicittaṃ vā, abhicetasi jātāni ābhicetasikāni, abhiceto sannissitānīti vā ābhicetasikāni. Tenevāha “uttamacittanissitāna”nti. Diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārānanti diṭṭhadhamme sukhavihārānaṃ. Diṭṭhadhammoti paccakkho attabhāvo vuccati, tattha sukhavihārānanti attho. Rūpāvacarajjhānānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tāni hi appetvā nisinnā jhāyino imasmiṃyeva attabhāve asaṃkiliṭṭhaṃ nekkhammasukhaṃ vindanti, tasmā “diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārānī”ti vuccanti.

179. In the ninth, as to ābhicetasikāni: abhiceto is said to be the excellent, purified mind, or the higher mind (adhicittaṃ). Ābhicetasikāni are things born in the higher mind, or things dependent on the higher mind. For that reason it is said: ‘dependent on the highest mind.’ Pleasant abidings in the present life (diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārāni): Diṭṭhadhamma is said to be one’s own present existence; the meaning is pleasant abidings therein. This is a designation for the form-sphere jhānas. For meditators who sit having attained them find the undefiled bliss of renunciation in this very life. Therefore they are called ‘pleasant abidings in the present life.’

Catubbidhamerayanti pupphāsavo, phalāsavo, guḷāsavo, madhvāsavoti evaṃ catuppabhedaṃ merayaṃ. Pañcavidhañca suranti pūvasurā, piṭṭhasurā, odanasurā, kiṇṇapakkhittā, sambhārasaṃyuttāti evaṃ pañcappabhedaṃ suraṃ. Puññaṃ attho etassāti puññattho. Yasmā panesa puññena atthiko nāma hoti, tasmā vuttaṃ “puññena atthikassā”ti. Sesamettha uttānameva.

Four kinds of liquor (meraya): liquor from flowers, from fruits, from molasses, and from honey—thus liquor is of four kinds. And five kinds of fermented drink (sura): fermented drink from cakes, from flour, from cooked rice, that to which yeast has been added, and that blended with ingredients—thus fermented drink is of five kinds. Puññattho means one for whom merit is the goal. Since he is one who has need of merit, it is therefore said, ‘of one who has need of merit.’ The rest here is of obvious meaning.

Gihisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Gihisutta is concluded.

10. Gavesīsuttavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Gavesī Sutta

180. Dasame sukāraṇanti bodhiparipācanassa ekantikaṃ sundaraṃ kāraṇaṃ. Mandahasitanti īsakaṃ [V 3.0053] hasitaṃ. Kahaṃ kahanti hāsasaddassa anukaraṇametaṃ. Haṭṭhappahaṭṭhākāramattanti haṭṭhassa pahaṭṭhākāramattaṃ. Yathā gahitasaṅketā “pahaṭṭho bhagavā”ti sañjānanti, evaṃ ākāranidassanamattaṃ.

180. In the tenth, 'a good reason' means a certain excellent reason for the maturing of enlightenment. 'A gentle smile' means a slight smile. 'Kahaṃ, kahaṃ' is an imitation of the sound of laughter. 'Merely the appearance of joy and delight' means just the appearance of being joyful and delighted. It is merely an indication of an expression, so that those who have grasped the sign recognize, 'The Blessed One is delighted.'

Idāni iminā pasaṅgena hāsasamuṭṭhānaṃ vibhāgato dassetuṃ “hasitañca nāmeta”ntiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha ajjhupekkhanavasenapi hāso na sambhavati, pageva domanassavasenāti āha “terasahi somanassasahagatacittehī”ti. Nanu ca keci kodhavasenapi hasantīti? Na, te sampiyanti kodhavatthuṃ tattha “mayaṃ dāni yathākāmakāritaṃ āpajjissāmā”ti duviññeyyantarena somanassacitteneva hāsassa uppajjanato. Tesūti [M 3.0055] pañcasu somanassasahagatakiriyacittesu. Balavārammaṇeti uḷāratame ārammaṇe yamakapāṭihāriyasadise. Dubbalārammaṇeti anuḷāraārammaṇe.

Now, in this connection, to show the arising of laughter by way of classification, the passage beginning 'Laughter, namely...' is commenced. Therein, laughter does not arise even by way of equanimity, still less by way of displeasure; hence it is said, 'with thirteen consciousnesses accompanied by joy.' But do some not laugh even out of anger? No. They take delight in the object of anger, thinking, 'Now we will get to act as we please'; for laughter arises only from a consciousness of joy with a hard-to-discern inner reason. 'Among these' means among the five functional consciousnesses accompanied by joy. 'With a strong object' means with a most sublime object, like the Twin Miracle. 'With a weak object' means with a non-sublime object.

“Imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne…pe… uppādetī”ti idaṃ porāṇaṭṭhakathāyaṃ tathā āgatattā vuttaṃ, na sahetukasomanassasahagatacittehi bhagavato sitaṃ na hotīti dassanattaṃ. Abhidhammaṭīkāyaṃ (dha. sa. mūlaṭī. 968) pana “atītaṃsādīsu appaṭihataṃ ñāṇaṃ vatvā ‘imehi dhammehi samannāgatassa buddhassa bhagavato sabbaṃ kāyakammaṃ ñāṇapubbaṅgamaṃ ñāṇānuparivattī’tiādivacanato (mahāni. 156; paṭi. ma. 3.5) ‘bhagavato idaṃ cittaṃ uppajjatī’ti vuttavacanaṃ vicāretabba”nti vuttaṃ. Tattha iminā hasituppādacittena pavattiyamānampi bhagavato sitakaraṇaṃ pubbenivāsaanāgataṃsasabbaññutaññāṇānaṃ anuvattakattā ñāṇānuparivattiyevāti evaṃ pana ñāṇānuparivattibhāve sati na koci pāḷiaṭṭhakathānaṃ virodho. Tathā hi abhidhammaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 568) “tesaṃ ñāṇānaṃ ciṇṇapariyante idaṃ cittaṃ uppajjatī”ti vuttaṃ. Avassañcetaṃ evaṃ icchitabbaṃ, aññathā āvajjanacittassapi bhagavato tathārūpe kāle na yujjeyya. Tassapi hi viññattisamuṭṭhāpakabhāvassa nicchitattā. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “evañca katvā manodvārāvajjanassapi viññattisamuṭṭhāpakattaṃ upapannaṃ hotī”ti (dha. sa. mūlaṭī. 1 kāyakammadvārakathāvaṇṇanā) na ca viññattisamuṭṭhāpakatte taṃsamuṭṭhānakāyaviññattiyā kāyakammādibhāvaṃ āpajjanabhāvo vissajjatīti.

'But in this case... he produces...' This is said because it is so stated in the ancient commentary, not to show that the Blessed One's smile does not occur with consciousnesses accompanied by joy and having a root-cause. However, in the Abhidhamma Subcommentary it is said: 'Having stated that knowledge of the past, etc., is unobstructed, and based on passages like, "For the Blessed One, the Buddha, endowed with these qualities, all bodily action is preceded by knowledge and follows knowledge," the statement "This consciousness arises in the Blessed One" should be examined.' Here, even the Blessed One's act of smiling, which proceeds from this smile-producing consciousness, is indeed governed by knowledge because it follows upon the knowledges of past lives, future destinies, and omniscience. When it is thus governed by knowledge, there is no contradiction with the Pāli and the commentaries. For in the Abhidhamma commentary it is said: 'This consciousness arises at the culmination of the exercise of those knowledges.' And this must certainly be accepted in this way; otherwise, even the adverting consciousness of the Blessed One would not be fitting at such a time, for its nature of producing intimation has been determined. For it is said: 'And having done so, mind-door adverting also becomes a producer of intimation.' Nor, when it is a producer of intimation, is the fact that the bodily intimation arising from it becomes bodily action, etc., relinquished.

Hasitanti sitameva sandhāya vadati. Tenāha “evaṃ appamattakampī”ti. Samosaritā vijjulatā. Sā hi itaravijjulatā viya khaṇaṭṭhitiyā sīghanirodhā ca na hoti, apica kho dandhanirodhā, na ca sabbakālikā. Dīdhiti pāvakamahāmeghato vā cātuddīpikamahāmeghato vā [V 3.0054] niccharati. Tenāha “cātuddīpikamahāmeghamukhato”ti. Ayaṃ kira tāsaṃ rasmīnaṃ dhammatā, yadidaṃ tikkhattuṃ sīsaṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā dāṭhaggesuyeva antaradhānaṃ. Sesamettha suviññeyyameva.

'Laughter' is said referring only to a smile. Hence it is said, 'even so slightly moved.' An assembled lightning flash. For it is not, like other lightning flashes, of momentary duration and quick cessation, but rather it ceases slowly and is not perpetual. The radiance issues from a great cloud of fire or from a great cloud covering the four continents. Hence it is said, 'from the mouth of the great cloud covering the four continents.' This, it seems, is the nature of those rays: namely, that after circumambulating the head three times clockwise, they disappear right at the tips of the eye-teeth. The rest here is easy to understand.

Gavesīsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Gavesī Sutta is concluded.

Upāsakavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Chapter on Lay Followers is concluded.

(19) 4. Araññavaggo

(19) 4. The Forest Chapter

1. Āraññikasuttavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Sutta on the Forest Dweller

181. Catutthassa [M 3.0056] paṭhame appīcchataṃyeva nissāyātiādīsu “iti appiccho bhavissāmī”ti idaṃ me āraññikaṅgaṃ appicchatāya saṃvattissati, “iti santuṭṭho bhavissāmī”ti idaṃ me āraññikaṅgaṃ santuṭṭhiyā saṃvattissati, “iti kilese sallikhissāmī”ti idaṃ me āraññikaṅgaṃ kilesasallikhanatthāya saṃvattissatīti āraññiko hoti. Aggoti jeṭṭhako. Sesāni tasseva vevacanāni.

181. In the first sutta of the fourth chapter, in the passage beginning 'relying on fewness of wishes': one becomes a forest-dweller thinking: '"Thus I will have few wishes"—this ascetic practice of forest-dwelling of mine will conduce to fewness of wishes'; '"Thus I will be content"—this ascetic practice of forest-dwelling of mine will conduce to contentment'; '"Thus I will scrape away the defilements"—this ascetic practice of forest-dwelling of mine will conduce to the scraping away of defilements.' 'Foremost' (aggo) means chief (jeṭṭhako). The rest are synonyms for it.

Gavā khīranti gāvito khīraṃ nāma hoti, na gāviyā dadhi. Khīramhā dadhītiādīsupi eseva nayo. Evamevanti yathā etesu pañcasu gorasesu sappimaṇḍo aggo, evamevaṃ imesu pañcasu āraññikesu yo ayaṃ appicchatādīni nissāya āraññiko hoti, ayaṃ aggo ceva seṭṭho ca mokkho ca pavaro ca. Imesu āraññikesu jātiāraññikā veditabbā, na āraññikanāmamattena āraññikāti veditabbā. Paṃsukūlikādīsupi eseva nayo.

'From a cow, milk' means that milk comes from a cow, not curd from a cow. The same principle applies to 'from milk, curd,' and so on. Just as, among these five cow-products, the cream of ghee is the foremost, so too, among these five kinds of forest-dwellers, the one who is a forest-dweller relying on fewness of wishes and so on is the foremost, the best, the chief, and the most excellent. Among these forest-dwellers, they should be known as genuine forest-dwellers, not as forest-dwellers in name only. The same principle applies to refuse-rag wearers and so on.

Āraññikasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Sutta on the Forest Dweller is concluded.

Araññavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Forest Chapter is concluded.

(20) 5. Brāhmaṇavaggo

(20) 5. The Brahmin Chapter

1. Soṇasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Soṇa Sutta

191. Pañcamassa [V 3.0055] paṭhame sampiyenevāti aññamaññapemeneva kāyena ca cittena ca missībhūtā saṅghaṭṭitā saṃsaṭṭhā hutvā saṃvāsaṃ vattenti, na appiyena niggahena vāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tenāha “piya”ntiādi. Udaraṃ avadihati upacinoti pūretīti udarāvadehakaṃ. Bhāvanapuṃsakañcetaṃ, udarāvadehakaṃ katvā udaraṃ pūretvāti attho. Tenāha “udaraṃ avadihitvā”tiādi.

191. In the first sutta of the fifth chapter, 'only affectionately' means: they dwell together having become mixed, joined, and united in body and mind only with mutual affection, not with dislike and censure. Thus it is said, 'affectionate,' etc. 'Udarāvadehakaṃ' means one who stuffs, heaps up, and fills the belly. And this is a neuter noun denoting an action; the meaning is 'having stuffed the belly full.' Thus it is said, 'having stuffed the belly,' etc.

Soṇasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Soṇa Sutta is finished.

2. Doṇabrāhmaṇasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Doṇa Sutta

192. Dutiye [M 3.0057] pavattāroti (dī. ni. ṭī. 1.285) pāvacanabhāvena vattāro. Yasmā te tesaṃ mantānaṃ pavattanakā, tasmā āha “pavattayitāro”ti. Sudde bahi katvā rahobhāsitabbaṭṭhena mantā eva taṃtaṃatthappaṭipattihetutāya mantapadaṃ. Anupanītāsādhāraṇatāya rahassabhāvena vattabbakiriyāya adhigamūpāyaṃ. Sajjhāyitanti gāyanavasena sajjhāyitaṃ. Taṃ pana udattānudattādīnaṃ sarānaṃ sampadāvaseneva icchitanti āha “sarasampattivasenā”ti. Aññesaṃ vuttanti pāvacanabhāvena aññesaṃ vuttaṃ. Samupabyūḷhanti saṅgahetvā uparūpari saññūḷhaṃ. Rāsikatanti iruvedayajuvedasāmavedādivasena, tatthāpi paccekaṃ mantabrahmādivasena, ajjhāyānuvākādivasena ca rāsikataṃ. Tesanti mantānaṃ kattūnaṃ. Dibbena cakkhunā oloketvāti dibbacakkhuparibhaṇḍena yathākammūpagañāṇena sattānaṃ kammassakatādiṃ, paccakkhato dassanaṭṭhena dibbacakkhusadisena pubbenivāsañāṇena atītakappe brāhmaṇānaṃ mantajjhenavidhiñca oloketvā. Pāvacanena saha saṃsandetvāti kassapasammāsambuddhassa yaṃ vacanaṃ vaṭṭasannissitaṃ, tena saha aviruddhaṃ katvā. Na hi tesaṃ vivaṭṭasannissito attho paccakkho hoti. Aparāpareti aṭṭhakādīhi aparāpare pacchimā okkākarājakālādīsu uppannā. Pakkhipitvāti aṭṭhakādīhi ganthitamantapadesu kilesasannissitapadānaṃ tattha tattha pade pakkhipanaṃ katvā. Viruddhe akaṃsūti [V 3.0056] brāhmaṇadhammikasuttādīsu (su. ni. brāhmaṇadhammikasuttaṃ 286 ādayo) āgatanayena saṃkilesatthadīpanato paccanīkabhūte akaṃsu.

192. In the second sutta: 'Those who proclaim' means those who speak in the sense of proclaiming the teaching. Because they are the originators of those mantras, it is said, 'proclaimers.' Having excluded the Suddas, the mantra-verses themselves are the basis for the practice of this or that purpose, on account of having to be spoken in private. It is a means of attainment through the act of speaking what is secret, because it is not common to the uninitiated. 'Recited' means recited in the manner of chanting. But that is desired only by way of the perfection of the tones—high, low, etc.—hence it is said, 'by way of the perfection of tones.' 'Spoken by others' means spoken by others in the sense of a proclamation. 'Piled up' means collected and heaped one upon another. 'Arranged in collections' means made into collections by way of the Rigveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda, etc., and there too, separately by way of mantras, brāhmaṇas, etc., and by way of chapters, sections, etc. 'Of them' means of the composers of the mantras. 'Having surveyed with the divine eye' means: having surveyed with the knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings according to their kamma, which is an accessory of the divine eye, the ownership of kamma by beings, etc.; and with the knowledge of past lives, which is like the divine eye in the sense of seeing directly, having surveyed the method of studying the mantras of the brahmins in past eons. 'Having compared it with the teaching' means: having made it consistent with the teaching of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One Kassapa, which is concerned with the round of existence. For the meaning that transcends the round is not directly apparent to them. 'Later and later' means the subsequent ones who arose after Aṭṭhaka and others, in the time of Okkākarāja and so on. 'Inserted' means having inserted words connected with the defilements here and there in the verses of the mantras composed by Aṭṭhaka and others. 'They made them contradictory' means they made them opposed, because they explained a meaning connected with defilement, in the way that has come down in the Brāhmaṇadhammika Sutta and other discourses.

Usūnaṃ asanakammaṃ issatthaṃ, dhanusippena jīvikā. Idha pana issatthaṃ viyāti issatthaṃ, sabbaāvudhajīvikāti āha “yodhājīvakammenā”ti, āvudhaṃ gahetvā upaṭṭhānakammenāti attho. Rājaporisaṃ nāma vinā āvudhena poroheccāmaccakammādirājakammaṃ katvā rājupaṭṭhānaṃ. Sippaññatarenāti gahitāvasesena hatthiassasippādinā. Kumārabhāvato pabhuti caraṇena komārabrahmacariyaṃ.

Archery (`issatthaṃ`) is the act of shooting arrows, a livelihood by the skill of the bow. Here, however, `issatthaṃ` means any livelihood by weapons; thus it is said, 'by the livelihood of a warrior,' the meaning of which is: by the work of service, having taken up a weapon. Royal service is service to the king by performing royal duties such as the work of a chaplain or minister, without weapons. 'By another skill' means by the remaining skills, such as the skill with elephants and horses. `Komārabrahmacariyaṃ` is the practice of the holy life from boyhood onwards.

Udakaṃ pātetvā dentīti dvāre ṭhitasseva brāhmaṇassa hatthe udakaṃ āsiñcantā “idaṃ te, brāhmaṇa, bhariyaṃ posāpanatthāya demā”ti vatvā [M 3.0058] denti. Kasmā pana te evaṃ brahmacariyaṃ caritvāpi dāraṃ pariyesanti, na yāvajīvaṃ brahmacārino hontīti? Micchādiṭṭhivasena. Tesañhī evaṃ diṭṭhi hoti “yo puttaṃ na uppādeti, so kulavaṃsacchedakaro hoti, tato niraye paccatī”ti. Cattāro kira abhāyitabbaṃ bhāyanti gaṇḍuppādako, kikī, kontinī, brāhmaṇoti. Gaṇḍuppādā kira mahāpathaviyā khayanabhayena mattabhojanā honti, na bahuṃ mattikaṃ khādanti. Kikī sakuṇikā ākāsapatanabhayena aṇḍassa upari uttānā seti. Kontinī sakuṇī pathavīkampanabhayena pādehi bhūmiṃ na suṭṭhu akkamati. Brāhmaṇā kulavaṃsūpacchedabhayena dāraṃ pariyesanti. Āhu cettha –

'Having poured water, they give' means: while the brahmin is standing at the door, they pour water into his hand and give, saying: 'This, brahmin, we give for the purpose of supporting a wife.' But why is it that, having practiced the holy life in this way, they still seek a wife and do not remain celibate for life? Because of wrong view. For they hold this view: 'One who does not beget a son becomes a destroyer of the family lineage, and on that account he is tormented in hell.' It is said that four beings fear what is not to be feared: the earthworm, the blue jay, the curlew, and the brahmin. Earthworms, it is said, fearing the depletion of the great earth, are moderate in eating and do not consume much soil. The blue jay, a bird, fearing that the sky might fall, lies on its back on top of its eggs. The curlew, a bird, fearing that the earth might quake, does not tread firmly on the ground with its feet. Brahmins, fearing the cutting off of their family lineage, seek a wife. And it is said on this matter:

“Gaṇḍuppādo kikī ceva, kontī brāhmaṇadhammiko;

Ete abhayaṃ bhāyanti, sammūḷhā caturo janā”ti. (su. ni. aṭṭha. 2.293);

"The earthworm, the blue jay, the curlew, and the pious brahmin: these four deluded beings fear what is not to be feared."

Sesamettha uttānameva.

The rest here is clear.

Doṇabrāhmaṇasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Doṇa Sutta is finished.

3. Saṅgāravasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Saṅgārava Sutta

193. Tatiye (saṃ. ni. ṭī. 2.5.236) paṭhamaññevāti puretaraṃyeva, asajjhāyakatānaṃ [V 3.0057] mantānaṃ appaṭibhānaṃ pageva paṭhamaṃyeva siddhaṃ, tattha vattabbameva natthīti adhippāyo. Pariyuṭṭhānaṃ nāma abhibhavo gahaṇanti āha “kāmarāgapariyuṭṭhitenāti kāmarāgaggahitenā”ti. Vikkhambheti apanetīti vikkhambhanaṃ, paṭipakkhato nissarati etenāti nissaraṇaṃ. Vikkhambhanañca taṃ nissaraṇañcāti vikkhambhananissaraṇaṃ. Tenāha “tatthā”tiādi. Sesapadadvayepi eseva nayo. Attanā araṇīyo pattabbo attho attattho. Tathā parattho veditabbo.

193. In the third sutta, the words 'paṭhamaññeva' mean "even earlier" (puretaraṃyeva). For those who do not recite the mantras, their lack of understanding is established from the very beginning; the meaning is that there is nothing to be said about that. 'Pariyuṭṭhāna' means obsession, a seizing. Thus it is said: 'kāmarāgapariyuṭṭhitena' means "seized by sensual lust." One suppresses (vikkhambheti), that is, one removes; hence 'vikkhambhana,' "suppression." One escapes (nissarati) from the opposite; hence 'nissaraṇa,' "escape." Suppression which is an escape is 'vikkhambhananissaraṇa.' Hence it is said, "there," and so on. The same principle applies to the other two terms. 'Attattho' (one's own welfare) is the goal (attho) to be attained (pattabbo) by oneself (attanā). 'Parattho' (the welfare of others) should be understood in the same way.

“Aniccato anupassanto niccasaññaṃ pajahatī”tiādīsu (paṭi. ma. 1.52) byāpādādīnaṃ anāgatattā byāpādavāre tadaṅganissaraṇaṃ na gahitaṃ. Kiñcāpi na gahitaṃ, paṭisaṅkhānavasena tassa vinodetabbatāya tadaṅganissaraṇampi labbhatevāti sakkā viññātuṃ. Ālokasaññā upacārappattā vā appanāppattā [M 3.0059] vā. Yo koci kasiṇajjhānādibhedo samatho. Dhammavavatthānaṃ upacārappanāppattavasena gahetabbaṃ.

In such passages as: “Contemplating as impermanent, one abandons the perception of permanence” (Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.52), since ill will and so on have not come up for discussion, in the section on ill will the escape by substitution of opposites is not included. Although it is not included, it can be understood that since this state is to be dispelled by way of reflection, the escape by substitution of opposites can still be obtained. The perception of light may have reached either access concentration or absorption concentration. Serenity is any kind of meditation such as the various kasiṇa absorptions. The determination of phenomena should be understood by way of reaching either access or absorption.

Kudhitoti tatto. Ussūrakajātoti tasseva kudhitabhāvassa ussūrakaṃ accuṇhataṃ patto. Tenāha “usumakajāto”ti. Tilabījakādibhedenāti tilabījakaṇṇikakesarādibhedena sevālena. Paṇakenāti udakapicchillena. Appasanno ākulatāya. Asannisinno kalaluppattiyā. Anālokaṭṭhāneti ālokarahite ṭhāne.

'Kudhito' means heated (tatto). 'Ussūrakajāto' means having reached a state of extreme heat, the burning heat of that very heated state. Hence it is said, 'usumakajāto' (having become steamy). 'Tilabījakādibhedena' means with various kinds of water-plants such as those resembling sesame seeds, flower-buds, and filaments. 'Paṇakena' means with water-slime. 'Appasanno' (unclear) is due to turbidity. 'Asannisinno' (not settled) is due to the arising of mud. 'Anālokaṭṭhāne' means in a place devoid of light.

Saṅgāravasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Saṅgārava Sutta is concluded.

4. Kāraṇapālīsuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Kāraṇapālī Sutta

194. Catutthe paṇḍito maññeti ettha maññeti idaṃ “maññatī”ti iminā samānatthaṃ nipātapadaṃ. Tassa iti-saddaṃ ānetvā atthaṃ dassento “paṇḍitoti maññatī”ti āha. Anumatipucchāvasena cetaṃ vuttaṃ. Tenevāha “udāhu no”ti. “Taṃ kiṃ maññati bhavaṃ piṅgiyānī samaṇassa gotamassa paññāveyyattiya”nti vuttamevatthaṃ puna gaṇhanto “paṇḍito maññe”ti āha, tasmā vuttaṃ “bhavaṃ piṅgiyānī samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ paṇḍitoti maññati udāhu no”ti, yathā te khameyya, tathā naṃ kathehīti adhippāyo. Ahaṃ ko nāma, mama avisayo esoti dasseti. Ko cāti hetunissakke paccattavacananti āha “kuto cā”ti. Tathā cāha “kena kāraṇena jānissāmī”ti, yena kāraṇena samaṇassa gotamassa paññāveyyattiyaṃ jāneyyaṃ[V 3.0058], taṃ kāraṇaṃ mayi natthīti adhippāyo. Buddhoyeva bhaveyya abuddhassa sabbathā buddhañāṇānubhāvaṃ jānituṃ asakkuṇeyyattāti. Vuttañhetaṃ – “appamattakaṃ panetaṃ, bhikkhave, oramattakaṃ sīlamattakaṃ, yena puthujjano tathāgatassa vaṇṇaṃ vadamāno vadeyya (dī. ni. 1.7). Atthi, bhikkhave, aññeva dhammā gambhīrā duddasā duranubodhā…pe… yehi tathāgatassa yathābhūtaṃ vaṇṇaṃ sammā vadamāno vadeyyā”ti (dī. ni. 1.28) ca. Etthāti “sopi nūnassa tādiso”ti etasmiṃ pade.

194. In the fourth, in the phrase ‘paṇḍito maññeti’ (he thinks him wise), the word ‘maññeti’ is a particle with the same meaning as ‘maññati’. To show its meaning, bringing in the word ‘iti’, the commentator says: ‘paṇḍito iti maññati’ (he thinks, “He is wise”). This is said by way of asking for agreement, which is why he says, “or not?” Taking up again the meaning of what was said—“What does the venerable Piṅgiyāni think of the recluse Gotama’s wisdom and competence?”—he says, “I think he is wise.” Therefore it is said: “Does the venerable Piṅgiyāni think the recluse Gotama is wise, or not?” The meaning is: “Speak of him in whatever way seems fit to you.” He indicates: “Who am I? This is beyond my scope.” The phrase ‘ko ca’ (and who?) is a term in the singular expressing a reason; thus he says ‘kuto ca’ (and from what cause?). Thus he says: “By what reason would I know?” The meaning is: “The reason by which I might know the recluse Gotama’s wisdom and competence does not exist in me.” For it must be a Buddha, since it is entirely impossible for a non-Buddha to know the power of a Buddha’s knowledge. For this has been said: “This, monks, is a trifling, insignificant matter, a mere matter of virtue, with which a worldling praising the Tathāgata might speak” (DN 1.7). And: “There are, monks, other things, deep, difficult to see, difficult to understand… with which one rightly praising the Tathāgata might speak of him as he really is” (DN 1.28). “Here” refers to the phrase: “He too, surely, must be like that.”

Pasatthappasatthoti [M 3.0060] pasatthehi pāsaṃsehi attano guṇeheva so pasattho, na tassa kittinā, pasaṃsāsabhāveneva pāsaṃsoti attho. Tenāha “sabbaguṇāna”ntiādi. Maṇiratananti cakkavattino maṇiratanaṃ.

‘Pasatthappasattho’ (praised by the praiseworthy) means: he is praised by the praiseworthy, by those who are themselves praiseworthy, on account of his own virtues, not on account of his fame. The meaning is that he is praiseworthy by the very nature of praise. Hence it is said, “of all virtues,” and so on. ‘Maṇiratana’ (the jewel) means the wheel-turning monarch’s jewel.

Sadevake pāsaṃsānampi pāsaṃsoti dassetuṃ “pasatthehi vā”ti dutiyavikappo gahito. Araṇīyato attho, so eva vasatīti vasoti atthavaso. Tassa tassa payogassa ānisaṃsabhūtaṃ phalanti āha “atthavasanti atthānisaṃsa”nti. Attho vā phalaṃ tadadhīnavuttitāya vaso etassāti atthavaso, kāraṇaṃ.

To show that he is praiseworthy even to the praiseworthy in the world with its gods, the second alternative, “or by the praiseworthy,” is taken. ‘Atthavaso’: ‘attho’ is the goal, since it is to be attained; ‘vaso’ is power, because one has power over it. He says ‘atthavasaṃ’ means ‘atthānisaṃsaṃ’ (the benefit of the goal), which is the fruit that is the benefit of this or that endeavor. Alternatively, ‘attho’ is the goal or fruit; ‘vaso’ is power, because one's state is dependent on it. Thus ‘atthavaso’ means the reason.

Khuddakamadhūti khuddakamakkhikāhi katadaṇḍakamadhu. Aneḷakanti niddosaṃ apagatamakkhikaṇḍakaṃ.

‘Khuddakamadhu’ (small honey) is stick-honey made by small bees. ‘Aneḷakaṃ’ means faultless, free from bee larvae and fragments.
