Udāharīyati ubbegapītivasenāti udānaṃ, tathā vā udāharaṇaṃ udānaṃ. Tenāha “udāhāraṃ udāharī”ti. Yathā pana taṃ vacanaṃ udānanti vuccati, taṃ dassetuṃ “yathā hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

An ‘udāna’ is so called because it is uttered out of overwhelming joy. Or, an utterance (‘udāharaṇaṃ’) is an ‘udāna’. Hence it is said: “he uttered an utterance” (‘udāhāraṃ udāharī’). To show how that statement is called an ‘udāna’, the words “just as,” and so on, were said. The rest is easily understood.

Kāraṇapālīsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Kāraṇapālī Sutta is concluded.

5. Piṅgiyānīsuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Piṅgiyāni Sutta

195. Pañcame sabbasaṅgāhikanti sarīragatassa ceva vatthālaṅkāragatassa cāti sabbassa nīlabhāvassa saṅgāhakavacanaṃ. Tassevāti nīlādisabbasaṅgāhikavasena vuttaatthasseva. Vibhāgadassananti pabhedadassanaṃ. Yathā te licchavirājāno apītādivaṇṇā eva keci keci vilepanavasena [V 3.0059] pītādivaṇṇā khāyiṃsu, evaṃ anīlādivaṇṇā eva keci vilepanavasena nīlādivaṇṇā khāyiṃsu. Te kira suvaṇṇavicittehi maṇiobhāsehi ekanīlā viya khāyanti.

195. In the fifth, “all-encompassing” refers to an expression encompassing all blueness, both that pertaining to the body and that pertaining to ornaments. “Of that very” refers to the meaning that has been stated in terms of encompassing all such as blue, etc. “Showing the distinction” means showing the divisions. Just as those Licchavi kings, although not of yellow colour, appeared of yellow colour due to ointments, so too, although not of blue colour, some appeared of blue colour due to ointments. It is said that they appeared uniformly blue due to the brilliance of gold ornamentation and jewels.

Kokanadanti vā padumavisesanaṃ yathā “kokāsaka”nti. Taṃ kira bahupattaṃ vaṇṇasampannaṃ ativiya sugandhañca hoti. Ayañhettha attho – yathā [M 3.0061] kokanadasaṅkhātaṃ padumaṃ pāto sūriyuggamanavelāya phullaṃ vikasitaṃ avītagandhaṃ siyā virocamānaṃ, evaṃ sarīragandhena guṇagandhena ca sugandhaṃ, saradakāle antalikkhe ādiccamiva attano tejasā tapantaṃ, aṅgehi niccharantajutitāya aṅgīrasaṃ sambuddhaṃ passāti.

“Kokanada,” or “kokāsaka,” is a specific kind of lotus. It is said to have many petals, excellent color, and a very pleasant fragrance. The meaning here is this: just as the lotus called “kokanada” blooms in the morning at sunrise, fully open, with unfading fragrance, and radiant, so too the Sambuddha, fragrant with bodily scent and the fragrance of virtues, shining like the autumn sun in the sky with his own radiance, Aṅgīrasa with light emanating from his limbs, is seen.

Piṅgiyānīsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Piṅgiyāni Sutta is finished.

6. Mahāsupinasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Mahāsupina Sutta

196. Chaṭṭhe dhātukkhobhakaraṇapaccayo nāma visabhāgabhesajjasenāsanāhārādipaccayo. Atthakāmatāya vā anatthakāmatāya vāti pasannā atthakāmatāya, kuddhā anatthakāmatāya. Atthāya vā anatthāya vāti sabhāvato bhavitabbāya atthāya vā anatthāya vā. Upasaṃharantīti attano devānubhāvena upanenti. Bodhisattamātā viya puttapaṭilābhanimittanti tadā kira pure puṇṇamāya sattamadivasato paṭṭhāya vigatasurāpānaṃ mālāgandhādivibhūtisampannaṃ nakkhattakīḷaṃ anubhavamānā bodhisattamātā sattame divase pātova uṭṭhāya gandhodakena nahāyitvā sabbālaṅkārabhūsitā varabhojanaṃ bhuñjitvā uposathaṅgāni adhiṭṭhāya sirigabbhaṃ pavisitvā sirisayane nipannā niddaṃ okkamamānā imaṃ supinaṃ addasa – cattāro kira naṃ mahārājāno sayaneneva saddhiṃ ukkhipitvā anotattadahaṃ netvā nahāpetvā dibbavatthaṃ nivāsetvā dibbagandhehi vilimpetvā dibbapupphāni piḷandhetvā tato avidūre rajatapabbato, tassa anto kanakavimānaṃ atthi, tasmiṃ pācīnato sīsaṃ katvā nipajjāpesuṃ. Atha bodhisatto setavaravāraṇo hutvā tato avidūre eko suvaṇṇapabbato, tattha caritvā tato oruyha rajatapabbataṃ āruhitvā kanakavimānaṃ pavisitvā mātaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā dakkhiṇapassaṃ phāletvā kucchiṃ paviṭṭhasadiso ahosi. Imaṃ supinaṃ sandhāya etaṃ vuttaṃ “bodhisattamātā viya puttapaṭilābhanimitta”nti.

196. In the sixth, the condition that causes disturbance of the elements is the condition of incompatible medicine, lodging, food, and so on. It arises either from a desire for benefit or a desire for harm—the pleased act from a desire for benefit, while the angry act from a desire for harm. It may be for benefit or harm—this should be understood as for benefit or harm according to its nature. “They bring it forth” means they present it through their own divine power. “Like the mother of the Bodhisatta, as a sign of obtaining a son”—at that time, it is said, in the past, from the seventh day before the full moon, the mother of the Bodhisatta, having abstained from intoxicants, and replete with garlands, perfumes, and other ornaments, enjoyed festive celebrations. On the seventh day, she rose early in the morning, bathed in scented water, adorned herself with all ornaments, ate excellent food, observed the Uposatha precepts, entered her auspicious chamber, lay down on an auspicious bed, and as she was falling asleep, she saw this dream: Four great kings, it is said, lifted her up along with her bed, took her to Lake Anotatta, bathed her, clothed her in divine garments, anointed her with divine perfumes, adorned her with divine flowers, and then, not far away, there was a silver mountain. Inside it was a golden mansion. There, they laid her down with her head to the east. Then the Bodhisatta, in the form of a magnificent white elephant, having wandered on a nearby golden mountain, descended from there, then climbed the silver mountain, entered the golden mansion, circumambulated his mother, split her right side, and was as if entering her womb. With reference to this dream, it was said: “like the mother of the Bodhisatta, a sign of obtaining a son.”

Kosalarājā [V 3.0060][M 3.0062] viya soḷasa supineti –

Like the king of Kosala, he saw sixteen dreams:

“Usabhā rukkhā gāviyo gavā ca,

Asso kaṃso siṅgālī ca kumbho;

Pokkharaṇī ca apākacandanaṃ,

Lābūni sīdanti silāplavanti.

“Bulls, trees, cows and calves, a horse, a bowl, a she-jackal and a jar, a pond and raw sandalwood, gourds sink, stones float.

“Maṇḍūkiyo kaṇhasappe gilanti,

Kākaṃ suvaṇṇā parivārayanti;

Tasā vakā eḷakānaṃ bhayā hī”ti. (jā. 1.1.77) –

“Female frogs swallow black snakes, golden swans surround a crow; timid wolves fear goats.”

Ime soḷasa supine passanto kosalarājā viya.

Like the king of Kosala seeing these sixteen dreams.

1. Ekadivasaṃ kira kosalamahārājā rattiṃ niddūpagato pacchimayāme soḷasa mahāsupine passi (jā. aṭṭha. 1.1.76 mahāsupinajātakavaṇṇanā). Tattha cattāro añjanavaṇṇā kāḷausabhā “yujjhissāmā”ti catūhi disāhi rājaṅgaṇaṃ āgantvā “usabhayuddhaṃ passissāmā”ti mahājane sannipatite yujjhanākāraṃ dassetvā naditvā gajjitvā ayujjhitvāva paṭikkantā. Imaṃ paṭhamaṃ supinaṃ addasa.

1. One day, it is said, the great king of Kosala, having fallen asleep at night, in the last watch saw sixteen great dreams (Jā. aṭṭha. 1.1.76 Mahāsupinajātakavaṇṇanā). Therein, four black bulls the color of collyrium, saying “We will fight,” came from the four directions to the royal courtyard. When a great crowd had gathered, thinking “We will see the bullfight,” they displayed the manner of fighting, roared, and bellowed, but without actually fighting, they turned back. This was the first dream he saw.

2. Khuddakā rukkhā ceva gacchā ca pathaviṃ bhinditvā vidatthimattampi ratanamattampi anuggantvāva pupphanti ceva phalanti ca. Imaṃ dutiyaṃ addasa.

2. He saw small trees and shrubs breaking through the earth and, having grown not even a span or a cubit, flowering and bearing fruit. This was the second dream he saw.

3. Gāviyo tadahujātānaṃ vacchānaṃ khīraṃ pivantiyo addasa. Ayaṃ tatiyo supino.

3. He saw cows drinking milk from calves born that very day. This was the third dream.

4. Dhuravāhe ārohapariṇāhasampanne mahāgoṇe yugaparamparāya ayojetvā taruṇe godamme dhure yojente addasa. Te dhuraṃ vahituṃ asakkontā chaḍḍetvā aṭṭhaṃsu, sakaṭāni nappavattiṃsu. Ayaṃ catuttho supino.

4. He saw that instead of yoking in succession the great bulls, accustomed to the yoke and endowed with height and girth, they yoked young, untrained bullocks to the pole. Unable to bear the yoke, they threw it off and stood still; the carts did not move. This was the fourth dream.

5. Ekaṃ ubhatomukhaṃ assaṃ addasa. Tassa ubhosu passesu yavasaṃ denti, so dvīhipi mukhehi khādati. Ayaṃ pañcamo supino.

5. He saw a horse with a mouth at both ends. They gave it fodder on both sides, and it ate with both mouths. This was the fifth dream.

6. Mahājano [V 3.0061][M 3.0063] satasahassagghanikaṃ suvaṇṇapātiṃ sammajjitvā “idha passāvaṃ karohī”ti ekassa jarasiṅgālassa upanāmesi. Taṃ tattha passāvaṃ karontaṃ addasa. Ayaṃ chaṭṭho supino.

6. He saw a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand, polished and presented by the people to an old jackal with the words, "Urinate here." He saw the jackal urinating in it. This was the sixth dream.

7. Eko puriso rajjuṃ vaṭṭetvā pādamūle nikkhipati. Tena nisinnapīṭhassa heṭṭhā sayitā chātasiṅgālī tassa ajānantasseva taṃ khādati. Imaṃ sattamaṃ supinaṃ addasa.

7. He saw a man coiling a rope and placing it at his feet. Beneath the man's seat, a hungry she-jackal, unbeknownst to him, was eating it. This was the seventh dream he saw.

8. Rājadvāre bahūhi tucchakumbhehi parivāretvā ṭhapitaṃ ekaṃ mahantaṃ pūritakumbhaṃ addasa. Cattāropi pana vaṇṇā catūhi disāhi catūhi anudisāhi ca ghaṭehi udakaṃ ānetvā pūritakumbhameva pūrenti, pūritaṃ pūritaṃ udakaṃ uttaritvā palāyati. Tepi punappunaṃ tattheva udakaṃ āsiñcanti, tucchakumbhe olokentāpi natthi. Ayaṃ aṭṭhamo supino.

8. At the palace gate, he saw a large, full pot placed and surrounded by many empty ones. People of all four castes brought water in pots from the four directions and the intermediate directions, filling only the full pot. The water, being filled again and again, overflowed and ran away, yet they repeatedly poured water into that very pot, not even looking at the empty pots. This was the eighth dream.

9. Ekaṃ pañcapadumasañchannaṃ gambhīraṃ sabbatotitthaṃ pokkharaṇiṃ addasa. Samantato dvipadacatuppadā otaritvā tattha pānīyaṃ pivanti. Tassa majjhe gambhīraṭṭhāne udakaṃ āvilaṃ, tīrappadese dvipadacatuppadānaṃ akkamanaṭṭhāne acchaṃ vippasannamanāvilaṃ. Ayaṃ navamo supino.

9. He saw a deep pond covered with five kinds of lotuses, with fords on all sides. From all around, two-footed and four-footed creatures went down and drank water there. In the middle, in the deepest part, the water was turbid, but near the shore, in the place where the two-footed and four-footed creatures stepped, it was clear, bright, and undisturbed. This was the ninth dream.

10. Ekissāyeva kumbhiyā paccamānaṃ odanaṃ apākaṃ addasa. “Apāka”nti vicāretvā vibhajitvā ṭhapitaṃ viya tīhākārehi paccamānaṃ ekasmiṃ passe atikilinno hoti, ekasmiṃ uttaṇḍulo, ekasmiṃ supakkoti. Ayaṃ dasamo supino.

10. He saw rice being cooked in a single pot that was not properly cooked; it was as if it had been divided, cooking in three ways: in one part it was soggy, in another the grains were hard, and in another it was perfectly cooked. This was the tenth dream.

11. Satasahassagghanakaṃ candanasāraṃ pūtitakkena vikkiṇante addasa. Ayaṃ ekādasamo supino.

11. He saw heartwood of sandalwood worth a hundred thousand being sold for spoiled buttermilk. This was the eleventh dream.

12. Tucchalābūni udake sīdantāni addasa. Ayaṃ dvādasamo supino.

12. He saw hollow gourds sinking in the water. This was the twelfth dream.

13. Mahantamahantā kūṭāgārappamāṇā ghanasilā nāvā viya udake plavamānā addasa. Ayaṃ terasamo supino.

13. He saw massive, solid boulders the size of gabled mansions floating on the water like boats. This was the thirteenth dream.

14. Khuddakamadhukapupphappamāṇā maṇḍūkiyo mahante kaṇhasappe vegena anubandhitvā uppalanāḷe viya chinditvā maṃsaṃ khāditvā gilantiyo addasa. Ayaṃ cuddasamo supino.

14. He saw small female frogs, the size of small madhuka flowers, swiftly chasing large black snakes, severing them as if they were lotus stalks, and eating and swallowing their flesh. This was the fourteenth dream.

15. Dasahi [V 3.0062][M 3.0064] asaddhammehi samannāgataṃ gāmagocaraṃ kākaṃ kañcanavaṇṇavaṇṇatāya “suvaṇṇā”ti laddhanāme suvaṇṇarājahaṃse parivārente addasa. Ayaṃ pannarasamo supino.

15. He saw a village-frequenting crow, endowed with ten unwholesome qualities, being attended upon by royal golden swans, who had received the name 'Suvaṇṇa' on account of their golden color. This was the fifteenth dream.

16. Pubbe dīpino eḷake khādanti. Te pana eḷake dīpino anubandhitvā muramurāti khādante addasa. Athaññe tasā vakā eḷake dūratova disvā tasitā tāsappattā hutvā eḷakānaṃ bhayā palāyitvā gumbagahanāni pavisitvā nilīyiṃsu. Ayaṃ soḷasamo supino.

16. Formerly, leopards would eat goats. But then he saw goats chasing those leopards and devouring them with a crunching sound. And other timid wolves, seeing the goats from afar, became terrified and overcome with fear, and fleeing in fear of the goats, they entered thickets and dense bushes and hid. This was the sixteenth dream.

1. Tattha adhammikānaṃ rājūnaṃ, adhammikānañca manussānaṃ kāle loke viparivattamāne kusale osanne akusale ussanne lokassa parihānakāle devo na sammā vasissati, meghapādā pacchijjissanti, sassāni milāyissanti, dubbhikkhaṃ bhavissati, vassitukāmā viya catūhi disāhi meghā uṭṭhahitvā itthikāhi ātape patthaṭānaṃ vīhiādīnaṃ temanabhayena antopavesitakāle purisesu kudālapiṭake ādāya āḷibandhanatthāya nikkhantesu vassanākāraṃ dassetvā gajjitvā vijjulatā nicchāretvā usabhā viya ayujjhitvā avassitvāva palāyissanti. Ayaṃ paṭhamassa vipāko.

1. In that case, in the time of unrighteous kings and unrighteous people, when the world is in upheaval, when the wholesome has declined and the unwholesome has arisen, in the time of the world's decay, the heavens will not rain properly, the rain clouds will be cut off, the crops will wither, and there will be a famine. As if wishing to rain, clouds will rise from the four directions, and at the time when women, fearing they will get wet, bring inside the rice and other grains that were spread in the sun, and when men go out with spades and baskets to build up the dikes, the clouds will show the appearance of raining, and having thundered and emitted lightning, having fought like bulls, they will flee without having rained at all. This is the result of the first dream.

2. Lokassa parihīnakāle manussānaṃ parittāyukakāle sattā tibbarāgā bhavissanti, asampattavayāva kumāriyo purisantaraṃ gantvā utuniyo ceva gabbhiniyo ca hutvā puttadhītāhi vaḍḍhissanti. Khuddakarukkhānaṃ pupphaṃ viya hi tāsaṃ utunibhāvo, phalaṃ viya ca puttadhītaro bhavissanti. Ayaṃ dutiyassa vipāko.

2. In the time of the world's decay, when the lifespan of humans is short, beings will be intensely lustful. Girls, before even reaching the proper age, will go to other men, and having become menstruous and pregnant, they will be augmented by sons and daughters. For their menstruation will be like the flower of a small tree, and their sons and daughters will be like the fruit. This is the result of the second dream.

3. Manussānaṃ jeṭṭhāpacāyikakammassa naṭṭhakāle sattā mātāpitūsu vā sassusasuresu vā lajjaṃ anupaṭṭhapetvā sayameva kuṭumbaṃ saṃvidahantāva ghāsacchādanamattampi mahallakānaṃ dātukāmā dassanti, adātukāmā na dassanti. Mahallakā anāthā hutvā asayaṃvasī dārake ārādhetvā jīvissanti tadahujātānaṃ vacchakānaṃ khīraṃ pivantiyo mahāgāviyo viya. Ayaṃ tatiyassa vipāko.

3. When the practice of revering elders has disappeared among human beings, beings will not show respect toward their parents or parents-in-law. Managing the household themselves, they will give a mere measure of food and clothing to the elderly if they wish to give, but if they do not wish to give, they will not. The elderly, having become helpless and dependent, will have to live by gratifying the young, like great cows drinking the milk of their own newborn calves. This is the result of the third dream.

4. Adhammikarājūnaṃ [M 3.0065] kāle adhammikarājāno paṇḍitānaṃ paveṇikusalānaṃ kammanittharaṇasamatthānaṃ mahāmattānaṃ yasaṃ na dassanti, dhammasabhāyaṃ vinicchayaṭṭhānepi paṇḍite vohārakusale mahallake amacce na ṭhapessanti, tabbiparītānaṃ pana taruṇataruṇānaṃ yasaṃ dassanti, tathārūpe eva ca vinicchayaṭṭhāne ṭhapessanti. Te rājakammāni ceva yuttāyuttañca ajānantā [V 3.0063] neva taṃ yasaṃ ukkhipituṃ sakkhissanti, na rājakammāni nittharituṃ. Te asakkontā kammadhuraṃ chaḍḍessanti, mahallakāpi paṇḍitāmaccā yasaṃ alabhantā kiccāni nittharituṃ samatthāpi “kiṃ amhākaṃ etehi, mayaṃ bāhirakā jātā, abbhantarikā taruṇadārakā jānissantī”ti uppannāni kammāni na karissanti. Evaṃ sabbathāpi tesaṃ rājūnaṃ hāniyeva bhavissati, dhuraṃ vahituṃ asamatthānaṃ vacchadammānaṃ dhure yojitakālo viya dūravāhānañca mahāgoṇānaṃ yugaparamparāya ayojitakālo viya bhavissati. Ayaṃ catutthassa vipāko.

4. In the time of unrighteous kings, unrighteous rulers will not grant honor to their great ministers who are wise, skilled in tradition, and capable of accomplishing tasks. In the hall of justice, they will not appoint wise, judicious, and elderly ministers to positions of judgment. Instead, they will grant honor to their opposites, the very young, and will appoint such persons to positions of judgment. Not knowing the duties of kingship nor what is proper and improper, they will be unable to uphold that honor or to accomplish the royal duties. Being unable, they will cast off the yoke of their work. And the elderly wise ministers, though capable of accomplishing their duties, will not receive honor and will think, 'What is this to us? We have become outsiders; the young boys on the inside will know.' Thus they will not perform the duties that arise. In every way, this will lead only to the decline of those kings. It will be like a time when young bullocks unable to bear the yoke are yoked to the pole, and when great draft oxen are left unyoked from the succession of yokes. This is the result of the fourth dream.

5. Adhammikarājakāleyeva adhammikabālarājāno adhammike lolamanusse vinicchaye ṭhapessanti, te pāpapuññesu anādarā bālā sabhāyaṃ nisīditvā vinicchayaṃ dentā ubhinnampi atthapaccatthikānaṃ hatthato lañjaṃ gahetvā khādissanti asso viya dvīhi mukhehi yavasaṃ. Ayaṃ pañcamassa vipāko.

5. In the time of unrighteous kings, foolish and unrighteous rulers will appoint unrighteous and greedy men to judicial posts. These foolish men, having no regard for demerit and merit, will sit in the assembly giving judgment and will take and devour bribes from the hands of both litigants, like a horse that eats fodder with both mouths. This is the result of the fifth dream.

6. Adhammikāyeva vijātirājāno jātisampannānaṃ kulaputtānaṃ āsaṅkāya yasaṃ na dassanti, akulīnānaṃyeva dassanti. Evaṃ mahākulāni duggatāni bhavissanti, lāmakakulāni issarāni. Te ca kulīnapurisā jīvituṃ asakkontā “ime nissāya jīvissāmā”ti akulīnānaṃ dhītaro dassanti, iti tāsaṃ kuladhītānaṃ akulīnehi saddhiṃ saṃvāso jarasiṅgālassa suvaṇṇapātiyaṃ passāvakaraṇasadiso bhavissati. Ayaṃ chaṭṭhassa vipāko.

6. Unrighteous kings of base birth, out of suspicion, will not grant honor to the well-born sons of good families but will grant it only to those of low birth. Thus great families will become impoverished, while base families will become powerful. Then the men of good birth, unable to support themselves, will give their daughters to those of low birth, thinking, 'We will live by depending on them.' Thus the cohabitation of these daughters of good families with men of low birth will be like an old jackal urinating into a golden bowl. This is the result of the sixth dream.

7. Gacchante gacchante kāle itthiyo purisalolā surālolā alaṅkāralolā visikhālolā āmisalolā bhavissanti dussīlā durācārā. Tā sāmikehi kasigorakkhādīni kammāni katvā kicchena [M 3.0066] kasirena sambhataṃ dhanaṃ jārehi saddhiṃ suraṃ pivantiyo mālāgandhavilepanaṃ dhārayamānā antogehe accāyikampi kiccaṃ anoloketvā gehaparikkhepassa uparibhāgenapi chiddaṭṭhānehipi jāre upadhārayamānā sve vapitabbayuttakaṃ bījampi koṭṭetvā yāgubhattakhajjakāni pacitvā khādamānā vilumpissanti heṭṭhāpīṭhake nipannachātasiṅgālī viya vaṭṭetvā vaṭṭetvā pādamūle nikkhittarajjuṃ. Ayaṃ sattamassa vipāko.

7. As time goes on, women will become lustful for men, fond of liquor, fond of adornments, fond of gadding about, and greedy for material things; they will be immoral and ill-behaved. While their husbands toil at farming and cattle-herding, gathering wealth with difficulty and hardship, these women will drink liquor with their lovers, wear garlands, and use perfumes and unguents. They will neglect even urgent duties in the house, and watching for their lovers through openings in the house's enclosure, they will pound even the seed grain that should be sown the next day, cook gruel, rice, and savories, and eat them. They will thus plunder the household, just as a hungry she-jackal lying on a low stool might twist and turn a leather strap left at the foot of the bed. This is the result of the seventh dream.

8. Gacchante gacchante kāle loko parihāyissati, raṭṭhaṃ nirojaṃ bhavissati, rājāno duggatā kapaṇā bhavissanti. Yo issaro bhavissati, tassa bhaṇḍāgāre satasahassamattā bhavissanti. Te evaṃduggatā sabbe jānapade attanova kammaṃ kāressanti, upaddutā manussā sake kammante chaḍḍetvā rājūnaṃyeva atthāya pubbaṇṇāparaṇṇāni vapantā rakkhantā lāyantā maddantā [V 3.0064] pavesentā ucchukkhettāni karontā yantāni vāhentā phāṇitādīni pacantā pupphārāme phalārāme ca karontā tattha tattha nipphannāni pubbaṇṇādīni āharitvā rañño koṭṭhāgārameva pūressanti. Attano gehesu tucchakoṭṭhe olokentāpi na bhavissanti, tucchakumbhe anoloketvā pūritakumbhapūraṇasadisameva bhavissati. Ayaṃ aṭṭhamassa vipāko.

8. As time goes on, the world will decline, the kingdom will become devoid of vigor, and kings will become poor and wretched. Whoever is the ruler will have only a hundred thousand in his treasury. Being so poor, they will make all the people of the countryside work for them. The afflicted people will have to abandon their own work and labor only for the sake of the kings: sowing and reaping early and late crops, guarding them, threshing them, and bringing them in; making sugarcane fields, operating the mills, and boiling molasses; and making flower gardens and fruit orchards. They will gather the various crops produced here and there and fill only the king's granaries. In their own houses, they will not even look at their empty granaries. Their work will be just like filling up a pot that is already full, while ignoring their own empty pots. This is the result of the eighth dream.

9. Gacchante gacchante kāle rājāno adhammikā bhavissanti, chandādivasena agatiṃ gacchantā rajjaṃ kāressanti, dhammena vinicchayaṃ nāma na dassanti lañjavittakā bhavissanti dhanalolā, raṭṭhavāsikesu tesaṃ khantimettānuddayā nāma na bhavissanti, kakkhaḷā pharusā ucchuyante ucchubhaṇḍikā viya manusse pīḷentā nānappakāraṃ baliṃ uppādetvā dhanaṃ gaṇhissanti. Manussā balipīḷitā kiñci dātuṃ asakkontā gāmanigamādayo chaḍḍetvā paccantaṃ gantvā vāsaṃ kappessanti. Majjhimajanapado suñño bhavissati, paccanto ghanavāso seyyathāpi pokkharaṇiyā majjhe udakaṃ āvilaṃ pariyante vippasannaṃ. Ayaṃ navamassa vipāko.

9. As time goes on, kings will become unrighteous. They will rule by following the wrong courses, swayed by desire and other biases. They will not give judgment in accordance with the Dhamma but will be eager for bribes and greedy for wealth. They will have no patience, loving-kindness, or compassion for the inhabitants of their kingdom. They will be rough and harsh, and they will crush the people to extract wealth by imposing various kinds of taxes, just as one crushes a bundle of sugarcane in a press. Oppressed by taxes and unable to pay, the people will abandon their villages, towns, and so on, and will flee to the border regions to live. The central region of the country will become deserted, while the border regions will become densely populated, just like a pond that is turbid in the middle and clear at the edges. This is the result of the ninth dream.

10. Gacchante gacchante kāle rājāno adhammikā bhavissanti, tesu adhammikesu rājayuttāpi brāhmaṇagahapatikāpi negamajānapadāpīti samaṇabrāhmaṇe [M 3.0067] upādāya sabbe manussā adhammikā bhavissanti. Tato tesaṃ ārakkhadevatā, balipaṭiggāhikadevatā, rukkhadevatā, ākāsaṭṭhadevatāti evaṃ devatāpi adhammikā bhavissanti. Adhammikarājūnaṃ rajje vātā visamā kharā vāyissanti, te ākāsaṭṭhakavimānāni kampessanti. Tesu kampitesu devatā kupitā devaṃ vassituṃ na dassanti. Vassamānopi sakalaraṭṭhe ekappahāreneva na vassissati, vassamānopi sabbattha kasikammassa vā vappakammassa vā upakāro hutvā na vassissati. Yathā ca raṭṭhe, evaṃ janapadepi gāmepi ekataḷākasarepi ekappahārena na vassissati, taḷākassa uparibhāge vassanto heṭṭhābhāge na vassissati, heṭṭhā vassanto upari na vassissati. Ekasmiṃ bhāge sassaṃ ativassena nassissati, ekasmiṃ avassanena milāyissati, ekasmiṃ sammā vassamāno sampādessati. Evaṃ ekassa rañño rajje vuttasassā vipāko. Tippakārā bhavissanti ekakumbhiyā odano viya. Ayaṃ dasamassa vipāko.

10. As time goes on, kings will become unrighteous. When the kings are unrighteous, the royal officials, brahmins, householders, and the people of the towns and countryside—all human beings, including ascetics and brahmins—will become unrighteous. Then their guardian deities, the deities who receive offerings, the tree deities, and the deities dwelling in space will also become unrighteous. In the realm of unrighteous kings, the winds will blow unevenly and fiercely, shaking the celestial mansions of the space-dwelling deities. When these are shaken, the deities will become angry and will not allow it to rain. When it does rain, it will not fall over the entire country at once, nor will it fall in a way that benefits agriculture and sowing everywhere. Just as in the country, so too in a district, a village, or even a single pond or lake, the rain will not fall all at once. If it rains on the upper part of a pond, it will not rain on the lower part; if it rains on the lower part, it will not rain on the upper part. In one area the crops will be ruined by too much rain; in another they will wither from lack of rain; in another they will be perfected by just the right amount of rain. Thus the crops sown in the realm of a single king will have a threefold outcome, like rice cooked in a single pot. This is the result of the tenth dream.

11. Gacchante gacchanteyeva kāle sāsane parihāyante paccayalolā alajjikā bahū bhikkhū bhavissanti. Te bhagavatā paccayaloluppaṃ nimmathetvā kathitadhammadesanaṃ cīvarādicatupaccayahetu paresaṃ desessanti. Paccayehi mucchitvā nittharaṇapakkhe ṭhitā nibbānābhimukhaṃ katvā desetuṃ na sakkhissanti. Kevalaṃ “padabyañjanasampattiñceva madhurasaddañca sutvā [V 3.0065] mahagghāni cīvarādīni dassanti”iccevaṃ desessanti. Apare antaravīthicatukkarājadvārādīsu nisīditvā kahāpaṇaaḍḍhakahāpaṇapādamāsakarūpādīnipi nissāya desessanti. Iti bhagavatā nibbānagghanakaṃ katvā desitaṃ dhammaṃ catupaccayatthāya ceva kahāpaṇādiatthāya ca vikkiṇitvā desentā satasahassagghanakaṃ candanasāraṃ pūtitakkena vikkiṇantā viya bhavissanti. Ayaṃ ekādasamassa vipāko.

11. As time goes on and the Teaching declines, there will be many shameless bhikkhus who are greedy for requisites. For the sake of the four requisites, such as robes, they will teach to others the very Dhamma teaching spoken by the Blessed One for crushing greed for requisites. Infatuated by requisites, though they belong to the party of deliverance, they will be unable to teach with Nibbāna as their goal. They will teach only with the thought: 'Having heard our accomplishment in words and phrases and our sweet voices, people will give us expensive robes and other things.' Others will sit at crossroads, in the middle of streets, and at the king's gate, and teach the Dhamma in exchange for kahāpaṇas, half-kahāpaṇas, quarter-kahāpaṇas, māsakas, and other coins. Thus they will teach by selling the Dhamma—which was taught by the Blessed One as having the value of Nibbāna—for the sake of the four requisites and for the sake of coins. They will be like those who sell sandalwood core worth a hundred thousand for sour buttermilk. This is the result of the eleventh dream.

12. Adhammikarājakāle loke viparivattanteyeva rājāno jātisampannānaṃ kulaputtānaṃ yasaṃ na dassanti, akulīnānaññeva dassanti. Te issarā bhavissanti, itarā daliddā. Rājasammukhepi rājadvārepi amaccasammukhepi vinicchayaṭṭhānepi tucchalābusadisānaṃ akulīnānaṃyeva kathā osīditvā ṭhitā viya niccalā suppatiṭṭhitā bhavissati. Saṅghasannipātepi saṅghakammagaṇakammaṭṭhānesu [M 3.0068] ceva pattacīvarapariveṇādivinicchayaṭṭhānesu ca dussīlānaṃ pāpapuggalānaṃyeva kathā niyyānikā bhavissati, na lajjibhikkhūnanti evaṃ sabbatthāpi tucchalābūnaṃ sīdanakālo viya bhavissati. Ayaṃ dvādasamassa vipāko.

12. In a time of unrighteous kings, when the world is being overturned, kings will not grant honor to sons of good family endowed with high birth, but will grant it only to those of low birth. The latter will become influential, while the former will be impoverished. In the presence of the king, at the royal gate, in the presence of ministers, and in the courts of justice, the word of the low-born—who are like empty gourds—will sink in and stand firm, as if immovable and well-established. In the assembly of the Sangha, too, in places for formal acts of the Sangha and acts of a chapter, and in places for deciding matters concerning bowls, robes, monastic cells, and the like, the word of immoral, evil persons will be conclusive, not that of conscientious bhikkhus. Thus everywhere it will be like a time for the sinking of empty gourds. This is the result of the twelfth dream.

13. Tādiseyeva kāle adhammikarājāno akulīnānaṃ yasaṃ dassanti. Te issarā bhavissanti, kulīnā duggatā. Tesu na keci gāravaṃ karissanti, itaresuyeva karissanti. Rājasammukhe vā amaccasammukhe vā vinicchayaṭṭhāne vā vinicchayakusalānaṃ ghanasilāsadisānaṃ kulaputtānaṃ kathā na ogāhitvā patiṭṭhahissati. Tesu kathentesu “kiṃ ime kathentī”ti itare parihāsameva karissanti. Bhikkhusannipātepi vuttappakāresu ṭhānesu neva pesale bhikkhū garukātabbe maññissanti, nāpi nesaṃ kathā pariyogāhitvā patiṭṭhahissati, silānaṃ plavanakālo viya bhavissati. Ayaṃ terasamassa vipāko.

13. In such a time, unrighteous kings will grant honor to the low-born. The latter will become influential, while the high-born will be wretched. No one will show respect to the high-born; they will show it only to the others. In the presence of the king, or of ministers, or in a court of justice, the word of sons of good family who are skilled in judgment—men like solid rock—will not sink in and become established. When they speak, the others will only mock them, saying, ‘What are these fellows saying?’ In the assembly of bhikkhus, too, in the kinds of places mentioned above, they will not consider amiable bhikkhus as worthy of respect, nor will their word be taken to heart and established. It will be like a time for stones to float. This is the result of the thirteenth dream.

14. Loke parihāyanteyeva manussā tibbarāgādijātikā kilesānuvattakā hutvā taruṇānaṃ attano bhariyānaṃ vase vattissanti. Gehe dāsakammakārādayopi gomahiṃsādayopi hiraññasuvaṇṇampi sabbaṃ tāsaṃyeva āyattaṃ bhavissati. “Asukaṃ hiraññasuvaṇṇaṃ vā paricchadādijātaṃ vā kaha”nti vutte “yattha vā tattha vā hotu, kiṃ tuyhiminā byāpārena, tvaṃ mayhaṃ ghare santaṃ vā asantaṃ vā jānitukāmo jāto”ti vatvā nānappakārehi akkositvā mukhasattīhi koṭṭetvā dāsaceṭake viya vase katvā attano issariyaṃ pavattessanti. Evaṃ madhukapupphappamāṇānaṃ maṇḍūkīnaṃ āsivise kaṇhasappe gilanakālo viya bhavissati. Ayaṃ cuddasamassa vipāko.

14. When the world is declining, men, being of a nature of intense lust and other defilements and followers of the defilements, will fall under the sway of their own young wives. In the house, the slaves, workers, and so on, the cattle, buffaloes, and so on, and the gold and silver—everything will be under their control. If the husband asks, ‘Where is such-and-such gold, silver, or household requisite?’ she will reply: ‘Let it be wherever it is! What business is it of yours? Have you become keen to know what is and what is not in my house?’ Then, having reviled him in various ways and struck him with sharp words, bringing him under their control like a male or female slave, they will exercise their own authority. Thus it will be like a time for female frogs the size of a madhuka flower to swallow venomous black snakes. This is the result of the fourteenth dream.

15. Dubbalarājakāle [V 3.0066] pana rājāno hatthisippādīsu akusalā yuddhesu avisāradā bhavissanti. Te attano rājādhipaccaṃ āsaṅkamānā samānajātikānaṃ kulaputtānaṃ issariyaṃ adatvā attano pādamūlikanahāpanakappakādīnaṃ dassanti. Jātigottasampannā kulaputtā rājakule patiṭṭhaṃ alabhamānā jīvikaṃ kappetuṃ asamatthā hutvā issariye ṭhite jātigottahīne akulīne upaṭṭhahantā vicarissanti, suvaṇṇarājahaṃsehi kākassa parivāritakālo viya bhavissati. Ayaṃ pannarasamassa vipāko.

15. Then, in a time of weak kings, the rulers will be unskilled in arts such as elephantry and inexperienced in battle. Fearing for their own royal sovereignty, they will not grant authority to sons of good family of equal birth, but will give it to their own foot-servants, bath attendants, barbers, and the like. Then sons of good family, endowed with high birth and clan, unable to gain a footing in the royal court and incapable of making a living, will wander about attending on those of low birth and clan who are established in authority. It will be like a time when a crow is attended upon by golden royal swans. This is the result of the fifteenth dream.

16. Adhammikarājakāleyeva [M 3.0069] ca akulīnāva rājavallabhā issarā bhavissanti, kulīnā apaññātā duggatā. Te rājānaṃ attano kathaṃ gāhāpetvā vinicchayaṭṭhānādīsu balavanto hutvā dubbalānaṃ paveṇiāgatāni khettavatthādīni “amhākaṃ santakānī”ti abhiyuñjitvā te “na tumhākaṃ, amhāka”nti āgantvā vinicchayaṭṭhānādīsu vivadante vettalatādīhi paharāpetvā gīvāyaṃ gahetvā apakaḍḍhāpetvā “attano pamāṇaṃ na jānātha, amhehi saddhiṃ vivadatha, idāni vo paharāpetvā rañño kathetvā hatthapādacchedādīni kāressāmā”ti santajjessanti. Te tesaṃ bhayena attano santakāni vatthūni “tumhākaṃyeva tāni, gaṇhathā”ti niyyātetvā attano gehāni pavisitvā bhītā nipajjissanti. Pāpabhikkhūpi pesale bhikkhū yathāruci viheṭhessanti. Pesalā bhikkhū paṭisaraṇaṃ alabhamānā araññaṃ pavisitvā gahanaṭṭhānesu nilīyissanti. Evaṃ hīnajaccehi ceva pāpabhikkhūhi ca upaddutānaṃ jātimantakulaputtānañceva pesalabhikkhūnañca eḷakānaṃ bhayena tasavakānaṃ palāyanakālo viya bhavissati. Ayaṃ soḷasamassa vipāko. Evaṃ tassa tassa anatthassa pubbanimittabhūte soḷasa mahāsupine passi. Tena vuttaṃ “kosalarājā viya soḷasa supine”ti. Ettha ca pubbanimittato attano atthānatthanimittaṃ supinaṃ passanto attano kammānubhāvena passati. Kosalarājā viya lokassa atthānatthanimittaṃ supinaṃ passanto pana sabbasattasādhāraṇakammānubhāvena passatīti veditabbaṃ.

16. And in a time of unrighteous kings, it will be the low-born who become royal favorites and influential, while the high-born will be unknown and destitute. Having made the king accept their word, they will become powerful in the courts of justice and so on. They will lay claim to the fields, lands, and so on that have come down by tradition to the weak, saying, ‘These are ours!’ When the owners come and dispute this in the courts of justice, saying, ‘They are not yours, they are ours,’ the powerful will have them beaten with canes and the like, seize them by the neck, drag them away, and threaten them, saying: ‘You do not know your own measure! You dispute with us! Now we will have you flogged, and after speaking to the king, we will have your hands and feet cut off!’ Out of fear of them, the owners will hand over their own property, saying, ‘They are yours, take them,’ and entering their own houses, they will lie down terrified. Evil bhikkhus, too, will harass amiable bhikkhus as they please. Finding no refuge, the amiable bhikkhus will enter the forest and hide in impenetrable places. Thus for the high-born sons of good family and the amiable bhikkhus, oppressed by the base-born and by evil bhikkhus, it will be like a time when jackals flee in fear of rams. This is the result of the sixteenth dream. Thus he saw these sixteen great dreams, which were portents of this and that disaster. Therefore it is said: ‘like King Kosala, sixteen dreams.’ Herein, it should be understood that one who sees a dream that is a portent of his own welfare or harm sees it through the power of his own kamma. But one who, like King Kosala, sees a dream that is a portent of the welfare or harm of the world sees it through the power of kamma common to all beings.

Kuddhā hi devatāti mahānāgavihāre mahātherassa kuddhā devatā viya. Rohaṇe kira mahānāgavihāre mahāthero bhikkhusaṅghaṃ anapaloketvāva ekaṃ nāgarukkhaṃ chindāpesi. Rukkhe adhivatthā devatā therassa kuddhā paṭhamameva naṃ saccasupinena palobhetvā pacchā “ito te sattadivasamatthake upaṭṭhāko rājā marissatī”ti supine ārocesi. Thero taṃ kathaṃ āharitvā rājorodhānaṃ ācikkhi. Tā ekappahāreneva mahāviravaṃ viraviṃsu. Rājā “kiṃ eta”nti pucchi. Tā “evaṃ therena vutta”nti ārocayiṃsu. Rājā divasaṃ gaṇāpetvā sattāhe vītivatte therassa hatthapāde chindāpesi. Ekantaṃ saccameva hotīti phalassa saccabhāvato vuttaṃ, dassanaṃ [M 3.0070] pana vipallatthameva[V 3.0067]. Teneva pahīnavipallāsā pubbanimittabhūtampi supinaṃ na passanti. Dvīhi tīhipi kāraṇehi kadāci supinaṃ passatīti āha “saṃsaggabhedato”ti. “Asekhā na passanti pahīnavipallāsattā”ti vacanato catunnampi kāraṇānaṃ vipallāsā eva mūlakāraṇanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

A deity was angry: this is like the deity at the Mahānāga Vihāra who was angry with the great elder. It is said that at the Mahānāga Vihāra in Rohaṇa, a great elder had a certain nāga-tree cut down without having sought permission from the community of bhikkhus. The deity dwelling in the tree became angry with the elder. First she enticed him with a true dream, and then later she announced to him in a dream: ‘Seven days from now your royal patron will die.’ The elder took this message and reported it to the king’s harem. They at once raised a great cry. The king asked, ‘What is this?’ and they told him, ‘This is what the elder has said.’ The king had the days counted, and when seven days had passed, he had the elder’s hands and feet cut off. It is said, ‘It is absolutely true,’ because of the truth of the result, but the vision itself was distorted. For that reason, those who have abandoned distortion do not see even a dream that is a portent. When it is said, ‘Sometimes one sees a dream for two or three reasons,’ he says this refers to ‘from a break in association.’ From the statement, ‘Those beyond training do not see dreams because they have abandoned distortion,’ it should be understood that distortion is the root cause of all four reasons.

Tanti supinakāle pavattaṃ bhavaṅgacittaṃ. Rūpanimittādiārammaṇanti kammakammanimittagatinimittato aññaṃ rūpanimittādiārammaṇaṃ na hoti. Īdisānīti paccakkhato anubhūtapubbaparikappitarūpādiārammaṇāni ceva rāgādisampayuttāni ca. Sabbohārikacittenāti pakaticittena.

That: the life-continuum consciousness that occurs at the time of a dream. An object such as a sign of form: it does not have as its object a sign of form, etc., that is other than kamma, the sign of kamma, or the sign of destiny. Such as these: objects such as forms that have been previously experienced directly or have been conceived, and which are associated with lust and so on. With conventional consciousness: that is, with the normal consciousness.

Dvīhi antehi muttoti kusalākusalasaṅkhātehi dvīhi antehi mutto. Āvajjanatadārammaṇakkhaṇeti idaṃ yāva tadārammaṇuppatti, tāva pavattacittavāraṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. “Supineneva diṭṭhaṃ viya me, sutaṃ viya meti kathanakāle pana abyākatoyeva āvajjanamattasseva uppajjanato”ti vadanti. Evaṃ vadantehi pañcadvāre dutiyamoghavāre viya manodvārepi āvajjanaṃ dvattikkhattuṃ uppajjitvā javanaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā bhavaṅgaṃ otaratīti adhippetanti daṭṭhabbaṃ ekacittakkhaṇikassa āvajjanassa uppattiyaṃ “diṭṭhaṃ viya me, sutaṃ viya me”ti kappanāya asambhavato. Ettha ca “supinantepi tadārammaṇavacanato paccuppannavasena atītavasena vā sabhāvadhammā supinante ārammaṇaṃ hontī”ti vadanti. “Yadipi supinante vibhūtaṃ hutvā upaṭṭhite rūpādivatthumhi tadārammaṇaṃ vuttaṃ, tathāpi supinante upaṭṭhitanimittassa parikappavasena gahetabbatāya dubbalabhāvato dubbalavatthukattāti vutta”nti vadanti. Keci pana “karajakāyassa nirussāhasantabhāvappattito tannissitahadayavatthu na suppasannaṃ hoti, tato tannissitāpi cittappavatti na suppasannā asuppasannavaṭṭinissitadīpappabhā viya, tasmā dubbalavatthukattāti ettha dubbalahadayavatthukattā”ti atthaṃ vadanti. Vīmaṃsitvā yuttataraṃ gahetabbaṃ.

Freed from two ends: freed from the two ends designated as wholesome and unwholesome. At the moments of adverting and registration: this is said with reference to the cognitive process that occurs up to the arising of registration. Some say: “At the time of saying, ‘It is as if I saw it in a dream, as if I heard it,’ only a moment of adverting arises, which is indeterminate.” It should be understood that those who say this hold that, just as in the second ‘vain process’ at the five sense doors, so at the mind door, adverting arises two or three times, stands in the place of impulsion, and then sinks into the life-continuum; for if only a single moment of adverting arose, the conceiving, ‘It is as if I saw it, as if I heard it,’ would be impossible. And here some say: “Because registration is mentioned even in a dream, real phenomena become an object in a dream in either a present or a past mode.” Others say: “Although registration is mentioned when a form-object, etc., has appeared clearly in a dream, still, because the sign that appears in a dream must be grasped by way of conception, it is said to have a weak basis on account of its weakness.” But some explain the meaning thus: “Because the body produced by kamma has reached a state of exhaustion and listlessness, the heart-base on which it depends is not very clear; therefore the process of consciousness dependent on it is also not very clear, like the light of a lamp dependent on an unclean wick. Therefore, ‘on account of having a weak basis’ here means on account of having a weak heart-base.” Having investigated, the more suitable meaning should be adopted.

Supinantacetanāti manodvārikajavanavasena pavattā supinantacetanā. Supinañhi passanto manodvārikeneva javanena passati, na pañcadvārikena. Paṭibujjhanto ca manodvārikeneva paṭibujjhati, na pañcadvārikena. Niddāyantassa hi mahāvaṭṭiṃ jāletvā dīpe cakkhusamīpaṃ upanīte paṭhamaṃ cakkhudvārikaṃ āvajjanaṃ bhavaṅgaṃ na āvaṭṭeti, manodvārikameva āvaṭṭeti. Atha javanaṃ javitvā bhavaṅgaṃ otarati. Dutiyavāre cakkhudvārikaāvajjanaṃ bhavaṅgaṃ āvaṭṭeti[M 3.0071], tato cakkhuviññāṇādīni javanapariyosānāni pavattanti, tadanantaraṃ bhavaṅgaṃ pavattati. Tatiyavāre manodvārikaāvajjanena bhavaṅge āvaṭṭite manodvārikajavanaṃ javati. Tena cittena “kiṃ ayaṃ imasmiṃ ṭhāne āloko”ti jānāti. Tathā niddāyantassa kaṇṇasamīpe tūriyesu paggahitesu[V 3.0068], ghānasamīpe sugandhesu vā duggandhesu vā pupphesu upanītesu, mukhe sappimhi vā phāṇite vā pakkhitte, piṭṭhiyaṃ pāṇinā pahāre dinne paṭhamaṃ sotadvārikādīni āvajjanāni bhavaṅgaṃ na āvaṭṭenti, manodvārikameva āvaṭṭeti, atha javanaṃ javitvā bhavaṅgaṃ otarati. Dutiyavāre sotadvārikādīni āvajjanāni bhavaṅgaṃ āvaṭṭenti, tato sotaghānajivhākāyaviññāṇādīni javanapariyosānāni pavattanti, tadanantaraṃ bhavaṅgaṃ vattati. Tatiyavāre manodvārikaāvajjanena bhavaṅge āvaṭṭite manodvārikajavanaṃ javati, tena cittena ñatvā “kiṃ ayaṃ imasmiṃ ṭhāne saddo, saṅkhasaddo bherisaddo”ti vā “kiṃ ayaṃ imasmiṃ ṭhāne gandho, mūlagandho”ti vā “kiṃ idaṃ mayhaṃ mukhaṃ pakkhittaṃ, sappīti vā phāṇita”nti vā “kenamhi piṭṭhiyaṃ pahaṭo, atibaddho me pahāro”ti vā vattā hoti. Evaṃ manodvārikajavaneneva paṭibujjhati, na pañcadvārikena. Supinampi teneva passati, na pañcadvārikena. Sesamettha suviññeyyameva.

Volition in a dream is volition that occurs by way of mind-door impulsion. For one who sees a dream sees it only through mind-door impulsion, not through the five doors. And when one awakens, one awakens only through the mind-door, not through the five doors. For when someone is asleep, even if a lamp with a large wick is lit and brought near the eye, at first the eye-door advertence does not turn the life-continuum; only the mind-door advertence turns it. Then, after impulsion has run its course, it sinks into the life-continuum. On the second occasion, the eye-door advertence turns the life-continuum, then eye-consciousness and so on, ending with impulsion, arise. After that, the life-continuum occurs. On the third occasion, when the life-continuum is turned by mind-door advertence, mind-door impulsion runs. With that consciousness one knows: 'What is this light in this place?' Similarly, when someone is asleep and musical instruments are played near the ear, or fragrant or foul-smelling flowers are brought near the nose, or ghee or molasses is placed in the mouth, or a blow is given on the back with the hand, at first the ear-door advertences and so on do not turn the life-continuum; only the mind-door advertence turns it. Then, after impulsion has run its course, it sinks into the life-continuum. On the second occasion, the ear-door advertences and so on turn the life-continuum, then ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and so on, ending with impulsion, arise. After that, the life-continuum occurs. On the third occasion, when the life-continuum is turned by mind-door advertence, mind-door impulsion runs. Having known with that consciousness, one says: 'What is this sound in this place? A conch sound? A drum sound?' or 'What is this smell in this place? A root-smell?' or 'What is this placed in my mouth? Ghee or molasses?' or 'By whom have I been struck on the back? The blow to me was very hard!' Thus one awakens only through mind-door impulsion, not through the five doors. One sees a dream, too, only through that, not through the five doors. The rest here is easy to understand.

Mahāsupinasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Mahāsupina Sutta is finished.

7. Vassasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Vassa Sutta

197. Sattame utusamuṭṭhānanti vassike cattāro māse uppannaṃ. Akālepīti cittavesākhamāsesupi. Vassavalāhakadevaputtānañhi attano ratiyā kīḷitukāmatācitte uppanne akālepi devo vassati. Tatridaṃ vatthu – eko kira vassavalāhakadevaputto vākarakuṭakavāsikhīṇāsavattherassa santikaṃ gantvā vanditvā aṭṭhāsi. Thero “kosi tva”nti pucchi. Ahaṃ, bhante, vassavalāhakadevaputtoti. Tumhākaṃ kira cittena devo vassatīti. Āma, bhanteti. Passitukāmā mayanti. Temissatha, bhanteti. Meghasīsaṃ vā gajjitaṃ vā na paññāyati, kathaṃ temissāmāti. Bhante, amhākaṃ cittena devo vassati, tumhe paṇṇasālaṃ pavisathāti. “Sādhu, devaputtā”ti pāde dhovitvā paṇṇasālaṃ [M 3.0072] pāvisi. Devaputto tasmiṃ pavisanteyeva ekaṃ gītaṃ gāyitvā hatthaṃ ukkhipi, samantā tiyojanaṭṭhānaṃ ekameghaṃ ahosi. Thero addhatinto paṇṇasālaṃ paviṭṭhoti.

197. In the seventh, arisen from the season means arisen during the four months of the rainy season. Even out of season means even in the months of Citta and Vesākha. For when the thought 'I want to play for my own enjoyment' arises in the minds of the rain-cloud devaputtas, rain falls even out of season. Here is the story: It is said that a certain rain-cloud devaputta went to the elder Vākarakuṭakavāsī, an arahant, paid homage to him, and stood to one side. The elder asked: 'Who are you?' 'I am, venerable sir, a rain-cloud devaputta.' 'Is it true that rain falls by your will?' 'Yes, venerable sir.' 'We wish to see it.' 'You will get drenched, venerable sir.' 'No cloud-head or thunder is seen. How will I get drenched?' 'Venerable sir, rain falls by our will. You should enter the leaf-hut.' 'Very well, devaputta.' Having washed his feet, he entered the leaf-hut. Just as he was entering, the devaputta sang a song and raised his hand, and a single cloud formed over an area of three yojanas all around. The elder entered the leaf-hut half-drenched.

Vassasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Vassa Sutta is finished.

8-9. Vācāsuttādivaṇṇanā

8–9. Commentary on the Vācā Sutta, etc.

198-9. Aṭṭhame [V 3.0069] aṅgehīti kāraṇehi. Aṅgīyanti hetubhāvena ñāyantīti aṅgāni, kāraṇāni. Kāraṇatthe ca aṅga-saddo. Pañcahīti hetumhi nissakkavacanaṃ. Samannāgatāti samanuāgatā pavattā yuttā ca. Vācāti samullapana-vācā. Yā “vācā girā byappatho”ti (dha. sa. 636) ca, “nelā kaṇṇasukhā”ti (dī. ni. 1.9) ca āgacchati. Yā pana “vācāya ce kataṃ kamma”nti (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 1 kāyakammadvāra) evaṃ viññatti ca, “yā catūhi vacīduccaritehi ārati…pe… ayaṃ vuccati sammāvācā”ti (dha. sa. 299) evaṃ virati ca, “pharusavācā, bhikkhave, āsevitā bhāvitā bahulīkatā nirayasaṃvattanikā hotī”ti (a. ni. 8.40) evaṃ cetanā ca vācāti āgatā, na sā idha adhippetā. Kasmā? Abhāsitabbato. “Subhāsitā hoti, no dubbhāsitā”ti hi vuttaṃ. Subhāsitāti suṭṭhu bhāsitā. Tenassā atthāvahataṃ dīpeti. Anavajjāti rāgādiavajjarahitā. Imināssa kāraṇasuddhiṃ agatigamanādippavattadosābhāvañca dīpeti. Rāgadosādivimuttañhi yaṃ bhāsato anurodhavivajjanato agatigamanaṃ durasamussitamevāti. Ananuvajjāti anuvādavimuttā. Imināssā sabbākārasampattiṃ dīpeti. Sati hi sabbākārasampattiyaṃ ananuvajjatāti. Viññūnanti paṇḍitānaṃ. Tena nindāpasaṃsāsu bālā appamāṇāti dīpeti.

198–199. In the eighth, by factors means by causes. They are 'factors' (aṅgāni) because they are known as causes (hetu); they are reasons. The word 'aṅga' also has the meaning of cause. By five: this is the ablative of cause. Endowed means accompanied by, occurring with, and connected. Speech means conversational speech, which comes up as 'speech, utterance, expression' (Dhs 636) and as 'eloquent, pleasing to the ear' (DN 1:9). But the 'speech' that comes up as intimation, as in 'a deed done by speech' (Dhs-a 1, on the door of bodily action); or as abstinence, as in 'the abstinence from the four kinds of verbal misconduct… this is called right speech' (Dhs 299); or as volition, as in 'Harsh speech, bhikkhus, when cultivated, developed, and practiced frequently, is conducive to hell' (AN 8.40)—that is not intended here. Why? Because it is not what is spoken. For it is said: 'It is well-spoken, not ill-spoken.' Well-spoken means spoken well. This shows that it brings benefit. Blameless means free from the fault of lust, etc. This shows the purity of its cause and the absence of faults such as proceeding from bias. For when one speaks speech that is free from lust, hatred, etc., because one avoids partiality and opposition, proceeding from bias is completely set aside. Unreproachable means free from censure. This shows its perfection in all aspects. For when there is perfection in all aspects, it is unreproachable. By the wise means by the learned. This shows that in blame and praise, fools are no measure.

Imehi khotiādīni tāni aṅgāni paccakkhato dassento taṃ vācaṃ nigameti. Yañca aññe paṭiññādīhi avayavehi, nāmādīhi padehi, liṅgavacanavibhattikālakārakasampattīhi ca samannāgataṃ musāvādādivācampi subhāsitanti maññanti, taṃ paṭisedheti. Avayavādisamannāgatāpi hi tathārūpī [M 3.0073] vācā dubbhāsitāva hoti attano ca paresañca anatthāvahattā. Imehi pana pañcahaṅgehi samannāgatā sacepi milakkhubhāsāpariyāpannā ghaṭaceṭikāgītikapariyāpannāpi hoti, tathāpi subhāsitāva lokiyalokuttarahitasukhāvahattā. Tathā hi maggapasse sassaṃ rakkhantiyā sīhaḷaceṭikāya sīhaḷakeneva jātijarāmaraṇayuttaṃ gītikaṃ gāyantiyā saddaṃ sutvā maggaṃ gacchantā saṭṭhimattā vipassakabhikkhū arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu.

With the words beginning 'Indeed, with these,' he concludes about that speech, directly showing those factors. And he refutes what others consider well-spoken: speech endowed with parts such as a thesis, with words such as nouns, and with the perfections of gender, number, case, tense, and agent, even when it is false speech, etc. For even when endowed with such parts, etc., such speech is still ill-spoken because it brings harm to oneself and others. But speech endowed with these five factors, even if it is comprised in a barbarian language or comprised in the songs of pot-making servant girls, is still well-spoken because it brings worldly and supramundane welfare and happiness. For example, some sixty bhikkhus practicing insight meditation, who were walking along a road, attained arahantship upon hearing the sound of a Sinhalese servant girl guarding the crops by the roadside singing a song in Sinhalese about being connected with birth, aging, and death.

Tathā tisso nāma āraddhavipassako bhikkhu padumassarasamīpena gacchanto padumassare padumāni bhañjitvā –

Similarly, a bhikkhu named Tissa, an insight meditator, was walking near a lotus pond. A servant girl, plucking lotuses in the lotus pond, was singing:

“Pātova [V 3.0070] phullitakokanadaṃ,

Sūriyālokena bhijjiyate;

Evaṃ manussattaṃ gatā sattā,

Jarābhivegena maddīyantī”ti. (saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.213; su. ni. aṭṭha. 2.452 subhāsitasuttavaṇṇanā) –

“Just as a red lotus blooming at dawn is shattered by the sunlight, so beings who have reached the human state are crushed by the force of old age.”

Imaṃ gītiṃ gāyantiyā ceṭikāya sutvā arahattaṃ patto.

Having heard this song sung by the servant girl, he attained arahantship.

Buddhantarepi aññataro puriso sattahi puttehi saddhiṃ aṭavito āgamma aññatarāya itthiyā musalena taṇḍule koṭṭentiyā –

Also in the time of another Buddha, a certain man, having come from the forest with his seven sons, encountered a certain woman who was pounding rice with a pestle and singing:

“Jarāya parimadditaṃ etaṃ, milātacammanissitaṃ;

Maraṇena bhijjati etaṃ, maccussa ghāsamāmisaṃ.

“This is crushed by old age, dependent on withered skin; this is broken by death, food and flesh for the Death God.

“Kimīnaṃ ālayaṃ etaṃ, nānākuṇapena pūritaṃ;

Asucibhājanaṃ etaṃ, tadalikkhandhasamaṃ ida”nti. (saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.213; su. ni. aṭṭha. 2.452 subhāsitasuttavaṇṇanā) –

“This is an abode of worms, filled with various kinds of corpses; this is a vessel of impurity, like a rotten palm-trunk.”

Imaṃ gītaṃ sutvā paccavekkhanto saha puttehi paccekabodhiṃ patto. Evaṃ imehi pañcahi aṅgehi samannāgatā vācā sacepi milakkhubhāsāya pariyāpannā ghaṭaceṭikāgītikapariyāpannā vācā hoti, tathāpi subhāsitāti veditabbā. Subhāsitā eva anavajjā ananuvajjā ca viññūnaṃ atthatthikānaṃ kulaputtānaṃ atthappaṭisaraṇānaṃ, no byañjanappaṭisaraṇānanti. Navamaṃ uttānameva.

Having heard this song and reflecting on it, he attained paccekabodhi together with his sons. Thus, it should be understood that speech endowed with these five factors is well-spoken, even if it is comprised in a barbarian language or in the songs of pot-making servant girls. It is well-spoken, blameless, and unreproachable for the wise, for clansmen who seek the meaning, who have the meaning as their resort, not the letter as their resort. The ninth is self-evident.

Vācāsuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Vācā Sutta and others is concluded.

10. Nissāraṇīyasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Nissāraṇīya Sutta

200. Dasame [M 3.0074] nissarantīti nissaraṇīyāti vattabbe dīghaṃ katvā niddeso. Kattari hesa anīya-saddo yathā “niyyāniyā”ti. Tenāha “nissaṭā”ti. Kuto pana nissaṭā? Yathāsakaṃ paṭipakkhato. Nijjīvaṭṭhena dhātuyoti āha “attasuññasabhāvā”ti. Atthato pana dhammadhātumanoviññāṇadhātuviseso[V 3.0071]. Tādisassa bhikkhuno kilesavasena kāmesu manasikāro natthīti āha “vīmaṃsanattha”nti, “nekkhammaniyataṃ idāni me cittaṃ, kiṃ nu kho kāmavitakkopi uppajjissatī”ti vīmaṃsantassāti attho. Pakkhandanaṃ nāma anuppaveso. So pana tattha natthīti āha “nappavisatī”ti. Pasīdanaṃ nāma abhiruci. Santiṭṭhanaṃ patiṭṭhānaṃ. Vimuccanaṃ adhimuccananti. Taṃ sabbaṃ paṭikkhipanto vadati “pasādaṃ nāpajjatī”tiādi. Evaṃbhūtaṃ panassa cittaṃ tassa kathaṃ tiṭṭhatīti āha “yathā”tiādi.

200. In the tenth sutta, when ‘nissaraṇiyā’ should be said for ‘nissaranti’ (they escape), the exposition is made by lengthening the vowel to ‘nissaraṇīyā.’ Here this suffix -anīya is in the agent sense, as in ‘niyyāniyā.’ Therefore it says ‘nissaṭā’ (escaped). But from what has it escaped? From its respective opposing factors. Because of its lifeless quality, it is an element; thus it is said to have a 'nature empty of self.' In meaning, however, it is a specific instance of the dhamma-element and the mind-consciousness-element. For such a bhikkhu, there is no attention to sensual pleasures on account of the defilements; thus it is said 'for the purpose of investigation.' The meaning is: of one who investigates thus: 'My mind is now committed to renunciation; I wonder, could a sensual thought still arise?' Pakkhandana means entering. But since that is not present there, it says 'it does not enter.' Pasīdana means delight. Santiṭṭhana means settling. Vimuccana means being resolved upon. Rejecting all that, it says 'it does not find delight,' and so on. But how does the mind of such a one remain steady? This is explained with 'just as,' and so on.

Tanti paṭhamajjhānaṃ. Assāti bhikkhuno. Cittaṃ pakkhandatīti parikammacittena saddhiṃ jhānacittaṃ ekattavasena ekajjhaṃ katvā vadati. Gocare gatattāti attano ārammaṇe eva pavattattā. Ahānabhāgiyattāti ṭhitibhāgiyattā. Suṭṭhu vimuttanti vikkhambhanavimuttiyā sammadeva vimuttaṃ. Cittassa ca kāyassa ca vihananato vighāto. Dukkhaṃ paridahanato pariḷāho. Kāmavedanaṃ na vediyati anuppajjanato. Nissaranti tatoti nissaraṇaṃ. Ke nissaranti? Kāmā. Evañca kāmānanti kattusāmivacanaṃ suṭṭhu yujjati. Yadaggena kāmā tato nissaṭāti vuccanti, tadaggena jhānampi kāmato nissaṭanti vattabbataṃ labhatīti vuttaṃ “kāmehi nissaṭattā”ti. Evaṃ vikkhambhanavasena kāmanissaraṇaṃ vatvā idāni samucchedavasena accantato nissaraṇaṃ dassetuṃ “yo panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Sesapadesūti sesakoṭṭhāsesu.

That is the first jhāna. ‘Assā’ means 'of the bhikkhu.' When it says 'the mind leaps forward,' it is speaking of the jhāna-mind together with the preliminary-mind, making them one by way of unity. 'Because it has gone to its pasture' means because it proceeds only in its own object. 'Because it is not liable to decline' means because it partakes of stability. 'Well liberated' means rightly liberated by the liberation of suppression. Vighāta (vexation) is from the vexing of mind and body. Pariḷāha (fever) is from the burning up of suffering. One does not feel sensual feeling because it does not arise. From that they escape (nissaranti); hence it is an escape (nissaraṇaṃ). What escapes? Sensual pleasures. And so, the word ‘kāmānaṃ’ is very fitting as a genitive of the agent. In the same way that sensual pleasures are said to be escaped from, so too the jhāna can be said to be escaped from sensual pleasures; thus it is said, 'because of being escaped from sensual pleasures.' Having thus spoken of the escape from sensual pleasures by way of suppression, now, to show the complete escape by way of eradication, it says 'But whoever...,' and so on. 'In the remaining passages' means in the remaining sections.

Ayaṃ pana visesoti visesaṃ vadantena taṃ jhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvātiādiko avisesoti katvā dutiyatatiyavāresu sabbaso anāmaṭṭho, catutthavāre pana ayampi visesoti dassetuṃ “accantanissaraṇañcettha arahattaphalaṃ yojetabba”nti vuttaṃ. Yasmā arūpajjhānaṃ [M 3.0075] pādakaṃ katvā aggamaggaṃ adhigantvā arahatte ṭhitassa cittaṃ sabbaso rūpehi nissaṭaṃ nāma hoti. Tassa hi phalasamāpattito vuṭṭhāya vīmaṃsanatthaṃ rūpābhimukhaṃ cittaṃ pesentassa. Idamakkhātanti samathayānikānaṃ vasena heṭṭhā cattāro vārā gahitā. Idaṃ pana sukkhavipassakassa vasenāti āha “suddhasaṅkhāre”tiādi. “Puna sakkāyo natthī”ti uppannanti “idāni me sakkāyappabandho natthī”ti vīmaṃsantassa uppannaṃ.

But this is the distinction: because the statement 'having made that jhāna the basis,' and so on, is taken as not being a distinction, it is not touched upon at all in the second and third cases. In the fourth case, however, to show that this too is a distinction, it is said: 'And here the complete escape should be connected with the fruit of arahantship.' For when one has made a formless jhāna the basis, attained the supreme path, and is established in arahantship, one's mind is indeed completely escaped from all forms. This is for one who, having emerged from the attainment of fruition, sends the mind towards form for the purpose of investigation. 'This has been stated': the four cases below have been taken in terms of the serenity-vehicle practitioner. But this is in terms of the dry-insight practitioner; thus it says 'mere formations,' and so on. The arising of 'Again there is no personality-identity' means it arises for one who investigates, 'Now for me there is no continuity of personality-identity.'

Nissāraṇīyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Nissāraṇīya Sutta is concluded.

Brāhmaṇavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Brāhmaṇa Vagga is concluded.

Catutthapaṇṇāsakaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Fourth Fifty is concluded.

5. Pañcamapaṇṇāsakaṃ

5. The Fifth Fifty

(21) 1. Kimilavaggo

(21) 1. The Kimila Vagga

1-4. Kimilasuttādivaṇṇanā

1-4. Commentary on the Kimila Sutta and others

201-4. Pañcamassa [V 3.0072][M 3.0076] paṭhamadutiyāni uttānatthāneva. Tatiye adhivāsanaṃ khamanaṃ, paresaṃ dukkaṭaṃ duruttañca paṭivirodhākaraṇena attano upari āropetvā vāsanaṃ adhivāsanaṃ, tadeva khantīti adhivāsanakkhanti. Subhe ratoti sūrato, suṭṭhu vā pāpato orato virato sorato, tassa bhāvo soraccaṃ. Tenāha “soraccenāti sucisīlatāyā”ti. Sā hi sobhanakammaratatā, suṭṭhu vā pāpato oratabhāvo viratatā. Catutthe natthi vattabbaṃ.

201-4. The first and second suttas of the fifth vagga are of obvious meaning. In the third, adhivāsana is enduring. Adhivāsana is enduring by taking upon oneself the wrongdoing and harsh speech of others without making opposition; that itself is patience (khanti), hence adhivāsanakkhanti (enduring patience). Sūrata is one who delights in the good. Or, sorata is one who is well (suṭṭhu) restrained (orato), abstinent (virato) from evil (pāpato); the state of that is soracca (gentleness). Therefore it says: 'soraccena means by pure virtue.' For that is delight in beautiful actions, or the state of being well restrained from evil, abstinence. In the fourth, there is nothing to say.

Kimilasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Kimila Sutta and others is concluded.

5. Cetokhilasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Cetokhila Sutta

205. Pañcame cetokhilā nāma atthato vicikicchā kodho ca. Te pana yasmiṃ santāne uppajjanti, tassa kharabhāvo kakkhaḷabhāvo hutvā upatiṭṭhanti, pageva attanā sampayuttacittassāti āha “cittassa thaddhabhāvā”ti. Yathā lakkhaṇapāripūriyā gahitāya sabbā satthu rūpakāyasirī gahitā eva nāma hoti evaṃ sabbaññutāya sabbadhammakāyasirī gahitā eva nāma hotīti tadubhayavatthukameva kaṅkhaṃ dassento “sarīre kaṅkhamāno”tiādimāha. Vicinantoti dhammasabhāvaṃ vīmaṃsanto. Kicchatīti kilamati. Vinicchetuṃ na sakkotīti sanniṭṭhātuṃ na sakkoti. Ātapati kileseti ātappaṃ, sammāvāyāmoti āha “ātappāyāti kilesasantāpanavīriyakaraṇatthāyā”ti. Punappunaṃ yogāyāti bhāvanaṃ punappunaṃ yuñjanāya. Satatakiriyāyāti bhāvanāya nirantarappayogāya.

205. In the fifth sutta, cetokhilā (mental barrenness) in meaning are doubt and anger. When they arise in a person's mental continuum, they present themselves as harshness and roughness, let alone for the mind associated with them; thus it says 'because of the mind's rigidity.' Just as when the perfection of the characteristics is grasped, all the splendor of the Teacher's physical body is thereby grasped, so too when omniscience is grasped, all the splendor of the Dhamma-body is thereby grasped. Thus, showing doubt with a twofold basis, it says 'doubting about the body,' and so on. Vicinanto (doubting) means investigating the nature of phenomena. Kicchati means to be troubled. 'He is not able to decide' means he is not able to conclude. Ātappa (ardor) is that which burns and torments the defilements; it is right effort. Thus it says: 'ātappāya means for the purpose of making the effort that torments the defilements.' 'For repeated application' means for repeatedly yoking oneself to cultivation. 'For constant practice' means for uninterrupted application to cultivation.

Paṭivedhadhamme kaṅkhamānoti ettha kathaṃ lokuttaradhamme kaṅkhā pavattīti? Na ārammaṇakaraṇavasena[V 3.0073], anussutākāraparivitakkaladdhe parikappitarūpe kaṅkhā [M 3.0077] pavattatīti dassento āha “vipassanā…pe… vadanti, taṃ atthi nu kho natthīti kaṅkhatī”ti. Sikkhāti cettha pubbabhāgasikkhā veditabbā. Kāmañcettha visesuppattiyā mahāsāvajjatāya ceva saṃvāsanimittaṃ ghaṭanāhetu abhiṇhuppattikatāya ca sabrahmacārīsūti kopassa visayo visesetvā vutto, aññatthāpi kopo na cetokhiloti na sakkā viññātunti keci. Yadi evaṃ vicikicchāyapi ayaṃ nayo āpajjati, tasmā yathārutavasena gahetabbaṃ.

'Doubting the Dhamma of penetration': here, how does doubt about the supramundane Dhamma proceed? Showing that it does not proceed by way of making it an object, but that doubt proceeds concerning a conceived form obtained by reflection on what has been heard, he said: 'Insight... and so on... they say; he doubts, "I wonder, does it exist or not?"' Here, by 'training' the preliminary training should be understood. And here, the object of anger is specified as 'towards one's companions in the holy life' because of its great faultiness in regard to the arising of special attainments, because it is a cause of conflict in communal living, and because of its frequent occurrence. Some say that it cannot be known that anger in other cases is not a mental barrenness. If so, this same method would apply to doubt as well; therefore, it should be taken as it is stated.

Cetokhilasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Cetokhila Sutta is concluded.

6-8. Vinibandhasuttādivaṇṇanā

6-8. Commentary on the Vinibandha Sutta and Others

206-8. Chaṭṭhe pavattituṃ appadānavasena kusalacittaṃ vinibandhantīti cetasovinibandhā. Taṃ pana vinibandhantā muṭṭhiggāhaṃ gaṇhantā viya hontīti āha “cittaṃ vinibandhitvā”tiādi. Kāmagiddho puggalo vatthukāmepi kilesakāmepi assādeti abhinandatīti vuttaṃ “vatthukāmepi kilesakāmepī”ti. Attano kāyeti attano nāmakāye, attabhāve vā. Bahiddhārūpeti paresaṃ kāye anindriyabaddharūpe ca. Udaraṃ avadihati upacinoti pūretīti udarāvadehakaṃ. Seyyasukhanti seyyāya sayanavasena uppajjanakasukhaṃ. Samparivattakanti samparivattitvā. Paṇidhāyāti taṇhāvaseneva paṇidahitvā. Iti pañcavidhopi lobhaviseso eva “cetovinibandho”ti vuttoti veditabbo. Sattamaṭṭhamesu natthi vattabbaṃ.

206-8. In the sixth, they are called 'mental bondages' because they bind the wholesome mind, preventing it from proceeding, by way of not giving. And in binding it, they are like those who make a firm grasp; thus it is said: 'having bound the mind,' etc. A person greedy for sensual pleasures enjoys and delights in both sensual pleasures as objects and sensual pleasures as defilements; thus it is said: 'in sensual pleasures as objects and in sensual pleasures as defilements.' 'In one's own body' means in one's own mental body, or in one's individual existence. 'In external form' means in the bodies of others and in inanimate form. 'Gorging one's belly' means one accumulates, one fills. 'The pleasure of lying down' is the pleasure that arises from the act of lying down. 'Tossing and turning' means having turned over and over. 'Having made an aspiration' means having made an aspiration out of craving. Thus, it should be understood that these five specific kinds of greed are called 'mental bondage.' There is nothing to be said about the seventh and eighth suttas.

Vinibandhasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Vinibandha Sutta and others is concluded.

9-10. Gītassarasuttādivaṇṇanā

9-10. Commentary on the Gītassara Sutta and others

209-210. Navame āyatako nāma gītassaro taṃ taṃ vattaṃ bhinditvā akkharāni vināsetvā pavattoti āha “āyatakenā”tiādi. Dhammehi suttavattaṃ nāma atthi, gāthāvattaṃ nāma atthi, taṃ vināsetvā atidīghaṃ kātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Dhammañhi bhāsantena caturassena vattena parimaṇḍalāni [M 3.0078] padabyañjanāni dassetabbāni. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, sarabhañña”nti (cūḷava. 249) ca vacanato sarena dhammaṃ bhaṇituṃ vaṭṭati. Sarabhaññe kira taraṅgavattadhotakavattabhāgaggahakavattādīni [V 3.0074] dvattiṃsa vattāni atthi. Tesu yaṃ icchati, taṃ kātuṃ labhatīti. Dasame natthi vattabbaṃ.

209-210. In the ninth, a long-drawn-out singing tone is one that proceeds by breaking up the proper meter and ruining the syllables; thus it is said: 'with a long-drawn-out tone,' etc. In the Dhamma there is what is called sutta meter and what is called verse meter; it is not proper to ruin these and make them excessively long. For when reciting the Dhamma, the well-rounded words and phrases should be presented with a balanced, four-square meter. And because it is said, 'Bhikkhus, I allow chanting' (Cv V.3.1), it is permissible to recite the Dhamma with a melodic tone. It is said that in chanting there are thirty-two meters, such as the wave meter, the washed meter, the portion-taking meter, and so on. One may use whichever of these one wishes. There is nothing to be said about the tenth sutta.

Gītassarasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Gītassara Sutta and others is concluded.

Kimilavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Kimila Chapter is concluded.

(22) 2. Akkosakavaggo

(22) 2. The Chapter on Abuse

1-2. Akkosakasuttādivaṇṇanā

1-2. Commentary on the Akkosaka Sutta and others

211-2. Dutiyassa paṭhame dasahi akkosavatthūhi akkosakoti “bālosi, mūḷhosi, oṭṭhosi, goṇosi, gadrabhosī”tiādinā dasahi akkosavatthūhi akkosako. “Hotu, muṇḍakasamaṇa, adaṇḍo ahanti karosi, idāni te rājakulaṃ gantvā daṇḍaṃ āropessāmī”tiādīni vadanto paribhāsako nāmāti āha “bhayadassanena paribhāsako”ti. Lokuttaradhammā apāyamaggassa paripanthabhāvato paripantho nāmāti āha “lokuttaraparipanthassa chinnattā”ti, lokuttarasaṅkhātassa apāyamaggaparipanthassa chinnattāti attho. Dutiye natthi vattabbaṃ.

211-2. In the first of the second, an 'abuser' is one who abuses with the ten grounds for abuse, saying such things as: 'You are a fool, you are confused, you are a camel, you are an ox, you are a donkey.' One who reviles by saying such things as, 'So, shaveling ascetic, you act as if you are immune to punishment; now I will go to the royal court and have you punished!' is called a 'reviler'; thus it is said: 'a reviler by making threats.' The supramundane Dhamma is called an 'obstacle' because it is an obstacle to the path to the plane of misery. Thus it is said: 'because the obstacle to the supramundane is cut off,' which means, 'because the obstacle to the path to the plane of misery, which is designated as 'supramundane,' has been cut off.' There is nothing to be said about the second sutta.

Akkosakasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Akkosaka Sutta and others is concluded.

3-10. Sīlasuttādivaṇṇanā

3-10. Commentary on the Sīla Sutta and others

213-220. Tatiye (dī. ni. ṭī. 2.149) dussīloti ettha du-saddo abhāvattho “duppañño”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.449) viya, na garahaṇatthoti āha “asīlo nissīlo”ti. Bhinnasaṃvaroti ettha samādinnasīlo kenaci kāraṇena sīlabhedaṃ patto, so tāva bhinnasaṃvaro hotu. Yo pana sabbena sabbaṃ asamādinnasīlo ācārahīno, so kathaṃ bhinnasaṃvaro nāma hotīti[M 3.0079]? Sopi sādhusamācārassa pariharaṇīyassa bheditattā bhinnasaṃvaro eva nāma. Vinaṭṭhasaṃvaro saṃvararahitoti hi vuttaṃ hoti. Taṃ taṃ sippaṭṭhānaṃ. Māghātakāleti “mā ghātetha pāṇīna”nti [V 3.0075] evaṃ māghātaghosanaṃ ghositadivase. Abbhuggacchati pāpako kittisaddo. Ajjhāsayena maṅku hotiyeva vippaṭisāribhāvato.

213-220. In the third (cf. DN-ṭ 2.149), regarding 'immoral' (dussīla), the prefix 'du-' has the meaning of absence, as in 'unwise' (duppañña) and so on (cf. MN 1.449), not the meaning of censure; hence it is explained as 'without virtue' (asīlo) or 'devoid of virtue' (nissīlo). Here, 'one whose restraint is broken' (bhinnasaṃvaro) is one who has undertaken the moral precepts but for some reason has arrived at a breach of virtue; such a one is one whose restraint is broken. But how can one who has not undertaken the moral precepts at all and is devoid of good conduct be called 'one whose restraint is broken'? He too is so called because he has broken with the good conduct that should be maintained. For it is said that 'one whose restraint is ruined' means 'one who is devoid of restraint.' 'His particular craft' refers to various arts and crafts. 'At a time of non-killing' means on a day when a proclamation against killing has been announced, such as 'Do not kill living beings!' An evil reputation spreads. He is certainly troubled in his disposition because he is remorseful.

Tassāti dussīlassa. Samādāya vattitaṭṭhānanti uṭṭhāya samuṭṭhāya katakāraṇaṃ. Āpāthaṃ āgacchatīti taṃ manaso upaṭṭhāti. Ummīletvā idhalokanti ummīlanakāle attano puttadārādivasena idhalokaṃ passati. Nimīletvā paralokanti nimīlanakāle gatinimittupaṭṭhānavasena paralokaṃ passati. Tenāha “cattāro apāyā”tiādi. Pañcamapadanti “kāyassa bhedā”tiādinā vutto pañcamo ādīnavakoṭṭhāso. Vuttavipariyāyenāti vuttatthāya ādīnavakathāya vipariyāyena “appamatto taṃ taṃ kasivaṇijjādiṃ yathākālaṃ sampādetuṃ sakkotī”tiādinā. Pāsaṃsaṃ sīlamassa atthīti sīlavā. Sīlasampannoti sīlena samannāgato sampannasīloti evamādikaṃ pana atthavacanaṃ sukaranti anāmaṭṭhaṃ. Catutthādīni uttānatthāneva.

'Of him' means of the immoral person. 'The sphere in which he has conducted himself' means the reason for what he has done after getting up and arising. 'It comes into range' means it presents itself to the mind. 'Opening his eyes to this world' means that at the time of opening his eyes, he sees this world in terms of his children, wife, and so on. 'Closing his eyes to the next world' means that at the time of closing his eyes, he sees the next world by way of the appearance of the sign of his future destination. Therefore it is said: 'the four planes of misery,' etc. 'The fifth item' is the fifth section on dangers, stated with the words 'with the breakup of the body,' etc. 'By way of the opposite' means in the opposite way to the stated talk on dangers, as in: 'Being heedful, he is able to accomplish his farming, trade, etc., at the proper time.' 'He has praiseworthy virtue,' thus he is 'virtuous' (sīlavā). 'Endowed with virtue' (sīlasampanno) means possessed of virtue, accomplished in virtue. Such explanations of the meaning are easy and so have not been discussed. The fourth and following suttas are clear in meaning.

Sīlasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Sīla Sutta and others is concluded.

Akkosakavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Akkosaka Chapter is concluded.

(23) 3. Dīghacārikavaggo

(23) 3. The Chapter on Long Wandering

1-10. Paṭhamadīghacārikasuttādivaṇṇanā

1-10. Commentary on the First Discourse on Long Wandering and so forth

221-230. Tatiyassa paṭhamādīni suviññeyyāni. Pañcame raho nisajjāya āpajjatīti “yo pana bhikkhu mātugāmena saddhiṃ eko ekāya raho nisajjaṃ kappeyya, pācittiya”nti imasmiṃ sikkhāpade (pāci. 290) vuttaṃ āpattiṃ āpajjati. Paṭicchanne āsane āpajjatīti “yo pana bhikkhu mātugāmena raho paṭicchanne āsane nisajjaṃ kappeyya, pācittiya”nti imasmiṃ vuttaṃ āpattiṃ āpajjati. Mātugāmassa uttari chappañcavācāhi dhammaṃ desento [M 3.0080] āpajjatīti ‘yo pana bhikkhu mātugāmassa uttari chappañcavācāhi dhammaṃ deseyya aññatra [V 3.0076] viññunā purisaviggahenā”ti (pāci. 63) evaṃ vuttaṃ āpattiṃ āpajjati. Tenāha “tesaṃ tesaṃ sikkhāpadānaṃ vasena veditabbānī”ti. Chaṭṭhādīni uttānatthāni.

221-230. The first and so on of the third chapter are easy to understand. In the fifth, one incurs an offense by sitting in seclusion: 'Whatever bhikkhu should sit down in seclusion, alone with a woman, it is an offense of expiation'—one incurs the offense stated in this training rule (Pāc. 44). One incurs an offense by sitting on a concealed seat: 'Whatever bhikkhu should sit down with a woman in seclusion on a concealed seat, it is an offense of expiation'—one incurs the offense stated in this rule (Pāc. 45). One incurs an offense by teaching the Dhamma to a woman with more than five or six words: 'Whatever bhikkhu should teach the Dhamma to a woman in more than five or six words, unless a knowledgeable man is present' (Pāc. 7)—one incurs the offense thus stated. Therefore it is said: 'These are to be understood in accordance with their respective training rules.' The sixth and so on are clear in meaning.

Paṭhamadīghacārikasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the First Discourse on Long Wandering and so forth is concluded.

Dīghacārikavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Chapter on Long Wandering is concluded.

231-302. Catutthavaggādīni uttānatthāni.

231-302. The fourth chapter and so on are clear in meaning.

Iti manorathapūraṇiyā aṅguttaranikāya-aṭṭhakathāya

Thus in the Manorathapūraṇī, the commentary on the Aṅguttara Nikāya:

Pañcakanipātavaṇṇanāya anuttānatthadīpanā samattā.

The explanation of profound meanings in the commentary on the Book of Fives is concluded.

. Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa.

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.

Aṅguttaranikāye

In the Aṅguttara Nikāya

Chakkanipāta-ṭīkā

Subcommentary on the Book of the Sixes

1. Paṭhamapaṇṇāsakaṃ

1. The First Fifty

1. Āhuneyyavaggo

1. The Chapter on Those Worthy of Offerings

1. Paṭhamaāhuneyyasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the First Discourse on Those Worthy of Offerings

1. Chakkanipātassa [V 3.0077][M 3.0081] paṭhame cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvāti nissayavohārena vuttaṃ. Sasambhārakaniddesoyaṃ yathā “dhanunā vijjhatī”ti, tasmā nissayasīsena nissitassa gahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tenāyamattho “cakkhudvāre rūpārammaṇe āpāthagate taṃ rūpaṃ cakkhuviññāṇena disvā”ti. Neva sumano hotīti javanakkhaṇe iṭṭhe ārammaṇe rāgaṃ anuppādento neva sumano hoti gehassitapemavasenapi maggena sabbaso rāgassa samucchinnattā. Na dummanoti aniṭṭhe adussanto na dummano. Pasādaññathattavasenapi iṭṭhepi aniṭṭhepi majjhattepi ārammaṇe na samaṃ sammā ayoniso gahaṇaṃ asamapekkhanaṃ. Ayañcassa paṭipatti sativepullappattiyā paññāvepullappattiyā [V 3.0078] cāti āha “sato sampajāno hutvā”ti. Satiyā yuttattā sato. Sampajaññena yuttattā sampajāno. Ñāṇuppattipaccayarahitakālepi pavattibhedanato “satatavihāro kathito”ti vuttaṃ. Satatavihāroti khīṇāsavassa niccavihāro sabbadā pavattanakavihāro. Ṭhapetvā hi samāpattivelaṃ bhavaṅgavelañca khīṇāsavā imināva chaḷaṅgupekkhāvihārena viharanti.

1. In the first sutta of the Book of Sixes, the phrase 'having seen a form with the eye' is stated as a figurative expression of dependence. This is an explanation including the instrument, as in 'one shoots with a bow'; therefore, the grasping of the dependent should be understood by way of the heading of dependence. Hence this is the meaning: 'when a form-object has come into the range of the eye-door, one sees that form with eye-consciousness.' 'He is not glad' means that at the moment of impulsion, by not generating lust towards a desirable object, he is not glad—even by way of affection associated with the household life—because lust has been completely extirpated by the path. 'Nor is he sad' means that by not being vexed at an undesirable object, he is not sad. And due to the alteration of the sensitive faculty, towards a desirable, undesirable, or neutral object, there is no equal reaction, nor a proper but unwise grasping, nor a lack of consideration. This practice of his is due to the attainment of an abundance of mindfulness and an abundance of wisdom; thus it is said: 'being mindful and clearly comprehending.' He is 'mindful' because he is endowed with mindfulness. He is 'clearly comprehending' because he is endowed with clear comprehension.
