Even at a time devoid of a condition for the arising of knowledge, because of the variety of its occurrence, it is said, 'a constant dwelling is spoken of.' 'Constant dwelling' means the perpetual dwelling of one whose taints are destroyed, a dwelling that is always in operation. For, apart from the time of attainment and the time of the life-continuum, those whose taints are destroyed dwell by means of this very dwelling in six-factored equanimity.

Ettha ca “chasu dvāresupi upekkhako viharatī”ti iminā chaḷaṅgupekkhā kathitā. “Sampajāno”ti vacanato pana cattāri ñāṇasampayuttacittāni labbhanti tehi vinā sampajānatāya asambhavato. Satatavihārabhāvato aṭṭha mahākiriyacittāni labbhanti. “Neva sumano na dummano”ti vacanato aṭṭha mahākiriyacittāni, hasituppādo, voṭṭhabbanañcāti dasa cittāni labbhanti. Rāgadosasahajātānaṃ somanassadomanassānaṃ abhāvo tesampi sādhāraṇoti chaḷaṅgupekkhāvasena āgatānaṃ imesaṃ satatavihārānaṃ somanassaṃ kathaṃ labbhatīti ce? Āsevanato. Kiñcāpi [M 3.0082] khīṇāsavo iṭṭhāniṭṭhepi ārammaṇe majjhatto viya bahulaṃ upekkhako viharati attano parisuddhapakatibhāvāvijahanato, kadāci pana tathā cetobhisaṅkhārābhāve yaṃ taṃ sabhāvato iṭṭhaṃ ārammaṇaṃ, tassa yāthāvasabhāvaggahaṇavasenapi arahato cittaṃ pubbāsevanavasena somanassasahagataṃ hutvā pavattateva.

Here, by the phrase 'he dwells equanimous at the six doors,' six-factored equanimity is spoken of. From the statement 'clearly comprehending,' four types of consciousness associated with knowledge are obtained, since clear comprehension is impossible without them. Because it is a constant dwelling, the eight great functional consciousnesses are obtained. From the phrase 'neither glad nor sad,' the eight great functional consciousnesses, the smile-producing consciousness, and the determining consciousness—thus ten types of consciousness are obtained. If the absence of pleasure and displeasure co-arisen with lust and hatred is common to these too, how then is pleasure obtained in these constant dwellings that are described in terms of six-factored equanimity? Through repeated practice. Although one whose taints are destroyed dwells for the most part equanimous, like one who is neutral, toward desirable and undesirable objects—because he does not abandon his own naturally pure state—sometimes, when there is no such mental volition, the mind of an arahant, by grasping the real nature of an object that is intrinsically desirable, does arise accompanied by pleasure on account of prior practice.

Paṭhamaāhuneyyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the First Discourse on Those Worthy of Offerings is concluded.

2-7. Dutiyaāhuneyyasuttādivaṇṇanā

2-7. Commentary on the Second to Seventh Discourses on Those Worthy of Offerings

2-7. Dutiye (visuddhi. 2.380) anekavihitanti anekavidhaṃ nānappakāraṃ. Iddhividhanti iddhikoṭṭhāsaṃ. Paccanubhotīti paccanubhavati, phusati sacchikaroti pāpuṇātīti attho. Idānissa anekavihitabhāvaṃ dassento “ekopi hutvā”tiādimāha. Tattha “ekopi hutvā”ti iminā karaṇato pubbeva pakatiyā ekopi hutvā. Bahudhā hotīti bahūnaṃ santike caṅkamitukāmo vā sajjhāyaṃ kātukāmo vā pañhaṃ pucchitukāmo vā hutvā satampi sahassampi hoti. Āvibhāvaṃ tirobhāvanti ettha āvibhāvaṃ karoti, tirobhāvaṃ karotīti ayamattho. Idameva hi sandhāya paṭisambhidāyaṃ (paṭi. ma. 3.11) vuttaṃ – “āvibhāvanti kenaci anāvuṭaṃ hoti appaṭicchannaṃ vivaṭaṃ, tirobhāvanti kenaci āvuṭaṃ hoti paṭicchannaṃ pihitaṃ paṭikujjita”nti. Tirokuṭṭaṃ tiropākāraṃ tiropabbataṃ asajjamāno gacchati seyyathāpi ākāseti ettha tirokuṭṭanti parakuṭṭaṃ, kuṭṭassa parabhāganti vuttaṃ hoti. Esa nayo itaresu. Kuṭṭoti ca gehabhittiyā [V 3.0079] etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Pākāroti gehavihāragāmādīnaṃ parikkhepapākāro. Pabbatoti paṃsupabbato vā pāsāṇapabbato vā. Asajjamānoti alaggamāno seyyathāpi ākāse viya.

2-7. In the second sutta, 'manifold' (anekavihitaṃ) means of various kinds, of diverse sorts. 'The kinds of psychic power' (iddhividhaṃ) means the portion of psychic power. 'He experiences' (paccanubhoti) means he experiences, touches, realizes, attains. Now, to show its manifold nature, the text says, 'being one, he becomes many,' and so on. Therein, 'being one' means being one by nature even before the act of creation. 'He becomes many' means that when he wishes to do walking meditation, or to recite, or to ask a question in the presence of many, he becomes a hundred or even a thousand. 'Appearance and disappearance': here the meaning is that he makes himself appear and he makes himself disappear. It is with reference to this that it is said in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: 'Appearance means it is not enclosed by anything, it is uncovered, open. Disappearance means it is enclosed by something, it is covered, hidden, concealed.' 'He goes unhindered through a wall, a rampart, a mountain, as if through space': here 'through a wall' (tirokuṭṭaṃ) means to the other side of the wall; 'the far side of the wall' is what is said. This is the method for the other terms as well. 'Wall' (kuṭṭa) is a term for the wall of a house. 'Rampart' (pākāra) is the enclosing wall of a residence, a monastery, a village, etc. 'Mountain' (pabbata) is a mountain of earth or a mountain of rock. 'Unhindered' (asajjamāno) means not getting stuck, as if in open space.

Ummujjanimujjanti ettha ummujjanti uṭṭhānaṃ vuccati. Nimujjanti saṃsīdanaṃ. Ummujjañca nimujjañca ummujjanimujjaṃ. Udakepi abhijjamāneti ettha yaṃ udakaṃ akkamitvā saṃsīdati, taṃ bhijjamānanti vuccati, viparītaṃ abhijjamānaṃ. Pallaṅkena gacchati. Pakkhī [M 3.0083] sakuṇoti pakkhehi yuttasakuṇo. Imepi candimasūriye evaṃmahiddhike evaṃmahānubhāve pāṇinā parāmasatīti ettha candimasūriyānaṃ dvācattālīsayojanasahassassa upari caraṇena mahiddhikatā, tīsu dīpesu ekakkhaṇe ālokakaraṇena mahānubhāvatā veditabbā. Evaṃ uparicaraṇaālokakaraṇehi mahiddhike mahānubhāve. Parāmasatīti gaṇhāti, ekadese vā chupati. Parimajjatīti samantato ādāsatalā viya parimajjati. Yāva brahmalokāpīti brahmalokampi paricchedaṃ katvā. Kāyena vasaṃ vattetīti tatra brahmaloke kāyena attano vasaṃ vatteti.

Regarding 'diving down and popping up' (ummujjanimujjaṃ): here 'popping up' (ummujjana) means rising up; 'diving down' (nimujjana) means sinking down. 'Diving down and popping up' is the compound of both. 'On water without it parting' (udakepi abhijjamāne): here, water that parts when one walks on it and one sinks is called 'parting' (bhijjamāna); the opposite is 'not parting' (abhijjamāna). 'He goes cross-legged' (pallaṅkena gacchati). 'A winged bird' (pakkhī sakuṇo) means a bird endowed with wings. 'He touches and strokes with his hand these moon and sun, so mighty and powerful': here, the might (mahiddhikatā) of the moon and sun should be understood from their travelling forty-two thousand leagues above, and their power (mahānubhāvatā) from their illuminating three continents in a single moment. Thus they are mighty and powerful on account of travelling above and illuminating. 'He touches' (parāmasati) means he takes hold of, or touches a part of them. 'He strokes' (parimajjati) means he rubs all over, like the surface of a mirror. 'Even up to the Brahmā world' (yāva brahmalokāpi) means having made even the Brahmā world his domain. 'He wields mastery with his body' (kāyena vasaṃ vatteti) means that he exercises his own mastery with his body there in the Brahmā world.

Dibbāya sotadhātuyāti ettha dibbasadisattā dibbā. Devatānañhi sucaritakammanibbattā pittasemharuhirādīhi apalibuddhā upakkilesavimuttatāya dūrepi ārammaṇasampaṭicchanasamatthā dibbā pasādasotadhātu hoti. Ayañcāpi imassa bhikkhuno vīriyabhāvanābalena nibbattā ñāṇasotadhātu tādisāyevāti dibbasadisattā dibbā. Apica dibbavihāravasena paṭiladdhattā attanā ca dibbavihārasannissitattāpi dibbā. Savanaṭṭhena nijjīvaṭṭhena ca sotadhātu. Sotadhātukiccakaraṇena sotadhātu viyātipi sotadhātu. Tāya sotadhātuyā. Visuddhāyāti suddhāya nirupakkilesāya. Atikkantamānusikāyāti manussūpacāraṃ atikkamitvā saddasavane mānusikaṃ maṃsasotadhātuṃ atikkantāya vītivattetvā ṭhitāya. Ubho sadde suṇātīti dve sadde suṇāti. Katame dve? Dibbe ca mānuse ca, devānañca manussānañca saddeti vuttaṃ hoti. Etena padesapariyādānaṃ veditabbaṃ. Ye dūre santike cāti ye saddā dūre paracakkavāḷepi, ye ca santike antamaso sadehasannissitapāṇakasaddāpi, te suṇātīti vuttaṃ hoti. Etena nippadesapariyādānaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Regarding 'with the divine ear-element' (dibbāya sotadhātuyā): here, it is 'divine' (dibbā) because it is like the divine. For the divine ear-element of the deities, produced by their wholesome kamma, is unobstructed by bile, phlegm, blood, and so on; being free from imperfections, it is capable of receiving objects even from afar. This knowledge-ear-element, too, produced in this bhikkhu by the power of his energy and meditation development, is just like that; hence it is 'divine' because of its similarity to the divine. Moreover, it is 'divine' because it is attained by means of the divine abiding and because it is itself dependent on the divine abiding. It is the 'ear-element' (sotadhātu) in the sense of hearing and in the sense of being non-sentient. It is also like the ear-element because it performs the function of the ear-element. 'With that ear-element.' 'Purified' (visuddhāya) means clean, without imperfections. 'Surpassing the human' (atikkantamānusikāya) means that in hearing sounds it has surpassed the human sphere, that it stands having gone beyond the human ear-element of flesh. 'He hears both sounds' means he hears two kinds of sounds. Which two? Divine and human; that is, the sounds of deities and of humans. By this, a partial inclusion should be understood. 'Those that are far and near': this means he hears sounds that are far away, even in other world-systems, and those that are near, down to the sounds of creatures dwelling in his own body. By this, a complete inclusion should be understood.

Parasattānanti attānaṃ ṭhapetvā sesasattānaṃ. Parapuggalānanti idampi iminā ekatthameva. Veneyyavasena pana desanāvilāsena ca byañjananānattaṃ kataṃ. Cetasā cetoti attano cittena tesaṃ cittaṃ. Pariccāti paricchinditvā. Pajānātīti sarāgādivasena nānappakārato jānāti. Sarāgaṃ vā cittantiādīsu pana aṭṭhalobhasahagatacittaṃ sarāgaṃ cittanti veditabbaṃ. Avasesaṃ cātubhūmakaṃ [V 3.0080] kusalābyākatacittaṃ vītarāgaṃ. Dve [M 3.0084] domanassacittāni, dve vicikicchuddhaccacittānīti imāni pana cattāri cittāni imasmiṃ duke saṅgahaṃ na gacchanti. Keci pana therā tānipi saṅgaṇhanti. Duvidhaṃ pana domanassacittaṃ sadosaṃ cittaṃ nāma. Sabbampi cātubhūmakaṃ kusalābyākatacittaṃ vītadosaṃ. Sesāni dasa akusalacittāni imasmiṃ duke saṅgahaṃ na gacchanti. Keci pana therā tānipi saṅgaṇhanti. Samohaṃ vītamohanti ettha pana pāṭipuggalikanayena vicikicchuddhaccasahagatadvayameva samohaṃ. Mohassa pana sabbākusalesu sambhavato dvādasavidhampi akusalacittaṃ samohaṃ cittanti veditabbaṃ. Avasesaṃ vītamohaṃ. Thinamiddhānugataṃ pana saṃkhittaṃ, uddhaccānugataṃ vikkhittaṃ. Rūpāvacarārūpāvacaraṃ mahaggataṃ, avasesaṃ amahaggataṃ. Sabbampi tebhūmakaṃ sauttaraṃ, lokuttaraṃ anuttaraṃ. Upacārappattaṃ appanāppattañca samāhitaṃ, ubhayamappattaṃ asamāhitaṃ. Tadaṅgavikkhambhanasamucchedappaṭippassaddhinissaraṇavimuttiṃ pattaṃ pañcavidhampi etaṃ vimuttaṃ, vimuttimappattaṃ vā avimuttanti veditabbaṃ.

'Other beings' means all beings apart from oneself. 'Other individuals' has the same meaning as this. However, the variation in wording is made for the sake of adapting to the audience and for elegance in the teaching. 'With mind, the mind' means with one's own mind, their mind. `Paricca` means having encompassed. 'He understands' means he understands in various ways, such as in terms of lust and so on. In the phrase 'a mind with lust,' etc., a mind accompanied by the eight kinds of greed should be understood as 'a mind with lust.' The remaining wholesome and indeterminate minds of the four planes are 'without lust.' However, the two minds accompanied by displeasure and the two minds accompanied by doubt and restlessness—these four minds—do not fall under this pair. But some elders include them too. The two kinds of minds accompanied by displeasure are called 'minds with aversion.' All wholesome and indeterminate minds of the four planes are 'without aversion.' The remaining ten unwholesome minds do not fall under this pair. But some elders include them too. Regarding 'a mind with delusion' and 'a mind without delusion,' here, from an individual perspective, only the two minds accompanied by doubt and restlessness are 'with delusion.' However, since delusion is present in all unwholesome states, all twelve types of unwholesome minds should be understood as 'minds with delusion.' The rest are 'without delusion.' A mind accompanied by sloth and torpor is 'contracted,' while one accompanied by restlessness is 'scattered.' Form-sphere and formless-sphere minds are 'exalted,' while the rest are 'not exalted.' All minds pertaining to the three planes are 'with a superior,' while the supramundane is 'without a superior.' A mind that has attained access concentration or full absorption is 'concentrated,' while one that has attained neither is 'unconcentrated.' A mind that has attained any of these five kinds of liberation—liberation by substitution, by suppression, by cutting off, by tranquillization, and by escape—is 'liberated'; one that has not attained liberation is to be understood as 'unliberated'.

Anekavihitanti (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.12) anekavidhaṃ, anekehi vā pakārehi pavattitaṃ saṃvaṇṇitanti attho. Pubbenivāsanti samanantarātītabhavaṃ ādiṃ katvā tattha tattha nivutthasantānaṃ. Anussaratīti khandhapaṭipāṭivasena, cutipaṭisandhivasena vā anugantvā anugantvā sarati. Seyyathidaṃ – ekampi jātiṃ…pe… pubbenivāsaṃ anussaratīti. Tattha ekampi jātinti ekampi paṭisandhimūlaṃ cutipariyosānaṃ ekabhavapariyāpannaṃ khandhasantānaṃ. Esa nayo dvepi jātiyotiādīsupi. Anekepi saṃvaṭṭakappetiādīsu pana parihāyamāno kappo saṃvaṭṭakappo, vaḍḍhamāno vivaṭṭakappoti veditabbo. Tattha saṃvaṭṭena saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyī gahito hoti taṃmūlakattā, vivaṭṭena vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī. Evañhi sati yāni tāni “cattārimāni, bhikkhave, kappassa asaṅkhyeyyāni. Katamāni cattāri? Saṃvaṭṭo saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyī vivaṭṭo vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī”ti (a. ni. 4.156) vuttāni, tāni pariggahitāni honti.

'Of various kinds' (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 1.12) means of many kinds, or described as having occurred in various ways. 'Past lives' means the continuity of beings who have lived here and there, beginning with the immediately preceding existence. 'He recollects' means he recollects by following the succession of aggregates or by the process of death and rebirth. For example: 'He recollects one birth... up to recollecting past lives.' Here, 'one birth' refers to a single continuum of aggregates, from the root of rebirth-linking to the end of death, encompassing one complete existence. The same principle applies to 'two births,' etc. In the case of 'many cycles of contraction and expansion,' a declining eon should be understood as a 'cycle of contraction,' while an increasing eon is a 'cycle of expansion.' Here, by 'contraction,' the period of remaining contracted is taken, because it is its root; and by 'expansion,' the period of remaining expanded. Thus, when it is said, 'Monks, there are these four incalculable aeons. Which four? The aeon of contraction, the aeon of remaining contracted, the aeon of expansion, and the aeon of remaining expanded' (A. Ni. 4.156), these are included.

Amutrāsinti amumhi saṃvaṭṭakappe ahaṃ amumhi bhave vā yoniyā vā gahiyā vā viññāṇaṭṭhitiyā vā sattāvāse vā sattanikāye vā āsiṃ. Evaṃnāmoti tisso vā phusso vā. Evaṃgottoti gotamo vā kaccāyano vā kassapo vā. Idamassa atītabhave attano nāmagottānussaraṇavasena vuttaṃ. Sace pana tasmiṃ kāle attano vaṇṇasampattilūkhapaṇītajīvikabhāvaṃ [M 3.0085] sukhadukkhabahulataṃ appāyukadīghāyukabhāvaṃ vā anussaritukāmo hoti, tampi anussaratiyeva. Tenāha “evaṃvaṇṇo…pe… evamāyupariyanto”ti. Tattha evaṃvaṇṇoti odāto vā sāmo vā. Evamāhāroti sālimaṃsodanāhāro vā pavattaphalabhojano vā. Evaṃsukhadukkhappaṭisaṃvedīti [V 3.0081] anena pakārena kāyikacetasikānaṃ sāmisanirāmisādippabhedānaṃ sukhadukkhānaṃ paṭisaṃvedī. Evamāyupariyantoti evaṃ vassasataparimāṇāyupariyanto vā caturāsītikappasahassāyupariyanto vā. So tato cuto amutra udapādinti so ahaṃ tato bhavato yonito gahito viññāṇaṭṭhitito sattāvāsato sattanikāyato vā cuto punaamukasmiṃ nāma bhave yoniyā gatiyā viññāṇaṭṭhitiyā sattāvāse sakkanikāye vā udapādiṃ. Tatrāpāsinti tatrāpi bhave yoniyā gatiyā viññāṇaṭṭhitiyā sattāvāse sattanikāye vā puna ahosiṃ. Evaṃnāmotiādi vuttanayameva.

'There I was' means 'I was in that cycle of contraction; or in that existence, womb, destination, station of consciousness, abode of beings, or class of beings.' 'With such a name' means, for example, Tissa or Phussa. 'Of such a clan' means, for example, Gotama, Kaccāyana, or Kassapa. This is said with reference to recollecting one’s own name and clan in past existences. If one wishes to recollect one’s excellence of appearance, whether one's livelihood was coarse or refined, the abundance of pleasure and pain, or whether one had a short or long lifespan at that time, one recollects that too. Hence it is said: 'With such an appearance... up to with such a lifespan.' Here, 'with such an appearance' means fair or dark. 'With such food' means eating rice and meat or consuming fruits that naturally occur. 'Experiencing such pleasure and pain' means experiencing physical and mental pleasure and pain, whether worldly or unworldly, and so forth, in such a way. 'With such a lifespan' means living for a hundred years or up to eighty-four thousand eons. 'Having passed away from there, I arose elsewhere' means 'I, having passed away from that existence, womb, destination, station of consciousness, abode of beings, or class of beings, was reborn in such-and-such an existence, womb, destination, station of consciousness, abode of beings, or class of beings.' 'There too I was' means 'I was also in that existence, womb, destination, station of consciousness, abode of beings, or class of beings.' 'With such a name,' etc., follows the same pattern as before.

Apica amutrāsinti idaṃ anupubbena ārohantassa yāvadicchakaṃ anussaraṇaṃ. So tatoti paṭinivattantassa paccavekkhaṇaṃ, tasmā “idhūpapanno”ti imissā idhūpapattiyā anantarameva uppattiṭṭhānaṃ sandhāya “amutra udapādi”nti idaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Tatrāpāsinti evamādi panassa tatrāpi imissā upapattiyā antare upapattiṭṭhāne nāmagottādīnaṃ anussaraṇadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. So tato cuto idhūpapannoti svāhaṃ tato anantaruppattiṭṭhānato cuto idha amukasmiṃ nāma khattiyakule vā brāhmaṇakule vā nibbattoti. Itīti evaṃ. Sākāraṃ sauddesanti nāmagottavasena sauddesaṃ, vaṇṇādivasena sākāraṃ. Nāmagottena hi satto “tisso kassapo”ti uddisīyati, vaṇṇādīhi “sāmo odāto”ti nānattato paññāyati, tasmā nāmagottaṃ uddeso, itare ākārā.

Moreover, 'there I was' refers to the successive recollection of one ascending as far as desired. 'He, from there' is a reviewing for one turning back. Therefore, it should be understood that the phrase 'there he arose' is said with reference to the place of arising immediately preceding this rebirth here. 'There too I was,' and so on, is said to show the recollection of name, clan, and so on, in the intermediate places of rebirth before this current one. 'Having passed away from there, he was reborn here' means 'I, having passed away from that immediately preceding place of rebirth, was born here in such-and-such a khattiya or brahmin family.' 'Thus' means in this way. 'With features and details' means with details by name and clan, and with features by complexion and so on. For a being is designated by name and clan as, for example, 'Tissa Kassapa,' but is distinguished by variations such as 'dark or fair' through complexion and other traits. Therefore, the name and clan are the designation, while the rest are the features.

Dibbenātiādīsu dibbasadisattā dibbaṃ. Devatānañhi sucaritakammanibbattaṃ pittasemharuhirādīhi apalibuddhaṃ upakkilesavimuttatāya dūrepi ārammaṇasampaṭicchanasamatthaṃ dibbaṃ pasādacakkhu hoti. Idañcāpi vīriyabhāvanābalena nibbattaṃ ñāṇacakkhu tādisamevāti dibbasadisattā dibbaṃ. Dibbavihāravasena paṭiladdhattā attano ca dibbavihārasannissitattāpi dibbaṃ. Ālokapariggahena mahājutikattāpi [M 3.0086] dibbaṃ. Tirokuṭṭādigatarūpadassanena mahāgatikattāpi dibbaṃ. Taṃ sabbaṃ saddasatthānusārena veditabbaṃ. Dassanaṭṭhena cakkhu. Cakkhukiccakaraṇena cakkhumivātipi cakkhu. Cutūpapātadassanena diṭṭhivisuddhihetuttā visuddhaṃ. Yo hi cutimeva passati, na upapātaṃ, so ucchedadiṭṭhiṃ gaṇhāti. Yo upapātameva passati, na cutiṃ, so navasattapātubhāvadiṭṭhiṃ gaṇhāti. Yo pana tadubhayaṃ passati, so yasmā duvidhampi taṃ diṭṭhigataṃ ativattati, tasmā taṃ dassanaṃ diṭṭhivisuddhihetu hoti. Ubhayampi cetaṃ buddhaputtā passanti. Tena vuttaṃ “cutūpapātadassanena diṭṭhivisuddhihetuttā visuddha”nti. Manussūpacāraṃ atikkamitvā rūpadassanena atikkantamānusakaṃ, mānusaṃ vā maṃsacakkhuṃ atikkantattā [V 3.0082] atikkantamānusakanti veditabbaṃ. Tena dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena.

In the term 'divine' (dibba), it is called 'divine' because it resembles the divine. For the divine eye of sensitivity (pasādacakkhu), which arises from the wholesome deeds of deities, is unhindered by bile, phlegm, blood, and so forth, and being free from defilements, it is capable of perceiving objects even from afar. This eye of wisdom (ñāṇacakkhu), too, produced through the power of energy and cultivation, is similar, and thus it is called 'divine' because it resembles the divine. It is also called 'divine' because it is attained through divine abiding (dibbavihāra) and because it relies on divine abiding. Due to its great radiance in capturing light, it is also 'divine.' Because it sees forms beyond walls and other obstacles, it is also 'divine' due to its great range. All this should be understood in accordance with the science of words. In the sense of seeing, it is an 'eye.' Because it performs the function of an eye, it is also like an 'eye.' Because it sees the passing away and rebirth of beings, it is 'purified' (visuddha), as it is the cause for purity of view. For one who sees only passing away but not rebirth holds the view of annihilation. One who sees only rebirth but not passing away holds the view of the arising of a new being. But one who sees both transcends both kinds of wrong view, and thus this seeing becomes a cause for purity of view. Both of these are seen by the Buddha's children. Therefore, it is said, 'Because it sees the passing away and rebirth of beings, it is purified as the cause for purity of view.' By transcending the human sphere and seeing forms, it is called 'transcending the human' (atikkantamānusaka), or it should be understood as 'transcending the human' because it transcends the human fleshly eye. Thus, with this divine eye, purified and transcending the human...

Satte passatīti manussānaṃ maṃsacakkhunā viya satte oloketi. Cavamāne upapajjamāneti ettha cutikkhaṇe vā upapattikkhaṇe vā dibbacakkhunā daṭṭhuṃ na sakkā. Ye pana āsannacutikā idāni cavissanti, te cavamānāti, ye ca gahitappaṭisandhikā sampatinibbattā ca, te upapajjamānāti adhippetā. Te evarūpe cavamāne upapajjamāne ca passatīti dasseti. Hīneti mohanissandayuttattā hīnānaṃ jātikulabhogādīnaṃ vasena hīḷite uññāte. Paṇīteti amohanissandayuttattā tabbiparīte. Suvaṇṇeti adosanissandayuttattā iṭṭhakantamanāpavaṇṇayutte. Dubbaṇṇeti dosanissandayuttattā aniṭṭhākantāmanāpavaṇṇayutte, virūpavirūpetipi attho. Sugateti sugatigate, alobhanissandayuttattā vā aḍḍhe mahaddhane. Duggateti duggatigate, lobhanissandayuttattā vā dalidde appannapāne.

'He sees beings' means he observes beings as if with the human fleshly eye. In the phrase 'passing away and being reborn,' it is not possible to see with the divine eye at the moment of decease or the moment of rebirth. But those who are near death and will decease now are intended as 'passing away,' and those who have grasped rebirth-linking and have newly arisen are intended as 'being reborn.' It shows that one sees such beings passing away and being reborn. 'Inferior' means those who are despised and looked down upon due to low birth, family, wealth, and so forth, because they are connected with the outflow of delusion. 'Superior' means the opposite of the former, being connected with the outflow of non-delusion. 'Beautiful' means those endowed with agreeable, pleasing, and attractive complexions, being connected with the outflow of non-hatred. 'Ugly' means those endowed with disagreeable, unattractive complexions, being connected with the outflow of hatred; the meaning also includes deformed and misshapen. 'Fortunate' means those who have gone to a good destination, or who are rich and very wealthy, being connected with the outflow of non-greed. 'Unfortunate' means those who have gone to a bad destination, or who are poor and lacking food and drink, being connected with the outflow of greed.

Yathākammūpageti yaṃ yaṃ kammaṃ upacitaṃ, tena tena upagate. Kāyaduccaritenātiādīsu duṭṭhu caritaṃ kilesapūtikattāti duccaritaṃ. Kāyena duccaritaṃ, kāyato vā uppannaṃ duccaritanti kāyaduccaritaṃ. Itaresupi eseva nayo. Samannāgatāti samaṅgibhūtā. Ariyānaṃ upavādakāti buddhapaccekabuddhasāvakānaṃ ariyānaṃ antamaso gihisotāpannānampi anatthakāmā hutvā antimavatthunā vā guṇaparidhaṃsanena vā upavādakā, akkosakā garahakāti vuttaṃ hoti. Micchādiṭṭhikāti viparītadassanā[M 3.0087]. Micchādiṭṭhikammasamādānāti micchādiṭṭhivasena samādinnanānāvidhakammā, yepi micchādiṭṭhimūlakesu kāyakammādīsu aññepi samādāpenti.

As one is led by one's kamma: one fares on in accordance with whatever kamma one has accumulated. In 'bodily misconduct,' and so forth, it is misconduct (duccarita) because it is badly conducted (duṭṭhu caritaṃ), being putrid with defilements. Bodily misconduct is misconduct by way of the body, or misconduct that has arisen from the body; the same method applies to the others. 'Endowed' means possessed of. 'Those who revile the noble ones' means those who, wishing them harm, revile, abuse, or censure the noble ones—Buddhas, paccekabuddhas, and disciples, down to lay stream-enterers—either with the ultimate accusation or by disparaging their virtues. 'Those of wrong view' are those with a perverted view. 'Those who undertake actions based on wrong view' are those who, on account of wrong view, undertake various kinds of kamma, and who also incite others to undertake bodily kamma, and so forth, rooted in wrong view.

Kāyassa bhedāti upādinnakkhandhapariccāgā. Paraṃ maraṇāti tadanantaraṃ abhinibbattakkhandhaggahaṇā. Atha vā kāyassa bhedāti jīvitindriyassūpacchedā. Paraṃ maraṇāti cuticittato uddhaṃ. Apāyanti evamādi sabbaṃ nirayavevacanameva. Nirayo hi saggamokkhahetubhūtā puññasammatā ayā apetattā, sukhānaṃ vā āyassa abhāvā apāyo. Dukkhassa gati paṭisaraṇanti duggati, dosabahulatāya vā duṭṭhena kammena nibbattā gatīti duggati. Vivasā nipatanti tattha dukkaṭṭakārinoti vinipāto, vinassantā vā ettha patanti sambhijjamānaṅgapaccaṅgāti vinipāto. Natthi ettha assādasaññito ayoti nirayo.

'With the breakup of the body' means with the relinquishment of the clung-to aggregates. 'After death' means with the grasping of the newly arisen aggregates immediately after that. Alternatively, 'with the breakup of the body' means with the cutting off of the life faculty. 'After death' means subsequent to the death-consciousness. 'State of deprivation,' and so on, are all synonyms for the nether world. For the nether world is called a 'state of deprivation' (apāya) because it is devoid of the good fortune which is approved as merit, the cause for heaven and liberation; or it is an apāya because of the absence of the fortune of happiness. It is a 'bad destination' (duggati) because it is a destination and resort for suffering; or it is a duggati because it is a destination produced by bad kamma due to an abundance of hatred. It is the 'abyss' (vinipāta) because evildoers fall there helplessly; or it is a vinipāta because beings fall there perishing, with their limbs and members shattering. It is 'hell' (niraya) because there is no fortune called gratification here.

Atha vā apāyaggahaṇena tiracchānayoniṃ dīpeti. Tiracchānayoni hi apāyo sugatito apetattā[V 3.0083], na duggati mahesakkhānaṃ nāgarājādīnaṃ sambhavato. Duggatiggahaṇena pettivisayañca. So hi apāyo ceva duggati ca sugatito apetattā dukkhassa ca gatibhūtattā, na tu vinipāto asurasadisaṃ avinipatitattā. Vinipātaggahaṇena asurakāyaṃ. So hi yathāvuttena atthena apāyo ceva duggati ca sabbasamussayehi vinipatitattā vinipātoti vuccati. Nirayaggahaṇena avīciādikamanekappakāraṃ nirayamevāti. Upapannāti upagatā, tattha abhinibbattāti adhippāyo. Vuttavipariyāyena sukkapakkho veditabbo. Ayaṃ pana viseso – tattha sugatiggahaṇena manussāgatipi saṅgayhati, saggaggahaṇena devagatiyeva. Tattha sundarā gatīti sugati. Rūpādīhi visayehi suṭṭhu aggoti saggo. So sabbopi lujjanappalujjanaṭṭhena lokoti ayamettha saṅkhepo. Vitthāro pana sabbākārena visuddhimaggasaṃvaṇṇanāto gahetabbo. Tatiyādīni uttānatthāni.

Alternatively, by the term 'state of deprivation' it indicates the animal realm. For the animal realm is a state of deprivation because it is devoid of a good destination, but it is not a bad destination because powerful beings such as nāga kings are found there. By the term 'bad destination' it also indicates the sphere of ghosts. This is both a state of deprivation and a bad destination because it is devoid of a good destination and is a destination of suffering, but it is not the abyss because it has not fallen into ruin like the asuras. By the term 'abyss' it indicates the host of asuras. For the reason stated, this is both a state of deprivation and a bad destination, and it is called the 'abyss' because it has fallen from all its eminences. By the term 'hell' it indicates the many kinds of hells, such as Avīci. 'Reborn' means having gone there; the intention is 'newly arisen there.' The bright side should be understood in the reverse way to what has been stated. But there is this distinction: here, by the term 'good destination,' the human destination is also included, while by the term 'heaven,' only the divine destination is meant. There, a 'good destination' (sugati) is a beautiful destination. 'Heaven' (sagga) is so called because it is exceedingly excellent with regard to such objects as forms. All this is called 'world' (loka) in the sense of wearing away and breaking up. This is the summary here. The detailed account, however, should be taken in all its aspects from the explanation in the Visuddhimagga. The third and following suttas are clear in meaning.

Dutiyaāhuneyyasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Second Āhuneyya Sutta and others is finished.

8. Anuttariyasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Anuttariya Sutta

8. Aṭṭhame [M 3.0088] natthi etesaṃ uttarāni visiṭṭhānīti anuttarāni, anuttarāni eva anuttariyāni yathā “anantameva anantariya”nti āha “niruttarānī”ti. Dassanānuttariyaṃ nāma phalavisesāvahattā. Esa nayo sesesupi. Sattavidhaariyadhanalābhoti sattavidhasaddhādilokuttaradhanalābho. Sikkhāttayassa pūraṇanti adhisīlasikkhādīnaṃ tissannaṃ sikkhānaṃ pūraṇaṃ. Tattha pūraṇaṃ nippariyāyato asekkhānaṃ vasena veditabbaṃ. Kalyāṇaputhujjanato paṭṭhāya hi satta sekhā tisso sikkhā pūrenti nāma, arahā paripuṇṇasikkhoti. Iti imāni anuttariyāni lokiyalokuttarāni kathitāni.

8. In the eighth sutta: They are 'unsurpassable' (anuttarāni) because there are no other superior or more distinguished things than these. 'Unsurpassable things' (anuttariyāni) are just the unsurpassable (anuttarāni), just as it is said, 'the infinite (ananta) is indeed the infinite (ānantariya).' He said 'without a superior' (niruttarāni). 'The unsurpassable seeing' is so called because it brings about a special fruit. This method applies to the rest as well. 'The attainment of the sevenfold noble wealth' is the attainment of the seven kinds of supramundane wealth beginning with faith. 'The fulfillment of the threefold training' is the fulfillment of the three trainings, namely, the training in higher virtue, and so forth. Here, fulfillment should be understood in the primary sense with reference to the non-learner (asekha). For beginning from the virtuous worldling, the seven learners fulfill the three trainings only in name, but the arahant is one whose training is fulfilled. Thus these unsurpassable things, both worldly and supramundane, have been spoken of.

Anuttariyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Anuttariya Sutta is finished.

9. Anussatiṭṭhānasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Anussatiṭṭhāna Sutta

9. Navame anussatiyo eva diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikādihitasukhānaṃ kāraṇabhāvato ṭhānānīti anussatiṭṭhānāni. Buddhaguṇārammaṇā satīti yathā buddhānussati visesādhigamassa ṭhānaṃ hoti, evaṃ “itipi so bhagavā”tiādinā buddhaguṇe ārabbhe uppannā sati. Evaṃ anussarato [V 3.0084] hi pīti uppajjati, so taṃ pītiṃ khayato vayato paṭṭhapetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti. Upacārakammaṭṭhānaṃ nāmetaṃ gihīnampi labbhati. Upacārakammaṭṭhānanti ca paccakkhato upacārajjhānāvahaṃ kammaṭṭhānaparamparāya sammasanaṃ yāva arahattā lokiyalokuttaravisesāvahaṃ. Esa nayo sabbattha.

9. In the ninth sutta: The recollections themselves are 'bases' because they are causes for welfare and happiness in this present life and in lives to come; hence 'bases for recollection.' 'Mindfulness with the qualities of the Buddha as its object': just as the recollection of the Buddha is a basis for special attainments, so too is the mindfulness that has arisen having taken as its object the qualities of the Buddha, beginning with 'The Blessed One is such....' For one who recollects in this way, rapture arises. By making that rapture a basis for insight into its destruction and vanishing, one attains arahantship. This is called an access meditation subject, and it is obtained even by householders. And 'access meditation subject' is the contemplation of the sequence of meditation subjects that directly brings about access concentration and jhāna, and leads all the way to arahantship, bringing about worldly and supramundane special attainments. This method applies in all cases.

Anussatiṭṭhānasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Anussatiṭṭhāna Sutta is finished.

10. Mahānāmasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Mahānāma Sutta

10. Dasame tasmiṃ samayeti buddhāguṇānussaraṇasamaye. Rāgapariyuṭṭhitanti rāgena pariyuṭṭhitaṃ. Pariyuṭṭhānappattipi, rāgena vā saṃhitaṃ cittaṃ [M 3.0089] araññamiva corehi tena pariyuṭṭhitanti vuttaṃ, tassa pariyuṭṭhānaṭṭhānabhāvatopi pariyuṭṭhitarāganti attho. Byañjanaṃ pana anādiyitvā atthamattaṃ dassento “uppajjamānena rāgena uṭṭhahitvā gahita”nti āha. Ujukamevāti pageva kāyavaṅkādīnaṃ apanītattā cittassa ca anujubhāvakarānaṃ mānādīnaṃ abhāvato, rāgādipariyuṭṭhānābhāvena vā oṇatiuṇṇativirahato ujubhāvameva gataṃ. Atha vā ujukamevāti kammaṭṭhānassa thinaṃ middhaṃ otiṇṇatāya līnuddhaccavigamato majjhimasamathanimittappaṭipattiyā ujubhāvameva gataṃ. Aṭṭhakathaṃ nissāyāti bhavajātiādīnaṃ padānaṃ atthaṃ nissāya. Atthavedanti vā hetuphalaṃ paṭicca uppannaṃ tuṭṭhimāha. Dhammavedanti hetuṃ paṭicca uppannaṃ tuṭṭhiṃ. “Ārakattā araha”nti anussarantassa hi yadidaṃ bhagavato kilesehi ārakattaṃ, so hetu. Ñāpako cettha hetu adhippeto, na kārako sampāpako. Tatonena ñāyamāno arahattattho phalaṃ. Iminā nayena sesapadesupi hetuso phalavipāko veditabbo. Dhammānussatiādīsupi hi ādimajjhapariyosānakalyāṇatādayo suppaṭipattiādayo ca tattha tattha hetubhāvena niddiṭṭhāyeva. Dhammūpasaṃhitanti yathāvuttahetuphalasaṅkhātaguṇūpasaṃhitaṃ.

10. In the tenth section, “at that time” refers to the moment of recollecting the qualities of the Buddha. “Overcome by lust” means “overwhelmed by lust.” It can also mean that the mind, like a forest infested with thieves, is seized by lust; thus, it signifies that lust has taken hold, making it a place where lust takes hold, hence “overcome by lust.” Without dwelling on the phrasing, the meaning is simply that “lust arises and takes hold.” “Straightened” means free from bodily crookedness and mental distortions like conceit, or free from being oppressed by lust, thus becoming upright, without being bent or elevated. Alternatively, “straightened” refers to the meditation subject being free from sloth and torpor, sluggishness, and restlessness, and thus proceeding along the middle path of the sign of calm. “Relying on the commentary” means depending on the meaning of terms such as “existence” and “birth.” “Delighting in meaning” refers to satisfaction arising from understanding cause and effect. “Delighting in the Dhamma” means satisfaction arising from understanding the cause. “Because he is far from defilements, he is worthy”—for one who recollects thus, the cause is the Blessed One’s distance from defilements. Here, the indicator is intended as the cause, not the agent or accomplisher. From this, the meaning of arahantship, being understood, is the result. In this way, the relationship between cause and effect should be understood in the remaining phrases as well. For in the recollections of the Dhamma, etc., the excellence at the beginning, middle, and end, as well as proper practice, etc., are already explained as causes in their respective contexts. “Connected with the Dhamma” means connected with the qualities described as cause and effect.

Mahānāmasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Mahānāma Sutta is finished.

Āhuneyyavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Āhuneyyavagga is finished.

2. Sāraṇīyavaggo

2. The Sāraṇīya Vagga

1. Paṭhamasāraṇīyasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the First Sāraṇīya Sutta

11. Dutiyassa [V 3.0085] paṭhame saritabbayuttakāti anussaraṇārahā. Mijjati siniyhati etāyāti mettā, mittabhāvo. Mettā etassa atthīti mettaṃ, kāyakammaṃ. Taṃ pana yasmā mettāsahagatacittasamuṭṭhānaṃ, tasmā vuttaṃ “mettena cittena kātabbaṃ kāyakamma”nti. Esa nayo sesadvayepi. Imānīti mettakāyakammādīni. Bhikkhūnaṃ vasena āgatāni tesaṃ seṭṭhaparisabhāvato. Yathā pana bhikkhunīsupi labbhanti, evaṃ gihīsupi labbhanti catuparisasādhāraṇattāti taṃ dassento “bhikkhūnañhī”tiādimāha. Bhikkhuno [M 3.0090] sabbampi anavajjakāyakammaṃ ābhisamācārikakammantogadhamevāti āha “mettena cittena…pe… kāyakammaṃ nāmā”ti. Bhattivasena pavattiyamānā cetiyabodhīnaṃ vandanā mettāsiddhāti katvā tadatthāya gamanaṃ “mettaṃ kāyakamma”nti vuttaṃ. Ādi-saddena cetiyabodhibhikkhūsu vuttāvasesāpacāyanādivasena pavattamettāvasena pavattaṃ kāyikaṃ kiriyaṃ saṅgaṇhāti.

11. In the second sutta, at the first point, “worthy of recollection” means “fit for recollection.” “One is affectionate, one is fond through this” is loving-kindness, the state of being a friend. “There is loving-kindness in this” is “metta,” a bodily action. But because it arises from a mind accompanied by loving-kindness, therefore it is said: “Bodily action should be done with a mind of loving-kindness.” The same method applies to the remaining two. “These” refers to bodily actions of loving-kindness, etc. They come in connection with the monks, due to their being the foremost assembly. Just as they are obtainable among nuns, so too among householders, because they are common to the four assemblies. To show this, it is said: “For monks indeed...” and so on. All blameless bodily actions of a monk are included within the rules of good conduct, hence it is said: “With a mind of loving-kindness... is called bodily action.” The veneration of shrines and Bodhi trees, occurring in connection with offerings, is accomplished through loving-kindness; therefore, going for that purpose is called “bodily action of loving-kindness.” By the word “etc.,” it includes bodily actions that occur through loving-kindness, such as the remaining acts of reverence towards shrines, Bodhi trees, and monks that have been mentioned.

Tepiṭakampi buddhavacanaṃ kathiyamānanti adhippāyo. Tepiṭakampi buddhavacanaṃ paripucchanaatthakathanavasena pavattiyamānameva mettaṃ vacīkammaṃ nāma hitajjhāsayena pavattitabbato. Tīṇi sucaritānīti kāyavacīmanosucaritāni. Cintananti evaṃ cintanamattampi manokammaṃ, pageva paṭipannā bhāvanāti dasseti.

The intention is that the entire Tipiṭaka, when being spoken, is the word of the Buddha. The entire Tipiṭaka, proceeding by way of questioning and explaining the meaning, is itself called loving verbal action, since it should proceed with a beneficial intention. “Three good conducts” means good bodily, verbal, and mental conduct. “Thinking” means even mere thinking is mental action, how much more so the practice of development—this is shown.

Āvīti pakāsaṃ. Pakāsabhāvo cettha yaṃ uddissa taṃ kāyakammaṃ karīyati, tassa sammukhabhāvatoti āha “sammukhā”ti. Rahoti appakāsaṃ. Appakāsatā ca yaṃ uddissa taṃ kāyakammaṃ karīyati, tassa apaccakkhabhāvatoti āha “parammukhā”ti. Sahāyabhāvagamanaṃ tesaṃ purato. Tesu karontesuyeva hi sahāyabhāvagamanaṃ sammukhā kāyakammaṃ nāma hoti. Ubhayehīti navakehi therehi ca. Paggayhāti paggaṇhitvā uddhaṃ katvā kevalaṃ “devo”ti avatvā guṇehi thirabhāvajotanaṃ “devatthero”ti vacanaṃ paggayha vacanaṃ. Mamattabodhanaṃ vacanaṃ mamāyanavacanaṃ. Ekantaparammukhassa manokammassa sammukhatā nāma viññattisamuṭṭhāpanavasena hoti, tañca kho loke kāyakammanti pākaṭaṃ paññātaṃ. Hatthavikārādīni anāmasitvā eva dassento “nayanāni ummīletvā”tiādimāha. Kāmaṃ mettāsinehasiniddhānaṃ nayanānaṃ ummīlanā pasannena mukhena olokanañca [V 3.0086] mettaṃ kāyakammameva, yassa pana cittassa vasena nayanānaṃ mettāsinehasiniddhatā mukhassa ca pasannatā, taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “mettaṃ manokammaṃ nāmā”ti.

“Āvī” means “manifest.” The nature of manifestation here refers to the bodily action performed intending for those present; hence, it is called “face-to-face.” “Raho” means “unmanifest.” The nature of being unmanifest refers to the bodily action performed intending for those absent; hence, it is called “behind-the-back.” The act of associating with companions is done in their presence. For when one performs actions in their company, that act of associating is called a face-to-face bodily action. “By both” means by both the newly ordained monks and the elders. “Paggayha” means having lifted up, elevating—not merely saying “deva” but, by illuminating the state of steadfastness with virtues, thus saying “devatthero” is an elevated utterance. The utterance that awakens possessiveness is the speech of claiming “mine.” The face-to-face nature of a purely behind-the-back mental action occurs through the arising of an intimation, yet in the world, it is clearly known and understood as a bodily action. Without resorting to gestures like hand movements, it is shown simply by “opening the eyes” and so on. Indeed, the opening of eyes filled with loving-kindness and affection, and a serene gaze with a bright face, is itself a bodily action of loving-kindness. However, regarding the state of mind that causes the eyes to be filled with loving-kindness and affection, and the face to be serene, it is said, “loving-kindness is called a mental action.”

Lābha-saddo kammasādhano “lābhā vata, bho, laddho”tiādīsu viya. So cettha “dhammaladdhā”ti vacanato atītakālikoti āha “cīvarādayo laddhapaccayā”ti. Dhammato āgatāti dhammikā, parisuddhagamanā paccayā. Tenāha “dhammaladdhā”ti. Imameva hi atthaṃ dassetuṃ “kuhanādī”tiādi [M 3.0091] vuttaṃ. Na sammā gayhamānā hi dhammaladdhā nāma na hontīti tappaṭisedhanatthaṃ pāḷiyaṃ “dhammaladdhā”ti vuttaṃ. Deyyaṃ dakkhiṇeyyañca appaṭivibhattaṃ katvā bhuñjatīti appaṭivibhattabhogī nāma hoti. Tenāha “dve paṭivibhattāni nāmā”tiādi. Cittena vibhajananti etena cittuppādamattenapi vibhajanaṃ paṭivibhattaṃ nāma, pageva payogatoti dasseti. Cittena vibhajanapubbakaṃ vā kāyena vibhajananti mūlameva dassetuṃ “evaṃ cittena vibhajana”nti vuttaṃ. Tena cittuppādamattena paṭivibhāgo kātabboti dasseti. Appaṭivibhattanti bhāvanapuṃsakaniddeso, appaṭivibhattaṃ lābhaṃ bhuñjatīti kammaniddeso vā. Taṃ neva gihīnaṃ deti attano ājīvasodhanatthaṃ. Na attanā paribhuñjati “mayhaṃ asādhāraṇabhogitā mā hotū”ti. Paṭiggaṇhanto ca…pe… passatīti iminā āgamanato paṭṭhāya sādhāraṇabuddhiṃ upaṭṭhāpeti. Evaṃ hissa sādhāraṇabhogitā sukarā, sāraṇīyadhammo cassa pūro hoti.

The word 'lābha' (gain) is derived in the sense of the object, as in such phrases as, 'Indeed, friends, a gain has been obtained.' Here, the phrase 'righteously obtained' (dhammaladdhā) indicates the past tense; thus, it is said, 'requisites such as robes have been obtained.' What comes from the Dhamma is righteous (dhammika), meaning requisites of pure acquisition. Hence, it is said, 'righteously obtained.' To illustrate this very meaning, 'through deceit, etc.' (kuhanādi) and so on is stated. For things not rightly taken are not called 'righteously obtained'; therefore, to negate this, the Pāli text states 'righteously obtained.' One who consumes without having separated what is to be given (deyya) and what is worthy of an offering (dakkhiṇeyya) is called 'one who enjoys without dividing' (appaṭivibhattabhogī). Hence, it is said, 'there are two kinds of divisions,' and so on. 'Dividing with the mind'—by this it is shown that even a division by the mere arising of a thought is a division, let alone by physical action. Or, to show the very root, 'dividing with the body, preceded by dividing with the mind,' it is said, 'thus dividing with the mind.' This shows that a division should be made by the mere arising of a thought. 'Without dividing' (appaṭivibhattaṃ) is a neuter abstract noun, or it is an accusative of the object, as in 'consumes a gain without dividing.' He neither gives it to laypeople for the sake of purifying his livelihood, nor does he consume it himself, thinking, 'May I not be one who enjoys things not held in common.' 'And when receiving... up to... he sees'—by this, from the moment of its arrival, he establishes a mindset of sharing. For in this way, his practice of sharing becomes easy, and his principle conducive to cordiality is fulfilled.

Atha vā paṭiggaṇhanto ca…pe… passatīti iminā tassa lābhassa tīsu kālesu sādhāraṇato ṭhapanaṃ dassitaṃ. Paṭiggaṇhanto ca saṅghena sādhāraṇaṃ hotūti iminā paṭiggahaṇakālo dassito. Gahetvā…pe… passatīti iminā paṭiggahitakālo. Tadubhayaṃ pana tādisena pubbabhāgena vinā na hotīti atthasiddho purimakālo. Tayidaṃ paṭiggahaṇato pubbevassa hoti “saṅghena sādhāraṇaṃ hotūti paṭiggaṇhissāmī”ti, paṭiggaṇhantassa hoti “saṅghena sādhāraṇaṃ hotūti paṭiggaṇhāmī”ti, paṭiggahetvā hoti “saṅghena sādhāraṇaṃ hotūti hi paṭiggahitaṃ mayā”ti. Evaṃ tilakkhaṇasampannaṃ katvā laddhaṃ lābhaṃ osāraṇalakkhaṇaṃ avikopetvā paribhuñjanto sādhāraṇabhogī appaṭivibhattabhogī ca hoti.

Alternatively, by 'when receiving... up to... he sees,' the establishment of that gain as common in the three times is shown. By the thought, 'While receiving, may it be common to the Saṅgha,' the time of receiving is shown. By 'having taken... up to... he sees,' the time after receiving is shown. But since these two do not occur without such a preliminary part, the prior time is established by implication. This is as follows: before receiving, it occurs to him, 'I will receive it so that it may be common to the Saṅgha'; while receiving, it occurs to him, 'I am receiving it so that it may be common to the Saṅgha'; after having received, it occurs to him, 'It has been received by me so that it may be common to the Saṅgha.' Thus, having made the obtained gain possessed of these three characteristics, one who enjoys it without violating the characteristic of dedication becomes one who enjoys in common and one who enjoys without dividing.

Imaṃ pana sāraṇīyadhammanti imaṃ catutthaṃ saritabbayuttadhamaṃ. Na hi…pe… gaṇhanti, tasmā sādhāraṇabhogitā dussīlassa natthīti ārambhopi tāva na sambhavati, kuto pūraṇanti adhippāyo. Parisuddhasīloti iminā lābhassa dhammikabhāvaṃ dasseti. Vattaṃ akhaṇḍentoti iminā appaṭivibhattabhogitaṃ sādhāraṇabhogitañca dasseti. Sati pana tadubhaye sāraṇīyadhammo pūrito eva [V 3.0087] hotīti āha “pūretī”ti. Odissakaṃ katvāti etena anodissakaṃ katvā pituno, ācariyupajjhāyādīnaṃ vā [M 3.0092] therāsanato paṭṭhāya dentassa sāraṇīyadhammoyeva hotīti dasseti. Dātabbanti avassaṃ dātabbaṃ. Sāraṇīyadhammo panassa na hoti paṭijaggaṭṭhāne odissakaṃ katvā dinnattā. Tenāha “palibodhajagganaṃ nāma hotī”ti. Muttapalibodhassa vaṭṭati amuttapalibodhassa pūretuṃ asakkuṇeyyattā. Yadi evaṃ sabbena sabbaṃ sāraṇīyadhammaṃ pūrentassa odissakadānaṃ vaṭṭati, na vaṭṭatīti? No na vaṭṭati yuttaṭṭhāneti dassento “tena panā”tiādimāha. Iminā odissakadānaṃ panassa na sabbattha vāritanti dasseti. Gilānādīnañhi odissakaṃ katvā dānaṃ appaṭivibhāgapakkhikaṃ “asukassa na dassāmī”ti paṭikkhepassa abhāvato. Byatirekappadhāno hi paṭibhāgo. Tenāha “avasesa”ntiādi. Adātumpīti pi-saddena dātumpi vaṭṭatīti dasseti. Tañca kho karuṇāyanavasena, na vattaparipūraṇavasena, tasmā dussīlassapi atthikassa sati sambhave dātabbaṃ. Dānañhi nāma na kassaci nivāritaṃ.

Now, 'this principle conducive to cordiality' means this fourth state that should be remembered. 'Indeed… they do not grasp'; therefore, for an immoral person there is no common enjoyment of requisites. Thus, the intention is that even the beginning is not possible, so how could there be fulfillment? By 'one of pure virtue,' he shows the righteous nature of the gain. By 'not breaking the observance,' he shows both enjoyment without dividing and common enjoyment. When both are present, the principle conducive to cordiality is indeed fulfilled; thus he says, 'he fulfills.' 'Having made a specific designation': by this he shows that for one who gives without making a specific designation, starting from the elder's seat, to one's father, teacher, preceptor, and so on, it is indeed a principle conducive to cordiality. 'It should be given' means it must be given. But for him it is not a principle conducive to cordiality, because it was given with a specific designation in a case of caretaking. Therefore he said, 'it is called tending to an obstruction.' It is allowable for one who is free from obstruction, since it is impossible for one who is not free from obstruction to fulfill it. If so, for one who fulfills the principle conducive to cordiality in every way, is giving with a specific designation allowable or not? To show that it is indeed allowable in a suitable case, he said, 'But by that…' and so on. By this he shows that giving with a specific designation is not prohibited for him in all cases. For giving to the sick and others with a specific designation belongs to the side of non-division, because there is no refusal with the thought, 'I will not give to so-and-so.' For a share is primarily based on exclusion. Therefore he said, 'the remainder…' and so on. 'Even not to give': by the particle 'pi,' he shows that it is also allowable to give. And that is on account of compassion, not for the sake of fulfilling the observance. Therefore, it should be given even to an immoral person who is in need, if possible. For giving is indeed not prohibited to anyone.

Susikkhitāyāti sāraṇīyapūraṇavidhimhi susikkhitāya, sukusalāyāti attho. Idāni tassa kosallaṃ dassetuṃ “susikkhitāya hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Dvādasahi vassehi pūrehi, na tato oranti iminā tassa duppūrataṃ dasseti. Tathā hi so mahapphalo mahānisaṃso diṭṭhadhammikehipi tāvagarutarehi phalānisaṃsehi anugatoti taṃsamaṅgī ca puggalo visesalābhī ariyapuggalo viya loke acchariyabbhutadhammasamannāgato hoti. Tathā hi so duppajahadānamayassa sīlamayassa puññassa paṭipakkhadhammaṃ sudūre vikkhambhitaṃ katvā visuddhena cetasā loke pākaṭo paññāto hutvā viharati. Tassimamatthaṃ byatirekato anvayato ca vibhāvetuṃ “sace hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Taṃ suviññeyyameva.

'Well-trained' means well-trained in the method of fulfilling the principles conducive to cordiality; the meaning is 'very skillful.' Now, to show that skill, it is said, 'For one who is well-trained…' and so on. 'For twelve full years, not less than that': by this he shows the difficulty of its fulfillment. For indeed, it is of great fruit and great benefit, and is accompanied even in this very life by such very weighty fruits and benefits. And a person endowed with it becomes possessed of wonderful and marvelous qualities in the world, like a noble person who has obtained a special attainment. For indeed, having suppressed far away the states opposed to the merit consisting of difficult-to-relinquish giving and the merit consisting of virtue, he dwells with a purified mind, manifest and renowned in the world. To clarify this meaning by way of negative and positive formulation, it is said, 'For if…' and so on. That is very easy to understand.

Idānissa samparāyike diṭṭhadhammike ca ānisaṃse dassetuṃ “evaṃ pūritasāraṇīyadhammassā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Neva issā na macchariyaṃ hoti cirakālabhāvanāya vidhutabhāvato. Manussānaṃ piyo hoti pariccāgasīlatāya vissutattā. Tenāha “dadaṃ piyo hoti bhajanti naṃ bahū”tiādi (a. ni. 5.34). Sulabhapaccayo hoti dānavasena uḷārajjhāsayānaṃ paccayalābhassa idhānisaṃsasabhāvato dānassa. Pattagatamassa diyyamānaṃ [M 3.0093] na khīyati pattagatasseva dvādasavassikassa mahāvattassa avicchedena pūritattā. Aggabhaṇḍaṃ labhati devasikaṃ dakkhiṇeyyānaṃ aggato paṭṭhāya dānassa dinnattā. Bhaye vā…pe… āpajjanti deyyappaṭiggāhakavikappaṃ akatvā attani nirapekkhacittena cirakālaṃ dānassa pūritatāya pasāritacittattā.

Now, to show his benefits in future lives and in this present life, it is said, 'For one who has thus fulfilled the principles conducive to cordiality…' and so on. There is neither envy nor stinginess, because these have been shaken off by long-term cultivation. He becomes dear to people because he is renowned for his generous nature. Therefore it is said: 'Giving, one becomes dear; many resort to him,' and so on (AN 5.34). He easily obtains requisites, because for those with noble intentions, the obtaining of requisites is by nature a benefit of giving in this very life. What is given and placed in his bowl is not exhausted, because the great twelve-year observance concerning what is placed in the bowl has been fulfilled without interruption. He obtains the best goods daily because giving was done to those worthy of offerings, starting from the foremost among them. In times of danger… they do not fall into peril… because their mind is expansive, as they have fulfilled giving for a long time with a mind unconcerned for themselves, without making a distinction between what is to be given and the recipient.

Tatrāti [V 3.0088] tesu ānisaṃsesu vibhāvetabbesu. Imāni phalāni vatthūni kāraṇāni. Mahāgirigāmo nāma nāgadīpapasse eko gāmova. Alabhantāpīti appapuññatāya alābhino samānāpi. Bhikkhācāramaggasabhāganti sabhāgaṃ tabbhāgiyaṃ bhikkhācāramaggaṃ jānanti. Anuttarimanussadhammattā therānaṃ saṃsayavinodanatthañca “sāraṇīyadhammo me, bhante, pūrito”ti āha. Tathā hi dutiyavatthusmimpi therena attā pakāsito. Daharakāle evaṃ kira sāraṇīyadhammapūrako ahosi. Manussānaṃ piyatāya sulabhapaccayatāyapi idaṃ vatthumeva. Pattagatākhīyanassa pana visesaṃ vibhāvanato “idaṃ tāva…pe… ettha vatthū”ti vuttaṃ.

‘Therein’ means: among these benefits to be clarified. These are the fruits, the stories, the reasons. Mahāgirigāma is a village near Nāgadīpa. ‘Even though not obtaining’ means: even while being without gain due to little merit. ‘Sharing the alms-round path’ means: they know the alms-round path that is suitable, that they share in. Because of the elder's state of having an extraordinary human quality and in order to dispel the doubt of the elders, he said: ‘Venerable sir, the principle conducive to cordiality has been fulfilled by me.’ For in the second story, too, the elder revealed himself. It is said that he was a fulfiller of the principles conducive to cordiality even in his youth. This same story also illustrates his being dear to people and his easily obtaining requisites. But because it clarifies the special point about what is placed in the bowl not being exhausted, it is said: ‘This, for now… here is the story.’

Giribhaṇḍamahāpūjāyāti cetiyagirimhi sakalalaṅkādīpe yojanappamāṇe samudde ca nāvāsaṅghāṭādike ṭhapetvā dīpapupphagandhādīhi kariyamānāya mahāpūjāya. Tassā ca paṭipattiyā avañjhabhāvavibhāvanatthaṃ “ete mayhaṃ pāpuṇissantī”ti āha. Pariyāyenapi lesenapi. Anucchavikanti “sāraṇīyadhammapūrako”ti yathābhūtapavedanaṃ tumhākaṃ anucchavikanti attho.

‘At the Giribhaṇḍa Great Offering’ means: at the great offering made with lamps, flowers, incense, and so on, at Cetiyagiri, after placing them on ships, rafts, etc., in the sea for a yojana around the entire island of Laṅkā. And to clarify the unfailing nature of that practice, he said, ‘These will reach me.’ This was said indirectly or by a hint. ‘Suitable’ means: the truthful declaration, ‘a fulfiller of the principles conducive to cordiality,’ is suitable for you.

Anārocetvāva palāyiṃsu corabhayena. “Attano dujjīvikāyā”tipi vadanti. Ahaṃ sāraṇīyadhammapūrikā, mama pattapariyāpannenapi sabbāpimā bhikkhuniyo yāpessantīti āha “mā tumhe tesaṃ gatabhāvaṃ cintayitthā”ti. Vaṭṭissatīti kappissati. Therī sāraṇīyadhammapūrikā ahosi, therassa pana sīlatejeneva devatā ussukkaṃ āpajji.

Without informing anyone, they fled out of fear of thieves. Some also say: ‘Because of their own difficult livelihood.’ She said: ‘I am a fulfiller of the principles conducive to cordiality; I will sustain all these nuns even with what has come into my bowl,’ thus she said, ‘Do not worry about their having gone.’ ‘It will be sufficient’ means it will suffice. The elder nun was a fulfiller of the principles conducive to cordiality, but in the elder's case, it was solely through the power of his virtue that the deity became zealous.

Natthi etesaṃ khaṇḍanti akhaṇḍāni. Taṃ pana nesaṃ khaṇḍaṃ dassetuṃ “yassā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha upasampannasīlānaṃ uddesakkamena ādiantā veditabbā. Tenāha “sattasū”tiādi. Na hi añño koci āpattikkhandhānaṃ [M 3.0094] anukkamo atthi, anupasampannasīlānaṃ samādānakkamenapi ādiantā labbhanti. Pariyante chinnasāṭako viyāti tatrante dasante vā chinnavatthaṃ viya. Visadisudāharaṇañcetaṃ “akhaṇḍānī”ti imassa adhikatattā. Evaṃ sesānampi udāharaṇāni. Khaṇḍikatā bhinnatā khaṇḍaṃ, taṃ etassa atthīti khaṇḍaṃ, sīlaṃ. Chiddantiādīsupi eseva nayo. Vemajjhe bhinnaṃ vinivijjhanavasena. Visabhāgavaṇṇena gāvī viyāti sambandho. Visabhāgavaṇṇena upaḍḍhaṃ tatiyabhāgagataṃ sambhinnavaṇṇaṃ sabalaṃ, visabhāgavaṇṇeheva bindūhi antarantarāhi vimissaṃ kammāsaṃ. Ayaṃ imesaṃ viseso. Sabalarahitāni asabalāni, tathā akammāsāni. Sīlassa taṇhādāsabyato mocanaṃ vivaṭṭūpanissayabhāvāpādanaṃ, tasmā taṇhādāsabyato mocanavacanena tesaṃ sīlānaṃ vivaṭṭūpanissayatamāha. Bhujissabhāvakaraṇatoti iminā bhujissakarāni bhujissānīti uttarapadalopenāyaṃ [V 3.0089] niddesoti dasseti. Yasmā vā taṃsamaṅgipuggalo serī sayaṃvasī bhujisso nāma hoti, tasmāpi bhujissāni. Aviññūnaṃ appamāṇatāya “viññuppasatthānī”ti vuttaṃ. Suparisuddhabhāvena vā sampannattā viññūhi pasatthānīti viññuppasatthāni.

‘There is no break in them,’ thus they are unbroken. But to show a break in them, it is said, ‘Of which…’ and so on. Herein, the beginning and end of the virtues of the fully ordained should be understood by the order of recitation. Therefore he said, ‘In the seven…’ and so on. For there is no other sequence of the classes of offenses. For the virtues of the unordained, the beginning and end can be obtained by the order of undertaking. ‘Like a garment torn at the edge’ means like a cloth torn at its end or border. And this is a dissimilar example because of the superiority of the term ‘unbroken.’ The other examples should be understood in the same way. A state of being broken, a state of being shattered, is a break; virtue that has this is ‘broken.’ The same method applies to ‘perforated,’ etc. Broken in the middle by way of being pierced through. ‘Like a cow of variegated color’ is the connection. A cow of which half or a third is of a mixed color is ‘dappled’; one mixed with spots of variegated color here and there is ‘spotted.’ This is the difference between them. Those without dappling are ‘undappled’; likewise, ‘unspotted.’ The liberation of virtue from servitude to craving is the production of a state that is a decisive support for the rolling back of saṃsāra; therefore, by the words ‘liberating from servitude to craving,’ he states that those virtues are a decisive support for the rolling back. ‘Because they make one a free person’: by this he shows that this is a designation with the elision of the final member of the compound, so that ‘making one free’ is called ‘liberating.’ Or, because a person endowed with them is independent, self-mastered, and called a ‘free person,’ they are also ‘liberating.’ Because they are not assessed by the unwise, it is said, ‘praised by the wise.’ Or, because they are endowed with a state of supreme purity, they are praised by the wise, thus ‘praised by the wise.’

Taṇhādiṭṭhīhi aparāmaṭṭhattāti “imināhaṃ sīlena devo vā bhavissāmi devaññataro vā”ti taṇhāparāmāsena, “imināhaṃ sīlena devo hutvā tattha nicco dhuvo sassato bhavissāmī”ti diṭṭhiparāmāsena ca aparāmaṭṭhattā. Parāmaṭṭhunti “ayaṃ te sīlesu doso”ti catūsu vipattīsu yāya kāyaci vipattiyā dassanena parāmaṭṭhuṃ, anuddhaṃsetuṃ codetunti attho. Sīlaṃ nāma avippaṭisārādipārampariyena yāvadeva samādhisampādanatthanti āha “samādhisaṃvattanikānī”ti. Samādhisaṃvattanappayojanāni samādhisaṃvattanikāni.

‘Because of not being misapprehended by craving and views’ means because of not being misapprehended by the misapprehension of craving with the thought, ‘By this virtue I will become a deva or some other deva,’ or by the misapprehension of views with the thought, ‘By this virtue, having become a deva, I will be permanent, stable, and eternal there.’ ‘To find fault with’ means to censure or admonish by pointing out a fault in the virtues by way of any of the four kinds of failure, saying, ‘This is a fault in your virtues.’ Virtue is for the purpose of accomplishing concentration, through the sequence beginning with non-remorse; thus he said, ‘conducive to concentration.’ Those things that have the purpose of leading on to concentration are ‘conducive to concentration.’

Samānabhāvo sāmaññaṃ, paripuṇṇacatupārisuddhibhāvena majjhe bhinnasuvaṇṇassa viya bhedābhāvato sīlena sāmaññaṃ sīlasāmaññaṃ, taṃ gato upagatoti sīlasāmaññagato. Tenāha “samānabhāvūpagatasīlo”ti, sīlasampattiyā samānabhāvaṃ upagatasīlo sabhāgavuttikoti attho. Kāmaṃ puthujjanānampi catupārisuddhisīle nānattaṃ na siyā, taṃ pana na ekantikaṃ, idaṃ ekantikaṃ niyatabhāvatoti āha “natthi [M 3.0095] maggasīle nānatta”nti. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttanti maggasīlaṃ sandhāya taṃ “yāni tāni sīlānī”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Commonality means a state of sameness. Because of the absence of any division, owing to the state of fourfold perfect purity—just as there is no difference in quality in a piece of gold broken in the middle—sameness by way of virtue is commonality in virtue. One who has gone to it, approached it, is one who has attained commonality in virtue. Therefore he said, ‘one whose virtue has attained a state of sameness,’ meaning one whose virtue has attained a state of sameness through the accomplishment of virtue, having a similar mode of conduct. Although for worldlings too there might be no diversity in the fourfold purification virtue, that is not certain; this, however, is certain, being of a fixed nature. Therefore he said, ‘There is no diversity in the virtue of the path.’ It was said referring to that; that is, ‘Whatever those virtues are,’ etc., was said referring to the virtue of the path.

Yāyanti yā ayaṃ mayhañceva tumhākañca paccakkhabhūtā. Diṭṭhīti maggasammādiṭṭhi. Niddosāti niddhutadosā, samucchinnarāgādipāpadhammāti attho. Niyyātīti vaṭṭadukkhato nissarati niggacchati. Sayaṃ niyyantīyeva hi taṃsamaṅgipuggalaṃ vaṭṭadukkhato niyyāpetīti vuccati. Yā satthu anusiṭṭhi, taṃ karotīti takkaro, tassa, yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipajjantassāti attho. Samānadiṭṭhibhāvanti sadisadiṭṭhibhāvaṃ saccasampaṭivedhena abhinnadiṭṭhibhāvaṃ.

‘Yāyanti’ means this which is directly evident to both me and you. ‘Diṭṭhi’ means the right view of the path. ‘Niddosā’ means free from faults, that is, having cut off defilements such as lust and other evil states. ‘Niyyāti’ means it escapes and departs from the suffering of the round. For it is said that, while itself leading out, it leads the person endowed with it out of the suffering of the round. A ‘takkara’ is one who does what the Teacher instructs; that is, one who practices as instructed. ‘Samānadiṭṭhibhāva’ means a state of similar view, a state of undivided view through the penetration of the truths.

Paṭhamasāraṇīyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the First Discourse on Amiability is concluded.

2. Dutiyasāraṇīyasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Second Discourse on Amiability

12. Dutiye sabrahmacārīnanti sahadhammikānaṃ. Piyaṃ piyāyitabbakaṃ karontīti piyakaraṇā. Garuṃ garuṭṭhāniyaṃ karontīti garukaraṇā. Saṅgaṇhanatthāyāti saṅgahavatthuvisesabhāvato sabrahmacārīnaṃ [V 3.0090] saṅgahaṇāya saṃvattantīti sambandho. Avivadanatthāyāti saṅgahavatthubhāvato eva na vivadanatthāya. Sati ca avivadanahetubhūtasaṅgahakatte tesaṃ vasena sabrahmacārīnaṃ samaggabhāvo bhedābhāvo siddhoyevāti āha “sāmaggiyā”tiādi.

12. In the second sutta, ‘sabrahmacārīnaṃ’ means ‘of fellow practitioners of the Dhamma.’ They are ‘piyakaraṇā’ because they make one dear and beloved. They are ‘garukaraṇā’ because they make one respected and venerable. ‘For winning over’: the connection is that because these states are a special basis of harmony, they conduce to winning over one's fellow practitioners. ‘For non-dispute’: precisely because they are a basis of harmony, they are for the sake of not disputing. And when there is this winning over that is the cause of non-dispute, by means of these things the unity and absence of division among one's fellow practitioners is certainly accomplished. Hence he said, ‘for harmony,’ etc.

Dutiyasāraṇīyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Second Discourse on Amiability is concluded.

3. Nissāraṇīyasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Discourse on Deliverance

13. Tatiye vaḍḍhitāti bhāvanāpāripūrivasena paribrūhitā. Punappunaṃ katāti bhāvanāya bahulīkaraṇena aparāparaṃ pavattitā. Yuttayānasadisā katāti yathā yuttamājaññayānaṃ chekena sārathinā adhiṭṭhitaṃ yathāruci pavattati, evaṃ yathāruci pavattirahaṃ gahitā. Vatthukatāti vā adhiṭṭhānaṭṭhena vatthu viya katā, sabbaso upakkilesavisodhanena iddhivisesatāya pavattiṭṭhānabhāvato suvisodhitaparissayavatthu viya katāti vuttaṃ hoti. Adhiṭṭhitāti paṭipakkhadūrībhāvato [M 3.0096] subhāvitabhāvena taṃtaṃadhiṭṭhānayogyatāya ṭhapitā. Samantato citāti sabbabhāgena bhāvanūpacayaṃ gamitā. Tenāha “upacitā’ti. Suṭṭhu samāraddhāti iddhibhāvanāsikhāppattiyā sammadeva sambhāvitā. Abhūtabyākaraṇaṃ byākarotīti “mettā hi kho me cetovimutti bhāvitā”tiādinā attani avijjamānaguṇābhibyāhāraṃ byāharati. Cetovimuttisaddaṃ apekkhitvā “nissaṭā”ti vuttaṃ. Puna byāpādo natthīti idāni mama byāpādo nāma sabbaso natthīti ñatvā.

13. In the third, `developed` means augmented by way of fulfilling the development. `Repeatedly done` means made to occur again and again by making much of the development. `Made like a yoked vehicle` means: just as a yoked thoroughbred vehicle, attended by a skilled driver, proceeds as desired, so it has been taken up as fit to proceed as desired. `Made a basis` means made like a basis in the sense of a foundation; or, it is said to be made like a well-purified ground free from dangers, because it is a place for the occurrence of the special attainment of spiritual power through the complete purification from defilements. `Established` means established in suitability for this or that resolve by being well-developed, since opposition is far away. `Accumulated all around` means brought to an accumulation of development in every part. Hence he said, `upacitā` (accumulated). `Well undertaken` means properly generated by reaching the peak of the development of spiritual power. `He makes a declaration about what is not factual` means he utters a statement about a quality not existing in himself, such as, 'My liberation of mind by loving-kindness has been developed.' With reference to the word 'liberation of mind,' it is said, `nissaṭā` (released). `There is no more ill will` means knowing: 'Now for me there is absolutely no such thing as ill will.'

Balavavipassanāti bhayatupaṭṭhāne ñāṇaṃ, ādīnavānupassane ñāṇaṃ muccitukamyatāñāṇaṃ, bhaṅgañāṇanti catunnaṃ ñāṇānaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Yesaṃ nimittānaṃ abhāvena arahattaphalasamāpattiyā animittatā, taṃ dassetuṃ “sā hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha rāgassa nimittaṃ, rāgo eva vā nimittaṃ rāganimittaṃ. Ādi-saddena dosanimittādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Rūpavedanādisaṅkhāranimittaṃ rūpanimittādi. Tesaṃyeva niccādivasena upaṭṭhānaṃ niccanimittādi. Tayidaṃ nimittaṃ yasmā sabbena sabbaṃ arahattaphale natthi, tasmā vuttaṃ “sā hi…pe… animittā”ti. Nimittaṃ anussarati anugacchati ārabbha pavattati sīlenāti nimittānusārī. Tenāha “vuttappabhedaṃ nimittaṃ anusaraṇasabhāva”nti.

`Powerful insight` is a designation for these four kinds of knowledge: the knowledge of appearance as terror, the knowledge of contemplation of danger, the knowledge of desire for deliverance, and the knowledge of dissolution. To show the signlessness of the attainment of the fruit of arahantship, which is due to the absence of those signs, it was said, 'For it...,' etc. Herein, `the sign of lust` is either the object of lust or lust itself as a sign. By the word 'etc.' the inclusion of the sign of hatred, etc., should be understood. The sign of formations such as form, feeling, etc., is the sign of form, etc. The appearance of those very things as permanent, etc., is the sign of permanence, etc. Since this sign is in every way completely absent in the fruit of arahantship, it was therefore said: 'For it... is signless.' One who follows a sign (`nimittānusārī`) is one who by nature recollects a sign, follows it, and proceeds in dependence on it. Therefore he said, 'having the nature of following a sign of the kind explained.'

Asmimānoti “asmī”ti pavatto attavisayo māno. Ayaṃ nāma ahamasmīti rūpalakkhaṇo [V 3.0091] vedanādīsu vā aññataralakkhaṇo ayaṃ nāma attā ahaṃ asmīti. Asmimāno samugghātīyati etenāti asmimānasamugghāto, arahattamaggo. Puna asmimāno natthīti tassa anuppattidhammatāpādanaṃ kittento samugghātattameva vibhāveti.

"The conceit 'I am'" is the conceit concerning self that proceeds as "I am." Namely, the idea "such and such am I," characterized by form, or characterized by any of feeling, etc., as "this is the self, I am." "The eradication of the conceit 'I am'" is the path to arahantship, because it eradicates this conceit. Furthermore, by declaring "there is no more conceit 'I am'," he reveals precisely its eradication through the establishment of the natural state of its non-occurrence.

Nissāraṇīyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Discourse on Deliverance is concluded.

4-5. Bhaddakasuttādivaṇṇanā

4-5. The Commentary on the Bhaddaka Sutta and Others

14-15. Catutthe āramitabbaṭṭhena vā kammaṃ ārāmo etassāti kammārāmo. Kamme rato na ganthadhure vipassanādhure vāti kammarato. Punappunaṃ yuttoti tapparabhāvena anu anu yutto pasuto. Ālāpasallāpoti itthivaṇṇapurisavaṇṇādivasena punappunaṃ lapanaṃ. Pañcame natthi vattabbaṃ.

14-15. In the fourth: Or, `kammārāma` (one who delights in work) means one for whom work (kammaṃ) is a delight (ārāma) in the sense that it is to be undertaken. `Kammarata` (fond of work) means one who delights in work, not in the burden of the books or the burden of insight. 'Repeatedly engaged' means devotedly and eagerly involved, being intent on that. `Ālāpasallāpa` (talk and chatter) means repeated chatter about such things as the beauty of women and the beauty of men. In the fifth, there is nothing to be said.

Bhaddakasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Bhaddaka Sutta and others is concluded.

6. Nakulapitusuttavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Nakulapitu Sutta

16. Chaṭṭhe [M 3.0097] visabhāgavedanuppattiyā kakaceneva catuiriyāpathaṃ chindanto ābādhayatīti ābādho, so yassa atthīti ābādhiko. Taṃsamuṭṭhānadukkhena dukkhito. Adhimattagilānoti dhātusaṅkhayena parikkhīṇasarīro.

16. In the sixth: `Ābādha` (affliction) is so called because it afflicts, cutting through the four postures like a saw, due to the arising of a disagreeable feeling. One who has this is an `ābādhika` (an afflicted one). 'Tormented' by the suffering that arises from that. `Adhimattagilāna` (gravely ill) means one whose body is worn out through the depletion of the elements.

Sappaṭibhayakantārasadisā soḷasavatthukā aṭṭhavatthukā ca vicikicchā tiṇṇā imāyāti tiṇṇavicikicchā. Vigatā samucchinnā pavattiādīsu “evaṃ nu kho na nu kho”ti evaṃ pavattikā kathaṃkathā assāti vigatakathaṃkathā. Sārajjakarānaṃ pāpadhammānaṃ pahīnattā rāgavikkhepesu sīlādiguṇesu ca tiṭṭhakattā vesārajjaṃ, visāradabhāvaṃ veyyattiyaṃ pattāti vesārajjappattā. Attanā eva paccakkhato diṭṭhattā na paraṃ pacceti, nassa paro paccetabbo atthīti aparappaccayā.

`Tiṇṇavicikicchā` (one who has crossed over doubt): one is so called because one has crossed over the sixteen-grounded and eight-grounded doubt, which is like a perilous wilderness. `Vigatakathaṃkathā` (one whose questioning is removed): one is so called because for him questioning—which proceeds as 'Is it so? Is it not so?' concerning occurrence and so on—has departed and been cut off. `Vesārajjappattā` (one who has attained fearlessness): one is so called because one has attained fearlessness, confidence, and proficiency, since evil states that cause diffidence have been abandoned and one is established in virtues such as moral discipline and in regard to the distractions of lust. `Aparappaccayā` (not reliant on another): one is so called because, having seen for oneself directly, one does not rely on another, nor is there another on whom one must rely.

Gilānā vuṭṭhitoti gilānabhāvato vuṭṭhāya ṭhito. Bhāvappadhāno hi ayaṃ niddeso. Gilāno hutvā vuṭṭhitoti idaṃ pana atthamattanidassanaṃ.

'Having risen from illness' means one who stands firm, having risen from the state of illness. For this explanation emphasizes the state. But the phrase 'having been ill and then risen' is merely an illustration of the meaning.

Nakulapitusuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Nakulapitu Sutta is concluded.

7. Soppasuttavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Soppa Sutta

17. Sattame [V 3.0092] paṭisallānā vuṭṭhitoti ettha paṭisallānanti tehi tehi saddhivihārikaantevāsikaupāsakādisattehi ceva rūpārammaṇādisaṅkhārehi ca paṭinivattitvā apasakkitvā nilīyanaṃ vivecanaṃ. Kāyacittehi tato vivitto ekībhāvo pavivekoti āha “ekībhāvāyā”tiādi. Ekībhāvatoti ca iminā kāyavivekato vuṭṭhānamāha. Dhammanijjhānakkhantitotiādinā cittavivekato. Vuṭṭhitoti tato duvidhavivekato bhavaṅguppattiyā sabrahmacārīhi samāgamena upeto.

17. In the seventh: Herein, regarding 'having emerged from seclusion,' 'seclusion' means withdrawing, drawing back, and hiding away—which is separation—from those various beings such as co-residents, pupils, and lay followers, and also from formations such as form-objects. Because solitude is being alone, secluded from that in body and mind, he said 'for the sake of solitude,' etc. And by 'from being alone,' he speaks of emerging from bodily seclusion. By 'patient endurance in the contemplation of phenomena,' etc., he speaks of emerging from mental seclusion. 'Emerged' means that, having emerged from that twofold seclusion, one is endowed with association with one's fellows in the holy life through the arising of the life-continuum.

Soppasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Soppa Sutta is concluded.

8. Macchabandhasuttavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Macchabandha Sutta

18. Aṭṭhame [M 3.0098] macchaghātakanti macchabandhaṃ kevaṭṭaṃ. Orabbhikādīsu urabbhā vuccanti eḷakā, urabbhe hantīti orabbhiko. Sūkarikādīsupi eseva nayo.

18. In the eighth: `Macchaghātaka` (fish-killer) means a fisherman, a `kevaṭṭa`. Among such as sheep-butchers, rams are called `urabbhā`; one who kills rams is an `orabbhika`. The same method applies to pig-butchers and so on.

Macchabandhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Macchabandha Sutta is concluded.

9. Paṭhamamaraṇassatisuttavaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the First Discourse on Mindfulness of Death

19. Navame evaṃnāmake gāmeti nātikānāmakaṃ gāmaṃ nissāya. Dvinnaṃ cūḷapitimahāpitiputtānaṃ dve gāmā, tesu ekasmiṃ gāme. Ñātīnañhi nivāsaṭṭhānabhūto gāmo ñātiko, ñātikoyeva nātiko ña-kārassa na-kārādeso “animittā na nāyare”tiādīsu (visuddhi. 1.174; saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.20; jā. aṭṭha. 2.2.34) viya. So kira gāmo yesaṃ tadā tesaṃ pubbapurisena attano ñātīnaṃ sādhāraṇabhāvena nivasito, tena ñātikoti paññāyittha. Atha pacchā dvīhi dāyādehi dvidhā vibhajitvā paribhutto. Giñjakā vuccati iṭṭhakā, giñjakāhiyeva kato āvasathoti giñjakāvasatho. So hi āvāso yathā sudhāparikammena payojanaṃ natthi, evaṃ iṭṭhakāhi eva cinitvā chādetvā kato. Tasmiṃ kira padese mattikā sakkharamarumpavālukādīhi asammissā kathinā saṇhasukhumā, tāya katāni kulālabhājanānipi silāmayāni viya daḷhāni. Tasmā te upāsakā tāya mattikāya dīghaputhū [V 3.0093] iṭṭhakā kāretvā ṭhapetvā ṭhapetvā dvāravātapānakavāṭatulāyo sabbaṃ dabbasambhārena vinā tāhi iṭṭhakāhiyeva pāsādaṃ kāresuṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “iṭṭhakāmaye pāsāde”ti.

19. In the ninth: 'In the village so named' means near the village named Nātika. The two sons of Cūḷapiti and Mahāpiti had two villages; it was in one of those villages. Indeed, a village that is a residence for relatives is a `ñātika`. `Nātika` is just `ñātika`, with the letter `na` substituted for the letter `ña`, as in such cases as 'animittā na nāyare.' It is said that village was established by their ancestor for his relatives to live in common, thus it became known as Ñātika. Then later it was divided in two and used by two heirs. `Giñjakā` means brick. A residence made only of bricks is a `giñjakāvasatha` (brick hall). That residence was made by stacking and covering with bricks alone, such that there was no need for plasterwork. It is said that in that region the clay is hard, fine, and smooth, unmixed with gravel, pebbles, sand, and the like. Even pottery vessels made from it are as strong as if made of stone. Therefore those lay followers had long, thick bricks made from that clay and, by stacking them, built a mansion entirely from those bricks—including doors, windows, shutters, and lintels—without any wooden material. Hence it was said: 'in a brick mansion.'

Rattindivanti ekarattidivaṃ. Bhagavato sāsananti ariyamaggappaṭivedhāvahaṃ satthu ovādaṃ. Bahu vata me kataṃ assāti bahu vata mayā attahitaṃ pabbajitakiccaṃ kataṃ bhaveyya.

'A night and day' means a single night and day. 'The Blessed One's teaching' means the Teacher's instruction that leads to the penetration of the noble path. 'Much indeed would have been done by me' means: 'Much indeed of the duty of one gone forth, for my own welfare, would have been done by me.'

Tadantaranti tattakaṃ velaṃ. Ekapiṇḍapātanti ekaṃ divasaṃ yāpanappahonakaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ. Yāva anto paviṭṭhavāto bahi nikkhamati, bahi nikkhantavāto [M 3.0099] vā anto pavisatīti ekasseva pavesanikkhamo viya vuttaṃ, taṃ nāsikāvātabhāvasāmaññenāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

'The interval' means just that much time. 'A single alms-meal' means an alms-meal sufficient to last for a single day. The time it takes for an in-breath that has entered to go out, or for an out-breath that has gone out to enter, is spoken of as if it were a single entering and exiting. This should be understood as being due to the common nature of the breath in the nose.

Paṭhamamaraṇassatisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the First Discourse on Mindfulness of Death is concluded.

10. Dutiyamaraṇassatisuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Second Discourse on Mindfulness of Death

20. Dasame nikkhanteti vītivatte. Patigatāyāti paccāgatāya, sampattāyāti attho. Tenāha “paṭipannāyā”ti.
