So mamassa antarāyoti yathāvuttā na kevalaṃ kālakiriyāva, mama atidullabhaṃ khaṇaṃ labhitvā tassa satthusāsanamanasikārassa ceva jīvitassa ca saggamokkhānañca antarāyo assa, bhaveyyāti attho. Tenāha “tividho antarāyo”tiādi. Vipajjeyyāti vipattiṃ gaccheyya. Satthakena viya aṅgapaccaṅgānaṃ kantanakārakā kāye sandhibandhanacchedakavātā satthakavātā. Kattukamyatāchandoti niyyānāvaho kattukamyatākusalacchando. Payogavīriyanti bhāvanānuyogavīriyaṃ. Na paṭivāti na paṭinivattatīti appaṭivānī, antarā vosānānāpajjanavīriyaṃ. Tenāha “anukkaṇṭhanā appaṭisaṅgharaṇā”ti.

20. In the tenth [discourse], 'nikkhante' means 'having passed beyond.' 'Patigatāya' means 'having returned,' which has the meaning 'having arrived.' Therefore, it is said, 'paṭipannāya.' 'So mamassa antarāyo' means not merely death, as stated, but having obtained this extremely rare moment, it would be an obstacle to the attention to the Teacher's dispensation, to life, and to heaven and liberation; that is the meaning. Therefore, it is said, 'the threefold obstacle,' and so on. 'Vipajjeyya' means 'would meet with ruin.' Like a knife that cuts the limbs major and minor, the winds that sever the joint-ligaments in the body are called 'knife-like winds' (satthakavātā). 'Kattukamyatāchando' means the wholesome desire of wishing to do, which leads to release. 'Payogavīriya' means the energy of application to meditation. 'Na paṭivāti' means 'it does not turn back,' hence 'appaṭivānī,' the energy that does not come to an end in between. Therefore, it is said, 'not shrinking back, not holding back'.

Dutiyamaraṇassatisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Second Discourse on Mindfulness of Death is concluded.

Sāraṇīyavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Sāraṇīyavagga is concluded.

3. Anuttariyavaggo

3. The Chapter on the Unsurpassed

1-2. Sāmakasuttādivaṇṇanā

1-2. Commentary on the Sāmaka Sutta and others

21-22. Tatiyassa [V 3.0094] paṭhame kevalakappanti ettha kevala-saddo anavasesattho, kappa-saddo samantabhāvattho. Tasmā kevalakappaṃ pokkharaṇiyanti evamattho daṭṭhabbo. Anavasesaṃ pharituṃ samatthassapi obhāsassa kenaci kāraṇena ekadesapharaṇampi siyā, ayaṃ pana sabbasova pharatīti dassetuṃ samantattho kappa-saddo gahito. Attano obhāsena pharitvāti vatthālaṅkārasarīrasamuṭṭhitena obhāsena pharitvā, candimā [M 3.0100] viya ekobhāsaṃ ekapajjotaṃ karitvāti attho. Samanuññoti sammadeva katamanuñño. Tenāha “samānacitto”ti, samānajjhāsayoti attho. Dukkhaṃ vaco etasminti dubbaco, tassa kammaṃ dovacassaṃ, tassa puggalassa anādariyavasena pavattā cetanā, tassa bhāvo atthitā dovacassatā. Atha vā dovacassameva dovacassatā. Sā atthato saṅkhārakkhandho hoti. Cetanāpadhāno hi saṅkhārakkhandho. Catunnaṃ vā khandhānaṃ apadakkhiṇaggāhitākārena pavattānaṃ etaṃ adhivacananti vadanti. Pāpā assaddhādayo puggalā etassa mittāti pāpamitto, tassa bhāvo pāpamittatā. Sāpi atthato dovacassatā viya daṭṭhabbā. Yāya hi cetanāya puggalo pāpamitto pāpasampavaṅko nāma hoti, sā cetanā pāpamittatā. Cattāropi vā arūpino khandhā tadākārappavattā pāpamittatā. Dutiyaṃ uttānameva.

21-22. In the first [discourse] of the third [vagga], regarding 'kevalakappaṃ,' here the word 'kevala' has the meaning 'without remainder,' and the word 'kappa' has the meaning 'all-encompassing.' Therefore, the meaning of 'kevalakappaṃ pokkharaṇiyaṃ' should be understood in this way. Even if a light is capable of pervading without remainder, its pervading of only one part might occur due to some reason; but here, to show that this one pervades entirely, the word 'kappa' is taken in the sense of 'all-encompassing.' 'Attano obhāsena pharitvā' means having pervaded with the light arisen from one's clothing, ornaments, and body, like the moon making a single radiance, a single effulgence; that is the meaning. 'Samanuñño' means 'truly made agreeable.' Therefore, it is said, 'samānacitto,' meaning 'of the same mind,' that is, 'of the same inclination.' 'Dukkhaṃ vaco etasmiṃ' means 'speech is difficult for him,' hence 'dubbaco' (one difficult to admonish). His action is 'dovacassaṃ' (difficulty in being admonished). The intention that proceeds by way of disrespect for that person, its state, its existence, is 'dovacassatā' (the state of being difficult to admonish). Alternatively, 'dovacassatā' is simply 'dovacassaṃ.' In essence, it is the aggregate of formations. For the aggregate of formations is led by intention. Or, some say, this is a designation for the four aggregates functioning in a manner of improper grasping. 'Pāpā assaddhādayo puggalā etassa mittā' means 'evil, faithless persons, etc., are his friends,' hence 'pāpamitto' (one with evil friends). His state is 'pāpamittatā' (the state of having evil friends). This too should be seen essentially like 'dovacassatā.' For the intention by which a person is called an evil friend, one with evil associations, that intention is 'pāpamittatā.' Or the four immaterial aggregates functioning in that manner are 'pāpamittatā.' The second [discourse] is quite clear.

Sāmakasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Sāmaka Sutta and others is concluded.

3. Bhayasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Bhaya Sutta

23. Tatiye sambhavati jātimaraṇaṃ etenāti sambhavo, upādānanti āha “jātiyā ca maraṇassa ca sambhave paccayabhūte”ti. Anupādāti anupādāya. Tenāha “anupādiyitvā”ti. Jātimaraṇāni sammā khīyanti etthāti jātimaraṇasaṅkhayo, nibbānanti āha “jātimaraṇānaṃ saṅkhayasaṅkhāte nibbāne”ti. Sabbadukkhaṃ upaccagunti sakalampi vaṭṭadukkhaṃ atikkantā carimacittanirodhena vaṭṭadukkhalesassapi asambhavato.

23. In the third [discourse], 'sambhavo' (arising) is so called because birth and death arise through this; it is 'upādāna' (clinging). It is said: 'being a condition for the arising of birth and death.' 'Anupādā' means 'anupādāya' (not having clung). Therefore, it is said, 'anupādiyitvā' (not having clung). 'Jātimaraṇasaṅkhayo' (the destruction of birth and death) is so called because birth and death are completely destroyed here; it is 'nibbāna.' It is said: 'in Nibbāna, which is designated as the destruction of birth and death.' 'Sabbadukkhaṃ upaccaguṃ' means they have transcended all the suffering of the round of existence, because with the cessation of the final consciousness, there is no arising of even a trace of the suffering of the round.

Bhayasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Bhaya Sutta is concluded.

4. Himavantasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Himavanta Sutta

24. Catutthe [V 3.0095] samāpattikusalo hotīti samāpajjanakusalo hoti. Tenāha “samāpajjituṃ kusalo”ti. Tattha antogatahetuattho ṭhiti-saddo, tasmā ṭhapanakusaloti atthoti āha “samādhiṃ ṭhapetuṃ sakkotīti attho”ti. Tattha ṭhapetuṃ sakkotīti sattaṭṭhaaccharāmattaṃ [M 3.0101] khaṇaṃ jhānaṃ ṭhapetuṃ sakkoti adhiṭṭhānavasibhāvassa nipphāditattā. Yathāparicchedenāti yathāparicchinnakālena. Vuṭṭhātuṃ sakkoti vuṭṭhānavasibhāvassa nipphāditattā. Kallaṃ sañjātaṃ assāti kallitaṃ, tasmiṃ kallite kallitabhāve kusalo kallitakusalo. Hāsetuṃ tosetuṃ sampahaṃsetuṃ. Kallaṃ kātunti samādhānassa paṭipakkhadhammānaṃ dūrīkaraṇena sahakārīkāraṇānañca samappadhānena samāpajjane cittaṃ samatthaṃ kātuṃ. Samādhissa gocarakusaloti samādhismiṃ nipphādetabbe tassa gocare kammaṭṭhānasaññite pavattiṭṭhāne bhikkhācāragocare satisampajaññayogato kusalo cheko. Tenāha “samādhissa asappāye anupakārake dhamme vajjetvā”tiādi. Paṭhamajjhānādisamādhiṃ abhinīharitunti paṭhamajjhānādisamādhiṃ visesabhāgiyatāya abhinīharituṃ upanetuṃ.

24. In the fourth [discourse], 'samāpattikusalo hoti' means one is skilled in entering. Therefore, it is said, 'skilled in entering.' Here, the word 'ṭhiti' has the meaning of an included cause; therefore, the meaning is 'skilled in establishing,' and it is said: 'the meaning is, "is able to establish concentration."' There, 'is able to establish' means one is able to establish the jhāna for a moment lasting as long as seven or eight finger-snaps, because mastery in determination has been accomplished. 'Yathāparicchedena' means 'according to the determined time.' 'Is able to emerge' means because mastery in emerging has been accomplished. 'Kallaṃ sañjātaṃ assa' means 'it has become ready,' hence 'kallitaṃ.' Being skilled in that ready state is 'kallitakusalo.' 'To gladden, to please, to delight.' 'Kallaṃ kātuṃ' means to make the mind capable of entering into concentration by removing the opposing factors and by giving equal prominence to the supporting factors. 'Samādhissa gocarakusalo' means one is skilled and expert, through the application of mindfulness and clear comprehension, in the sphere of concentration to be accomplished, in its sphere which is the place of practice designated as the meditation subject, and in the sphere of the alms-round. Therefore, it is said, 'having avoided things unfavorable and unhelpful to concentration,' and so on. 'Paṭhamajjhānādisamādhiṃ abhinīharituṃ' means to direct or lead the first jhāna and other concentrations toward a state of distinction.

Himavantasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Himavanta Sutta is concluded.

5. Anussatiṭṭhānasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Anussatiṭṭhāna Sutta

25. Pañcame anussatikāraṇānīti anussatiyo eva diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikādihitasukhānaṃ hetubhāvato kāraṇāni. Nikkhantanti nissaṭaṃ. Muttanti vissaṭṭhaṃ. Vuṭṭhitanti apetaṃ. Sabbametaṃ vikkhambhanameva sandhāya vadati. Gedhamhāti pañcakāmaguṇato. Idampīti buddhānussativasena laddhaṃ upacārajjhānamāha. Ārammaṇaṃ karitvāti paccayaṃ karitvā, pādakaṃ katvāti attho.

25. In the fifth [sutta], 'anussatikāraṇāni' (causes for recollection) means the recollections themselves are causes, because they are the cause for welfare and happiness in this life, the next life, and so forth. 'Nikkhantaṃ' (departed) means escaped. 'Muttaṃ' (released) means detached. 'Vuṭṭhitaṃ' (emerged) means withdrawn. All this is said with reference to suppression itself. 'Gedhamhā' (from greed) means from the five cords of sensual pleasure. 'Idampi' (this too) refers to the access concentration attained by means of the recollection of the Buddha. 'Ārammaṇaṃ karitvā' (having made it an object) means having made it a condition, having made it a foundation; that is the meaning.

Anussatiṭṭhānasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Anussatiṭṭhāna Sutta is concluded.

6. Mahākaccānasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Mahākaccāna Sutta

26. Chaṭṭhe sambādheti vā taṇhāsaṃkilesādīnaṃ sampīḷe saṅkare gharāvāse. Okāsā vuccantīti maggaphalasukhādhigamāya okāsabhāvato okāsāti vuccanti. Okāsādhigamoti lokuttaradhammassa [V 3.0096] adhigamāya adhigantabbaokāso. Visujjhanatthāyāti rāgādīhi malehi abhijjhāvisamalobhādīhi [M 3.0102] ca upakkiliṭṭhacittānaṃ visuddhatthāya. Sā panāyaṃ cittassa visuddhi sijjhamānā yasmā sokādīnaṃ anupādāya saṃvattati, tasmā vuttaṃ “sokaparidevānaṃ samatikkamāyā”tiādi. Tattha socanaṃ ñātibyasanādinimittaṃ cetaso santāpo antotāpo antonijjhānaṃ soko, ñātibyasanādinimittameva socikatā. “Kahaṃ ekaputtakā”tiādinā (ma. ni. 2.353-354; saṃ. ni. 2.63) paridevanavasena lapanaṃ paridevo. Samatikkamanatthāyāti pahānāya. Āyatiṃ anuppajjanañhi idha samatikkamo. Dukkhadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamāyāti kāyikadukkhassa ca cetasikadomanassassa cāti imesaṃ dvinnaṃ atthaṅgamāya, nirodhāyāti attho. Ñāyati nicchayena kamati nibbānaṃ, taṃ vā ñāyati paṭivijjhati etenāti ñāyo, ariyamaggo. Idha pana saha pubbabhāgena ariyamaggo gahitoti āha “sahavipassanakassa maggassa adhigamanatthāyā”ti. Apaccayaparinibbānassāti anupādisesanibbānaṃ sandhāya vadati. Paccayavasena anuppannaṃ asaṅkhataṃ amatadhātumeva. Sesamettha uttānameva.

26. In the sixth [sutta], `sambādheti` (it is crowded) refers to the oppression by craving, defilements, and so forth, or the congestion in household life. “Opportunities” (okāsā) are so called because they are opportunities for the attainment of the happiness of the path and fruition. “Gaining opportunity” (okāsādhigamo) refers to the opportunity to be attained for the realization of the supramundane Dhamma. “For the purpose of purification” (visujjhanatthāya) means for the purification of minds defiled by stains such as lust and so forth, and by covetousness, unrighteous greed, and so forth. This purification of the mind, when accomplished, leads to the non-arising of sorrow and so forth; hence it is said, “for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation,” and so forth. Here, sorrow (soko) is the inner burning, inner torment, and inner anguish of the mind due to the loss of relatives and so forth; it is the state of being sorrowful due to the loss of relatives and so forth. Lamentation (paridevo) is the wailing expressed through words like, “Where is my only child?” and so forth. “For the purpose of overcoming” (samatikkamanatthāya) means for abandoning; for here, overcoming is non-arising in the future. “For the cessation of suffering and displeasure” (dukkhadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamāya) means for the cessation of these two—bodily suffering and mental displeasure; that is, for their cessation. The path (ñāyo) is so called because it decisively goes to Nibbāna, or because one knows and penetrates Nibbāna by it; it is the Noble Path. Here, however, the Noble Path is taken together with its preliminary aspect; hence it is said, “for the attainment of the path accompanied by insight.” The term `apaccaya-parinibbānassa` refers to Nibbāna without residue. It is simply the unconditioned, unborn, deathless element that has not arisen by way of conditions. The rest here is evident.

Mahākaccānasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Mahākaccāna Sutta is concluded.

7. Paṭhamasamayasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Explanation of the First Assembly Sutta.

27. Sattame vaḍḍhetīti manaso vivaṭṭanissitaṃ vaḍḍhiṃ āvahati. Manobhāvanīyoti vā manasā bhāvito sambhāvito. Yañca āvajjato manasi karoto cittaṃ vinīvaraṇaṃ hoti. Imasmiṃ pakkhe kammasādhano sambhāvanattho bhāvanīya-saddo. “Thinamiddhavinodanakammaṭṭhāna”nti vatvā tadeva vibhāvento “ālokasaññaṃ vā”tiādimāha. Vīriyārambhavatthuādīnaṃ vāti ettha ādi-saddena idha avuttānaṃ atibhojane nimittaggāhādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Vuttañhetaṃ “cha dhammā thinamiddhassa pahānāya saṃvattanti atibhojane nimittaggāho, iriyāpathasamparivattanatā, ālokasaññāmanasikāro, abbhokāsavāso, kalyāṇamittatā, sappāyakathā”ti (itivu. aṭṭha. 111). Antarāyasaddapariyāyo idha antarā-saddoti āha “anantarāyenā”ti.

27. In the seventh [sutta], `vaḍḍheti` (it increases) means it brings about growth dependent on the turning away of the mind. Or, `manobhāvanīyo` (to be developed by the mind) means cultivated and developed by the mind. And when one reflects and attends, the mind becomes free from hindrances. In this alternative, the word `bhāvanīya` is formed in the objective sense with the meaning of 'to be developed.' Having stated, “the meditation subject for dispelling sloth and torpor,” he elaborates on that very point by saying, “the perception of light,” and so forth. Regarding “or of the bases for initiating energy, and so forth,” here, the word “and so forth” should be understood to include what is not mentioned here, such as overeating, grasping at signs, and so forth. For it is said: “Six things lead to the abandoning of sloth and torpor: overeating, grasping at signs, changing postures, attending to the perception of light, dwelling in the open, good friendship, and suitable talk” (Itivuttaka Commentary 111). The word `antarā` here is a synonym for the word `antarāya` (obstacle); hence he says, `anantarāyena` (without obstacle).

Paṭhamasamayasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the First Assembly Sutta is concluded.

8. Dutiyasamayasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Explanation of the Second Assembly Sutta.

28. Aṭṭhame [V 3.0097][M 3.0103] maṇḍalasaṇṭhānamāḷasaṅkhepena katā bhojanasālā maṇḍalamāḷāti adhippetāti āha “bhojanasālāyā”ti. Sesamettha suviññeyyameva.

28. In the eighth [sutta], the dining hall made with a construction resembling a circular pavilion is what is intended by the term `maṇḍalamāḷa`; hence he says, “in the dining hall” (bhojanasālāyā). The rest here is easily understood.

Dutiyasamayasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Second Assembly Sutta is concluded.

9. Udāyīsuttavaṇṇanā

9. Explanation of the Udāyī Sutta.

29. Navame diṭṭhadhammo vuccati paccakkho attabhāvoti āha “imasmiṃyeva attabhāve”ti. Sukhavihāratthāyāti nikkilesatāya nirāmisena sukhena vihāratthāya. Ālokasaññaṃ manasi karotīti sūriyacandapajjotamaṇiukkāvijjuādīnaṃ āloko divā rattiñca upaladdho, yathāladdhavaseneva ālokaṃ manasi karoti, citte ṭhapeti. Tathā ca naṃ manasi karoti, yathāssa subhāvitālokakasiṇassa viya kasiṇāloko yathicchakaṃ yāvadicchakañca so āloko rattiyaṃ upatiṭṭhati. Yena tattha divāsaññaṃ ṭhapeti, divāriva vigatathinamiddho hoti. Tenāha “yathā divā tathā ratti”nti. Divāti saññaṃ ṭhapetīti vuttanayena manasi katvā divāriva saññaṃ uppādeti. Yathānena divā…pe… tatheva taṃ manasi karotīti yathānena divā upaladdho sūriyāloko, evaṃ rattimpi divā diṭṭhākāreneva taṃ ālokaṃ manasi karoti. Yathā canena rattiṃ…pe… manasi karotīti yathā rattiyaṃ candāloko upaladdho, evaṃ divāpi rattiṃ diṭṭhākāreneva taṃ ālokaṃ manasi karoti, citte ṭhapeti. Vivaṭenāti thinamiddhena apihitattā vivaṭena. Anonaddhenāti asañchāditena. Sahobhāsakanti saññāṇobhāsaṃ. Dibbacakkhuñāṇaṃ rūpagatassa dibbassa itarassa ca dassanaṭṭhena idha ñāṇadassananti adhippetanti āha “dibbacakkhusaṅkhātassā”tiādi.

29. In the ninth [sutta], `diṭṭhadhammo` (visible in this very life) is said to be the present existence; hence he says, “in this very existence” (imasmiṃyeva attabhāve). “For the sake of dwelling happily” (sukhavihāratthāya) means for the purpose of dwelling with the happiness that is unworldly and free from defilements. “He attends to the perception of light” (ālokasaññaṃ manasi karoti) means that the light of the sun, moon, lamps, gems, meteors, lightning, and so forth, is perceived by day and night; he simply attends to that light as it is perceived, fixing it in the mind. He attends to it in such a way that, like the light of a well-developed light-kasiṇa, that light appears to him at night as he wishes and for as long as he wishes. By this, he establishes the perception of day, and thus, even at night, he is free from sloth and torpor. Hence it is said, “as by day, so by night” (yathā divā tathā rattiṃ). “He establishes the perception of day” (divāti saññaṃ ṭhapeti) means having attended to it in the manner stated, he generates the perception as if it were day. “Just as by day… so he attends to it” (yathā divā… tatheva taṃ manasi karoti) means just as the light of the sun is perceived by day, so at night he attends to that light in the same way as seen by day. “Just as by night… he attends to it” (yathā rattiṃ… manasi karoti) means just as the light of the moon is perceived by night, so by day he attends to that light in the same way as seen by night, fixing it in the mind. “With an open mind” (vivaṭena) means open because it is not covered by sloth and torpor. “Unobstructed” (anonaddhenāti) means not obscured. “With co-arisen illumination” (sahobhāsakaṃ) means the illumination of consciousness. The knowledge of the divine eye is intended here as “knowledge and vision” (ñāṇadassana) in the sense of seeing forms, whether divine or other. Hence he says, “designated as the divine eye” (dibbacakkhusaṅkhātassa), and so forth.

Uddhaṃ jīvitapariyādānāti jīvitakkhayato upari maraṇato paraṃ. Samuggatenāti uṭṭhitena. Dhumātattāti uddhaṃ uddhaṃ dhumātattā sūnattā[M 3.0104]. Setarattehi viparibhinnaṃ vimissitaṃ nīlaṃ, purimavaṇṇavipariṇāmabhūtaṃ vā nīlaṃ vinīlaṃ, vinīlameva vinīlakanti ka-kārena padavaḍḍhanamāha anatthantarato yathā “pītakaṃ lohitaka”nti. Paṭikūlattāti jigucchanīyattā. Kucchitaṃ vinīlaṃ vinīlakanti kucchanattho vā ayaṃ ka-kāroti dassetuṃ vuttaṃ yathā “pāpako kittisaddo abbhuggacchatī”ti (dī. ni. 3.316; a. ni. 5.213). Paribhinnaṭṭhānehi kākadhaṅkādīhi[V 3.0098]. Vissandamānaṃ pubbanti vissavantapubbaṃ, tahaṃ tahaṃ paggharantapubbanti attho. Tathābhāvanti vissandamānapubbataṃ.

“Beyond the exhaustion of life” (uddhaṃ jīvitapariyādānā) means beyond the destruction of life, after death. “Having risen” (samuggatena) means having arisen. “Bloated” (dhumātattā) means swollen upwards and upwards, bloated. A discolored corpse (`vinīlaka`) is one that is discolored and mixed with white and red. Or, `vinīla` means blue that has undergone a transformation from its original color; `vinīlaka` is merely `vinīla`, which he says is a word-extension with the suffix `-ka` without difference in meaning, just as in “yellowish” (pītakaṃ) and “reddish” (lohitakaṃ). “Repulsive” (paṭikūlattā) means being disgusting. Or, to show that this suffix `-ka` in `vinīlaka` has the meaning of “contemptible” (kucchitaṃ), it is said, just as “an evil (pāpako) reputation arises” (Dīgha Nikāya 3.316; Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.213). The phrase `paribhinnaṭṭhānehi kākadhaṅkādīhi` means being devoured by crows, vultures, and so forth, at the places where it is torn apart. “Oozing pus” (vissandamānaṃ pubbaṃ) means pus oozing, pus flowing here and there—this is the meaning. “Such is its nature” (tathābhāvaṃ) refers to the state of oozing pus.

So bhikkhūti yo “passeyya sarīraṃ sīvathikāya chaḍḍita”nti vutto, so bhikkhu. Upasaṃharati sadisataṃ. Ayampi khotiādi upasaṃharaṇākāradassanaṃ. Āyūti rūpajīvitindriyaṃ. Arūpajīvitindriyaṃ panettha viññāṇagatikameva. Usmāti kammajatejo. Evaṃpūtikasabhāvoti evaṃ ativiya pūtisabhāvo āyuādivigame viyāti adhippāyo. Ediso bhavissatīti evaṃbhāvīti āha “evamevaṃ uddhumātādibhedo bhavissatī”ti.

“That monk” (so bhikkhu) refers to the monk who is spoken of as “he might see a corpse discarded in a charnel ground.” “He applies it to himself” (upasaṃharati) means he applies the similarity. “This body too…” (`Ayampi kho...`) and so forth, shows the method of application. “Life faculty” (āyu) refers to the material life faculty. The immaterial life faculty here is simply the course of consciousness. “Heat” (usmā) means the heat produced by kamma. “Of such a foul nature” (evaṃpūtikasabhāvo) means thus, an exceedingly foul state as if upon the cessation of life, and so forth—this is the intention. “It will be of such a kind” (ediso bhavissati) means it will be of such a nature; thus he says, “it will become thus, of the kind that is bloated, and so forth.”

Luñcitvā luñcitvāti uppāṭetvā uppāṭetvā. Sesāvasesamaṃsalohitayuttanti sabbaso akkhāditattā tahaṃ tahaṃ sesena appāvasesena maṃsalohitena yuttaṃ. Aññena hatthaṭṭhikanti avisesena hatthaṭṭhikānaṃ vippakiṇṇatā jotitāti anavasesato tesaṃ vippakiṇṇataṃ dassento “catusaṭṭhibhedampī”tiādimāha. Terovassikānīti tirovassagatāni. Tāni pana saṃvaccharaṃ vītivattāni hontīti āha “atikkantasaṃvaccharānī”ti. Purāṇatāya ghanabhāvavigamena vicuṇṇatā idha pūtibhāvo. So yathā hoti, taṃ dassento “abbhokāse”tiādimāha. Anekadhātūnanti cakkhudhātuādīnaṃ, kāmadhātuādīnaṃ vā. Satiyā ca ñāṇassa ca atthāyāti “abhikkante paṭikkante sampajānakārī hotī”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.214; 2.376; ma. ni. 1.109) vuttāya sattaṭṭhānikāya satiyā ceva taṃsampayuttañāṇassa ca atthāya.

“Plucking it again and again” (luñcitvā luñcitvā) means tearing it apart repeatedly. “With remnants of flesh and blood” (sesāvasesamaṃsalohitayuttaṃ) means that since it has not been entirely consumed, it is still connected here and there by small remnants of flesh and blood. “A hand-bone in one place” (aññena hatthaṭṭhikaṃ) refers to the indiscriminate scattering of hand bones, and so forth, showing their complete dispersal; and to show their complete dispersal, he says, “broken into sixty-four parts,” and so forth. “A year old” (terovassikāni) means having passed beyond a year. And because they have passed a year, he says, “having passed beyond a year” (atikkantasaṃvaccharāni). Here, “putrefaction” (pūtibhāvo) refers to being pulverized through the loss of solidity due to old age. To show how this happens, he says, “exposed to the open air,” and so forth. “Of many elements” (anekadhātūnaṃ) refers to the eye element and so forth, or the sense-sphere element and so forth. “For the sake of mindfulness and wisdom” (satiyā ca ñāṇassa ca atthāya) means for the purpose of the seven-based mindfulness and the wisdom associated with it, as stated in “one acts with clear comprehension when going forward or returning,” and so forth (Dīgha Nikāya 1.214; 2.376; Majjhima Nikāya 1.109).

Udāyīsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Udāyī Sutta is concluded.

10. Anuttariyasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Anuttariya Sutta

30. Dasame [M 3.0105] nihīnanti lāmakaṃ, kiliṭṭhaṃ vā. Gāmavāsikānanti bālānaṃ. Puthujjanānaṃ idanti pothujjanikaṃ. Tenāha “puthujjanānaṃ santaka”nti, puthujjanehi sevitabbattā tesaṃ santakanti vuttaṃ hoti. Anariyanti na niddosaṃ. Niddosaṭṭho hi ariyaṭṭho. Tenāha “na uttamaṃ na parisuddha”nti. Ariyehi vā na sevitabbanti anariyaṃ. Anatthasaṃhitanti diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikādivividhavipulānatthasahitaṃ. Tādisañca atthasannissitaṃ na hotīti āha “na atthasannissita”nti. Na vaṭṭe nibbindanatthāyāti catusaccakammaṭṭhānābhāvato. Asati pana vaṭṭe nibbidāya virāgādīnaṃ asambhavoyevāti āha “na virāgāyā”tiādi.

30. In the tenth discourse, ‘inferior’ (nihīnaṃ) means base or defiled. ‘Of village dwellers’ (gāmavāsikānaṃ) means of the ignorant. ‘This is of ordinary people’ (puthujjanānaṃ idaṃ) means common to ordinary people (pothujjanikaṃ). Therefore, he says, ‘belonging to ordinary people’ (puthujjanānaṃ santakaṃ); because it is to be frequented by ordinary people, it is said to belong to them. ‘Not noble’ (anariyaṃ) means not faultless. For the meaning of ‘noble’ is the meaning of ‘faultless’. Therefore, he says, ‘not supreme, not pure.’ Or, because it is not frequented by the noble ones, it is not noble. ‘Not connected with benefit’ (anatthasaṃhitaṃ) means connected with various extensive disadvantages, such as those pertaining to the present life and future lives. And because it is not grounded in such benefit, he says, ‘not grounded in benefit’ (na atthasannissitaṃ). ‘Not for the purpose of disenchantment with the round of existence’ (na vaṭṭe nibbindanatthāya) means due to the absence of the meditation subject of the four truths. But in the absence of disenchantment with the round of existence, dispassion and so forth are impossible; hence he says, ‘not for dispassion’ (na virāgāya), and so forth.

Anuttamaṃ [V 3.0099] anuttariyanti āha “etaṃ anuttara”nti. Hatthisminti nimittatthe bhummanti āha “hatthinimittaṃ sikkhitabba”nti. Hatthivisayattā hatthisannissitattā ca hatthisippaṃ “hatthī”ti gahetvā “hatthismimpi sikkhatī”ti vuttaṃ. Tasmā hatthisippe sikkhatīti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo.

‘Supreme, unsurpassed’ (anuttamaṃ anuttariyaṃ)—therefore he says, ‘this is unsurpassed’ (etaṃ anuttaraṃ). Regarding ‘on an elephant’ (hatthismiṃ), the locative case (bhummaṃ) is in the sense of an object (nimittatthe); therefore he says, ‘the subject of elephants is to be trained in’ (hatthinimittaṃ sikkhitabbaṃ). Because it is the domain of elephants and is based on elephants, the elephant craft (hatthisippaṃ) is taken as ‘elephant’ (hatthī), and thus it is said, ‘He trains in what pertains to the elephant’ (hatthismimpi sikkhatī). Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as: he trains in the elephant craft. The same method applies to the remaining terms.

Liṅgabyattayena vibhattibyattayena pāricariyeti vuttanti āha “pāricariyāya paccupaṭṭhitā”ti. Sesamettha suviññeyyameva.

Because it is stated as ‘pāricariyā’ with a change of gender and a change of case inflection, he says, ‘attended with service’ (pāricariyāya paccupaṭṭhitā). The rest here is easily understood.

Anuttariyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Anuttariya Sutta is concluded.

Anuttariyavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Anuttariya Vagga is concluded.

4. Devatāvaggo

4. The Chapter on Deities

1-4. Sekhasuttādivaṇṇanā

1–4. Commentary on the Sekha Sutta and Others

31-34. Catutthassa paṭhame sekhānaṃ paṭiladdhaguṇassa parihāni nāma natthīti āha “uparūpariguṇaparihānāyā”ti, uparūpariladdhabbānaṃ maggaphalānaṃ parihānāya anuppādāyāti attho. Tatiyādīni uttānatthāneva.

31–34. In the first of the fourth discourse, he says there is no such thing as decline of a quality attained by trainees; hence it is said, ‘for the decline of higher and higher qualities’ (uparūpariguṇaparihānāya). The meaning is: for the decline, that is, the non-arising, of the paths and fruits that are to be attained higher and higher. The third and following discourses are of clear meaning.

Sekhasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Sekha Sutta and Others is concluded.

5. Vijjābhāgiyasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Vijjābhāgiya Sutta

35. Pañcame [M 3.0106] sampayogavasena vijjaṃ bhajanti, sahajātaaññamaññanissayasampayuttaatthiavigatādipaccayavasena tāya saha ekībhāvaṃ gacchantīti vijjābhāgiyā. Atha vā vijjābhāge vijjākoṭṭhāse vattanti vijjāsabhāgatāya tadekadese vijjākoṭṭhāse pavattantīti vijjābhāgiyā. Tattha vipassanāñāṇaṃ, manomayiddhi, cha abhiññāti aṭṭha vijjā. Purimena atthena tāhi sampayuttadhammā vijjābhāgiyā. Pacchimena atthena tāsu yā kāci ekāva vijjā [V 3.0100] vijjā, sesā vijjābhāgiyā. Evaṃ vijjāpi vijjāya sampayuttadhammāpi “vijjābhāgiyā”tveva veditabbā. Idha pana vipassanāñāṇasampayuttā saññāva vijjābhāgiyāti āgatā, saññāsīsena sesasampayuttadhammāpi vuttā evāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Aniccānupassanāñāṇeti aniccānupassanāñāṇe nissayapaccayabhūte uppannasaññā, tena sahagatāti attho. Sesesupi eseva nayo.

35. In the fifth discourse, because they partake of wisdom (vijjaṃ) by way of association (sampayogavasena), becoming one with it through conditions such as co-nascence, mutual dependence, support, association, presence, and non-disappearance, they are ‘sharers in wisdom’ (vijjābhāgiyā). Or alternatively, they abide in the share of wisdom, in the portion of wisdom; because they share the nature of wisdom, they proceed in a part of it, in the portion of wisdom; thus they are ‘sharers in wisdom’. Herein, there are eight kinds of wisdom: insight knowledge, mind-made power, and the six higher knowledges. According to the first meaning, the states associated with these are ‘sharers in wisdom’. According to the latter meaning, any single one of these is wisdom, and the rest are ‘sharers in wisdom’. Thus, both wisdom itself and the states associated with wisdom should be understood as ‘sharers in wisdom’. Here, however, only the perception associated with insight knowledge is given as a ‘sharer in wisdom’, but it should be understood that by mentioning perception as the chief, the remaining associated states are also stated. ‘In the knowledge of the contemplation of impermanence’ (aniccānupassanāñāṇe) means the perception that has arisen with the knowledge of the contemplation of impermanence as its support condition, and is co-nascent with it. The same method applies in the remaining cases.

Vijjābhāgiyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Vijjābhāgiya Sutta is concluded.

6. Vivādamūlasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Discourse on the Root of Disputes

36. Chaṭṭhe kodhanoti kujjhanasīlo. Yasmā so appahīnakodhatāya adhigatakodho nāma hoti, tasmā “kodhena samannāgato”ti āha. Upanāho etassa atthīti upanāhī, upanayhanasīloti vā upanāhī. Vivādo nāma uppajjamāno yebhuyyena paṭhamaṃ dvinnaṃ vasena uppajjatīti vuttaṃ “dvinnaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ vivādo”ti. So pana yathā bahūnaṃ anatthāvaho hoti, taṃ nidassanamukhena nidassento “katha”ntiādimāha. Abbhantaraparisāyāti parisabbhantare.

36. In the sixth discourse, ‘an angry person’ (kodhano) means one who is habitually angry. Because, not having abandoned anger, one is said to be overcome by anger, he says, ‘endowed with anger’ (kodhena samannāgato). ‘One who bears a grudge’ (upanāhī) is one for whom there is a grudge, or one who is habitually resentful. A dispute, when it arises, generally arises first between two people, thus it is said, ‘a dispute between two monks’ (dvinnaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ vivādo). But to show how it brings harm to many, he speaks beginning with ‘how?’, and so forth. ‘Within the assembly’ (abbhantaraparisāya) means inside the assembly.

Guṇamakkhanāya pavattopi attano kārakaṃ gūthena paharantiṃ gūtho viya paṭhamataraṃ makkhetīti makkho, so etassa atthīti makkhī. Paḷāsatīti paḷāso, parassa guṇe ḍaṃsitvā viya apanetīti attho. So etassa atthīti paḷāsī. Paḷāsī puggalo hi dutiyassa dhuraṃ na deti, samaṃ haritvā ativadati. Tenāha “yugaggāhalakkhaṇena paḷāsena samannāgato”ti. Issatīti issukī. Maccharāyatīti maccharaṃ, taṃ etassa atthīti [M 3.0107] maccharī. Saṭhayati na sammā bhāsatīti saṭho aññathā santaṃ attānaṃ aññathā pavedanato. Māyā etassa atthī māyāvī. Micchā pāpikā viññugarahitā etassa diṭṭhīti micchādiṭṭhi, kammapathapariyāpannāya “natthi dinna”ntiādivatthukāya micchattapariyāpannāya aniyyānikāya diṭṭhiyā samannāgatoti attho. Tenāha “natthikavādī”tiādi.

Because, though it proceeds to denigrate another’s virtue, it first smears its own agent, like dung smears one who strikes with dung, it is called ‘disparagement’ (makkho). One who has this is ‘disparaging’ (makkhī). ‘He is competitive’ (paḷāsati), thus it is ‘rivalry’ (paḷāso); the meaning is that one takes away another’s virtues as if by biting them. One who has this is ‘rivalrous’ (paḷāsī). A rivalrous person does not yield the foremost place to another; though carrying an equal load, he speaks down to him. Hence he says, ‘endowed with rivalry characterized by seizing the yoke-end’ (yugaggāhalakkhaṇena paḷāsena). ‘He is jealous’ (issatīti), thus he is ‘envious’ (issukī). ‘He is avaricious’ (maccharāyati), thus it is ‘stinginess’ (maccharaṃ); one who has this is ‘stingy’ (maccharī). ‘He deceives, he does not speak correctly’ (saṭhayati na sammā bhāsati), thus he is ‘deceitful’ (saṭho), because he presents himself as other than he is. One who has ‘deceit’ (māyā) is ‘deceitful’ (māyāvī). His view is wrong, evil, and censured by the wise, thus he is of ‘wrong view’ (micchādiṭṭhi); the meaning is that he is endowed with a view that is included in the course of action, comprised in wrongness, and does not lead to liberation, based on such tenets as ‘there is nothing given,’ and so forth. Hence he says, ‘one who is a nihilist’ (natthikavādī), and so forth.

Saṃ attano diṭṭhiṃ, sayaṃ vā attanā yathāgahitaṃ parāmasati, sabhāvaṃ atikkamitvā parato āmasatīti sandiṭṭhīparāmāsī. Ādhānaṃ daḷhaṃ gaṇhātīti ādhānaggāhī, daḷhaggāhī, “idameva sacca”nti thiraggāhīti attho. Yuttaṃ kāraṇaṃ disvāva laddhiṃ paṭinissajjatīti paṭinissaggī, dukkhena kicchena kasirena bahumpi kāraṇaṃ dassetvā na sakkā paṭinissaggaṃ kātunti [V 3.0101] duppaṭinissaggī. Yo attano uppannadiṭṭhiṃ “idameva sacca”nti daḷhaṃ gaṇhitvā api buddhādīhi kāraṇaṃ dassetvā vuccamāno na paṭinissajjati. Tassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tādiso hi puggalo yaṃ yadeva dhammaṃ vā adhammaṃ vā suṇāti, taṃ sabbaṃ “evaṃ amhākaṃ ācariyehi kathitaṃ, evaṃ amhehi suta”nti kummova aṅgāni sake kapāle antoyeva samodahati. Yathā hi kacchapo attano hatthapādādike aṅge kenaci ghaṭite sabbāni aṅgāni attano kapāleyeva samodahati, na bahi nīharati, evamayampi “na sundaro tava gāho, chaḍḍehi na”nti vutto taṃ na vissajjati, antoyeva attano hadaye eva ṭhapetvā vicarati, kumbhīlaggāhaṃ gaṇhāti. Yathā susumārā gahitaṃ na paṭinissajjanti, evaṃ gaṇhāti.

He clings to his own view, or he grasps what he has taken up by himself; having gone beyond its true nature, he clings to it from another's standpoint—thus he is one who clings to his own view. He firmly holds onto his adherence—this is the meaning of being an adherent, holding firmly, thinking, 'This alone is the truth,' holding steadfastly. One who, upon seeing a valid reason, abandons his belief is called one who lets go. But one who, even after much difficulty, effort, and hardship, even after being shown many reasons, cannot abandon his belief is called one who is hard to relinquish. Whoever firmly grasps his own arisen view, thinking, 'This alone is the truth,' and even when the Buddha or others present reasons and admonish him, does not relinquish it—this is his designation. Such a person, whatever teaching—whether Dhamma or not-Dhamma—he hears, he simply says, 'This is how our teachers have spoken, this is how we have heard it,' like a tortoise drawing its limbs into its own shell. Just as a tortoise, when its limbs or head are struck by something, draws all its limbs into its own shell and does not extend them outward, so too does this person, when told, 'Your grasp is not good, release it,' refuse to release it. Instead, he keeps it locked in his heart and wanders about, seizing it with a crocodile's grip. Just as crocodiles do not release what they have seized, so does he hold on.

Vivādamūlasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on the Root of Disputes is concluded.

7. Chaḷaṅgadānasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Discourse on the Six-Limbed Gift

37. Sattame dakkhanti vaḍḍhanti etāyāti dakkhiṇā, pariccāgamayaṃ puññaṃ, tassūpakaraṇabhūto deyyadhammo ca. Idha pana deyyadhammo adhippeto. Tenevāha “dakkhiṇaṃ patiṭṭhāpetī”ti. Ito uṭṭhitenāti ito khettato uppannena. Rāgo vinayati etenāti rāgavinayo, rāgassa samucchedikā paṭipadā. Tenāha “rāgavinayapaṭipadaṃ paṭipannā”ti.

37. In the seventh, they see and grow by means of this; therefore it is called 'dakkhiṇā,' an offering. The merit consists of relinquishment, and the gift is the supporting factor for that. Here, however, the gift is intended. Therefore, he said, 'He establishes an offering.' 'Arising from this' means arising from this field. Lust is disciplined by this; therefore it is called 'rāgavinayo,' the disciplining of lust—the practice that eradicates lust. Therefore, he said, 'They have undertaken the practice for the disciplining of lust.'

“Pubbeva dānā sumano”tiādigāthāya pubbeva dānā muñcacetanāya pubbe dānūpakaraṇasambharaṇato paṭṭhāya sumano “sampattīnaṃ nidānaṃ anugāmikadānaṃ [M 3.0108] dassāmī”ti somanassito bhaveyya. Dadaṃ cittaṃ pasādayeti dadanto deyyadhammaṃ dakkhiṇeyyahatthe patiṭṭhāpento “asārato dhanato sārādānaṃ karomī”ti attano cittaṃ pasādeyya. Datvā attamano hotīti dakkhiṇeyyānaṃ deyyadhammaṃ pariccajitvā “paṇḍitapaññattaṃ nāma mayā anuṭṭhitaṃ, aho sādhu suṭṭhū”ti attamano pamudito pītisomanassajāto hoti. Esāti yā ayaṃ pubbacetanā muñcacetanā aparacetanāti imāsaṃ kammaphalānaṃ saddhānugatānaṃ somanassapariggahitānaṃ tividhānaṃ cetanānaṃ pāripūrī, esā.

By the verse beginning, 'Even before giving, one is joyful,' before giving, from the very preparation of the gift with the intention to give, one should be joyful, thinking, 'I will give this gift, which is the cause of prosperity and follows the giver,' and thus become gladdened. While giving, one gladdens the mind—as one places the gift in the hands of the worthy recipient, one thinks, 'I am taking the essence from essenceless wealth,' and thus gladdens one's own mind. Having given, one is delighted—after relinquishing the gift to the worthy recipients, one thinks, 'I have done what is commended by the wise—how good, how well!' and becomes delighted, joyful, and filled with rapture and gladness. This is the fulfillment of these three kinds of intentions—the intention before giving, the intention during giving, and the intention after giving—which are accompanied by faith, embraced by joy, and result in kamma.

Sīlasaññamenāti kāyikavācasikasaṃvarena. Hatthapādeti dakkhiṇeyyānaṃ hatthapāde. Mukhaṃ vikkhāletvāti tesaṃyeva mukhaṃ vikkhāletvā, attanāva mukhodakaṃ datvāti adhippāyo.

By restraint of moral conduct—this refers to bodily and verbal restraint. Hands and feet—this refers to the hands and feet of those worthy of offerings. Having washed the face—this means having washed their faces; the meaning is that one offers them water for the face oneself.

Chaḷaṅgadānasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Chaḷaṅgadāna Sutta is concluded.

8-11. Attakārīsuttādivaṇṇanā

8-11. Commentary on the Attakārī Sutta and others

38-41. Aṭṭhame [V 3.0102] kusalakiriyāya ādiārambhabhāvena pavattavīriyaṃ ṭhitasabhāvatāya sabhāvadhāraṇaṭṭhena dhātūti vuttanti āha – “ārambhadhātūti ārabhanavasena pavattavīriya”nti. Laddhāsevanaṃ vīriyaṃ balappattaṃ hutvā paṭipakkhe vidhamatīti āha “nikkamadhātūti kosajjato nikkhamanasabhāvaṃ vīriya”nti. Parakkamanasabhāvoti adhimattatarānaṃ paṭipakkhadhammānaṃ vidhamanasamatthatāya paṭupaṭutarabhāvena paraṃ paraṃ ṭhānaṃ akkamanasabhāvo. Navamādīsu natthi vattabbaṃ.

38-41. In the eighth, it is said that the energy that arises as the initial commencement in performing wholesome deeds is called a 'dhātu' because of its steadfast nature, in the sense of maintaining its inherent quality. He says: 'The element of initiative is the energy that arises by way of commencement.' He also says that the energy that has been cultivated, having attained strength, dispels the opposing factors: 'The element of exertion is the energy whose nature is to depart from sloth.' Its nature of striving is the nature of overcoming one position after another with ever greater skill, due to its capability of dispelling even more intense opposing states. In the ninth and so on, there is nothing to be said.

Attakārīsuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Attakārī Sutta and others is concluded.

12. Nāgitasuttavaṇṇanā

12. Commentary on the Nāgita Sutta

42. Dvādasame māhaṃ nāgita yasena samāgamanti mā ahaṃ yasena samāgamanaṃ patthemi. Mā ca mayā yasoti yaso ca mayā mā samāgacchatūti [M 3.0109] attho. Iminā attano lābhasakkārena anatthikataṃ vibhāveti. Pañcahi vimuttīhīti tadaṅgavimuttiādīhi pañcahi vimuttīhi. Sesamettha uttānameva.

42. In the twelfth, the phrase 'May I not meet with fame, Nāgita' means 'I do not long for association with fame.' And 'May fame not come to me' means 'fame should not come together with me.' By this, he reveals his lack of desire for gain and honor. 'By the five kinds of liberations' means by the five kinds of liberations such as liberation by substitution of opposites, etc. The rest here is self-evident.

Nāgitasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Nāgita Sutta is concluded.

Devatāvaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Devatā Vagga is concluded.

5. Dhammikavaggo

5. The Chapter on the Righteous

1. Nāgasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Nāga Sutta

43. Pañcamassa paṭhame parisiñcitunti (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.272) yo cuṇṇamattikādīhi gattāni ubbaṭṭento mallakamuṭṭhādīhi vā ghaṃsanto nahāyati, so “nahāyatī”ti vuccati. Yo tathā akatvā pakatiyāva nahāyati, so “parisiñcatī”ti vuccati[V 3.0103]. Bhagavato ca sarīre tathā haritabbaṃ rajojallaṃ nāma nupalimpati acchachavibhāvato, utuggahaṇatthaṃ pana bhagavā kevalaṃ udake otarati. Tenāha “gattāni parisiñcitu”nti.

43. In the first section of the fifth, regarding 'to sprinkle': one who bathes by rubbing the limbs with powder, clay, and so on, or scrubbing with a wrestler’s fist and the like, is said to 'bathe.' One who, without doing so, bathes in the ordinary way is said to 'sprinkle.' However, dust and impurities that would need to be removed in such a way do not cling to the Blessed One’s body because of its clear-skinned radiance. The Blessed One enters the water solely for the purpose of regulating his temperature. Hence, it is said, 'to sprinkle the limbs.'

Pubbakoṭṭhakoti pācīnakoṭṭhako. Sāvatthiyaṃ kira jetavanavihāro kadāci mahā, kadāci khuddako. Tathā hi so vipassissa bhagavato kāle yojaniko ahosi, sikhissa tigāvuto, vessabhussa aḍḍhayojaniko, kakusandhassa gāvutappamāṇo, koṇāgamanassa aḍḍhagāvutappamāṇo, kassapassa vīsatiusabhappamāṇo, amhākaṃ bhagavato kāle aṭṭhakarīsappamāṇo jāto. Tampi nagaraṃ tassa vihārassa kadāci pācīnato hoti, kadāci dakkhiṇato, kadāci pacchimato, kadāci uttarato. Jetavanagandhakuṭiyaṃ pana catunnaṃ mañcapādānaṃ patiṭṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ acalameva. Cattāri hi acalacetiyaṭṭhānāni nāma mahābodhipallaṅkaṭṭhānaṃ, isipatane dhammacakkappavattanaṭṭhānaṃ, saṅkassanagare devorohanakāle sopānassa patiṭṭhānaṭṭhānaṃ, mañcapādaṭṭhānanti. Ayaṃ pana pubbakoṭṭhako kassapadasabalassa vīsatiusabhavihārakāle pācīnadvārakoṭṭhako ahosi. So idāni “pubbakoṭṭhako”tveva paññāyati.

`Pubbakoṭṭhako` means the eastern gate-tower. In Sāvatthī, it is said, the Jetavana monastery was sometimes large and sometimes small. For instance, during the time of the Buddha Vipassī, it was a league in size; for Sikhī, three gāvutas; for Vessabhū, half a league; for Kakusandha, a gāvuta in extent; for Koṇāgamana, half a gāvuta in extent; for Kassapa, twenty usabhas; and in our Blessed One’s time, it was eight karīsas. Moreover, that city was sometimes to the east, sometimes to the south, sometimes to the west, and sometimes to the north of that monastery. However, the spot in the Gandhakuṭī at Jetavana where the four legs of the couch were placed is indeed immovable. There are four immovable shrine sites: the site of the great Bodhi throne, the site of the Turning of the Wheel of the Dhamma at Isipatana, the place where the stairs were established at the time of the descent from the deva world in Saṅkassanagara, and the site of the couch legs. This eastern gate-tower was the eastern gate-tower during the time of the twenty-usabha monastery of Kassapa, the one of Ten Powers. Now it is simply known as the 'eastern gate-tower'.

Kassapadasabalassa [M 3.0110] kāle aciravatī nagaraṃ parikkhipitvā sandamānā pubbakoṭṭhakaṃ patvā udakena bhinditvā mahantaṃ udakarahadaṃ māpesi samatittikaṃ anupubbagambhīraṃ. Tattha ekaṃ rañño nhānatitthaṃ, ekaṃ nāgarānaṃ, ekaṃ bhikkhusaṅghassa, ekaṃ buddhānanti evaṃ pāṭiekkāni nhānatitthāni honti ramaṇīyānivippakiṇṇarajatapaṭṭasadisavālukāni. Iti bhagavatā āyasmatā ānandena saddhiṃ yena ayaṃ evarūpo pubbakoṭṭhako, tenupasaṅkami gattāni parisiñcituṃ. Athāyasmā ānando udakasāṭikaṃ upanāmesi. Bhagavā surattadupaṭṭaṃ apanetvā udakasāṭikaṃ nivāsesi. Thero dupaṭṭena saddhiṃ mahācīvaraṃ attano hatthagataṃ akāsi. Bhagavā udakaṃ otari, sahotaraṇenevassa udake macchakacchapā sabbe suvaṇṇavaṇṇā ahesuṃ, yantanāḷikāhi suvaṇṇarasadhārāni siñcanakālo viya suvaṇṇapaṭappasāraṇakālo viya ca ahosi. Atha bhagavato nahānavattaṃ dassetvā paccuttiṇṇassa thero surattadupaṭṭaṃ upanāmesi. Bhagavā taṃ nivāsetvā vijjullatāsadisaṃ kāyabandhanaṃ bandhitvā mahācīvaraṃ antantena saṃharitvā padumagabbhasadisaṃ katvā upanītaṃ dvīsu kaṇṇesu gahetvā aṭṭhāsi. Tena vuttaṃ “pubbakoṭṭhake gattāni parisiñcitvā ekacīvaro aṭṭhāsī”ti.

At the time of Kassapa the Ten-Powered One, the Aciravati River, flowing around the city, surged towards the eastern gate-tower. Breaking through with its waters, it formed a vast lake, level-brimmed and gradually deepening. There, one bathing place was for the king, one for the city-dwellers, one for the community of monks, and one for the Buddhas—thus, the bathing places were separately designated, delightful, with sand resembling scattered silver plates. Then the Blessed One, accompanied by the Venerable Ānanda, approached this eastern gate-tower to bathe his limbs. The Venerable Ānanda offered a bathing cloth. The Blessed One removed his well-dyed upper robe and put on the bathing cloth. The elder took the great robe, together with the upper robe, into his own hands. The Blessed One entered the water, and with his entry, all the fish and turtles in the water turned golden in color. It was as if golden streams were pouring from mechanical pipes, or as if golden cloths were being unfurled. When the Blessed One had emerged, having completed the custom of bathing, the elder offered him the well-dyed upper robe. The Blessed One put it on, fastened his body-band like a flash of lightning, gathered the great robe at its edges, made it like the calyx of a lotus, and held it by the two corners as he stood. Thus it is said: 'Having bathed his limbs at the eastern gate-tower, he stood clad in a single robe.'

Evaṃ ṭhitassa pana bhagavato sarīraṃ vikasitapadumapupphasadisaṃ sabbapāliphullaṃ pāricchattakaṃ, tārāmarīcivikasitañca gaganatalaṃ siriyā avahasamānaṃ viya virocittha, byāmappabhāparikkhepavilāsinī [V 3.0104] cassa dvattiṃsavaralakkhaṇamālā ganthitvā ṭhapitā dvattiṃsa candimā viya, dvattiṃsa sūriyā viya, paṭipāṭiyā ṭhapitadvattiṃsacakkavattidvattiṃsadevarājadvattiṃsamahābrahmāno viya ca ativiya virocittha. Yasmā ca bhagavato sarīraṃ sudhantacāmīkarasamānavaṇṇaṃ, suparisodhitapavāḷaruciratoraṇaṃ, suvisuddhanīlaratanāvalisadisakesatanuruhaṃ, tasmā tahaṃ tahaṃ viniggatasujātajātihiṅgulakarasūpasobhitaṃ upari satamegharatanāvalisucchāditaṃ jaṅgamamiva kanakagirisikharaṃ virocittha. Tasmiñca samaye dasabalassa sarīrato nikkhamitvā chabbaṇṇarasmiyo samantato asītihatthappamāṇe padese ādhāvantī vidhāvantī ratanāvaliratanadāmaratanacuṇṇavippakiṇṇaṃ viya pasāritaratanacittakañcanapaṭṭamiva āsiñcamānalākhārasadhārācittamiva ukkāsatanipātasamākulamiva nirantaravippakiṇṇakaṇikārakiṅkiṇikapupphamiva vāyuvegasamuddhatacinapiṭṭhacuṇṇarañjitamiva [M 3.0111] indadhanuvijjullatāvitānasanthatamiva ca gaganatalaṃ, taṃ ṭhānaṃ pavanañca sammā pharanti. Vaṇṇabhūmi nāmesā. Evarūpesu ṭhānesu buddhānaṃ sarīravaṇṇaṃ vā guṇavaṇṇaṃ vā cuṇṇiyapadehi vā gāthāhi vā atthañca upamāyo ca kāraṇāni ca āharitvā paṭibalena dhammakathikena pūretvā kathetuṃ vaṭṭati. Evarūpesu hi ṭhānesu dhammakathikassa thāmo veditabbo. Pubbasadisāni kurumānoti nirudakāni kurumāno, sukkhāpayamānoti attho. Sodake gatte cīvaraṃ pārupantassa hi cīvare kaṇṇikāni uṭṭhahanti, parikkhārabhaṇḍaṃ dussati, buddhānaṃ pana sarīre rajojallaṃ na upalimpati, padumapatte ukkhittaudakabindu viya udakaṃ vinivaṭṭetvā gacchati. Evaṃ santepi sikkhāgāravatāya bhagavā “pabbajitavattaṃ nāmeta”nti mahācīvaraṃ ubhosu kaṇṇesu gahetvā purato kāyaṃ paṭicchādetvā aṭṭhāsi.

The Blessed One’s body, standing thus, shone like a fully bloomed lotus flower, like the Pāricchattaka tree in full bloom. The sky, brightened by the rays of the stars, shone as if mocking its splendor. The garland of his thirty-two excellent marks, shining with a surrounding fathom-wide radiance, appeared as if thirty-two moons, thirty-two suns, or thirty-two universal monarchs, thirty-two kings of the devas, and thirty-two great Brahmās were arranged in succession, all glowing exceedingly. Because the Blessed One’s body was the color of refined gold, like a radiant gateway of well-polished coral, with hair and body-hair like a garland of perfectly pure blue gems, it shone like a moving golden mountain peak, adorned here and there with the finest vermilion powder and covered above by a hundred gem-garlands like clouds. At that moment, six-colored rays emanated from the body of the Ten-Powered One, spreading in all directions for eighty cubits. They raced and danced about, like scattered gem-garlands, gem-festoons, and gem-powder; like a spread-out golden cloth adorned with gems; like a painting with streams of poured lac dye; like a sky filled with falling meteors; like a continuous scattering of kaṇikāra flowers with little bells; like powdered cinnabar stirred up by the force of the wind; or like a canopy of rainbows and lightning-creepers spread across the sky—filling that place and the forest completely. This is called the 'ground of description.' In such places, a skilled Dhamma speaker should describe the beauty of the Buddha’s body or his virtues, whether in prose or verse, bringing forth meanings, similes, and reasons to fulfill the discourse. For in such places, the strength of a Dhamma speaker is to be known. ‘Making them like before’ means making them without water, that is, drying them. For if one drapes a robe on a moist body, creases will arise in the robe and the requisite will be spoiled. But dust and stains do not cling to the bodies of the Buddhas—like a drop of water on a lotus leaf, the water rolls off and goes away. Even so, out of respect for the training, the Blessed One, reflecting, 'This is the duty of one who has gone forth,' took the great robe by both corners, covered his body in front, and stood there.

Tāḷitañca vāditañca tāḷitavāditaṃ, tūriyānaṃ tāḷitavāditaṃ tūriyatāḷitavāditaṃ. Mahantañca taṃ tūriyatāḷitavāditañcāti mahātūriyatāḷitavāditaṃ. Tenāha “mahantenā”tiādi. Atha vā bherimudiṅgapaṇavāditūriyānaṃ tāḷitaṃ vīṇāveḷugomukhiādīnaṃ vāditañca tūriyatāḷitavāditanti vā evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

The beaten and the played is 'the beaten-and-played.' The beaten-and-played of musical instruments is 'the musical instruments' beaten-and-played.' And that great beaten-and-played of musical instruments is 'the great beaten-and-played of musical instruments.' Hence it is said, 'with great,' and so on. Alternatively, the beating of musical instruments such as kettledrums, tabors, and small drums, and the playing of lutes, flutes, cow-horn trumpets, and the like is 'the beaten-and-played of musical instruments.' Thus the meaning here should be understood.

Abhiññāpāraṃ gatoti abhiññāpāragū. Evaṃ sesesupi. So hi bhagavā sabbadhamme abhijānanto gatoti abhiññāpāragū. Tesu pañcupādānakkhandhe parijānanto gatoti pariññāpāragū. Sabbakilese pajahanto gatoti pahānapāragū. Cattāro magge bhāvento gatoti bhāvanāpāragū. Nirodhaṃ sacchikaronto gatoti sacchikiriyāpāragū. Sabbasamāpattiṃ samāpajjanto gatoti samāpattipāragū. Subrahmadevaputtādayoti ettha so kira devaputto accharāsaṅghaparivuto nandanakīḷitaṃ katvā pāricchattakamūle paññattāsane nisīdi. Taṃ pañcasatā parivāretvā nisinnā[V 3.0105], pañcasatā rukkhaṃ abhiruhitvā madhurassarena gāyitvā pupphāni pātenti. Tāni gahetvā itarā ekatovaṇṭikamālāva ganthenti. Atha rukkhaṃ abhiruḷhā upacchedakavasena ekappahāreneva kālaṃ katvā avīcimhi nibbattā mahādukkhaṃ anubhavanti. Atha kāle gacchante devaputto “imāsaṃ neva saddo suyyati[M 3.0112], na pupphāni pātenti, kahaṃ nu kho gatā”ti āvajjento niraye nibbattabhāvaṃ disvā piyavatthukasokena ruppamāno cintesi – “etā tāva yathākammena gatā, mayhaṃ āyusaṅkhāro kittako”ti. So “sattame divase mayāpi avasesāhi pañcasatāhi saddhiṃ kālaṃ katvā tattheva nibbattitabba”nti disvā balavatarena sokena samappito. “Imaṃ mayhaṃ sokaṃ sadevake loke aññatra tathāgatā nibbāpetuṃ samattho natthī”ti cintetvā satthu santikaṃ gantvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ ṭhito –

'He has gone to the far shore of direct knowledge' means he is a 'far-shore-goer in direct knowledge' (abhiññāpāragū). The same applies to the rest. Indeed, the Blessed One, having gone by directly knowing all phenomena, is a far-shore-goer in direct knowledge. Having gone by fully understanding the five aggregates of clinging, he is a far-shore-goer in full understanding. Having gone by abandoning all defilements, he is a far-shore-goer in abandoning. Having gone by developing the four paths, he is a far-shore-goer in development. Having gone by realizing cessation, he is a far-shore-goer in realization. Having gone by attaining all meditative attainments, he is a far-shore-goer in attainment. Regarding 'Subrahma, the deva’s son, and others': here, it is said that this deva’s son, surrounded by a company of celestial nymphs, having enjoyed the sport of the Nandana Grove, sat down on a prepared seat at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree. Five hundred nymphs sat surrounding him, while another five hundred climbed the tree, singing in sweet voices and scattering flowers. Gathering these, the others wove them into garlands from a single stalk. Then, those who had climbed the tree, by way of a life-interrupting kamma, died all at once and were reborn in Avīci, where they experienced great suffering. When some time had passed, the deva’s son, reflecting, 'Neither are their voices heard, nor do they scatter flowers—where can they have gone?' saw that they had been reborn in hell. Afflicted with grief for his beloved ones, he thought: 'They have gone according to their kamma. How long is my own life-span?' Seeing that 'On the seventh day, I too, along with the remaining five hundred, must die and be reborn right there,' he was overcome by even stronger sorrow. Thinking, 'In this world with its devas, no one apart from the Tathāgata is capable of extinguishing this sorrow of mine,' he went to the Teacher, paid homage, and stood to one side.

“Niccaṃ utrastamidaṃ cittaṃ, niccaṃ ubbiggamidaṃ mano;

Anuppannesu kicchesu, atho uppatitesu ca;

Sace atthi anutrastaṃ, taṃ me akkhāhi pucchito”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.98) –

'Ever terrified is this mind, ever agitated is this heart; concerning troubles not yet arisen, and also those that have arisen. If there is a state free from terror, that, being asked, please declare to me.'

Imaṃ gāthamabhāsi. Bhagavāpissa –

He spoke this verse. And the Blessed One said to him:

“Nāññatra bojjhā tapasā, nāññatrindriyasaṃvarā;

Nāññatra sabbanissaggā, sotthiṃ passāmi pāṇina”nti. (saṃ. ni. 1.98) –

'Not otherwise than through awakening and austerity, not otherwise than through restraint of the faculties, not otherwise than through the relinquishment of all, do I see safety for living beings.'

Dhammaṃ desesi. So desanāpariyosāne vigatasoko pañcahi accharāsatehi saddhiṃ sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāya bhagavantaṃ namassamāno aṭṭhāsi. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ “dukkhappattā subrahmadevaputtādayo”ti. Ādi-saddena candasūriyadevaputtādayo saṅgaṇhāti. Catūhi kāraṇehīti ārakattā, arīnaṃ arānañca hatattā, paccayādīnaṃ arahattā, pāpakaraṇe rahābhāvāti imehi catūhi kāraṇehi.

He taught the Dhamma. At the end of the teaching, free from sorrow, he stood paying homage to the Blessed One, having been established in the fruit of stream-entry along with five hundred celestial nymphs. With reference to this, it was said: 'The Subrahma devaputtas and others who had experienced suffering.' By the word 'and others,' the Candasuriya devaputtas and others are included. By four reasons—due to being far (from defilements), due to the destruction of enemies and the spokes (of the wheel of existence), due to the worthiness of requisites, and due to the absence of secrecy in doing evil—by these four reasons.

Dasavidhasaṃyojanānīti orambhāgiyuddhambhāgiyabhedato dasavidhasaṃyojanāni. Sabbe accarucīti sabbasatte atikkamitvā pavattaruci. Aṭṭhamakanti sotāpattimaggaṭṭhaṃ sandhāya vadati. Sotāpannoti phalaṭṭho gahito.

The tenfold fetters—the tenfold fetters divided into lower fetters and higher fetters. 'All-surpassing delight' means delight arising having surpassed all beings. 'The eighth' refers to one established in the path of stream-entry. 'A stream-enterer' means one established in the fruit is taken.

Soraccanti [V 3.0106] “tattha katamaṃ soraccaṃ? Yo kāyiko avītikkamo, vācasiko avītikkamo, kāyikavācasiko avītikkamo, idaṃ vuccati soraccaṃ, sabbāpi sīlasaṃvaro soracca”nti (dha. sa. 1349) vacanato sucisīlaṃ “soracca”nti vuttaṃ. Karūṇāti karuṇābrahmavihāramāha. Karuṇāpubbabhāgoti tassa pubbabhāgaṃ upacārajjhānaṃ vadati.

Gentleness—'Here, what is gentleness? Non-transgression by way of body, non-transgression by way of speech, non-transgression by way of body and speech—this is called gentleness; all restraint of virtue is gentleness.' Thus, pure virtue is called 'gentleness.' Compassion—he refers to the Brahma-abiding of compassion. 'With compassion as its preliminary part' refers to its preliminary part, the access jhāna.

Duvidhena [M 3.0113] jhānenāti ārammaṇūpanijjhānalakkhaṇūpanijjhānabhedato duvidhena jhānamanena. Pañcavidhamicchājīvavasenāti kuhanālapanānemittikatānippesikatālābhenalābhaṃnijigīsanatāsaṅkhāta- pañcavidhamicchājīvavasena. Na lippatīti na allīyati anusayato ārammaṇakaraṇato vā taṇhādiṭṭhiabhinivesābhāvato. Sesamettha uttānameva.

'By twofold meditation' means through twofold meditation distinguished as meditation dwelling on the object and meditation dwelling on the characteristic mark. 'By fivefold wrong livelihood' means through fivefold wrong livelihood consisting of scheming, flattery, hinting, disparaging, and the pursuit of gain with gain. 'He does not cling' means he does not adhere through latent tendency or by making it an object, due to the absence of craving, views, or insistence. The rest here is self-evident.

Nāgasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Nāga Sutta is concluded.

2. Migasālāsuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Migasālā Sutta

44. Dutiye samasamagatiyāti ka-kārassa ya-kāravasena niddesoti āha “samabhāveneva samagatikā”ti. Bhavissantīti atītatthe anāgatavacanaṃ katanti āha “bhavissantīti jātā”ti. Purāṇassa hi isidattassa ca samagatikaṃ sandhāya sā evamāha.

44. In the second instance, regarding 'samasamagati,' explaining the 'ka' syllable by means of the 'ya' syllable, he says, 'equal in nature, equal in destiny.' 'Bhavissanti'—using the future tense for the past meaning, he says, '“bhavissanti” means “they were.”' For she spoke thus referring to the equal destiny of Purāṇa and Isidatta.

Ammakāti mātugāmo. Upacāravacanañhetaṃ. Itthīsu yadidaṃ ammakā mātugāmo jananī janikāti. Tenāha “itthī hutvā itthisaññāya eva samannāgatā”ti.

'Ammaka' means 'woman.' This is a term of familiar address. Among women, indeed, 'ammaka' means woman, progenitor, birth-giver. Therefore, it is said, 'Being a woman, possessing the perception of a woman.'

Diṭṭhiyā paṭivijjhitabbaṃ appaṭividdhaṃ hotīti atthato kāraṇato ca paññāya paṭivijjhitabbaṃ appaṭividdhaṃ hoti, nijjaṭaṃ niggumbaṃ katvā yāthāvato aviditaṃ hoti. Samaye samaye kilesehi vimuccanakaṃ pītipāmojjaṃ idha sāmāyikaṃ ma-kāre akārassa dīghaṃ katvā. Tenāha – “sāmāyikampi vimuttiṃ na labhatīti kālānukālaṃ dhammassavanaṃ nissāya pītipāmojjaṃ na labhatī”ti. Pamiṇantīti ettha ārambhattho pa-saddoti āha “tuletuṃ ārabhantī”ti. Paṇītoti visiṭṭho.

That 'what should be penetrated by view remains unpenetrated' means that what should be penetrated by wisdom, in its meaning and its reason, remains unpenetrated; it is not known as it truly is, after making it disentangled and free of thickets. The joy and delight of being liberated from defilements from time to time is here called 'temporary' (sāmāyikaṃ), formed by lengthening the 'a' in the 'ma' syllable. Therefore, it is said: 'One does not attain even temporary liberation,' which means one does not gain joy and delight by relying on the timely hearing of the Dhamma. As for 'pamiṇantīti,' here the prefix 'pa' indicates commencement; thus it is said, 'they begin to weigh.' 'Paṇīta' means distinguished.

Tadantaranti vacanavipallāsena upayogatthe sāmivacanaṃ katanti āha “taṃ antaraṃ taṃ kāraṇa”nti[V 3.0107]. Lobhassa aparāparuppattiyā bahuvacanavasena “lobhadhammā”ti vuttā. Sīlena visesī ahosi methunadhammaviratiyā samannāgatattā.

'Tadantaraṃ' is said through a distortion of language, using the genitive case in the sense of connection; thus it is said, 'that is the interval, that is the cause.' Because of the successive arising of greed, it is spoken of in the plural as 'greed-states.' He was distinguished by virtue, being endowed with abstaining from the sexual act.

Migasālāsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Migasālā Sutta is concluded.

3-6. Iṇasuttādivaṇṇanā

3-6. Commentary on the Debt Discourse and Others

45-48. Tatiye [M 3.0114] daliddo nāma duggato, tassa bhāvo dāliddiyaṃ. Na etassa sakaṃ sāpateyyanti assako, asāpateyyo. Tenāha “attano santakena rahito”ti. “Buddho dhammo saṅgho”ti vutte “sammāsambuddho bhagavā, svākkhāto dhammo, suppaṭipanno saṅgho”ti kenaci akampiyabhāvena okappanaṃ ratanattayaguṇe ogāhetvā kappanaṃ okappanasaddhā nāma. “Idaṃ akusalaṃ kammaṃ no sakaṃ, idaṃ pana kammaṃ saka”nti evaṃ byatirekato anvayato ca kammassakatajānanapaññā kammassakatapaññā. Tividhañhi duccaritaṃ attanā katampi sakakammaṃ nāma na hoti atthabhañjanato. Sucaritaṃ sakakammaṃ nāma atthajananato. Iṇādānasminti paccattavacanatthe etaṃ bhummanti āha “iṇaggahaṇaṃ vadāmī”ti.

In the third instance, 'daliddo' means 'destitute,' and his state is 'poverty.' He does not own any property—he is without property, devoid of ownership. Hence it is said, 'bereft of his own possessions.' When 'Buddha, Dhamma, Sangha' is spoken of, the firm establishment, by someone with an unshakable nature, having plunged into the qualities of the Triple Gem—that the Blessed One is perfectly self-enlightened, the Dhamma is well-expounded, the Sangha is practicing rightly—is called 'okappanasaddhā' (conviction-faith). The wisdom of knowing ownership of actions—discriminating and understanding, 'This unwholesome action is not my own, but this wholesome action is my own'—is called 'kammassakatapaññā' (wisdom of ownership of actions). For unwholesome conduct, though done by oneself, is not called one's own action because it is destructive of benefit. Wholesome conduct is called one's own action because it generates benefit. Regarding 'iṇādānasminti,' taking the sense of the individual speaking, it is included in the locative case; hence it is said, 'I speak of debt-taking.'

Kaṭaggāhoti kataṃ sabbaso siddhameva katvā gahaṇaṃ. So pana vijayalābho hotīti āha “jayaggāho”ti. Hirimano etassāti hirimanoti āha “hirisampayuttacitto”ti, pāpajigucchanalakkhaṇāya hiriyā sampayuttacittoti attho. Ottappati ubbijjati bhāyati sīlenāti ottappī, ottappena samannāgato. Nirāmisaṃ sukhanti tatiyajjhānasukhaṃ dūrasamussāritakāmāmisattā. Upekkhanti catutthajjhānupekkhaṃ, na yaṃ kiñci upekkhāvedananti āha “catutthajjhānupekkha”nti. Āraddhavīriyoti paggahitaparipuṇṇakāyikacetasikavīriyoti attho. Yo gaṇasaṅgaṇikaṃ vinodetvā catūsu iriyāpathesu aṭṭhaārambhavatthuvasena ekako hoti, tassa kāyikaṃ vīriyaṃ āraddhaṃ nāma hoti. Cittasaṅgaṇikaṃ vinodetvā aṭṭhasamāpattivasena ekako hoti. Gamane uppannakilesassa ṭhānaṃ pāpuṇituṃ na deti, ṭhāne uppannakilesassa nisajjaṃ, nisajjāya uppannakilesassa sayanaṃ pāpuṇituṃ na deti, uppannaṭṭhāneyeva kilese niggaṇhāti. Ayaṃ cetasikaṃ vīriyaṃ āraddhaṃ nāma hoti. Paṭipakkhadūrībhāvena seṭṭhaṭṭhena ca eko udetīti ekodi, ekaggatā. Tassa yogato ekaggacitto idha ekodi. Paṭipakkhato attānaṃ nipāti, taṃ vā nipayati visosetīti nipako. Aññataraṃ kāyādibhedaṃ ārammaṇaṃ sātisayāya satiyā saratīti sato. Tenāha “ekaggacitto”tiādi.

'Kaṭaggāho' means taking what has been fully accomplished as accomplished. That is called 'jayaggāho' because it is the attainment of victory. 'Hirimanoti' means 'endowed with a mind associated with shame,' that is, a mind connected with shame, which has the characteristic of disgust toward evil. 'Ottappī' means one who is fearful, anxious, and afraid of wrongdoing—endowed with moral dread. 'Nirāmisaṃ sukhaṃ' refers to the happiness of the third jhāna, because it is far removed from sensual pleasures. 'Upekkhā' is the equanimity of the fourth jhāna—not just any neutral feeling—hence it is called 'the equanimity of the fourth jhāna.' 'Āraddhavīriyo' means one whose bodily and mental energy is fully exerted. For one who, having abandoned group activities, remains alone in the four postures based on the eight grounds of exertion, their bodily energy is called 'exerted.' For one who, having abandoned mental distractions, remains alone in the eight attainments, not allowing arisen defilements to reach a standing position while walking, a sitting position while standing, or a lying position while sitting—but restraining the defilements right where they arise—their mental energy is called 'exerted.' 'Ekodi' means 'solitary' because it arises alone, being supreme in distancing from opposition and being excellent. From this practice, one becomes 'ekaggacitto'—unified in mind. 'Nipako' means one who wards off opposition, or dissolves it. 'Sato' means one who recollects any object—such as the body—with abundant mindfulness. Hence it is said: 'ekaggacitto,' etc.

Akuppā [V 3.0108] me vimuttīti mayhaṃ arahattaphalavimutti akuppatāya akuppārammaṇatāya ca akuppā. Sā hi rāgādīhi na kuppatīti akuppatāyapi akuppā[M 3.0115]. Akuppaṃ nibbānamassā ārammaṇanti akuppārammaṇatāyapi akuppā. Tenevāha “akuppārammaṇattā”tiādi. Bhavasaṃyojanānanti kāmarāgapaṭighamānadiṭṭhivicikicchāsīlabbataparāmāsabhavarāgaissāmacchariya- avijjāsaṅkhātānaṃ dasannaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ. Imāni hi satte bhavesu saṃyojenti upanibandhanti bhavābhavena saṃyojenti, tasmā bhavasaṃyojanānīti vuccanti. Khīṇāsavo uttamaaṇaṇo kilesaiṇānaṃ abhāvato. Aññe hi sattā yāva na kilesā pahīyanti, tāva saiṇā nāma aserivihārabhāvato. Catutthādīni uttānatthāni.

'My liberation is unshakeable'—this refers to my liberation through the fruit of arahantship, which is unshakeable because of its unshakeable nature and because its object is unshakeable. For it is not shaken by lust and the like, thus it is unshakeable in its nature. And because its object is the unshakeable Nibbāna, it is unshakeable because its object is unshakeable. Hence it is said, 'because its object is unshakeable,' and so on. 'The fetters of existence'—these are the ten fetters: sensual desire, ill will, conceit, wrong view, doubt, attachment to rites and rituals, craving for existence, envy, stinginess, and ignorance. These bind beings to existences, tethering them to repeated becoming, thus they are called the fetters of existence. 'One whose taints are destroyed, the supreme debt-free one,' because of the absence of the debts of defilements. Other beings, as long as their defilements are not abandoned, are called 'indebted' because they lack the state of freedom. The remaining terms (from the fourth onward) are clear in meaning.

Iṇasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Iṇasutta and similar suttas is concluded.

7. Khemasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Explanation of the Khema Sutta

49. Sattame vutthabrahmacariyavāsoti nivutthabrahmacariyavāso. Katakaraṇīyoti ettha karaṇīyanti pariññāpahānabhāvanāsacchikiriyamāha. Taṃ pana yasmā catūhi maggehi paccekaṃ catūsu saccesu kattabbattā soḷasavidhaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tenāha “catūhi maggehi kattabba”nti. Khandhakilesaabhisaṅkhārasaṅkhātā tayo osīdāpanaṭṭhena bhārā viyāti bhārā. Te ohitā oropitā nikkhittā pātitā etenāti ohitabhāro. Tenāha “khandhabhāraṃ…pe… otāretvā ṭhito”ti. Anuppatto sadatthanti anuppattasadattho. Sadatthoti ca sakatthamāha ka-kārassa da-kāraṃ katvā. Ettha hi arahattaṃ attano yonisomanasikārāyattattā attūpanibandhaṭṭhena sasantānapariyāpannattā attānaṃ avijahanaṭṭhena attano uttamatthena ca attano atthattā “sakattho”ti vuccati. Tenāha “sadattho vuccati arahatta”nti. Sammadaññā vimuttoti sammā aññāya vimutto, acchinnabhūtāya maggapaññāya sammā yathābhūtaṃ dukkhādīsu yo yathā jānitabbo, tathā jānitvā vimuttoti attho. Tenāha “sammā hetunā”tiādi. Vimuttoti ca dve vimuttiyo sabbassa cittasaṃkilesassa maggo nibbānādhimutti ca. Nibbāne adhimuccanaṃ tattha ninnapoṇapabbhāratāya. Arahā sabbakilesehi vimuttacittattā cittavimuttiyā vimutto. Nibbānaṃ adhimuttattā nibbāne vimutto. Sesamettha uttānameva.

49. In the seventh sutta, 'vutthabrahmacariyavāso' means 'nivutthabrahmacariyavāso,' one who has lived the holy life. Here, 'katakaraṇīya' refers to what must be done, namely, full understanding, abandoning, developing, and realizing. Since this must be done by each of the four paths in relation to the four truths, it should be understood as sixteenfold. Hence it is said, 'to be done by the four paths.' The three burdens, known as the aggregates, defilements, and formations, are called burdens because they cause sinking. They are laid down, cast off, removed, and discarded by him—thus, 'one who has laid down the burden.' Hence it is said, 'having laid down the burden of the aggregates... and stands having cast it off.' 'Anuppatto sadatthanti' means 'anuppattasadattho,' one who has attained one's own welfare. And 'sadattho' means 'sakattho,' changing the 'ka' syllable to 'da.' Here, arahantship is called 'one's own welfare' because it depends on one's own wise attention, is connected to oneself by being included in one's own continuum, does not abandon oneself, is the highest for oneself, and is one's own welfare. Hence it is said, ''one's own welfare' is called arahantship.' 'Sammadaññā vimuttoti' means 'sammā aññāya vimutto,' liberated by right understanding—liberated by rightly understanding, with the unbroken wisdom of the path, what should be known as it truly is regarding suffering and so forth. Hence it is said, 'rightly by reason,' etc. And 'vimutto' refers to two kinds of liberation: the path from all mental defilements, and inclination towards Nibbāna. Inclination towards Nibbāna is being inclined and directed toward it. The arahant is liberated by liberation of mind because the mind is freed from all defilements, and is liberated in Nibbāna due to being inclined toward it. The rest here is clear.

Khemasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Khemasutta Commentary is concluded.

8. Indriyasaṃvarasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Indriyasaṃvarasutta

50. Aṭṭhame [V 3.0109][M 3.0116] upanisīdati phalaṃ etthāti kāraṇaṃ upanisā. Yathābhūtañāṇadassananti yathāsabhāvajānanasaṅkhātaṃ dassanaṃ. Etena taruṇavipassanaṃ dasseti. Taruṇavipassanā hi balavavipassanāya paccayo hoti. Taruṇavipassanāti nāmarūpapariggahe ñāṇaṃ, paccayapariggahe ñāṇaṃ, sammasane ñāṇaṃ, maggāmagge vavatthapetvā ṭhitañāṇanti catunnaṃ ñāṇānaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Nibbindati etāyāti nibbidā. Balavavipassanāti bhayatupaṭṭhāne ñāṇaṃ ādīnavānupassane ñāṇaṃ muccitukamyatāñāṇaṃ saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇanti catunnaṃ ñāṇānaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Paṭisaṅkhānupassanā pana muccitukamyatāpakkhikā eva. “Yāva maggāmaggañāṇadassanavisuddhi, tāva taruṇavipassanā”ti hi vacanato upakkilesavimuttaudayabbayañāṇato balavavipassanā. Virajjati ariyo saṅkhārato etenāti virāgo, ariyamaggo. Arahattaphalanti ukkaṭṭhaniddesato vuttaṃ. Indriyasaṃvarassa sīlarakkhaṇahetuttā vuttaṃ “sīlānurakkhaṇaindriyasaṃvaro kathito”ti.

50. In the eighth sutta, 'upanisā' is the cause, meaning 'that by which the fruit is approached.' 'Knowledge and vision of things as they really are' refers to seeing characterized by knowing according to their own nature. This indicates preliminary insight. For preliminary insight serves as a condition for strong insight. 'Preliminary insight' (taruṇavipassanā) is a term for four kinds of knowledge: knowledge of the discernment of name and form, knowledge of the discernment of conditions, knowledge of comprehension, and knowledge that remains after distinguishing the path and the non-path. One becomes disenchanted through this—thus, disenchantment (nibbidā). 'Strong insight' (balavavipassanā) is a term for four kinds of knowledge: knowledge of the appearance of danger, knowledge of contemplation of drawbacks, knowledge of the desire for deliverance, and knowledge of equanimity toward formations. However, contemplation of re-observation belongs only to the side of the desire for deliverance. For it is said, 'As long as there is purification of knowledge and vision of the path and non-path, so long is it preliminary insight.' Strong insight begins from the knowledge of arising and passing away, free from corruptions. The noble one becomes dispassionate toward formations through this—thus, dispassion (virāgo), the noble path. 'The fruit of arahantship' is stated by way of the highest description. The guarding of the senses is mentioned as the cause for protecting virtue, hence it is said, 'The guarding of the senses is taught as the protection of virtue.'

Indriyasaṃvarasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Indriyasaṃvarasutta Commentary is concluded.

9. Ānandasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Ānanda Sutta

51. Navame therā bhikkhū viharanti bahussutā āgatāgamātiādipāḷipadesu imināva nayena attho daṭṭhabbo – sīlādiguṇānaṃ thirabhāvappattiyā therā. Suttageyyādi bahu sutaṃ etesanti bahussutā. Vācuggatadhāraṇena sammadeva garūnaṃ santike āgamitabhāvena āgato pariyattidhammasaṅkhāto āgamo etesanti āgatāgamā. Suttātidhammasaṅkhātassa dhammassa dhāraṇena dhammadharā. Vinayadhāraṇena vinayadharā. Tesaṃyeva dhammavinayānaṃ mātikāya dhāraṇena mātikādharā. Tattha tattha dhammaparipucchāya paripucchati. Taṃ atthaparipucchāya paripañhati vīmaṃsati vicāreti. Idaṃ, bhante, kathaṃ, imassa kvatthoti paripucchanapañhanākāradassanaṃ. Āvivaṭañceva pāḷiyā atthaṃ padesantarapāḷidassanena āgamato vivaranti. Anuttānīkatañca yuttivibhāvanena uttānīkaronti. Kaṅkhāṭṭhāniyesu dhammesu saṃsayuppattiyā [M 3.0117] hetuyā gaṇṭhiṭṭhānabhūtesu pāḷipadesu yāthāvato vinicchayadānena kaṅkhaṃ paṭivinodenti.

51. In the ninth sutta, the meaning in passages such as 'the elder monks dwell as learned, bearers of the tradition,' etc., should be understood in this way: 'elders' (therā) due to the firm attainment of virtues such as morality. They are 'learned' (bahussutā) because they have heard much, such as the Suttas and Geyya. 'Bearers of the tradition' (āgatāgamā) because they have properly received the teaching-tradition, known as the tradition, from their teachers through vocal recitation and retention. They are 'bearers of the Dhamma' (dhammadharā) by retaining the Dhamma, which includes the Suttas and the Abhidhamma. They are 'bearers of the Vinaya' (vinayadharā) by retaining the Vinaya. They are 'bearers of the matrices' (mātikādharā) by retaining the mātikā of these very Dhamma and Vinaya. They inquire about the Dhamma here and there. They examine, investigate, and reflect on it through questioning about the meaning. This is how they see the manner of questioning and answering: 'Venerable sir, how is this? What is the meaning of this?' They 'open up what is unopened' by revealing the meaning of the text through seeing other passages in other parts of the scriptures. They 'make clear what is unclear' by clarifying with reasoning. In scriptural passages that are knots of uncertainty due to the arising of doubt in matters where doubt can arise, they dispel uncertainty by giving a decisive judgment.

Ānandasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Ānandasutta Commentary is concluded.

10. Khattiyasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Khattiya Sutta

52. Dasame [V 3.0110] bhoge adhippāyo etesanti bhogādhippāyā. Paññatthāya etesaṃ mano upavicaratīti paññūpavicārā. Pathaviyā dāyatthāya vā cittaṃ abhiniveso etesanti pathavībhinivesā. Mantā adhiṭṭhānaṃ patiṭṭhā etesanti mantādhiṭṭhānā. Iminā nayena sesapadānipi veditabbāni. Sesaṃ uttānameva.

52. In the tenth sutta, their intention is for possessions, thus they are 'possession-intentioned.' Their mind ranges for the sake of wisdom, thus they are 'wisdom-ranging.' Their mind is intent on the inheritance of the earth, thus they are 'earth-intent.' Mantras are their determination and foundation, thus they are 'mantra-determined.' The remaining terms should be understood in this manner. The rest is clear.

Khattiyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Khattiyasutta Commentary is concluded.

11. Appamādasuttavaṇṇanā

11. Commentary on the Appamāda Sutta

53. Ekādasame jaṅgalānanti ettha yo nipicchalo na anūpo nirudakatāya thaddhalūkho bhūmippadeso, so “jaṅgalo”ti vuccati. Tabbahulatāya pana idha sabbo bhūmippadeso jaṅgalo. Tasmiṃ jaṅgale jātā bhavāti vā jaṅgalā, tesaṃ jaṅgalānaṃ. Evañhi nadicarānampi hatthīnaṃ saṅgaho kato hoti samodhātabbānaṃ viya samodhāyakānampi idha jaṅgalaggahaṇena gahetabbato. Pathavītalacārīnanti iminā jalacārino ca nivatteti adissamānapādattā. “Pāṇāna”nti sādhāraṇavacanampi “padajātānī”ti saddantarasannidhānena visesaniviṭṭhameva hotīti āha “sapādakapāṇāna”nti. “Muttagata”ntiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.119; a. ni. 9.11) gata-saddo viya idha jāta-saddo anatthantaroti āha “padajātānīti padānī”ti. Samodhānanti samavarodhaṃ, antogadhaṃ vā. Tenāha “odhānaṃ upanikkhepaṃ gacchantī”ti. Kūṭaṅgamāti pārimantena kūṭaṃ upagacchanti. Kūṭaninnāti kūṭacchiddamagge pavisanavasena kūṭe ninnā. Kūṭasamosaraṇāti chidde anupavisanavasena ca āhacca avatthānena ca kūṭe samodahitvā ṭhitā. Vaṇṭe [M 3.0118] patamāne sabbāni bhūmiyaṃ patantīti āha “vaṇṭānuvattakāni bhavantī”ti.

53. In the eleventh sutta, regarding 'jaṅgalānaṃ' (of the wilderness-dwellers): here, any terrain that is not slippery, not marshy, and is dry, hard, and rough due to lack of water is called 'jaṅgala' (wilderness). But here, due to the abundance of such terrain, the entire area is 'jaṅgala.' Those born or existing in that wilderness are 'jaṅgalā' (wilderness-dwellers); 'tesaṃ jaṅgalānaṃ' means 'of the wilderness-dwellers.' Thus, even elephants living along rivers are included, as those who are to be gathered, as well as those who gather them, are to be included here by the term 'jaṅgala-dwelling.' Regarding 'pathavītalacārīnaṃ' (ground-walkers): by this, water-dwellers are excluded, as their feet are unseen.
