Though 'pāṇānaṃ' (beings) is a general term, with the proximity of the word 'padajātāni' (footed beings), it becomes specifically qualified; hence it is said, 'sapādakapāṇānaṃ' (beings with feet). Just as the word 'gata' (gone) in 'muttagata' (gone free), etc., the word 'jāta' (born) here makes no difference in meaning; hence it is said, ''padajātāni' means 'padāni'' (footprints). 'Samodhānaṃ' means crowding together, or being contained within. Hence it is said, 'they go to the place of depositing, the trap.' 'Kūṭaṅgamā' (approaching the peak) means they approach the peak entirely. 'Kūṭaninnā' (sloping towards the peak) means they are sloping towards the peak by entering through the hole leading to the peak. 'Kūṭasamosaraṇā' (assembling at the peak) means they stand assembled at the peak without entering the hole, remaining by striking against it. Regarding 'vaṇṭe patamāne sabbāni bhūmiyaṃ patanti' (when the stalk falls, all fall to the ground), it is said, 'they become followers of the stalk.'

Appamādasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Appamādasutta Commentary is concluded.

12. Dhammikasuttavaṇṇanā

12. Commentary on the Dhammika Sutta

54. Dvādasame jātibhūmiyanti ettha jananaṃ jāti, jātiyā bhūmi jātibhūmi, jātaṭṭhānaṃ. Taṃ kho panetaṃ neva kosalamahārājādīnaṃ, na caṅkibrāhmaṇādīnaṃ, na sakkasuyāmasantusitādīnaṃ[V 3.0111], na asītimahāsāvakānaṃ, na aññesaṃ sattānaṃ “jātibhūmī”ti vuccati. Yassa pana jātadivase dasasahassī lokadhātu ekaddhajamālāvippakiṇṇakusumavāsacuṇṇagaṇasugandhā sabbapāliphullamiva nandanavanaṃ virocamānā paduminipaṇṇe udakabindu viya akampittha, jaccandhādīnañca rūpadassanādīni anekāni pāṭihāriyāni pavattiṃsu. Tassa sabbaññubodhisattassa jātaṭṭhānaṃ, sātisayassa pana janakakapilavatthusannissayo “jātibhūmī”ti vuccati. Jātibhūmakā upāsakāti jātibhūmivāsino upāsakā. Santanetvā sabbaso tanetvā pattharitvā ṭhitamūlāni mūlasantānakāni. Tāni pana atthato mūlāniyevāti āha “mūlasantānakānanti mūlāna”nti.

54. In the twelfth, regarding 'jātibhūmiyaṃ': here, 'jāti' is birth; the ground of birth is 'jātibhūmi', the place of birth. However, this is not called the 'birthplace' of King Kosala and others, nor of the brahmin Caṅkī and others, nor of Sakka, Suyāma, Santusita, and others, nor of the eighty great disciples, nor of other beings. But on the day of his birth, the ten-thousandfold world-system trembled like a drop of water on a lotus leaf, shining like the Nandana grove in full bloom, fragrant with masses of scattered flags, garlands, flowers, and scented powders; and many miracles occurred, such as the congenitally blind seeing forms. The place of birth of that All-Knowing Bodhisatta, the exceedingly distinguished one, near Kapilavatthu, the city of his father, is called the 'birthplace'. 'Jātibhūmakā upāsakā' means lay devotees dwelling in the birthplace. `Mūlasantānakāni` are the continuations of the roots, established after having been thoroughly extended and spread out. These, however, in meaning are simply the roots; thus it is said, '`mūlasantānakānanti mūlānaṃ`' (the continuations of the roots means the roots).

Jātadivase āvudhānaṃ jotitattā, rañño aparimitassa ca sattakāyassa anatthato paripālanasamatthatāya ca “jotipālo”ti laddhanāmattā vuttaṃ “nāmena jotipālo”ti. Govindoti govindiyābhisekena abhisitto, govindassa ṭhāne ṭhapanābhisekena abhisittoti attho. Taṃ kira tassa brāhmaṇassa kulaparamparāgataṃ ṭhānantaraṃ. Tenāha “ṭhānena mahāgovindo”ti. Gavaṃ paññañca vindati paṭilabhatīti govindo, mahanto govindoti mahāgovindo. Goti hi paññāyetaṃ adhivacanaṃ “gacchati atthe bujjhatī”ti katvā. Mahāgovindo ca amhākaṃ bodhisattoyeva. So kira disampatissa nāma rañño purohitassa govindabrāhmaṇassa putto hutvā attano pitussa ca rañño ca accayena tassa putto reṇu, sahāyā [M 3.0119] cassa sattabhū, brahmadatto, vessabhū, bharato, dve dhataraṭṭhāti ime satta rājāno yathā aññamaññaṃ na vivadanti. Evaṃ rajje patiṭṭhāpetvā tesaṃ atthadhamme anusāsante jambudīpatale sabbesaṃ rājāva raññaṃ, brahmāva brāhmaṇānaṃ, devova gahapatikānaṃ sakkato garukato mānito pūjito apacito uttamagāravaṭṭhānaṃ ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ “reṇuādīnaṃ sattannaṃ rājūnaṃ purohito”ti. Imeva satta bhāradhārā mahārājāno. Vuttañhetaṃ –

On his birthday, because weapons were illuminated, and because he was capable of protecting the immeasurable multitude of beings from harm, he was given the name 'Jotipāla'. Hence it is said, 'by name, Jotipāla'. 'Govinda' means he was anointed with the Govinda consecration; that is, he was consecrated to the position of Govinda. It is said that this was a hereditary position in that brahmin's family. Therefore, it is stated, 'by position, Mahāgovinda'. 'Govinda' means one who finds and acquires `go` (which is knowledge). 'Mahāgovinda' means the great Govinda. For 'go' is indeed a term for knowledge, derived from 'gacchati' (to go) in the sense of comprehending meaning. And our Mahāgovinda was the Bodhisatta himself. It is said that he was the son of Govinda the brahmin, the chaplain of King Disampati. After the passing of both his father and the king, the king's son Reṇu, and his friends—Sattabhū, Brahmadatta, Vessabhū, Bharata, and the two Dhataraṭṭhas—these seven became kings in such a way that they did not quarrel among themselves. Having established them in kingship and advising them in matters of benefit and righteousness, he was revered by all in Jambudīpa as the king of kings, the Brahmā of brahmins, and the deity of householders—honored, respected, esteemed, worshipped, and venerated, occupying the highest position of reverence. Therefore, it is said, 'the chaplain of the seven kings beginning with Reṇu'. These seven great kings were the Bhāradhārās. For it is said—

“Sattabhū brahmadatto ca, vessabhū bharato saha;

Reṇu dve ca dhataraṭṭhā, tadāsuṃ satta bhāradhā”ti. (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.308);

“Sattabhū, Brahmadatta, and Vessabhū, together with Bharata; Reṇu and the two Dhataraṭṭhas: these were the seven Bhāradhās.” (Dīgha Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā 2.308)

Rañño diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikatthānaṃ puro vidhānato pure saṃvidhānato purohito. Kodhāmagandhenāti kodhasaṅkhātena pūtigandhena. Karuṇā assa atthīti karuṇanti sapubbabhāgakaruṇajjhānaṃ vuttanti āha “karuṇāya ca karuṇāpubbabhāge ca ṭhitā”ti. Yakāro sandhivasena āgatoti āha “yeteti ete”ti. Arahattato paṭṭhāya sattamoti sakadāgāmī. Sakadāgāmiṃ [V 3.0112] upādāyāti sakadāgāmibhāvaṃ paṭicca. Sakadāgāmissa hi pañcindriyāni sakadāgāmibhāvaṃ paṭicca mudūni nāma honti. Sesamettha suviññeyyameva.

Because he arranges (`vidhānato`) and plans (`saṃvidhānato`) beforehand (`puro`, `pure`) the king's welfare in this life and the next, he is a 'purohita' (chaplain). 'Kodhāmagandhena' (by the stench of anger) means by the foul odor known as anger. 'Karuṇā assa atthīti karuṇā' (he has compassion, thus he is compassionate) refers to the compassion-jhāna with its preliminary stages; thus it is said, 'established in compassion and in the preliminary stages of compassion'. The letter 'ya' comes for the sake of euphonic combination; thus it is said, '`yeteti` means `ete`'. 'Arahattato paṭṭhāya sattamo' (the seventh counting from arahantship) refers to a once-returner. 'Sakadāgāmiṃ upādāya' (with reference to the once-returner) means on account of the state of a once-returner. For, on account of the state of a once-returner, the five faculties of a once-returner are called 'mild' (`mudūni`). The rest here is easily understood.

Dhammikasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Dhammika Sutta is concluded.

Dhammikavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Dhammika Vagga is concluded.

Paṭhamapaṇṇāsakaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The First Fifty is concluded.

2. Dutiyapaṇṇāsakaṃ

2. The Second Fifty

6. Mahāvaggo

6. The Great Chapter

1. Soṇasuttavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Soṇa Sutta

55. Chaṭṭhassa [V 3.0113][M 3.0120] paṭhame nisīdi bhagavā paññatte āsaneti ettha kiṃ taṃ āsanaṃ paṭhamameva paññattaṃ, udāhu bhagavantaṃ disvā paññattanti ce? Bhagavato dharamānakāle padhānikabhikkhūnaṃ vattametaṃ, yadidaṃ attano vasanaṭṭhāne buddhāsanaṃ paññapetvāva nisīdananti dassento āha “padhānikabhikkhū”tiādi. Buddhakāle kira yattha yattha ekopi bhikkhu viharati, sabbattha buddhāsanaṃ paññattameva hoti. Kasmā? Bhagavā hi attano santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā phāsukaṭṭhāne viharante manasi karoti – “asuko mayhaṃ santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā gato, asakkhi nu kho visesaṃ nibbattetuṃ, no”ti. Atha naṃ passati kammaṭṭhānaṃ vissajjetvā akusalavitakkaṃ vitakkayamānaṃ, tato “kathañhi nāma mādisassa satthu santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā viharantaṃ imaṃ kulaputtaṃ akusalavitakkā adhibhavitvā anamatagge vaṭṭadukkhe saṃsāressantī”ti tassa anuggahatthaṃ tattheva attānaṃ dassetvā taṃ kulaputtaṃ ovaditvā ākāsaṃ uppatitvā puna attano vasanaṭṭhānameva gacchati. Athevaṃ ovadiyamānā te bhikkhū cintayiṃsu “satthā amhākaṃ manaṃ jānitvā āgantvā amhākaṃ samīpe ṭhitaṃyeva attānaṃ dasseti. Tasmiṃ khaṇe, ‘bhante, idha nisīdatha nisīdathā’ti āsanapariyesanaṃ nāma bhāro”ti. Te āsanaṃ paññapetvāva viharanti. Yassa pīṭhaṃ atthi, so taṃ paññapeti. Yassa natthi, so mañcaṃ vā phalakaṃ vā pāsāṇaṃ vā vālikāpuñjaṃ vā paññapeti. Taṃ alabhamānā purāṇapaṇṇānipi saṃkaḍḍhitvā tattha paṃsukūlaṃ pattharitvā ṭhapenti.

55. Regarding the first words of the sixth sutta, 'The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat': here, was that seat prepared beforehand, or was it prepared upon seeing the Blessed One? To show that during the Blessed One’s lifetime it was the custom of diligent monks to prepare a Buddha-seat in their own dwelling place before sitting down, it is said, 'diligent monks,' etc. In the Buddha's time, it is said, wherever even a single monk was dwelling, a Buddha-seat was always prepared. Why? Because the Blessed One would direct his mind towards those who, having taken a meditation subject from him, were dwelling in a suitable place, thinking: 'So-and-so took a meditation subject from me and left; has he been able to bring about a special attainment, or not?' Then, if he saw that monk had abandoned the meditation subject and was thinking unwholesome thoughts, he would think: 'How can it be that unwholesome thoughts should overpower this clansman, who is dwelling after having taken a meditation subject from a teacher like me, and cause him to transmigrate in the beginningless round of suffering?' For his benefit, the Blessed One would manifest himself right there, advise that clansman, and then rise into the sky and return to his own dwelling place. Being advised in this way, those monks reflected: 'The Teacher, knowing our minds, comes and manifests himself, standing right beside us. At that moment, searching for a seat, thinking, “Venerable sir, please sit here, sit here,” is a burden.' Thus, they would dwell only after preparing a seat. Whoever had a stool would prepare that. Whoever did not would prepare a cot, a plank, a stone, or a pile of sand. If they could not get those, they would gather old leaves, spread a rag from a dust-heap over them, and set it in place.

Satta sarāti – chajjo, usabho, gandhāro, majjhimo, pañcamo, dhevato, nisādoti ete satta sarā. Tayo gāmāti – chajjagāmo, majjhimagāmo, sādhāraṇagāmoti tayo gāmā, samūhāti attho. Manussaloke vīṇāvādanā ekekassa sarassa vasena tayo tayo mucchanāti katvā ekavīsati mucchanā. Devaloke vīṇāvādanā pana samapaññāsa mucchanāti vadanti. Tattha hi [V 3.0114] ekekassa sarassa vasena satta [M 3.0121] satta mucchanā, antarassa sarassa ca ekāti samapaññāsa mucchanā. Teneva sakkapañhasuttasaṃvaṇṇanāyaṃ (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.345) “samapaññāsa mucchanā mucchetvā”ti pañcasikhassa vīṇāvādanaṃ dassentena vuttaṃ. Ṭhānā ekūnapaññāsāti ekekasseva sarassa satta satta ṭhānabhedā, yato sarassa maṇḍalatāvavatthānaṃ hoti. Ekūnapaññāsaṭṭhānaviseso tisso duve catasso catasso tisso duve catassoti dvāvīsati sutibhedā ca icchitā.

Seven notes (`sarā`): Chajja, Usabha, Gandhāra, Majjhima, Pañcama, Dhevata, and Nisāda—these are the seven notes. Three scales (`gāmā`): Chajjagāma, Majjhimagāma, and Sādhāraṇagāma—these are the three scales, meaning groups. In the human world, when playing the lute, there are three modulations (`mucchanā`) for each note, making twenty-one modulations. In the celestial world, however, they say there are fifty modulations when playing the lute. There, for each note, there are seven modulations, plus one for the intermediate (`antara`) note, making fifty modulations. Thus, in the commentary on the Sakkapañha Sutta, it is said, 'having modulated fifty `mucchanā`,' when describing Pañcasikha’s lute-playing. There are forty-nine positions (`ṭhānā`): for each note, there are seven distinct positions, from which the range of the note is established. The forty-nine distinct positions are accepted, and also the twenty-two divisions of microtonal intervals (`suti`), which are distributed as three, two, four, four, three, two, and four.

Atigāḷhaṃ āraddhanti thinamiddhachambhitattānaṃ vūpasamatthaṃ ativiya āraddhaṃ. Sabbattha niyuttā sabbatthikā. Sabbena vā līnuddhaccapakkhiyena atthetabbā sabbatthikā. Samathoyeva samathanimittaṃ. Evaṃ sesesupi. Khayā rāgassa vītarāgattāti ettha yasmā bāhirako kāmesu vītarāgo na khayā rāgassa vītarāgo sabbaso avippahīnarāgattā. Vikkhambhitarāgo hi so. Arahā pana khayā eva, tasmā vuttaṃ “khayā rāgassa vītarāgattā”ti. Esa nayo dosamohesupi.

Regarding 'they exert excessively': this means it is exerted too intensely for the pacification of sloth, torpor, and consternation. 'Sabbatthikā' means 'applied everywhere'. Or, they are 'sabbatthikā' because they are to be understood in every way, without inclining towards sluggishness and restlessness. 'Samathoyeva' (calmness itself) means 'samathanimittaṃ' (the sign of calmness). The same applies to the rest. Regarding 'Through the destruction of lust, one is free from lust': here, because an outsider is free from lust regarding sense pleasures, he is not free 'through the destruction of lust,' since his lust is not entirely abandoned. For he has only suppressed lust. But an arahant is free through destruction; therefore, it is said, 'Through the destruction of lust, one is free from lust.' The same principle applies to hatred and delusion.

Lābhasakkārasilokaṃ nikāmayamānoti ettha labbhati pāpuṇīyatīti lābho, catunnaṃ paccayānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Sakkaccaṃ kātabboti sakkāro. Paccayā eva hi paṇītapaṇītā sundarasundarā abhisaṅkharitvā katā “sakkāro”ti vuccati, yā ca parehi attano gāravakiriyā, pupphādīhi vā pūjā. Silokoti vaṇṇabhaṇanaṃ. Taṃ lābhañca, sakkārañca, silokañca, nikāmayamāno, pavattayamānoti attho. Tenevāha “catupaccayalābhañca…pe… patthayamāno”ti.

Here, 'lābhasakkārasilokaṃ nikāmayamānoti' means desiring gain, honor, and praise. 'Lābho' refers to what is obtained or acquired; it is a term for the four requisites. 'Sakkāro' means doing something carefully. Indeed, requisites that are prepared with great effort—the finest and most beautiful—are called 'sakkāro.' It also includes the respect shown by others or offerings such as flowers. 'Siloko' means the utterance of praise. Thus, 'nikāmayamāno' means desiring and pursuing gain, honor, and praise. Therefore, it is said: 'desiring the gain of the four requisites...pe... aspiring for it.'

Thūṇanti pasūnaṃ bandhanatthāya nikhātatthambhasaṅkhātaṃ thūṇaṃ. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

Regarding 'thūṇaṃ' (post): this refers to a post, that is, a pillar dug into the ground for the purpose of tethering animals. The rest is easily understood.

Soṇasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Soṇa Sutta is concluded.

2. Phaggunasuttavaṇṇanā

2. The commentary on the Phagguna Sutta

56. Dutiye samadhosīti samantato adhosi. Sabbabhāgena pariphandanacalanākārena apacitiṃ dasseti. Vattaṃ kiretaṃ bāḷhagilānenapi vuḍḍhataraṃ [M 3.0122] disvā uṭṭhitākārena apaciti dassetabbā. Tena pana “mā cali mā calī”ti vattabbo, taṃ pana calanaṃ uṭṭhānākāradassanaṃ hotīti [V 3.0115] āha “uṭṭhānākāraṃ dassetī”ti. Santimāni āsanānīti paṭhamameva paññatthāsanaṃ sandhāya vadati. Buddhakālasmiñhi ekassapi bhikkhuno vasanaṭṭhāne – “sace satthā āgacchissati, āsanaṃ paññattameva hotū”ti antamaso phalakamattampi paṇṇasanthāramattampi paññattameva. Khamanīyaṃ yāpanīyanti kacci dukkhaṃ khamituṃ, iriyāpathaṃ vā yāpetuṃ sakkāti pucchati. Sīsavedanāti kutoci nikkhamituṃ alabhamānehi vātehi samuṭṭhāpitā balavatiyo sīsavedanā honti.

56. In the second sutta, 'samadhosīti' means it trembled all around. It shows reverence in every aspect by way of trembling and shaking movement. It is said to be the custom that even a gravely ill person, upon seeing an elder, should show reverence by making a motion of rising. But that person should be told, 'Do not move, do not move,' for that movement is a showing of the act of rising—hence it is said, 'shows the act of rising.' 'These seats are ready'—here, he speaks referring to the seat already prepared. For in the Buddha's time, in the dwelling place of even a single monk, a seat—even if it were just a plank or a spread of leaves—was always prepared with the thought, 'If the Teacher were to come, let a seat be ready.' 'Is it bearable, is it endurable?'—he asks, 'Is it possible to bear the suffering or to sustain the posture?' 'Pains in the head'—these are severe pains in the head caused by powerful winds arising when they are unable to find any way out.

Phaggunasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Phagguna Sutta is concluded.

2. Chaḷabhijātisuttavaṇṇanā

2. The commentary on the Chaḷabhijāti Sutta

57. Tatiye abhijātiyoti ettha abhi-saddo upasaggamattaṃ, na atthavisesajotakoti āha “cha jātiyo”ti. Abhijāyatīti etthāpi eseva nayo.

57. In the third sutta, regarding 'abhijāti,' the word 'abhi' is merely a prefix, not indicating any special meaning, as it is said, 'six kinds of births.' The same principle applies to 'abhijāyati.'

Urabbhe hanantīti orabbhikā. Evaṃ sūkarikādayo veditabbā. Rodenti kururakammantatāya sappaṭibaddhe satte assūni mocentīti ruddā, te eva luddā ra-kārassa la-kāraṃ katvā. Iminā aññepi ye keci māgavikā nesādā vuttā, te pāpakammappasutatāya “kaṇhābhijātī”ti vadati.

They kill sheep, hence they are called sheep-butchers (orabbhikā). Similarly, pig-butchers (sūkarikā) and others should be understood. Because they make creatures connected to them through cruel work cry and shed tears, they are called 'ruddā' (the cruel). These very 'ruddā' are called 'luddā' (hunters) by changing the 'r' sound to an 'l' sound. By this, others such as deer-hunters (māgavikā) and fowlers (nesādā) are also mentioned. Due to their dedication to evil deeds, they are called 'of dark birth.'

Bhikkhūti ca buddhasāsane bhikkhū. Te kira sacchandarāgena paribhuñjantīti adhippāyena catūsu paccayesu kaṇṭake pakkhipitvā khādantīti “kaṇṭakavuttikā”ti vadati. Kasmāti ce? Yasmā te paṇīte paccaye paṭisevantīti tassa micchāgāho. Ñāyaladdhepi paccaye bhuñjamānā ājīvakasamayassa vilomaggāhitāya paccayesu kaṇṭake pakkhipitvā khādanti nāmāti vadatīti. Atha vā kaṇṭakavuttikā evaṃnāmakā eke pabbajitā, ye savisesaṃ attakilamathānuyogaṃ anuyuttā. Tathā hi te kaṇṭake vattantā viya hontīti “kaṇṭakavuttikā”ti vuttā. Imameva ca atthavikappaṃ sandhāyāha “kaṇṭakavuttikāti samaṇā nāmete”ti.

And 'bhikkhus' refers to bhikkhus in the Buddha’s dispensation. He calls them 'thorn-practitioners' with the meaning that, because they enjoy the four requisites with their own craving and desire, it is as if they eat them after inserting thorns. Why is that? Because he has the wrong view that they make use of excellent requisites. He says that even while they are consuming requisites obtained lawfully, due to his own perverse grasp of the Ājīvaka doctrine, it is as if they are eating the requisites after inserting thorns. Alternatively, 'thorn-practitioners' is the name of certain renunciates who are especially devoted to the practice of self-mortification. For indeed, they are as if living amidst thorns; thus they are called 'thorn-practitioners.' It is with reference to this very alternative explanation that it is said: 'These ascetics are called thorn-practitioners.'

Lohitābhijāti [M 3.0123] nāma nigaṇṭhā ekasāṭakāti vuttā. Te kira ṭhatvā bhuñjananahānappaṭikkhepādivatasamāyogena purimehi dvīhi paṇḍaratarā.

The Nigaṇṭhas called Lohitābhijāti (of red birth) are said to wear a single garment. They are said to be whiter than the previous two due to adhering to vows such as eating while standing and refusing to bathe.

Acelakasāvakāti [V 3.0116] ājīvakasāvake vadati. Te kira ājīvakaladdhiyā suvisuddhacittatāya nigaṇṭhehipi paṇḍaratarā. Evañca katvā attano paccayadāyake nigaṇṭhehipi jeṭṭhakatare karoti.

The term 'Acelakasāvakā' refers to the disciples of the Ājīvakas. It is said that, due to the Ājīvaka doctrine and their very pure minds, they were even whiter than the Nigaṇṭhas. And having done so, they cause their own supporters to be superior to the Nigaṇṭhas.

Ājīvakā ājīvakiniyo “sukkābhijātī”ti vuttā. Te kira purimehi catūhi paṇḍaratarā. Nandādayo hi tathārūpaṃ ājīvakappaṭipattiṃ ukkaṃsaṃ pāpetvā ṭhitā, tasmā nigaṇṭhehi ājīvakasāvakehi ca paṇḍaratarāti “paramasukkābhijātī”ti vuttā.

The Ājīvakas and Ājīvikinīs were called 'Sukkābhijātī' (of white birth). It is said that they were whiter than the previous four. For Nandā and others, having brought such Ājīvaka practices to the highest point, stood out as whiter than the Nigaṇṭhas and the Ājīvaka disciples, hence they were called 'Paramasukkābhijātī' (of supremely white birth).

Bilaṃ olaggeyyunti maṃsabhāgaṃ nhārunā vā kenaci vā ganthitvā purisassa hatthe vā kese vā olambanavasena bandheyyuṃ. Iminā satthadhammaṃ nāma dasseti. Satthavāho kira mahākantāraṃ paṭipanno antarāmagge goṇe mate maṃsaṃ gahetvā sabbesaṃ satthikānaṃ “idaṃ khāditvā ettakaṃ mūlaṃ dātabba”nti koṭṭhāsaṃ olambati. Goṇamaṃsaṃ nāma khādantāpi atthi, akhādantāpi atthi, khādantāpi mūlaṃ dātuṃ sakkontāpi asakkontāpi. Satthavāho yena mūlena goṇo gahito, taṃ mūlaṃ satthikehi dhāraṇatthaṃ sabbesaṃ balakkārena koṭṭhāsaṃ datvā mūlaṃ gaṇhāti. Ayaṃ satthadhammo.

'Bilaṃ olaggeyyunti' means they would tie a piece of meat with sinew or something similar, fastening it to a man's hand or hair so it hangs. This illustrates what is called the 'satthadhamma' (caravan custom). It is said that when a caravan leader traveling through a great wilderness had an ox die along the way, he would take the meat and hang portions for all the caravan members, saying, 'After eating this, so much value must be given.' Some would eat the ox meat, some would not; among those who ate it, some could pay the value, and some could not. The caravan leader, in order to recover from the caravan members the price for which the ox was purchased, would forcibly distribute portions to all and collect the price. This is the caravan custom.

Kaṇhābhijātiyo samānoti kaṇhe nīcakule jāto hutvā. Kaṇhadhammanti paccatte upayogavacananti āha “kaṇhasabhāvo hutvā abhijāyatī”ti, taṃ antogadhahetuatthaṃ padaṃ, uppādetīti attho. Tasmā kaṇhaṃ dhammaṃ abhijāyatīti kāḷakaṃ dasadussīlyadhammaṃ uppādeti. Sukkaṃ dhammaṃ abhijāyatīti etthāpi iminā nayena attho veditabbo. So hi “ahaṃ pubbepi puññānaṃ akatattā nīcakule nibbatto, idāni puññaṃ karissāmī”ti puññasaṅkhātaṃ paṇḍaradhammaṃ karoti.

'Kaṇhābhijātiyo samāno' means being born into a low, dark family. 'Kaṇhadhammanti' is a term of reflexive application, as it is said, 'Being of a dark nature, he is born.' This phrase has an internal causal meaning; the meaning is 'he generates.' Therefore, 'he is born to dark dhammas' means he produces the ten dark states of bad morality. 'He is born to white dhammas'—here too, the meaning should be understood in the same way. For he thinks, 'Because I did no merit in the past, I was born into a low family; now I will do merit,' and thus performs the white dhammas, which are designated as merit.

Akaṇhaṃ asukkaṃ nibbānanti sace kaṇhaṃ bhaveyya, kaṇhavipākaṃ dadeyya yathā dasavidhaṃ dussīlyadhammaṃ. Sace sukkaṃ, sukkavipākaṃ dadeyya yathā dānasīlādikusalakammaṃ. Dvinnampi appadānato “akaṇhaṃ asukka”nti vuttaṃ. Nibbānañca nāma imasmiṃ atthe arahattaṃ adhippetaṃ “abhijāyatī”ti vacanato[M 3.0124]. Tañhi kilesanibbānante jātattā nibbānaṃ nāma yathā “rāgādīnaṃ khayante jātattā rāgakkhayo, dosakkhayo, mohakkhayo”ti. Paṭippassambhanavasena vā kilesānaṃ nibbāpanato nibbānaṃ. Taṃ esa abhijāyati pasavati. Idhāpi hi antogadhahetu atthaṃ “jāyatī”ti padaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “jāyatī”ti imassa pāpuṇātīhi atthaṃ [V 3.0117] gahetvāva “nibbānaṃ pāpuṇātī”ti vuttaṃ. Sukkābhijātiyo samānoti sukke uccakule jāto hutvā. Sesamettha suviññeyyameva.

Not black, not white, is Nibbāna—if it were black, it would yield a black result like the ten kinds of unwholesome conduct. If it were white, it would yield a white result like wholesome deeds such as generosity and virtue. Because it gives no result of either, it is called 'not black, not white.' Here, Nibbāna refers to Arahantship, as indicated by the term 'abhijāyati' (is born). For it is called Nibbāna because it is born at the extinction of the defilements, just as 'the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion' are so called because they are born at their extinction. Alternatively, it is called Nibbāna because of the stilling of the defilements. This (Arahantship) is born or produced. Here, the word 'jāyati' (is born) implies its cause. In the commentary, however, the meaning of 'jāyati' is taken as 'attains,' so it is said, 'one attains Nibbāna.' 'Of bright birth' means having been born in a high or noble family. The rest here is easily understood.

Chaḷabhijātisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Chaḷabhijāti Sutta is concluded.

4. Āsavasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Discourse on the Taints

58. Catutthe saṃvarenāti saṃvarena hetubhūtena vā. Idhāti ayaṃ idha-saddo sabbākārato indiyasaṃvarasaṃvutassa puggalassa sannissayabhūtasāsanaparidīpano, aññassa tathābhāvappaṭisedhano vāti vuttaṃ “idhāti idhasmiṃ sāsane”ti. Paṭisaṅkhāti paṭisaṅkhāya. Saṅkhā-saddo ñāṇakoṭṭhāsapaññattigaṇanādīsu dissati “saṅkhāyekaṃ paṭisevatī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.168) hi ñāṇe dissati. “Papañcasaññāsaṅkhā samudācarantī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.202, 204) koṭṭhāse. “Tesaṃ tesaṃ dhammānaṃ saṅkhā samaññā”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 1313-1315) paññattiyaṃ. “Na sukaraṃ saṅkhātu”ntiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 2.128) gaṇanāya. Idha pana ñāṇe daṭṭhabbo. Tenevāha “paṭisañjānitvā paccavekkhitvāti attho”ti. Ādīnavapaccavekkhaṇā ādīnavapaṭisaṅkhāti yojanā. Sampalimaṭṭhanti ghaṃsitaṃ. Anubyañjanasoti hatthapādasitaālokitavilokitādippakārabhāgaso. Tañhi ayonisomanasikaroto kilesānaṃ anubyañjanato “anubyañjana”nti vuccati. Nimittaggāhoti itthipurisanimittassa subhanimittādikassa vā kilesavatthubhūtassa nimittassa gāho. Ādittapariyāyenāti ādittapariyāye (saṃ. ni. 4.28; mahāva. 54) āgatanayena veditabbo.

58. In the fourth, 'by restraint' means by restraint as a cause. Here, the word 'here' illuminates the teaching as the foundation for a person restrained with sense-restraint in all aspects, and it denies such a state for others, as stated: 'Here means in this teaching.' 'Reflects' means by reflecting. The term 'saṅkhā' is seen in contexts such as knowledge, categories, designations, and counting. For example, in 'he partakes after reflection,' it refers to knowledge. In 'conceptual proliferations and designations arise,' it refers to categories. In 'the designation and name of these various phenomena,' it refers to designation. In 'it is not easy to count,' it refers to counting. Here, however, it should be understood as knowledge. Hence, it is said: 'It means knowing and reviewing.' The examination of dangers is to be understood as the reflection on dangers. 'Touched' means rubbed. 'Secondary characteristics' refers to aspects such as the movements of hands and feet, smiling, gazing, and so forth. For one who attends improperly, these become the secondary manifestations of defilements; hence, they are called 'secondary characteristics.' 'Grasping at signs' means seizing upon the signs of a woman or man, or any attractive sign that becomes a basis for defilements. 'By the simile of the burning' should be understood according to the method described in the 'Discourse on the Burning' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.28; Mahāvagga 54).

Yathā itthiyā indriyaṃ itthindriyaṃ, na evamidaṃ, idaṃ pana cakkhumeva indriyanti cakkhundriyaṃ. Tenāha “cakkhumeva indriya”nti. Yathā āvāṭe niyataṭṭhitiko kacchapo “āvāṭakacchapo”ti vuccati, evaṃ tappaṭibaddhavuttitāya taṃ ṭhāno [M 3.0125] saṃvaro cakkhundriyasaṃvaro. Tenāha “cakkhundriye saṃvaro cakkhundriyasaṃvaro”ti. Nanu ca cakkhundriye saṃvaro vā asaṃvaro vā natthi. Na hi cakkhupasādaṃ nissāya sati vā muṭṭhassaccaṃ vā uppajjati. Apica yadā rūpārammaṇaṃ cakkhussa āpāthaṃ āgacchati, tadā bhavaṅge dvikkhattuṃ uppajjitvā niruddhe kiriyamanodhātu āvajjanakiccaṃ sādhayamānā uppajjitvā nirujjhati. Tato cakkhuviññāṇaṃ dassanakiccaṃ, tato vipākamanodhātu sampaṭicchanakiccaṃ, tato vipākamanoviññāṇadhātu santīraṇakiccaṃ, tato kiriyāhetukamanoviññāṇadhātu voṭṭhabbanakiccaṃ sādhayamānā uppajjitvā nirujjhati[V 3.0118], tadanantaraṃ javanaṃ javati. Tatthāpi neva bhavaṅgasamaye, na āvajjanādīnaṃ aññatarasamaye ca saṃvaro vā asaṃvaro vā atthi. Javanakkhaṇe pana sace dussīlyaṃ vā muṭṭhassaccaṃ vā aññāṇaṃ vā akkhanti vā kosajjaṃ vā uppajjati, asaṃvaro hoti. Tasmiṃ pana sīlādīsu uppannesu saṃvaro hoti, tasmā “cakkhundriye saṃvaro”ti kasmā vuttanti āha “javane uppajjamānopi hesa…pe… cakkhundriyasaṃvaroti vuccatī”ti.

Just as the faculty of a woman is called the female faculty, it is not so in this case; here, the eye itself is the faculty, hence it is called the eye faculty. Therefore, it is said, 'the eye itself is the faculty.' Just as a tortoise settled in a pit is called a 'pit-tortoise,' similarly, because its function is bound to that, that state of restraint is the restraint of the eye faculty. Therefore, it is said, 'restraint in the eye faculty is the restraint of the eye faculty.' But is there really restraint or non-restraint in the eye faculty? For neither mindfulness nor lack of mindfulness arises dependent on the eye-sensitivity. Moreover, when a visible object comes into the range of the eye, after the life-continuum has arisen and ceased twice, the functional mind-element arises, accomplishing the function of adverting, and then ceases. After that, eye-consciousness arises, performing the function of seeing; then the resultant mind-element, performing the function of receiving; then the resultant mind-consciousness-element, performing the function of investigating; and then the functional rootless mind-consciousness-element, performing the function of determining—each arises and ceases. Immediately after that, the impulsion (javana) flashes forth. Even then, neither at the time of the life-continuum nor at the time of adverting and so on, is there restraint or non-restraint. However, at the moment of impulsion, if immorality, lack of mindfulness, ignorance, impatience, or laziness arises, there is non-restraint. But if morality and so on arise at that time, there is restraint. Therefore, why is it said, 'restraint in the eye faculty'? It is said, 'Even though it arises in the impulsive moment... it is called the restraint of the eye faculty.'

Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā nagare catūsu dvāresu asaṃvutesu kiñcāpi antogharadvārakoṭṭhakagabbhādayo susaṃvutā, tathāpi antonagare sabbaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ arakkhitaṃ agopitameva hoti. Nagaradvārena hi pavisitvā corā yadicchakaṃ kareyyuṃ, evamevaṃ javane dussīlyādīsu uppannesu tasmiṃ asaṃvare sati dvārampi aguttaṃ hoti bhavaṅgampi āvajjanādīni vīthicittānipi. Yathā pana nagaradvāresu saṃvutesu kiñcāpi antogharādayo asaṃvutā, tathāpi antonagare sabbaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ surakkhitaṃ sugopitameva hoti. Nagaradvāresu hi pihitesu corānaṃ paveso natthi, evamevaṃ javane sīlādīsu uppannesu dvārampi suguttaṃ hoti bhavaṅgampi āvajjanādīni vīthicittānipi, tasmā javanakkhaṇe uppajjamānopi cakkhundriyasaṃvaroti vuttoti.

This is what is said: Just as in a city with four gates left unguarded, even though the inner doors, storerooms, and chambers are well-guarded, all goods within the city remain unprotected and unguarded. For thieves can enter through the city gates and do as they please. Similarly, when unwholesome qualities such as immorality arise in the javana, if there is non-restraint, the sense door is unguarded, as are the life-continuum, adverting, and other cognitive process consciousnesses. On the other hand, just as when the city gates are well-guarded, even if the inner rooms and so on are unguarded, all goods within the city remain well-protected and well-guarded. For when the city gates are closed, thieves cannot enter. Similarly, when wholesome qualities such as morality arise in the javana, the sense door is well-guarded, as are the life-continuum, adverting, and other cognitive process consciousnesses. Therefore, it is said that it is 'restraint of the eye faculty' even though it arises at the moment of javana.

Saṃvarena samannāgato puggalo saṃvutoti āha “upeto”ti. Ayamevettha attho sundarataroti upari pāḷiyaṃ sandissanato vuttaṃ. Tenāha “tathā hī”tiādi.

A person endowed with restraint is called restrained; thus it is said 'upeto' (meaning 'endowed'). This very meaning here is the more beautiful one, as is evident from its occurrence in the Pāli text above. Therefore, it is said, 'Thus indeed,' and so on.

Yanti ādesoti iminā liṅgavipallāsena saddhiṃ vacanavipallāso katoti dasseti, nipātapadaṃ vā etaṃ puthuvacanatthaṃ. Vighātakarāti cittavighātakarā[M 3.0126], kāyacittadukkhanibbattakā vā. Yathāvuttakilesahetukā dāhānubandhā vipākā eva vipākapariḷāhā. Yathā panettha āsavā aññe ca vighātakarā kilesapariḷāhā sambhavanti, taṃ dassetuṃ “cakkhudvārasmiñhī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Taṃ suviññeyyameva. Ettha ca saṃvaraṇūpāyo, saṃvaritabbaṃ, saṃvaro, yato so saṃvaro, yattha saṃvaro, yathā saṃvaro, yañca saṃvaraphalanti ayaṃ vibhāgo veditabbo. Kathaṃ? “Paṭisaṅkhā yoniso”ti hi saṃvaraṇūpāyo. Cakkhundriyaṃ saṃvaritabbaṃ. Saṃvaraggahaṇena gahitā sati saṃvaro. “Asaṃvutassā”ti saṃvaraṇāvadhi. Asaṃvarato hi saṃvaraṇaṃ. Saṃvaritabbaggahaṇasiddho idha saṃvaravisayo. Cakkhundriyañhi saṃvaraṇaṃ ñāṇaṃ rūpārammaṇe saṃvarayatīti avuttasiddhoyamattho. Āsavatannimittakilesapariḷāhābhāvo phalaṃ. Evaṃ sotadvārādīsu yojetabbaṃ. Sabbatthevāti manodvāre pañcadvāre cāti sabbasmiṃ dvāre.

"Yanti ādesoti" – This shows that an inversion of number has been made along with an inversion of gender. Alternatively, this is a particle used in the sense of plurality. "Vighātakarāti" – Causing distress to the mind, or producing suffering in body and mind. The results, connected with burning and caused by the aforementioned defilements, are themselves the torments of results. And here, to show that taints and other distress-causing torments of defilements arise, it is said, "In the eye-door," and so on. This is easily understood. Here, this distinction should be understood: the means of restraint, what should be restrained, restraint, from what that restraint arises, where restraint is, how restraint is, and what the fruit of restraint is. How? "Reflecting wisely" is the means of restraint. The eye faculty should be restrained. Mindfulness, which is grasped through the term 'restraint', is restraint itself. "For one who is unrestrained" is the limit for restraint, for restraint is from non-restraint. Here, the object of restraint is established by grasping what should be restrained. For the eye faculty is what is to be restrained, and knowledge restrains in regard to a form-object—this meaning is established though not explicitly stated. The absence of the torments of defilements that are signs of taints is the fruit. In the same way, this should be applied to the ear-door and so on. "Sabbatthevāti" – In every case, meaning in the mind-door and the five sense-doors—in every door.

Paṭisaṅkhā [V 3.0119] yoniso cīvarantiādīsu “sītassa paṭighātāyā”tiādinā paccavekkhaṇameva yoniso paṭisaṅkhā. Īdisanti evarūpaṃ iṭṭhārammaṇaṃ. Bhavapatthanāya assādayatoti bhavapatthanāmukhena bhāvitaṃ ārammaṇaṃ assādentassa. Cīvaranti nivāsanādi yaṃ kiñcicīvaraṃ. Paṭisevatīti nivāsanādivasena paribhuñjati. Yāvadevāti payojanaparimāṇaniyamanaṃ. Sītappaṭighātādiyeva hi yogino cīvarappaṭisevanappayojanaṃ. Sītassāti sītadhātukkhobhato vā utupariṇāmato vā uppannassa sītassa. Paṭighātāyāti paṭighātanatthaṃ tappaccayassa vikārassa vinodanatthaṃ. Uṇhassāti aggisantāpato uppannassa uṇhassa. Ḍaṃsādayo pākaṭāyeva. Puna yāvadevāti niyatappayojanaparimāṇaniyamanaṃ. Niyatañhi payojanaṃ cīvaraṃ paṭisevantassa hirikopīnappaṭicchādanaṃ, itaraṃ kadāci. Hirikopīnanti sambādhaṭṭhānaṃ. Yasmiñhi aṅge vivaṭe hirī kuppati vinassati, taṃ hiriyā kopanato hirikopīnaṃ, taṃpaṭicchādanatthaṃ cīvaraṃ paṭisevati.

Reflecting wisely on the robe and so forth: the very reflection, 'for the warding off of cold,' and so on, is wise reflection. Such means such a pleasing object. For the sake of desiring existence, one savors: this refers to one who savors an object developed by way of the aspiration for existence. Robe means any kind of robe, such as a lower garment. One uses means one wears it as a lower garment and so on. Only for: this is the limitation of the extent of the purpose. For a yogi, the purpose of using a robe is indeed only for the warding off of cold and so on. Of cold: of the cold that has arisen from a disturbance of the cold element or from a change of season. For warding off: for the purpose of warding off, for the purpose of dispelling the affliction caused by it. Of heat: of the heat that has arisen from the heat of a fire. Gadflies and so on are self-evident. Again, only for: this is the limitation of the extent of the definite purpose. For one using a robe, the definite purpose is the covering of the private parts; the other is occasional. Private parts means the shameful place. For when that limb is exposed, modesty is agitated and is lost; because it agitates modesty, it is called the 'agitator of modesty' (hirikopīna). One uses the robe for the purpose of covering that.

Piṇḍapātanti yaṃ kiñci āhāraṃ. So hi piṇḍolyena bhikkhuno patte patanato, tattha tattha laddhabhikkhāpiṇḍānaṃ pāto sannipātoti vā “piṇḍapāto”ti vuccati. Neva davāyāti na kīḷanāya. Na madāyāti na balamadamānamadapurisamadatthaṃ. Na maṇḍanāyāti na aṅgapaccaṅgānaṃ pīṇanabhāvatthaṃ. Na vibhūsanāyāti na tesaṃyeva sobhatthaṃ, chavisampattiatthanti attho[M 3.0127]. Imāni yathākkamaṃ mohadosasaṇṭhānavaṇṇarāgūpanissayappahānatthāni veditabbāni. Purimaṃ vā dvayaṃ attano saṃkilesuppattinisedhanatthaṃ, itaraṃ parassapi. Cattāripi kāmasukhallikānuyogassa pahānatthaṃ vuttānīti veditabbāni. Kāyassāti rūpakāyassa. Ṭhitiyā yāpanāyāti pabandhaṭṭhitatthañceva pavattiyā avicchedanatthañca, cirakālaṭṭhitatthaṃ jīvitindriyassa pavattāpanatthaṃ. Vihiṃsūparatiyāti jighacchādukkhassa uparamatthaṃ. Brahmacariyānuggahāyāti sāsanamaggabrahmacariyānaṃ anuggaṇhanatthaṃ. Itīti evaṃ iminā upāyena. Purāṇañca vedanaṃ paṭihaṅkhāmīti purāṇaṃ abhuttapaccayā uppajjanakavedanaṃ paṭihanissāmi. Navañca vedanaṃ na uppādessāmīti navaṃ bhuttapaccayā uppajjanakavedanaṃ na uppādessāmi. Tassā hi anuppajjanatthameva āhāraṃ paribhuñjati. Ettha abhuttapaccayā uppajjanakavedanā nāma yathāvuttajighacchānimittā vedanā. Sā hi abhuñjantassa bhiyyo bhiyyopavaḍḍhanavasena uppajjati, bhuttapaccayā anuppajjanakavedanāpi khudānimittāva aṅgadāhasūlādivedanā appavattā. Sā hi bhuttapaccayā anuppannāva na uppajjissati. Vihiṃsānimittatā cetāsaṃ vihiṃsāya viseso.

Almsfood means any kind of food. It is called 'almsfood' (piṇḍapāta) either because of the falling (pāta) of lumps (piṇḍa) into the monk's bowl, or because it is a gathering (pāta) of alms-lumps obtained here and there. Not for amusement means not for play. Not for intoxication means not for the intoxication of strength, the intoxication of conceit, or the intoxication of manhood. Not for beautification means not for the purpose of making the major and minor limbs plump. Not for adornment means not for their beauty, that is, for the sake of perfecting the complexion. These should be understood as being, respectively, for the purpose of abandoning the supporting conditions for delusion, hatred, lust for form, and lust for appearance. The first two are for preventing the arising of one's own defilements; the others, for those of others. All four should be understood as being stated for the purpose of abandoning indulgence in sensual pleasure. Of this body means of the physical body. For its maintenance and sustenance means for the purpose of its continuous existence and for the non-interruption of its process; for its lasting for a long time and for causing the life faculty to proceed. For the cessation of harm means for the purpose of ending the suffering of hunger. For supporting the holy life means for supporting the holy life of the Dispensation and the Path. Thus means in this way. I will ward off the old feeling: I will ward off the old feeling that arises from the condition of not having eaten. And I will not produce a new feeling: I will not produce a new feeling that arises from the condition of having eaten. For one consumes food for the very purpose of its non-arising. Here, the feeling that arises from the condition of not having eaten is the feeling caused by hunger as described. For one who does not eat, it arises by way of increasing more and more. The feeling that does not arise conditioned by having eaten is also the un-arisen feeling caused by hunger, such as bodily burning, stabbing pains, and so on. For that, being unarisen due to the condition of having eaten, will not arise. The fact that these are caused by affliction is their distinction from affliction.

Yātrā ca me bhavissatīti yāpanā ca me catunnaṃ iriyāpathānaṃ bhavissati. “Yāpanāyā”ti [V 3.0120] iminā jīvitindriyayāpanā vuttā, idha catunnaṃ iriyāpathānaṃ avicchedasaṅkhātā yāpanāti ayametāsaṃ viseso. Anavajjatā ca phāsuvihāro cāti ayuttapariyesanappaṭiggahaṇaparibhogaparivajjanena anavajjatā, parimitaparibhogena phāsuvihāro. Asappāyāparimitabhojanapaccayā aratitandīvijambhitāviññugarahādidosābhāvena vā anavajjatā. Sappāyaparimitabhojanapaccayā kāyabalasambhavena phāsuvihāro. Yāvadatthaṃ udarāvadehakabhojanaparivajjanena vā seyyasukhapassasukhamiddhasukhādīnaṃ abhāvato anavajjatā. Catupañcālopamattaūnabhojanena catuiriyāpathayogyatāpādanato phāsuvihāro. Vuttañhetaṃ –

And there will be maintenance for me means: and there will be sustenance of the four postures for me. By 'for sustenance' (yāpanāya), the sustenance of the life faculty was stated; here, sustenance is described as the non-interruption of the four postures—this is the distinction between them. And blamelessness and a comfortable abiding: blamelessness is through the avoidance of improper seeking, accepting, and consuming; a comfortable abiding is through moderate consumption. Or, blamelessness is through the absence of the faults of discontent, lethargy, yawning, censure by the wise, and so on, which are conditioned by unsuitable and immoderate eating. A comfortable abiding is through the arising of bodily strength conditioned by suitable and moderate eating. Or, blamelessness is from the absence of the pleasure of lying down, the pleasure of lying on one's side, the pleasure of torpor, and so on, through avoiding eating to fill the belly. A comfortable abiding is from producing suitability for the four postures by eating four or five morsels less. As it is said:

“Cattāro pañca ālope, abhutvā udakaṃ pive;

Alaṃ phāsuvihārāya, pahitattassa bhikkhuno”ti. (theragā. 983; mi. pa. 6.5.10);

Having left four or five morsels uneaten, one should drink water; this is sufficient for the comfortable abiding of a monk with a resolute mind.

Ettāvatā [M 3.0128] ca payojanapariggaho, majjhimā ca paṭipadā dīpitā hoti. Yātrā ca me bhavissatīti payojanapariggahadīpanā. Yātrā hi naṃ āhārūpayogaṃ payojeti. Dhammikasukhāpariccāgahetuko phāsuvihāro majjhimā paṭipadā antadvayaparivajjanato.

By this much, the grasping of the purpose and the Middle Way are shown. And there will be maintenance for me is the showing of the grasping of the purpose. For maintenance indeed directs one to the use of food. The comfortable abiding, which is caused by the non-abandonment of righteous happiness, is the Middle Way, because it avoids the two extremes.

Senāsananti senañca āsanañca. Yattha vihārādike seti nipajjati āsati nisīdati, taṃ senāsanaṃ. Utuparissayavinodanappaṭisallānārāmatthanti utuyeva parisahanaṭṭhena parissayo sarīrābādhacittavikkhepakaro, tassa vinodanatthaṃ, anuppannassa anuppādanatthaṃ, uppannassa vūpasamanatthañcāti attho. Atha vā yathāvutto utu ca sīhabyagghādipākaṭaparissayo ca rāgadosādipaṭicchannaparissayo ca utuparissayo, tassa vinodanatthañceva ekībhāvaphāsukatthañca. Cīvarappaṭisevane hirīkopīnappaṭicchādanaṃ viya taṃ niyatapayojananti puna “yāvadevā”ti vuttaṃ.

Lodging means both a resting place and a seat. That wherein, in a monastery and so on, one lies down, reclines, or sits, is a lodging. For dispelling the dangers of the climate and for delight in seclusion: the climate itself is a danger (parissaya) in the sense that it is oppressive, causing bodily affliction and mental distraction; the purpose is to dispel it, meaning to prevent the unarisen from arising and to calm the arisen. Or, the dangers of the climate (utuparissaya) are the climate as described, the manifest dangers from lions, tigers, and so on, and the concealed dangers of lust, hatred, and so on; the purpose is both to dispel them and for the sake of comfort in solitude. Just as covering the private parts is the definite purpose when using the robe, so this is its definite purpose; therefore it is again said, 'only for'.

Gilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhāranti rogassa paccanīkappavattiyā gilānapaccayo, tato eva bhisakkassa anuññātavatthutāya bhesajjaṃ, jīvitassa parivārasambhārabhāvehi parikkhāro cāti gilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhāro, taṃ. Veyyābādhikānanti veyyābādhato dhātukkhobhato ca taṃnibbattakuṭṭhagaṇḍapīḷakādirogato uppannānaṃ. Vedanānanti dukkhavedanānaṃ. Abyābajjhaparamatāyāti niddukkhaparamabhāvāya. Yāva taṃ dukkhaṃ sabbaṃ pahīnaṃ hoti, tāva paṭisevāmīti yojanā. Evamettha saṅkhepeneva pāḷivaṇṇanā veditabbā. Navavedanuppādatopīti na kevalaṃ āyatiṃ eva vipākapariḷāhā[V 3.0121], atha kho atibhojanapaccayā alaṃsāṭakādīnaṃ viya navavedanuppādatopi veditabbā.

The requisite of medicine as a support for the sick: it is a support for the sick (gilānapaccayo) by counteracting illness; it is medicine (bhesajjaṃ) because it is a substance permitted by a physician; and it is a requisite (parikkhāro) because it is an accessory and provision for life. Of those arising from affliction: of those that have arisen from diseases such as leprosy, boils, and abscesses, which are produced from affliction and from a disturbance of the elements. Of feelings: of painful feelings. For the supreme state of non-affliction: for the supreme state of being without suffering. The construction is: 'I will use it until all that suffering is abandoned.' Thus, the explanation of the Pāli should be understood here in brief. From the arising of a new feeling: it should be understood not only as the future fever of result, but also as the arising of a new feeling conditioned by overeating, like that from unsuitable clothing and so on.

Kammaṭṭhānikassa calanaṃ nāma kammaṭṭhānapariccāgoti āha “calati kampati kammaṭṭhānaṃ vijahatī”ti. “Khamo hoti sītassa uṇhassā”ti ettha ca lomasanāgattherassa vatthu kathetabbaṃ. Thero kira cetiyapabbate piyaṅguguhāya padhānaghare viharanto antaraṭṭhake himapātasamaye lokantarikanirayaṃ paccavekkhitvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ avijahantova abbhokāse vītināmesi. Gimhasamaye ca pacchābhattaṃ bahicaṅkame kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikaroto sedāpissa kacchehi muccanti. Atha naṃ antevāsiko āha – “idha, bhante, nisīdatha, sītalo okāso”ti. Thero “uṇhabhayenevamhi, āvuso, idha nisinno”ti avīcimahānirayaṃ paccavekkhitvā [M 3.0129] nisīdiyeva. Uṇhanti cettha aggisantāpova veditabbo sūriyasantāpassa parato vuccamānattā. Sūriyasantāpavasena panetaṃ vatthu vuttaṃ.

For one who practices a meditation subject, wavering means abandoning the meditation subject, as it is said: 'It wavers, it shakes, the meditation subject is abandoned.' Regarding 'He is able to endure cold and heat'—here the story of the Elder Lomasanāga should be told. The elder, it is said, while dwelling in a striving-hut at the Piyaṅgu Cave on Cetiyapabbata, during the eight-day cold spell when snow was falling, reflected on the interspace hell without abandoning his meditation subject and spent the time in the open. And in the summer, after his meal, while attending to his meditation subject on the outer walking path, sweat poured from his armpits. Then his attendant said to him, 'Venerable sir, sit here, the place is cool.' The elder replied, 'Friend, it is precisely out of fear of the heat that I am sitting here,' and after reflecting on the Avīci great hell, he sat down right there. Here, 'heat' should be understood as the torment of fire, for the sun's heat is spoken of later. But this story is told in the context of the sun's heat.

Yo ca dve tayo vāre bhattaṃ vā pānīyaṃ vā alabhamānopi anamatagge saṃsāre attano pettivisayūpapattiṃ paccavekkhitvā avedhanto kammaṭṭhānaṃ na vijahatiyeva. Ḍaṃsamakasavātātapasamphassehi phuṭṭho cepi tiracchānūpapattiṃ paccavekkhitvā avedhanto kammaṭṭhānaṃ na vijahatiyeva. Sarīsapasamphassena phuṭṭho cāpi anamatagge saṃsāre sīhabyagghādimukhesu anekavāraṃ parivattitapubbabhāvaṃ paccavekkhitvā avedhanto kammaṭṭhānaṃ na vijahatiyeva padhāniyatthero viya, ayaṃ “khamo jighacchāya…pe… sarīsapasamphassāna”nti veditabbo. Theraṃ kira khaṇḍacelavihāre kaṇikārapadhāniyaghare ariyavaṃsadhammaṃ suṇantaññeva ghoraviso sappo ḍaṃsi. Thero jānitvāpi pasannacitto nisinno dhammaṃyeva suṇāti, visavego thaddho ahosi. Thero upasampadamāḷaṃ ādiṃ katvā sīlaṃ paccavekkhitvā “visuddhasīlomhī”ti pītiṃ uppādesi, saha pītuppādā visaṃ nivattitvā pathaviṃ pāvisi. Thero tattheva cittekaggataṃ labhitvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi.

And he who, even when not obtaining food or drink for two or three times, reflects on his rebirth in the realm of spirits in the beginningless cycle of rebirths and, unshaken, does not abandon his meditation subject; and who, even when touched by gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, and the sun's heat, reflects on rebirth as an animal and, unshaken, does not abandon his meditation subject; and who, even when touched by a reptile, reflects on his former state of having been turned over countless times in the mouths of lions, tigers, and so on in the beginningless cycle of rebirths and, unshaken, does not abandon his meditation subject, like the striving elder—this one is to be understood as ‘one who is patient with hunger… and the touch of reptiles.’ It is said that while the elder was listening to the Dhamma of the Noble Lineage in the Kaṇikāra striving-house at Khaṇḍacelavihāra, a highly venomous snake bit him. Though aware of it, the elder, with a serene mind, remained seated and continued listening to the Dhamma. The force of the venom was arrested. The elder, reflecting on his virtue from his higher ordination onwards, gave rise to joy, thinking, ‘I am one of purified virtue.’ With the arising of joy, the venom receded and entered the earth. Right there, the elder attained one-pointedness of mind, developed insight, and reached arahantship.

Yo pana akkosavasena durutte duruttattāyeva ca durāgate api antimavatthusaññite vacanapathe sutvā khantiguṇaṃyeva paccavekkhitvā na vedhati dīghabhāṇakaabhayatthero viya, ayaṃ “khamo duruttānaṃ durāgatānaṃ vacanapathāna”nti veditabbo. Thero kira paccayasantosabhāvanārāmatāya mahāariyavaṃsappaṭipadaṃ kathesi, sabbo mahāgāmo āgacchati, therassa mahāsakkāro uppajji. Taṃ aññataro mahāthero adhivāsetuṃ asakkonto “dīghabhāṇako [V 3.0122] ‘ariyavaṃsaṃ kathemī’ti sabbarattiṃ kolāhalaṃ karotī”tiādīhi akkosi. Ubhopi ca attano attano vihāraṃ gacchantā gāvutamattaṃ ekapathena agamaṃsu. Sakalagāvutampi so taṃ akkosiyeva. Tato yattha dvinnaṃ vihārānaṃ maggo bhijjati, tattha ṭhatvā dīghabhāṇakatthero taṃ vanditvā “eso, bhante, tumhākaṃ maggo”ti āha. So assuṇanto [M 3.0130] viya agamāsi. Theropi vihāraṃ gantvā pāde pakkhāletvā nisīdi. Tamenaṃ antevāsiko “kiṃ, bhante, sakalagāvutaṃ paribhāsantaṃ na kiñci avocutthā”ti āha. Thero “khantiyevāvuso, mayhaṃ bhāro, na akkhanti, ekapaduddhārepi kammaṭṭhānaviyogaṃ na passāmī”ti āha.

But he who, upon hearing harsh words spoken as abuse, and offensive words that are simply harsh, even paths of speech designated as a matter of final defeat, reflects only on the virtue of patience and does not tremble, like Elder Abhaya the Dīgha-reciter, he is to be understood as ‘one who endures harsh and offensive paths of speech.’ It is said that the Elder, due to his delight in developing contentment with requisites, taught the practice of the Great Noble Lineage. The entire great village came, and great honor arose for the Elder. Another great elder, unable to endure it, reviled him, saying, 'This Dīgha-reciter, saying “I will teach the noble lineage,” makes a commotion all night long,' and so on. Both, going to their respective monasteries, traveled together along a single path for about a gāvuta. Throughout that entire gāvuta, he kept reviling him. Then, where the path forked for the two monasteries, Elder Dīghabhāṇaka stood, paid respects to him, and said, 'Venerable sir, this is your path.' He went on as if not hearing. The Elder, having gone to his monastery, washed his feet and sat down. His attendant asked him, 'Venerable sir, why did you not say anything while he was reviling you for the entire gāvuta?' The Elder replied, 'Friend, patience is my burden, not impatience. Even in uttering a single word in response, I see no separation from my meditation subject.'

Vacanameva tadatthaṃ ñāpetukāmānañca patho upāyoti āha “vacanameva vacanapatho”ti. Asukhaṭṭhena vā tibbā. Yañhi na sukhaṃ, taṃ aniṭṭhaṃ tibbanti vuccati. Adhivāsakajātiko hotīti yathāvuttavedanānaṃ adhivāsakasabhāvo hoti. Cittalapabbate padhāniyattherassa kira rattiṃ padhānena vītināmetvā ṭhitassa udaravāto uppajjati. So taṃ adhivāsetuṃ asakkonto āvattati parivattati. Tamenaṃ caṅkamanapasse ṭhito piṇḍapātiyatthero āha – “āvuso, pabbajito nāma adhivāsanasīlo hotī”ti. So “sādhu, bhante”ti adhivāsetvā niccalo sayi. Vāto nābhito yāva hadayaṃ phālesi. Thero vedanaṃ vikkhambhetvā vipassanto muhuttena anāgāmī hutvā parinibbāyi. Evaṃ sabbatthāti “uṇhena phuṭṭhassa sītaṃ patthayato”tiādinā sabbattha uṇhādinimittaṃ kāmāsavuppatti veditabbā. Natthi sugatibhave sītaṃ vā uṇhaṃ vāti aniṭṭhaṃ sītaṃ vā uṇhaṃ vā natthīti adhippāyo. Attaggāhe sati attaniyaggāhoti āha “mayhaṃ sītaṃ uṇhanti gāho diṭṭhāsavo”ti.

The word itself is the path and means for those who wish to convey that meaning; hence it is said, 'The word itself is the path of speech.' Or, words are intense in the sense of being unpleasant. For what is not pleasant is called undesirable and intense. He is of a patient nature—meaning he has the inherent quality of enduring the aforementioned feelings. It is said that on Cittalapabbata, for a striving elder who had spent the night in exertion, abdominal wind arose. Unable to endure it, he tossed and turned. Then, the alms-gathering elder who was standing on the nearby walking path said to him, 'Friend, one who has gone forth is by nature patient.' He replied, 'Very well, venerable sir,' and enduring it, lay down motionless. The wind split him from the navel up to the heart. The elder, suppressing the pain and practicing insight, in a moment became a non-returner and passed away. Thus, in all cases—as in 'one touched by heat longs for cold' and so on—the sign of heat, etc., should be understood as the arising of the taint of sensual desire. In a fortunate rebirth, there is no cold or heat—meaning there is no undesirable cold or heat. When there is grasping of self, there is grasping of what belongs to self—hence it is said, 'The grasping “my cold, my heat” is the taint of wrong view.'

Ahaṃ samaṇoti “ahaṃ samaṇo, kiṃ mama jīvitena vā maraṇena vā”ti evaṃ cintetvāti adhippāyo. Paccavekkhitvāti gāmappavesappayojanādiñca paccavekkhitvā. Paṭikkamatīti hatthiādīnaṃ samīpagamanato apakkamati. Ṭhāyanti etthāti ṭhānaṃ, kaṇṭakānaṃ ṭhānaṃ kaṇṭakaṭṭhānaṃ, yattha kaṇṭakāni santi, taṃ okāsanti vuttaṃ hoti. Amanussaduṭṭhānīti amanussasañcārena dūsitāni, saparissayānīti attho. Aniyatavatthubhūtanti aniyatasikkhāpadassa kāraṇabhūtaṃ. Vesiyādibhedatoti vesiyāvidhavāthullakumārikāpaṇḍakapānāgārabhikkhunibhedato. Samānanti samaṃ, avisamanti attho. Akāsi vāti tādisaṃ anācāraṃ akāsi vā. Sīlasaṃvarasaṅkhātenāti kathaṃ parivajjanaṃ sīlaṃ? Anāsanaparivajjanena hi [M 3.0131] anācāraparivajjanaṃ vuttaṃ. Anācārāgocaraparivajjanaṃ cārittasīlatāya sīlasaṃvaro. Tathā hi bhagavatā “pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuto viharatī”ti (vibha. 508) sīlasaṃvaravibhajane ācāragocarasampattiṃ [V 3.0123] dassentena “atthi anācāro, atthi agocaro”tiādinā (vibha. 513-514) ācāragocarā vibhajitvā dassitā. “Caṇḍaṃ hatthiṃ parivajjetī”ti vacanato hatthiādiparivajjanampi bhagavato vacanānuṭṭhānanti katvā ācārasīlamevāti veditabbaṃ.

'I am a recluse' means with the intention of thinking thus: 'What is life or death to me?' 'Having reflected' means having considered the purpose of entering the village and so on. 'He retreats' means he turns away from approaching elephants and so on. A place (ṭhāna) is where things are established (ṭhāyanti). A place of thorns (kaṇṭakaṭṭhāna) is a place where there are thorns; this is what is meant by the location. 'Haunted by non-humans' means corrupted by the movement of non-humans, that is, perilous. 'A matter related to an uncertain rule' means something that is the cause for an uncertain training rule. 'From the types such as prostitutes' means from distinctions such as prostitutes, widows, mature unmarried women, young girls, eunuchs, taverns, and nuns. 'Equal' means the same, not unequal. 'He may have done' means he may have done such misconduct. Regarding ‘restraint consisting of virtue’: how is avoidance virtue? By the avoidance of inappropriate seats, the avoidance of misconduct is stated. And the avoidance of a resort for misconduct, being a matter of conduct-virtue, is restraint in virtue. Thus, indeed, the Blessed One, when showing the accomplishment of conduct and resort in the analysis of restraint in virtue, said: 'He dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha,' and then showed conduct and resort divided up, saying, 'There is misconduct, there is an improper resort,' and so on. From the statement, 'He avoids a fierce elephant,' it should be known that avoiding elephants and so on is also the fulfillment of the Blessed One's word, and thus it is indeed conduct-virtue.

Itipīti imināpi kāraṇena ayonisomanasikārasamuṭṭhitattāpi, lobhādisahagatattāpi, kusalappaṭipakkhatopītiādīhi kāraṇehi ayaṃ vitakko akusaloti attho. Iminā nayena sāvajjotiādīsupi attho veditabbo. Ettha ca akusalotiādinā diṭṭhadhammikaṃ kāmavitakkassa ādīnavaṃ dasseti, dukkhavipākoti iminā samparāyikaṃ. Attabyābādhāya saṃvattatītiādīsupi imināva nayena ādīnavavibhāvanā veditabbā. Uppannassa kāmavitakkassa anadhivāsanaṃ nāma puna tādisassa anuppādanaṃ. Taṃ panassa pahānaṃ vinodanaṃ byantikaraṇaṃ anabhāvagamananti ca vattuṃ vaṭṭatīti pāḷiyaṃ – “uppannaṃ kāmavitakkaṃ nādhivāsetī”ti vatvā “pajahatī”tiādi vuttanti tamatthaṃ dassento “anadhivāsento kiṃ karotī”tiādimāha. Pahānañcettha vikkhambhanameva, na samucchedoti dassetuṃ “vinodetī”tiādi vuttanti vikkhambhanavaseneva attho dassito. Uppannuppanneti tesaṃ pāpavitakkānaṃ uppādāvatthāgahaṇaṃ vā kataṃ siyā anavasesaggahaṇaṃ vā. Tesu paṭhamaṃ sandhāyāha “uppannamatte”ti, sampatijāteti attho. Anavasesaggahaṇaṃ byāpanicchāyaṃ hotīti dassetuṃ “satakkhattumpi uppannuppanne”ti vuttaṃ.

'Therefore' means that because it arises from unwise attention, is associated with greed and other defilements, and opposes wholesome states, and so on, this thought is unwholesome—this is the meaning. In the same way, the meanings of 'blameworthy' and so on should be understood. Here, by 'unwholesome' and so on, the danger of sensual thoughts in this very life is shown, while by 'resulting in suffering' their future danger is indicated. Similarly, by 'leads to self-harm' and so on, the explanation of dangers should be understood in the same way. The non-endurance of an arisen sensual thought means preventing such a thought from arising again. That its abandonment, removal, eradication, and making it disappear can be spoken of is because in the Pāli, after saying, 'He does not endure an arisen sensual thought,' it says, 'he abandons it,' and so on. To clarify this meaning, it is said, 'Not enduring it, what does one do?' and so on. Here, abandoning refers only to suppression, not to eradication—hence terms like 'removes' and so on are used, and thus the meaning is explained in terms of suppression. 'Arisen and arisen' may refer either to the taking of the state of arising of those evil thoughts or to their taking without remainder. Regarding the first, it is said, 'as soon as it has arisen,' meaning newly arisen. To show that taking without remainder is meant, it is said, 'even if arisen a hundred times.'

Ñātivitakkoti “amhākaṃ ñātayo sukhajīvino sampattiyuttā”tiādinā gehassitapemavasena ñātake ārabbha uppannavitakko. Janapadavitakkoti “amhākaṃ janapado subhikkho sampannasasso ramaṇīyo”tiādinā gehassitapemavasena janapadaṃ ārabbha uppannavitakko. Ukkuṭikappadhānādīhi dukkhe nijjiṇṇe samparāye sattā sukhī honti amarāti dukkarakārikāya paṭisaṃyutto amaratthāya vitakko. Taṃ vā ārabbha amarāvikkhepadiṭṭhisahagato amaro ca so vitakko cāti [M 3.0132] amarāvitakko. Parānuddayatāpaṭisaṃyuttoti paresu upaṭṭhākādīsu sahananditādivasena pavatto anuddayatāpatirūpako gehassitapemappaṭisaṃyutto vitakko. Lābhasakkārasilokappaṭisaṃyuttoti cīvarādilābhena ca sakkārena ca kittisaddena ca ārammaṇakaraṇavasena paṭisaṃyutto. Anavaññattippaṭisaṃyuttoti “aho vata maṃ pare na avajāneyyuṃ, na heṭṭhā katvā maññeyyuṃ, pāsāṇacchattaṃ viya garuṃ kareyyu”nti uppannavitakko.

The thought of relatives is the thought that arises regarding relatives due to affection connected with household life, such as, 'Our relatives live happily and are prosperous,' and so on. The thought of the homeland is the thought that arises regarding one's homeland due to affection connected with household life, such as, 'Our homeland is abundant in food, rich in crops, and delightful,' and so on. The thought of immortality is the thought connected with performing difficult deeds for the sake of immortality, such as: 'When suffering is overcome by difficult practices like the squatting posture, beings are happy and immortal in the future.' Alternatively, it is a thought of immortality regarding that, associated with the view of endless wriggling about immortality, being both an immortal (view) and a thought. The thought connected with pseudo-compassion is the thought that arises in relation to attendants and so on, proceeding as rejoicing with them, which is a semblance of compassion connected to affection for household life. The thought connected with gain, honor, and fame is the thought associated with the gain of robes and so on, with honor, and with the sound of praise, by way of making them an object. The thought connected with not being despised is the thought that arises, such as, 'Oh, may others not despise me, may they not think of me as inferior, may they treat me with respect like a royal parasol!'

Kāmavitakko [V 3.0124] kāmasaṅkappanasabhāvato kāmāsavappattiyā sātisayattā ca kāmanākāroti āha “kāmavitakko panettha kāmāsavo”ti. Tabbisesoti kāmāsavaviseso bhavasabhāvattāti adhippāyo. Kāmavitakkādike vinodeti attano santānato nīharati etenāti vinodanaṃ, vīriyanti āha “vīriyasaṃvarasaṅkhātena vinodanenā”ti.

The thought of sensual pleasure, because of its nature of intending sensual pleasures and its excessiveness in leading to the attainment of the influx of sensual pleasure, is a form of craving; hence, it is said, 'The thought of sensual pleasure here is the influx of sensual pleasure.' 'That distinction' means a particular kind of influx of sensual pleasure, due to its nature as becoming; this is the meaning. 'One dispels thoughts of sensual pleasure and so on' means one removes them from one's own mental continuum. That by which one does this is 'dispelling.' This is energy; hence, it is said, 'by the dispelling designated as restraint by energy.'

“Satta bojjhaṅgā bhāvitā bahulīkatā vijjāvimuttiyo paripūrentī”ti vacanato vijjāvimuttīnaṃ anadhigamo tato ca sakalavaṭṭadukkhānativatti abhāvanāya ādīnavo. Vuttavipariyāyena bhagavato orasaputtabhāvādivasena ca bhāvanāya ānisaṃso veditabbo. Thomentoti āsavapahānassa dukkarattā tāya eva dukkarakiriyāya taṃ abhitthavanto. Saṃvareneva pahīnāti saṃvarena pahīnā eva. Tena vuttaṃ “na appahīnesuyeva pahīnasaññī”ti.

Because it is said, 'Seven factors of enlightenment, when developed and cultivated, fulfill knowledge and liberation,' the disadvantage of not developing them is the non-attainment of knowledge and liberation, and consequently not transcending all the suffering in the cycle of existence. The advantage of development should be understood in the opposite way, and as being a true-born son of the Blessed One and so on. 'They praise' means they extol that very difficult act of abandoning the influxes, because it is difficult to abandon them. 'They are abandoned by restraint' means they are indeed abandoned by restraint. Therefore, it is said, 'One should not perceive as abandoned what is not yet abandoned.'

Āsavasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Āsava Sutta is concluded.

5. Dārukammikasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Dārukammika Sutta

59. Pañcame puttasambādhasayananti puttehi sambādhasayanaṃ. Ettha puttasīsena dārapariggahaṃ puttadāresu uppilo viya. Tena tesaṃ rogādihetu sokābhibhavena ca cittassa saṃkiliṭṭhataṃ dasseti. Kāmabhogināti iminā pana rāgābhibhavanti. Ubhayenapi vikkhittacittataṃ dasseti. Kāsikacandananti ujjalacandanaṃ. Taṃ kira vaṇṇavisesasamujjalaṃ hoti pabhassaraṃ, tadatthameva naṃ saṇhataraṃ karonti. Tenevāha “saṇhacandana”nti[M 3.0133], kāsikavatthañca candanañcāti attho. Mālāgandhavilepananti vaṇṇasobhatthañceva sugandhabhāvatthañca mālaṃ, sugandhabhāvatthāya gandhaṃ, chavirāgakaraṇatthañceva subhatthañca vilepanaṃ dhārentena. Jātarūparajatanti suvaṇṇañceva avasiṭṭhadhanañca sādiyantena. Sabbenapi kāmesu abhigiddhabhāvameva pakāseti.

59. In the fifth sutta, 'a bed crowded with children' means a bed crowded by children. Here, by 'children's heads' is meant the taking of a wife, which is like a boil among children and wives. Thus, it shows the mind's defilement from being overwhelmed by sorrow caused by their diseases and so on. By 'sensual enjoyer' is indicated being overwhelmed by lust. By both, a distracted mind is shown. 'Kāsika sandalwood' means bright sandalwood. It is said to be radiant and luminous with a special color; for that very purpose, they make it even smoother. Therefore, it is said 'smooth sandalwood'—the meaning is Kāsi cloth and sandalwood. 'Garlands, perfumes, and ointments' means by one who wears garlands for beauty and fragrance, perfumes for fragrance, and ointments for coloring the skin and for beauty. 'Gold and silver' means by one who delights in gold and the remaining wealth. By all this, a state of excessive greed for sensual pleasures is revealed.

Dārukammikasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Dārukammika Sutta is concluded.

6. Hatthisāriputtasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Hatthisāriputta Sutta

60. Chaṭṭhe hatthiṃ sāretīti hatthisārī, tassa puttoti hatthisāriputto. So kira sāvatthiyaṃ hatthiācariyassa putto bhagavato santike pabbajitvā tīṇi piṭakāni uggahetvā sukhumesu [V 3.0125] khandhadhātuāyatanādīsu atthantaresu kusalo ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ – “therānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ abhidhammakathaṃ kathentānaṃ antarantarā kathaṃ opātetī”ti. Tattha antarantarā kathaṃ opātetīti therehi vuccamānassa kathāpabandhassa antare antare attano kathaṃ pavesetīti attho. Pañcahi saṃsaggehīti savanasaṃsaggo, dassanasaṃsaggo, samullāpasaṃsaggo, sambhogasaṃsaggo, kāyasaṃsaggoti imehi pañcahi saṃsaggehi. Kiṭṭhakhādakoti kiṭṭhaṭṭhāne uppannasassañhi kiṭṭhanti vuttaṃ kāraṇūpacārena. Sippiyo suttiyo. Sambukāti saṅkhamāha.

60. In the sixth sutta, 'one who trains elephants' is an elephant trainer; his son is Hatthisāriputta. It is said that he, the son of an elephant master in Sāvatthī, having gone forth in the presence of the Blessed One, mastered the three Piṭakas and became skilled in the subtle meanings of the aggregates, elements, sense bases, and so forth. Therefore, it is said: 'While the elder bhikkhus were discussing the Abhidhamma, he would interject his own words in between.' Here, 'interjecting his own words in between' means inserting his own discourse in the intervals of the ongoing discussion being spoken by the elders. 'Through five kinds of association' refers to these five: association through hearing, association through seeing, association through speaking together, association through partaking together, and association through physical contact. 'Eating what is grown': The crop that grows in a tilled place is called 'what is grown' by a metaphor of the cause. 'Sippiyo' are pearl oysters. 'Sambukā' refers to conch shells.

Gihibhāve vaṇṇaṃ kathesīti (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.422) kassapasammāsambuddhassa kira sāsane dve sahāyakā ahesuṃ, aññamaññaṃ samaggā ekatova sajjhāyanti. Tesu eko anabhirato gihibhāve cittaṃ uppādetvā itarassa ārocesi. So gihibhāve ādīnavaṃ, pabbajjāya ānisaṃsaṃ dassetvā ovadi. So taṃ sutvā abhiramitvā puna ekadivasaṃ tādise citte uppanne taṃ etadavoca – “mayhaṃ, āvuso, evarūpaṃ cittaṃ uppajjati, imāhaṃ pattacīvaraṃ tuyhaṃ dassāmī”ti. So pattacīvaralobhena tassa gihibhāve ānisaṃsaṃ dassetvā pabbajjāya ādīnavaṃ kathesi. Tassa taṃ sutvāva gihibhāvato cittaṃ nivattetvā pabbajjāyameva abhirami. Evamesa tadā sīlavantassa bhikkhuno gihibhāve [M 3.0134] ānisaṃsakathāya kathitattā idāni cha vāre vibbhamitvā sattamavāre pabbajitvā mahāmoggallānassa mahākoṭṭhikattherassa ca abhidhammakathaṃ kathentānaṃ antarantarā kathaṃ opātesi. Atha naṃ mahākoṭṭhikatthero apasādesi. So mahāsāvakassa kathite patiṭṭhātuṃ asakkonto vibbhamitvā gihi jāto. Poṭṭhapādassa panāyaṃ gihisahāyako ahosi, tasmā vibbhamitvā dvīhatīhaccayena poṭṭhapādassa santikaṃ gato. Atha naṃ so disvā – “samma, kiṃ tayā kataṃ, evarūpassa nāma satthu sāsanā apasakkantosi, ehi pabbajituṃ dāni te vaṭṭatī”ti taṃ gahetvā bhagavato santikaṃ agamāsi. Tasmiṃ ṭhāne pabbajitvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ “sattame vāre pabbajitvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇī”ti.

'He spoke in praise of the householder's life' (gihibhāve vaṇṇaṃ kathesīti)—so it is said (Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 1.422). It is said that in the dispensation of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddha Kassapa, there were two friends, harmonious and united, who studied together. Among them, one, being discontent, conceived a desire for the householder's life and informed the other. The other then pointed out the drawbacks of the householder's life and the benefits of renunciation, advising him. Hearing this, he was delighted, but one day, when such a thought arose again, he said to him, 'Friend, such a thought has arisen in me. I will give you my bowl and robe.' Out of greed for the bowl and robe, the other then extolled the benefits of the householder's life and spoke of the drawbacks of renunciation. Hearing that, his mind turned away from the householder's life, and he found joy in renunciation alone. Thus, because at that time praise of the householder's life had been spoken by a virtuous bhikkhu, now, after falling away six times, he renounced on the seventh occasion. While the Abhidhamma discourse was being given by the great disciples Mahāmoggallāna and Mahākoṭṭhika Thera, he repeatedly interrupted their discussion. Then, Mahākoṭṭhika Thera rebuked him. Unable to remain steadfast under the great disciple’s words, he fell away and became a householder. This man had been the householder friend of Poṭṭhapāda, so after falling away, he went to Poṭṭhapāda within two or three days. Seeing him, Poṭṭhapāda said, 'Friend, what have you done? You have strayed from such a Teacher’s dispensation. Come, now it is proper for you to renounce.' Taking him, he went to the presence of the Blessed One. Ordained on the spot, he attained Arahantship. Hence it is said, 'Having renounced on the seventh occasion, he attained Arahantship.'

Hatthisāriputtasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Hatthisāriputta Sutta is concluded.

7. Majjhesuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Majjhe Sutta

61. Sattame mantāti ya-kāralopena niddeso, karaṇatthe vā etaṃ paccattavacanaṃ. Tenāha “tāya ubho ante viditvā”ti. Phassavasena nibbattattāti dvayadvayasamāpattiyaṃ aññamaññaṃ samphassavasena nibbattattā, “phassapaccayā taṇhā, taṇhāpaccayā upādānaṃ, upādānapaccayā bhavo[V 3.0126], bhavapaccayā jātī”ti iminā cānukkamena phassasamuṭṭhānattā imassa kāyassa phassavasena nibbattattāti vuttaṃ. Eko antoti ettha ayaṃ anta-saddo antaabbhantaramariyādalāmakaabhāvakoṭṭhāsapadapūraṇasamīpādīsu dissati. “Antapūro udarapūro”tiādīsu (su. ni. 197) hi ante antasaddo. “Caranti loke parivārachannā anto asuddhā, bahi sobhamānā”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.122) abbhantare. “Kāyabandhanassa anto jīrati (cūḷava. 278) sā haritantaṃ vā panthantaṃ vā selantaṃ vā udakantaṃ vā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.304) mariyādāyaṃ. “Antamidaṃ, bhikkhave, jīvikāna”ntiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 3.80; itivu. 91) lāmake. “Esevanto dukkhassā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.393; saṃ. ni. 2.51) abhāve. Sabbapaccayasaṅkhayo hi dukkhassa abhāvo [M 3.0135] koṭītipi vuccati. “Tayo antā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 3.305) koṭṭhāse. “Iṅgha tāva suttantaṃ vā gāthāyo vā abhidhammaṃ vā pariyāpuṇassu, suttante okāsaṃ kārāpetvā”ti (pāci. 442) ca ādīsu padapūraṇe. “Gāmantaṃ vā osaṭo (pārā. 409-410; cūḷava. 343) gāmantasenāsana”ntiādīsu (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.410) samīpe. Svāyamidha koṭṭhāse vattatīti ayameko koṭṭhāsoti.

61. In the seventh sutta, the word `mantā` (in `mantāti`) is a designation involving the elision of the letter 'ya' [from `mantāya`], or it is the accusative case used in the instrumental sense. Hence it is said, 'Having known both ends by that.' 'Arising by way of contact' (`Phassavasena nibbattattā`) means that in the dual attainments, each arises through mutual contact. And by this sequence—'Contact conditions craving, craving conditions clinging, clinging conditions becoming, becoming conditions birth'—because it originates from contact, it is said that this body arises through contact. 'One end' (`eko anto`): Here, the word `anta` is seen in various senses such as end, interior, boundary, worthlessness, absence, part, filling of a word, and proximity. For example: In phrases like 'Antapūro udarapūro' (Snp 197), `anta` means 'end.' In 'Caranti loke parivārachannā anto asuddhā, bahi sobhamānā' (SN 1.122), it means 'interior.' In 'Kāyabandhanassa anto jīrati' (Cv 278) or 'sā haritantaṃ vā panthantaṃ vā selantaṃ vā udakantaṃ vā' (MN 1.304), it means 'boundary.' In 'Antamidaṃ, bhikkhave, jīvikānaṃ' (SN 3.80; Iti 91), it means 'worthlessness.' In 'Esevanto dukkhassā' (MN 3.393; SN 2.51), it means 'absence,' for the cessation of all conditions is called the absence of suffering, and also its culmination. In 'Tayo antā' (DN 3.305), it means 'part.' In 'Iṅgha tāva suttantaṃ vā gāthāyo vā abhidhammaṃ vā pariyāpuṇassu, suttante okāsaṃ kārāpetvā' (Pāc. 442), it refers to 'filling a word.' In 'Gāmantaṃ vā osaṭo' (Pārā. 409-410; Cv 343) or 'gāmantasenāsanaṃ' (Pārā Aṭṭha 2.410), it means 'proximity.' Here, it is used in the sense of a 'part.' Thus, this is one part.

Santo paramatthato vijjamāno dhammasamūhoti sakkāyo, pañcupādānakkhandhā. Tenāha “tebhūmakavaṭṭa”nti. Sesamettha suviññeyyameva.

`Sakkāya` is the group of phenomena existing in the ultimate sense, that is, the five aggregates subject to clinging. Hence, it is said 'the round of the three planes' (`tebhūmakavaṭṭa`). The rest here is easily understood.

Majjhesuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Majjhe Sutta is concluded.

8. Purisindriyañāṇasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Discourse on the Knowledge of the Faculties of a Person

62. Aṭṭhame nibbattivasena apāyasaṃvattaniyena vā kammunā apāyesu niyuttoti āpāyiko nerayikoti etthāpi eseva nayo. Avīcimhi uppajjitvā tattha āyukappasaññitaṃ antarakappaṃ tiṭṭhatīti kappaṭṭho. Nirayūpapattipariharaṇavasena tikicchituṃ asakkuṇeyyoti atekiccho. Akhaṇḍānīti ekadesenapi akhaṇḍitāni. Bhinnakālato paṭṭhāya bījaṃ bījatthāya na upakappati. Apūtīnīti udakatemanena apūtikāni. Pūtikañhi bījaṃ bījatthāya na upakappati. Avātātapahatānīti vātena ca ātapena ca na hatāni nirojataṃ na pāpitāni. Nirojañhi kasaṭaṃ bījaṃ bījatthāya na upakappati. “Sārādānī”ti vattabbe ā-kārassa rassattaṃ katvā pāḷiyaṃ “sāradānī”ti vuttanti āha “sārādānī”ti. Taṇḍulasārassa ādānato [V 3.0127] sārādāni, gahitasārāni patiṭṭhitasārāni. Nissarañhi bījaṃ bījatthāya na upakappati. Sukhasayitānīti cattāro māse koṭṭhe pakkhittaniyāmeneva sukhasayitāni suṭṭhu sannicitāni. Maṇḍakhetteti ūsakhārādidosehi aviddhaste sārakkhette. Abhidoti abhi-saddena samānatthanipātapadanti āha “abhiaḍḍharatta”nti. Natthi etassa bhidāti vā abhido. “Abhidaṃ aḍḍharatta”nti vattabbe upayogatthe paccattavacanaṃ. Aḍḍharattanti [M 3.0136] ca accantasaṃyogavacanaṃ, bhummatthe vā. Tasmā abhido aḍḍharattanti abhinne aḍḍharattasamayeti attho. Puṇṇamāsiyañhi gaganamajjhassa purato vā pacchato vā cande ṭhite aḍḍharattasamayo bhinno nāma hoti, majjhe eva pana ṭhite abhinno nāma.

62. In the eighth sutta, `āpāyiko` means one bound for the planes of misery, that is, one consigned to the planes of misery by kamma that leads to rebirth or is conducive to the planes of misery. For `nerayiko` (one bound for hell), this same method of explanation applies. Having been born in Avīci, one remains there for an interim eon designated as an eon of life-span—hence, `kappaṭṭho` (lasting an eon). Unable to be treated by any means to prevent rebirth in hell—hence, `atekiccho` (incurable). `Akhaṇḍāni` (unbroken) means not even partially broken. From the time it is split, a seed is no longer suitable for its purpose as a seed. `Apūtīni` (unspoiled) means not rotted by water moisture. For a spoiled seed is not suitable for its purpose as a seed. `Avātātapahatāni` (unscorched by wind and sun) means not withered by wind and heat, not reduced to a sapless state. For a sapless, worthless seed is not suitable for its purpose as a seed. When it should be called `sārādānī`, the shortening of the vowel 'ā' in the Pāli results in `sāradānī`; it is said as `sārādānī`. `Sārādānī` means taking the essence of the grain, possessing essence, well-established in essence. For an essenceless seed is not suitable for its purpose as a seed. `Sukhasayitāni` (comfortably stored) means stored well in a granary for four months, thoroughly accumulated according to fixed practice. `Maṇḍakhette` (in a fertile field) means a field free from defects like saltiness or alkaline soil, rich in essence. `Abhido` is an indeclinable word having the same meaning as `abhi`, as in `abhiaḍḍharatta`. Or, `abhido` means 'there is no division of it.' When it should be said `abhidaṃ aḍḍharatta`, the accusative case is used in the sense of usage. And `aḍḍharatta` is a term indicating absolute connection, or alternatively, it is used in the locative sense. Therefore, `abhido aḍḍharatta` means 'at the time of the undivided middle of the night.' For on the full moon night, when the moon stands either before or after the middle of the sky, the time of the middle of the night is called 'divided,' but when it stands exactly in the middle, it is called 'undivided.'

Suppabuddhasunakkhattādayoti ettha (dha. pa. aṭṭha. 2.127 suppabuddhasakyavatthu) suppabuddho kira sākiyo “mama dhītaraṃ chaḍḍetvā nikkhanto, mama puttaṃ pabbājetvā tassa veriṭṭhāne ṭhito cā”ti imehi dvīhi kāraṇehi satthari āghātaṃ bandhitvā ekadivasaṃ “na dāni nimantitaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā bhuñjituṃ dassāmī”ti gamanamaggaṃ pidahitvā antaravīthiyaṃ suraṃ pivanto nisīdi.
