Athassa satthari bhikkhusaṅghaparivute taṃ ṭhānaṃ āgate “satthā āgato”ti ārocesuṃ. So āha – “purato gacchāti tassa vadetha, nāyaṃ mayā mahallakataro, nāssa maggaṃ dassāmī”ti. Punappunaṃ vuccamānopi tatheva nisīdi. Satthā mātulassa santikā maggaṃ alabhitvā tatova nivatti. Sopi carapurisaṃ pesesi – “gaccha tassa kathaṃ sutvā ehī”ti. Satthāpi nivattanto sitaṃ katvā ānandattherena – “ko nu kho, bhante, sitapātukamme paccayo”ti puṭṭho āha – “passasi, ānanda, suppabuddha”nti. Passāmi, bhante. Bhāriyaṃ tena kammaṃ kataṃ mādisassa buddhassa maggaṃ adentena, ito sattame divase heṭṭhāpāsāde pāsādamūle pathaviyā pavisissatī”ti ācikkhi.

Here, in reference to Suppabuddha, Sunakkhatta, and others (DhpA 2.127, Suppabuddha the Sakyan's story): It is said that Suppabuddha the Sakyan harbored hatred toward the Teacher for two reasons: "He abandoned my daughter and left, and he ordained my son, standing in the position of his enemy." One day, thinking, "Now I will not let him go and eat at the invited place," he blocked the path and sat drinking liquor in the middle of the street. Then, when the Teacher, surrounded by the community of bhikkhus, arrived at that place, they announced to him, "The Teacher has come." He said, "Tell him to go ahead. He is not older than me, and I will not give way to him." Though repeatedly urged, he remained seated. The Teacher, unable to obtain the path from his maternal uncle, turned back from there. Suppabuddha then sent a spy, saying, "Go, listen to what he says, and return." As the Teacher turned back, he smiled. When Venerable Ānanda asked, "Venerable sir, what is the cause for this smile?" the Teacher replied, "Do you see, Ānanda, Suppabuddha?" "I see, Venerable sir." "He has done a grave deed by not giving way to a Buddha like me. On the seventh day from now, he will sink into the earth at the base of the palace, in the lower palace," the Teacher declared.

Sunakkhattopi (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.147) pubbe bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā dibbacakkhuparikammaṃ pucchi. Athassa bhagavā kathesi. So dibbacakkhuṃ nibbattetvā ālokaṃ vaḍḍhetvā olokento devaloke nandanavanacittalatāvanaphārusakavanamissakavanesu dibbasampattiṃ anubhavamāne devaputte ca devadhītaro ca disvā – “etesaṃ evarūpāya attabhāvasampattiyā ṭhitānaṃ kira madhuro nu kho saddo bhavissatī”ti saddaṃ sotukāmo hutvā dasabalaṃ upasaṅkamitvā dibbasotadhātuparikammaṃ pucchi. Bhagavā panassa – “dibbasotadhātussa upanissayo natthī”ti ñatvā parikammaṃ na kathesi. Na hi buddhā yaṃ na bhavissati, tassa parikammaṃ kathenti. So bhagavati āghātaṃ bandhitvā cintesi – “ahaṃ samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ paṭhamaṃ dibbacakkhuparikammaṃ [V 3.0128] pucchiṃ, so mayhaṃ ‘sampajjatu vā mā vā sampajjatū’ti kathesi. Ahaṃ pana paccattapurisakārena taṃ nibbattetvā dibbasotadhātuparikammaṃ pucchiṃ, taṃ me na kathesi. Addhā evaṃ [M 3.0137] hoti ‘ayaṃ rājapabbajito dibbacakkhuñāṇaṃ nibbattetvā, dibbasotañāṇaṃ nibbattetvā, cetopariyakammañāṇaṃ nibbattetvā, āsavānaṃ khaye ñāṇaṃ nibbattetvā, mayā samasamo bhavissatī’ti issāmacchariyavasena mayhaṃ na kathetī”ti bhiyyoso āghātaṃ bandhitvā kāsāyāni chaḍḍetvā gihibhāvaṃ patvāpi na tuṇhībhūto vihāsi. Dasabalaṃ pana asatā tucchena abbhācikkhitvā apāyūpago ahosi. Tampi bhagavā byākāsi. Vuttañhetaṃ – “evampi kho, bhaggava, sunakkhatto licchaviputto mayā vuccamāno apakkameva imasmā dhammavinayā, yathā taṃ āpāyiko”ti (dī. ni. 3.6). Tena vuttaṃ “aparepi suppabuddhasunakkhattādayo bhagavatā ñātāvā”ti. Ādi-saddena kokālikādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo.

Sunakkhatta too (MN.A. 1.147) formerly approached the Blessed One and asked about the preparatory work for the divine eye. Then the Blessed One explained it to him. Having developed the divine eye and increased his vision, he looked around and saw devas in the heavenly realms—Nandana Grove, Cittalata Grove, Phārusaka Grove, and Missaka Grove—enjoying divine pleasures, along with sons and daughters of the devas. Seeing them, he thought, "For those abiding in such a state of personal excellence, their voices must surely be sweet." Desiring to hear their voices, he approached the Ten-Powered One and asked about the preparatory work for the divine ear-element. But the Blessed One, knowing that "there is no underlying basis for him to develop the divine ear-element," did not explain the preparatory work to him. For the Buddhas do not teach preparatory work for what will not come to be. Conceiving a hatred for the Blessed One, he thought, "First, I asked the ascetic Gotama about the preparatory work for the divine eye, and he explained it to me, as if indifferent to whether it would succeed or not. But when I, through my own personal effort, developed it and then asked about the preparatory work for the divine ear-element, he did not explain it to me. Surely, it must be like this: 'This one, having gone forth from royal life, will develop the knowledge of the divine eye, the knowledge of the divine ear, the knowledge of knowing others' minds, and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints—then he will become equal to me.' Out of jealousy and stinginess, he did not teach me." Increasing his anger, he discarded his ochre robes, returned to lay life, and still did not remain silent. Instead, he falsely accused the Ten-Powered One with what was untrue and empty and became one bound for a state of misery. The Blessed One also declared this. For it is said: "Even so, Bhaggava, Sunakkhatta the Licchavi, when spoken to by me, departed from this Dhamma and Discipline, as is fitting for one bound for misery" (DN 3.6). Therefore, it is said: "Others, too, like Suppabuddha and Sunakkhatta, were known by the Blessed One." By the word "and so on," one should understand the inclusion of others like Kokālika.

Susīmo paribbājakoti (saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 2.2.70) evaṃnāmako vedaṅgesu kusalo paṇḍito paribbājako. Aññatitthiyā hi parihīnalābhasakkārasilokā “samaṇo gotamo na jātigottādīni ārabbha lābhaggappatto jāto, kaviseṭṭho panesa uttamakavitāya sāvakānaṃ bandhaṃ bandhitvā deti. Te taṃ uggaṇhitvā upaṭṭhākānaṃ upanisinnakathampi anumodanampi sarabhaññampīti evamādīni kathenti. Te tesaṃ pasannānaṃ lābhaṃ upasaṃharanti. Sace mayaṃ yaṃ samaṇo gotamā jānāti, tato thokaṃ jāneyyāma, attano samayaṃ tattha pakkhipitvā mayampi upaṭṭhākānaṃ katheyyāma. Tato etehi lābhitarā bhaveyyāma. Ko nu kho samaṇassa gotamassa santike pabbajitvā khippameva uggaṇhituṃ sakkhissatī”ti evaṃ cintetvā “susimo paṭibalo”ti disvā upasaṅkamitvā evamāhaṃsu “ehi tvaṃ, āvuso susīma, samaṇe gotame brahmacariyaṃ cara, tvaṃ dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇitvā amhe vāceyyāsi, taṃ mayaṃ dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇitvā gihīnaṃ bhāsissāma, evaṃ mayampi sakkatā bhavissāma garukatā mānitā pūjitā lābhino cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhārāna”nti (saṃ. ni. 2.70).

The wanderer Susīma (S.A. 2.2.70) was a learned wanderer named Susīma, skilled in the Vedangas. Other sectarians, indeed, whose gains, honor, and fame had declined, thought: "The ascetic Gotama has attained the highest gains not through birth or lineage, but as the foremost poet; he composes and gives his disciples excellent verses, binding them to him. Having learned these, they speak to their supporters of discourses delivered while sitting nearby, words of appreciation, melodious chanting, and so forth. They thus procure gains from those who are pleased with them. If we knew even a little of what the ascetic Gotama knows, and incorporated our own doctrine into it, we too could speak to our supporters. Then we would gain even more than they do. Who is capable of going forth in the presence of the ascetic Gotama and quickly learning?" Thinking thus, they saw Susīma as capable and approached him, saying: "Come, friend Susīma, live the holy life under the ascetic Gotama. Having mastered the Dhamma, teach it to us. Having learned the Dhamma, we will speak to householders. Thus, we too will be respected, revered, honored, worshipped, and obtain robes, alms-food, dwellings, and medicinal requisites."

Atha susīmo paribbājako tesaṃ vacanaṃ sampaṭicchitvā yenānando tenupasaṅkami, upasaṅkamitvā pabbajjaṃ yāci. Thero ca taṃ ādāya bhagavantaṃ [M 3.0138] upasaṅkamitvā etamatthaṃ ārocesi. Bhagavā pana cintesi “ayaṃ paribbājako titthiyasamaye ‘ahaṃ pāṭiekko satthā’ti paṭijānamāno carati, ‘idheva maggabrahmacariyaṃ carituṃ icchāmī’ti kira vadati, kiṃ nu kho mayi pasanno, udāhu mayhaṃ vā mama sāvakānaṃ dhammakathāya pasanno”ti. Athassa ekaṭṭhānepi pasādābhāvaṃ ñatvā “ayaṃ mama sāsane ‘dhammaṃ thenessāmī’ti pabbajati, itissa āgamanaṃ [V 3.0129] aparisuddhaṃ, nipphatti nu kho kīdisā”ti olokento “kiñcāpi ‘dhammaṃ thenessāmī’ti pabbajati, katipāheneva pana ghaṭetvā arahattaṃ gaṇhissatī”ti ñatvā “tenahānanda, susīmaṃ pabbājethā”ti āha. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ “evaṃ bhagavatā ko ñāto? Susīmo paribbājako”ti.

Then the wanderer Susīma, accepting their words, approached Venerable Ānanda. Having approached, he requested ordination. The elder, taking him, approached the Blessed One and informed him of the matter. The Blessed One reflected: "This wanderer, during the time of the sectarians, used to go about claiming, ‘I am a unique teacher.’ And now he says, ‘I wish to lead the holy life here.’ I wonder, is he inspired by me, or by the Dhamma-teaching of me or my disciples?" Then, knowing that he had no inspiration in any respect, he investigated: "This one is going forth in my Dispensation thinking, ‘I will steal the Dhamma.’ His motive for coming is thus impure. What, I wonder, will be his attainment?" Perceiving that even though he goes forth thinking, ‘I will steal the Dhamma,’ in just a few days he would strive and attain arahantship, he said: "Then, Ānanda, ordain Susīma." Referring to this, it was said: "How was Susīma the wanderer known by the Blessed One?"

Santatimahāmattoti (dha. pa. aṭṭha. 2.141 santatimahāmattavatthu) so kira ekasmiṃ kāle rañño pasenadissa paccantaṃ kupitaṃ vūpasametvā āgato. Athassa rājā tuṭṭho satta divasāni rajjaṃ datvā ekaṃ naccagītakusalaṃ itthiṃ adāsi. So satta divasāni surāmadamatto hutvā sattame divase sabbālaṅkārappaṭimaṇḍito hatthikkhandhavaragato nahānatitthaṃ gacchanto satthāraṃ piṇḍāya pavisantaṃ dvārantare disvā hatthikkhandhavaragatova sīsaṃ cāletvā vandi. Satthā sitaṃ katvā “ko nu kho, bhante, sitapātukaraṇe hetū”ti ānandattherena puṭṭho sitakāraṇaṃ ācikkhanto āha – “passasi, ānanda, santatimahāmattaṃ, ajjeva sabbābharaṇappaṭimaṇḍito mama santikaṃ āgantvā cātuppadikagāthāvasāne arahattaṃ patvā parinibbāyissatī”ti. Tena vuttaṃ “evaṃ ko ñāto bhagavatāti? Santatimahāmatto”ti.

The story of the great minister Santati (Dha. Pa. Aṭṭha. 2.141, Santatimahāmattavatthu): It is said that on one occasion, having quelled a disturbance in the border region for King Pasenadi, he returned. Pleased, the king granted him kingship for seven days and gave him a woman skilled in dancing and singing. For seven days, he was intoxicated with liquor. On the seventh day, adorned with all ornaments and mounted on a superb elephant, he went to the bathing place. Seeing the Teacher entering for alms at the city gate, he bowed his head while still on the superb elephant’s back. The Teacher smiled. When the Elder Ānanda asked, “What, venerable sir, is the cause for the manifestation of a smile?”, the Teacher, explaining the cause of the smile, said, “Do you see, Ānanda, the great minister Santati? Today, adorned with all ornaments, he will come to me and, at the end of a four-lined verse, attain arahantship and pass into final Nibbāna.” Therefore it was said: “Who was thus known by the Blessed One?” “The great minister Santati.”

Purisindriyañāṇasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Purisindriyañāṇa Sutta is concluded.

9. Nibbedhikasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Nibbedhika Sutta

63. Navame parihāyati attano phalaṃ pariggahetvā vattati, tassa vā kāraṇabhāvaṃ upagacchatīti pariyāyoti idha kāraṇaṃ vuttanti āha “nibbijjhanakāraṇa”nti.

63. In the ninth (sutta), 'it declines, having grasped its own fruit, it proceeds,' or 'it attains the state of being its cause'—the term 'pariyāya' here means 'cause'; thus it is said, 'the cause of penetration.'

“Anujānāmi[M 3.0139], bhikkhave, ahatānaṃ vatthānaṃ diguṇaṃ saṅghāṭi”nti ettha hi paṭalaṭṭho guṇaṭṭho. “Accenti kālā tarayanti rattiyo, vayoguṇā anupubbaṃ jahantī”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.4) ettha rāsaṭṭho guṇaṭṭho. “Sataguṇā dakkhiṇā pāṭikaṅkhitabbā”ti (ma. ni. 3.379) ettha ānisaṃsaṭṭho. “Antaṃ antaguṇaṃ (dī. ni. 2.377; ma. ni. 1.110; khu. pā. 3.dvattiṃsākāro), kayirā mālāguṇe bahū”ti (dha. pa. 53) ettha bandhanaṭṭho guṇaṭṭho. Idhāpi esova adhippetoti āha “bandhanaṭṭhena guṇā”ti. Kāmarāgassa saṃyojanassa paccayabhāvena vatthukāmesupi bandhanaṭṭho rāsaṭṭho vā guṇaṭṭho daṭṭhabbo. Cakkhuviññeyyāti vā cakkhuviññāṇataṃdvārikaviññāṇehi jānitabbā. Sotaviññeyyātiādīsupi eseva nayo. Iṭṭhārammaṇabhūtāti [V 3.0130] sabhāveneva iṭṭhārammaṇajātikā, iṭṭhārammaṇabhāvaṃ vā pattā. Kamanīyāti kāmetabbā. Manavaḍḍhanakāti manoharā. Etena parikappanatopi iṭṭhārammaṇabhāvaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Piyajātikāti piyāyitabbasabhāvā. Kāmūpasañhitāti kāmarāgena upecca sambandhanīyā sambandhā kātabbā. Tenāha “ārammaṇaṃ katvā”tiādi. Saṅkapparāgoti vā subhādivasena saṅkappitavutthamhi uppannarāgo. Evamettha vatthukāmaṃ paṭikkhipitvā kilesakāmo vutto tasseva vasena tesampi kāmabhāvasiddhito, kilesakāmassapi iṭṭhavedanā diṭṭhādisampayogabhedena pavattiākārabhedena ca atthi vicittakāti tato visesetuṃ “citravicitrārammaṇānī”ti āha, nānappakārāni rūpādiārammaṇānīti attho.

'I allow, bhikkhus, a double-layered outer robe of unused cloth.' Here, the meaning of 'guṇa' is 'layer.' 'Times pass, nights glide by, the stages of life successively abandon us.' Here, the meaning of 'guṇa' is 'accumulation.' 'A hundredfold offering should be expected.' Here, the meaning of 'guṇa' is 'benefit.' 'The end, the final limit, one should make many garlands.' Here, the meaning of 'guṇa' is 'binding.' Here too, this is the intended meaning; thus it is said, 'guṇā in the sense of binding.' As a condition for the fetter of sensual lust, 'guṇa' should be understood in the sense of binding or accumulation even in the case of objective sensual pleasures. 'Known by the eye' means to be known by eye-consciousness or by consciousness through the eye-door. The same method applies to 'known by the ear,' and so forth. 'Having become a pleasing object' means that by their very nature they are of the class of pleasing objects, or they have attained the state of being a pleasing object. 'Desirable' means they should be desired. 'Delighting the mind' means charming. By this, it includes the state of being a pleasing object even from the aspect of mental construction. 'Of a lovable nature' means having the characteristic of being loved. 'Connected with sensual pleasures' means they are to be approached and connected by sensual lust, a connection is to be made. Therefore it is said, 'having made it the object,' and so forth. 'Lust of thought' refers to lust arising in a thing conceived as beautiful, etc. Thus, here, having rejected objective sensual pleasures, defilement-sensual pleasure is spoken of, because by its influence, even those (objective sensual pleasures) are established as sensual pleasures. And because defilement-sensual pleasure also exists in various ways—through association with pleasant feelings, views, etc., and through diverse modes of manifestation—therefore, to distinguish it further, it is said, 'with varied and diverse objects,' meaning objects of various kinds such as forms, etc.

Athettha dhīrā vinayanti chandanti atha etesu ārammaṇesu dhitisampannā paṇḍitā chandarāgaṃ vinayanti.

And here the wise dispel desire: that is, regarding these objects, the discerning, endowed with steadfastness, dispel desire and passion.

Tajjātikanti taṃsabhāvaṃ, atthato pana tassa kāmassa anurūpanti vuttaṃ hoti. Puññassa bhāgo puññabhāgo, puññakoṭṭhāso. Tena nibbatto, tattha vā bhavoti puññabhāgiyo. Apuññabhāgiyoti etthāpi eseva nayo. Vipākoyeva vepakkanti āha “vohāravipāka”nti.

'Of that kind' (tajjātika) means 'of that nature' (taṃsabhāva); but in meaning, it is said to be 'suitable for that desire' (tassa kāmassa anurūpa). A portion of merit is 'merit-portion' (puññabhāga), a share of merit (puññakoṭṭhāsa). One born from that, or existing therein, is 'partaking of merit' (puññabhāgiya). The same method applies to 'partaking of demerit' (apuññabhāgiya). The result itself is 'ripening' (vepakka); thus it is said, 'conventional result' (vohāravipāka).

Sabbasaṅgāhikāti kusalākusalasādhāraṇā. Saṃvidahanacetanāti sampayuttadhammesu saṃvidahanalakkhaṇā cetanā. Urattāḷinti uraṃ tāḷetvā[M 3.0140]. Ekapadanti ekapadacitaṃ mantaṃ. Tenāha “ekapadamantaṃ vā”tiādi.

'All-inclusive' (sabbasaṅgāhika) means common to both wholesome and unwholesome. 'Coordinating volition' (saṃvidahanacetanā) means the volition having the characteristic of coordinating associated states. 'Striking the chest' (urattāḷi) means having struck the chest. 'Single word' (ekapada) means a mantra consisting of a single word. Therefore it is said, 'or a mantra consisting of a single word,' and so forth.

Nibbedhikasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Nibbedhika Sutta is concluded.

10. Sīhanādasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Sīhanāda Sutta

64. Dasame tathāgatabalānīti aññehi asādhāraṇāni tathāgatasseva balāni. Nanu cetāni sāvakānampi ekaccāni uppajjantīti? Kāmaṃ uppajjanti, yādisāni pana buddhānaṃ ṭhānāṭṭhānañāṇādīni, na tādisāni tadaññesaṃ kadāci uppajjantīti aññehi asādhāraṇāni. Imameva hi yathāvuttaṃ lesaṃ apekkhitvā sādhāraṇabhāvato āsayānusayañāṇādīsu eva asādhāraṇasamaññā niruḷhā. Yathā pubbabuddhānaṃ balāni puññassa sampattiyā āgatāni, tathā āgatabalānīti vā tathāgatabalāni. Usabhassa idaṃ āsabhaṃ, seṭṭhaṭṭhānaṃ. Pamukhanādanti seṭṭhanādaṃ[V 3.0131]. Paṭivedhañāṇañceva desanāñāṇañcāti ettha paññāya pabhāvitaṃ attano ariyaphalāvahaṃ paṭivedhañāṇaṃ. Karuṇāya pabhāvitaṃ sāvakānaṃ ariyaphalāvahaṃ desanāñāṇaṃ. Tattha paṭivedhañāṇaṃ uppajjamānaṃ uppannanti duvidhaṃ. Tañhi abhinikkhamanato yāva arahattamaggā uppajjamānaṃ, phalakkhaṇe uppannaṃ nāma. Tusitabhavanato yāva mahābodhipallaṅke arahattamaggā uppajjamānaṃ, phalakkhaṇe uppannaṃ nāma. Dīpaṅkarato paṭṭhāya yāva arahattamaggā uppajjamānaṃ, phalakkhaṇe uppannaṃ nāma. Desanāñāṇampi pavattamānaṃ pavattanti duvidhaṃ. Tañhi yāva aññātakoṇḍaññassa sotāpattimaggā pavattamānaṃ, phalakkhaṇe pavattaṃ nāma. Tesu paṭivedhañāṇaṃ lokuttaraṃ, desanāñāṇaṃ lokiyaṃ. Ubhayampi panetaṃ aññehi asādhāraṇaṃ, buddhānaññeva orasañāṇaṃ.

64. In the tenth (sutta), 'the powers of the Tathāgata' means the powers unique to the Tathāgata alone, not shared by others. But do not some of these arise even in disciples? Yes, they do arise. However, such knowledge as the Buddhas' knowledge of what is possible and impossible, etc., never arises in others in the same way; hence, they are unshared. Indeed, it is by considering this very aspect as stated that the designation 'unshared' has become established, even though knowledges like that of inclinations and latent tendencies are shared. Or, the powers of the Tathāgata are so called because they have come about through the perfection of merit, just as the powers of past Buddhas came about. This 'bull-like' (āsabhaṃ) refers to the bull (usabha), meaning the supreme state. 'Foremost roar' (pamukhanāda) means 'supreme roar' (seṭṭhanāda). Regarding 'the knowledge of penetration' (paṭivedhañāṇa) and 'the knowledge of teaching' (desanāñāṇa): here, the knowledge of penetration is that which, developed by wisdom, brings the noble fruits to oneself. The knowledge of teaching is that which, developed by compassion, brings the noble fruits to disciples. In this context, the knowledge of penetration is twofold: 'arising' and 'arisen.' For it is called 'arising' from the time of renunciation until the path of arahantship, and 'arisen' at the moment of the fruit. It is called 'arising' from the Tusita abode until the path of arahantship at the great seat of enlightenment, and 'arisen' at the moment of the fruit. It is called 'arising' from Dīpaṅkara onwards until the path of arahantship, and 'arisen' at the moment of the fruit. The knowledge of teaching is also twofold: 'proceeding' and 'proceeded.' For it is called 'proceeding' until Aññāta Koṇḍañña's attainment of the path of stream-entry, and 'proceeded' at the moment of the fruit. Among these, the knowledge of penetration is supramundane, while the knowledge of teaching is mundane. Yet both are unshared by others—they are the Buddhas' own true knowledge.

Ṭhānañca ṭhānato pajānātīti kāraṇañca kāraṇato pajānāti. Yasmā tattha phalaṃ tiṭṭhati tadāyattavuttitāya uppajjati ceva pavattati ca, tasmā ṭhānanti vuccati. Bhagavā “ye ye dhammā yesaṃ yesaṃ dhammānaṃ hetū paccayā uppādāya, taṃ taṃ ṭhānaṃ, ye ye dhammā yeyaṃ yeyaṃ dhammānaṃ na hetū na paccayā uppādāya, taṃ taṃ aṭṭhāna”nti pajānanto ṭhānato aṭṭhānato yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti.

'He understands the possible as possible' means he understands the cause as cause. Because the result stands there, and arises and proceeds in dependence on that, therefore it is called 'the possible' (ṭhāna). The Blessed One, understanding thus: 'Whatever phenomena are a cause and condition for the arising of whatever phenomena, that is a possible cause (ṭhāna); whatever phenomena are not a cause and not a condition for the arising of whatever phenomena, that is an impossible cause (aṭṭhāna),' understands the possible and the impossible as they actually are.

Samādiyantīti [M 3.0141] samādānāni, tāni pana samādiyitvā katāni hontīti āha “samādiyitvā katāna”nti. Kammameva vā kammasamādānanti etena “samādāna”nti saddassa apubbatthābhāvaṃ dasseti muttagatasadde gatasaddassa viya. Gatīti nirayādigatiyo. Upadhīti attabhāvo. Kāloti kammassa vipaccanārahakālo. Payogoti vipākuppattiyā paccayabhūtā kiriyā.

'They undertake' (samādiyanti) means 'undertakings' (samādānāni); and since these are done by undertaking, it is said, 'of those undertaken and done.' Or, 'undertaking of action' (kammasamādāna) is simply the action itself; by this, it shows that the word 'samādāna' does not have a meaning distinct from its components, like the word 'gata' in the compound 'muttagata.' 'Destination' (gati) refers to destinations such as hell, etc. 'Substratum' (upadhi) means individual existence. 'Time' (kāla) is the time when the action is fit for ripening. 'Application' (payoga) refers to the action that serves as a condition for the arising of the result.

Catunnaṃ jhānānanti paccanīkajjhāpanaṭṭhena ārammaṇūpanijjhānaṭṭhena ca catunnaṃ rūpāvacarajjhānānaṃ. Catukkanayena hetaṃ vuttaṃ. Aṭṭhannaṃ vimokkhānanti “rūpī rūpāni passatī”tiādīnaṃ (ma. ni. 2.248; 3.312; dha. sa. 248; paṭi. ma. 1.209) aṭṭhannaṃ vimokkhānaṃ. Tiṇṇaṃ samādhīnanti savitakkasavicārādīnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ samādhīnaṃ. Navannaṃ anupubbasamāpattīnanti paṭhamajjhānasamāpattiādīnaṃ navannaṃ anupubbasamāpattīnaṃ. Ettha ca paṭipāṭiyā aṭṭhannaṃ samādhītipi nāmaṃ, samāpattītipi cittekaggatāsabbhāvato, nirodhasamāpattiyā tadabhāvato na samādhīti nāmaṃ. Hānabhāgiyaṃ dhammanti appaguṇehi paṭhamajjhānādīhi vuṭṭhitassa saññāmanasikārānaṃ kāmādipakkhandanaṃ. Visesabhāgiyaṃ dhammanti paguṇehi paṭhamajjhānādīhi vuṭṭhitassa saññāmanasikārānaṃ dutiyajjhānādipakkhandanaṃ. Iti saññāmanasikārānaṃ [V 3.0132] kāmādidutiyajjhānādipakkhandanāni hānabhāgiyavisesabhāgiyadhammāti dassitāni. Tehi pana jhānānaṃ taṃsabhāvatā dhammasaddena vuttā. Tasmāti vuttamevatthaṃ hetubhāvena paccāmasati. Vodānanti paguṇatāsaṅkhātaṃ vodānaṃ. Tañhi paṭhamajjhānādīhi vuṭṭhahitvā dutiyajjhānādīnaṃ adhigamassa paccayattā “vuṭṭhāna”nti vuttaṃ. Ye pana “nirodhato phalasamāpattiyā vuṭṭhānanti pāḷi natthī”ti vadanti. Te “nirodhā vuṭṭhahantassa nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ phalasamāpattiyā anantarapaccayena paccayo”ti imāya pāḷiyaṃ (paṭṭhā. 1.1.417) paṭisedhetabbā.

Of the four jhānas: in the sense of burning up opposition and in the sense of closely examining the object, these are the four form-sphere jhānas. This is said by way of the fourfold method. Of the eight liberations: the eight liberations such as 'one having form sees forms' (MN 2.248; 3.312; DhS 248; Paṭis 1.209). Of the three concentrations: the three concentrations such as those with initial and sustained thought. Of the nine successive attainments: the nine successive attainments beginning with the first jhāna attainment. Here, in sequence, the eight are also called concentrations, and they are called attainments because of the existence of mental one-pointedness; but the attainment of cessation is not called a concentration because of its absence. A state connected with decline: when emerging from the first jhāna, etc., which are of lesser quality, the perceptions and attention incline toward sensual pleasures, etc. A state connected with distinction: when emerging from the first jhāna, etc., which are well-mastered, the perceptions and attention incline toward the second jhāna, etc. Thus, the inclining of perceptions and attention toward sensual pleasures, etc., or toward the second jhāna, etc., are shown as states connected with decline and distinction. By these, however, the nature of the jhānas as such is expressed by the word 'state'. Therefore: this refers back to the very meaning just stated as the reason. Purification: purification is that which is designated as proficiency. For it is called 'emergence' because it is a condition for attaining the second jhāna, etc., after emerging from the first jhāna, etc. But those who say, 'There is no canonical text stating emergence from cessation into fruition attainment,' should be refuted by this canonical text (Paṭṭh 1.1.417): 'For one emerging from cessation, the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is a condition for fruition attainment by way of immediate conditionality.'

Sīhanādasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Lion's Roar Discourse is completed.

Mahāvaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Great Chapter is completed.

7. Devatāvaggo

7. The Chapter on Deities

1-3. Anāgāmiphalasuttādivaṇṇanā

1-3. Commentary on the Discourse on the Fruit of Non-Returning, and so on.

65-67. Sattamassa [M 3.0142] paṭhamādīni uttānatthāni. Tatiye abhisamācāre uttamasamācāre bhavaṃ ābhisamācārikaṃ, vattappaṭipattivattaṃ. Tenāha “uttamasamācārabhūta”ntiādi. Sekhapaṇṇattisīlanti sekhiyavasena paññattasīlaṃ.

65-67. The first terms of the seventh section and so on are clear in meaning. In the third discourse, on 'abhisamācāra' (higher conduct): that which pertains to excellent conduct is 'ābhisamācārika,' the practice of duties and observances. Therefore, he said, 'being of the nature of excellent conduct,' and so on. 'Sekhapaṇṇattisīla' means the virtue laid down by way of the training rules (sekhiya).

Anāgāmiphalasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on the Fruit of Non-Returning, and so on, is concluded.

4-5. Saṅgaṇikārāmasuttādivaṇṇanā

4-5. Commentary on the Discourse at Saṅgaṇikārāma, and so on.

68-69. Catutthe gaṇena saṅgaṇaṃ samodhānaṃ gaṇasaṅgaṇikā, sā āramitabbaṭṭhena ārāmo etassāti gaṇasaṅgaṇikārāmo. Saṅgaṇikāti vā sakaparisasamodhānaṃ. Gaṇoti nānājanasamodhānaṃ. Sesamettha suviññeyyameva. Pañcamaṃ uttānatthameva.

68-69. In the fourth discourse: 'gaṇasaṅgaṇikā' is associating with a group, a coming together. Because that association is a resort (ārāma) for one, in the sense of being resorted to, it is called 'gaṇasaṅgaṇikārāmo'. Or, 'saṅgaṇikā' means the assembling of one's own following. 'Gaṇa' means the assembling of diverse people. The rest here is quite easy to understand. The fifth discourse is clear in meaning.

Saṅgaṇikārāmasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse at Saṅgaṇikārāma, and so on, is concluded.

6. Samādhisuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Discourse on Concentration

70. Chaṭṭhe [V 3.0133] paṭippassambhanaṃ paṭippassaddhīti atthato ekanti āha “na paṭippassaddhiladdhenāti kilesappaṭippassaddhiyā aladdhenā”ti. Sukkapakkhe santenātiādīsu aṅgasantatāya ārammaṇasantatāya sabbakilesasantatāya ca santena, atappaniyaṭṭhena paṇītena, kilesappaṭippassaddhiyā laddhattā, kilesappaṭippassaddhibhāvaṃ vā laddhattā paṭippassaddhiladdhena, passaddhikilesena vā arahatā laddhattā paṭippassaddhiladdhena, ekodibhāvena adhigatattā ekodibhāvādhigatenāti evamattho daṭṭhabbo.

70. In the sixth discourse, regarding 'paṭippassambhanaṃ' (calming) and 'paṭippassaddhī' (tranquility), he says they are one in meaning: 'na paṭippassaddhiladdhena' means 'not by one who has not attained the tranquility of defilements.' In phrases beginning with 'in the bright side, by the peaceful,' 'by the peaceful' (santena) refers to being peaceful through the calmness of the factors, the calmness of the object, and the calmness of all defilements; 'by the sublime' (paṇītena) in the sense of being without torment; 'attained by tranquility' (paṭippassaddhiladdhena) because it is attained through the tranquility of defilements, or because the state of tranquility of defilements is attained. Alternatively, 'attained by tranquility' because it is attained by an arahant whose defilements have been tranquilized; 'attained by unification' (ekodibhāvādhigatena) because it is attained by unification. This is how the meaning should be understood.

Samādhisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on Concentration is concluded.

7-10. Sakkhibhabbasuttādivaṇṇanā

7-10. Commentary on the Discourse on the Capability to Witness, and so on.

71-74. Sattame [M 3.0143] tasmiṃ tasmiṃ viseseti tasmiṃ tasmiṃ sacchikātabbe visese. Sakkhibhāvāya paccakkhakāritāya bhabbo sakkhibhabbo, tassa bhāvo sakkhibhabbatā. Taṃ sakkhibhabbataṃ. Sati satiāyataneti sati satikāraṇe. Kiñcettha kāraṇaṃ? Abhiññā vā abhiññāpādakajjhānaṃ vā, avasāne pana chaṭṭhābhiññāya arahattaṃ vā kāraṇaṃ, arahattassa vipassanā vāti veditabbaṃ. Yañhi taṃ tatra tatra sakkhibhabbatāsaṅkhātaṃ iddhividhapaccanubhavanādi, tassa abhiññā kāraṇaṃ. Atha iddhividhapaccanubhavanādi abhiññā, evaṃ sati abhiññāpādakajjhānaṃ kāraṇaṃ. Arahattampi “kudāssu nāmāhaṃ tadāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharissāmī”ti anuttaresu vimokkhesu pihaṃ upaṭṭhapetvā chaṭṭhābhiññaṃ nibbattentassa kāraṇaṃ. Idañca sabbasādhāraṇaṃ na hoti, sādhāraṇavasena pana arahattassa vipassanā kāraṇaṃ. Atha vā sati āyataneti tassa tassa visesādhigamassa upanissayasaṅkhāte kāraṇe satīti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

71-74. In the seventh discourse, 'tasmiṃ tasmiṃ visese' (in each specific case) means 'in each specific distinction to be realized' (tasmiṃ tasmiṃ sacchikātabbe visese). One is capable of witnessing, capable of making things directly present (sakkhibhabbo); the state of being so is 'sakkhibhabbatā'. That is 'sakkhibhabbataṃ'. 'Sati āyatane' means 'when there is a cause' (sati kāraṇe). What is the cause here? It should be understood that either direct knowledge (abhiññā) or the jhāna that is the basis for direct knowledge is the cause; or, ultimately, arahantship by means of the sixth direct knowledge is the cause; or it is the insight leading to arahantship. For whatever is designated as 'witness-capability' in various instances—such as experiencing the kinds of psychic power—direct knowledge is the cause. If the experience of the kinds of psychic power and so on is direct knowledge, then in that case the jhāna that is the basis for direct knowledge is the cause. Even arahantship becomes the cause for one who produces the sixth direct knowledge after having established a longing for the unsurpassed liberations with the thought, 'When will I enter and dwell in that sphere?' And this is not common to all; in a general sense, however, the insight leading to arahantship is the cause. Alternatively, 'sati āyatane' means 'when there is a cause,' that is, a supporting condition for achieving each specific distinction. This is how the meaning should be understood here.

Hānabhāgiyādīsu “paṭhamajjhānassa lābhiṃ kāmasahagatā saññāmanasikārā samudācaranti, hānabhāgiyo samādhi. Tadanudhammatā sati santiṭṭhati, ṭhitibhāgiyo samādhi. Avitakkasahagatā saññāmanasikārā samudācaranti, visesabhāgiyo samādhi. Nibbidāsahagatā saññāmanasikārā samudācaranti virāgūpasaṃhitā, nibbedhabhāgiyo samādhī”ti (vibha. 799) iminā nayena sabbasamāpattiyo vitthāretvā hānabhāgiyādiattho veditabbo. Tattha paṭhamajjhānassa lābhinti [V 3.0134] yvāyaṃ appaguṇassa paṭhamassa jhānassa lābhī, taṃ. Kāmasahagatā saññāmanasikārā samudācarantīti tato vuṭṭhitaṃ ārammaṇavasena kāmasahagatā hutvā saññāmanasikārā samudācaranti tudanti, tassa kāmānatītassa kāmānupakkhandānaṃ saññāmanasikārānaṃ vasena so paṭhamajjhānasamādhi hāyati parihāyati, tasmā hānabhāgiyo vutto. Tadanudhammatāti tadanurūpasabhāvo. Sati santiṭṭhatīti idaṃ micchāsatiṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Yassa hi paṭhamajjhānānurūpasabhāvā paṭhamajjhānaṃ santato paṇītato disvā assādayamānā abhinandamānā nikanti hoti, tassa nikantivasena so paṭhamajjhānasamādhi neva hāyati na vaḍḍhati, ṭhitikoṭṭhāsiko hoti. Tena vuttaṃ [M 3.0144] “ṭhitibhāgiyo samādhī”ti. Avitakkasahagatāti avitakkaṃ dutiyajjhānaṃ santato paṇītato manasikaroto ārammaṇavasena avitakkasahagatā. Saññāmanasikārā samudācarantīti paguṇapaṭhamajjhānato vuṭṭhitaṃ dutiyajjhānādhigamatthāya codenti tudanti. Tassa upari dutiyajjhānānupakkhandānaṃ saññāmanasikārānaṃ vasena so paṭhamajjhānasamādhi visesabhūtassa dutiyajjhānassa uppattipadaṭṭhānatāya “visesabhāgiyo”ti vutto.

In the section on decline and so forth, the meaning of 'associated with decline' and so on should be understood by elaborating all attainments in this way, as stated: 'For one who has attained the first jhāna, perceptions and attention connected with sensuality arise—this is concentration associated with decline. When mindfulness in accordance with that nature persists—this is concentration associated with stability. Perceptions and attention connected with the absence of thought arise—this is concentration associated with distinction. Perceptions and attention connected with disenchantment arise, directed toward dispassion—this is concentration associated with penetration.' (Vibh 799). Here, 'one who has attained the first jhāna' refers to one who has attained the first jhāna of lesser quality. 'Perceptions and attention connected with sensuality arise' means that after emerging from it, perceptions and attention connected with sensuality arise through the object, assailing him. For one who has not transcended sensual pleasures, due to those perceptions and attention that incline toward sensual pleasures, his first jhāna concentration declines and deteriorates. Therefore, it is called 'associated with decline.' 'In accordance with that nature' means having a nature corresponding to it. 'When mindfulness persists' is said with reference to wrong mindfulness. For one who, seeing the first jhāna as peaceful and sublime in accordance with its nature, delights in it, enjoys it, and has a craving for it—due to that craving, his first jhāna concentration neither declines nor grows but remains in a state of stability. Hence, it is called 'concentration associated with stability.' 'Connected with the absence of thought' refers to one who attends to the second jhāna, which is free of thought, as peaceful and sublime; through the object, his attention is connected with the absence of thought. 'Perceptions and attention arise' means they urge and prod one who has emerged from a proficient first jhāna for the purpose of attaining the second jhāna. Due to those perceptions and attention that incline toward the higher second jhāna, his first jhāna concentration is called 'associated with distinction' because it serves as the basis for the arising of the distinguished second jhāna.

Nibbidāsahagatāti tameva paṭhamajjhānalābhiṃ jhānato vuṭṭhitaṃ nibbidāsaṅkhātena vipassanāñāṇena sahagatā. Vipassanāñāṇañhi jhānaṅgesu pabhedena upaṭṭhahantesu nibbindati ukkaṇṭhati, tasmā “nibbidā”ti vuccati. Samudācarantīti nibbānasacchikiriyatthāya codenti tudanti. Virāgūpasaṃhitāti virāgasaṅkhātena nibbānena upasaṃhitā. Vipassanāñāṇañhi sakkā iminā maggena virāgaṃ nibbānaṃ sacchikātunti pavattito “virāgūpasaṃhita”nti vuccati. Taṃsampayuttā saññāmanasikārā virāgūpasaṃhitā eva nāma. Tassa tesaṃ saññāmanasikārānaṃ vasena paṭhamajjhānasamādhi ariyamaggappaṭivedhassa padaṭṭhānatāya “nibbedhabhāgiyo”ti vutto. Hānaṃ bhajantīti hānabhāgiyā, hānabhāgo vā etesaṃ atthīti hānabhāgiyā, parihānakoṭṭhāsikāti attho. Iminā nayena ṭhitibhāgiyo veditabbo. Aṭṭhamādīni uttānatthāneva.

'Accompanied by disenchantment' (nibbidāsahagatā) means they are accompanied by the insight knowledge called 'disenchantment' (nibbidā) for that same attainer of the first jhāna who has emerged from the jhāna. For when the factors of jhāna appear distinctly, insight knowledge becomes disenchanted and weary of them; hence it is called 'disenchantment.' 'They occur' (samudācaranti) means they urge and prod for the sake of realizing Nibbāna. 'Connected with dispassion' (virāgūpasaṃhitā) means connected with Nibbāna, which is designated as 'dispassion.' Because insight knowledge proceeds with the thought, 'By this path, it is possible to realize dispassion, Nibbāna,' it is called 'connected with dispassion.' The perceptions and attentions associated with it are indeed called 'connected with dispassion.' On account of these perceptions and attentions, the concentration of the first jhāna, being a basis for the penetration of the noble path, is called 'partaking of penetration' (nibbedhabhāgiyo). 'Partaking of decline' (hānabhāgiyā) means 'they partake of decline' (hānaṃ bhajanti), or 'they have a share in decline' (hānabhāgo vā etesaṃ atthi); the meaning is 'belonging to the portion of decline.' In this way, 'partaking of stability' (ṭhitibhāgiyo) should be understood. The eighth and following are clear in meaning.

Sakkhibhabbasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Sakkhibhabba Sutta and so forth is concluded.

Devatāvaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Devatā Vagga is concluded.

8. Arahattavaggo

8. The Chapter on Arahantship

1-3. Dukkhasuttādivaṇṇanā

1–3. Commentary on the Dukkha Sutta and so forth.

75-77. Aṭṭhamassa [V 3.0135] paṭhamādīsu natthi vattabbaṃ. Tatiye tividhaṃ kuhanavatthunti paccayappaṭisevanasāmantajappanairiyāpathappavattanasaṅkhātaṃ tividhaṃ kuhanavatthuṃ. Ukkhipitvāti “mahākuṭumbiko mahānāviko mahādānapatī”tiādinā paggaṇhitvā lapanaṃ. Avakkhipitvāti “kiṃ imassa jīvitaṃ, bījabhojano nāmāya”nti hīḷetvā lapanaṃ.

75–77. Regarding the first and following points of the eighth sutta, there is nothing to be said. In the third, 'the threefold basis for deceit' means the threefold basis for deceit designated as the use of requisites, hinting, and the adoption of postures. 'Having extolled' (ukkhipitvā) means speaking after praising with phrases such as, “A great householder, a great shipowner, a great benefactor.” 'Having disparaged' (avakkhipitvā) means speaking after belittling with phrases such as, “What is this life of his? He is a mere seed-eater.”

Dukkhasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Dukkha Sutta and so forth is concluded.

4. Sukhasomanassasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Sukhasomanassa Sutta

78. Catutthe [M 3.0145] yathāvuttadhammādīsu tassa kilesanimittaṃ dukkhaṃ anavassananti “sukhasomanassabahulo viharatī”ti vuttaṃ. Kāyikasukhañceva cetasikasomanassañca bahulaṃ assāti sukhasomanassabahulo. Yavati tena phalaṃ missitaṃ viya hotīti yoni, ekantikaṃ kāraṇaṃ. Assāti yathāvuttassa bhikkhuno. Paripuṇṇanti avikalaṃ anavasesaṃ.

78. In the fourth, regarding the qualities as stated, because the suffering that is the sign of his defilements does not flow down, it is said, “He dwells abundant in pleasure and joy.” 'Abundant in pleasure and joy' (sukhasomanassabahulo) means he has abundant bodily pleasure and mental joy. 'Source' (yoni) is the decisive cause, so called because the fruit is, as it were, blended with it. 'His' (assa) refers to the aforementioned bhikkhu. 'Complete' (paripuṇṇaṃ) means without deficiency, without remainder.

Sukhasomanassasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Sukhasomanassa Sutta is concluded.

5. Adhigamasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Adhigama Sutta

79. Pañcame āgacchanti etena kusalā vā akusalā vāti āgamanaṃ, kusalākusalānaṃ uppattikāraṇaṃ. Tattha kusaloti āgamanakusalo. Evaṃ dhamme manasikaroto kusalā vā akusalā vā dhammā abhivaḍḍhantīti evaṃ jānanto. Apagacchanti kusalā vā akusalā vā etenāti apagamanaṃ. Tesaṃ eva anuppattikāraṇaṃ, tattha kusaloti apagamanakusalo. Evaṃ dhamme manasikaroto kusalā vā akusalā vā dhammā nābhivaḍḍhantīti evaṃ [V 3.0136] jānanto. Upāyakusaloti ṭhānuppattikapaññāsamannāgato. Idañca accāyikakicce vā bhaye vā uppanne tassa tikicchanatthaṃ ṭhānuppattiyā kāraṇajānanavasena veditabbaṃ.

79. In the fifth, 'coming' (āgamana) is so called because 'by this, wholesome or unwholesome states come.' It is the cause for the arising of wholesome and unwholesome states. Herein, 'skillful' means skillful in coming; that is, knowing thus: 'When one attends to things in this way, wholesome or unwholesome states increase.' 'Departing' (apagamana) is so called because 'by this, wholesome or unwholesome states depart.' It is the cause for their non-arising. Herein, 'skillful' means skillful in departing; that is, knowing thus: 'When one attends to things in this way, wholesome or unwholesome states do not increase.' 'Skillful in means' (upāyakusalo) means endowed with the wisdom of ready wit. And this should be understood as knowing the reason for a ready response in order to remedy an urgent matter or a danger that has arisen.

Adhigamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Adhigama Sutta is concluded.

6-7. Mahantattasuttādivaṇṇanā

6–7. Commentary on the Mahantatta Sutta and so forth.

80-81. Chaṭṭhe sampatteti kilese sampatte. Sattamaṃ uttānameva.

80–81. In the sixth, 'when encountered' (sampatte) means when defilements are encountered. The seventh is clear in meaning.

Mahantattasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Mahantatta Sutta and so forth is concluded.

8-10. Dutiyanirayasuttādivaṇṇanā

8–10. Commentary on the Second Niraya Sutta and so forth.

82-84. Aṭṭhame [M 3.0146] kāyapāgabbhiyādīhīti ādi-saddena vacīpāgabbhiyaṃ manopāgabbhiyañca saṅgaṇhāti. Navamādīni uttānatthāneva.

82–84. In the eighth, in the phrase 'with bodily impudence, and so forth,' the word 'and so forth' includes verbal impudence and mental impudence. The ninth and following are clear in meaning.

Dutiyanirayasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Second Niraya Sutta and so forth is concluded.

Arahattavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Chapter on Arahantship is concluded.

9. Sītivaggo

9. The Chapter on Coolness

1. Sītibhāvasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Sītibhāva Sutta

85. Navamassa paṭhame sītibhāvanti nibbānaṃ, kilesavūpasamaṃ vā. Niggaṇhātīti accāraddhavīriyatādīhi uddhataṃ cittaṃ uddhaccapakkhato rakkhaṇavasena niggaṇhāti. Paggaṇhātīti atisithilavīriyatādīhi līnaṃ cittaṃ kosajjapātato rakkhaṇavasena paggaṇhāti. Sampahaṃsetīti samappavattacittaṃ tathāpavattiyaṃ paññāya toseti uttejeti vā. Yadā vā paññāpayogamandatāya [V 3.0137] upasamasukhānadhigamena vā nirassādaṃ cittaṃ bhāvanāya na pakkhandati, tadā jātiādīni saṃvegavatthūni paccavekkhitvā sampahaṃseti samuttejeti. Ajjhupekkhatīti yadā pana cittaṃ alīnaṃ anuddhataṃ anirassādaṃ ārammaṇe samappavattaṃ sammadeva bhāvanāvītiṃ otiṇṇaṃ hoti, tadā paggahaniggahasampahaṃsanesu kiñci byāpāraṃ akatvā samappavattesu assesu sārathī viya ajjhupekkhati, upekkhakova hoti. Paṇītādhimuttikoti paṇīte uttame maggaphale adhimutto ninnapoṇapabbhāro.

85. In the first of the ninth, 'the state of coolness' (sītibhāvaṃ) means Nibbāna, or the stilling of defilements. 'One restrains' (niggaṇhāti) means that with excessive energy and so forth, one restrains the agitated mind, guarding it from the side of restlessness. 'One encourages' (paggaṇhāti) means that with overly slack energy and so forth, one encourages the sluggish mind, guarding it from falling into laziness. 'One gladdens' (sampahaṃseti) means one delights or inspires a properly engaged mind with wisdom in that very engagement. Or, when the mind, due to dullness in the application of wisdom or through not attaining the bliss of tranquility, is without relish and does not leap toward meditation, then one reflects on the grounds for spiritual urgency, such as birth, and so forth, and gladdens and inspires it. 'One looks on with equanimity' (ajjhupekkhati) means that when the mind is neither sluggish nor agitated nor without relish, but is properly engaged in the object and has rightly entered upon the path of meditation, then, without making any effort in encouraging, restraining, or gladdening, one looks on with equanimity, like a charioteer with well-behaved horses; one becomes equanimous. 'Resolved on the sublime' (paṇītādhimuttiko) means one is resolved on, inclined to, sloping towards, and bent on the sublime, the supreme path and fruit.

Sītibhāvasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Sītibhāva Sutta is concluded.

2-11. Āvaraṇasuttādivaṇṇanā

2–11. Commentary on the Āvaraṇa Sutta and so forth.

86-95. Dutiye acchandikoti kattukamyatākusalacchandarahito. Uttarakurukā manussā acchandikaṭṭhānaṃ paviṭṭhā. Duppaññoti bhavaṅgapaññāya parihīno[M 3.0147]. Bhavaṅgapaññāya pana paripuṇṇāyapi yassa bhavaṅgaṃ lokuttarassa paccayo na hoti, sopi duppañño eva nāma. Abhabbo niyāmaṃ okkamituṃ kusalesu dhammesu sammattanti kusalesu dhammesu sammattaniyāmasaṅkhātaṃ ariyamaggaṃ okkamituṃ adhigantuṃ abhabbo. Na kammāvaraṇatāyātiādīsu abhabbavipariyāyena attho veditabbo. Catutthādīni uttānatthāni.

86–95. In the second, 'without desire' (acchandiko) means devoid of wholesome desire, which is the wish to act. The humans of Uttarakuru have entered the state of being without desire. 'Of weak wisdom' (duppañño) means deficient in the wisdom of the life-continuum. However, even one whose wisdom of the life-continuum is complete, if his life-continuum is not a condition for the supramundane, he too is called 'of weak wisdom.' 'Incapable of entering the fixed course of rightness in wholesome states' means incapable of entering, of attaining, the noble path, which is designated as the fixed course of rightness in wholesome states. In phrases such as 'not due to the obstruction of kamma,' the meaning should be understood as the opposite of 'incapable.' The fourth and following are clear in meaning.

Āvaraṇasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Āvaraṇa Sutta and so forth is concluded.

Sītivaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Sītivagga is concluded.

10. Ānisaṃsavaggo

10. The Chapter on Advantages

1-11. Pātubhāvasuttādivaṇṇanā

1–11. Commentary on the Pātubhāva Sutta and so forth.

96-106. Dasamassa paṭhamādīsu natthi vattabbaṃ. Aṭṭhame mettā etassa atthīti mettāvā, tassa bhāvo mettāvatā, mettāpaṭipatti, tāya. Sā pana mettāvatā mettāvasena pāricariyāti [V 3.0138] āha “mettāyuttāya pāricariyāyā”ti. Paricaranti vippakatabrahmacariyattā. Pariciṇṇasatthukena sāvakena nāma satthuno yāva dhammena kātabbā pāricariyā, tāya sammadeva sampāditattā. Navamādīni uttānatthāni.

96-106. Regarding the tenth section, from the first sutta onwards, there is nothing to be said. In the eighth, `mettāvā` is one for whom there is loving-kindness (`mettā etassa atthīti`); its state is `mettāvatā`, that is, the practice of loving-kindness; by that. But that `mettāvatā` is service by way of loving-kindness; thus it is said, 'by service endowed with loving-kindness' (`mettāyuttāya pāricariyāyā`ti). They serve because their holy life is incomplete. For the service that should be rendered to the Teacher by a disciple who has served the Teacher is, by that, perfectly accomplished as is proper. The ninth and subsequent sections are clear in meaning.

Pātubhāvasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Pātubhāva Sutta and others is concluded.

Ānisaṃsavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Ānisaṃsa Vagga is concluded.

107-116. Ekādasamavaggo uttānatthoyeva.

107-116. The eleventh chapter is entirely clear in meaning.

Iti manorathapūraṇiyā aṅguttaranikāya-aṭṭhakathāya

Thus, in the Manorathapūraṇī, the commentary on the Aṅguttara Nikāya,

Chakkanipātavaṇṇanāya anuttānatthadīpanā samattā.

the elucidation of unclear meanings for the commentary on the Book of the Sixes is completed.

. Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa.

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

1. The First Fifty

1. Commentary on the Chapter on Wealth

1-10. Sattakanipātassa [V 3.0139] paṭhamo vaggo uttānattho.

1-10. The first chapter of the Book of the Sevens has an easily understood meaning.

2. Anusayavaggo

2. The Section on Underlying Tendencies

4.Puggalasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Puggala Sutta.

14. Dutiyassa [M 3.0149] catutthe ubhato ubhayathā, ubhato ubhohi bhāgehi vimuttoti ubhatobhāgavimutto ekadesasarūpekasesanayena. Dvīhi bhāgehīti karaṇe nissakke cetaṃ bahuvacanaṃ[V 3.0140]. Āvuttiādivasena ayaṃ niyamo veditabboti āha “arūpasamāpattiyā”tiādi. Etena “samāpattiyā vikkhambhanavimokkhena, maggena samucchedavimokkhena vimuttattā ubhatobhāgavimutto”ti evaṃ pavatto tipiṭakacūḷanāgattheravādo, “nāmakāyato rūpakāyato ca vimuttattā ubhatobhāgavimutto”ti evaṃ pavatto tipiṭakamahārakkhitattheravādo, “samāpattiyā vikkhambhanavimokkhena ekavāraṃ, maggena samucchedavimokkhena ekavāraṃ vimuttattā ubhatobhāgavimutto”ti evaṃ pavatto tipiṭakacūḷābhayattheravādo cāti imesaṃ tiṇṇampi theravādānaṃ ekajjhaṃ saṅgaho katoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ettha ca paṭhamavāde dvīhi bhāgehi vimutto ubhatobhāgavimutto vutto, dutiyavāde ubhato bhāgato vimuttoti ubhatobhāgavimutto, tatiyavāde dvīhi bhāgehi dve vāre vimuttoti ayametesaṃ visesoti. Vimuttoti kilesehi vimutto, kilesavikkhambhanasamucchedanehi vā kāyato vimuttohi attho.

14. In the fourth sutta of the second vagga, `ubhatobhāgavimutto` (released both ways) means released from both (`ubhato`), in both ways (`ubhayathā`); released from both parts (`ubhohi bhāgehi`), by way of the `ekasesa` method where one part represents the whole of a similar kind. The plural 'by two parts' is in the instrumental case, and this is in the sense of 'without remainder'. This rule should be understood by way of repetition and so forth, thus it is said: 'by the formless attainment,' and so on. By this, it should be understood that the view of the Elder Cūḷanāga of the Tipiṭaka—'one is called released both ways because one is released by the suppression-liberation of attainment and by the eradication-liberation of the path'—the view of the Elder Mahārakkhita of the Tipiṭaka—'one is called released both ways because one is released from the mental body and the physical body'—and the view of the Elder Cūḷābhaya of the Tipiṭaka—'one is called released both ways because one is released once by the suppression-liberation of attainment and once by the eradication-liberation of the path'—that these three elders' views have been brought together as one. And here, in the first view, 'released both ways' is said of one released by two parts; in the second view, 'released both ways' is one released from both parts; in the third view, it is one released by two parts two times—this is the distinction among them. 'Released' means released from defilements, or the meaning is released from the body by the suppression and eradication of defilements.

Soti ubhatobhāgavimutto. Kāmañcettha rūpāvacaracatutthajjhānampi arūpāvacarajjhānaṃ viya duvaṅgikaṃ āneñjappattanti vuccati. Taṃ pana padaṭṭhānaṃ katvā arahattaṃ patto ubhatobhāgavimutto nāma na hoti rūpakāyato [M 3.0150] avimuttattā. Tañhi kilesakāyatova vimuttaṃ, na rūpakāyato, tasmā tato vuṭṭhāya arahattaṃ patto ubhatobhāgavimutto na hotīti āha “catunnaṃ arūpa…pe… pañcavidho hotī”ti. Arūpasamāpattīnanti niddhāraṇe sāmivacanaṃ. Arahattaṃ pattaanāgāminoti bhūtapubbagatiyā vuttaṃ. Na hi arahattaṃ patto anāgāmī nāma hoti. “Rūpī rūpāni passatī”tiādike nirodhasamāpattiante aṭṭha vimokkhe vatvā –

He is one released both ways. Here, even the fourth jhāna of the form realm, like a formless jhāna, is called 'attained to imperturbability' due to having two factors. However, one who attains arahantship based on that is not called 'released both ways,' because one is not released from the form body. For one is released only from the body of defilements, not from the form body; therefore, one who emerges from that and attains arahantship is not 'released both ways.' Hence, it is said, 'Of the four formless... it is fivefold.' The term 'of the formless attainments' is a genitive expression used in determination. 'A non-returner who has attained arahantship' is said with reference to a previous state. For one who has attained arahantship is not called a non-returner. Having spoken of the eight liberations, from 'One with form sees forms' up to the attainment of cessation—

“Yato ca kho, ānanda, bhikkhu ime aṭṭha vimokkhe kāyena phusitvā viharati, paññāya cassa disvā āsavā parikkhīṇā honti. Ayaṃ vuccati, ānanda, bhikkhu ubhatobhāgavimutto”ti –

And when, Ānanda, a bhikkhu dwells having contacted these eight liberations with his body, and his taints are destroyed through having seen with wisdom, this bhikkhu, Ānanda, is called one released both ways.

Yadipi mahānidāne (dī. ni. 2.130) vuttaṃ, taṃ pana ubhatobhāgavimuttaseṭṭhavasena vuttanti, idha pana sabbaubhatobhāgavimutte saṅgahaṇatthaṃ “pañcavidho hotī”ti vatvā “pāḷi panettha…pe… aṭṭhavimokkhalābhino vasena āgatā”ti āha. Majjhimanikāye pana kīṭāgirisutte (ma. ni. 2.182) –

Even though it is stated in the Mahānidāna (Dī. Ni. 2.130), that, however, is said in terms of the foremost of those released both ways. Here, however, to include all those released both ways, having said 'There are five kinds,' it is explained, 'The Pāli here... up to... comes in terms of those who attain the eight liberations.' In the Majjhima Nikāya, however, in the Kīṭāgiri Sutta (Ma. Ni. 2.182)—

“Katamo ca, bhikkhave, puggalo ubhatobhāgavimutto? Idha, bhikkhave, ekacco puggalo ye te santā vimokkhā atikkamma rūpe āruppā, te kāyena phusitvā viharati[V 3.0141], paññāya cassa disvā āsavā parikkhīṇā honti. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, puggalo ubhatobhāgavimutto”ti –

And what, bhikkhus, is the person released in both ways? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person, transcending forms, contacts with his body those peaceful liberations that are formless, and his taints are destroyed by seeing with wisdom. This, bhikkhus, is called the person released in both ways.

Arūpasamāpattivasena cattāro ubhatobhāgavimuttā, seṭṭho ca vutto vuttalakkhaṇūpapattito. Yathāvuttesu hi pañcasu purimā cattāro samāpattisīsaṃ nirodhaṃ na samāpajjantīti pariyāyena ubhatobhāgavimuttā nāma. Aṭṭhasamāpattilābhī anāgāmī taṃ samāpajjitvā tato vuṭṭhāya vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pattoti nippariyāyena ubhatobhāgavimuttaseṭṭho nāma.

By means of the formless attainments, four are released both ways, and the foremost is declared due to possessing the characteristics as stated. Indeed, among the five mentioned, the first four do not attain cessation at the peak of attainment; thus, they are called 'released both ways' in a qualified sense. An anāgāmī who has gained the eight attainments, having attained them and arisen from them, develops insight and attains arahantship; this is called the foremost 'released both ways' in an unqualified sense.

Katamo ca puggalotiādi puggalapaññattipāḷi. Tattha katamoti pucchāvacanaṃ. Puggaloti asādhāraṇato pucchitabbavacanaṃ. Idhāti idhasmiṃ sāsane. Ekaccoti eko. Aṭṭha vimokkhe kāyena phusitvā viharatīti [M 3.0151] aṭṭha samāpattiyo samāpajjitvā nāmakāyato paṭilabhitvā viharati. Paññāya cassa disvā āsavā parikkhīṇā hontīti vipassanāpaññāya saṅkhāragataṃ, maggapaññāya cattāri saccāni passitvā cattāropi āsavā parikkhīṇā honti. Disvāti dassanahetu. Na hi āsave paññāya passanti, dassanakāraṇā pana parikkhīṇā disvā parikkhīṇāti vuttā dassanāyattaparikkhayattā. Evañhi dassanaṃ āsavānaṃ khayassa purimakiriyābhāvena vuttaṃ.

And what is a person? This is the Person-Designation text. Therein, 'what' is a question. 'Person' is a term to be specifically asked about. 'Here' means in this Dispensation. 'Some' means one. 'Having contacted with his body the eight liberations, he dwells' means he attains the eight meditative attainments and dwells, having obtained them by way of the mental body. 'And through wisdom, having seen, his taints are destroyed' means through insight wisdom, seeing conditioned phenomena, and through path wisdom, seeing the four truths, all four taints are destroyed. 'Having seen' means 'due to seeing.' For taints are not seen by wisdom itself, but because they are destroyed due to seeing, it is said 'having seen, they are destroyed'—because their destruction is dependent on seeing. Thus, seeing is said to be the prior action in the destruction of the taints.

Paññāvimuttoti visesato paññāya eva vimutto, na tassa adhiṭṭhānabhūtena aṭṭhavimokkhasaṅkhātena sātisayena samādhināti paññāvimutto. Yo ariyo anadhigataaṭṭhavimokkho sabbaso āsavehi vimutto, tassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Adhigatepi hi rūpajjhānavimokkhe na so sātisayasamādhinissitoti na tassa vasena ubhatobhāgavimuttatā hotīti vuttovāyamattho. Arūpajjhānesu pana ekasmimpi sati ubhatobhāgavimuttoyeva nāma hoti. Tena hi aṭṭhavimokkhekadesena taṃnāmadānasamatthena aṭṭhavimokkhalābhītveva vuccati. Samudāye hi pavatto vohāro avayavepi dissati yathā taṃ “sattisayo”ti anavasesato āsavānaṃ parikkhīṇattā. Aṭṭhavimokkhapaṭikkhepavaseneva na ekadesabhūtarūpajjhānappaṭikkhepavasena. Evañhi arūpajjhānekadesābhāvepi aṭṭhavimokkhapaṭikkhepo na hotīti siddhaṃ hoti. Arūpāvacarajjhānesu hi ekasmimpi sati ubhatobhāgavimuttoyeva nāma hoti.

'Released by wisdom' means one released specifically by wisdom alone, not by the superior concentration that serves as its foundation, known as the eight liberations; thus one is 'released by wisdom.' This is a designation for a noble one who has not attained the eight liberations but is completely released from all taints. For even when the form-jhāna liberations are attained, since one is not dependent on superior concentration, one is not 'released both ways' by means of that; this meaning has already been stated. But if even one of the formless jhānas is present, one is indeed called 'released both ways.' Therefore, by a part of the eight liberations that is capable of conferring that name, one is indeed called an 'obtainer of the eight liberations.' For a conventional expression that applies to the whole is also seen to apply to a part, as in the case of 'a forest of spears.' This is because the taints are utterly destroyed. The exclusion is by way of rejecting the eight liberations as a whole, not by way of rejecting the form jhānas which are a part of them. Thus it is established that even in the absence of a part of the formless jhānas, there is no rejection of the eight liberations. For if even one of the formless-sphere jhānas is present, one is indeed called 'released both ways'.

Phuṭṭhantaṃ sacchikatoti phuṭṭhānaṃ anto phuṭṭhanto, phuṭṭhānaṃ arūpajjhānānaṃ anantaro kāloti adhippāyo. Accantasaṃyoge cetaṃ upayogavacanaṃ. Taṃ phuṭṭhānantarakālameva sacchikātabbaṃ sacchikato [V 3.0142] sacchikaraṇūpāyenāti vuttaṃ hoti, bhāvanapuṃsakaṃ vā etaṃ “ekamantaṃ nisīdī”tiādīsu viya. Yo hi arūpajjhānena rūpakāyato nāmakāyekadesato ca vikkhambhanavimokkhena vimutto, tena nirodhasaṅkhāto vimokkho ālocito pakāsito viya hoti, na pana kāyena sacchikato. Nirodhaṃ pana ārammaṇaṃ katvā ekaccesu āsavesu khepitesu tena so sacchikato hoti, tasmā so sacchikātabbaṃ nirodhaṃ yathāālocitaṃ nāmakāyena sacchi karotīti “kāyasakkhī”ti vuccati, na [M 3.0152] tu “vimutto”ti ekaccānaṃ āsavānaṃ aparikkhīṇattā. Tenāha “jhānaphassaṃ paṭhamaṃ phusati, pacchā nirodhaṃ nibbānaṃ sacchikarotī”ti. Ayaṃ catunnaṃ arūpasamāpattīnaṃ ekekato vuṭṭhāya saṅkhāre sammasitvā kāyasakkhibhāvaṃ pattānaṃ catunnaṃ, nirodhā vuṭṭhāya aggamaggappattaanāgāmino ca vasena ubhatobhāgavimutto viya pañcavidho nāma hotīti vuttaṃ abhidhammaṭīkāyaṃ (pu. pa. mūlaṭī. 24) “kāyasakkhimhipi eseva nayo”ti. Ekacce āsavāti heṭṭhimamaggavajjhā āsavā.

“The end of what is touched is realized” means the end of the act of touching, that is, the time immediately after the immaterial jhānas have been experienced. This is a term of application denoting complete connection. It is said that what should be realized is to be realized at the very moment immediately after touching—through the means of realization—or this is a neuter verbal noun indicating a state, like in phrases such as “sat down to one side.” For one liberated through the immaterial jhāna, suppressing the form-body and a part of the mental body by way of liberation by suppression, the liberation called cessation is discerned and revealed, but not realized with the body. However, by making cessation the object and having eradicated some taints, one realizes it. Therefore, one who realizes with the mental body the cessation that is to be realized—as it has been discerned—is called a “body-witness,” but not “liberated,” because some taints remain uneradicated. Hence, it is said: “First, one contacts the jhāna-contact, then realizes cessation, Nibbāna.” This refers to the four types of individuals who emerge from each of the four immaterial attainments, contemplate formations, and attain the state of a body-witness, as well as the non-returner who attains the highest path after emerging from cessation. Thus, there are five types, similar to the one liberated in both ways, as stated in the Abhidhamma subcommentary (Puggalapaññatti Mūlaṭīkā 24): “The same method applies to the body-witness.” “Some taints” refers to the taints that are to be abandoned by the lower paths.

Diṭṭhantaṃ pattoti dassanasaṅkhātassa sotāpattimaggañāṇassa anantaraṃ pattoti vuttaṃ hoti. “Diṭṭhattā patto”tipi pāṭho. Etena catusaccadassanasaṅkhātāya diṭṭhiyā nirodhassa pattataṃ dīpeti. Tenāha “dukkhā saṅkhārā”tiādi. Tattha paññāyāti maggapaññāya. Paṭhamaphalaṭṭhato paṭṭhāya yāva aggamaggaṭṭhā diṭṭhippatto. Tenāha “sopi kāyasakkhī viya chabbidho hotī”ti. Yathā pana paññāvimutto, evaṃ ayampi sukkhavipassako catūhi arūpajjhānehi vuṭṭhāya diṭṭhippattabhāvappattā cattāro cāti pañcavidho hotīti veditabbo. Saddhāvimuttepi eseva nayo. Idaṃ dukkhanti ettakaṃ dukkhaṃ, na ito uddhaṃ dukkhanti. Yathābhūtaṃ pajānātīti ṭhapetvā taṇhaṃ upādānakkhandhapañcakaṃ dukkhasaccanti yāthāvato pajānāti. Yasmā pana taṇhā dukkhaṃ janeti nibbatteti, tato taṃ dukkhaṃ samudeti, tasmā naṃ “ayaṃ dukkhasamudayo”ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Yasmā pana idaṃ dukkhañca samudayo ca nibbānaṃ patvā nirujjhati, appavattiṃ gacchati, tasmā na “ayaṃ dukkhanirodho”ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Ariyo pana aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo taṃ dukkhanirodhaṃ gacchati, tena taṃ “ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā”ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Ettāvatā nānākkhaṇe saccavavatthānaṃ dassitaṃ. Idāni taṃ ekakkhaṇe dassetuṃ “tathāgatappaveditā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tathāgatappaveditāti tathāgatena bodhimaṇḍe paṭividdhā viditā pākaṭā katā. Dhammāti catusaccadhammā. Vodiṭṭhā hontīti sudiṭṭhā. Vocaritāti sucaritā, paññāya suṭṭhu carāpitāti attho. Ayanti ayaṃ evarūpo puggalo diṭṭhippattoti.

“One who has attained the end of seeing” means one who has attained immediately after the knowledge of the path of stream-entry, which is designated ‘seeing.’ There is also the reading ‘attained through seeing.’ This indicates the attainment of cessation through the view known as the vision of the four truths. Hence, it is said, “Formations are suffering,” and so on. Here, ‘by wisdom’ means by the wisdom of the path. From the stage of the first fruition up to the stage of the highest path, one is called a ‘view-attainer.’ Therefore, it is said, “He too, like the body-witness, is sixfold.” Just as the one liberated by wisdom, so too this dry-insight meditator, along with the four who attain the state of a view-attainer after emerging from the four formless attainments, becomes fivefold—this should be understood. The same method applies to the one liberated by faith. “This is suffering” means this much is suffering, not more than this. “He understands as it really is” means, setting aside craving, he rightly comprehends the five aggregates of clinging as the truth of suffering. Because craving produces and generates suffering, from that, suffering arises. Therefore, he understands as it really is: “This is the origin of suffering.” Because this suffering and its origin cease upon reaching Nibbāna and come to non-arising, he understands as it really is: “This is the cessation of suffering.” The noble eightfold path leads to the cessation of suffering. Therefore, he understands as it really is: “This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.” Thus far, the determination of the truths at different moments has been shown. Now, to present them at a single moment, it is said: “Proclaimed by the Tathāgata,” and so on. “Proclaimed by the Tathāgata” means penetrated, known, and made manifest by the Tathāgata at the seat of enlightenment. “Dhammas” means the four noble truths. “Are well-seen” means are clearly seen. “Are well-practiced” means are well-cultivated, that is, thoroughly made to be practiced by wisdom. “This” means a person of such a kind is called a ‘view-attainer.’”

Saddhāya vimuttoti saddahanavasena vimutto. Etena sabbathā avimuttassapi saddhāmattena vimuttabhāvaṃ [V 3.0143] dasseti. Saddhāvimuttoti vā saddhāya adhimuttoti [M 3.0153] attho. Kiṃ pana nesaṃ kilesappahāne nānattaṃ atthīti? Natthi. Atha kasmā saddhāvimutto diṭṭhippattaṃ na pāpuṇātīti? Āgamanīyanānattena. Diṭṭhippatto hi āgamanamhi kilese vikkhambhento appadukkhena akasirena akilamantova sakkoti vikkhambhituṃ, saddhāvimutto pana dukkhena kasirena kilamanto sakkoti vikkhambhituṃ, tasmā saddhāvimutto diṭṭhippattaṃ na pāpuṇāti. Tenāha “etassa hī”tiādi. Saddahantassāti “ekaṃsato ayaṃ paṭipadā kilesakkhayaṃ āvahati sammāsambuddhena bhāsitattā”ti evaṃ saddahantassa. Yasmā panassa aniccānupassanādīhi niccasaññāpahānavasena bhāvanāya pubbenāparaṃ visesaṃ passato tattha tattha paccakkhatāpi atthi, tasmā vuttaṃ “saddahantassa viyā”ti. Sesapadadvayaṃ tasseva vevacanaṃ. Ettha ca pubbabhāgamaggabhāvanāti vacanena āgamanīyanānattena diṭṭhippattasaddhāvimuttānaṃ paññānānattaṃ hotīti dassitaṃ. Abhidhammaṭṭhakathāyampi (pu. pa. aṭṭha. 28) “nesaṃ kilesappahāne nānattaṃ natthi, paññāya nānattaṃ atthiyevā”ti vatvā “āgamanīyanānatteneva saddhāvimutto diṭṭhippattaṃ na pāpuṇātīti sanniṭṭhānaṃ kata”nti vuttaṃ.

“One liberated by faith” means one liberated by way of faith. By this, it is shown that even one not liberated in all ways can have a state of liberation through mere faith. “Liberated by faith” means “one resolved by faith.” But is there any difference for them in the abandonment of defilements? There is not. Then why does one liberated by faith not attain the status of a view-attainer? Due to the difference in the preliminary path. For a view-attainer, while suppressing defilements on the preliminary path, is able to suppress them with little difficulty, without trouble, and without weariness. But one liberated by faith is able to suppress them only with difficulty, with trouble, and with weariness. Therefore, one liberated by faith does not attain the status of a view-attainer. Hence it is said, “For this one…” etc. “Of one who has faith” means of one who has faith thus: “This path certainly leads to the destruction of defilements because it was spoken by the Perfectly Enlightened One.” Moreover, because for him there is also direct experience in various respects as he sees the progressive distinction in his development by abandoning the perception of permanence through the contemplation of impermanence, etc., it is said, “like one who has faith.” The remaining two phrases are synonyms for the same. Here, by the statement about the development of the preliminary part of the path, it is shown that there is a difference in wisdom between the view-attainer and the one liberated by faith due to the difference in the preliminary path. In the Abhidhamma commentary as well (Puggalapaññatti Aṭṭhakathā 28), after saying: “There is no difference for them in the abandonment of defilements, but there is indeed a difference in wisdom,” it is concluded: “It is solely due to the difference in the preliminary path that one liberated by faith does not attain the status of a view-attainer.”

Ārammaṇaṃ yāthāvato dhāreti avadhāretīti dhammo, paññā. Taṃ paññāsaṅkhātaṃ dhammaṃ adhimattatāya pubbaṅgamaṃ hutvā pavattaṃ anussaratīti dhammānusārī. Tenāha “dhammo”tiādi. Paññāpubbaṅgamanti paññāpadhānaṃ. “Saddhaṃ anussarati, saddhāpubbaṅgamaṃ maggaṃ bhāvetī”ti imamatthaṃ eseva nayoti atidisati. Paññaṃ vāhetīti paññāvāhī, paññaṃ sātisayaṃ pavattetīti attho. Tenāha “paññāpubbaṅgamaṃ ariyamaggaṃ bhāvetī”ti. Paññā vā puggalaṃ vāheti nibbānābhimukhaṃ gametīti paññāvāhī. Saddhāvāhīti etthāpi iminā nayeneva attho veditabbo. Ubhatobhāgavimuttādikathāti ubhatobhāgavimuttādīsu āgamanato paṭṭhāya vattabbakathā. Tasmāti visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 2.773, 889) vuttattā. Tato eva visuddhimaggasaṃvaṇṇanāyaṃ (visuddhi. mahāṭī. 2.773) vuttanayeneva cettha attho veditabbo.

That which bears and determines the object as it really is, is Dhamma, that is, wisdom. One who follows that Dhamma, designated as wisdom, which proceeds having become the forerunner due to its excellence, is a Dhamma-follower. Hence, it is said, “the Dhamma,” etc. “Wisdom as the forerunner” means wisdom as predominant. He applies this same method to the meaning of “One follows faith, develops the path with faith as the forerunner.” A `paññāvāhī` is one who makes wisdom proceed; the meaning is that one causes wisdom to proceed exceedingly. Hence, it is said, “one develops the noble path with wisdom as the forerunner.” Or, wisdom leads the individual, causing them to go towards Nibbāna; thus, one is a `paññāvāhī`. The meaning of `saddhāvāhī` should also be understood in this same way. The discussion on the one liberated in both ways, etc., is the discussion that should be stated, beginning from the scriptures on the one liberated in both ways and so on. Therefore, because it is stated in the Visuddhimagga (Vism. 2.773, 889), the meaning here should be understood according to the method stated in the commentary on the Visuddhimagga (Visuddhimagga-mahāṭīkā 2.773).

Puggalasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Puggalasutta is finished.

5. Udakūpamāsuttavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Discourse with the Simile of Water

15. Pañcame [M 3.0154] ekantakāḷakehīti natthikavādaahetukavādaakiriyavādasaṅkhātehi niyatamicchādiṭṭhidhammehi. Tenāha “niyatamicchādiṭṭhiṃ sandhāya vutta”nti. Evaṃ puggaloti iminā kāraṇena [V 3.0144] ekavāraṃ nimuggo nimuggoyeva so hoti. Etassa hi puna bhavato vuṭṭhānaṃ nāma natthīti vadanti makkhaligosālādayo viya. Heṭṭhā heṭṭhā narakaggīnaṃyeva āhāro. Sādhu saddhā kusalesūti kusaladhammesu saddhā nāma sāhu laddhakāti ummujjati, so tāvattakeneva kusalena ummujjati nāma. Sādhu hirītiādīsupi eseva nayo. Caṅkavāreti rajakānaṃ khāraparissāvane, surāparissāvane vā. Evaṃ puggaloti “evaṃ sādhu saddhā”ti imesaṃ saddhādīnaṃ vasena ekavāraṃ ummujjitvā tesaṃ parihāniyā puna nimujjatiyeva devadattādayo viya. Devadatto hi aṭṭha samāpattiyo pañca ca abhiññāyo nibbattetvāpi puna buddhānaṃ paṭipakkhatāya tehi guṇehi parihīno ruhiruppādakammaṃ saṅghabhedakammañca katvā kāyassa bhedā dutiyacittavārena cuticittamanantarā niraye nibbatto. Kokāliko dve aggasāvake upavaditvā padumaniraye nibbatto.

15. In the fifth case, with “completely dark,” it refers to the doctrines of nihilism, causelessness, and inaction, which are known as fixed wrong views. Thus it is said, “referring to one with fixed wrong views.” Thus, this person, for this reason, once submerged, remains submerged. Indeed, for such a one there is no rising again from existence, so say those like Makkhali Gosāla and others. Their food is only the fires of hell below, lower and lower. “Good is faith in wholesome qualities”: faith in wholesome qualities is called ‘good’ when it is obtained, and by that much wholesome action one emerges, as it were. The same method applies to “Good is moral shame,” and so forth. “Like a dyer’s vat” means in the straining of lye by dyers, or in the straining of liquor. Thus, this person, having emerged once by means of these qualities such as faith, as in “Good is faith,” submerges again due to their decline, like Devadatta and others. For Devadatta, though he produced the eight attainments and the five higher knowledges, later, due to his opposition to the Buddhas, he declined from those qualities, and having committed the deed of causing blood to flow and the deed of causing a schism in the Saṅgha, upon the breakup of the body, he was reborn in hell immediately after the death-consciousness, in the second thought-moment. Kokālika, having slandered the two chief disciples, was reborn in the Paduma hell.

Neva hāyati no vaḍḍhatīti appahonakakālepi na hāyati, pahonakakālepi na vaḍḍhati. Ubhayampi panetaṃ agārikenapi anagārikenapi dīpetabbaṃ. Ekacco hi agāriko appahonakakāle pakkhikabhattaṃ vassikaṃ vā upanibandhāpesi, so pacchā pahonakakālepi pakkhikabhattādimattameva pavatteti. Anagārikopi ādimhi appahonakakāle uddesaṃ dhutaṅgaṃ vā gaṇhāti, medhāvī balavīriyasampattiyā pahonakakāle tato uttariṃ na karoti. Evaṃ puggaloti evaṃ imāya saddhādīnaṃ ṭhitiyā puggalo ummujjitvā ṭhito nāma hoti. Ummujjitvā pataratīti sakadāgāmipuggalo kilesatanutāya uṭṭhahitvā gantabbadisābhimukho tarati nāma.

“It does not decline nor does it increase”: even in a time of scarcity it does not decline, and even in a time of abundance it does not increase. Both of these should be explained with reference to both householders and the homeless. For a certain householder, in a time of scarcity, arranges for fortnightly meals or annual supplies, and later, even in a time of abundance, he continues only with fortnightly meals and the like. Likewise, a homeless one, at the beginning in a time of scarcity, takes up a subject of study or an ascetic practice; and in a time of abundance, though wise and endowed with strength and energy, he does not do more than that. Thus, this person, by means of this stability of faith and so forth, is said to have emerged and stood firm. “Having emerged, he crosses over”: the once-returner, due to the attenuation of defilements, rises up and is said to cross over, facing the direction he must go.

Paṭigādhappatto hotīti anāgāmipuggalaṃ sandhāya vadati. Ime pana satta puggalā udakopamena dīpitā. Satta kira jaṅghavāṇijā addhānamaggappaṭipannā antarāmagge ekaṃ puṇṇanadiṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Tesu paṭhamaṃ otiṇṇo udakabhīruko puriso otiṇṇaṭṭhāneyeva nimujjitvā puna saṇṭhātuṃ nāsakkhi, avassaṃva macchakacchapabhattaṃ jāto. Dutiyo otiṇṇaṭṭhāne nimujjitvā [M 3.0155] sakiṃ uṭṭhahitvā puna nimuggo uṭṭhātuṃ nāsakkhi, antoyeva macchakacchapabhattaṃ jāto. Tatiyo nimujjitvā uṭṭhito majjhe nadiyā ṭhatvā neva orato āgantuṃ, na pāraṃ gantuṃ asakkhi. Catuttho uṭṭhāya ṭhito uttaraṇatitthaṃ olokesi. Pañcamo uttaraṇatitthaṃ oloketvā patarati. Chaṭṭho taṃ disvā pārimatīraṃ gantvā kaṭippamāṇe udake ṭhito. Sattamo pārimatīraṃ gantvā gandhacuṇṇādīhi nhatvā varavatthādīni nivāsetvā surabhivilepanaṃ vilimpitvā nīluppalamālādīni pilandhitvā nānālaṅkārappaṭimaṇḍito mahānagaraṃ pavisitvā pāsādamāruhitvā uttamabhojanaṃ bhuñjati.

“He has reached a firm footing” refers to the non-returner. These seven persons, however, are illustrated by the simile of water. It is said that seven foot-merchants, having set out on a road journey, came upon a full river in the middle of the road. Among them, the first, a man afraid of water, sank immediately upon entering and could not manage to stand again; he certainly became food for fish and turtles. The second, having sunk at the entering place, managed to rise once but sank again and could not rise; he certainly became food for fish and turtles inside the water. The third, having sunk and risen, stood in the middle of the river, unable either to return to this shore or to go to the far shore. The fourth, having risen and stood, looked for a ford to cross. The fifth, having looked for a ford to cross, proceeded across. The sixth, having seen that, reached the far shore and stood in water up to his hips. The seventh, having reached the far shore, bathed with perfumed powders and such, dressed in fine garments and such, applied fragrant unguents, adorned himself with blue lotus garlands and such, ornamented with various ornaments, entered the great city, ascended the palace, and enjoyed the finest food.

Tattha [V 3.0145] jaṅghavāṇijā viya ime satta puggalā, nadī viya vaṭṭaṃ, paṭhamassa udakabhīrukassa purisassa otiṇṇaṭṭhāneyeva nimujjanaṃ viya micchādiṭṭhikassa vaṭṭe nimujjanaṃ, ummujjitvā nimujjanapuriso viya saddhādīnaṃ uppattimatthakena ummujjitvā tāsaṃ hāniyā nimuggapuggalo, majjhe nadiyā ṭhatvā viya saddhādīnaṃ ṭhitiyā ṭhitipuggalo, uttaraṇatitthaṃ olokento viya sotāpanno, patarantapuriso viya kilesakāmāvaṭṭatāya pataranto sakadāgāmī, taritvā kaṭimatte udake ṭhitapuriso viya anāvaṭṭadhammattā anāgāmī, nhatvā pārimatīraṃ uttaritvā thale ṭhitapuriso viya cattāro oghe atikkamitvā nibbānathale ṭhito khīṇāsavabrāhmaṇo, thale ṭhitapurisassa nagaraṃ pavisitvā pāsādaṃ āruyha uttamabhojanabhuñjanaṃ viya khīṇāsavassa nibbānārammaṇasamāpattiṃ appetvā vītināmanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

There, these seven persons are like foot-merchants; the round of existence is like a river. Just as the first man, afraid of water, sinks in the very place he enters, so the one with wrong view sinks in the cycle. Like the man who emerges and then sinks, so is the person who emerges by means of the arising of faith and so forth, but sinks due to their decline. Like one standing in the middle of the river, so is the person who stands firm due to the stability of faith and so forth. Like one looking for a ford to cross, so is the stream-enterer. Like the man who crosses over, so is the once-returner, crossing over due to the cycle of defilements and sensual pleasures. Like a man who has crossed and stands with the water at waist-level, so is the non-returner, due to not having the nature of returning. Like the man who has bathed, crossed to the far shore, and stands on the dry land, so is the Brahmin with taints destroyed, standing on the dry land of Nibbāna, having crossed the four floods. Like the man standing on dry land who enters a city, ascends to a palace, and enjoys the finest food, so it should be understood that the one with taints destroyed passes the time by attaining the absorption with Nibbāna as its object.

Udakūpamāsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Discourse on the Simile of Water is concluded.

6-9. Aniccānupassīsuttādivaṇṇanā

6-9. Commentary on the Aniccānupassī Sutta and Other Discourses

16-19. Chaṭṭhe “idha samasīsī kathito”ti vatvā evaṃ samasīsitaṃ vibhajitvā idhādhippetaṃ dassetuṃ “so catubbidho hotī”tiādimāha. Rogavasena samasīsī rogasamasīsī. Esa nayo sesesupi. Ekappahārenevāti ekavelāyameva. Yo cakkhurogādīsu aññatarasmiṃ sati “ito anuṭṭhito arahattaṃ pāpuṇissāmī”ti vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapesi, athassa arahattañca rogato vuṭṭhānañca ekakālameva hoti[M 3.0156], ayaṃ rogasamasīsī nāma. Iriyāpathassa pariyosānanti iriyāpathantarasamāyogo. Yo ṭhānādīsu iriyāpathesu aññataraṃ adhiṭṭhāya “avikopetvāva arahattaṃ pāpuṇissāmī”ti vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapesi. Athassa arahattappatti ca iriyāpathavikopanañca ekappahāreneva hoti, ayaṃ iriyāpathasamasīsī nāma. Jīvitasamasīsī nāmāti ettha “palibodhasīsaṃ māno, parāmāsasīsaṃ diṭṭhi, vikkhepasīsaṃ uddhaccaṃ, kilesasīsaṃ avijjā, adhimokkhasīsaṃ saddhā, paggahasīsaṃ vīriyaṃ, upaṭṭhānasīsaṃ sati, avikkhepasīsaṃ samādhi, dassanasīsaṃ paññā, pavattasīsaṃ jīvitindriyaṃ, cutisīsaṃ vimokkho, saṅkhārasīsaṃ nirodho”ti paṭisambhidāyaṃ (paṭi. ma. 3.33) vuttesu sattarasasu sīsesu pavattasīsaṃ kilesasīsanti dve sīsāni idhādhippetāni – “apubbaṃ acarimaṃ āsavapariyādānañca hoti jīvitapariyādānañcā”ti vacanato. Tesu kilesasīsaṃ arahattamaggo pariyādiyati, pavattasīsaṃ jīvitindriyaṃ cuticittaṃ pariyādiyati.
