Tattha avijjāpariyādāyakaṃ cittaṃ jīvitindriyaṃ pariyādātuṃ na sakkoti, jīvitindriyapariyādāyakaṃ avijjaṃ pariyādātuṃ na sakkoti[V 3.0146]. Aññaṃ avijjāpariyādāyakaṃ cittaṃ, aññaṃ jīvitandriyapariyādāyakaṃ. Yassa cetaṃ sīsadvayaṃ samaṃ pariyādānaṃ gacchati, so jīvitasamasīsī nāma.

16-19. In the sixth section, having stated, “Here, one who is equal-headed is spoken of,” and having thus divided ‘equal-headedness,’ in order to show what is intended here, it is said, “He is of four kinds,” and so on. The roga-samasīsī is the equal-headed one by way of illness. This method applies to the rest as well. “By a single stroke” means at one time. If someone, when afflicted by an eye disease or the like, establishes insight meditation, thinking, “Without having arisen from this, I will attain arahantship,” then for him, the attainment of arahantship and recovery from the illness occur at the same time. This is called the roga-samasīsī. “The termination of the posture” means the conjunction with another posture. If someone, having resolved upon one of the postures such as standing, establishes insight meditation, thinking, “Without disturbing this posture, I will attain arahantship,” then for him, the attainment of arahantship and the changing of the posture occur in a single stroke. This is called the iriyāpatha-samasīsī. As for the jīvita-samasīsī, here, among the seventeen heads mentioned in the Paṭisambhidāmagga (Paṭi. Ma. 3.33)—“The head of obstruction is conceit, the head of grasping is wrong view, the head of distraction is restlessness, the head of defilements is ignorance, the head of determination is faith, the head of exertion is energy, the head of establishment is mindfulness, the head of non-distraction is concentration, the head of vision is wisdom, the head of continuity is the life faculty, the head of passing away is liberation, the head of formations is cessation”—the head of continuity (the life faculty) and the head of defilements are the two intended here, as stated by the phrase, “There is both the exhaustion of the taints and the exhaustion of life, without prior or subsequent.” Among these, the path of arahantship exhausts the head of defilements, and the dying consciousness exhausts the head of continuity (the life faculty). There, the mind that exhausts ignorance cannot exhaust the life faculty, and the mind that exhausts the life faculty cannot exhaust ignorance. One mind exhausts ignorance, another mind exhausts the life faculty. He for whom these two heads are exhausted equally is called the jīvita-samasīsī.

Kathaṃ panidaṃ samaṃ hotīti? Vārasamatāya. Yasmiñhi vāre maggavuṭṭhānaṃ hoti, sotāpattimagge pañca paccavekkhaṇāni, sakadāgāmimagge pañca, anāgāmimagge pañca, arahattamagge cattārīti ekūnavīsatime paccavekkhaṇañāṇe patiṭṭhāya bhavaṅgaṃ otaritvā parinibbāyato imāya vārasamatāya idaṃ ubhayasīsapariyādānampi samaṃ hotīti imāya vārasamatāya. Vārasamavuttidāyakena hi maggacittena attano anantaraṃ viya nipphādetabbā paccavekkhaṇavārā ca kilesapariyādānasseva vārāti vattabbataṃ arahati. “Vimuttasmiṃ vimuttamiti ñāṇaṃ hotī”ti (ma. ni. 1.78; saṃ. ni. 3.12, 14) vacanato paccavekkhaṇaparisamāpanena kilesapariyādānaṃ sampāpitaṃ nāma hotīti imāya vāravuttiyā samatāya kilesapariyādānajīvitapariyādānānaṃ samatā veditabbā. Tenevāha “yasmā panassa…pe... tasmā evaṃ vutta”nti.

How then is this equal? By the equality of turns. For in whichever turn emergence from the path occurs—five reflections regarding the stream-entry path, five regarding the once-returner path, five regarding the non-returner path, and four regarding the arahant path—for one who, being established in these nineteen reflection knowledges, has descended into the life-continuum and attains final Nibbāna, by this equality of turns, this cessation of both heads is also equal. For the path-consciousness, as the giver of an equal turn, is to produce the turns of reflection as if immediately after itself, and the turns of reflection deserve to be called the turns of the very exhaustion of defilements. In accordance with the statement, “In one who is liberated, the knowledge arises, ‘I am liberated,’” the exhaustion of defilements is indeed accomplished by the completion of the reflections. By this equality in the occurrence of turns, the equality of the exhaustion of defilements and the exhaustion of life should be understood. Therefore, it was said: “Because for him…pe... therefore, it is thus stated.”

Āyuno vemajjhaṃ anatikkamitvā antarāva kilesaparinibbānena parinibbāyatīti antarāparinibbāyī. Tenāha “yo pañcasu suddhāvāsesū”tiādi[M 3.0157]. Vemajjheti avihādīsu yattha uppanno, tattha āyuno vemajjhe. Āyuvemajjhaṃ upahacca atikkamitvā tattha parinibbāyatīti upahaccaparinibbāyī. Tenāha “yo tatthevā”tiādi. Asaṅkhārena appayogena anussāhena akilamanto tikkhindriyatāya sukheneva parinibbāyatīti asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī. Tenāha “yo tesaṃyevā”tiādi. Tesaṃyeva puggalānanti niddhāraṇe sāmivacanaṃ. Appayogenāti adhimattappayogena vinā appakasirena. Sasaṅkhārena sappayogena kilamanto dukkhena parinibbāyatīti sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī. Uddhaṃvāhibhāvena uddhamassa taṇhāsotaṃ vaṭṭasotañcāti, uddhaṃ vā gantvā paṭilabhitabbato uddhamassa maggasotanti uddhaṃbhoto. Paṭisandhivasena akaniṭṭhaṃ gacchatīti akaniṭṭhagāmī.

Without passing the middle of the lifespan, one attains final Nibbāna by the final Nibbāna of defilements in the interim—thus, one is an 'interim attainer of Nibbāna' (antarāparinibbāyī). Hence it is said: “He who is reborn among the five Pure Abodes,” etc. 'In the middle' means in the middle of the lifespan in whichever of the Aviha and other realms one has been reborn. Having struck and surpassed the middle of the lifespan, one attains final Nibbāna there—thus, one is a 'one who attains Nibbāna after reducing the lifespan' (upahaccaparinibbāyī). Hence it is said: “He who attains Nibbāna right there,” etc. Without exertion, without application, without striving, without tiring, due to keen faculties, one attains final Nibbāna with ease—thus, one is a 'one who attains Nibbāna without exertion' (asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī). Hence it is said: “He who is one of them,” etc. “Among those very persons” is a genitive of specification. “Without application” means without excessive application, with little difficulty. With exertion, with application, striving, one attains final Nibbāna with difficulty—thus, one is a 'one who attains Nibbāna with exertion' (sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī). Because of the nature of flowing upward, his stream of craving and stream of the cycle of existence are upward; or because the path-stream is to be obtained by going upward, his stream is upward—thus, one is an 'upstream-goer' (uddhaṃsoto). By way of rebirth-linking, one goes to Akaniṭṭha—thus, one is a 'goer to Akaniṭṭha' (akaniṭṭhagāmī).

Ettha pana catukkaṃ veditabbaṃ. Yo hi avihato paṭṭhāya cattāro devaloke sodhetvā akaniṭṭhaṃ gantvā parinibbāyati, ayaṃ uddhaṃsoto akaniṭṭhagāmī nāma. Ayañhi avihesu kappasahassaṃ vasanto arahattaṃ pattuṃ asakkuṇitvā atappaṃ gacchati, tatrāpi dve kappasahassāni vasanto arahattaṃ pattuṃ asakkuṇitvā sudassaṃ gacchati, tatrāpi cattāri kappasahassāni vasanto arahattaṃ pattuṃ asakkuṇitvā sudassiṃ gacchati, tatrāpi aṭṭha kappasahassāni vasanto arahattaṃ [V 3.0147] pattuṃ asakkuṇitvā akaniṭṭhaṃ gacchati, tattha vasanto aggamaggaṃ adhigacchati. Tattha yo avihato paṭṭhāya dutiyaṃ vā catutthaṃ vā devalokaṃ gantvā parinibbāyati, ayaṃ uddhaṃsoto na akaniṭṭhagāmī nāma. Yo kāmabhavato cavitvā akaniṭṭhesu parinibbāyati, ayaṃ na uddhaṃsoto akaniṭṭhagāmī nāma. Yo heṭṭhā catūsu devalokesu tattha tattheva nibbattitvā parinibbāyati, ayaṃ na uddhaṃsoto na akaniṭṭhagāmīti.

Here, however, a fourfold distinction should be understood. One who, starting from the Aviha realm, having passed through the four deva worlds, and reaching Akaniṭṭha attains final Nibbāna—this one is called an 'upstream-goer, a goer to Akaniṭṭha.' For this one, dwelling in Aviha for a thousand eons, being unable to attain arahantship, proceeds to Atappa. There too, dwelling for two thousand eons, being unable to attain arahantship, proceeds to Sudassa. There too, dwelling for four thousand eons, being unable to attain arahantship, proceeds to Sudassī. There too, dwelling for eight thousand eons, being unable to attain arahantship, proceeds to Akaniṭṭha. Dwelling there, one attains the supreme path. Here, one who, starting from Aviha, reaches the second or the fourth deva world and attains final Nibbāna—this one is called an 'upstream-goer,' but not a 'goer to Akaniṭṭha.' One who passes away from the realm of sensual existence and attains final Nibbāna in Akaniṭṭha—this one is called a 'goer to Akaniṭṭha,' but not an 'upstream-goer.' One who is reborn in any of the four lower deva worlds below and there itself attains final Nibbāna—this one is neither an 'upstream-goer' nor a 'goer to Akaniṭṭha.'

Ete pana avihesu uppannasamanantaraāyuvemajjhaṃ appatvāva parinibbāyanavasena tayo antarāparinibbāyino, eko upahaccaparinibbāyī, eko uddhaṃsototi pañcavidho, asaṅkhārasasaṅkhāraparinibbāyivibhāgena dasa honti, tathā atappasudassasudassīsūti cattāro dasakāti cattārīsaṃ. Akaniṭṭhe pana uddhaṃsoto natthi, tayo antarāparinibbāyino, eko [M 3.0158] upahaccaparinibbāyīti cattāro, asaṅkhārasasaṅkhāraparinibbāyivibhāgena aṭṭhāti aṭṭhacattārīsaṃ anāgāmino. Sattamādīsu natthi vattabbaṃ.

Among these, in the Aviha realm, there are three types of one who attains Nibbāna in the interim, one who attains Nibbāna after reducing the lifespan, and one who is an upstream-goer; thus, there are five types. When divided by way of attaining Nibbāna without exertion and with exertion, they become ten. Similarly, in Atappa, Sudassa, and Sudassī, there are four sets of ten, making forty in total. In the Akaniṭṭha realm, however, there is no upstream-goer. There, the three types of one who attains Nibbāna in the interim and the one who attains Nibbāna after reducing the lifespan make four. When divided by way of attaining Nibbāna without exertion and with exertion, they become eight. Thus, there are forty-eight non-returners. As for the seventh discourse and the rest, there is nothing further to be said.

Aniccānupassīsuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Aniccānupassī Sutta and others is concluded.

10. Niddasavatthusuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Niddasavatthu Sutta

20. Dasame niddasavatthūnīti ādisaddalopenāyaṃ niddesoti āha “niddasādivatthūnī”ti. Natthi idāni imassa dasāti niddaso. Pañhoti ñātuṃ icchito attho. Puna dasavasso na hotīti tesaṃ matimattametanti dassetuṃ “so kirā”ti kirasaddaggahaṇaṃ. Niddasoti cetaṃ vacanamattaṃ. Tassa nibbīsādibhāvassa viya ninnavādibhāvassa ca icchitattāti dassetuṃ “na kevalañcā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Gāme vicarantoti gāme piṇḍāya caranto. Na idaṃ titthiyānaṃ adhivacanaṃ tesu tannimittassa abhāvā, sāsanepi sekhassapi na idaṃ adhivacanaṃ, kimaṅgaṃ pana puthujjanassa. Yassa panetaṃ adhivacanaṃ yena ca kāraṇena, taṃ dassetuṃ “khīṇāsavasseta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Appaṭisandhikabhāvo hissa paccakkhato kāraṇaṃ. Paramparāya itarāni yāni pāḷiyaṃ āgatāniṃ.

20. In the tenth, regarding 'niddasavatthūni,' he says 'niddasādivatthūni' to indicate that this is an explanation where the word 'ādi' (etc.) has been elided. 'Niddaso' means 'there are no ten (dasa) for him now.' 'Pañho ti' means: the question is about the meaning one wishes to know. Again, to show that the idea 'he is not a ten-year-old' is merely their opinion, the particle 'kira' is used in 'so kirā.' And 'niddaso' is merely a word. To show that the desired state is not only that of being without dejection, etc., but also of being humble, it is said, 'na kevalañcā,' etc. 'Gāme vicarantoti' means wandering in the village for alms. This is not a designation for heretics, since they lack the cause for it, nor is it a designation for a learner in the Dispensation, let alone for an ordinary person. But to show for whom it is a designation and for what reason, it is said, 'khīṇāsavasseta,' etc. His state of non-rebirth is the direct cause. The others, which have come down in the Pāli text, are indirect causes.

Sikkhāya sammadeva ādānaṃ sikkhāsamādānaṃ. Taṃ panassā pāripūriyā veditabbanti āha “sikkhāttayapūraṇe”ti. Sikkhāya vā sammadeva ādito paṭṭhāya rakkhaṇaṃ sikkhāsamādānaṃ. Tañca atthato pūraṇena paricchinnaṃ arakkhaṇe sabbena sabbaṃ abhāvato, rakkhaṇe [V 3.0148] ca paripūraṇato. Balavacchandoti daḷhacchando. Āyatinti anantarānāgatadivasādikālo adhippeto, na anāgatabhavoti āha “anāgate punadivasādīsupī”ti. Sikkhaṃ paripūrentassa tattha nibaddhabhattitā avigatapematā. Tebhūmakadhammānaṃ aniccādivasena sammadeva nijjhānaṃ dhammanisāmanāti āha “vipassanāyetaṃ adhivacana”nti. Taṇhāvinayeti bhaṅgānupassanāñāṇānubhāvasiddhe taṇhāvikkhambhane. Ekībhāveti gaṇasaṅgaṇikākilesasaṅgaṇikāvigamasiddhe vivekavāse. Vīriyārambheti sammappadhānassa paggaṇhane[M 3.0159]. Taṃ pana sabbaso vīriyassa paribrūhanaṃ hotīti āha “kāyikacetasikassa vīriyassa pūraṇe”ti. Satiyañceva nipakabhāve cāti satokāritāya ceva sampajānakāritāya ca. Satisampajaññabaleneva hi vīriyārambho ijjhati. Diṭṭhipaṭivedheti maggasammādiṭṭhiyā paṭivijjhane. Tenāha “maggadassane”ti.

The proper undertaking of the training is 'sikkhāsamādāna.' And that should be understood by way of its fulfillment; hence it is said, 'sikkhāttayapūraṇe' (in the fulfillment of the triple training). Or, 'sikkhāsamādāna' is the proper protection of the training from the very beginning. And that is defined in meaning by fulfillment, because without protection there is a complete absence of it, and with protection there is its complete fulfillment. 'Balavacchando' means strong desire. 'Āyati' refers to a future time, such as the next day, etc., not a future existence; hence it is said, 'anāgate punadivasādīsupi' (even in future days, etc.). For one fulfilling the training, there is constant devotion and undiminished affection for it. The proper reflection on the phenomena of the three realms as impermanent, etc., is 'dhammanisāmanā;' hence it is said, 'vipassanāyetaṃ adhivacanaṃ' (this is a designation for insight). 'Taṇhāvinaye' (in the removal of craving) means in the suppression of craving accomplished through the power of the knowledge of contemplation of dissolution. 'Ekībhāve' (in solitude) means in dwelling in seclusion, accomplished by the removal of association with groups and association with defilements. 'Vīriyārambhe' (in the arousal of energy) means in the undertaking of right effort. And that is the complete development of energy; hence it is said, 'kāyikacetasikassa vīriyassa pūraṇe' (in the fulfillment of bodily and mental energy). 'Satiyañceva nipakabhāve cāti' (in mindfulness and in the state of being prudent) means through acting with mindfulness and acting with clear comprehension. For the arousal of energy succeeds only through the power of mindfulness and clear comprehension. 'Diṭṭhipaṭivedhe' (in the penetration of view) means in the penetration of the right view of the path. Hence it is said, 'maggadassane' (in the seeing of the path).

Niddasavatthusuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Niddasavatthu Sutta is concluded.

Anusayavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Anusayavagga is concluded.

3. Vajjisattakavaggo

3. The Vajjian Chapter on Sevens

1. Sārandadasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Sārandada Sutta

21. Tatiyassa paṭhame devāyatanabhāvena cittattā lokassa cittīkāraṭṭhānatāya ca cetiyaṃ ahosi. Yāvakīvanti (dī. ni. ṭī. 2.134) ekamevetaṃ padaṃ aniyamato parimāṇavācī. Kālo cettha adhippetoti āha “yattakaṃ kāla”nti. Abhiṇhaṃ sannipātāti niccasannipātā. Taṃ pana niccasannipātataṃ dassetuṃ “divasassā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Sannipātabahulāti pacurasannipātā. Vosānanti saṅkocaṃ. “Vuddhiyevā”tiādinā vuttamatthaṃ byatirekamukhena dassetuṃ “abhiṇhaṃ asannipatantā hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ākulāti khubhitā na pasannā. Bhijjitvāti vaggabandhato vibhajja visuṃ visuṃ hutvā.

21. In the first (discourse) of the third (chapter), because of its being a divine abode, being beautiful, and a place of veneration for the world, it was a shrine. 'Yāvakīvaṃ' (Dī. Ni. Ṭī. 2.134) is a single word indicating an indefinite quantity. Here, time is the intended meaning; hence, it is said, 'yattakaṃ kālaṃ' (for as long as). 'Abhiṇhaṃ sannipātā' means constant gatherings. To show this constant gathering, 'divasassa,' etc., is said. 'Sannipātabahulā' means frequent gatherings. 'Vosānaṃ' means shrinking. To illustrate the meaning stated by 'vuddhiyeva' (growth alone), etc., through contrast, it is said, 'abhiṇhaṃ asannipatantā hi' (for not gathering frequently), etc. 'Ākulā' means agitated, not serene. 'Bhijjitvā' means having broken apart from factional ties and become separate.

Sannipātabheriyāti sannipātārocanabheriyā. Addhabhuttā vāti sāmibhuttā vā. Osīdamāneti hāyamāne.

'Sannipātabheriyā' means the drum announcing the assembly. 'Addhabhuttā vā' means 'or half-eaten.' 'Osīdamāne' means 'while declining.'

Suṅkanti [V 3.0149] bhaṇḍaṃ gahetvā gacchantehi pabbatakhaṇḍanādititthagāmadvārādīsu rājapurisānaṃ dātabbabhāgaṃ. Balinti nipphannasassādito chabhāgaṃ sattabhāgantiādinā laddhabbakaraṃ. Daṇḍanti dasavīsatikahāpaṇādikaṃ aparādhānurūpaṃ gahetabbadhanadaṇḍaṃ. Vajjidhammanti vajjirājadhammaṃ. Idāni apaññattapaññāpanādīsu tappaṭikkhepe ca ādīnavānisaṃse ca vitthārato dassetuṃ “tesa”ntiādi [M 3.0160] vuttaṃ. Pāricariyakkhamāti upaṭṭhānakkhamā. Porāṇaṃ vajjidhammanti ettha pubbe kira vajjirājāno “ayaṃ coro”ti ānetvā dassite “gaṇhatha naṃ cora”nti avatvā vinicchayamahāmattānaṃ denti. Te vinicchinitvā sace acoro hoti, vissajjenti. Sace coro, attanā kiñci akatvā vohārikānaṃ denti, tepi vinicchinitvā acoro ce, vissajjenti. Coro ce, suttadharānaṃ denti. Tepi vinicchinitvā acoro ce, vissajjenti. Coro ce, aṭṭakulikānaṃ denti, tepi tatheva katvā senāpatissa, senāpati uparājassa, uparājā rañño. Rājā vinicchinitvā sace acoro hoti, vissajjeti. Sace pana coro hoti, paveṇipaṇṇakaṃ vācāpeti. Tattha “yena idaṃ nāma kataṃ, tassa ayaṃ nāmadaṇḍo”ti likhitaṃ. Rājā tassa kiriyaṃ tena samānetvā tadanucchavikaṃ daṇḍaṃ karoti. Iti etaṃ porāṇaṃ vajjidhammaṃ samādāya vattantānaṃ manussā na ujjhāyanti. Paramparāgatesu aṭṭakulesu jātā agatigamanaviratā aṭṭamahallakapurisā aṭṭakulikā.

'Suṅkaṃ' means the portion to be given to the king's officers by those carrying goods through mountain passes, fords, village gates, and so forth. 'Baliṃ' means the tax to be obtained, such as one-sixth or one-seventh, from the harvested crops. 'Daṇḍaṃ' means the monetary fine to be taken, such as ten or twenty kahāpaṇas, according to the offense. 'Vajjidhammaṃ' means the law of the Vajjian kings. Now, to explain in detail the dangers and benefits concerning the establishment of what has not been established and the rejection thereof, the passage begins with 'tesaṃ,' and so on. 'Pāricariyakkhamā' means capable of serving. Regarding 'porāṇaṃ vajjidhammaṃ,' the ancient law of the Vajjis: in the past, it is said, when someone was brought and shown to the Vajjian kings with the accusation, 'This is a thief,' they would not say, 'Seize this thief,' but would hand him over to the judicial ministers. If, after investigating, they found he was not a thief, they would release him. If he was a thief, without doing anything themselves, they would hand him over to the legal experts. If they too, after investigating, found he was not a thief, they would release him. If he was a thief, they would hand him over to the keepers of the law-books. If they too, after investigating, found he was not a thief, they would release him. If he was a thief, they would hand him over to the council of eight families. They, having done likewise, would hand him over to the commander-in-chief, the commander-in-chief to the viceroy, and the viceroy to the king. The king, after investigating, if he was not a thief, would release him. But if he was a thief, he would have the book of precedents read out. Therein it is written: 'For one who has done such-and-such a deed, this is the penalty.' The king, comparing the person's action with that, imposes a suitable penalty. Thus, for those who conducted themselves according to this ancient Vajjian law, the people did not complain. The 'aṭṭakulikā' were the eight elder men, born into eight families of unbroken lineage, who refrained from going astray into partiality.

Sakkāranti upakāraṃ. Garubhāvaṃ paccupaṭṭhapetvāti “ime amhākaṃ garuno”ti tattha garubhāvaṃ paṭi paṭi upaṭṭhapetvā. Mānessantīti sammānessanti. Taṃ pana sammānanaṃ tesu nesaṃ attamanatāpubbakanti āha “manena piyāyissantī”ti. Nipaccakāraṃ paṇipātaṃ. Dassentīti garucittabhāraṃ dassenti. Sandhānetunti sambandhaṃ avicchinnaṃ katvā ghaṭetuṃ.

'Sakkāraṃ' means assistance. 'Garubhāvaṃ paccupaṭṭhapetvā' means having repeatedly established reverence, thinking, 'These are our venerable ones.' 'Mānessanti' means they will properly esteem. That esteem, however, is preceded by their satisfaction in them; hence, it is said, 'manena piyāyissanti' (they will cherish them with their minds). 'Nipaccakāraṃ' means prostration. 'Dassenti' means they display the weight of a respectful mind. 'Sandhānetuṃ' means to join together, making the connection unbroken.

Pasayhakārassāti balakkārassa. Kāmaṃ vuddhiyā pūjanīyatāya “vuddhihāniyo”ti vuttaṃ, attho pana vuttānukkameneva yojetabbo. Pāḷiyaṃ vā yasmā “vuddhiyeva pāṭikaṅkhā, no parihānī”ti vuttaṃ, tasmā tadanukkamena “vuddhihāniyo”ti vuttaṃ.

'Pasayhakārassa' means of one who uses force. Although 'vuddhihāniyo' (growth and decline) is said with 'growth' placed first due to its venerability, the meaning should nevertheless be construed according to the sequence stated. Or, because it is said in the Pāḷi text, 'Only growth is to be expected, not decline,' it is therefore said 'vuddhihāniyo' following that sequence.

Vipaccituṃ aladdhokāse pāpakamme, tassa kammassa vipāke vā anavasarova devasopasaggo. Tasmiṃ pana laddhokāse siyā devatopasaggassa avasaroti āha “anuppannaṃ…pe… vaḍḍhentī”ti. Eteneva anuppannaṃ sukhanti etthāpi attho veditabbo. Balakāyassa diguṇatiguṇatādassanaṃ paṭibhayabhāvadassananti evamādinā devatānaṃ saṅgāmasīse sahāyatā veditabbā.

When an evil deed has not found an opportunity to ripen, there is no occasion for divine affliction regarding the result of that kamma. But when it has found an opportunity, there may be an occasion for divine affliction; hence, it is said: 'anuppannaṃ…pe… vaḍḍhenti' (unarisen…they increase). By this same principle, the meaning of 'anuppannaṃ sukhaṃ' (unarisen happiness) should also be understood here. The assistance of deities at the head of the battle should be understood through such things as the appearance of the army's strength as double or triple, the appearance of a terrifying nature, and so on.

Anicchitanti [V 3.0150][M 3.0161] aniṭṭhaṃ. Āvaraṇatoti nisedhanato. Dhammato anapetā dhammiyāti idha “dhammikā”ti vuttā. Migasūkarādighātāya sunakhādīnaṃ kaḍḍhitvā vanacaraṇaṃ vājo, tattha niyuttā, te vā vājentīti vājikā, migavadhacārino.

'Anicchitaṃ' means unwanted. 'Āvaraṇato' means by way of prevention. 'Dhammiyā' means not deviating from the Dhamma; here they are called 'dhammikā' (righteous). 'Vājo' is roaming in the forest, having dragged along dogs and so on for the slaughter of deer, boars, and other animals; those engaged therein, or those who drive them on, are 'vājikā' (hunters), those who roam about for the killing of animals.

Sārandadasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Sārandada Sutta is concluded.

2. Vassakārasuttavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Vassakāra Sutta.

22. Dutiye abhiyātukāmoti ettha abhi-saddo abhibhavanattho “anabhividitu”ntiādīsu viyāti āha “abhibhavanatthāya yātukāmo”ti. Vajjirājānoti “vajjetabbā ime”ti ādito pavattaṃ vacanaṃ upādāya vajjīti laddhanāmā rājāno, vajjiraṭṭhassa vā rājāno vajjirājāno. Raṭṭhassa pana vajjisamaññā tannivāsirājakumāravasena veditabbā. Rājiddhiyāti rājabhāvānugatena pabhāvena. So pana pabhāvo nesaṃ gaṇarājānaṃ mitho sāmaggiyā loke pākaṭo. Ciraṭṭhāyī ca ahosīti “samaggabhāvaṃ kathetī”ti vuttaṃ. Anu anu taṃsamaṅgino bhāveti vaḍḍhetīti anubhāvo, anubhāvo eva ānubhāvo, patāpo. So pana nesaṃ patāpo hatthiassādivāhanasampattiyā tattha ca subhikkhitabhāvena loke pākaṭo jātoti “etena…pe… kathetī”ti vuttaṃ. Tāḷacchiggaḷenāti kuñcikāchiddena. Asananti saraṃ. Atipātayissantīti atikkāmenti. Poṅkhānupoṅkhanti poṅkhassa anupoṅkhaṃ, purimasarassa poṅkhapadānugatapoṅkhaṃ itaraṃ saraṃ katvāti attho. Avirādhitanti avirajjhitaṃ. Ucchindissāmīti ummūlanavasena kulasantatiṃ chindissāmi. Ayanaṃ vaḍḍhanaṃ ayo, tappaṭipakkhena anayoti āha “avaḍḍhi”nti. Ñātīnaṃ byasanaṃ vināso ñātibyasanaṃ.

22. In the second (section), regarding 'abhiyātukāmo' (desiring to attack), the prefix 'abhi-' has the meaning of overcoming, as in 'anabhividituṃ,' etc.; hence, it is said, 'abhibhavanatthāya yātukāmo' (desiring to go for the purpose of overcoming). 'Vajjirājāno' (the Vajjian kings) are kings who obtained the name 'Vajjī' based on the saying that originated, 'ime vajjetabbā' (these are to be avoided); or, they are the kings of the Vajjian country. The designation 'Vajjī' for the country, however, should be understood on account of the royal princes who resided there. 'Rājiddhiyā' (by royal power) means by the influence associated with the state of being a king. That influence of those republican kings became manifest in the world through their mutual harmony, and it was long-lasting; thus it is said, 'it speaks of their state of harmony.' 'Anubhāvo' is so called because it repeatedly (anu anu) cultivates (bhāveti) and increases (vaḍḍheti) those endowed with it; anubhāvo is the same as ānubhāvo, meaning majesty (patāpo). That majesty of theirs became manifest in the world through their wealth of conveyances such as elephants and horses, and through the abundance of food there; thus it is said, 'by this… it speaks of…' 'Tāḷacchiggaḷena' means through a keyhole. 'Asanaṃ' means an arrow. 'Atipātayissanti' means they will make it pass beyond. 'Poṅkhānupoṅkhaṃ' means feather after feather; the meaning is having made the feather of the next arrow follow the feather-base of the previous arrow. 'Avirādhitaṃ' means unhindered. 'Ucchindissāmi' means I will cut off the family lineage by way of uprooting. 'Ayanaṃ' is growth (vaḍḍhanaṃ), thus 'ayo'; its opposite is 'anayo,' hence it says 'avaḍḍhi' (decline). 'Ñātibyasanaṃ' is the ruin (byasanaṃ) or destruction (vināso) of relatives.

Gaṅgāyāti gaṅgāsamīpe. Paṭṭanagāmanti sakaṭapaṭṭanagāmaṃ. Tatrāti tasmiṃ paṭṭane. Balavāghātajātoti uppannabalavakodho. Meti mayhaṃ. Gatenāti gamanena. Sītaṃ vā uṇhaṃ vā natthi tāya velāya. Abhimukhaṃ yuddhenāti abhimukhaṃ ujukameva saṅgāmakaraṇena. Upalāpanaṃ sāmaṃ dānañcāti dassetuṃ “ala”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Bhedopi idha upāyo evāti [M 3.0162] vuttaṃ “aññatra mithubhedā”ti. Yuddhassa pana anupāyatā pageva pakāsitā. Idanti “aññatra upalāpanāya aññatra mithubhedā”ti idaṃ vacanaṃ. Kathāya nayaṃ labhitvāti “yāvakīvañca [V 3.0151] …pe… parihānī”ti imāya bhagavato kathāya upāyaṃ labhitvā. Anukampāyāti vajjirājesu anuggahena.

'Gaṅgāya' means near the Ganges. 'Paṭṭanagāmaṃ' means the port village of Sakaṭapaṭṭana. 'Tatrā' means in that port town. 'Balavāghātajāto' means one in whom strong anger has arisen. 'Me' means 'my' or 'for me.' 'Gatena' means by going. 'There is neither cold nor heat at that time.' 'Abhimukhaṃ yuddhena' means by making battle directly face-to-face. To show that conciliation, peaceful negotiation, and giving are sufficient means, the statement beginning with 'alaṃ' (enough) is made. That dissension is also a means here is stated by 'aññatra mithubhedā' (except for mutual dissension). The ineffectiveness of battle, however, has already been shown. 'Idaṃ' refers to this statement: 'except for conciliation, except for mutual dissension.' 'Kathāya nayaṃ labhitvā' means having obtained a method from this discourse of the Blessed One: 'As long as… no decline…' 'Anukampāya' means out of favour towards the Vajjian kings.

Rājāpi tameva pesetvā sabbe…pe… pāpesīti rājā taṃ attano santikaṃ āgataṃ “kiṃ, ācariya, bhagavā avacā”ti pucchi. So “yathā bho samaṇassa gotamassa vacanaṃ na sakkā vajjī kenaci gahetuṃ, apica upalāpanāya vā mithubhedena vā sakkā”ti āha. Tato naṃ rājā “upalāpanāya amhākaṃ hatthiassādayo nassissanti, bhedeneva te gahessāmi, kiṃ karomā”ti pucchi. Tena hi, mahārāja, tumhe vajjī ārabbha parisati kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpetha, tato ahaṃ “kiṃ te, mahārāja, tehi, attano santakena kasivaṇijjādīni katvā jīvantu ete rājāno”ti vatvā pakkamissāmi. Tato tumhe “kiṃ nu, bho, esa brāhmaṇo vajjī ārabbha pavattaṃ kathaṃ paṭibāhatī”ti vadeyyātha. Divasabhāge cāhaṃ tesaṃ paṇṇākāraṃ pesessāmi, tampi gāhāpetvā tumhepi mama dosaṃ āropetvā bandhanatāḷanādīni akatvāva kevalaṃ khuramuṇḍaṃ maṃ katvā nagarā nīharāpetha, athāhaṃ “mayā te nagare pākāro parikhā ca kāritā, ahaṃ thiradubbalaṭṭhānañca uttānagambhīraṭṭhānañca jānāmi, na cirassaṃ dāni taṃ ujuṃ karissāmī”ti vakkhāmi. Taṃ sutvā tumhe “gacchatū”ti vadeyyāthāti. Rājā sabbaṃ akāsi.

Regarding the passage, 'The king, having sent him, brought all... to ruin and disaster': The king asked him when he arrived in his presence, "What, teacher, did the Blessed One say?" He replied, "According to the word of the ascetic Gotama, the Vajjis cannot be captured by anyone, but it is possible by means of flattery or by causing dissension." Then the king asked him, "If we use flattery, our elephants, horses, and so forth will be lost. I will capture them by causing dissension alone. What should we do?" "Then, great king, you should raise a discussion in the assembly concerning the Vajjis. Then I will say, 'What is it to you, great king? Let these kings live by their own means, farming and trading.' Having said this, I will leave. Then you should say, 'Why does this brahmin obstruct the discussion concerning the Vajjis?' During the day, I will send them a gift. Seize that too, and accuse me as well. Without binding or beating me, just shave my head and banish me from the city. Then I will say, 'I had the walls and moats built for your city. I know the strong and weak points, the shallow and deep places. Before long I will set it right.' Hearing this, you should say, 'Let him go.'" The king did everything.

Licchavī tassa nikkhamanaṃ sutvā “saṭho brāhmaṇo, mā tassa gaṅgaṃ uttāretuṃ adatthā”ti āhaṃsu. Tatra ekaccehi “amhe ārabbha kathitattā kira so evaṃ karotī”ti vutte “tena hi bhaṇe etū”ti vadiṃsu. So gantvā licchavī disvā “kimāgatatthā”ti pucchito taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesi. Licchavino “appamattakena nāma evaṃ garuṃ daṇḍaṃ kātuṃ na yutta”nti vatvā “kiṃ te tatra ṭhānantara”nti pucchiṃsu. Vinicchayamahāmaccohamasmīti. Tadeva te ṭhānantaraṃ hotūti. So suṭṭhutaraṃ vinicchayaṃ karoti. Rājakumārā tassa santike sippaṃ uggaṇhanti. So patiṭṭhitaguṇo hutvā ekadivasaṃ ekaṃ licchaviṃ gahetvā ekamantaṃ gantvā “dārakā [M 3.0163] kasantī”ti pucchi. Āma, kasanti. Dve goṇe yojetvāti. Āma, dve goṇe yojetvāti. Ettakaṃ vatvā nivatto. Tato tamañño “kiṃ ācariyo āhā”ti pucchitvā tena vuttaṃ – asaddahanto “na meso yathābhūtaṃ kathetī”ti tena saddhiṃ bhijji.

The Licchavis, hearing of his departure, said, "That brahmin is deceitful; do not allow him to cross the Ganges." Some there remarked, "It seems he is acting this way because it was said about us." They then said, "Well then, let him come." He went and, seeing the Licchavis, was asked, "Why have you come?" He explained the situation to them. The Licchavis, saying, "It is not right to inflict such a heavy punishment for such a trifling matter," asked, "What was your position there?" "I was the chief minister of justice," he replied. "Let that very position be yours," they said. He gave judgments very well. The princes learned skills from him. Having established his good reputation, one day he took a Licchavi aside and asked, "Are the boys plowing?" "Yes, they are plowing." "With two oxen yoked?" "Yes, with two oxen yoked." Having said this much, he returned. Then another asked him, "What did the teacher say?" and not believing what was said, thinking, "He does not tell me what actually happened," he broke with him.

Brāhmaṇo aparampi ekadivasaṃ ekaṃ licchaviṃ ekamantaṃ netvā “kena byañjanena bhuttosī”ti pucchitvā nivatto. Tampi añño pucchitvā asaddahanto tatheva bhijji. Brāhmaṇo aparampi divasaṃ ekaṃ licchaviṃ ekamantaṃ netvā “atiduggatosi kirā”ti pucchi. Ko evamāhāti[V 3.0152]. Asuko nāma licchavīti. Aparampi ekamantaṃ netvā “tvaṃ kira bhīrujātiko”ti pucchi. Ko evamāhāti? Asuko nāma licchavīti. Evaṃ aññena akathitameva aññassa kathento tīhi saṃvaccharehi te rājāno aññamaññaṃ bhinditvā yathā dve ekamaggena na gacchanti, tathā katvā sannipātabheriṃ carāpesi. Licchavino “issarā sannipatantu, sūrā sannipatantū”ti vatvā na sannipatiṃsu. Brāhmaṇo “ayaṃ dāni kālo, sīghaṃ āgacchatū”ti rañño sāsanaṃ peseti. Rājā sutvāva balabheriṃ carāpetvā nikkhami. Vesālikā sutvā “rañño gaṅgaṃ uttarituṃ na dassāmā”ti bheriṃ carāpesuṃ. Te sutvā “gacchantu sūrarājāno”tiādīni vatvā na sannipatiṃsu. “Nagarappavesanaṃ na dassāma, dvārāni pidahissāmā”ti bheriṃ carāpesuṃ. Ekopi na sannipati. Yathāvivaṭehi dvārehi pavisitvā sabbe anayabyasanaṃ pāpetvā gato. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ – “rājāpi tameva pesetvā sabbepi bhinditvā gantvā anayabyasanaṃ pāpesī”ti.

The brahmin took another Licchavi aside one day and asked, "With what relish did you eat?" and then withdrew. Another asked that Licchavi what was said, and not believing him, he too broke away. The brahmin took yet another Licchavi aside one day and asked, "Are you said to be extremely poor?" "Who says so?" "Such-and-such a Licchavi." Again, he took another aside and asked, "Are you said to be of a cowardly nature?" "Who says so?" "Such-and-such a Licchavi." Thus, by relating to one what another had not said, within three years he caused those kings to become divided from each other. He made them so divided that two would not walk the same path together, and then he had the assembly drum sounded. The Licchavis, saying, "Let the powerful assemble, let the brave assemble," did not assemble. The brahmin sent a message to the king, saying, "Now is the time, come quickly!" Upon hearing this, the king had the drum of war sounded and set out. The people of Vesālī heard it and had a drum sounded, saying, "We will not allow the king to cross the Ganges!" Hearing this, they said, "Let the heroic kings go forth," and so on, but they did not assemble. They had a drum sounded, saying, "We will not allow entry into the city, we will close the gates." Not even one assembled. The king entered through the gates as they were open, brought them all to ruin and disaster, and then departed. With reference to this it was said: "The king sent him and, having divided them all, went and brought them to ruin and disaster."

Vassakārasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Vassakāra Sutta is concluded.

2. Paṭhamasattakasuttavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the First Sutta of the Sevens

23. Tatiye aparihānāya hitāti aparihāniyā (dī. ni. ṭī. 2.136), na parihāyanti etehīti vā aparihāniyā. Evaṃ saṅkhepato vuttamatthaṃ vitthārato dassento “idhāpi cā”tiādimāha. Tattha tatotiādi disāsu āgatasāsane vuttavacanaṃ vuttakathanaṃ. Vihārasīmā ākulā yasmā[M 3.0164], tasmā uposathapavāraṇā ṭhitā. Olīyamānakoti pāḷito atthato ca vinassamānako. Ukkhipāpentāti paguṇabhāvakaraṇena atthasaṃvaṇṇanāvasena ca paggaṇhantā.

23. In the third point, aparihānāya hitā means aparihāniyā (for non-decline) (Dī. Ni. Ṭī. 2.136); or, because they do not decline by these means, it is aparihāniyā. Explaining in detail the meaning thus stated in brief, he says, 'And here also,' and so on. Therein, tato, and so on, refers to the spoken word and the spoken teaching in the Dispensation that has come to the various regions. Because the monastery boundary is congested, the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā are therefore established. Olīyamānako means perishing both in terms of the Pāli text and its meaning. Ukkhipāpentā means supporting them by making them proficient and by way of explaining the meaning.

Sāvatthiyaṃ bhikkhū viya (pārā. 565) pācittiyaṃ desāpetabboti paññāpentā. Vajjiputtakā viya (cūḷava. 446) dasavatthudīpanena. Tathā akarontāti navaṃ katikavattaṃ vā sikkhāpadaṃ vā amaddantā dhammavinayato sāsanaṃ dīpentā khuddakampi ca sikkhāpadaṃ asamūhanantā. Āyasmā mahākassapo viya cāti “suṇātu me, āvuso, saṅgho, santāmhākaṃ sikkhāpadāni gihigatāni. Gihinopi jānanti ‘idaṃ vo samaṇānaṃ sakyaputtikānaṃ kappati, idaṃ vo na kappatī’ti. Sacepi hi mayaṃ khuddānukhuddakāni sikkhāpadāni samūhanissāma, bhavissanti vattāro ‘dhūmakālikaṃ samaṇena gotamena sāvakānaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññattaṃ, yāvimesaṃ satthā aṭṭhāsi, tāvime sikkhāpadesu sikkhiṃsu. Yato imesaṃ satthā parinibbuto, na dānime sikkhāpadesu [V 3.0153] sikkhantī’ti. Yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ, saṅgho apaññattaṃ na paññapeyya, paññattaṃ na samucchindeyya, yathāpaññattesu sikkhāpadesu samādāya vatteyyā”ti imaṃ (cūḷava. 442) tantiṃ ṭhapento āyasmā mahākassapo viya ca.

Like the monks at Sāvatthī (Pārā. 565), who decree that a pācittiya offense should be confessed. Like the Vajjiputtakas (Cūḷava. 446), by elucidating the ten points. Similarly, those who do not act thus—not rejecting a new customary rule or training rule, elucidating the Teaching from the Dhamma and Vinaya, and not uprooting even a minor training rule—and like the Venerable Mahākassapa, who, establishing this standard (Cūḷava. 442), said: "Friends, let the Sangha listen to me. Our training rules have become known to householders. Even householders know, 'This is allowable for you, the Sakyan ascetics; this is not allowable for you.' If we were to uproot even the minor training rules, there would be those who say, 'The training rule laid down by the ascetic Gotama for his disciples was temporary, like smoke. As long as their teacher was present, they trained in these training rules. But now that their teacher has passed away, they no longer train in the training rules.' If it seems timely to the Sangha, the Sangha should not lay down what has not been laid down, nor abolish what has been laid down, but should proceed, having undertaken the training rules as they have been laid down."

Thirabhāvappattāti sāsane thirabhāvaṃ anivattitabhāvaṃ upagatā. Therakārakehīti therabhāvasādhakehi sīlādiguṇehi asekkhadhammehi. Bahū rattiyoti pabbajitā hutvā bahū rattiyo jānanti. Sīlādiguṇesu patiṭṭhāpanameva sāsane pariṇāyakatāti āha “tīsu sikkhāsu pavattentī”ti. Ovādaṃ na denti abhājanabhāvato. Paveṇikathanti ācariyaparamparābhataṃ sammāpaṭipattidīpanaṃ dhammakathaṃ. Sārabhūtaṃ dhammapariyāyanti samathavipassanāmaggaphalasampāpanena sāsane sārabhūtaṃ bojjhaṅgakosallaanuttarasītibhāva- (a. ni. 6.85) adhicittasuttādidhammatantiṃ. Ādikaṃ ovādanti ādi-saddena “evaṃ te āloketabbaṃ, evaṃ te viloketabbaṃ, evaṃ te samiñjitabbaṃ, evaṃ te pasāretabbaṃ, evaṃ te saṅghāṭipattacīvaraṃ dhāretabba”nti ovādaṃ saṅgaṇhāti.

"Attained steadfastness" means they have reached a steadfast, non-returning state in the Dispensation. "By qualities that make one an elder" refers to the virtues such as morality that establish the state of an elder, and the qualities of one beyond training. "Many nights" means they have known many nights since going forth. Establishing others in virtues such as morality is itself leadership in the Dispensation; thus it is said, “causing them to proceed in the three trainings.” "They do not give advice" because the recipients are unfit. "Traditional talk" refers to the Dhamma talk that illuminates right practice, handed down through the lineage of teachers. "The essential Dhamma exposition" means the Dhamma teaching that is essential in the Dispensation by leading to the attainment of serenity, insight, the path, and fruition—such as skill in the enlightenment factors, the unsurpassed coolness (AN 6.85), the suttas on the higher mind, and other such Dhamma texts. "The initial advice" includes, by the word "initial," instructions such as: "Thus should you look forward, thus should you look around, thus should you bend, thus should you stretch, thus should you wear your patchwork robe, bowl, and outer robe."

Punabbhavadānaṃ punabbhavo uttarapadalopena. Itareti ye na paccayavasikā na āmisacakkhukā, te na gacchanti taṇhāya vasaṃ.

The term `punabbhavadāna` means rebirth, with the elision of the latter part of the compound. Those others, who are not controlled by requisites, nor have an eye for material things, do not come under the power of craving.

Āraññakesūti [M 3.0165] araññabhāgesu araññapariyāpannesu. Nanu yattha katthacipi taṇhā sāvajjā evāti codanaṃ sandhāyāha “gāmantasenāsanesu hī”tiādi. Tena “anuttaresu vimokkhesu pihaṃ upaṭṭhāpayato”ti ettha vuttapihādayo piya āraññakasenāsanesu sālayatā sevitabbapakkhikā evāti dasseti.

"In forest dwellings" means in forest regions, in places included within the forest. In reference to the objection, “Surely, is not craving blameworthy wherever it may be?” it is said, “For in dwellings at the village outskirts...” and so on. By this, it shows that longing and so on, mentioned in the phrase “arousing longing for the unsurpassed liberations,” are also on the side of what is to be cultivated by one who delights in forest dwellings.

Attanāvāti sayameva. Tena parehi anussāhitānaṃ saraseneva anāgatānaṃ pesalānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ āgamanaṃ, āgatānañca phāsuvihāraṃ paccāsīsantīti dasseti. Imināva nīhārenāti imāya paṭipattiyā. Aggahitadhammaggahaṇanti aggahitassa pariyattidhammassa uggahaṇaṃ. Gahitasajjhāyakaraṇanti uggahitassa suṭṭhu atthacintanaṃ. Cintarattho hi ayaṃ sajjhāyasaddo. Entīti upagacchanti. Nisīdanti āsanapaññāpanādinā.

"By oneself" means by oneself alone. This shows that they expect the arrival of virtuous monks who have come of their own accord, not having been encouraged by others, and a comfortable abiding for those who have arrived. "By this very method" means by this practice. "Grasping the ungrasped Dhamma" means learning the ungrasped scriptural Dhamma. "Reciting what has been grasped" means thoroughly reflecting on the meaning of what has been learned, for this word "recitation" has the meaning of reflection. "They come" means they approach. "They sit down" implies the arranging of seats and so on.

Paṭhamasattakasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the First Sutta of the Septet is concluded.

4-6. Dutiyasattakasuttādivaṇṇanā

4-6. Commentary on the Second Sutta of the Septet, etc.

24-26. Catutthe [V 3.0154] karontoyevāti yathāvuttaṃ tiracchānakathaṃ kathentoyeva. Atiracchānakathābhāvepi tassa tattha tapparabhāvadassanatthaṃ avadhāraṇavacanaṃ. Pariyantakārīti sapariyantaṃ katvā vattā. “Pariyantavatiṃ vācaṃ bhāsitā”ti (dī. ni. 1.9, 194) hi vuttaṃ. Appabhassovāti parimitakathoyeva ekantena kathetabbasseva kathanato. Samāpattisamāpajjanaṃ ariyo tuṇhībhāvo. Niddāyatiyevāti niddokkamane anādīnavadassī niddāyatiyeva, iriyāpathaparivattanādinā na naṃ vinodeti. Evaṃ saṃsaṭṭhovāti vuttanayena gaṇasaṅgaṇikāya saṃsaṭṭho eva viharati. Dussīlā pāpicchā nāmāti sayaṃ nissīlā asantaguṇasambhāvanicchāya samannāgatattā pāpā lāmakā icchā etesanti pāpicchā. Pāpapuggalehi mittikaraṇato pāpamittā. Tehi sadā sahapavattanena pāpasahāyā. Tattha ninnatādinā tadadhimuttatāya pāpasampavaṅkā. Pañcamādīni uttānatthāniyeva.

24-26. "In the fourth case, he does just that" means he engages in low talk as previously described. Even in the absence of low talk, the emphatic particle is used to show his dedication to it. "One who speaks within limits" means one who speaks after setting limits. As it is said, "he speaks speech that has a limit." "Speaking little" means speaking only a limited amount, because of speaking only what absolutely needs to be spoken. "Noble silence" is entering into a meditative attainment. "He just sleeps" means, not seeing the danger in giving way to sleep, he just sleeps and does not dispel it by changing posture, etc. "Thus, he associates" means he lives associating closely with groups and company in the manner described. "The immoral, of evil wishes": they are themselves devoid of virtue and are endowed with a desire for the estimation of non-existent qualities; therefore, their wishes are evil and base, thus they are of 'evil wishes'. "Evil friends" are those who befriend wicked people. "Evil companions" are those who constantly associate with them. "Inclined to evil" are those inclined towards them due to their disposition, etc., and their conviction in them. The meaning of the fifth and following terms is clear.

Dutiyasattakasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Second Sutta of the Septet, etc., is concluded.

7-11. Saññāsuttādivaṇṇanā

7-11. Commentary on the Sutta on Perceptions, etc.

27-31. Sattame [M 3.0166] aniccāti anupassati etāyāti aniccānupassanā. Tathāpavattavipassanā pana yasmā attanā sahagatasaññāya bhāvitāya bhāvitā eva hoti, tasmā vuttaṃ “aniccānupassanādīhi sahagatasaññā”ti. Imā satta lokiyavipassanāpi honti “anicca”ntiādinā pavattanato. “Etaṃ santaṃ etaṃ paṇītaṃ yadidaṃ sabbasaṅkhārasamatho”ti āgatavasena panettha dve lokuttarā hontīti veditabbā. “Virāgo nirodho”ti hi tattha nibbānaṃ vuttanti idha virāgasaññā, tā vuttasaññā nibbānārammaṇāpi siyuṃ. Sesamettha suviññeyyameva. Aṭṭhamādīni uttānatthāneva.

27-31. In the seventh, ‘by this one contemplates “impermanent”’—thus it is the contemplation of impermanence. However, since the insight that proceeds in such a way is developed only when the perception associated with it has been developed, therefore it is said, “perception associated with the contemplation of impermanence, etc.” These seven are also mundane insights, because they proceed with terms like “impermanent.” It should be understood that two here are supramundane, according to the passage: “This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, the stilling of all formations.” For there, Nibbāna is described as “dispassion, cessation”—thus, the perception of dispassion here, and the perceptions mentioned, may also have Nibbāna as their object. The rest here is easily understood. The eighth and those following are clear in meaning.

Saññāsuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Sutta on Perceptions, etc., is concluded.

Vajjisattakavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Chapter of the Septet on the Vajjis is concluded.

4. Devatāvaggo

4. The Chapter on Deities

5. Paṭhamamittasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the First Sutta on a Friend

36. Catutthassa [V 3.0155] pañcame attano guyhaṃ tassa āvikarotīti attano guyhaṃ nigguhituṃ yuttakathaṃ aññassa akathetvā tasseva ācikkhati. Tassa guyhaṃ aññesaṃ nācikkhatīti tena kathitaguyhaṃ yathā aññe na jānanti, evaṃ anāvikaronto chādeti.

36. In the fourth, regarding the fifth point: ‘one reveals one’s own secret to him’ means that without telling another a matter fit to be kept hidden, one discloses it to that very person. ‘Does not tell his secret to others’ means one conceals what has been told by him, not revealing it, so that others do not know.

Paṭhamamittasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the First Sutta on a Friend is concluded.

6-11. Dutiyamittasuttādivaṇṇanā

6-11. Commentary on the Second Sutta on a Friend, etc.

37-42. Chaṭṭhe piyo ca hoti manāpo cāti kalyāṇamittalakkhaṇaṃ dassitaṃ. Kalyāṇamitto hi saddhāsampanno ca hoti sīlasampanno sutasampanno cāgasampanno vīriyasampanno satisampanno samādhisampanno paññāsampanno. Tattha saddhāsampattiyā saddahati tathāgatassa sambodhiṃ kammañca kammaphalañca, tena sambodhiyā hetubhūtaṃ sattesu hitasukhaṃ na pariccajati[M 3.0167]. Sīlasampattiyā sattānaṃ piyo hoti garu bhāvanīyo codako pāpagarahī vattā vacanakkhamo. Sutasampattiyā saccapaṭiccasamuppādādipaṭisaṃyuttānaṃ gambhīrānaṃ kathānaṃ kattā hoti. Cāgasampattiyā appiccho hoti santuṭṭho pavivitto asaṃsaṭṭho. Vīriyasampattiyā āraddhavīriyo hoti attahitaparahitapaṭipattiyaṃ. Satisampattiyā upaṭṭhitassatī hoti. Samādhisampattiyā avikkhitto hoti samāhitacito. Paññāsampattiyā aviparītaṃ pajānāti. So satiyā kusalākusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ gatiyo samannesamāno paññāya sattānaṃ hitāhitaṃ yathābhūtaṃ jānitvā samādhinā tattha ekaggacitto hutvā vīriyena satte ahite nisedhetvā hite niyojeti. Tena vuttaṃ “piyo…pe… niyojetī”ti. Sattamādīni uttānatthāni.

37-42. In the sixth, the characteristics of a good friend are shown as “dear and agreeable.” For a good friend is endowed with faith, virtue, learning, generosity, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. Herein, through the attainment of faith, one has faith in the enlightenment of the Tathāgata and in kamma and its results; thus, one does not abandon the welfare and happiness of beings, which is a cause for enlightenment. Through the attainment of virtue, one becomes dear to beings, respected, esteemed, an exhorter, a reprover of evil, a speaker, and patient of others' speech. Through the attainment of learning, one becomes a speaker of profound discourses connected with truth, dependent origination, and so forth. Through the attainment of generosity, one has few wants, is content, secluded, and unentangled. Through the attainment of energy, one is energetic in the practice for one’s own and others' welfare. Through the attainment of mindfulness, one is established in mindfulness. Through the attainment of concentration, one is undistracted and has a composed mind. Through the attainment of wisdom, one understands without distortion. Investigating with mindfulness the courses of wholesome and unwholesome states, one knows with wisdom the benefit and harm for beings as they truly are; becoming one-pointed in mind there with concentration, with energy one restrains beings from what is unbeneficial and guides them to what is beneficial. Therefore, it is said: “dear… guides.” The seventh and following are clear in meaning.

Dutiyamittasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Second Sutta on a Friend, etc., is concluded.

Devatāvaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Chapter on Deities is concluded.

5. Mahāyaññavaggo

5. The Chapter on the Great Sacrifice

1. Sattaviññāṇaṭṭhitisuttavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Sutta on the Seven Stations of Consciousness

44. Pañcamassa [V 3.0156] paṭhame yasmā nidassanatthe nipāto (dī. ni. ṭī. 2.127) tasmā seyyathāpi manussāti yathā manussāti vuttaṃ hoti. Viseso hotiyeva satipi bāhirassa kāraṇassa abhede ajjhattikassa bhinnattā. Nānattaṃ kāye etesaṃ, nānatto vā kāyo etesanti nānattakāyā. Iminā nayena sesapadesupi attho veditabbo. Nesanti manussānaṃ. Nānattā saññā etesaṃ atthīti nānattasaññino. Sukhasamussayato vinipāto etesaṃ atthīti vinipātikā satipi devabhāve dibbasampattiyā abhāvato. Apāyesu vā gato natthi nipāto etesanti vinipātikā. Tenāha “catuapāyavinimuttā”ti. Piyaṅkaramātādīnaṃ viyāti piyaṅkaramātā kira yakkhinī paccūsasamaye anuruddhattherassa dhammaṃ sajjhāyato sutvā –

44. In the first of the fifth, because the particle is used in the sense of illustration (Dī. Ni. Ṭī. 2.127), therefore, ‘just as humans’ means ‘like humans’ is stated. There is indeed a distinction even when the external cause is the same, due to the difference in the internal cause. ‘Those with diverse bodies’ means there is diversity in their bodies, or the body is diverse among them. In this way, the meaning of the remaining phrases should also be understood. ‘Nesam’ means ‘of humans.’ ‘Nānattasaññino’ means ‘they have diverse perceptions’ because ‘diverse perceptions exist for them.’ ‘Vinipātikā’ means ‘prone to downfall’ because ‘a downfall from the accumulation of happiness is theirs,’ even though they are devas, due to the absence of divine attainments. Or, ‘vinipātikā’ means ‘for them there is no falling into the states of woe.’ Therefore, it is said, ‘freed from the four states of woe.’ Like Piyaṅkaramātā and others—it is said that Piyaṅkaramātā, a yakkhinī, heard the Venerable Anuruddha reciting the Dhamma at dawn—

“Mā [M 3.0168] saddamakarī piyaṅkara, bhikkhu dhammapadāni bhāsati;

Api dhammapadaṃ vijāniya, paṭipajjema hitāya no siyā.

“Make no noise, Piyaṅkara, the monk is reciting verses of Dhamma; having understood a verse of Dhamma, may we practice it for our welfare.

“Pāṇesu ca saṃyamāmase, sampajānamusā na bhaṇāmase;

Sikkhema susīlyamattano, api muccema pisācayoniyā”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.240) –

“We should restrain ourselves with regard to living beings, and knowingly speak no lies; let us train ourselves in good conduct, and perhaps be freed from the ghost realm.” (Saṃ. Ni. 1.240)

Evaṃ puttakaṃ saññāpetvā taṃ divasaṃ sotāpattiphalaṃ pattā. Uttaramātā pana bhagavato dhammaṃ sutvāva sotāpannā jātā.

Thus, having instructed her son, that day she attained the fruit of stream-entry. Uttaramātā, however, became a stream-enterer just upon hearing the Blessed One’s Dhamma.

Brahmakāye paṭhamajjhānanibbatte brahmasamūhe, brahmanikāye vā bhavāti brahmakāyikā. Mahābrahmuno parisāya bhavāti brahmapārisajjā tassa paricārakaṭṭhāne ṭhitattā. Mahābrahmuno purohitaṭṭhāne ṭhitāti brahmapurohitā. Āyuvaṇṇādīhi mahantā brahmānoti mahābrahmāno. Satipi tesaṃ tividhānampi paṭhamena jhānena gantvā nibbattabhāve jhānassa pana pavattibhedena ayaṃ visesoti dassetuṃ “brahmapārisajjā panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Parittenāti hīnena. Sā cassa hīnatā chandādīnaṃ hīnatāya veditabbā. Paṭiladdhamattaṃ vā hīnaṃ. Kappassāti asaṅkhyeyyakappassa[V 3.0157]. Hīnapaṇītānaṃ majjhe bhavattā majjhimaṃ. Sā cassa majjhimatā chandādīnaṃ majjhimatāya veditabbā. Paṭilabhitvā nātisubhāvitaṃ vā majjhimaṃ. Upaḍḍhakappoti asaṅkhyeyyakappassa upaḍḍhakappo. Vipphārikataroti brahmapārisajjehi pamāṇato vipulataro sabhāvato uḷārataro ca hoti. Sabhāvenapi hi uḷāratamova. Taṃ panettha appamāṇaṃ. Tassa hi parittābhādīnaṃ parittasubhādīnañca kāye satipi sabhāvavematte ekattavaseneva vavatthapīyatīti “ekattakāyā”tveva te vuccanti. Paṇītenāti ukkaṭṭhena. Sā cassa ukkaṭṭhatā chandādīnaṃ ukkaṭṭhatāya veditabbā. Subhāvitaṃ vā, sammadeva, vasibhāvaṃ pāpitaṃ paṇītaṃ “padhānabhāvaṃ nīta”nti katvā. Idhāpi kappo asaṅkhyeyyakappavaseneva veditabbo paripuṇṇamahākappassa asambhavato. Itīti evaṃ vuttappakārena. Teti “brahmakāyikā”ti vuttā tividhāpi brahmāno. Saññāya ekattāti tihetukabhāvena ekasabhāvattā. Na hi tassā sampayuttadhammavasena aññopi koci bhedo atthi. Evanti iminā nānattakāyā ekattasaññino gahitāti dasseti.

In the Brahma realm, ‘Brahmakāyikā’ means those who are born in the group of Brahmās or the assembly of Brahmās, having arisen from the first jhāna. ‘Brahmāpārisajjā’ means those who are part of Mahābrahmā’s retinue, because they stand in the position of his attendants. ‘Brahmapurohitā’ means those who stand in the position of Mahābrahmā’s chief ministers. ‘Mahābrahmāno’ means those who are great in lifespan, appearance, and other qualities. Even though these three types are born by going there through the first jhāna, to show that this distinction is due to a difference in the practice of the jhāna, it is said: ‘Brahmāpārisajjā,’ etc. ‘Paritta’ means inferior. This inferiority should be understood as the inferiority of their zeal and other qualities, or as merely having attained. ‘Kappassa’ refers to an incalculable eon. ‘Majjhima’ means being in the middle between the inferior and the superior. This middling nature should be understood as the middling nature of their zeal and other qualities, or as having attained but not being very well developed. ‘Upaḍḍhakappo’ means half of an incalculable eon. ‘Vipphārikatara’ means more extensive than the Brahmāpārisajjā in measure and more sublime in nature. For in nature, it is indeed most sublime, and that sublimity is here immeasurable. For although there are bodies of the Parittābhā and others with limited radiance and bodies of the Parittasubhā and others with limited beauty, due to the unity in their essential nature, they are designated simply as ‘ekattakāyā’ (having a single body). ‘Paṇīta’ means superior. This superiority should be understood as the superiority of their zeal and other qualities, or as well-developed, rightly brought to a state of mastery, having been ‘brought to a state of prominence.’ Here too, ‘kappa’ should be understood as an incalculable eon, since a full great eon is impossible. ‘Iti’ means in this manner. ‘Te’ refers to the three types of Brahmās called ‘Brahmakāyikā.’ ‘Saññāya ekattā’ means their unity in perception due to their being three-rooted and thus having a single nature, for there is no other distinction based on associated mental states. ‘Evaṃ’ indicates that by this, those with diverse bodies but unified perception are included.

Daṇḍaukkāyāti [M 3.0169] daṇḍadīpikāya. Sarati dhāvati, vissarati vippakiṇṇā viya dhāvati. Dve kappāti dve mahākappā. Ito paresupi eseva nayo. Idhāti imasmiṃ sutte. Ukkaṭṭhaparicchedavasena ābhassaraggahaṇeneva sabbepi te parittābhāappamāṇābhāpi gahitā.

‘Daṇḍaukkāya’ means by a torch-stick. ‘Sarati’ means ‘it rushes’; ‘vissarati’ means ‘it rushes as if dispersed.’ ‘Two kappas’ means two great eons. This same method applies to what follows. ‘Idha’ means ‘in this sutta.’ By grasping the Ābhassara realm by way of the highest limit, all those—even the Parittābhā and Appamāṇābhā—are included.

Sundarā pabhā subhā, tāya kiṇṇā subhākiṇṇāti vattabbe. Bhā-saddassa rassattaṃ antima-ṇa-kārassa ha-kārañca katvā “subhakiṇhā”ti vuttā. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana niccalāya ekagghanāya pabhāya subhoti pariyāyavacananti “subhena okiṇṇā vikiṇṇā”ti attho vutto. Etthāpi antima-ṇa-kārassa ha-kārakaraṇaṃ icchitabbameva. Na chijjitvā pabhā gacchati ekagghanattā. Catutthaviññāṇaṭṭhitimeva bhajanti kāyassa saññāya ca ekarūpattā. Vipulasantasukhāyuvaṇṇādiphalattā vehapphalā. Etthāti viññāṇaṭṭhitiyaṃ.

A beautiful radiance is ‘subhā’; strewn with that, it should be said ‘subhākiṇṇā’. Having shortened the word ‘bhā’ and changed the final ‘ṇa’ to ‘ha,’ it is said ‘subhakiṇhā.’ In the commentary, however, ‘subhā’ is a synonymous term for steady and solid light, hence the meaning is given as ‘strewn or scattered with loveliness.’ Here too, the changing of the final ‘ṇa’ to ‘ha’ is to be accepted. The light does not break and go, because of its solid nature. They partake of the fourth station of consciousness, because of the uniformity of body and perception. ‘Vehapphalā’ means they are the fruit of abundant, peaceful happiness, life, beauty, and so forth. ‘Ettha’ means ‘in this station of consciousness.’

Vivaṭṭapakkhe ṭhitā apunarāvattanato. “Na sabbakālikā”ti vatvā tameva asabbakālikattaṃ vibhāvetuṃ “kappasatasahassampī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Soḷasakappasahassaccayena uppannānaṃ suddhāvāsabrahmānaṃ parinibbāyanato aññesañca tattha anuppajjanato buddhasuññe loke suññaṃ taṃ ṭhānaṃ hoti, tasmā suddhāvāsā na sabbakālikā. Khandhāvāraṭṭhānasadisā honti suddhāvāsabhūmiyo. Iminā suttena suddhāvāsānaṃ sattāvāsabhāvadīpaneneva viññāṇaṭṭhitibhāvopi dīpito hoti, tasmā suddhāvāsāpi sattasu viññāṇaṭṭhitīsu catutthaviññāṇaṭṭhitiṃ, navasu sattāvāsesu catutthasattāvāsañca bhajanti.

They stand on the side of the evolving eon, because there is no returning. Having stated that they are ‘not perpetual,’ it is further clarified with ‘even for a hundred thousand eons,’ etc., to explain that very imperpetuity. After the passing of sixteen thousand eons, the Pure Abode Brahmās who arose there attain final Nibbāna, and since no others arise there, that place becomes empty in a world empty of Buddhas. Therefore, the Pure Abodes are not perpetual. The Pure Abode realms are like sites of encampments. By this sutta, merely by indicating the state of the Pure Abodes as abodes for beings, their state as stations of consciousness is also indicated. Therefore, the Pure Abodes also partake of the fourth station of consciousness among the seven stations of consciousness, and the fourth abode of beings among the nine abodes of beings.

Sukhumattāti [V 3.0158] saṅkhārāvasesasukhumabhāvappattattā. Paribyattaviññāṇakiccābhāvato neva viññāṇaṃ, na sabbaso aviññāṇaṃ hotīti nāviññāṇaṃ, tasmā paripphutaviññāṇakiccavantīsu viññāṇaṭṭhitīsu na vuttaṃ.

‘Because of subtlety’ means because of having attained a state of subtlety as residual formations. Because there is an absence of the function of manifest consciousness, it is neither consciousness nor entirely non-consciousness, hence it is not non-consciousness. Therefore, it is not mentioned among the stations of consciousness, in which the function of consciousness is pervasive.

Sattaviññāṇaṭṭhitisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Sutta on the Seven Stations of Consciousness is concluded.

2. Samādhiparikkhārasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Discourse on the Accessories of Concentration

45. Dutiye samādhiparikkhārāti ettha tayo parikkhārā. “Ratho sīlaparikkhāro, jhānakkho cakkavīriyo”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.4) hi ettha alaṅkāro parikkhāro [M 3.0170] nāma. “Sattahi nagaraparikkhārehi suparikkhataṃ hotī”ti (a. ni. 7.67) ettha parivāro parikkhāro nāma. “Gilānapaccaya…pe… jīvitaparikkhārā”ti (ma. ni. 1.191-192) ettha sambhāro parikkhāro nāma. So idha adhippetoti āha “maggasamādhissa sambhārā”ti. Parivāraparikkhāropi vaṭṭatiyeva. Parivāro hi sammādiṭṭhādayo maggadhammā sammāsamādhissa sahajātādipaccayabhāvena parikaraṇato abhisaṅkharaṇato. Parikkhatāti parivāritā. Ayaṃ vuccati ariyo sammāsamādhīti ayaṃ sattahi ratanehi parivuto cakkavattī viya sattahi aṅgehi parivuto ariyo sammāsamādhīti vuccati. Upecca nissīyatīti upanisā, saha upanisāyāti saupaniso, saupanissayo attho, saparivāroyevāti vuttaṃ hoti. Sahakārikāraṇabhūto hi dhammasamūho idha “upaniso”ti adhippeto.

45. In the second, regarding ‘requisites for concentration,’ there are three kinds of requisites. Here, in ‘The chariot is the requisite of virtue, jhāna the axle, energy the wheel’ (Saṃ. Ni. 5.4), a requisite is named ornamentation. Here, in ‘fortified with seven city requisites’ (A. Ni. 7.67), a requisite is named an enclosure. Here, in ‘support for the sick... requisites for life’ (Ma. Ni. 1.191-192), a requisite is named provisions. That this is intended here is stated as ‘the provisions for the concentration of the path.’ The enclosure-requisite also applies. For the enclosure consists of the path factors, such as right view, which serve as accessories to right concentration by being its co-nascent conditions and by preparing it. ‘Parikkhata’ means encompassed. This is called noble right concentration—just as a wheel-turning monarch is surrounded by seven treasures, noble right concentration is said to be surrounded by seven factors. That which one approaches and relies upon is `upanisā` (support). `Saha upanisāya` (together with its support) is `saupaniso`, which has the meaning of `saupanissayo` (with its support), and it is said to be `saparivāro` (with its retinue). Here, the collection of dhammas that function as cooperative causes is intended by ‘upanisā’.

Samādhiparikkhārasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Discourse on the Accessories of Concentration is concluded.

3. Paṭhamaaggisuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the First Fire Discourse

46. Tatiye anuḍahanaṭṭhenāti kāmaṃ āhuneyyaggiādayo tayo aggī brāhmaṇehipi icchitā santi. Te pana tehi icchitamattāva, na sattānaṃ tādisā atthasādhakā. Ye pana sattānaṃ atthasādhakā, te dassetuṃ “āhunaṃ vuccatī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha ānetvā hunanaṃ pūjanaṃ “āhuna”nti vuttaṃ, taṃ āhunaṃ arahantī mātāpitaro. Tenāha bhagavā – “āhuneyyāti, bhikkhave, mātāpitūnaṃ etaṃ adhivacana”nti (itivu. 106). Yadaggena ca te puttānaṃ bahūpakāratāya [V 3.0159] āhuneyyāti, tesu sammāpaṭipatti nesaṃ hitasukhāvahā, tadaggena tesu micchāpaṭipatti ahitadukkhāvahāti āha “tesu…pe… nibbattantī”ti.

46. In the third section, 'in the sense of not burning up,' although the three fires—the fire worthy of offerings, etc.—are desired by brahmins, they are desired merely as such and do not truly benefit beings. To show those fires that do benefit beings, it is said, 'āhuna is called...' Here, 'āhuna' refers to the act of bringing near and offering, which is honoring. Parents are worthy of that āhuna. Therefore, the Blessed One said, '“Worthy of offerings,” monks, this is a designation for parents' (Itivuttaka 106). Because parents, through their great service to their children, are worthy of offerings, right conduct toward them brings welfare and happiness, while wrong conduct toward them brings harm and suffering—thus it is said, 'toward them... are produced.'

Svāyamattho (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 3.305) mittavindakavatthunā veditabbo. Mittavindako hi mātarā, “tāta, ajja uposathiko hutvā vihāre sabbarattiṃ dhammassavanaṃ suṇohi, sahassaṃ te dassāmī”ti vutto dhanalobhena uposathaṃ samādāya vihāraṃ gantvā “idaṃ ṭhānaṃ akutobhaya”nti sallakkhetvā dhammāsanassa heṭṭhā nipanno sabbarattiṃ niddāyitvā gharaṃ [M 3.0171] agamāsi. Mātā pātova yāguṃ pacitvā upanāmesi. So sahassaṃ gahetvāva pivi. Athassa etadahosi “dhanaṃ saṃharissāmī”ti. So nāvāya samuddaṃ pakkhanditukāmo ahosi. Atha naṃ mātā, “tāta, imasmiṃ kule cattālīsakoṭidhanaṃ atthi, alaṃ gamanenā”ti nivāreti. So tassā vacanaṃ anādiyitvā gacchati eva. Sā purato aṭṭhāsi. Atha naṃ kujjhitvā “ayaṃ mayhaṃ purato tiṭṭhatī”ti pādena paharitvā patitaṃ antaraṃ katvā agamāsi.

This meaning should be understood through the story of Mittavindaka (as found in Dīgha Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā 3.305). Mittavindaka was told by his mother, 'Dear son, today, having become an observer of the Uposatha, listen to the Dhamma in the monastery all night, and I will give you a thousand.' Out of greed for money, he undertook the Uposatha and went to the monastery. Thinking, 'This place is safe from all dangers,' he lay down beneath the Dhamma seat, slept all night, and then returned home. In the morning, his mother prepared rice gruel and offered it to him. He took the thousand and then drank it. Then this thought occurred to him: 'I will accumulate wealth.' He wanted to board a ship and set out to sea. His mother tried to stop him, saying, 'Dear son, in this family there is a fortune of forty crores; there is no need to go.' But he disregarded her words and went anyway. She stood in front of him. Then, angered, thinking 'This one stands in my way,' he struck her with his foot, knocked her down, and went on his way.

Mātā uṭṭhahitvā “mādisāya mātari evarūpaṃ kammaṃ katvā gatassa te gataṭṭhāne sukhaṃ bhavissatīti evaṃsaññī nāma tvaṃ puttā”ti āha. Tassa nāvaṃ āruyha gacchato sattame divase nāvā aṭṭhāsi. Atha te manussā “addhā ettha pāpapuggalo atthi, salākaṃ dethā”ti āhaṃsu. Salākā dīyamānā tasseva tikkhattuṃ pāpuṇi. Te tassa uḷumpaṃ datvā taṃ samudde pakkhipiṃsu. So ekaṃ dīpaṃ gantvā vimānapetīhi saddhiṃ sampattiṃ anubhavanto tāhi “purato purato mā agamāsī”ti vuccamānopi taddiguṇaṃ taddiguṇaṃ sampattiṃ passanto anupubbena khuracakkadharaṃ ekaṃ addasa. Taṃ cakkaṃ padumapupphaṃ viya upaṭṭhāsi. So taṃ āha, “ambho, idaṃ tayā piḷandhitaṃ padumaṃ mayhaṃ dehī”ti. Na idaṃ, sāmi, padumaṃ, khuracakkaṃ etanti. So “vañcesi maṃ tvaṃ, kiṃ mayā padumaṃ na diṭṭhapubba”nti vatvā “tvaṃ lohitacandanaṃ vilimpitvā piḷandhanaṃ padumapupphaṃ mayhaṃ na dātukāmo”ti āha. So cintesi “ayampi mayā katasadisaṃ kammaṃ katvā tassa phalaṃ anubhavitukāmo”ti. Atha naṃ “gaṇha, re”ti vatvā tassa matthake cakkaṃ khipi. Tena vuttaṃ –

His mother got up and said, 'Having committed such an act against a mother like me, are you really of the opinion, my son, that you will find happiness in the place you are going?' As he sailed on the ship, on the seventh day, the ship stopped. Then the people said, 'Surely, there is a wicked person here; let us draw lots.' As the lots were cast, it fell to him three times. They gave him a raft and threw him into the sea. He reached an island where he enjoyed prosperity with celestial spirits. Though they warned him, 'Do not go further ahead,' seeing the prosperity double and then double again, he gradually saw one bearing a razor-wheel. The wheel appeared to him like a lotus flower. He said to him, 'Hey, give me that lotus you are wearing.' 'This is not a lotus, lord, it is a razor-wheel.' He replied, 'You deceive me—have I never seen a lotus before? You have smeared yourself with red sandalwood and are unwilling to give me the lotus flower you are wearing.' The other thought, 'This one, too, must have done a deed similar to mine and wishes to experience its fruit.' Then, saying, 'Take it, you wretch!', he hurled the wheel onto his head. Thus it was said:

“Catubbhi aṭṭhajjhagamā, aṭṭhāhi pica soḷasa;

Soḷasāhi ca bāttiṃsa, atricchaṃ cakkamāsado;

Icchāhatassa posassa, cakkaṃ bhamati matthake”ti. (jā. 1.1.104; 1.5.103);

'From four he came to eight, and from eight to sixteen; from sixteen to thirty-two. Through excessive greed, he came upon the wheel. For a man smitten by craving, the wheel spins upon his head.' (Jātaka 1.1.104; 1.5.103)

Soti [V 3.0160] gehasāmiko bhattā. Purimanayenevāti anuḍahanassa paccayatāya. Tatridaṃ vatthu – kassapabuddhakāle sotāpannassa upāsakassa bhariyā aticāraṃ carati. So taṃ paccakkhato disvā “kasmā evaṃ karosī”ti āha. Sā “sacāhaṃ evarūpaṃ karomi, ayaṃ me sunakho viluppamāno [M 3.0172] khādatū”ti vatvā kālakatā kaṇṇamuṇḍakadahe vemānikapetī hutvā nibbattā divā sampattiṃ anubhavati, rattiṃ dukkhaṃ. Tadā bārāṇasirājā migavaṃ caranto araññaṃ pavisitvā anupubbena kaṇṇamuṇḍakadahaṃ sampatto tāya saddhiṃ sampattiṃ anubhavati. Sā taṃ vañcetvā rattiṃ dukkhaṃ anubhavati. So ñatvā “kattha nu kho gacchatī”ti piṭṭhito piṭṭhito gantvā avidūre ṭhito kaṇṇamuṇḍakadahato nikkhamitvā taṃ “paṭapaṭa”nti khādamānaṃ ekaṃ sunakhaṃ disvā asinā dvidhā chindi, dve ahesuṃ. Puna chinne cattāro, puna chinne aṭṭha, puna chinne soḷasa ahesuṃ. Sā “kiṃ karosi, sāmī”ti āha. So “kiṃ ida”nti āha. Sā “evaṃ akatvā kheḷapiṇḍaṃ bhūmiyaṃ niṭṭhubhitvā pādena ghaṃsāhī”ti āha. So tathā akāsi. Sunakhā antaradhāyiṃsu. Muṭṭhiyogo kirāyaṃ tassa sunakhantaradhānassa, yadidaṃ kheḷapiṇḍaṃ bhūmiyaṃ niṭṭhubhitvā pādena ghaṃsanaṃ, taṃ divasaṃ tassā kammaṃ khīṇaṃ. Rājā vippaṭisārī hutvā gantuṃ āraddho. Sā “mayhaṃ, sāmi, kammaṃ khīṇaṃ, mā agamāsī”ti āha. Rājā assutvāva gato.

'So' means the householder, her husband. 'In the same way as before' refers to being a condition for not burning up. Here is the story: During the time of the Buddha Kassapa, the wife of a stream-enterer lay follower committed adultery. He saw her in the act and asked, 'Why are you doing this?' She replied, 'If I am doing such a thing, may this dog devour me, tearing me apart!' After saying this, she died and was reborn as a celestial spirit in Kaṇṇamuṇḍaka Lake, enjoying prosperity by day and suffering by night. At that time, the king of Bārāṇasī, while hunting, entered the forest and gradually reached Kaṇṇamuṇḍaka Lake, where he enjoyed prosperity with her. She deceived him, and at night, she suffered. The king, realizing this, thought, 'Where can she be going?' and followed her from behind. Standing not far away, he saw a dog emerge from Kaṇṇamuṇḍaka Lake and devour her with a 'snap-snap' sound. He cut the dog in two with his sword, and it became two. When he cut them again, they became four, then eight, then sixteen. She asked, 'What are you doing, my lord?' He replied, 'What is this?' She said, 'Instead of doing that, spit a lump of saliva on the ground and rub it with your foot.' He did so, and the dogs disappeared. This, it seems, was a secret technique for making the dogs disappear, namely, spitting a lump of saliva on the ground and rubbing it with the foot. That day, her kamma was exhausted. The king, filled with remorse, started to leave. She said, 'My lord, my kamma is exhausted; do not go!' But the king left without listening.

Dakkhiṇāti cattāro paccayā dīyamānā dakkhanti etehi hitasukhānīti, taṃ dakkhiṇaṃ arahatīti dakkhiṇeyyo, bhikkhusaṅgho.

A 'dakkhiṇā' (gift) is so called because when the four requisites are given, they see (dakkhanti) welfare and happiness through them. One who is worthy of such a gift (dakkhiṇaṃ) is called 'dakkhiṇeyyo' (worthy of gifts); this refers to the Sangha of monks.

Paṭhamaaggisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the First Fire Sutta is concluded.

4-5. Dutiyaaggisuttādivaṇṇanā

4-5. Commentary on the Second Fire Sutta, etc.

47-48. Catutthe yaññavāṭaṃ sampādetvā mahāyaññaṃ uddissa saviññāṇakāni aviññāṇakāni ca yaññūpakaraṇāni sajjitānīti āha pāḷiyaṃ “mahāyañño upakkhaṭo”ti. Taṃ upakaraṇaṃ tesaṃ tathāsajjananti āha “upakkhaṭoti paccupaṭṭhito”ti. Vacchatarasatānīti yuvabhāvappattāni nātibalavavacchasatāni. Te pana vacchā eva honti, na dammā, balībaddā vā. Urabbhāti taruṇameṇḍakā vuccanti. Upanītānīti ṭhapanatthāya upanītāni. Vihiṃsaṭṭhenāti hiṃsanaṭṭhena. Upavāyatūti upagantvā sarīradarathaṃ nibbāpento saṇhasītalā vāto vāyatu. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva. Pañcame natthi vattabbaṃ.

47-48. In the fourth sutta, it is said in the Pāli, 'a great sacrifice is ready,' meaning that having prepared the sacrificial enclosure with a great sacrifice in mind, both sentient and insentient sacrificial materials were arranged. That those materials were so arranged is what is meant by 'ready means prepared.' 'Hundreds of young calves' means hundreds of calves that had reached youth but were not yet very strong. They were just calves, not tamed bullocks or oxen. 'Rams' refers to young rams. 'Brought forward' means brought for the purpose of being placed there. 'With the intent to harm' means with the intention of harming. 'Let the breeze blow' means may a soft, cool wind approach and, extinguishing the fever of the body, blow. The rest is easily understood. In the fifth, there is nothing to be said.

Dutiyaaggisuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Second Fire Sutta, etc., is concluded.

6. Dutiyasaññāsuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Second Perception Sutta

49. Chaṭṭhe [V 3.0161][M 3.0173] nhāruvilekhananti cammaṃ likhantānaṃ cammaṃ likhitvā chaḍḍitakasaṭaṃ. “Esohamasmī”tiādinā ahaṃkaraṇaṃ ahaṅkāro. “Etaṃ mamā”ti mamaṃkaraṇaṃ mamaṅkāro. Tenāha “ahaṅkāradiṭṭhito”tiādi. Tisso vidhāti seyyasadisahīnavasena tayo mānā. “Ekavidhena rūpasaṅgaho”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 584) koṭṭhāso “vidhā”ti vutto. “Kathaṃvidhaṃ sīlavantaṃ vadanti, kathaṃvidhaṃ paññavantaṃ vadantī”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.95) pakāro. “Tisso imā, bhikkhave, vidhā. Katamā tisso? Seyyohamasmīti vidhā”ti (vibha. 920) ettha māno “vidhā”ti vutto. Idhāpi mānova adhippeto. Māno hi vidahanato hīnādivasena tividhā. Tenākārena dahanato upadahanato “vidhā”ti vuccati.

49. In the sixth [sutta], ‘nhāruvilekhana’ means the scraping of the skin, the discarded scrapings after scraping the skin. By ‘Esohamasmī’ and so on, the I-making is egoism. ‘Etaṃ mamā’ (This is mine) is the mine-making, which is possessiveness. Therefore, it is said, ‘from the view of egoism,’ etc. ‘Tisso vidhā’ (three kinds) refers to the three kinds of conceit based on superior, equal, and inferior. In passages like ‘Ekavidhena rūpasaṅgaho’ (Dhammasaṅgaṇi 584), ‘vidhā’ is used to mean a category. In phrases such as ‘Kathaṃvidhaṃ sīlavantaṃ vadanti, kathaṃvidhaṃ paññavantaṃ vadantī’ (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.95), it denotes a kind or manner. In the passage, ‘Tisso imā, bhikkhave, vidhā. Katamā tisso? Seyyohamasmīti vidhā’ (Vibhaṅga 920), conceit is referred to as ‘vidhā.’ Here too, conceit is the intended meaning. For conceit is threefold, as it scorches (vidahanato) based on being inferior and so on. Therefore, due to scorching (dahanato) and intensely scorching (upadahanato), it is called ‘vidhā.’

Dutiyasaññāsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Second Perception Sutta is concluded.

7-8. Methunasuttādivaṇṇanā

7-8. Commentary on the Methuna Sutta, etc.

50-51. Sattame idhāti imasmiṃ loke. Ekaccoti eko. Samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vāti pabbajjāmattena samaṇo vā, jātimattena brāhmaṇo vā. Dvayaṃdvayasamāpattinti dvīhi dvīhi samāpajjitabbaṃ, methunanti attho. Na heva kho samāpajjatīti sambandho. Ucchādanaṃ ubbaṭṭanaṃ. Sambāhanaṃ parimaddanaṃ. Sādiyatīti adhivāseti. Tadassādetīti ucchādanādiṃ abhiramati. Nikāmetīti icchati. Vittinti tuṭṭhiṃ. Idampi khoti ettha idanti yathāvuttaṃ sādiyanādiṃ khaṇḍādibhāvavasena ekaṃ katvā vuttaṃ. Pi-saddo vakkhamānaṃ upādāya samuccayattho, kho-saddo avadhāraṇattho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yadetaṃ brahmacāripaṭiññassa asatipi dvayaṃdvayasamāpattiyaṃ mātugāmassa ucchādananahāpanasambāhanasādiyanādi. Idampi ekaṃsena tassa brahmacariyassa khaṇḍādibhāvāpādanato khaṇḍampi chiddampi sabalampi kammāsampīti. Evaṃ pana khaṇḍādibhāvāpattiyā so aparisuddhaṃ brahmacariyaṃ carati, na parisuddhaṃ, saṃyutto methunasaṃyogena, na [M 3.0174] visaṃyutto. Tato cassa na jātiādīhi parimuttīti dassento “ayaṃ vuccatī”tiādimāha.

50-51. In the seventh [sutta], ‘here’ means in this world. ‘Some’ means one. ‘An ascetic or a brahmin’ refers to either an ascetic by virtue of going forth, or a brahmin by birth. ‘Engaging in pairs’ means it should be engaged in by pairs of two, meaning sexual intercourse. ‘Does not actually engage’ is the connection. ‘Ucchādana’ means anointing. ‘Sambāhana’ means massaging. ‘Sādiyati’ means approves. ‘Tadassādeti’ means delights in anointing and so on. ‘Nikāmeti’ means desires. ‘Vitti’ means satisfaction. ‘This too,’ here, means that what was previously described—approving and so on—is stated as one by way of the qualities of being broken, etc. The particle ‘pi’ indicates inclusion by taking what will be said, while ‘kho’ emphasizes. This is what is said: for one who has taken the vow of celibacy, even without actually engaging in sexual intercourse, there is this matter of a woman's anointing, bathing, massaging, approving, and so on. This too, certainly, by causing the state of being broken and so on in that celibacy, is a break, a flaw, a stain, and an impurity. Thus, by falling into this state of being broken and so on, he lives an impure celibate life, not a pure one, bound by the bond of sexual intercourse, not unbound. To show that because of this he is not freed from birth and so on, it is said, ‘This is called...’ and so on.

Sañjagghatīti kilesavasena mahāhasitaṃ hasati. Saṃkīḷatīti kāyasaṃsaggavasena kīḷati. Saṃkelāyatīti sabbaso mātugāmaṃ kelāyanto viharati. Cakkhunāti attano cakkhunā. Cakkhunti [V 3.0162] mātugāmassa cakkhuṃ. Upanijjhāyatīti upecca nijjhāyati oloketi. Tirokuṭṭanti kuṭṭassa parato. Tathā tiropākāraṃ, “mattikāmayā bhitti kuṭṭaṃ, iṭṭhakāmayā pākāro”ti vadanti. Yā kāci vā bhitti porisakā diyaḍḍharatanappamāṇā kuṭṭaṃ, tato adhiko pākāro. Assāti brahmacāripaṭiññassa. Pubbeti vatasamādānato pubbe. Kāmaguṇehīti kāmakoṭṭhāsehi. Samappitanti suṭṭhu appitaṃ sahitaṃ. Samaṅgibhūtanti samannāgataṃ. Paricārayamānanti kīḷantaṃ, upaṭṭhahiyamānaṃ vā. Paṇidhāyāti patthetvā. Sīlenātiādīsu yamaniyamādisamādānavasena sīlaṃ, avītikkamavasena vataṃ. Ubhayampi vā sīlaṃ, dukkaracariyavasena pavattitaṃ vataṃ. Taṃtaṃakiccasammatato vā nivattilakkhaṇaṃ sīlaṃ, taṃtaṃsamādānavato vesabhojanakiccakaraṇādivisesappaṭipatti vataṃ. Sabbathāpi dukkaracariyā tapo. Methunā virati brahmacariyanti evampettha pāḷivaṇṇanā veditabbā. Aṭṭhamaṃ uttānameva.

‘Sañjagghati’ means he laughs loudly due to defilements. ‘Saṃkīḷati’ means he plays by way of physical contact. ‘Saṃkelāyati’ means he completely frolics with women. ‘Cakkhunā’ (with the eye) refers to his own eye. ‘Cakkhuṃ’ (the eye) refers to the woman’s eye. ‘Upanijjhāyati’ means he approaches and gazes intently, he observes. ‘Tirokuṭṭaṃ’ (beyond the wall) means on the other side of the wall. Similarly, ‘tiropākāraṃ’ (beyond the rampart)—they say, ‘A `kuṭṭa` is a wall made of clay, while a `pākāra` is a wall made of brick.’ Any wall that is a man's height, one and a half cubits in measure, is a `kuṭṭa`; anything taller is a `pākāra`. ‘Assa’ (his) refers to one who has taken a vow of celibacy. ‘Pubbe’ (formerly) means before undertaking the vow. ‘Kāmaguṇehi’ (with sensual pleasures) refers to the objects of sensual desire. ‘Samappitaṃ’ means well-fixed, connected. ‘Samaṅgibhūtaṃ’ means endowed. ‘Paricārayamānaṃ’ means playing, or being attended upon. ‘Paṇidhāya’ means having desired. In terms of ‘sīla’ (virtue) and so on—virtue (sīla) refers to undertaking restraints and precepts, while a vow (vata) refers to non-transgression. Both may also be called virtue, or a vow when practiced through difficult conduct. Alternatively, virtue (sīla) is characterized by abstaining from what is deemed improper, while a vow (vata) refers to specific practices like eating out of turn (vesabhojanakiccakaraṇādi) from one who has undertaken the vow.
