In all forms, difficult practice is austerity. Abstaining from sexual activity is celibacy—thus should the commentary on the text be understood here. The eighth is straightforward.

Methunasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Methuna Sutta, etc., is concluded.

9. Dānamahapphalasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Dānamahapphala Sutta

52. Navame “sāhu dāna”nti dānaṃ detīti “dānaṃ nāma sādhu sundara”nti dānaṃ detīti attho. Dānañhi datvā taṃ paccavekkhantassa pāmojjapītisomanassādayo uppajjanti, lobhadosaissāmaccherādayo vidūrībhavanti. Idāni dānaṃ anukūladhammaparibrūhanena paccanīkadhammavidūrīkaraṇena ca bhāvanācittassa upasobhanāya ca parikkhārāya ca hotīti “alaṅkārabhūtañceva parivārabhūtañca detī”ti vuttaṃ. Jhānānāgāmī nāma hoti jhānaṃ nibbattetvā [M 3.0175] brahmalokūpapannānaṃ ariyānaṃ heṭṭhā anuppajjanato. Imaṃ pecca paribhuñjissāmīti sāpekkhassa dānaṃ paralokaphalāsāya sātisayāya ca pubbācāravasena uppajjamānāya anubhavattā taṇhuttaraṃ nāma hotīti āha “paṭhamaṃ taṇhuttariyadāna”nti. Dānaṃ nāma buddhādīhi pasatthanti garuṃ cittīkāraṃ upaṭṭhapetvā dātabbattā “dutiyaṃ cittīkāradāna”nti vuttaṃ. Pubbakehi pitupitāmahehi dinnapubbaṃ katapubbaṃ jahāpetuṃ nāma nānucchavikanti attabhāvasabhāgavasena hirottappaṃ paccupaṭṭhapetvā dātabbato “tatiyaṃ hirottappadāna”nti vuttaṃ. “Ahaṃ pacāmi, na ime pacanti, nārahāmi pacanto apacantānaṃ dānaṃ adātu”nti evaṃsaññī hutvā dento niravasesaṃ katvā detīti āha “catutthaṃ niravasesadāna”nti. “Yathā tesaṃ pubbakānaṃ isīnaṃ tāni mahāyaññakāni ahesuṃ, evaṃ me ayaṃ dānaparibhogo bhavissatī”ti evaṃsaññino dānaṃ dakkhiṇaṃ arahesu dātabbato “pañcamaṃ dakkhiṇeyyadāna”nti vuttaṃ. “Imaṃ me dānaṃ dadato cittaṃ pasīdatī”tiādinā [V 3.0163] pītisomanassaṃ uppādetvā dentassa dānaṃ somanassabāhullappattiyā somanassupacāraṃ nāma hotīti āha “chaṭṭhaṃ somanassupavicāradāna”nti vuttaṃ.

52. In the ninth (explanation), the phrase 'sāhu dānaṃ' (good giving) means that one gives with the thought, 'Giving is indeed good and beautiful.' For when one gives and reflects on it, joy, rapture, and happiness arise, while greed, hatred, envy, stinginess, and other defilements vanish. Now, giving serves for the enhancement of favorable qualities, for the dispelling of opposing qualities, for the adornment of the mind, and as requisites for development. Thus, it is said that one gives 'as an adornment and as an accompaniment.' A jhānānāgāmī (one who has attained jhana and does not return) is so called because, having produced jhana, they are reborn in the Brahma realms and do not arise below the noble ones. Giving with anticipation, thinking, 'I will enjoy this after death,' is called 'the first, giving that transcends craving' because it arises from an intense hope for future rewards and from the experience of it being superior, in accordance with previous traditions. Giving is praised by the Buddhas and others; thus, because it should be given with great respect and veneration, it is called 'the second, giving with veneration.' Because it is improper to abandon what was previously given and done by ancestors like fathers and grandfathers, and because one should establish shame and moral dread in accordance with one's own nature before giving, it is called 'the third, giving with shame and moral dread.' Thinking, 'I cook, but they do not; it is unworthy for me, who cooks, not to give to those who do not,' one gives completely, without holding back. Thus, it is called 'the fourth, complete giving.' Believing, 'Just as those great sacrifices were for past sages, so will this offering of mine be,' one gives what should be given to worthy recipients. Thus, it is called 'the fifth, giving to the worthy of offerings.' When one gives, thinking, 'My mind brightens as I give,' and so on, generating joy and happiness, the giving, due to the attainment of an abundance of happiness, is called 'the sixth, giving associated with happiness.'

Dānamahapphalasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Dānamahapphala Sutta is concluded.

10. Nandamātāsuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Nandamātā Sutta

53. Dasame “vutthavasso pavāretvā…pe… nikkhamī”ti aṅguttarabhāṇakānaṃ matenetaṃ vuttaṃ. Majjhimabhāṇakā pana vadanti “bhagavā upakaṭṭhāya vassūpanāyikāya jetavanato bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto cārikaṃ nikkhami. Teneva ca akāle nikkhantattā kosalarājādayo vāretuṃ ārabhiṃsu. Pavāretvā hi caraṇaṃ buddhāciṇṇa”nti. Puṇṇāya sammāpaṭipattiṃ paccāsīsanto bhagavā “mama nivattanapaccayā tvaṃ kiṃ karissasī”ti āha. Puṇṇāpi…pe… pabbajīti ettha seṭṭhi “puṇṇāya bhagavā nivattito”ti sutvā taṃ bhujissaṃ katvā dhītuṭṭhāne ṭhapesi. Sā pabbajjaṃ yācitvā pabbaji, pabbajitvā vipassanaṃ ārabhi. Athassā satthā āraddhavipassakabhāvaṃ ñatvā imaṃ obhāsagāthaṃ vissajjesi –

53. In the tenth (explanation), the phrase 'having completed the rains retreat and held the Pavāraṇā ceremony... he departed' is stated according to the view of the Aṅguttara reciters. However, the Majjhima reciters say, 'The Blessed One, accompanied by the community of bhikkhus, set out on a wandering tour from Jetavana just before the rains retreat. Because he departed at an improper time, King Kosala and others began to restrain him. For it is the custom of the Buddhas to wander only after the Pavāraṇā.' Hoping for Puṇṇā’s proper practice, the Blessed One asked, 'What will you do on account of my turning back?' Puṇṇā also... she went forth. Here, the merchant, hearing that 'the Blessed One turned back because of Puṇṇā,' made her his freedwoman and appointed her to the position of his daughter. She requested ordination, went forth, and began practicing insight meditation. Then, knowing that she had begun insight meditation, the Teacher uttered this illuminating verse—

“Puṇṇe [M 3.0176] pūrassu saddhammaṃ, cando pannaraso yathā;

Paripuṇṇāya paññāya, dukkhassantaṃ karissasī”ti. (therīgā. 3);

“Puṇṇā, fill yourself with the good Dhamma, like the moon on the fifteenth day; with wisdom fully perfected, you will make an end of suffering.”

Sā gāthāpariyosāne arahattaṃ patvā abhiññātā sāvikā ahosi. Sesamettha suviññeyyameva.

At the conclusion of the verse, she attained arahantship and became a renowned disciple. The remainder here is easily understood.

Nandamātāsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Nandamātā Sutta is concluded.

Mahāyaññavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Chapter on the Great Sacrifice is concluded.

Paṭhamapaṇṇāsakaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The First Fifty is concluded.

6. Abyākatavaggo

6. The Chapter on the Undeclared

1-2. Abyākatasuttādivaṇṇanā

1–2. Commentary on the Discourses on the Undeclared, and so forth.

54-55. Chaṭṭhavaggassa [V 3.0164] paṭhamaṃ suviññeyyameva. Dutiye atīte attabhāve nibbattakaṃ kammanti “purimakammabhavasmiṃ moho avijjā, āyūhanā saṅkhārā, nikanti taṇhā, upagamanaṃ upādānaṃ, cetanā bhavo”ti evamāgataṃ saparikkhāraṃ pañcavidhaṃ kammavaṭṭamāha. Etarahi me attabhāvo na siyāti viññāṇanāmarūpasaḷāyatanaphassavedanāsahitaṃ paccuppannaṃ pañcavidhaṃ vipākavaṭṭamāha. Yaṃ atthikanti yaṃ paramatthato vijjamānakaṃ. Tenāha “bhūta”nti. Tañhi paccayanibbattatāya “bhūta”nti vuccati. Taṃ pajahāmīti tappaṭibaddhacchandarāgappahānena tato eva āyatiṃ anuppattidhammatāpādanavasena pajahāmi pariccajāmi. Haritantanti (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.303) haritameva. Anta-saddena padavaḍḍhanaṃ kataṃ yathā “vanantaṃ suttanta”nti, allatiṇādīni āgamma nibbāyatīti attho. Pathantanti mahāmaggaṃ. Selantanti pabbataṃ. Udakantanti udakaṃ. Ramaṇīyaṃ vā bhūmibhāganti tiṇagumbādirahitaṃ vivittaṃ abbhokāsabhūmibhāgaṃ. Anāhārāti apaccayā nirupādānā. Sesamettha uttānameva.

54–55. The first discourse of the sixth chapter is easily understood. In the second, regarding the kamma that produced existence in the past, it speaks of the fivefold cycle of kamma with its accessories, as stated: 'Delusion in the previous kamma-existence is ignorance; accumulation is volitional formations; delight is craving; approaching is clinging; volition is becoming.' It speaks of the present fivefold cycle of result, comprising consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling, as that whereby 'this present existence of mine would not be.' That which exists—that which is ultimately real. Therefore, he said 'existent' (bhūta). For it is called 'existent' because it arises from conditions. 'I abandon it' means I abandon and relinquish it by giving up the desire and lust connected to it, and thereby causing it not to arise in the future. 'Haritanta' (green) means simply 'green.' The word 'anta' is used as an augment, as in 'vananta' (forest) or 'suttanta' (discourse); the meaning is that it is extinguished by coming into contact with wet grass and the like. 'Pathanta' (path) means the great path. 'Selanta' (rock) means a mountain. 'Udakanta' (water) means water. 'A delightful area of ground' refers to a secluded, open space free of grass, bushes, and the like. 'Without sustenance' means without conditions or clinging. The remainder here is evident.

Abyākatasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourses on the Undeclared, and so forth, is concluded.

3. Tissabrahmāsuttavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Tissabrahma Sutta

56. Tatiye [M 3.0177] vivittāni tādisāni pana pariyantāni atidūrāni hontīti āha “antimapariyantimānī”ti. Ante bhavāni antimāni, antimāniyeva pariyantimāni. Ubhayenapi atidūrataṃ dasseti. Samannāhāre ṭhapayamānoti indriyaṃ samākārena vattento indriyasamataṃ paṭipādento nāma hoti. Vipassanācittasampayutto samādhi, satipi saṅkhāranimittāvirahe niccanimittādivirahato “animitto”ti vuccatīti āha “animittanti balavavipassanāsamādhi”nti.

56. In the third sutta, it is said that secluded boundaries are indeed such, but they are very far away, hence it is said, 'having ultimate and final boundaries.' Those that exist at the end are ultimate; indeed, the ultimate are the final. Both indicate great distance. By 'establishing harmonious application' is meant one who, causing the faculties to function harmoniously, establishes balance among the faculties. The concentration associated with insight consciousness, even when there is no sign of formations, is called 'signless' due to the absence of the sign of permanence and so forth. Hence it is said, 'signless means strong insight concentration.'

Tissabrahmāsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Tissabrahmā Sutta is concluded.

4-7. Sīhasenāpatisuttādivaṇṇanā

4-7. Commentary on the Sīhasenāpati Sutta and so forth

57-60. Catutthe [V 3.0165] kucchito ariyo kadariyo. Thaddhamacchariyasadisaṃ hi kucchitaṃ sabbanihīnaṃ natthi sabbakusalānaṃ ādibhūtassa nisedhanato. Sesamettha pañcamādīni ca uttānatthāneva.

57-60. In the fourth sutta, a miser is a despicable person. Indeed, there is nothing so despicable, so utterly base, as obstinate avarice, because it obstructs the origin of all wholesome qualities. The remaining terms, from the fifth onward, have obvious meanings.

Sīhasenāpatisuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Sīhasenāpati Sutta and so forth is concluded.

8. Pacalāyamānasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Pacalāyamāna Sutta

61. Aṭṭhame ālokasaññaṃ manasi kareyyāsīti divā vā rattiṃ vā sūriyapajjotacandamaṇiādīnaṃ ālokaṃ “āloko”ti manasi kareyyāsi. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – sūriyacandālokādiṃ divā rattiñca upaladdhaṃ yathāladdhavaseneva manasi kareyyāsi, citte ṭhapeyyāsi. Yathā te subhāvitālokakasiṇassa viya kasiṇāloko yadicchakaṃ yāvadicchakañca so āloko rattiyaṃ upatiṭṭhati, yena tattha divāsaññaṃ ṭhapeyyāsi, divā viya vigatathinamiddhova bhaveyyāsīti. Tenāha “yathā divā tathā ratti”nti. Iti vivaṭena cetasāti evaṃ apihitena cittena thinamiddhapidhānena apihitattā. Apariyonaddhenāti samantato anonaddhena asañchāditena. Sahobhāsanti sañāṇobhāsaṃ. Thinamiddhavinodanaālokopi vā hotu kasiṇālokopi [M 3.0178] vā parikammālokopi vā, upakkilesāloko viya sabboyaṃ āloko ñāṇasamuṭṭhānovāti. Yesaṃ akaraṇe puggalo mahājāniyo hoti, tāni avassaṃ kātabbāni. Yāni akātumpi vaṭṭanti, sati samavāye kātabbato tāni karaṇīyānīti āha “itarāni karaṇīyānī”ti. Atha vā kattabbāni kammāni karaṇaṃ arahantīti karaṇīyāni. Itarāni kiccānītipi vadanti.

61. In the eighth sutta, 'you should attend to the perception of light' means that whether by day or night, you should attend to the light of the sun, a lamp, the moon, a gem, and so forth, thinking 'light.' This is what is said: you should attend to the light of the sun, moon, etc., perceived by day and by night, just as it is perceived, and fix it in the mind. Just as for one who has well-developed the light kasiṇa, the light of the kasiṇa appears at will and for as long as desired during the night, so that you may establish the perception of day there and be free from sloth and torpor as if it were day. Hence it is said, 'as by day, so by night.' Thus, 'with an open mind' means with a mind not covered, not being concealed by the covering of sloth and torpor. 'Unenveloped' means not enveloped or obscured on all sides. 'With radiance' means with the radiance of knowledge. Whether it is the light that dispels sloth and torpor, or the light of the kasiṇa, or the light of preliminary practice, all this light, like the light of the corruptions of insight, arises from knowledge. Those things which, if not done, cause a person great loss, must certainly be done. Those which may be left undone, yet should be done when the opportunity arises—these are called 'other duties.' Alternatively, they are called 'duties' because they are actions that ought to be done. Others also call them 'tasks.'

Ādinayappavattā viggāhikakathāti “na tvaṃ imaṃ dhammavinayaṃ ājānāsi, ahaṃ imaṃ dhammavinayaṃ ājānāmi, kiṃ tvaṃ imaṃ dhammavinayaṃ ājānissasi, micchāpaṭipanno tvamasi, ahamasmi sammāpaṭipanno, sahitaṃ me, asahitaṃ te, purevacanīyaṃ pacchā avaca, pacchāvacanīyaṃ pure avaca, adhiciṇṇaṃ te viparāvattaṃ, āropito te vādo, niggahito tvamasi. Cara vādappamokkhāya, nibbeṭhehi vā sace pahosī”ti (dī. ni. 1.18; ma. ni. 3.41) evaṃpavattā kathā. Tattha sahitaṃ meti (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.18) mayhaṃ vacanaṃ sahitaṃ siliṭṭhaṃ, atthayuttaṃ kāraṇayuttanti attho. Sahitanti vā pubbāparāviruddhaṃ. Asahitaṃ teti tuyhaṃ vacanaṃ [V 3.0166] asahitaṃ asiliṭṭhaṃ. Adhiciṇṇaṃ te viparāvattanti yaṃ tuyhaṃ dīgharattāciṇṇavasena suppaguṇaṃ, taṃ mayhaṃ ekavacaneneva viparāvattaṃ parivattitvā ṭhitaṃ, na kiñci jānāsīti attho. Āropito te vādoti mayā tava vāde doso āropito. Cara vādappamokkhāyāti dosamocanatthaṃ cara vicara, tattha tattha gantvā sikkhāti attho. Nibbeṭhehi vā sace pahosīti atha sayaṃ pahosi, idāni eva nibbeṭhehīti attho.

Disputatious talk that proceeds by way of refutation is as follows: "You do not understand this Dhamma-Vinaya, but I understand it. How could you understand this Dhamma-Vinaya? You are practicing wrongly, while I am practicing rightly. My words are coherent, yours are incoherent. What should be said first, you said later; what should be said later, you said first. Your long-held position has been overturned. A charge has been brought against your argument. You are defeated. Go, try to free yourself from this argument—or disentangle it if you can!" (Dī. Ni. 1.18; Ma. Ni. 3.41). Here, "my words are coherent" (Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 1.18) means: "My statement is coherent, connected, meaningful, and logically sound." Alternatively, "coherent" means not contradicting what was said before or after. "Yours are incoherent" means: "Your statement is incoherent, unconnected." "Your long-held position has been overturned" means: "What you have habitually practiced for a long time and mastered has been overturned by my single statement—you know nothing!" "A charge has been brought against your argument" means: "I have imputed a fault to your argument." "Go, try to free yourself from this argument" means: "Go, wander about to free yourself from this fault—go here and there to learn." "Or disentangle it if you can" means: "But if you are capable, disentangle it right now!"

Taṇhā sabbaso khīyanti etthāti taṇhāsaṅkhayo, tasmiṃ. Taṇhāsaṅkhayeti ca idaṃ visaye bhummanti āha “taṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā”ti. Vimuttacittatāyāti sabbasaṃkilesehi vippayuttacittatāya. Aparabhāge paṭipadā nāma ariyasaccābhisamayo. Sā sāsanacārigocarā paccattaṃ veditabbatoti āha “pubbabhāgappaṭipadaṃ saṃkhittena desethāti pucchatī”ti. Akuppadhammatāya khayavayasaṅkhātaṃ antaṃ atītāti accantā, so eva aparihāyanasabhāvattā accantā niṭṭhā assāti accantaniṭṭhā. Tenāha “ekantaniṭṭho satataniṭṭhoti attho”ti. Na hi paṭividdhassa [M 3.0179] lokuttaradhammassa dassannaṃ kuppannaṃ nāma atthi. Accantameva catūhi yogehi khemo etassa atthīti accantayogakkhemī. Maggabrahmacariyassa vusitattā tassa ca aparihāyanasabhāvattā accantaṃ brahmacārīti accantabrahmacārī. Tenāha “niccabrahmacārīti attho”ti. Pariyosānanti maggabrahmacariyapariyapariyosānaṃ vaṭṭadukkhapariyosānañca.

Craving is completely destroyed herein; therefore, it is the destruction of craving. And regarding 'in the destruction of craving,' this is a locative of sphere, hence it is said, 'having made that the object.' 'Liberation of mind' means a mind disengaged from all defilements. In the subsequent part, the path is the realization of the noble truths. Because that path has the practice of the teaching as its domain and is to be known individually, he asks, 'Teach the preliminary practice in brief.' Having passed beyond the end, which is reckoned as destruction and cessation, by virtue of its unshakeable nature, it is called ultimate. And because it has an irreversible nature, it has an ultimate conclusion. Therefore, it is said, 'It means being absolutely concluded, eternally concluded.' Indeed, for one who has penetrated the supramundane Dhamma, there is no such thing as the wavering of vision. He possesses utter security from the four yokes—hence, he is 'utterly secure from the yokes.' Having lived the holy life of the path, and because of its irreversible nature, he is 'utterly a holy-life-farer.' Therefore, it is said, 'It means he is a perpetual holy-life-farer.' 'The conclusion' refers to both the culmination of the holy life of the path and the conclusion of the suffering of the round of rebirth.

Pañcakkhandhāti pañcupādānakkhandhā. Sakkāyasabbañhi sandhāya idha “sabbe dhammā”ti vuttaṃ vipassanāvisayassa adhippetattā. Tasmā āyatanadhātuyopi taggatikā eva daṭṭhabbā. Tenāha bhagavā “nālaṃ abhinivesāyā”ti. Na yuttā abhinivesāya “etaṃ mama, eso me attā”ti ajjhosānāya. “Alameva nibbindituṃ alaṃ virajjitu”ntiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.272; saṃ. ni. 2.124, 128, 134, 143) viya alaṃ-saddo yuttatthopi hotīti āha “na yuttā”ti. Sampajjantīti bhavanti. Yadipi “tatiyā catutthī”ti idaṃ visuddhidvayaṃ abhiññāpaññā, tassa pana sapaccayanāmarūpadassanabhāvato sati ca paccayapariggahe sapaccayattā aniccanti, nāmarūpassa aniccatāya dukkhaṃ, dukkhañca anattāti atthato lakkhaṇattayaṃ supākaṭameva hotīti āha “aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ anattāti ñātapariññāya abhijānātī”ti. Tatheva tīraṇapariññāyāti iminā aniccādibhāvena nālaṃ abhinivesāyāti nāmarūpassa upasaṃharati, na abhiññāpaññānaṃ sambhāradhammānaṃ. Purimāya hi atthato āpannaṃ lakkhaṇattayaṃ gaṇhāti salakkhaṇasallakkhaṇaparattā tassā. Dutiyāya sarūpato tassā lakkhaṇattayāropanavasena sammasanabhāvato. Ekacittakkhaṇikatāya abhinipātamattatāya ca [V 3.0167] appamattakampi. Rūpapariggahassa oḷārikabhāvato arūpapariggahaṃ dasseti. Dassento ca vedanāya āsannabhāvato, visesato sukhasārāgitāya, bhavassādagadhitamānasatāya ca therassa vedanāvasena nibbattetvā dasseti.

The five aggregates are the five aggregates subject to clinging. Here, 'all phenomena' is stated with reference to all that constitutes individuality, since it is intended as the domain of insight. Therefore, the sense bases and elements should also be seen as belonging to that same category. Hence, the Blessed One said, 'Not fit for attachment.' It is not suitable for attachment, for grasping with the thought, 'This is mine, this is my self.' As in phrases like 'It is enough to become disenchanted, enough to become dispassionate,' the word 'alaṃ' can also mean 'suitable'; hence, it is said, 'not suitable.' 'They come to be' means they are. Moreover, although 'the third and fourth' refers to the two purifications, which are the wisdom of higher knowledge, nevertheless, because of seeing name-and-form with its conditions, and when there is the grasping of conditions, because it is conditioned, it is impermanent; due to the impermanence of name-and-form, there is suffering, and what is suffering is non-self. Thus, the three characteristics become very clear in meaning. Hence, it is said, 'He fully knows by comprehension as known that it is impermanent, suffering, and non-self.' Similarly, by this comprehension by scrutiny, he applies to name-and-form the fact that, due to its nature of being impermanent and so on, it is not fit for attachment; he does not apply it to the constituent factors of the wisdom of higher knowledge. For the first grasps the three characteristics that are implicitly present, as it is concerned with discerning their individual characteristics. The second does so explicitly, as it involves scrutinizing by way of superimposing the three characteristics upon it. And even a little bit, due to its being momentary, lasting for a single mind-moment, and being a mere occurrence. Because the grasping of form is gross, he shows the grasping of the formless. And in showing this, because feeling is proximate, and especially because of craving for the essence of pleasure and the mind's greed for the taste of existence, the elder explains it by generating it in terms of feeling.

Khayavirāgoti khayasaṅkhāto virāgo saṅkhārānaṃ palujjanā. Yaṃ āgamma sabbaso saṅkhārehi virajjanā hoti, taṃ nibbānaṃ accantavirāgo. Nirodhānupassimhipīti nirodhānupassipadepi. Eseva nayoti atidisitvā taṃ [M 3.0180] ekadesena vivaranto “nirodhopi hi…pe… duvidhoyevā”ti āha. Khandhānaṃ pariccajanaṃ tappaṭibaddhakilesappahānavasenāti yenākārena vipassanā kilese pajahati, tenākārena taṃnimittakkhandhe ca pajahatīti vattabbataṃ arahatīti āha “sā hi…pe… vossajjatī”ti. Ārammaṇatoti kiccasādhanavasena ārammaṇakaraṇato. Evañhi maggato aññesaṃ nibbānārammaṇānaṃ pakkhandanavossaggābhāvo siddhova hoti. Pariccajanena pakkhandanena cāti dvīhipi vā kāraṇehi. Soti maggo. Sabbesaṃ khandhānaṃ vossajjanaṃ tappaṭibaddhasaṃkilesappahānena daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yasmā vā vipassanācittaṃ pakkhandatīti maggasampayuttacittaṃ sandhāyāha. Maggo ca samucchedavasena kilese khandhe ca pariccajati, tasmā yathākkamaṃ vipassanāmaggānañca vasena pakkhandanapariccāgavossaggāpi veditabbā. Tadubhayasamaṅgīti vipassanāsamaṅgī maggasamaṅgī ca. “Aniccānupassanāya niccasaññaṃ pajahatī”tiādivacanato (paṭi. ma. 1.52) hi yathā vipassanāya kilesānaṃ pariccāgappaṭinissaggo labbhati, evaṃ āyatiṃ tehi kilesehi uppādetabbakkhandhānampi pariccāgapaṭinissaggo vattabbo. Pakkhandanapaṭinissaggo pana magge labbhamānāya ekantakāraṇabhūtāya vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanāya vasena veditabbo. Magge pana tadubhayampi ñāyāgatameva nippariyāyatova labbhamānattā. Tenāha “tadubhayasamaṅgīpuggalo”tiādi. Pucchantassa ajjhāsayavasena “na kiñci loke upādiyatī”ti ettha kāmupādānavasena upādiyanaṃ paṭikkhipatīti āha “taṇhāvasena na upādiyatī”ti. Taṇhāvasena vā asati upādiyane diṭṭhivasena upādiyanaṃ anavakāsamevāti “taṇhāvasena”icceva vuttaṃ. Na parāmasatīti nādiyati. Diṭṭhiparāmāsavasena vā “nicca”ntiādinā na parāmasati. Saṃkhitteneva kathesīti tassa ajjhāsayavasena papañcaṃ akatvā kathesi.

'Destruction-dispassion' means dispassion designated as destruction, the perishing of formations. That, depending on which there is complete dispassion towards all formations, that Nibbāna is ultimate dispassion. 'In one contemplating cessation' means in the section on contemplating cessation. Having extended the application by saying 'This is the same method,' he then explains a part of it, saying, 'For cessation is indeed… twofold.' The abandoning of the aggregates is in the sense of abandoning the defilements connected with them. This means that in whatever way insight abandons defilements, in that same way it deserves to be said that it also abandons the aggregates that are their objects; therefore, he says, 'For it… relinquishes.' 'By way of object' means because of making it an object in the sense of accomplishing a function. For in this way, for others than the path that have Nibbāna as their object, the absence of plunging in and relinquishing is indeed established. Or by both causes, namely, by abandoning and by plunging in. That is the path. The relinquishing of all aggregates should be seen as the abandoning of the defilements connected with them. Or, because he says 'insight-consciousness plunges in,' he is referring to the consciousness associated with the path. And the path abandons defilements and aggregates by way of eradication. Therefore, plunging in, abandoning, and relinquishing should be understood respectively in terms of insight and the path. 'Endowed with both' means endowed with insight and endowed with the path. For from statements like 'Through the contemplation of impermanence, one abandons the perception of permanence,' just as the abandoning and relinquishing of defilements is obtained by insight, so too should the abandoning and relinquishing of the aggregates that would be produced by those defilements in the future be spoken of. The relinquishing that is plunging in, however, should be understood in terms of the insight leading to emergence, which is the decisive cause obtained in the course of the path. On the path, however, both are obtained directly and without ambiguity, as they are inherent in the method. Therefore, he says, 'a person endowed with both,' and so on. According to the questioner's disposition, in the phrase 'one does not cling to anything in the world,' he rejects clinging in the sense of sensual clinging; thus he says, 'one does not cling by way of craving.' Or, when there is no clinging by way of craving, there is no opportunity for clinging by way of views; thus, it is simply said, 'by way of craving.' 'Does not grasp' means does not take up. Or, one does not grasp by way of the grasping of views, with ideas such as 'permanent.' 'He spoke concisely' means he spoke according to that person's disposition, without elaboration.

Pacalāyamānasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Pacalāyamāna Sutta is concluded.

9. Mettasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Mettā Sutta.

62. Navame [V 3.0168] mā, bhikkhave, puññānanti (itivu. aṭṭha. 62) ettha māti paṭisedhe nipāto. Puñña-saddo “kusalānaṃ, bhikkhave, dhammānaṃ samādānahetu evamidaṃ puññaṃ pavaḍḍhatī”tiādīsu [M 3.0181] (dī. ni. 3.80) puññaphale āgato. “Avijjāgatoyaṃ, bhikkhave, purisapuggalo puññañce saṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkharotī”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 2.51) kāmarūpāvacarasucaritesu. “Puññūpagaṃ hoti viññāṇa”ntiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 2.51) sugativisesabhūte upapattibhave. “Tīṇimāni, bhikkhave, puññakiriyavatthūni dānamayaṃ puññakiriyavatthu, sīlamayaṃ puññakiriyavatthu, bhāvanāmayaṃ puññakiriyavatthū”tiādīsu (itivu. 60; dī. ni. 3.305; a. ni. 8.36) kusalacetanāyaṃ. Idha pana tebhūmakakusaladhamme veditabbo. Bhāyitthāti ettha duvidhaṃ bhayaṃ ñāṇabhayaṃ, sārajjabhayanti. Tattha “yepi te, bhikkhave, devā dīghāyukā vaṇṇavanto sukhabahulā uccesu vimānesu ciraṭṭhitikā, tepi tathāgatassa dhammadesanaṃ sutvā yebhuyyena bhayaṃ saṃvegaṃ santāsaṃ āpajjantī”ti (a. ni. 4.33) āgataṃ ñāṇabhayaṃ. “Ahudeva bhayaṃ, ahu chambhitattaṃ, ahu lomahaṃso”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.318) āgataṃ sārajjabhayaṃ. Idhāpi sārajjabhayameva. Ayañhettha attho – bhikkhave, dīgharattaṃ kāyavacīsaṃyamo vattappaṭivattapūraṇaṃ ekāsanaṃ ekaseyyaṃ indriyadamo dhutadhammehi cittassa niggaho satisampajaññaṃ kammaṭṭhānānuyogavasena vīriyārambhoti evamādīni yāni bhikkhunā nirantaraṃ pavattetabbāni puññāni, tehi mā bhāyittha, mā bhayaṃ santāsaṃ āpajjittha. Ekaccassa diṭṭhadhammasukhassa uparodhabhayena samparāyikanibbānasukhadāyakehi puññehi mā bhāyitthāti. Nissakke idaṃ sāmivacanaṃ.

62. In the ninth sutta: 'Monks, do not fear merits' (Itivuttaka Commentary 62). Here, 'mā' is a prohibitive particle. The word 'puñña' (merit) occurs in the sense of the fruit of merit in passages like 'Monks, because of undertaking wholesome qualities, this merit grows' (Dīgha Nikāya 3.80). In statements such as 'Monks, this person, bound by ignorance, generates a meritorious formation' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.51), it pertains to wholesome conduct in the sensual and fine-material realms. In expressions like 'Consciousness goes to merit' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.51), it denotes a superior rebirth, which is a special kind of existence. In passages such as 'Monks, there are these three bases of meritorious action: the basis of meritorious action consisting of giving, the basis of meritorious action consisting of virtue, and the basis of meritorious action consisting of mental development' (Itivuttaka 60; Dīgha Nikāya 3.305; Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.36), it signifies wholesome volition. Here, however, it should be understood as wholesome qualities pertaining to the three realms. 'Do not fear' (bhāyittha). Here, fear is of two kinds: fear arising from knowledge and fear arising from agitation. Regarding the first, the fear arising from knowledge is found in the passage: 'Monks, even those gods who are long-lived, beautiful, and abundant in happiness, long-abiding in lofty mansions, upon hearing the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dhamma, for the most part experience fear, a sense of urgency, and terror' (Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.33). The fear arising from agitation is found in passages like: 'There was indeed fear, there was trembling, there was hair-raising horror' (Dīgha Nikāya 2.318). Here, too, it is specifically fear arising from agitation. The meaning here is this: Monks, do not fear, do not be alarmed or terrified by those merits that a monk must continuously cultivate—such as long-term restraint of body and speech, the fulfillment of duties and observances, solitary sitting and solitary sleeping, restraint of the senses, control of the mind through ascetic practices, mindfulness and clear comprehension, and the rousing of energy through application to meditation subjects. Do not fear those merits which bestow the happiness of the future life and Nibbāna, out of fear that they might obstruct the happiness of the present life for someone. This is the Master's own utterance.

Idāni tato abhāyitabbabhāve kāraṇaṃ dassento “sukhasseta”ntiādimāha. Tattha sukha-saddo “sukho buddhānamuppādo, sukhā virāgatā loke”tiādīsu (dha. pa. 194) sukhamūle āgato. “Yasmā ca kho, mahāli, rūpaṃ sukhaṃ sukhānupatitaṃ sukhāvakkanta”ntiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 3.60) sukhārammaṇe. “Yāvañcidaṃ, bhikkhave, na sukaraṃ akkhānena pāpuṇituṃ yāva sukhā saggā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.255) sukhapaccayaṭṭhāne. “Sukho puññassa uccayo”tiādīsu (dha. pa. 118) sukhahetumhi. “Diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārā ete dhammā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.82) abyāpajje. “Nibbānaṃ paramaṃ sukha”ntiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.215; dha. pa. 203, 204) nibbāne. “Sukhassa ca pahānā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.232; ma. ni. 1.271; saṃ. ni. 2.152) sukhavedanāyaṃ. “Adukkhamasukhaṃ [V 3.0169] santaṃ, sukhamicceva bhāsita”ntiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 4.253; itivu. 53) upekkhāvedanāyaṃ. “Dvepi [M 3.0182] mayā, ānanda, vedanā vuttā pariyāyena sukhā vedanā dukkhā vedanā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.89) iṭṭhasukhesu. “Sukho vipāko puññāna”ntiādīsu (peṭako. 23) iṭṭhavipāke. Idhāpi iṭṭhavipāke eva daṭṭhabbo. Iṭṭhassātiādīsu icchitabbato ceva aniṭṭhappaṭipakkhato ca iṭṭhassa. Kamanīyato manasmiñca kamanato pavisanato kantassa. Piyāyitabbato santappanato ca piyassa. Mananīyato manassa vaḍḍhanato ca manāpassāti attho veditabbo. Yadidaṃ puññānīti puññānīti yadidaṃ vacanaṃ, etaṃ sukhassa iṭṭhassa vipākassa adhivacanaṃ nāmaṃ. Sukhassetaṃ yadidaṃ puññānīti phalena kāraṇassa abhedopacāraṃ vadati. Tena katūpacitānaṃ puññānaṃ avassaṃbhāviphalaṃ sutvā appamattena sakkaccaṃ puññāni kattabbānīti puññakiriyāyaṃ niyojeti, ādarañca nesaṃ tattha uppādeti.

Now, showing the reason why they should not be feared, he begins with “This is a synonym for happiness,” and so on. Herein, the word “sukha” (happiness) occurs in the sense of the root of happiness in passages like “Happy is the arising of the Buddhas, happy is dispassion in the world” (Dhammapada 194). In “Because, Mahāli, form is pleasant, associated with pleasure, inclined to pleasure” (Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.60), it refers to a pleasant object. In “Even up to this point, monks, it is not easy to attain by description how pleasant the heavens are” (Majjhima Nikāya 3.255), it refers to a condition of happiness. In “Happy is the accumulation of merit” (Dhammapada 118), it refers to the cause of happiness. In “These states are the blissful abiding in the present life” (Majjhima Nikāya 1.82), it refers to non-affliction. In “Nibbāna is the highest bliss” (Majjhima Nikāya 2.215; Dhammapada 203, 204), it refers to Nibbāna. In “And the abandoning of pleasure” (Dīgha Nikāya 1.232; Majjhima Nikāya 1.271; Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.152), it refers to pleasant feeling. In “Neither-painful-nor-pleasant, peaceful, yet called pleasant” (Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.253; Itivuttaka 53), it refers to equanimous feeling. In “I have spoken, Ānanda, of two kinds of feeling in a way: pleasant feeling and painful feeling” (Majjhima Nikāya 2.89), it refers to desirable pleasures. In “Happy is the result of merits” (Peṭakopadesa 23), it refers to desirable results. Here too, it should be understood as referring to desirable results. In “desirable” (iṭṭhassa), it means what is wished for and what is the opposite of the undesirable. In “charming” (kantassa), it means what is delightful and what enters the mind pleasingly. In “dear” (piyassa), it means what is to be cherished and what satisfies. In “agreeable” (manāpassa), it should be understood to mean what is mentally delightful and what increases the mind’s joy. The phrase “that is, merits” (yadidaṃ puññāni)—this utterance is a designation, a name, for the desirable result which is happiness. By “This is a synonym for happiness, that is, merits,” he speaks with a figurative expression of non-difference, identifying the cause with its fruit. Thereby, having heard of the inevitable fruit of merits that have been performed and accumulated, he enjoins one to perform meritorious deeds diligently and respectfully, and he inspires reverence for them therein.

Idāni attanā sunettakāle katena puññakammena dīgharattaṃ paccanubhūtaṃ bhavantarappaṭicchannaṃ uḷārataraṃ puññavipākaṃ udāharitvā tamatthaṃ pākaṭataraṃ karonto “abhijānāmi kho panāha”ntiādimāha. Tattha abhijānāmīti abhivisiṭṭhena ñāṇena jānāmi, paccakkhato bujjhāmi. Dīgharattanti cirakālaṃ. Puññānanti dānādīnaṃ kusaladhammānaṃ. Satta vassānīti satta saṃvaccharāni. Mettacittanti mijjatīti mettā, siniyhatīti attho. Mitte bhavā, mittassa vā esā pavattītipi mettā. Lakkhaṇādito pana hitākārappavattilakkhaṇā, hitūpasaṃhārarasā, āghātavinayapaccupaṭṭhānā, sattānaṃ manāpabhāvadassanapadaṭṭhānā. Byāpādūpasamo etissā sampatti, sinehasambhavo vipatti. Mettacittaṃ bhāvetvāti mettāsahagataṃ cittaṃ, cittasīsena samādhi vuttoti mettāsamādhiṃ metābrahmavihāraṃ uppādetvā ceva vaḍḍhetvā ca.

Now, making that meaning clearer by citing the more excellent fruit of merit—experienced for a long time, hidden by other existences, and due to the meritorious deeds done by himself in the time of Sunetta—he says, “Moreover, I recollect,” and so on. Herein, “I recollect” (abhijānāmi) means I know with distinct knowledge, I understand directly. “For a long time” (dīgharattaṃ) means for a long period. “Merits” (puññāni) refers to wholesome qualities such as generosity. “Seven years” (satta vassāni) means seven full years. “A mind of loving-kindness” (mettācittaṃ): mettā is so called because it is gentle (mijjati), meaning it endears (siniyhati). Mettā also means that it occurs in a friend, or it is the behavior of a friend. But from the perspective of its characteristics, it has the characteristic of promoting welfare, the function of bringing about benefit, the manifestation of the subsidence of aversion, and the proximate cause of seeing beings as agreeable. The subduing of ill-will is its accomplishment, while the arising of affection is its failure. “Having developed a mind of loving-kindness” (mettācittaṃ bhāvetvā) means having cultivated a mind accompanied by loving-kindness; since concentration is spoken of under the heading of 'mind,' it means having developed and increased the concentration of loving-kindness, the divine abiding of loving-kindness.

Satta saṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭakappeti satta mahākappe. Saṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭaggahaṇeneva hi saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyivivaṭṭaṭṭhāyinopi gahitā. Imaṃ lokanti kāmalokaṃ. Saṃvaṭṭamāne sudanti saṃvaṭṭamāne, sudanti nipātamattaṃ, vipajjamāneti attho. “Varasaṃvattaṭṭhāne suda”ntipi paṭhanti. Kappeti kāle. Kappasīsena hi kālo vutto, kāle khīyamāne sabbopi khīyateva. Yathāha – “kālo [M 3.0183] ghasati bhūtāni, sabbāneva sahattanā”ti (jā. 1.2.190). “Ābhassarūpago homī”ti vuttattā tejosaṃvaṭṭavasenettha kappavuṭṭhānaṃ veditabbaṃ. Ābhassarūpagoti tattha paṭisandhiggahaṇavasena ābhassarabrahmalokaṃ upagacchāmīti ābhassarūpago homi. Vivaṭṭamāneti saṇṭhahamāneti attho. Suññaṃ brahmavimānaṃ upapajjāmīti kassaci sattassa tattha nibbattassa abhāvato suññaṃ yaṃ paṭhamajjhānabhūmisaṅkhātaṃ [V 3.0170] brahmavimānaṃ ādito nibbattati, taṃ paṭisandhiggahaṇavasena upapajjāmi upemi.

“Seven eons of contraction and expansion” means seven great eons. By the term “contraction and expansion,” the periods of abiding in contraction and abiding in expansion are also included. “This world” refers to the sensual realm. “During contraction, indeed” means during contraction; sudaṃ is only a particle, meaning when it is being destroyed. Some read it as “during the excellent period of contraction, indeed.” “In the eon” (kappe) means in time. For time is spoken of under the heading of eons, and when time is exhausted, everything is exhausted. As it is said: “Time devours all beings, including itself” (Jā 1.2.190). Since it is said, “I become one who has gone to the Ābhassara realm,” here the emergence from the eon should be understood as occurring by way of the contraction by fire. “I become one who has gone to the Ābhassara realm” means I go to the Ābhassara Brahmā-world by way of taking rebirth there. “During expansion” means during the process of formation. “I am reborn in an empty Brahmā mansion” means that because no being had been born there, I am reborn, I go by way of taking rebirth, into the empty Brahmā mansion known as the plane of the first jhāna, which arises at the beginning.

Brahmāti kāmāvacarasattehi visiṭṭhaṭṭhena tathā tathā brūhitaguṇatāya brahmavihārato nibbattanaṭṭhena ca brahmā. Brahmapārisajjabrahmapurohitehi mahanto brahmāti mahābrahmā, tato eva te abhibhavitvā ṭhitattā abhibhū. Tehi na kenacipi guṇena abhibhūtoti anabhibhūto. Aññadatthūti ekaṃsavacane nipāto. Dassanato daso, atītānāgatapaccuppannānaṃ dassanasamattho abhiññāñāṇena passitabbaṃ passāmīti attho. Sesabrahmānaṃ iddhipādabhāvanābalena attano cittañca mama vase vattemīti vasavattī homīti yojetabbaṃ. Tadā kira bodhisatto aṭṭhasamāpattilābhīpi samāno tathā sattahitaṃ attano pāramipūraṇañca olokento tāsu eva dvīsu jhānabhūmīsu nikanti uppādetvā mettābrahmavihāravasena aparāparaṃ saṃsari. Tena vuttaṃ “satta vassāni…pe… vasavattī”ti.

Brahmā is so called because he is distinguished by an eminent state from beings in the realm of desire, because he possesses augmented virtues, and because of his arising from the divine abidings. Greater than the Brahmā's retinue and the Brahmā's ministers, he is called Mahābrahmā, and because he stands having overcome them, he is the Overcomer. He is unconquered because he is not overcome by any of them in virtue. “Indeed” (aññadatthu) is a particle with an emphatic meaning. The meaning of 'seer' (daso), from 'seeing,' is: 'I am capable of seeing the past, future, and present; with the knowledge of direct experience, I see what is to be seen.' The phrase 'I become a master of will' (vasavattī) should be construed as follows: 'By the power of developing the bases of psychic power, I make my own mind subject to my will and have mastery over the other Brahmās.' At that time, it is said, the Bodhisatta, even though possessing the eight attainments, contemplating both the welfare of beings and the fulfillment of his own perfections, repeatedly transmigrated by means of the divine abiding of loving-kindness, developing delight in those two jhāna planes. Therefore it is said, “For seven years... a master of will.”

Evaṃ bhagavā rūpāvacarapuññassa vipākamahantataṃ pakāsetvā idāni kāmāvacarapuññassapi vipākaṃ dassento “chattiṃsakkhattu”ntiādimāha. Tattha sakko ahosinti chattiṃsakkhattuṃ chattiṃsavāre aññattha anupapajjitvā nirantaraṃ sakko devānamindo tāvatiṃsadevarājā ahosiṃ. Rājā ahosintiādīsu catūhi acchariyadhammehi catūhi saṅgahavatthūhi ca lokaṃ rañjetīti rājā. Cakkaratanaṃ vatteti, catūhi sampatticakkehi vattati, tehi ca paraṃ vatteti, parahitāya ca iriyāpathacakkānaṃ vatto etasmiṃ atthīti cakkavattī. “Rājā”ti cettha sāmaññaṃ, “cakkavattī”ti visesaṃ. Dhammena caratīti dhammiko, ñāyena samena vattatīti attho. Dhammeneva rajjaṃ labhitvā rājā jātoti dhammarājā, dasavidhe kusaladhamme agarahite ca rājadhamme niyuttoti dhammiko. Tena ca dhammena sakalaṃ [M 3.0184] lokaṃ rañjetīti dhammarājā. Parahitadhammakaraṇena vā dhammiko, attahitadhammakaraṇena dhammarājā. Yasmā cakkavattī dhammena ñāyena rajjaṃ adhigacchati, na adhammena, tasmā vuttaṃ “dhammena laddharajjattā dhammarājā”ti.

Thus, the Blessed One, having shown the greatness of the fruit of form-realm merit, now reveals the fruit of sense-realm merit by saying, “Thirty-six times,” and so on. Herein, “I was Sakka” means that thirty-six times, on thirty-six occasions, without being reborn elsewhere, I was continually Sakka, the king of the devas, the lord of the Tāvatiṃsa devas. In the passages beginning “I was a king,” “king” (rājā) means one who delights (rañjeti) the world with the four marvelous qualities and the four bases of beneficence. He is a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavattī) because he turns the wheel-treasure; he proceeds with the four wheels of prosperity, and with them he causes others to proceed; and the proceeding of the wheels of conduct for the welfare of others exists in him. Here, “king” is general, “wheel-turning monarch” is specific. “Righteous” (dhammiko) means he conducts himself by Dhamma, meaning he acts with fairness and equity. “Righteous king” (dhammarājā) means he obtained kingship by Dhamma and was born a king; “righteous” (dhammiko) because he is devoted to the ten kinds of wholesome conduct and blameless royal duties. And by that righteousness, he delights the whole world—thus, a righteous king. Or, “righteous” because he performs duties for the welfare of others, and “righteous king” because he performs duties for his own welfare. Since the wheel-turning monarch attains kingship by Dhamma, justly, not unrighteously, it is said, “Because he obtained kingship righteously, he is a righteous king.”

Catūsu disāsu samuddapariyosānatāya cāturantā nāma tattha tattha dīpe mahāpathavīti āha “puratthima…pe… issaro”ti. Vijitāvīti vijetabbassa vijitavā, kāmakodhādikassa abbhantarassa paṭirājabhūtassa bāhirassa ca arigaṇassa vijayī vijinitvā ṭhitoti attho. Kāmaṃ cakkavattino kenaci yuddhaṃ nāma natthi, yuddhena pana sādhetabbassa vijayassa siddhiyā “vijitasaṅgāmo”ti vuttaṃ. Janapado vā catubbidhaacchariyadhammena samannāgato asmiṃ rājini thāvariyaṃ [V 3.0171] kenaci asaṃhāriyaṃ daḷhabhattibhāvaṃ patto, janapade vā attano dhammikāya paṭipattiyā thāvariyaṃ thirabhāvaṃ pattoti janapadatthāvariyappatto. Caṇḍassa hi rañño balidaṇḍādīhi lokaṃ pīḷayato manussā majjhimajanapadaṃ chaḍḍetvā pabbatasamuddatīrakandarādīni nissāya paccante vāsaṃ kappenti. Atimudukassa rañño corehi sāhasikadhanavilopapīḷitā manussā paccantaṃ pahāya janapadamajjhe vāsaṃ kappenti. Iti evarūpe rājini janapado thirabhāvaṃ na pāpuṇāti.

Because it is bounded by the ocean in the four directions, it is called 'Cāturanta.' The phrase 'the great earth on islands here and there' refers to the passage 'eastern... lord.' 'Vijitāvī' means one who has conquered what should be conquered—both the inner enemy, such as lust and anger, and the outer enemy, the hostile forces. Having conquered and remained steadfast is the meaning. Indeed, for a wheel-turning monarch, there is no battle; however, to signify the accomplishment of conquest that could be achieved through war, it is said, “victorious in battle.” Or, the populace, endowed with the four marvelous qualities, under this ruler attains stability—unshakable and unassailable by anyone, having attained a strong bond of devotion. Or, through the ruler’s righteous conduct, the populace attains stability, a state of firmness in the kingdom. For when a cruel king oppresses the world with taxes and punishments, people abandon the central lands and, relying on mountains, seacoasts, caves, and the like, make their dwellings in outlying districts. When a king is excessively lenient, people, harassed by thieves and violent plunder, abandon the borders and settle in the heart of the kingdom. Thus, under such rulers, the kingdom does not attain stability.

Sattaratanasamannāgatoti cakkaratanādīhi sattahi ratanehi samupeto. Tesu hi rājā cakkavattī cakkaratanena ajitaṃ jināti, hatthiassaratanehi vijite sukheneva anuvicarati, pariṇāyakaratanena vijitamanurakkhati, avasesehi upabhogasukhamanubhavati. Paṭhamena cassa ussāhasattiyogo, pacchimena mantasattiyogo, hatthiassagahapatiratanehi pabhusattiyogo suparipuṇṇo hoti. Itthimaṇiratanehi upabhogasukhamanubhavati, sesehi issariyasukhaṃ. Visesato cassa purimāni tīṇi adosakusalamūlajanitakammānubhāvena sampajjanti, majjhimāni alobhakusalamūlajanitakammānubhāvena, pacchimamekaṃ amohakusalamūlajanitakammānubhāvenāti.

Endowed with the seven treasures: equipped with the seven treasures such as the wheel-treasure. For indeed, a wheel-turning monarch conquers the unconquered with the wheel-treasure, roams the conquered territory with ease through the elephant- and horse-treasures, protects the conquered territory with the counselor-treasure, and experiences the pleasure of enjoyment with the remaining treasures. With the first, he is connected with the power of effort; with the last, he is connected with the power of counsel; with the elephant-, horse-, and householder-treasures, the power of his lordship is fully complete. With the woman-treasure and jewel-treasure, he experiences the pleasure of enjoyment; with the rest, the pleasure of sovereignty. Specifically, the first three arise from the power of deeds born of the wholesome root of non-aversion, the middle three from the power of deeds born of the wholesome root of non-greed, and the last one from the power of deeds born of the wholesome root of non-delusion.

Sūrāti sattivanto, nibbhayāti atthoti āha “abhīruno”ti. Aṅganti kāraṇaṃ. Yena kāraṇena “vīrā”ti vucceyyuṃ, taṃ vīraṅgaṃ. Tenāha “vīriyassetaṃ nāma”nti. Yāva cakkavāḷapabbatā cakkassa vattanato “cakkavāḷapabbataṃ sīmaṃ katvā ṭhitasamuddapariyanta”nti vuttaṃ. Adaṇḍenāti iminā dhanadaṇḍassa sarīradaṇḍassa ca akaraṇaṃ vuttaṃ. Asatthenāti iminā [M 3.0185] pana senāya yujjhanassāti tadubhayaṃ dassetuṃ “na daṇḍenā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – ye katāparādhe satte satampi sahassampi gaṇhanti, te dhanadaṇḍena rajjaṃ kārenti. Ye chejjabhejjaṃ anusāsanti, te satthadaṇḍena. Ahaṃ pana duvidhampi daṇḍaṃ pahāya adaṇḍena ajjhāvasiṃ. Ye ekatodhārādinā satthena paraṃ viheṭhenti, te satthena rajjaṃ kārenti nāma. Ahaṃ pana satthena khuddakamakkhikāya pivanamattampi lohitaṃ kassaci anuppādetvā dhammeneva “ehi kho, mahārājā”ti evaṃ paṭirājūhi sampaṭicchitāgamano vuttappakāraṃ pathaviṃ abhijinitvā ajjhāvasiṃ, abhivijinitvā sāmī hutvā vasinti.

`Sūra` means powerful; the meaning is 'without fear,' hence it is said, 'fearless.' `Aṅga` means cause. That which is the cause for beings to be called 'heroes' is the attribute of a hero. Therefore, it is said, “This is a term for energy.” It is said, “Having made the Cakkavāḷa mountain the boundary, and up to the limits of the ocean,” because the wheel turns as far as the Cakkavāḷa mountain. “Without a rod” means not using the rod of wealth or the rod of bodily punishment. But “without a weapon” shows that there is no fighting with an army, and to show both, it is said, “not with a rod,” etc. This is what is meant: Those who, when offenses are committed, seize even a hundred or a thousand beings, rule with the rod of wealth. Those who enforce punishments like cutting and piercing rule with the rod of the sword. But I, having abandoned both kinds of rods, dwell without a rod. Those who oppress others with weapons such as single-edged swords rule with the sword. But I, without causing even a drop of blood as small as a gnat’s sip to arise in anyone, righteously conquered the earth in the manner described, saying, “Come, great king,” and having received the submission of rival kings, I dwelt having thoroughly conquered, dwelling as its master.

Iti bhagavā attānaṃ kāyasakkhiṃ katvā puññānaṃ vipākamahantataṃ pakāsetvā idāni tamevatthaṃ gāthābandhanena dassento “passa, puññānaṃ vipāka”ntiādimāha. Sukhesinoti ālapanavacanametaṃ, tena sukhapariyesake satte āmanteti. Pāḷiyaṃ pana “passathā”ti vattabbe “passā”ti vacanabyattayo katoti daṭṭhabbo. Manussānaṃ ure satthaṃ ṭhapetvā icchitadhanaharaṇādinā vā [V 3.0172] sāhasakāritāya sāhasikā, tesaṃ kammaṃ sāhasikakammaṃ. Pathaviyā issaro pathabyoti āha “puthavisāmiko”ti.

Thus, the Blessed One, having made himself a bodily witness, revealed the greatness of the result of merits, and now showing that very meaning through verse, he said, “See, the result of merits,” and so on. “O seekers of happiness”—this is a term of address; with it, he addresses beings who seek happiness. In the Pāli, though “passathā” should be said, “passa” is used as a change of expression—this should be noted. Those who, placing a weapon at the chest of humans, commit violent acts such as forcibly taking desired wealth—they are reckless, and their actions are reckless actions. `Pathabyo` means 'lord of the earth'; he is called `puthavisāmiko`.

Mettasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Metta Sutta is concluded.

10. Bhariyāsuttavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Bhariyā Sutta

63. Dasame uccāsaddā mahāsaddā uddhaṃ uggatattā uccaṃ patthaṭattā mahantaṃ avinibbhogaṃ vinibhuñjitvā gahetuṃ asakkuṇeyyaṃ saddaṃ karontā vadanti. Vacīghosopi hi bahūhi ekajjhaṃ pavattito atthato ca saddato ca duravabodho kevalaṃ mahānigghoso eva hutvā sotapathamāgacchati. Macchavilopeti macche vilumpitvā viya gahaṇe, macchānaṃ vā vilumpane. Kevaṭṭānañhi macchapacchiṭṭhapitaṭṭhāne mahājano sannipatitvā “idha aññaṃ ekaṃ macchaṃ dehi, ekaṃ macchaphālaṃ dehi, etassa te mahā dinno, mayhaṃ khuddako”ti evaṃ uccāsaddamahāsaddaṃ karonti. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ “kevaṭṭānaṃ macchapacchiṃ otāretvā ṭhitaṭṭhāne”ti. Macchaggahaṇatthaṃ jāle pakkhittepi tasmiṃ ṭhāne kevaṭṭā ceva aññe ca “paviṭṭho na paviṭṭho[M 3.0186], gahito na gahito”ti mahāsaddaṃ karonti. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ “jāle vā…pe… mahāsaddo hotī”ti. Kattabbavattanti pādaparikammādikattabbakiccaṃ. Kharāti cittena vācāya ca kakkhaḷā. Sesamettha uttānameva.

63. In the tenth, `uccāsaddā mahāsaddā` means they speak making a sound that is 'high' because it has risen up and 'great' because it is spread out, a vast sound that is indistinguishable and impossible to grasp by analyzing it. For even the clamor of speech, when produced by many together, becomes difficult to understand in meaning and sound, becoming merely a great confused noise that reaches the ear. 'Macchavilope' means at the capture, which is like a plundering of fish, or at the plundering of fish. For in the place where fishermen have set down their fish baskets, a great crowd gathers and shouts loudly: 'Give me another fish here! Give me a piece of fish! This one of yours is big; mine is small!'—thus making a loud and great noise. This is said with reference to 'in the place where the fishermen have lowered their fish baskets.' Even when a net is cast to catch fish, both the fishermen and others standing there make a great noise, saying: 'It's in! It's not in! It's caught! It's not caught!' This is said with reference to 'or when a net… a great noise arises.' 'Kattabbavattaṃ' means the duty to be done, such as attending to the feet, and so on. 'Kharā' means harsh in mind and speech. The rest here is clear.

Bhariyāsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Bhariyā Sutta is concluded.

11. Kodhanasuttavaṇṇanā

11. The Commentary on the Kodhana Sutta

64. Ekādasame sapattakaraṇāti vā sapattehi kātabbā. Kodhananti kujjhanasīlaṃ. Kodhanoyanti kujjhano ayaṃ. Ayanti ca nipātamattaṃ. Kodhaparetoti kodhena anugato, parābhibhūto vā. Dubbaṇṇova hotīti pakatiyā vaṇṇavāpi alaṅkatappaṭiyattopi mukhavikārādivasena virūpo eva hoti. Etarahi āyatiñcāti kodhābhibhūtassa ekantamidaṃ phalanti dīpetuṃ “dubbaṇṇovā”ti avadhāraṇaṃ katvā puna “kodhābhibhūto”ti vuttaṃ.

64. In the eleventh, `sapattakaraṇā` means 'or to be done by enemies.' `Kodhanaṃ` means 'of an angry nature.' `Kodhanoyaṃ` means 'this one is angry.' And `ayaṃ` is merely a particle. `Kodhaparetoti` means one overcome by anger, or dominated by it. `Dubbaṇṇo va hotīti` means even if naturally beautiful or well-adorned, due to facial distortions and the like, one becomes ugly. To show that this is exclusively the result for one overcome by anger both now and in the future, after emphasizing with 'dubbaṇṇo vā,' it is further stated as 'kodhābhibhūto.'

Ayasabhāvanti akittimabhāvaṃ. Attano paresañca anatthaṃ janetīti anatthajanano. Antaratoti abbhantarato, cittato vā. Taṃ jano nāvabujjhatīti kodhasaṅkhātaṃ antarato abbhantare [V 3.0173] attano citteyeva jātaṃ anatthajananacittappakopanādibhayaṃ bhayahetuṃ ayaṃ bālamahājano na jānāti. Yanti yattha. Bhummatthe hi etaṃ paccattavacanaṃ. Yasmiṃ kāle kodho sahate naraṃ, andhatamaṃ tadā hotīti sambandho. Yanti vā kāraṇavacanaṃ, yasmā kodho uppajjamāno naraṃ sahate abhibhavati, tasmā andhatamaṃ tadā hoti, yadā kuddhoti attho yaṃ-taṃ-saddānaṃ ekantasambandhabhāvato. Atha vā yanti kiriyāparāmasanaṃ. Sahateti yadetaṃ kodhassa sahanaṃ abhibhavanaṃ, etaṃ andhatamaṃ bhavananti attho. Atha vā yaṃ naraṃ kodho sahate abhibhavati, tassa andhatamaṃ tadā hoti. Tato ca kuddho atthaṃ na jānāti, kuddho dhammaṃ na passatīti.

'Ayasabhāvaṃ' means the state of disrepute. 'Attano paresañca anatthaṃ janetīti anatthajanano' means he is a source of harm, generating harm for himself and others. 'Antarato' means internally, or in the mind. 'Taṃ jano nāvabujjhatīti' means this foolish multitude does not know this danger, this cause of fear, which is called anger, arisen within, in one's own mind, generating harm and agitating the mind. 'Yaṃ' means 'where.' In the sense of the locative, this is a singular term. 'Yasmiṃ kāle kodho sahate naraṃ, andhatamaṃ tadā hotīti' is the connection: 'When anger overcomes a man, then there is utter darkness.' 'Yaṃ' can also be a causal term, meaning, 'because anger arises and overwhelms a man, therefore, at that time, there is utter darkness.' The meaning is that when one is angry—this is due to the absolute connection of the words 'yaṃ' and 'tadā'. Alternatively, 'yaṃ' refers to the action. 'Sahateti' means that this overcoming, this subduing by anger, is utter darkness. Or, 'he whom anger overcomes'—for him, there is utter darkness at that time. Consequently, 'an angry man does not know what is beneficial, an angry man does not see the Dhamma.'

Bhūnaṃ vuccati vuddhi, tassa hananaṃ ghāto etesanti bhūnahaccāni. Tenāha “hatavuddhīnī”ti. Dama-saddena vuttamevatthaṃ vibhāvetuṃ paññāvīriyena [M 3.0187] diṭṭhiyāti vuttanti dassento “katarena damenā”tiādimāha. Anekattho hi dama-saddo. “Saccena danto damasā upeto, vedantagū vusitabrahmacariyo”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.195; su. ni. 467) ettha hi indriyasaṃvaro damoti vutto “manacchaṭṭhāni indriyāni dametī”ti katvā. “Yadi saccā damā cāgā, khantyā bhiyyodha vijjatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.246; su. ni. 191) ettha paññā damo “saṃkilesaṃ dameti pajahatī”ti katvā. “Dānena damena saṃyamena saccavajjena atthi puññaṃ, atthi puññassa āgamo”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.365) ettha uposathakammaṃ damo “upavasanavasena kāyakammādīni dametī”ti katvā. “Sakkhissasi kho tvaṃ, puṇṇa, iminā damūpasamena samannāgato sunāparantasmiṃ janapadantare viharitu”nti (ma. ni. 3.396; saṃ. ni. 4.88) ettha adhivāsanakkhanti damo “kodhūpanāhamakkhādike dameti vinodetī”ti katvā. “Na mānakāmassa damo idhatthi, na monamatthi asamāhitassā”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.9) ettha abhisambojjhaṅgādiko samādhipakkhiko dhammo damo “dammati cittaṃ etenā”ti katvā. Idhāpi “taṃ damena samucchinde, paññāvīriyena diṭṭhiyā”ti vacanato dama-saddena paññāvīriyadiṭṭhiyo vuttā.

'Bhūnaṃ' is said to be growth; their destruction is 'ghāta'; hence, 'bhūnahaccāni' (destroyers of growth). Therefore, it is said, 'hatavuddhīnī' (destroyers of growth). To clarify the meaning expressed by the word 'dama,' namely, 'through wisdom, energy, and right view,' he says, beginning with 'by which restraint?' For the word 'dama' has multiple meanings. In the passage, 'Restrained by truth, endowed with restraint, skilled in the Vedas, having lived the holy life' (Saṃ. Ni. 1.195; Su. Ni. 467), restraint is said to refer to sense control—'he restrains the six sense faculties.' In the verse, 'If truth, restraint, generosity, and patience exist here in abundance' (Saṃ. Ni. 1.246; Su. Ni. 191), restraint means wisdom—'it restrains and abandons defilements.' In the statement, 'There is merit in giving, restraint, self-control, and truthful speech; there is a source of merit' (Saṃ. Ni. 4.365), restraint refers to the observance of the uposatha—'it restrains bodily actions, etc., through the practice of uposatha.' In the passage, 'Will you be able, Puṇṇa, endowed with this restraint and calm, to dwell in the remote Sunāparanta country?' (Ma. Ni. 3.396; Saṃ. Ni. 4.88), restraint means forbearance—'it restrains and dispels anger, hostility, and resentment.' In the verse, 'For one desirous of pride, there is no restraint here; nor is there silence for the unconcentrated' (Saṃ. Ni. 1.9), restraint refers to the factors of enlightenment and other qualities allied with concentration—'the mind is tamed by this.' Here too, in the statement, 'Cut it off with restraint, with wisdom, energy, and right view,' the term 'dama' is said to refer to wisdom, energy, and right view.

Kodhanasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Kodhana Sutta is concluded.

Abyākatavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Chapter of the Unexplained is concluded.

7. Mahāvaggo

7. The Great Division

1-2. Hiriottappasuttādivaṇṇanā

1-2. Commentary on the Hiriottappa Sutta and others

65-66. Sattamassa [V 3.0174] paṭhamaṃ uttānameva. Dutiye tayo saṃvaṭṭāti āposaṃvaṭṭo, tejosaṃvaṭṭo, vāyosaṃvaṭṭoti tayo saṃvaṭṭā. Tisso saṃvaṭṭasīmāti ābhassarā, subhakiṇhā, vehapphalāti tisso saṃvaṭṭasīmā. Yadā hi kappo tejena saṃvaṭṭati vinassati, tadā ābhassarato heṭṭhā agginā ḍayhati. Yadā āpena saṃvaṭṭati, tadā subhakiṇhato heṭṭhā udakena vilīyati. Yadā vāyunā saṃvaṭṭati, tadā vehapphalato heṭṭhā vāyunā viddhaṃsati. Vitthārato pana sadāpi ekaṃ buddhakkhettaṃ vinassati. Buddhakkhettaṃ nāma tividhaṃ hoti jātikkhettaṃ āṇākkhettaṃ [M 3.0188] visayakkhettanti. Tattha jātikkhettaṃ nāma dasasahassacakkavāḷapariyantaṃ hoti, yaṃ tathāgatassa paṭisandhigahaṇādīsu kampati. Āṇākkhettaṃ koṭisahassacakkavāḷapariyantaṃ, yattha ratanasuttaṃ (khu. pā. 6.1 ādayo; su. ni. 224 ādayo) khandhaparittaṃ (a. ni. 4.67; cūḷava. 251) dhajaggaparittaṃ (saṃ. ni. 1.249). Āṭānāṭiyaparittaṃ (dī. ni. 3.275 ādayo), moraparittanti (jā. 1.2.17-18) imesaṃ parittānaṃ ānubhāvo vattati. Visayakkhettaṃ anantamaparimāṇaṃ, yaṃ “yāvatā vā pana ākaṅkheyyā”ti vuttaṃ. Evametesu tīsu buddhakkhettesu ekaṃ āṇākkhettaṃ vinassati. Tasmiṃ pana vinassante jātikkhettaṃ vinaṭṭhameva hoti. Vinassantañca ekatova vinassati, saṇṭhahantampi ekatova saṇṭhahati.

65-66. In the seventh, the first is self-evident. In the second, there are three dissolutions: dissolution by water, dissolution by fire, and dissolution by wind—these are the three dissolutions. The three boundaries of dissolution are the Ābhassara, the Subhakiṇha, and the Vehapphala—these are the three boundaries of dissolution. For when the aeon dissolves and perishes by fire, then it is burned by fire from below the Ābhassara. When it dissolves by water, then it is dissolved by water from below the Subhakiṇha. When it dissolves by wind, then it is shattered by wind from below the Vehapphala. In detail, however, at any one time a single Buddha-field is destroyed. A Buddha-field is of three kinds: the birth-field, the command-field, and the range-field. Among these, the birth-field extends to the limit of ten thousand world-systems, which trembles at the Tathāgata’s conception and so on. The command-field extends to the limit of a hundred thousand world-systems, where the power of protective recitations such as the Ratana Sutta, the Khandha Paritta, the Dhajagga Paritta, the Āṭānāṭiya Paritta, and the Mora Paritta prevails. The range-field is endless and immeasurable, as stated: "As far as one might desire." Thus, among these three Buddha-fields, one command-field is destroyed. When it is destroyed, the birth-field is already destroyed. And it is destroyed all at once, and it is re-established all at once.

Tīṇi saṃvaṭṭamūlānīti rāgadosamohasaṅkhātāni tīṇi saṃvaṭṭakāraṇāni. Rāgādīsu hi akusalamūlesu ussannesu loko vinassati. Tathā hi rāge ussannatare agginā vinassati, dose ussannatare udakena, mohe ussannatare vātena. Keci pana “dose ussannatare agginā, rāge udakenā”ti vadanti.

The three roots of dissolution are the three causes of dissolution, namely, greed, hatred, and delusion. For when these unwholesome roots become rampant, the world is destroyed. Specifically, when greed is very rampant, it is destroyed by fire; when hatred is very rampant, by water; and when delusion is very rampant, by wind. Some, however, say that when hatred is very rampant, it is destroyed by fire, and when greed is very rampant, by water.

Tīṇi kolāhalānīti kappakolāhalaṃ, buddhakolāhalaṃ, cakkavattikolāhalanti tīṇi kolāhalāni. Tattha “vassasatasahassamatthake kappuṭṭhānaṃ nāma bhavissatī”tiādinā devatāhi ugghositasaddo kappakolāhalaṃ nāma hoti. “Ito vassasatasahassamatthake loko vinassissati, mettaṃ, mārisā, bhāvetha karuṇaṃ muditaṃ upekkha”nti manussapathe devatā ghosantiyo caranti. “Vassasahassamatthake [V 3.0175] buddho uppajjissatī”ti buddhakolāhalaṃ nāma hoti. “Ito vassasahassamatthake buddho uppajjitvā dhammānudhammappaṭipanno saṅgharatanena parivārito dhammaṃ desento vicarissatī”ti devatā ugghosanti. “Vassasatamatthake pana cakkavattī uppajjissatī”ti cakkavattikolāhalaṃ nāma hoti. “Ito vassasatamatthake sattaratanasampanno cātuddīpissaro sahassaparivāro vehāsaṅgamo cakkavattī rājā uppajjissatī”ti devatā ugghosanti.

There are three great announcements: the announcement of the aeon, the announcement of the Buddha, and the announcement of the wheel-turning monarch. Among these, the announcement of the aeon is the sound proclaimed by the deities, beginning with, 'At the end of a hundred thousand years, a re-establishment of the aeon will occur.' Deities wander in the path of humans, proclaiming, 'At the end of a hundred thousand years from now, the world will perish. Dear ones, cultivate loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.' The announcement of the Buddha is the declaration, 'At the end of a thousand years, a Buddha will arise.' The deities proclaim, 'At the end of a thousand years from now, a Buddha will arise and, practicing in accordance with the Dhamma, surrounded by the Sangha jewel, will wander teaching the Dhamma.' The announcement of the wheel-turning monarch is the declaration, 'At the end of a hundred years, a wheel-turning monarch will arise.' The deities proclaim, 'At the end of a hundred years from now, a wheel-turning monarch will arise, endowed with the seven treasures, sovereign of the four continents, surrounded by a thousand followers, traveling through the sky.'

Aciraṭṭhena na dhuvāti udakabubbuḷādayo viya na ciraṭṭhāyitāya dhuvabhāvarahitā. Assāsarahitāti supinake pītapānīyaṃ viya anulittacandanaṃ viya ca assāsavirahitā.

'Not permanent' means not lasting long; like water bubbles and so on, because they do not endure for long, they are devoid of a permanent nature. 'Devoid of satisfaction' means devoid of gratification, like drinking water in a dream or like being anointed with sandalwood.

Upakappanameghoti [M 3.0189] kappavināsakameghaṃ sandhāya vadati. Yasmiñhi samaye kappo agginā nassati, āditova kappavināsakamahāmegho uṭṭhahitvā koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷe ekamahāvassaṃ vassati. Manussā tuṭṭhahaṭṭhā sabbabījāni nīharitvā vapanti. Sassesu pana gokhāyitakamattesu jātesu gadrabharavaṃ ravanto ekabindumpi na vassati, tadā pacchinnaṃ pacchinnameva vassaṃ hoti. Tenāha “tadā nikkhantabījaṃ..pe… ekabindumpi devo na vassatī”ti. “Vassasatasahassa accayena kappavuṭṭhānaṃ bhavissatī”tiādinā devatāhi vuttavacanaṃ sutvā yebhuyyena manussā ca bhummadevatā ca saṃvegajātā aññamaññaṃ muducittā hutvā mettādīni puññānī katvā devaloke nibbattanti, avīcito paṭṭhāya tuccho hotīti.

The term 'Upakappanamegha' is said in reference to the aeon-destroying cloud. For when the aeon is to be destroyed by fire, at the very beginning the great aeon-destroying cloud arises and pours down a single great rain over a hundred thousand million world-systems. People, delighted and joyful, take out all seeds and sow them. But when the crops have grown only to a height where a cow can eat them, the cloud roars like a donkey, but not even a single drop of rain falls; then the rain is completely cut off. Hence it is said, 'Then the seeds that were brought out... not even a single drop does the sky-god rain.' Hearing the words spoken by the deities, such as, 'After the passing of a hundred thousand years, the re-arising of the aeon will occur,' for the most part humans and earth-dwelling deities, filled with a sense of urgency, become gentle-hearted toward one another, perform meritorious deeds such as loving-kindness, and are reborn in the deva world. From Avīci upwards, it becomes empty.

Pañca bījajātānīti mūlabījaṃ khandhabījaṃ phaḷubījaṃ aggabījaṃ bījabījanti pañca bījāni jātāni. Tattha mūlabījanti vacā, vacattaṃ, haliddaṃ, siṅgiveranti evamādi. Khandhabījanti assattho, nigrodhoti evamādi. Phaḷubījanti ucchu, veḷu, naḷoti evamādi. Aggabījanti ajjukaṃ, phaṇijjakanti evamādi. Bījabījanti vīhiādi pubbaṇṇañceva muggamāsādiaparaṇṇañca. Paccayantarasamavāye visadisuppattiyā visesakāraṇabhāvato ruhanasamatthe sāraphale niruḷho bīja-saddo tadatthasiddhiyā mūlādīsupi kesuci pavattatīti mūlādito nivattanatthaṃ ekena bīja-saddena visesetvā vuttaṃ “bījabīja”nti “rūparūpaṃ (visuddhi. 2.449) dukkhadukkha”nti (saṃ. ni. 4.327) yathā. Yathā phalapākapariyantā osadhirukkhā veḷukadaliādayo.

There are five kinds of seeds: root-seed, stem-seed, joint-seed, tip-seed, and seed-seed. Herein, root-seed refers to things like sweet flag, orris root, turmeric, ginger, and so on. Stem-seed refers to things like the sacred fig, the banyan tree, and so on. Joint-seed refers to things like sugarcane, bamboo, reeds, and so on. Tip-seed refers to things like basil, marjoram, and so on. Seed-seed refers to both early-maturing crops such as rice, and late-maturing crops such as mung beans and other beans. The word 'seed' is established in the sense of the essential part in a fruit that is capable of sprouting, because it is the specific cause for the arising of a dissimilar plant when other conditions converge. To accomplish this meaning, it is also sometimes applied to roots and the like. In order to distinguish it from roots and so on, it is specified with the word 'seed' and called 'seed-seed,' just as in 'form-form' (Visuddhimagga 2.449) and 'suffering-suffering' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.327). Just as there are medicinal plants and trees whose life ends with the ripening of their fruit, such as bamboo, plantains, and so on.

Yaṃ kadācītiādīsu yanti nipātamattaṃ. Kadācīti kismiñci kāle. Karahacīti tasseva [V 3.0176] vevacanaṃ. Dīghassa addhunoti dīghassa kālassa. Accayenāti atikkamena. Sesamettha uttānameva.

In 'yaṃ kadāci,' etc., 'yaṃ' is merely a particle. 'Kadāci' means 'at some time.' 'Karahaci' is a synonym for that. 'Dīghassa addhuno' means 'of a long time.' 'Accayena' means 'by the passing of.' The rest here is self-evident.

Hiriottappasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Hiriottappa Sutta and others is concluded.

3. Nagaropamasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Discourse on the Simile of the City

67. Tatiye paccante bhavaṃ paccantimaṃ. “Ratho sīlaparikkhāro, jhānakkho cakkavīriyo”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 5.4) viya alaṅkāravacano parikkhārasaddoti āha “nagarālaṅkārehi alaṅkata”nti. Parivāravacanopi vaṭṭatiyeva “satta samādhiparikkhārā”tiādīsu [M 3.0190] (dī. ni. 3.330) viya. Nemaṃ vuccati thambhādīhi anupatabhūmippadesoti āha “gambhīraāvāṭā”ti, gambhīraṃ bhūmiṃ anuppaviṭṭhāti attho. Suṭṭhu sannisīdāpitāti bhūmiṃ nikhanitvā sammadeva ṭhapitā.

67. In the third section, `paccantimaṃ` means 'being in a border region.' Just as in such passages as, 'The chariot has virtue as its equipment, jhāna as its axle, energy as its wheels' (SN 5.4), the word `parikkhāra` is a term for adornment; thus it is said, 'adorned with the city's adornments.' It is also valid as a term for retinue, as in 'the seven requisites of concentration' (DN 3.330). `Nema` is said to be a region of ground not supported by pillars and so on; thus it is said, 'deep moats,' meaning 'having entered deep into the ground.' 'Well-sunken' means 'having dug into the ground and properly established'.

Anupariyāyeti etenāti anupariyāyo, soyeva pathoti anupariyāyapatho, parito pākārassa anuyāyamaggo.

One goes around by means of it, thus it is an `anupariyāya`; that very path is the `anupariyāyapatha`, the path that follows around the rampart.

Hatthiṃ ārohanti ārohāpayanti cāti hatthārohā (dī. ni. ṭī. 1.163). Yena hi payogena puriso hatthino ārohanayoggo hoti, hatthissa taṃ payogaṃ vidhāyantānaṃ sabbesampetesaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Tenāha “sabbepī”tiādi. Tattha hatthācariyā nāma ye hatthino hatthārohakānañca sikkhāpakā. Hatthivejjā nāma hatthibhisakkā. Hatthibandhā nāma hatthīnaṃ pādarakkhakā. Ādi-saddena hatthīnaṃ yavapadāyakādike saṅgaṇhāti. Assārohā rathikāti etthāpi eseva nayo. Rathe niyuttā rathikā. Ratharakkhā nāma rathassa āṇirakkhakā. Dhanuṃ gaṇhanti gaṇhāpenti cāti dhanuggahā, issāsā dhanusippassa sikkhāpakā ca. Tenāha “dhanuācariyā issāsā”ti. Celena celapaṭākāya yuddhe akanti gacchantīti celakāti āha – “ye yuddhe jayaddhajaṃ gahetvā purato gacchantī”ti. Yathā tathā ṭhite senike brūhakaraṇavasena tato tato calayanti uccālentīti calakā. Sakuṇagghiādayo viya maṃsapiṇḍaṃ parasenāsamūhaṃ sāhasikamahāyodhatāya chetvā chetvā dayanti uppatitvā gacchantīti piṇḍadāyakā. Dutiyavikappe piṇḍe dayanti janasammadde uppatantā viya gacchantīti piṇḍadāyakāti attho veditabbo. Uggatuggatāti thāmajavaparakkamādivasena ativiya uggatā, udaggāti attho. Pakkhandantīti attano [V 3.0177] vīrasūrabhāvena asajjamānā parasenaṃ anupavisantīti attho. Thāmajavabalaparakkamādisampattiyā mahānāgā viya mahānāgā. Ekasūrāti ekākisūrā attano sūrabhāveneva ekākino hutvā yujjhanakā. Sajālikāti savammikā. Saraparittāṇanti cammaparisibbitaṃ kheṭakaṃ, cammamayaṃ vā phalakaṃ. Gharadāsayodhāti attano dāsayodhā.

They mount elephants and have others mount them, hence they are called elephant riders (Dī. Ni. Ṭī. 1.163). For by whatever training a man becomes fit to mount an elephant, all those who impart that training to elephants are included. Therefore, it is said, 'all indeed,' and so forth. Herein, elephant trainers are those who train elephants and elephant riders. Elephant doctors are elephant physicians. Elephant binders are those who protect the feet of elephants. By the word 'etc.', those who provide fodder for elephants and the like are included. In the case of horse riders and charioteers too, the same principle applies. Those assigned to chariots are charioteers. Chariot guards are those who protect the chariot's linchpins. They take up bows and have others take them up, hence they are called bowmen; archers are those who instruct in the skill of archery. Therefore, it is said, 'bow instructors, archers.' Those who go into battle with a cloth banner are called `celakā`—thus it is said, 'those who go forth in battle holding the victory flag.' They make soldiers standing here and there move and stir by way of augmenting the ranks, hence they are called `calakā`. Like vultures and other birds of prey with a lump of flesh, they cut and tear apart the mass of the enemy army with their daring and great warrior-hood, and go forth leaping, hence they are called `piṇḍadāyakā`. In the second alternative, the meaning of `piṇḍadāyakā` should be understood as 'they tear apart the masses, going forth as if leaping in the crowd.' 'Uggatuggatā' means exceedingly exalted by way of strength, speed, vigor, and so forth; the meaning is 'udaggā' (uplifted). 'Pakkhandanti' means 'they enter the enemy ranks unhindered due to their own heroic and brave nature.' 'Mahānāgā' means they are like great elephants due to their possession of strength, speed, power, vigor, and so forth. 'Ekasūrā' means 'lone warriors,' those who fight alone, being solitary by their own bravery. 'Sajālikā' means 'savammikā' (armored). 'Saraparittāṇa' means a shield sewn with leather, or a leather-made board. 'Gharadāsayodhā' means 'their own household warriors'.

Sampakkhandanalakkhaṇāti saddheyyavatthuno evametanti sampakkhandanalakkhaṇā. Sampasādanalakkhaṇāti pasīditabbe vatthusmiṃ pasīdanalakkhaṇā. Okappanasaddhāti [M 3.0191] okkantitvā pakkhanditvā adhimuccanaṃ. Pasādanīye vatthusmiṃ pasīdanaṃ pasādasaddhā. Ayaṃ anudhammoti ayaṃ navannaṃ lokuttaradhammānaṃ anulomadhammo. Nibbidābahuloti ukkaṇṭhanābahulo. Saddhā bandhati pātheyyanti saddhā nāmāyaṃ sattassa maraṇavasena mahāpathaṃ saṃvajato mahākantāraṃ paṭipajjato mahāviduggaṃ pakkhandato pātheyyapuṭaṃ bandhati, sambalaṃ vissajjetīti attho. Saddhañhi uppādetvā dānaṃ deti, sīlaṃ rakkhati, uposathakammaṃ karoti. Tenetaṃ vuttaṃ “saddhā bandhati pātheyya”nti. Sirīti issariyaṃ. Issariye hi abhimukhībhūte thalatopi jalatopi bhogā āgacchantiyeva. Tenetaṃ vuttaṃ “sirī bhogānamāsayo”ti. Saddhā dutiyā purisassa hotīti purisassa devaloke, manussaloke ceva nibbānañca gacchantassa saddhā dutiyā hoti, sahāyakiccaṃ sādheti. Bhattapuṭādīti ādi-saddena dutiyikādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Anekasarasatāti anekasabhāvatā, anekakiccatā vā. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

'Sampakkhandanalakkhaṇā' means the characteristic of leaping forward, in the sense that it leaps forward toward the object of faith with the thought, 'It is so.' 'Sampasādanalakkhaṇā' means the characteristic of becoming serene toward an object in which one should be serene. 'Okappanasaddhā' means trust, which is entering, leaping forward, and resolving. 'Pasādasaddhā' is serenity toward an object that inspires serenity. 'Ayaṃ anudhammo' means this is the Dhamma in conformity with the nine supramundane Dhammas. 'Nibbidābahulo' means abounding in weariness. 'Faith ties the provisions' means that this faith, indeed, ties a provision bundle for a being who, on account of death, is traveling the great road, traversing the great wilderness, and venturing into the great impasse; the meaning is that it provides supplies. For having aroused faith, one gives gifts, observes virtue, and performs the Uposatha duty. Therefore, it is said, 'Faith ties the provisions.' 'Sirī' means sovereignty. For when sovereignty is manifest, wealth comes even from land and water. Therefore, it is said, 'Glory is the resting place of wealth.' 'Faith is a man’s companion' means that for a man going to the deva-world, the human world, and to Nibbāna, faith is his companion, accomplishing the duty of a friend. 'Bhattapuṭādi' (a bundle of food, etc.)—by the word 'etc.', the inclusion of a companion and so forth should be understood. 'Anekasarasatā' means having many natures or having many functions. The rest is easily understood.

Nagaropamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on the Simile of the City is concluded.

4. Dhammaññūsuttavaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Discourse on One Who Knows the Dhamma

68. Catutthe suttageyyādidhammaṃ jānātīti dhammaññū. Tassa tasseva suttageyyādinā bhāsitassa tadaññassa suttapadatthassa bodhakassa saddassa atthakusalatāvasena atthaṃ jānātīti atthaññū. “Ettakomhi sīlena samādhinā paññāyā”ti evaṃ yathā attano pamāṇajānanavasena attānaṃ jānātīti attaññū. Paṭiggahaṇaparibhogapariyesanavissajjanesu mattaṃ jānātīti mattaññū. Niddese pana paṭiggahaṇamattaññutāya eva paribhogādimattaññutā pabodhitā hotīti paṭiggahaṇamattaññutāva dassitā. “Ayaṃ kālo uddesassa, ayaṃ kālo paripucchāya, ayaṃ kālo yogassa adhigamāyā”ti evaṃ kālaṃ jānātīti kālaññū. Tattha pañca vassāni uddesassa kālo, dasa paripucchāya, idaṃ atisambādhaṃ, atikkhapaññassa tāvatā kālena tīretuṃ asakkuṇeyyattā [V 3.0178] dasa vassāni uddesassa kālo, vīsati paripucchāya, tato paraṃ yoge kammaṃ kātabbaṃ. Khattiyaparisādikaṃ [M 3.0192] aṭṭhavidhaṃ parisaṃ jānātīti parisaññū. Bhikkhuparisādikaṃ catubbidhaṃ, khattiyaparisādikaṃ manussaparisaṃyeva puna catubbidhaṃ gahetvā aṭṭhavidhaṃ vadanti apare. Niddese panassa khattiyaparisādicatubbidhaparisaggahaṇaṃ nidassanamattaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Imaṃ me sevantassa akusalā dhammā parihāyanti, kusalā dhammā abhivaḍḍhanti, tasmā ayaṃ puggalo sevitabbo, vipariyāyato añño asevitabbo”ti sevitabbāsevitabbapuggalaṃ jānātīti puggalaparoparaññū. Evañhi tesaṃ puggalānaṃ paroparaṃ ukkaṭṭhanihīnataṃ jānāti nāma. Niddesepissa sevitabbāsevitabbapuggale vibhāvanameva samaṇakathākatanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

68. In the fourth [sutta], one who knows the Dhamma, such as the suttas and geyyas, is a 'knower of the Dhamma' (dhammaññū). One who knows the meaning (atthaññū) is one who, through skill in meaning, knows the meaning of the sound that conveys the meaning of the sutta-passages spoken in those very suttas, geyyas, and so forth, and of others. One who knows oneself (attaññū) is one who knows oneself by knowing one's own measure, thinking, 'I am of such virtue, concentration, and wisdom.' One who knows moderation (mattaññū) is one who knows moderation in receiving, consuming, seeking, and giving. In the exposition, however, since knowing moderation in consuming and other aspects is implied by knowing moderation in receiving, only knowing moderation in receiving is shown. One who knows the time (kālaññū) is one who knows the time, thinking, 'This is the time for recitation, this is the time for questioning, this is the time for striving for attainment.' Here, five years is the time for recitation, ten for questioning. This is too constrained; since it is impossible even for one with keen wisdom to complete it in such a time, ten years is the time for recitation and twenty for questioning, after which one should engage in practice. One who knows the assembly (parisaññū) is one who knows the eightfold assembly, beginning with the assembly of khattiyas. The assembly of bhikkhus is fourfold, while others say that the assembly of khattiyas, being a human assembly, is again taken as fourfold, making eight in total. In the exposition, however, the inclusion of the fourfold assembly beginning with the assembly of khattiyas should be understood as merely an example. One who knows persons, superior and inferior (puggalaparoparaññū) is one who knows the person to be associated with or avoided, thinking, 'When I associate with this person, unwholesome qualities decline and wholesome qualities increase; therefore, this person should be associated with, and conversely, another should be avoided.' Thus, one truly knows the superiority and inferiority of such persons. In the exposition, it should be understood that the explanation of persons to be associated with and avoided is simply a discourse for ascetics.

Dhammaññūsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Dhammaññū Sutta is concluded.
