5-6. Pāricchattakasuttādivaṇṇanā

5-6. Commentary on the Pāricchattaka Sutta and so forth

69-70. Pañcame patitapalāsoti patitapatto. Ettha paṭhamaṃ paṇḍupalāsataṃ, dutiyaṃ pannapalāsatañca vatvā tatiyaṃ jālakajātatā, catutthaṃ khārakajātatā ca pāḷiyaṃ vuttā. Dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana mahāgovindasuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.294) imameva pāḷiṃ āharitvā dassentena paṭhamaṃ paṇḍupalāsataṃ, dutiyaṃ pannapalāsatañca vatvā tatiyaṃ khārakajātatā, catutthaṃ jālakajātatā ca dassitā. Evañhi tattha vuttaṃ – “pāricchattake pupphamāne ekaṃ vassaṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ gacchanti, te tassa paṇḍupalāsabhāvato paṭṭhāya attamanā honti. Yathāha –

69-70. In the fifth [sutta], 'patitapalāso' means 'fallen leaves.' Here, firstly, the state of being yellowed leaves; secondly, the state of being fallen leaves; thirdly, the state of being net-like; and fourthly, the state of being like a khāraka are stated in the Pāḷi. However, in the Dīghanikāya Commentary, in the explanation of the Mahāgovinda Sutta (Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 2.294), by citing this very Pāḷi passage, it is shown that firstly is the state of being yellowed leaves, secondly the state of being fallen leaves, thirdly the state of being like a khāraka, and fourthly the state of being net-like. For thus it is said there: 'When the Pāricchattaka tree is in bloom, they attend to it for a year, and from the state of its leaves turning yellow onwards, they become delighted. As it is said:'

Yasmiṃ, bhikkhave, samaye devānaṃ tāvatiṃsānaṃ pāricchattako koviḷāro, paṇḍupalāso hoti, attamanā, bhikkhave, devā tāvatiṃsā tasmiṃ samaye honti ‘paṇḍupalāso dāni pāricchattako, koviḷāro, na cirasseva pannapalāso bhavissatī’ti. Yasmiṃ samaye devānaṃ tāvatiṃsānaṃ pāricchattako, koviḷāro, pannapalāso hoti, jālakajāto hoti, khārakajāto hoti, kuṭumalakajāto hoti, korakajāto hoti, attamanā, bhikkhave[M 3.0193], devā tāvatiṃsā tasmiṃ samaye honti ‘korakajāto dāni pāricchattako koviḷāro, na cirasseva sabbapāliphullo bhavissatī’ti.

Monks, at the time when the Pāricchattaka koviḷāra tree of the Tāvatiṃsa gods has yellowed leaves, the Tāvatiṃsa gods are delighted at that time, thinking, 'Now the Pāricchattaka koviḷāra tree has yellowed leaves; before long it will have fallen leaves.' Monks, at the time when the Pāricchattaka koviḷāra tree of the Tāvatiṃsa gods has fallen leaves, has become net-like, has become like a khāraka, has produced large buds, has produced opening buds, the Tāvatiṃsa gods are delighted at that time, thinking, 'Now the Pāricchattaka koviḷāra tree has produced opening buds; before long it will be in full bloom with all its foliage.'

Līnatthappakāsiniyampi [V 3.0179] (dī. ni. ṭī. 2.294) ettha evamattho dassito – pannapalāsoti patitapatto. Khārakajātoti jātakhuddakamakuḷo. Ye hi nīlapattakā ativiya khuddakā makuḷā, te “khārakā”ti vuccanti. Jālakajātoti tehiyeva khuddakamakuḷehi jātajālako sabbaso jālo viya jāto. Keci pana “jālakajātoti ekajālo viya jāto”ti atthaṃ vadanti. Pāricchattako kira khārakaggahaṇakāle sabbatthakameva pallaviko hoti, te cassa pallavā pabhassarapavāḷavaṇṇasamujjalā honti. Tena so sabbaso samujjalanto tiṭṭhati. Kuṭumalajātoti sañjātamahāmakuḷo. Korakajātoti sañjātasūcibhedo sampativikasamānāvattho. Sabbapāliphulloti sabbaso phullitavikasitoti. Ayañca anukkamo dīghabhāṇakānaṃ vaḷañjanānukkamena dassito, na ettha ācariyassa virodho āsaṅkitabbo.

In the Līnatthappakāsinī (Dī. Ni. Ṭī. 2.294) too, the meaning is explained thus: 'Pannapalāso' means 'fallen leaves.' 'Khārakajāto' means 'having produced small buds.' For those very small buds with bluish leaves are called 'khārakā.' 'Jālakajāto' means 'having formed a network from those very small buds, having become entirely like a net.' Some, however, say the meaning of 'jālakajāto' is 'having become like a single net.' It is said that the Pāricchattaka tree, at the time of producing khāraka buds, is entirely covered with new foliage, and its new shoots shine brilliantly with a color like radiant coral. Thus, it stands completely resplendent. 'Kuṭumalajāto' means 'having produced large buds.' 'Korakajāto' refers to the stage where needle-like splits appear, the state of being just about to blossom. 'Sabbapāliphullo' means 'fully blossomed and open.' And this sequence is presented according to the customary sequence of the Dīghabhāṇakas, and no contradiction with the teacher’s view should be suspected here.

Kantanakavātoti devānaṃ puññakammapaccayā pupphānaṃ chindanakavāto. Kantatīti chindati. Sampaṭicchanakavātoti chinnānaṃ chinnānaṃ pupphānaṃ sampaṭiggaṇhakavāto. Cinantoti nānāvidhabhattisannivesavasena nicinaṃ karonto. Aññataradevatānanti nāmagottavasena apaññātadevatānaṃ. Reṇuvaṭṭīti reṇusaṅghāto. Kaṇṇikaṃ āhaccāti sudhammāya kūṭaṃ āhantvā.

'Kantanakavāta' means 'the wind that cuts flowers due to the meritorious deeds of the gods.' 'Kantati' means 'cuts' or 'severs.' 'Sampaṭicchanakavāta' means 'the wind that gathers the severed flowers.' 'Cinanto' means 'collecting them, making a heap, according to various artistic arrangements.' 'Aññataradevatānaṃ' refers to 'deities not known by name or clan.' 'Reṇuvaṭṭī' means 'a mass of pollen' or 'a pollen swirl.' 'Kaṇṇikaṃ āhacca' means 'having struck the gable ornament of the Sudhammā hall.'

Anupharaṇānubhāvoti khīṇāsavassa bhikkhuno kittisaddassa yāva brahmalokā anupharaṇasaṅkhāto ānubhāvo. Pabbajjānissitaṃ hotīti pabbajjāya catupārisuddhisīlampi dassitamevāti adhippāyo. Paṭhamajjhānasannissitantiādīsupi imināva nayena attho veditabbo. Idha pana ubhayato paricchedo heṭṭhā sīlato upari arahattato ca paricchedassa dassitattā. Tenetaṃ vuttanti tena kāraṇena etaṃ “catupārisuddhisīlaṃ pabbajjānissitaṃ hotī”tiādivacanaṃ vuttaṃ. Chaṭṭhaṃ uttānameva.

'Anupharaṇānubhāvo' refers to 'the power of pervading,' which is the influence of the fame of a monk whose defilements are destroyed, pervading as far as the Brahmā world. 'Pabbajjānissitaṃ hoti' means that 'even the fourfold purified morality is shown through the going forth'—this is the intention. Similarly, in cases such as 'dependent on the first jhāna' and so forth, the meaning should be understood in the same way. Here, however, the boundary is from both sides, since the boundary is shown below by virtue and above by arahantship. 'Tenetaṃ vuttaṃ' means that 'for that reason, this statement, "the fourfold purified morality is dependent on the going forth," and so forth, is said.' The sixth [sutta] is self-explanatory.

Pāricchattakasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Pāricchattaka Sutta and so forth is concluded.

7. Bhāvanāsuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Bhāvanā Sutta

71. Sattame [M 3.0194] atthassa asādhikā “bhāvanaṃ ananuyuttassā”ti vuttattā. Sambhāvanattheti “api nāma evaṃ siyā”ti vikappanattho sambhāvanattho. Evañhi loke siliṭṭhavacanaṃ hotīti ekameva saṅkhaṃ avatvā aparāya saṅkhāya saddhiṃ vacanaṃ loke siliṭṭhavacanaṃ hoti yathā “dve vā [V 3.0180] tīṇi vā udakaphusitānī”ti. Sammā adhisayitānīti pādādīhi attanā nesaṃ kiñci upaghātaṃ akarontiyā bahivātādiparissayapariharaṇatthaṃ sammadeva upari sayitāni. Upariattho hettha adhi-saddo. Utuṃ gaṇhāpentiyāti tesaṃ allasinehapariyādānatthaṃ attano kāyusmāvasena utuṃ gaṇhāpentiyā. Tenāha “usmīkatānī”ti. Sammā paribhāvitānīti sammadeva sabbaso kukkuṭavāsanāya vāsitāni. Tenāha “kukkuṭagandhaṃ gāhāpitānī”ti. Ettha ca sammāparisedanaṃ kukkuṭagandhaparibhāvanañca sammāadhisayanasammāparisedananipphattiyā ānubhāvanipphāditanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sammāadhisayaneneva hi itaradvayaṃ ijjhati. Na hi sammāadhisayanato visuṃ sammāparisedanassa sammāparibhāvanassa ca kāraṇaṃ atthi. Tena pana saddhiṃyeva itaresaṃ dvinnampi ijjhanato vuttaṃ.

71. In the seventh case, it is not conducive to the goal because it is said, 'for one not devoted to development.' The meaning of sambhāvanā is the meaning of considering, 'perhaps it might be so,' which is the meaning of possibility. For in the world, this is elegant speech: not stating just one number, but speaking along with another number is elegant speech in the world, as in 'two or three drops of water.' 'Properly sat upon' means they were properly sat upon from above by her, without causing them any harm with her feet and so on, in order to ward off external dangers such as wind. Here, the prefix 'adhi-' has the meaning of 'above.' 'Making them take on the heat' means making them take on the heat by means of her own body's warmth in order to dry up their moisture. Hence, it is said, 'warmed.' 'Properly imbued' means thoroughly imbued in every way with the scent of a hen. Hence, it is said, 'made to take on the scent of a hen.' And here, it should be understood that proper warming and imbuing with the scent of a hen are produced by the power of the accomplishment of proper sitting upon and proper warming. For the other two are accomplished precisely through proper sitting upon. Indeed, there is no cause for proper warming and proper imbuing separate from proper sitting upon. Therefore, it is said that the other two are accomplished together with it.

Tividhakiriyākaraṇenāti sammāadhisayanāditividhakiriyākaraṇenāti attho. Kiñcāpi “evaṃ aho vata me”tiādinā na icchā uppajjeyya kāraṇassa pana sampāditattā, atha kho bhabbāva te abhinibbhijjitunti yojanā. Kasmā bhabbāti āha “te hi yasmā tāyā”tiādi. Sayampīti aṇḍāni. Pariṇāmanti paripākaṃ bahinikkhamanayogyataṃ. Yathā kapālassa tanutā ālokassa anto paññāyamānassa kāraṇaṃ, tathā kapālassa tanutāya nakhasikhāmukhatuṇḍakānaṃ kharatāya ca allasinehapariyādānaṃ kāraṇavacananti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tasmāti ālokassa anto paññāyamānato sayañca paripākagatattā.

'By the performance of the threefold action' means by the performance of the threefold action beginning with proper sitting upon. Although the wish, 'Oh, if only it were so for me,' and so on, might not arise, yet because the cause has been provided, they are indeed capable of breaking through—this is the connection. Why are they capable? He said, 'Because they, by that...' and so on. 'By themselves' refers to the eggs. 'Maturation' means ripeness, the suitability for emerging outside. Just as the thinness of the shell is the cause for the light being visible inside, so too the thinness of the shell, the sharpness of the tips of their claws and beaks, and the drying up of moisture should be seen as the statement of the cause. Therefore: because the light is visible inside and because they have reached maturity by themselves.

Opammasampaṭipādananti opammatthassa upameyyena sammadeva paṭipādanaṃ. Tanti opammasampaṭipādanaṃ. Evanti idāni vuccamānākārena. Atthenāti upameyyatthena saṃsandetvā saha yojetvā. Sampādanena sampayuttadhammavasena ñāṇassa tikkhabhāvo veditabbo. Ñāṇassa hi sabhāvato satinepakkato ca tikkhabhāvo, samādhivasena kharabhāvo, saddhāvasena vippasannabhāvo. Pariṇāmakāloti balavavipassanākālo. Vaḍḍhikāloti [M 3.0195] vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanākālo. Anulomaṭṭhāniyā hi vipassanā gahitagabbhā nāma tadā maggagabbhassa gahitattā. Tajjātikanti tassa vipassanānuyogassa anurūpaṃ. Satthāpi avijjaṇḍakosaṃ paharati, desanāpi vineyyasantānagataṃ avijjaṇḍakosaṃ paharati, yathāṭhāne ṭhātuṃ na deti.

'The application of the simile' means the proper application of the meaning of the simile to the subject of comparison. That is the application of the simile. 'Thus' means in the manner now being stated. 'With the meaning' means by comparing and connecting it with the meaning of the subject of comparison. The sharpness of knowledge is to be understood by way of the states associated with its accomplishment. For the sharpness of knowledge comes from its nature and from mindfulness and prudence; its firmness comes from concentration; its clarity comes from faith. 'The time of maturation' is the time of powerful insight. 'The time of growth' is the time of insight leading to emergence. For insight in the stage of conformity is called 'having conceived the embryo,' because at that time the embryo of the path has been conceived. 'Of that kind' means corresponding to that practice of insight. The Teacher also strikes the eggshell of ignorance; the teaching also strikes the eggshell of ignorance present in the mental continuum of those to be trained, not allowing it to remain in its place.

Olambakasaṅkhātanti olambakasuttasaṅkhātaṃ. “Pala”nti hi tassa suttassa nāmaṃ. Cāretvā dāruno heṭṭhā dosajānanatthaṃ ussāpetvā. Gaṇḍaṃ haratīti palagaṇḍoti etena “palena gaṇḍahāro palagaṇḍoti pacchimapade uttarapadalopena niddeso”ti dasseti. Gahaṇaṭṭhāneti hatthena gahetabbaṭṭhāne[V 3.0181]. Sammadeva khipīyanti etena kāyaduccaritādīnīti saṅkhepo, pabbajjāva saṅkhepo pabbajjāsaṅkhepo. Tena vipassanaṃ anuyuñjantassa puggalassa ajānantasseva āsavānaṃ parikkhayo idha vipassanānisaṃsoti adhippeto.

'Called the Olambaka' means called the Olambaka Sutta. For 'Pala' is the name of that sutta. Having applied it and raised it up in order to know the fault underneath the wood. 'It removes the protuberance' (gaṇḍaṃ harati), hence it is a palagaṇḍa. By this, it is shown that 'palagaṇḍa is a designation with the elision of the latter part of the final word, from palena gaṇḍahāro (remover of the protuberance by the pala).' 'At the place of grasping' means at the place to be grasped by the hand. 'By this, bodily misconduct and so forth are rightly cast away' (khipīyanti): this is a casting away (saṅkhepa). Going forth itself is a casting away, hence 'the casting away of going forth' (pabbajjāsaṅkhepa). Thereby, it is intended here that the benefit of insight is the destruction of the taints for a person practicing insight, even without their knowing it.

Hemantikena kāraṇabhūtena, bhummatthe vā etaṃ karaṇavacanaṃ, hemantiketi attho. Paṭippassambhantīti paṭippassaddhaphalāni honti. Tenāha “pūtikāni bhavantī”ti. Mahāsamuddo viya sāsanaṃ agādhagambhīrabhāvato. Nāvā viya yogāvacaro mahoghuttarato. Pariyāyanaṃ viyāti parito aparāparaṃ yāyanaṃ viya. Khajjamānānanti khādantena viya udakena khepiyamānabandhanānaṃ. Tanubhāvoti pariyuṭṭhānapavattiyā asamatthatāya dubbalabhāvo. Vipassanāñāṇapītipāmojjehīti vipassanāñāṇasamuṭṭhitehi pītipāmojjehi. Okkhāyamāneti vipassanākammaṭṭhāne vīthippaṭipāṭiyā okkhāyamāne, paṭisaṅkhānupassanāya vā okkhāyamāne. Saṅkhārupekkhāya pakkhāyamāne. Dubbalatā dīpitā “appakasireneva saṃyojanāni paṭippassambhanti, pūtikāni bhavantī”ti vuttattā.

By 'in the winter season' (hemantikena), which is the cause; or this instrumental word has the meaning of the locative, meaning 'in the winter season.' 'They subside' means their results become pacified. Hence, he said, 'they become rotten.' The teaching is like the great ocean because of its unfathomable depth. The practitioner of yoga is like a ship because of crossing the great flood. 'Like going around' means like going around again and again. 'Of those being eaten' means of the bonds being swept away by the water as if by something eating. 'The state of being thin' means the state of weakness due to the inability for the manifestation of the obsessions to proceed. 'Through the joy and gladness of insight knowledge' means through the joy and gladness arisen from insight knowledge. 'When it is being cleared away' (okkhāyamāne) means when it is being cleared away in the sequence of the path in the insight meditation subject, or when it is being cleared away by the insight of reflection. When it is being wasted away (pakkhāyamāne) by equanimity towards formations. The weakness is shown because it is said, 'With little difficulty the fetters subside, they become rotten'.

Bhāvanāsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Bhāvanā Sutta is finished.

8-9. Aggikkhandhopamasuttādivaṇṇanā

8-9. Commentary on the Aggikkhandhopama Sutta and Similar Discourses

72-73. Aṭṭhame passatha nūti api passatha. Mahantanti vipulaṃ. Aggikkhandhanti aggisamūhaṃ. Ādittanti padittaṃ. Sampajjalitanti samantato pajjalitaṃ accivipphuliṅgāni [M 3.0196] muñcantaṃ. Sajotibhūtanti samantato uṭṭhitāhi jālāhi ekappabhāsamudayabhūtaṃ. Taṃ kiṃ maññathāti taṃ idāni mayā vuccamānatthaṃ kiṃ maññathāti anumatiggahaṇatthaṃ pucchati. Yadettha satthā aggikkhandhāliṅganaṃ kaññāliṅganañca ānesi, tamatthaṃ vibhāvetuṃ “ārocayāmī”tiādimāha.

72-73. In the eighth sutta: 'Do you see?' (passatha nū) means 'Do you indeed see?' 'Great' means extensive. 'Mass of fire' means a heap of fire. 'Blazing' means kindled. 'Fully ablaze' means blazing all around, emitting flames and sparks. 'Become a single mass of light' means become a single arising of radiance with flames risen up all around. 'What do you think of this?' means he asks to gain agreement, 'What do you think of this matter now being spoken by me?' In that the Teacher here introduced embracing a mass of fire and embracing a maiden, he said, 'I declare...' and so on, in order to clarify that meaning.

Dussīlassāti nissīlassa sīlavirahitassa. Pāpadhammassāti dussīlattā eva hīnajjhāsayatāya lāmakasabhāvassa. Asucisaṅkassarasamācārassāti aparisuddhatāya asuci hutvā saṅkāya saritabbasamācārassa. Dussīlo hi kiñcideva asāruppaṃ disvā “idaṃ asukena kataṃ bhavissatī”ti paresaṃ āsaṅkā hoti. Kenacideva karaṇīyena mantayante bhikkhū disvā “kacci nu kho ime mayā katakammaṃ jānitvā mantentī”ti attanoyeva saṅkāya saritabbasamācāro[V 3.0182]. Paṭicchannakammantassāti lajjitabbatāya paṭicchādetabbakammantassa. Assamaṇassāti na samaṇassa. Salākaggahaṇādīsu “ahampi samaṇo”ti micchāpaṭiññāya samaṇapaṭiññassa. Aseṭṭhacāritāya abrahmacārissa. Uposathādīsu “ahampi brahmacārī”ti micchāpaṭiññāya brahmacāripaṭiññassa. Pūtinā kammena sīlavipattiyā anto anupaviṭṭhattā antopūtikassa. Chadvārehi rāgādikilesānussavanena tintattā avassutassa. Sañjātarāgādikacavarattā sīlavantehi chaḍḍetabbattā ca kasambujātassa.

'Of one with bad virtue' means of one without virtue, devoid of virtue. 'Of one with evil qualities' means of one with a base nature because of having bad virtue and a low disposition. 'Of one with impure and suspect conduct' means of one whose conduct is to be remembered with suspicion, having become impure due to impurity. For a person of bad virtue, upon seeing something unsuitable, becomes suspicious of others, thinking, 'This must have been done by so-and-so.' Upon seeing monks conferring about some business, his own conduct is to be remembered with suspicion as he thinks, 'I wonder if they are conferring because they have found out about the deed I have done?' 'Of one with concealed actions' means of one whose actions are to be concealed because they are shameful. 'Of one who is not an ascetic' means not an ascetic. Of one who claims to be an ascetic with a false claim, 'I too am an ascetic,' in matters like the taking of voting-tickets. Of one who is not a celibate because of not having the best conduct. Of one who claims to be a celibate with a false claim, 'I too am a celibate,' during the Uposatha and so on. 'Rotten within' means one who is rotten inside because of having entered into the failure of virtue through putrid action. 'Leaky' means one who is soaked by the flowing in of defilements such as lust through the six doors. 'Become like rubbish' means one who has become like rubbish because of arisen lust and other refuse, and because he is to be discarded by the virtuous.

Vālarajjuyāti vālehi katarajjuyā. Sā hi kharatarā hoti. Ghaṃseyyāti mathanavasena ghaṃseyya. Teladhotāyāti telena nisitāya. Paccorasminti patiurasmiṃ, abhimukhe uramajjheti adhippāyo. Ayosaṅkunāti saṇḍāsena. Pheṇuddehakanti pheṇaṃ uddehetvā uddehetvā, anekavāraṃ pheṇaṃ uṭṭhāpetvāti attho. Evamettha saṅkhepato pāḷivaṇṇanā veditabbā. Navamaṃ uttānameva.

'By a rope of horsehair' means by a rope made of hairs. It is indeed very rough. 'He would rub' means he would rub by way of churning. 'Washed with oil' means sharpened with oil. 'Against the chest' means on the chest; the intention is 'in the middle of the chest, directly facing.' 'With an iron spike' means with tongs. 'Bringing up foam' means having drawn out foam, drawing out foam; the meaning is raising foam many times. Thus, the brief explanation of the Pāli should be understood here. The ninth is clear in itself.

Aggikkhandhopamasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Discourse on the Simile of the Mass of Fire, and others, is concluded.

10. Arakasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Araka Sutta.

74. Dasame parittanti ittaraṃ. Tenāha “appaṃ thoka”nti. Pabandhānupacchedassa paccayabhāvo idha jīvitassa raso kiccanti adhippetanti āha [M 3.0197] “sarasaparittatāyapī”ti. Tadadhīnavuttitāyapi hi “yo, bhikkhave, ciraṃ jīvati, so vassasataṃ appaṃ vā bhiyyo”ti vacanato parittaṃ khaṇaparittatāyapi. Paramatthato hi atiparitto sattānaṃ jīvitakkhaṇo ekacittakkhaṇappavattimattoyeva. Yathā nāma rathacakkaṃ pavattamānampi ekeneva nemippadesena pavattati, tiṭṭhamānampi ekeneva tiṭṭhati, evamevaṃ ekacittakkhaṇikaṃ sattānaṃ jīvitaṃ tasmiṃ citte niruddhamatte satto niruddhoti vuccati. Yathāha “atīte cittakkhaṇe jīvittha na jīvati na jīvissati. Anāgate cittakkhaṇe na jīvittha na jīvati jīvissati. Paccuppanne cittakkhaṇe na jīvittha jīvati na jīvissati.

74. In the tenth sutta, 'limited' means 'brief'. Therefore, he said, 'little, small.' The intended meaning is that here the function of life, its essence, is to be a condition for the non-interruption of continuity; this is why he said, 'even due to the limitedness of its essence.' For even in its state of dependence on that, according to the saying, 'Bhikkhus, one who lives long lives for a hundred years or a little more,' life is limited even by the limitation of moments. For in the ultimate sense, the life-moment of beings is extremely limited, lasting only for the duration of a single mind-moment. Just as a chariot wheel, when rolling, rolls on only one point of its rim, and when standing, stands on only one point, even so the life of beings lasts for a single mind-moment. When that mind-moment has ceased, the being is said to have ceased. As it is said: 'In a past mind-moment one lived; one does not live, nor will one live. In a future mind-moment one has not lived, one does not live, but one will live. In the present mind-moment one has not lived; one lives, but one will not live.'

“Jīvitaṃ attabhāvo ca, sukhadukkhā ca kevalā;

Ekacittasamāyuttā, lahuso vattate khaṇo.

Life and individuality, and all happiness and sorrow, are conjoined with a single mind-moment; swiftly the moment passes.

“Ye [V 3.0183] niruddhā marantassa, tiṭṭhamānassa vā idha;

Sabbepi sadisā khandhā, gatā appaṭisandhikā.

Those aggregates that have ceased for one who is dying, or for one who is living here—all are alike, gone without relinking.

“Anibbattena na jāto, paccuppannena jīvati;

Cittabhaṅgā mato loko, paññatti paramatthiyā”ti. (mahāni. 10);

By the unproduced, one is not born; by the present, one lives. At the breaking of the mind, the world is dead; this is a designation in the ultimate sense.

Lahusanti lahukaṃ. Tenāha “lahuṃ uppajjitvā nirujjhanato lahusa”nti. Parittaṃ lahusanti ubhayaṃ panetaṃ appakassa vevacanaṃ. Yañhi appakaṃ, taṃ parittañceva lahukañca hoti. Idha pana āyuno adhippetattā rassanti vuttaṃ hoti. Mantāyanti karaṇatthe etaṃ bhummavacananti āha “mantāya boddhabbaṃ, paññāya jānitabbanti attho”ti. Mantāyanti vā manteyyanti vuttaṃ hoti, mantetabbaṃ mantāya upaparikkhitabbanti attho. Paññāya jānitabbanti jānitabbaṃ jīvitassa parittabhāvo bahudukkhādibhāvo. Jānitvā ca pana sabbapalibodhe chinditvā kattabbaṃ kusalaṃ, caritabbaṃ brahmacariyaṃ. Yasmā itthi jātassa amaraṇaṃ, appaṃ vā bhiyyo vassasatato upari appaṃ aññaṃ vassasataṃ appatvā vīsaṃ vā tiṃsaṃ vā cattālīsaṃ vā paṇṇāsaṃ vā saṭṭhi vā vassāni jīvati, evaṃdīghāyuko pana atidullabho. “Asuko hi evaṃ ciraṃ jīvatī”ti tattha tattha gantvā daṭṭhabbo hoti. Tattha visākhā upāsikā vīsasataṃ jīvati, tathā pokkharasātibrāhmaṇo, brahmāyubrāhmaṇo, bāvariyabrāhmaṇo, ānandatthero, mahākassapattheroti[M 3.0198]. Anuruddhatthero pana vassasatañceva paṇṇāsañca vassāni. Bākulatthero vassasatañceva saṭṭhi ca vassāni, ayaṃ sabbadīghāyuko, sopi dve vassasatāni na jīvi.

'Swift' means 'quick'. Therefore, he said, 'it is swift because it arises and ceases quickly.' 'Limited' and 'swift'—both of these are synonyms for 'little'. For whatever is little is both limited and swift. Here, however, since the lifespan is intended, it means 'short'. Regarding 'mantāya', this is a locative expression in the sense of the instrumental; therefore, he said, 'the meaning is "it should be understood by wisdom, it should be known by discernment."' Or 'mantāya' means 'manteyya' (one should consider); the meaning is 'it should be considered, it should be examined by wisdom.' 'It should be known by discernment' means that the limited nature of life and its state of having much suffering and so on should be known. And having known this, after cutting off all obstacles, the wholesome should be done and the holy life should be lived. For one who is born, there is no such thing as not dying. One who lives long lives for a hundred years, or a little more. And how much more? Above a hundred years, a little, not reaching another hundred years, but living for twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, or sixty years. But such a long-lived person is exceedingly rare. One has to go to various places to see such a person, thinking, 'So-and-so lives for so long.' In this regard, the female lay disciple Visākhā lived for one hundred and twenty years, as did the brahmin Pokkharasāti, the brahmin Brahmāyu, the brahmin Bāvari, the Elder Ānanda, and the Elder Mahākassapa. The Elder Anuruddha, however, lived for one hundred and fifty years. The Elder Bākula lived for one hundred and sixty years; he was the longest-lived of all, yet even he did not live for two hundred years.

Arakasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Araka Sutta is concluded.

Mahāvaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Great Chapter is concluded.

8. Vinayavaggo

8. The Chapter on Discipline.

1-8. Paṭhamavinayadharasuttādivaṇṇanā

1-8. Commentary on the First Discourse on the Vinaya-Holder, and others.

75-82. Aṭṭhamassa [V 3.0184] paṭhamaṃ dutiyañca uttānatthameva. Tatiye vinayalakkhaṇe patiṭṭhito lajjibhāvena vinayalakkhaṇe ṭhito hoti. Alajjī (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.45) hi bahussutopi samāno lābhagarukatāya tantiṃ visaṃvādetvā uddhammaṃ ubbinayaṃ satthusāsanaṃ dīpetvā sāsane mahantaṃ upaddavaṃ karoti, saṅghabhedampi saṅgharājimpi uppādeti. Lajjī pana kukkuccako sikkhākāmo jīvitahetupi tantiṃ avisaṃvādetvā dhammameva vinayameva ca dīpeti, satthusāsanaṃ garuṃ katvā ṭhapeti. Evaṃ yo lajjī, so vinayaṃ ajahanto avokkamantova lajjibhāvena vinayalakkhaṇe ṭhito hoti patiṭṭhito.

75-82. The first and second of the eighth have a clear meaning. In the third, 'established in the characteristic of discipline' means one is situated in the characteristic of discipline through having a sense of shame. For the shameless one, even if very learned, due to being intent on gain, misrepresents the textual tradition and, by proclaiming non-Dhamma and non-Vinaya as the Teacher's teaching, causes great trouble in the dispensation, and even produces schism in the Sangha and strife in the Sangha. But the one with a sense of shame, being scrupulous and desirous of the training, does not misrepresent the textual tradition even for the sake of his life. Instead, he illuminates only the Dhamma and the Vinaya, holding the Teacher's teaching in high regard. Thus, one who has a sense of shame, by not abandoning or deviating from the discipline, is situated and established in the characteristic of discipline through that sense of shame.

Asaṃhīroti ettha saṃhīro nāma yo pāḷiyaṃ vā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vā heṭṭhā vā uparito vā padapaṭipāṭiyā vā pucchiyamāno vitthunati vipphandati, saṇṭhātuṃ na sakkoti, yaṃ yaṃ parena vuccati, taṃ taṃ anujānāti, sakavādaṃ chaḍḍetvā paravādaṃ gaṇhāti. Yo pana pāḷiyaṃ vā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vā heṭṭhupariyavasena vā padapaṭipāṭiyā vā pucchiyamāno na vitthunati na vipphandati, ekekalomaṃ saṇḍāsena gaṇhanto viya “evaṃ mayaṃ vadāma, evaṃ no ācariyā vadantī”ti vissajjeti. Yamhi pāḷi ca pāḷivinicchayo ca suvaṇṇabhājane pakkhittasīhavasā viya parikkhayaṃ pariyādānaṃ agacchanto tiṭṭhati, ayaṃ vuccati asaṃhīro. Yasmā pana evarūpo yaṃ yaṃ parena vuccati, taṃ taṃ nānujānāti, attanā suvinicchinitaṃ katvā gahitaṃ aviparītamatthaṃ na [M 3.0199] vissajjeti, tasmā vuttaṃ “na sakkoti gahitaggahaṇaṃ vissajjāpetu”nti. Catutthādīni suviññeyyāni.

Regarding 'unshaken': here, one called 'shaken' is a person who, when questioned on the Pāli or the commentary, on what comes before or after, or on the sequence of words, falters and wavers, is unable to stand firm, agrees with whatever others say, and, abandoning his own view, adopts the view of others. But one who, when questioned on the Pāli or the commentary, on what comes before or after, or on the sequence of words, does not falter or waver, but answers as if grasping each single hair with tongs, saying, 'This is what we say; this is what our teachers say'—one in whom the Pāli and the analysis of the Pāli stand without coming to destruction or exhaustion, like lion’s fat placed in a golden vessel—this one is called 'unshaken.' Because such a person does not agree with whatever others say, and does not relinquish the correct meaning he has grasped after having well ascertained it himself, therefore it is said: 'He cannot be made to relinquish what he has grasped.' The fourth and the following are easily understood.

Paṭhamavinayadharasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the First Discourse on the Vinaya-Holder, and others, is concluded.

9. Satthusāsanasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Discourse on the Teacher's Dispensation.

83. Navame vivekaṭṭhoti vivitto. Tenāha “dūrībhūto”ti. Satiavippavāse ṭhitoti kammaṭṭhāne [V 3.0185] satiṃ avijahitvā ṭhito. Pesitattoti kāye ca jīvite ca anapekkhatāya nibbānaṃ pesitacitto tanninno tappoṇo tappabbhāro.

83. In the ninth sutta, 'standing in seclusion' means 'secluded'. Therefore, he said, 'become distant.' 'Stands in non-absence of mindfulness' means he stands without having abandoned mindfulness on the meditation subject. 'One who has dispatched himself' means that, through lack of concern for body and life, his mind is dispatched towards Nibbāna, sloping towards it, inclining towards it, heading towards it.

Satthusāsanasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Discourse on the Teacher's Dispensation is concluded.

10. Adhikaraṇasamathasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Discourse on the Settling of Issues.

84. Dasame adhikarīyanti etthāti adhikaraṇāni. Ke adhikarīyanti? Samathā. Kathaṃ adhikarīyanti? Samanavasena. Tasmā te tesaṃ samanavasena pavattantīti āha “adhikaraṇāni samentī”tiādi. Uppannānaṃ uppanānanti uṭṭhitānaṃ uṭṭhitānaṃ. Samathatthanti samanatthaṃ. Dīghanikāye saṅgītisuttavaṇṇanāyampi (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 3.331) vitthāratoyevāti etthāyaṃ vitthāranayo – adhikaraṇesu tāva dhammoti vā adhammoti vā aṭṭhārasahi vatthūhi vivadantānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ yo vivādo, idaṃ vivādādhikaraṇaṃ nāma. Sīlavipattiyā vā ācāradiṭṭhiājīvavipattiyā vā anuvadantānaṃ yo anuvādo upavadanā ceva codanā ca, idaṃ anuvādādhikaraṇaṃ nāma. Mātikāyaṃ āgatā pañca, vibhaṅge dveti sattapi āpattikkhandhā, idaṃ āpattādhikaraṇaṃ nāma. Yaṃ saṅghassa apalokanādīnaṃ catunnaṃ kammānaṃ karaṇaṃ, idaṃ kiccādhikaraṇaṃ nāma.

84. In the tenth, 'adhikaraṇāni' (legal issues) are so called because 'they are dealt with therein.' What are dealt with? The means of settlement (samathā). How are they dealt with? By way of pacification. Therefore, since they proceed by way of pacification, it is said, 'legal issues are settled,' and so on. 'Of those arisen, arisen' means 'of those that have come up, that have come up.' 'For the purpose of settlement' means 'for the purpose of pacification.' In the commentary on the Saṅgīti Sutta in the Dīghanikāya, the detailed explanation is as follows: Regarding legal issues, first, the dispute of bhikkhus wrangling over eighteen grounds as to whether something is Dhamma or not Dhamma is called a 'dispute-based legal issue.' The accusation concerning a failure in virtue, conduct, view, or livelihood—which is both a reproach and an indictment—is called an 'accusation-based legal issue.' The five categories that come in the Mātikā and the two in the Vibhaṅga—that is, the seven groups of offenses—are called an 'offense-based legal issue.' The performance of the four kinds of formal acts of the Saṅgha, beginning with proclamation (apalokana), is called a 'duty-based legal issue'.

Tattha vivādādhikaraṇaṃ dvīhi samathehi sammati sammukhāvinayena ca yebhuyyasikāya ca. Sammukhāvinayeneva sammamānaṃ yasmiṃ vihāre uppannaṃ tasmiṃyeva [M 3.0200] vā, aññatra vūpasametuṃ gacchantānaṃ antarāmagge vā, yattha gantvā saṅghassa niyyātitaṃ, tattha saṅghena vā, saṅghe vūpasametuṃ asakkonte tattheva ubbāhikāya sammatapuggalehi vā vinicchitaṃ sammati. Evaṃ sammamāne ca panetasmiṃ yā saṅghasammukhato dhammasammukhato vinayasammukhatā puggalasammukhatā, ayaṃ sammukhāvinayo nāma. Tattha ca kārakasaṅghassa saṅghasāmaggivasena sammukhibhāvo saṅghasammukhatā. Sametabbassa vatthuno bhūtattā dhammasammukhatā. Yathā taṃ sametabbaṃ, tathevassa samanaṃ vinayasammukhatā. Yo ca vivadati, yena ca vivadati, tesaṃ ubhinnaṃ atthapaccatthikānaṃ sammukhībhāvo puggalasammukhatā. Ubbāhikāya vūpasame panettha saṅghasammukhatā parihāyati. Evaṃ tāva sammukhāvinayeneva sammati.

A dispute-based legal issue is settled by two means of settlement: by the face-to-face procedure and by the majority decision. When settling solely by the face-to-face procedure, a matter that has arisen in a certain monastery is settled either in that very monastery, or on the way while going elsewhere to settle it, or wherever it is presented to the Saṅgha—there it is settled by the Saṅgha. If the Saṅgha is unable to settle it there, then it is decided by individuals agreed upon by means of a committee. When settled in this way, the presence of the Saṅgha, the presence of the Dhamma, the presence of the Vinaya, and the presence of the individuals—this is called the face-to-face procedure. Here, the presence of the Saṅgha refers to the acting Saṅgha being present by way of its concord. The presence of the Dhamma refers to the matter to be settled being true. The presence of the Vinaya refers to its settlement being in accordance with how it should be settled. The presence of the individuals refers to both the disputing parties, the plaintiff and defendant, being face-to-face. However, in the case of settlement by a committee, the presence of the Saṅgha is lacking. Thus, it is first settled solely by the face-to-face procedure.

Sace panevampi na sammati, atha naṃ ubbāhikāya sammatā bhikkhū “na mayaṃ sakkoma vūpasametu”nti [V 3.0186] saṅghasseva niyyātenti. Tato saṅgho pañcaṅgasamannāgataṃ bhikkhuṃ salākaggāhāpakaṃ sammannati, tena guḷhakavivaṭakasakaṇṇajappakesu tīsu salākaggāhakesu aññataravasena salākaṃ gāhāpetvā sannipatitāya parisāya dhammavādīnaṃ yebhuyyatāya yathā te dhammavādino vadanti, evaṃ vūpasantaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ sammukhāvinayena ca yebhuyyasikāya ca vūpasantaṃ hoti. Tattha sammukhāvinayo vuttanayo eva. Yaṃ pana yebhuyyasikākammassa karaṇaṃ, ayaṃ yebhuyyasikā nāma. Evaṃ vivādādhikaraṇaṃ dvīhi samathehi sammati.

If even then it is not settled, then the bhikkhus appointed by committee declare, "We are unable to settle it," and refer it back to the Saṅgha. Then the Saṅgha appoints a bhikkhu endowed with five qualities as the ballot-taker. He has the ballots taken by one of three methods—secret, open, or whispering in the ear—and in the assembled company, the legal issue is settled according to the majority of those who speak in accordance with the Dhamma. Thus, the legal issue is settled by the face-to-face procedure and by the majority decision. Herein, the face-to-face procedure is as previously stated. The performance of the act of taking a majority vote is called the 'majority decision.' In this way, a dispute-based legal issue is settled by two means of settlement.

Anuvādādhikaraṇaṃ catūhi samathehi sammati sammukhāvinayena ca sativinayena ca amūḷhavinayena ca tassapāpiyasikāya ca. Sammukhāvinayeneva sammamānaṃ yo ca anuvadati, yañca anuvadati, tesaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā sace kāci āpatti natthi, ubho khamāpetvā, sace atthi ayaṃ nāmettha āpattīti evaṃ vinicchitaṃ vūpasammati. Tattha sammukhāvinayalakkhaṇaṃ vuttanayameva.

An accusation-based legal issue is settled by four means of settlement: by the face-to-face procedure, by the verdict of innocence based on mindfulness, by the verdict for past insanity, and by the procedure for the corrupt. When settling solely by the face-to-face procedure, if, after hearing the statements of both the accuser and the accused, there is no offense, both should be made to ask for forgiveness. If there is an offense, it is resolved by determining, 'This is indeed such an offense.' Here, the characteristic of the face-to-face procedure is as previously explained.

Yadā pana khīṇāsavassa bhikkhuno amūlikāya sīlavipattiyā anuddhaṃsitassa sativinayaṃ yācamānassa saṅgho ñatticatutthena kammena sativinayaṃ deti, tadā sammukhāvinayena ca sativinayena ca vūpasantaṃ hoti. Dinne pana sativinaye puna tasmiṃ puggale kassaci anuvādo na ruhati. Yadā ummattako bhikkhu ummādavasena kate assāmaṇake ajjhācāre “saratāyasmā evarūpiṃ āpatti”nti bhikkhūhi codiyamāno “ummattakena [M 3.0201] me, āvuso, etaṃ kataṃ, nāhaṃ taṃ sarāmī”ti bhaṇantopi bhikkhūhi codiyamānova puna acodanatthāya amūḷhavinayaṃ yācati, saṅgho cassa ñatticatutthena kammena amūḷhavinayaṃ deti. Tadā sammukhāvinayena ca amūḷhavinayena ca vūpasantaṃ hoti. Dinne pana amūḷhavinaye puna tasmiṃ puggale kassaci tappaccayā anuvādo na ruhati. Yadā pana pārājikena vā pārājikasāmantena vā codiyamānassa aññenaññaṃ paṭicarato pāpussannatāya pāpiyassa puggalassa “sacāyaṃ acchinnamūlo bhavissati, sammā vattitvā osāraṇaṃ labhissati. Sace chinnamūlo, ayamevassa nāsanā bhavissatī”ti maññamāno saṅgho ñatticatutthena kammena tassapāpiyasikaṃ karoti, tadā sammukhāvinayena ca tassapāpiyasikāya ca vūpasantaṃ hotīti. Evaṃ anuvādādhikaraṇaṃ catūhi samathehi sammati.

When a bhikkhu whose corruptions are destroyed is accused of a groundless transgression of morality, and he requests a verdict of innocence based on mindfulness, the Saṅgha grants it to him through a formal act consisting of one motion and three announcements. Then it is settled by the face-to-face procedure and by the verdict of innocence based on mindfulness. Once this verdict has been granted, no one can bring up an accusation against that individual based on that matter again. When an insane bhikkhu, due to his insanity, commits an act unbecoming of a renunciate, and other bhikkhus accuse him, saying, "Venerable, do you remember committing such an offense?"—even if he replies, "Friends, I was insane when I did that; I do not remember it"—but the bhikkhus continue to accuse him, and he requests a verdict for past insanity to avoid further accusations, the Saṅgha grants it to him by a formal act consisting of one motion and three announcements. Then it is settled by the face-to-face procedure and the verdict for past insanity. Once this verdict has been granted, no one can bring up an accusation against that individual based on that reason again. When a person accused of an offense entailing expulsion or bordering on expulsion evades the issue by making counter-accusations, and due to his being overcome by wickedness, the Saṅgha thinks, "If this person has not destroyed his wholesome roots, he may behave properly and obtain reinstatement. But if he has destroyed his wholesome roots, this will be his ruin"—then the Saṅgha imposes the procedure for the corrupt on him by a formal act consisting of one motion and three announcements. Then it is settled by the face-to-face procedure and the procedure for the corrupt. Thus, an accusation-based legal issue is settled by these four means of settlement.

Āpattādhikaraṇaṃ tīhi samathehi sammati sammukhāvinayena ca paṭiññātakaraṇena ca tiṇavatthārakena ca. Tassa sammukhāvinayeneva vūpasamo natthi. Yadā pana ekassa vā bhikkhuno [V 3.0187] santike saṅghagaṇamajjhesu vā bhikkhu lahukaṃ āpattiṃ deseti, tadā āpattādhikaraṇaṃ sammukhāvinayena ca paṭiññātakaraṇena ca vūpasammati. Tattha sammukhāvinaye tāva yo ca deseti, yassa ca deseti, tesaṃ sammukhībhāvo puggalasammukhato. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

An offense-based legal issue is settled by three means of settlement: by the face-to-face procedure, by the procedure based on acknowledgment, and by the procedure of covering over as with grass. There is no resolution for it solely by the face-to-face procedure. But when a bhikkhu confesses a light offense in the presence of an individual bhikkhu, or in the midst of a group or the Saṅgha, then the offense-based legal issue is settled by the face-to-face procedure and by the procedure based on acknowledgment. In this context, regarding the face-to-face procedure, the face-to-face presence of both the one who confesses and the one to whom it is confessed constitutes the presence of the individuals. The rest is as previously stated.

Puggalassa ca gaṇassa ca desanākāle saṅghasammukhato parihāyati. Yaṃ panettha “ahaṃ, bhante, itthannāmaṃ āpattiṃ āpanno”ti ca “passasī”ti ca “āma, passāmī”ti ca paṭiññātāya “āyatiṃ saṃvareyyāsī”ti karaṇaṃ, taṃ paṭiññātakaraṇaṃ nāma. Saṅghādisese parivāsādiyācanā paṭiññā, parivāsādīnaṃ dānaṃ paṭiññātakaraṇaṃ nāma.

At the time of confession to an individual or a group, the presence of the Saṅgha is lacking. Herein, the procedure based on acknowledgment—whereby one confesses, saying, 'Venerable sir, I have committed such-and-such an offense,' and upon being asked, 'Do you see it?' replies, 'Yes, I see it,' and is told, 'You should restrain yourself in the future'—is called the 'procedure based on acknowledgment.' In the case of a Saṅghādisesa offense, the request for probation and so forth is the acknowledgment, and the granting of probation and so forth is called the 'procedure based on acknowledgment.'

Dvepakkhajātā pana bhaṇḍanakārakā bhikkhū bahuṃ assāmaṇakaṃ ajjhācāraṃ caritvā puna lajjidhamme uppanne “sace mayaṃ imāhi āpattīhi aññamaññaṃ kāressāma, siyāpi taṃ adhikaraṇaṃ kakkhaḷattāya vāḷattāya saṃvatteyyā”ti aññamaññaṃ āpattiyā kārāpane dosaṃ disvā yadā bhikkhū tiṇavatthārakakammaṃ karonti, tadā āpattādhikaraṇaṃ sammukhāvinayena ca tiṇavatthārakena ca sammati. Tatra hi yattakā hatthapāsūpagatā “na metaṃ khamatī”ti evaṃ diṭṭhāvikammaṃ akatvā “dukkaṭaṃ kammaṃ puna kātabbaṃ kamma”nti [M 3.0202] na ukkoṭenti, niddampi okkantā honti, sabbesaṃ ṭhapetvā thullavajjañca gihipaṭisaṃyuttañca sabbāpattiyo vuṭṭhahanti. Evaṃ āpattādhikaraṇaṃ tīhi samathehi sammati.

But the quarrelsome monks who had formed two factions, having engaged in much unmonastic misconduct, when a sense of shame arose in them again, thought: 'If we cause each other to be charged with these offenses, that dispute might become harsh and violent.' Seeing the fault in causing each other to be charged with offenses, when the monks perform the procedure of covering over with grass, then the offense-related dispute is settled by face-to-face resolution and by the procedure of covering over with grass. For there, as many as are present in the assembly, without making a declaration of disagreement by saying, 'This does not satisfy me,' do not object, saying, 'This is a wrong deed, a deed that must be redone,' and they become tranquil. Except for gross offenses and those connected with laypeople, all offenses are absolved. Thus, the offense-related dispute is settled by three settlements.

Kiccādhikaraṇaṃ ekena samathena sammati sammukhāvinayeneva. Iti imāni cattāri adhikaraṇāni yathānurūpaṃ imehi sattahi samathehi sammanti. Tena vuttaṃ – “uppannuppannānaṃ adhikaraṇānaṃ samathāya vūpasamāya sammukhāvinayo dātabbo…pe… tiṇavatthārako”ti. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānameva.

A matter concerning duties is settled by one settlement, namely, the procedure of face-to-face resolution. Thus, these four kinds of disputes are settled appropriately by these seven settlements. Therefore, it was said: 'For the stilling and allaying of whatever disputes have arisen, the procedure of face-to-face resolution is to be given... [up to]... the covering over with grass.' The rest is clear in every case.

Adhikaraṇasamathasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Adhikaraṇasamatha Sutta is concluded.

Vinayavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Vinayavagga is concluded.

Iti manorathapūraṇiyā aṅguttaranikāya-aṭṭhakathāya

Thus, in the Manorathapūraṇī, the commentary on the Aṅguttara Nikāya,

Sattakanipātavaṇṇanāya anuttānatthadīpanā samattā.

the commentary on the Book of the Sevens, an illumination of the profound meaning, is concluded.
